Wall Lord Ilvriss’ tail lashed the ground as he bounced on the toes of his dancing boots. Lyonette finished lacing up the Highsteppers of House Lischelle, the new Heirloom Artifact she’d made that gave her three dances despite her weakened body and reflexes. The Wall Lord put his hands on his hips.
“I would have thought a [Princess], nay, a [Worldly Princess], would try more experiences, Miss Marquin. But it seems that you’re more hidebound than I thought.”
Oh snap. Ser Dalimont and Mrsha edged for the door as Lyonette’s cheeks flamed. Ilvriss regretted the comment at once. He had a bit of a…a sharp tongue. He hadn’t realized it until Nanette had pointed it out to him. Lyonette folded her arms as she hopped from foot to foot, like a [Boxer] warming up. He eyed her hands as she smiled sweetly.
“And you, Wall Lord Ilvriss, seem to keep projecting your Salazsarian values all over the people you meet. I suppose even when you’ve changed, you can’t help but look down on anyone who doesn’t share your exact culture, eh?”
That one stung. Because it dovetailed with Ilvriss’ entire experience in the town of Thirthoof and…well, the entire expedition. He stood still and didn’t jump into the first steps of the warmup song, Relz du Marqfin, as Ser Dalimont triggered the music.
Lyonette hesitated as she began to glide across the ground. She stopped, embarrassed.
“I—that might have been too far.”
“No, it’s quite accurate. I should have warned you rather than laughed about the bidet. I just wanted to give the opportunity, but it is high-and-mighty, isn’t it?”
“What? No, I’m just—”
Lyonette turned to Dalimont, and he gave her a thumbs up and motions to indicate she was on her own. She glared at him.
“I didn’t mean it, Ilvriss! And I admit, I was highly sheltered, so I never took advantage of the bidets when I could have. I apologize.”
“No, no, I do.”
“It’s a silly fight. I was just mad you were hiding from me, or so I felt—”
“Well, I was.”
He admitted that. Lyonette was a dancing fiend. Ever since she’d found out she could keep dancing despite her condition, she had him dancing.
And the Highstepper sucked. It was the most complicated, ankle-breaking dance Ilvriss had ever found in his life, and Lyonette insisted on practicing three dances with her boots…twice a day, since her boots would recharge enough for a second go-round after twelve hours.
One warmup dance, which was a ‘standard’ Terandrian or Izrilian dance, already damn complex. Next, the Highstepper. After Ilvriss stopped holding his shins and his heart-rate had dropped to under a hundred and eighty beats-per-minute, they tried Erin Solstice’s dance. After that, even Lyonette was so embarrassed she’d let him limp away to sit in a hot spring or collapse in the inn or something.
She just loved to dance. She was also highly competitive, and Ilvriss was somehow the only person who could dance in the entire damn inn.
No, wait, Dame Ushar and Ser Dalimont could do it. But the two Thronebearers refused to unless Lyonette or Ilvriss needed a sub-in for a second. Because they knew what would happen! Damn them! Weren’t they supposed to rise to any task?
Ilvriss brought this up after the first dance. Fifteen minutes of Relz du Marqfin—he was sweating despite the cold air!
“Lyonette, are you picking the longest songs to make those boots work longer?”
“Maybe. I admit the Relz is tiring. But we can do at least the first half of the Highstepper! In seven minutes. Ser Dalimont, the timer.”
“Of course, Your Highness. An orange?”
The man came around with orange slices, and Ilvriss eyed him.
“Surely, Ser Dalimont could oblige you by dancing when I’m not here, Lyonette.”
So you’re not so hellbent on me doing it? The [Knight] instantly smiled.
“Regretfully, Wall Lord, a Thronebearer must be in fine fettle to defend their charge. I cannot allow my legs to be compromised.”
“You damn Human.”
“This is surely a task only for a Drake, Wall Lord Ilvriss. I admit my inferiority with grace and happiness.”
Lyonette giggled at Ilvriss’ face. Then she nudged his leg a touch anxiously.
“You don’t mind it that much, do you, Ilvriss? We could cut it back, but I do look forwards to it…”
She seemed ready to desist, but so crestfallen that Ilvriss glanced at Ser Dalimont, then put a smile on his face.
“Not at all, Lyonette. It’s excellent footwork training. But maybe not the Highstepper every time? What if we did that only once a day?”
“I could do that. It does kill the limbs. Oh, what if we did some more Drake dances? There are Chandrarian ones I had Ushar buy manuals on to study—”
He groaned, but mildly. There was something to it when you got in the zone. When you knew all the steps and were whirling around, feet flying—
Then, he had to admit it, that’s when he felt like he was actually talented or—or had the same rush like you felt during some moment of extreme physical exertion. The sense of pure accomplishment, of knowing what came next.
It just embarrassed Ilvriss, because he could reach that height on the dance floor, but martial superiority on the battlefield had always eluded him. Then it was just tenseness, fighting underwater, swinging his sword, trying to take out his enemy and stay alive. Not the rush he sometimes heard other warriors, including his father, describe.
Grace.
When he rose to his feet, and the familiar Highstepper’s music came on, he and Lyonette saw someone watching them.
Colfa val Lischelle. And Himilt. The farmer nodded at the two, and Colfa called out.
“I had to drag Himilt here. I’ve wanted to dance in a real ballroom like this since I was a girl. No objections, Himilt.”
“I didn’t object to that, Colfa. I just objected to the part where you said it was the Highstepper.”
The Vampire was eying the grand ballroom floor, that glossy marble, with appreciation. No matter what he was, he was still a Vampire. And in his way, the quiet Himilt had a dignity unto royalty to match Lyonette and Ilvriss.
Who was he? At this moment, just another man suffering the Highstepper. Ilvriss locked eyes with Himilt and saw the Vampire grimacing as he stretched his hamstrings out. They nodded at each other as Lyonette and Colfa beamed.
 
——
 
“Come on, Wall Lord Ilvriss. Last dance.”
“No.”
He was curled up around his leg in pain. Colfa, panting, was trying to drag Himilt up by the leg.
“Stop being a baby, Himilt val Lischelle-Drakle. I forgot the Highstepper had that kick. Your leg isn’t broken.”
“It feels like it.”
“Well, you’ll heal in a minute. Up!”
Both men were on the floor. Holding hands. Ilvriss’ claw grasped Himilt’s gloved hand like a [Lover]. They held on as the [Princess] and Vampiress tried to drag them up.
Suffering. One of the Highstepper’s moves was the aforementioned swing-leg kick. A standby in line dances where you raised your leg, kicked out, kicked back, kicked to the side, to the left—an easy-enough move.
Everything the Highstepper did was to show off. So you did it so fast while facing each other before switching into another pattern that you had to be in perfect sync.
Do it out of order and you’d hit your partner with a boot to the shin with all your force. Which was enough to crack bones if Colfa did it. And Lyonette wasn’t far behind.
Ilvriss noted that he hadn’t hit Lyonette that hard. But he had a purple bruise on his scales. A huge one. He felt at the dented flesh as he sat up. Lyonette hesitated.
“Oh, um—I’m quite sorry, Ilvriss. Ushar? A small poultice, maybe? But we need to not heal ourselves or we’ll lose our muscle growth. Come on, we have three-fourths of the Highstepper down!”
They did. So Ilvriss got up after a moment, and they practiced Erin’s dance. Which was…something else.
All the frantic energy of the Highstepper, the intricate, maddening perfection of limb movements, wasn’t in Erin’s magical dance that Mrsha had found.
Oh, it was still high-energy. But there was something more graceful to it. It wasn’t for showing off. It was just—
Complex.
“Argh. Sorry—”
Lyonette performed a three-rotation spin into Ilvriss’ arms and hit his neck spines. Then she was a touch too slow when they went for a synchronized glide across the floor.
Colfa and Himilt watched; they had tried a more casual dance. This one…Ilvriss was sweating harder than he did practicing with the sword! But he seized Lyonette’s hand.
Walk four paces left, perform a three-step reversal, breakaway spin, and—
It was showy. Lyonette’s dress unfolded like a flower’s petals, and for a moment, he remembered Oteslia. The dance moved faster. It started slow, with the elegance of a Terandrian ballroom dance. Until—
He extended one leg as far as he could and stepped out, leaning back. Despite his weight being on the back foot, he pushed himself up until his front leg held the weight, and he spun his foot around, tracing a perfect circle.
His tail followed him, and the Wall Lord pushed off the ground. Twirled in the air. Landed—and Lyonette was there. She’d performed her half of the dance, and they met again. Locked eyes and smiled as he felt himself doing it.
Okay, this is amazing. They stepped sideways, minds straining to hold the dance together. It was supposed to be ten minutes of insanely complicated steps. Erin had fifty pages devoted to it, and it was so damn hard for Ilvriss to memorize that on top of everything else! Even Lyonette had problems, and she loved it.
But the more you danced it, the more you just sort of remembered what came next. Saw your partner doing it and fell into rhythm. Ilvriss swore he felt something as they strode backwards while facing each other. Like ice skaters moving backwards, despite looking forwards.
What had Kevin called it? Swing dancing, country, even a bit of disco—a blend of dance styles that even the Lord of the Dance would have had trouble cataloguing. Blended into one…
Gift of ghosts.
They were building to something, Ilvriss felt. The longer he and Lyonette stayed in-step for the dance, the more it felt natural. He forgot his aching shins, his tired limbs. He began to move, heedless of the vigor.
Stepping around her, like they were tracing a magical spell circle, turning, catching each other’s eyes, heart racing. Reaching for the impossible.
On the precipice—and then Ilvriss’ mind caught up to the dance’s flow. And he hesitated.
Just for a second.
Oh no.
Nononono, here it came—but he had to do it. It said that was the next part. He even had an audience today!
Damn you Erin Solstice! But he trusted her. He trusted that damn woman, so Ilvriss stopped whirling about. He turned to face Lyonette—threw up his arms—and began to shake his body left to right.
Like…a giant inflatable tube propelled upwards by hot air. Left, then right. Erin had even written a note that the Earthers had helpfully translated to Ilvriss.
‘Wacky inflatable tube dude dance’.
Woo! Woo! He did it from right to left, scales turning red as Colfa and Himilt stared at him. Ser Dalimont’s face was a study in perfect blankness. Then Ilvriss began to do Ksmvr’s dance. He squatted and shook his fists out up and down. First on his right side, then his left.
It wasn’t…a bad dance. And if you were an Antinium, you had a lot less mobility so it fit. It just wasn’t—
It wasn’t a fitting damn dance for this.
The humiliation of this moment might never be exceeded. Ilvriss had done it in front of the Goblin and Antinium staff, Mrsha, Nanette—it still burned his scales like Dragonfire.
But he did it because the sacred texts said to do it. His one consolation was seeing Lyonette, face red as a tomato, flapping her arms and shaking her posterior.
The quack-quack duck dance. They stared at each other until Colfa and Himilt couldn’t take it any longer and burst out laughing.
“Colfa!”
Lyonette shrieked, and they gave up doing the next moves, which were just as humiliating. And Ilvriss thought—
She has to have done that just to annoy them. Somehow, she knew Ilvriss would be the one doing this, and Erin had done this just to spite him. But there was a part of him that felt—
Horribly—
Like that was actually part of the dance. Somehow.
 
——
 
“I don’t get it. She put Ksmvr’s dance in there, and it was not invented until recently. She has to be lying. She has to be.”
After that dance, Ilvriss sat, gulping water and going over the dance again.
“It says there, in writing, Lyonette ‘must do this dance’.”
She glared at him.
“It also says, ‘hilarious, get Ulvama to do it’. It’s a prank!”
“Well, why does it feel halfway accurate?”
She threw up her hands.
“I don’t know! I’ll ask her next time she calls Ishkr, Mrsha, or Nanette! I’d ask, but—”
She paused, and Ilvriss stopped gulping water.
“You still haven’t told her? Your class?”
“I…don’t want to make her worry.”
“Lyonette, you have to—”
“She stresses! My turn’s coming up; she calls once a week, and she’s rotating through Ishkr, myself, Mrsha, and Nanette. Just give her time, Ilvriss. I…you do the wacky arms dance very well.”
“Thank you. And I admire your quack-quack dance.”
Red-faced, the [Princess] went to nudge him, then just sat next to Ilvriss. They were covered in sweat, and silly dances or not, Ilvriss had to admit he felt like he’d earned his supper. They breathed in and out.
“How’s the camp?”
“Marvus keeps attacking us. He hasn’t noticed the undead, but Nerul was right. He keeps coming, damnit. He’s too high-level.”
“I’m sorry, I don’t have a solution for—”
“It’s fine. My [Recruiters] say I have more workers coming, actually. A lot of them. With Emperor Godart’s people, we’ll have plenty of hands. So long as we counter the undead, it’s fine. And we’ve found a number of items the [Miners]—we think they were [Miners]—had. High-artifact grade objects. I’ve had our [Mages] looking at them. Nothing’s trapped. I wish we could prevail upon Fissival’s Scholarium, but…”
“Really? I thought it was hard to recruit.”
Ilvriss shrugged as he sat up.
“Apparently, some new hire made a splash. I’m riding back in the morning, and that’s good news. About the magical items—do you think Master Hedault would have time to look at them? My peers in Salazsar would cause a huge fuss about them, and I might not get the items back.”
“Hedault? Of course! And Valeterisa could do it.”
“She won’t steal them? Where is she, by the by?”
That worried Ilvriss, because he knew Valeterisa, but Lyonette just smiled.
“She’s in the mountains building her academy. Apparently, they’re actually making progress—Magus Grimalkin and Lady Pryde are there a lot too. If you have a chance, you should stay to greet them. I’ll have a word with her. If she wants funding, she’ll behave.”
And that was why this was all excusable, Ilvriss’ desire for company aside. He exhaled.
“In that case, I’ll ride back but send samples over here. With Welsca. It’s a good cover story. I’ll say it’s a reward for her latest Skill.”
“Oh, what did she get?”
“[Fast Travel]…”
They were chatting after their dancing as they had done for any number of his visits now. Ilvriss’ stomach growled, and Lyonette pointed at it.
“Let’s get some food in you.”
“What’s on the menu in the inn?”
“Nothing. I thought we’d go to Tails and Scales. If you’re free?”
“Are you sure?”
Didn’t she like to save money in the inn? And Chef Calescent had feelings, but Lyonette sighed.
“Actually, we want to give Calescent a break. He’s made food, but he needs a vacation! Imani is feeding him and the members of the staff. We had an incident with Liska. Everyone needs time off!”
“Excellent. Well, I won’t turn down Lasica’s cooking, and Rufelt does a wonderful non-alcoholic cocktail.”
“Didn’t you take my daughter there the other day?”
Lyonette eyed him, but before Ilvriss could apologize, she waved it off.
“I heard about Selys. Let’s talk it out over dinner. Ugh, and did you know Taimaguros is in Izril?”
“No. Do we hate them? I mean, more than I’m supposed to hate Terandrians in general as a good Drake? There are a few nations we extra-hate…I think Taimaguros is on the list? What’re they actually like, Lyonette?”
He pushed himself up, and Lyonette sighed.
“They’re very odd. Taima or Guros and no in-between. And between you and me, they’re one of the few kingdoms that actually practices prima nocta. I thought it was a joke—”
“Er, I don’t know that one.”
“Ah…how should I explain it?”
They were headed for the doors to the ballroom when Mrsha the Changed threw the doors open. She stood there as Wall Lord Ilvriss tensed for a disaster, and Lyonette blinked.
“Mrsha? What’s wrong?”
The girl held up a card.
Bidets are superior.
The Wall Lord felt a smile appear on his lips. His heart lifted, and his chest puffed out. Lyonette’s expression turned into a scowl.
“Mrsha, what happened to mother-daughter loyalty? Don’t you take Wall Lord Ilvriss’ side just because it’s novel. We don’t need one in the new inn! Give me one reason why it’s good.”
The girl gazed up at her mother solemnly.
Mother? I have fur.
“Ah. Well—”
Ilvriss shook Mrsha’s paw.
“Would you like to join us at Tails and Scales, Miss Mrsha? This uncivilized scion of Marquin the Radiant is keeping me company, but I would prefer a decent guest.”
Lyonette began to scold Mrsha and Ilvriss as they walked out the doors, smirking.
 
——
 
Those were the good moments. But there were always the bad ones, after.
Wall Lord Ilvriss stood in Liscor’s square and watched people throwing produce at Krshia Silverfang as she tried to deliver a speech. She dodged a rotten Yellat. Tried to keep speaking—but the rain of refuse got too heavy, and she had to retreat.
Then he saw Lism stepping forwards to jeers.
“Listen, you idiots—do you want the old Council back? What we do in private is our business!”
“Traitor!”
“We trusted you!”
They kept hurling objects. Wall Lord Ilvriss glanced around, wondering if there was a moment for him to say something. But there were Humans in the crowd. Gnolls and Drakes, and he wasn’t Liscorian. He watched Lism take a flying tomato, and then the two Councilmembers were covering each other. Making their way away.
When Ilvriss began his long ride back to the dig site, Welsca handed him something.
 
Two brawls. 86 injured. Undead attack—3 dead, 33 injured. Two urgent complaints from dig teams. Liuss’ family has responded via [Message] spell.
 
That last one—Wall Lord Ilvriss arranged for meetings. A tour of the wounded. Made sure the dead were being compensated, and scheduled a briefing with Major Shellc for whenever he was free. And arranged for the correspondence from Salazsar to be on his desk. And for Master Plumber Oidhol to be given whatever he needed to begin work right away. All of this was his regular work.
But the hard part was…Liuss.
 
——
 
Wall Lord Ilvriss knew how to deal with someone who had died in the line of duty or work. A disaster in the mines was horrible. It reflected on him and his company. If it could be prevented, he and Alrric would change things to ensure it didn’t happen again. If it was negligence, someone not following protocols, that would be uncovered.
Same with the monsters. People knew this was a dangerous dig. It was not…better. But it was easier, if that made sense. Because there were protocols to follow, as insulting as that might be to the individuals.
But Liuss?
Liuss was the Drake who’d climbed the fence at the cookout the Lischelles had hosted. Just a lad. A well-to-do family’s son who’d been part of Wall Lord Dramm’s crew. A fool who’d thought to ‘get back’ at the Lischelles the only way he knew how, egged on by his friends.
The bull had killed him very fast. It hadn’t been the Lischelles’ fault for once. They had been explicit enough with the warnings, and there’d been a fence.
No one went into a bull’s territory without using a [Sleep] wand first. So…it was not the boy’s fault. Ilvriss would never blame the dead.
But how did he explain it to the family? There was a temptation, which Ilvriss had half-embraced, to lie. If he said Liuss had been defending the camp or—or safeguarding House Gemscale’s interests, that was a nondescript way of saving face, right?
He couldn’t tell the boy’s parents that he’d died doing something stupid to no end. But lying—lying like that would mean those Drakes held it against the Lischelles and the north in general. It was also a disservice to the [Soldiers] who were risking their lives.
In the end, Ilvriss had compromised. He’d written vaguely about a horrible accident during negotiations. Let them dig and find out the whole story, but he’d added as much respect to Liuss’ name as possible.
That was not the end of it. The family had lost their boy. Liuss’ parents had written back. Asking questions—Ilvriss had put Wall Lord Dramm in charge of speaking to them personally. It was not his fault exactly, but he’d been there and the ranking Drake, damn it.
Communications continued. Ilvriss had taken a scrying orb call with the parents, a dry-eyed affair that was painfully polite. Eyes boring into him as he told the [Gem Merchant] duo how appalled he was. How Liuss had been so well loved.
Lie. But that’s what they wanted to hear, wasn’t it? That their son had been what he was to them: a hero. There had been questions.
Had the bull been unsupervised? Well, yes, damnit, it was a bull. Had it been charging? Maybe Liuss had been onto something—why were these Humans allowed to attack us?
Ilvriss had entertained it. Let them shape their own narratives. Right up until the last bit. Which was the final straw.
A missive had come for him, requesting that Wall Lord Ilvriss cite Liuss for a medal under Salazsar’s commendation system. Civilians and soldiers got different kinds of awards, often with a monetary reward because that was Drakes. For true heroism, you could even receive property or—
They wanted Ilvriss to commend their son with the Stoutscale Award, a medal for civilians who had performed acts of extreme valor despite risk to their life. It was a prestigious award—and half the recipients were posthumously awarded it. The [Representative] had written carefully to tell Wall Lord Ilvriss that all the grieving family wanted was his recommendation to the committee, nothing more.
And that they’d forgo the reward customary for the medal and donate it back to the city.
Wall Lord Ilvriss refused. He should have put his foot down before this. Shouldn’t have danced around the truth as much. Well, he’d tried to be respectful to the dead, to the family, but not this.
“No medals. Inform Wall Lord Dramm he is to withdraw his recommendation.”
“But sir—”
The young man who’d deliver the message was one of Liuss’ friends. Ilvriss glanced up, once, eyes flashing.
“Wall Lord Dramm will be asked to testify on truth stone if this proposal goes through. The scandal of a proposal being rejected after certification by Dramm is not one he wishes to have. The committee records such events.”
“Yes, Wall Lord.”
No medal. Ilvriss would not lie. He wrote a curt message back to the [Representative] informing him of that in no uncertain terms, and that he would not entertain similar untruths.
The next day, they put a story in the newspaper about him.
 
——
 
Wall Lord Ilvriss’ disastrous expedition in the north! 
That was the headline. Wall Lord Ilvriss stopped drinking tea and flipped the newspaper over. The Miner’s Report, the leading newspaper in Salazsar. The war with Fissival was on the bottom of the page. He went back to reading the subheadings.
 
Multiple brave sons and daughters of Salazsar dead. 
Daily brawls with Humans, unsanitary working conditions?
Allegations of an affair with a [Princess]?
Is this the Wall Lord we need?
 
He read in silence as Xesci and some of his staff waited. They were uncomfortable. Ilvriss just exhaled.
“Let me know if Alrric faces trouble.”
“Should we write to the newspaper, sir? We could complain—”
Ilvriss tossed the newspaper down.
“Let them talk. I’m sure I deserve some of it. They’ll keep talking until they get bored or I switch the narrative. That’s how it works. Has my Uncle sent a message?”
“No, Wall Lord.”
“Then we continue.”
The second Golem attack came shortly after he approved Osthia’s budget for a memorial service. Long-ranged arrows fired from some kind of Centaur-Golem sniper, according to witnesses.
Four. Ilvriss’ ring caught two. He dodged one.
The last one broke three ribs and, he imagined, hadn’t been meant to kill him. The arrowtips were blunted. He drank a healing potion and lay through the night in mild agony until Courier Salamani raced into camp with a healing scroll, courtesy of The Wandering Inn.
Got back to work. That was the day that Damia Reinhart rode into his camp.
 
——
 
Today was going to be an amazing day.
It took two days to travel from the door outside of the Cowpat Plains to Ilvriss’ base camp on foot. Well, foot, horse, wagon—theirs was a huge group.
Silverfangs, recruits from Liscor, Esthelm, Invrisil, and everywhere else that Damia had talked up Wall Lord Ilvriss’ campaign. Not to mention Varnie, the [Gang Boss] that Damia had so dramatically rescued from the noose.
That gave her some social credit. More than being a [Lady] or the one who’d recruited everyone. Enough for the Silverfangs to actually be open and friendly, despite their experiences in the north and Damia’s reputation as, well, a Reinhart.
And Gnolls were, like everything else in Liscor, interesting. Damia couldn’t get enough of talking to them.
“So all your Named-rank adventurers actually know each other and get along? Ours fight like Gnolls and Dr—I mean, Crelers and everything else!”
She put her foot in it and blushed, but Huntress Rayna just laughed.
“No offense taken, Lady Damia. That’s the one true saying you northerners have of the south. Our Named-ranks meet, yes. We make a point of introducing them to each other.”
“Like one introduces pets to each other. An analogy they do not care for, yes?”
Irit was riding with them. Rayna, Irit were both young leaders of this group in the north, and Damia had naturally fallen in with them. With so many Honored Gnolls who’d passed and the tribe split up between the Meeting of Tribes, their old mines, Liscor, and the north, there were a lot of younger Gnolls in authority.
Damia thought that was a good thing. It interested her that Rayna and Irit had openly wished for seniors to be around. It was, apparently, not fun to suddenly have to take charge when you weren’t ready for it.
“So they meet with, what, mediators?”
Irit nodded.
“[Shamans]. So they can get along, know each other, and if there is trouble, ally. They don’t have to like each other, but we are Gnolls. At the mercy of Drakes, you see? So when push comes to shove—”
“You don’t turn on each other. Well, obviously. Smart. Selphids do the same thing. If our Named-ranks did that, we’d have so much less infighting.”
“It’s not easy. There’s always one known grudge. Before the Meeting of Tribes, entire tribes held huge grudges. They still do, but we can’t afford it now. So we’re all one big, happy family.”
“About as functional as mine?”
More laughter. Damia revelled in it, even if it was self-deprecation. More than one Human was listening to her, including Binevy and Sule. She’d impressed them too. Not a bad thing.
Actually, the only unhappy person was Sule. He’d lasted about half a second against Primera when Damia had pulled her stunt, and the farm boy-turned-[Bodyguard] didn’t mind his job.
But he had sort of been hoping Damia was one of those licentious Reinharts. The ones who slept with their bodyguards.
…It took a curious sort to join House Reinhart.
However, Damia was a Level 16 [Sharp Dame]. Two levels from her recruiting, four from helping Varnie escape Lord Xitegen.
She sort of wished she’d gotten more, but six levels in such a short amount of time, even for someone as low-level as Damia? She’d take it.
One of the things she’d won was a loyalty-Skill for Varnie.
[Loyalty of the Low]. Slightly unflattering, but it sounded good. Another was [Bridge the Gap]—a Skill that Damia assumed was because she was being friendly with people?
Only, it worked on…both ideas as well as things. Damia had used it to be more at-home with the Gnolls, and she used it again now.
“Whoops, pothole.”
Her horse had nearly ridden into some stupid mudhole. Instead, its hooves clattered on pieces of wood, and everyone glanced down.
“Nice Skill, yes?”
“It’s called [Bridge the Gap]. It, uh, works? I wish it were more powerful.”
“Better than nothing.”
The others rode over the gap in the mudhole, calling out warnings as people walking behind skirted it. A lot of Gnolls were on foot, but Damia had secured a horse for herself and her people, and Rayna rode in case of trouble.
Rayna’s horse tried to walk on the artificial bridge of not-quite-perfect planks of wood, perhaps a symbol of Damia’s level, but it vanished after barely eight seconds. Her horse’s hooves splashed in the muck, and she cursed as it got on her fur.
“Turn my fur white—right before our meeting with the Wall Lord!”
“Rayna, you can’t say that anymore!”
Irit called over, and Rayna blushed as Damia fumbled for a water flask. But before she could offer it, someone jogged over at a speed that made her eyes boggle. Also, the Gnoll with a fur coat like a grizzly bear and stature to match was so tall he was almost of a height with her—mounted!
“Rayna, my hunting heart, your fur! Here. I didn’t see you this morning.”
“Thamert, I’m fine. It’s just mud.”
Embarrassed, the [Huntress] snatched the water flask the Gnoll held, and Damia eyed him.
Dead gods, he is the biggest Gnoll I have ever seen in my life. The Minotaur at that brothel seemed small-chested compared to him. He smiled at her.
“So this is Lady Damia? Greetings, Lady. I am Thamert, Rayna’s fiancé and [Mine Leader] in the north.”
“We’re not engaged anymore, Thamert!”
Rayna snapped at him. He flicked his ears and put a hand over his chest.
“I would raise a family with you, Rayna. Just tell me to go and I’ll—”
“Get out of here!”
She kicked at him, leaning over her horse, and he exhaled hugely. His head fell, and Damia eyed Rayna.
“If that’s the case—”
“Oh shut up, we’re not breaking up. Just get lost—you’re embarrassing me!”
His head rose once more, and the huge Gnoll beamed.
“My lovely, spirited, fiery huntress—”
Damia did her utmost not to laugh, and Irit bit his tongue as his shoulders shook. Rayna dared them to laugh as she rode forwards, wiping at her fur.
“That’s…he’s too important to ignore, despite how he acts. Never mind that. We’re just seeing each other. Not engaged.”
“That’s an Ekhtouch Gnoll, isn’t he?”
Damia took the time to ogle Thamert’s backside as he strode off. He had to be. Rayna nodded, and Irit explained.
“During the Meeting of Tribes, the Ekhtouch tribe and ours became friendly. It’s a custom of theirs to arrange marriages. It is, to them, what their tribe creates.”
Superior Gnolls. Damia nodded; she’d read up on the tribes. She glanced at Rayna.
“But you called it off?”
“Chieftain Gireulashia changed the practice. Plus, with the tribes in disarray, she lifted a bunch of restrictions on their clan. They can have more children, and she broke off engagements. Some of them left. Others stayed. I was engaged, but since we’re so busy, I don’t have time for children.”
“Ah, but you’re still seeing him?”
The [Huntress] grumbled as she shifted around in her saddle.
“Well…yes. He’s the one who wants children. He doesn’t have to grow them! Thamert’s a [Miner]. If you get a chance, watch him swing a pickaxe. He makes it look like a work of art.”
“I wouldn’t miss that for the world.”
Damia glanced back and got a boot in the leg. More laughter until a hither-to silent woman broke in.
“So that’s who the tall Gnolls are. Gave me itching down my spine. Yon [Miner] doesn’t look like he’s more than just a fellow who could throw a punch. The other one makes me nervous.”
Varnie. The [Gang Leader] was a bit subdued after having her gang destroyed, despite being saved. But she glanced over her shoulder, and this time, it was Rayna’s turn to grin.
“That’s Sadr. She throws things. Daggers, arrows—I saw her throw a stick straight through a wheel of cheese. She was also engaged, but she broke it all the way off. Came north because it was too awkward. She’s interested in you, Irit.”
The [Shaman] sighed.
“She just wants to be highly placed in the Silverfang tribe.”
“Eh, she likes you.”
Varnie glanced between the joking Gnolls, then turned to Damia.
“A Gnoll with a [Thrower] class? One of them fancy Gnolls? Mind if I recruit her for th’ gang, boss lady?”
The two Silverfangs went still and turned to Damia. The [Lady] smiled.
“You can make her an offer, Varnie, but I don’t want to offend our friends here. Next time, ask me in private.”
“Right, I suppose that’s a fancy way of doing that. So is that a yes or no…?”
“Mm, a yes. Very politely.”
Employees. Binevy was Damia’s right hand who kept things organized. Sule was her [Bodyguard]. And Varnie was the person who could do things. She’d said as much to Damia.
“Anyone who pulls me out of a noose deserves a fair turn. Can’t say I’ll be here forever, but let’s make a deal: I pay off my debt and see where you’re going. If I need to jump ship, I’ll do it nice and honorable, even if I run off in the night. No leavin’ with all your gold. Face’s honor.”
Damia just had to convince Varnie she wanted to work for the [Dame]. And she had a Face as an employee.
A wonderful day. Irit began to protest to Damia that they couldn’t just lose Sadr, whom he really didn’t mind, you know, it was just that she sometimes got pushy and he was his own Gnoll at the moment—when they finally spotted the dig site. Damia stood up in her saddle and gasped as she saw the huge piles of dirt excavated from the ground, orderly tents, and Drakes on patrol! She inhaled—
Then retched, and everyone laughed. All the Gnolls had nose plugs in.
“I think I swallowed a fly. Water, water!”
“You spat it out, Miss.”
Sule pointed, and Damia croaked at him.
“What do you think the flies live in? Water—water—”
Her stomach roiled at the very thought. Damia gargled, then felt so nauseous she leapt from the saddle as the Drakes saw them arrive and came out to greet the huge convoy of people. She rushed for the outhouses, clearly marked, and threw herself into one.
She did not vomit, but sat there as her stomach settled. Damia Reinhart schooled herself.
I’m meeting with Wall Lord Ilvriss. The Wall Lord Ilvriss.
He’s the closest thing to the inn besides Liska. Closer since he’s so important! I need to make a great first impression. Plus, he’s single.
She sat on the toilet, adjusting her riding dress, searching around for some perfume. The outhouse was actually very pleasant; it was newly-built of wood, it seemed, so fresh it gleamed. There was a sink to the side, a hanging charm that made it so no bad scents remained.
Dead gods, this is classier than many of the privies in our mansion! Damia stared at the working sink and turned a knob. Water began to flow at once!
“Is this…plumbing?”
Out here? In the middle of nowhere? She was dumbstruck! The newly-refurbished outhouse was classy! Was this all down to Salazsarian gold? She stared around, then noticed there was a handle on the toilet.
It flushed? And there was a button on the side of the outhouse. It had a bunch of little lines radiating upwards and a little tail lifting above it.
What the heck did that do? Damia pressed the button. Heard a gurgling sound. Then screamed.
 
——
 
“Silverfangs?”
Wall Lord Ilvriss stood outside his dig site, and [Clan Leader] Plisce looked worried.
“You, ah, did not send for us, Wall Lord?”
“Not specifically. My recruiters were searching for anyone with mining or digging Skills, and of course, if I’d thought to ask…! Welcome, Ancestors, come in! We’ll have to have a celebration in your honor! How is Chieftain Akrisa? And—how many Humans?”
There were so many! Ilvriss was astonished! And gratified! He’d heard they were numerous, but this was all down to—
“Lady Damia? I was told we hired her on a provisional basis, but I confess, I haven’t met her in person.”
He had to improvise. Reassure the worried Gnolls and others that this was all part of the plan. But internally, Ilvriss was a bit disconcerted.
Some [Lady] had hired the lot of these people. For what? The gold was his assumption. She was owed quite a sum of it. He just worried these people were here under false duress or something, or she’d made outlandish promises.
But Plisce assured Ilvriss he’d read the contract and just wanted to negotiate a bulk rate for his people.
“The [Lady] reminded us of your deeds at the Meeting of Tribe, Wall Lord, and I shall confess, we wished to see the Cowpat Plains. It has been…hard finding land.”
Ah, Ilvriss saw the issue now. He rubbed his neck spines wearily.
“The old rights issue, eh?”
“From south to north, nothing changes. But perhaps here—”
“The locals are not friendly to Drakes, just so you know, Clan Leader. Speaking frankly, associating with my company might poison the well ahead of time. If you want to enjoy our hospitality while you deliberate, I won’t hold you to any contracts. I’d be delighted to—not make introductions since that wouldn’t go well, but give you names and locations of the leaders here.”
The Gnoll smiled.
“Ah, there is some generosity. Let us see, Wall Lord. I do want to earn money, and yours is the only digging job around! As for the hostility, everyone claims we are welcome and that they are ‘not like those Drakes’. If they mean it, they shall prove it.”
Fair enough. Ilvriss shook hands with Plisce and was giving orders to get everyone settled. But where was Damia—?
A scream that sounded somewhat familiar came from the new outhouses that Master Plumber Oidhol had just laid. Ilvriss turned as a young woman exploded out of them. She turned, saw everyone staring, and put her hands behind her dress.
“I just pressed a button and—oh no. Run me over, it’s a bidet. I’ve heard of those!”
She had a rather visible stain on her—she must have been sitting on the toilet clothed and the button activated—Wall Lord Ilvriss saw Damia Reinhart turn, spot him, and turn crimson, then pale.
He coughed as he averted his eyes and waved for someone to run a towel over. Or something. Wall Lord Ilvriss was worried Damia was dangerous. But he had to admit, she seemed a bit…young.
 
——
 
Damia was so embarrassed by her first meeting with the Wall Lord she put her head under a pillow and refused to come out of the guest tent.
Good first impression—failure. She could only show him she was a friend of the inn. Someone he wanted to meet!
Certainly, the Wall Lord seemed to need to make use of her. He was speaking to Binevy, Clan Leader Plisce, and a representative from Riverfarm.
“—have had issues with, er, Drake culture from Salazsar with our workers before. I refuse to let any prejudices affect the Silverfangs we employ.”
“One thing to say it, another thing to act on it. I have heard your company does better than most with Gnolls, but we have our own ways. How would we do this, Wall Lord?”
Ilvriss glanced at Damia as Binevy waved the [Lady] over.
“Liaisons. Diligent oversight. My personal staff will take part, and I hope you would do the same and relay any complaints to me personally, Plisce. I have an expert named Xesci—and I believe I should like to request Lady Damia do the same.”
He wanted to make sure the Humans, Gnolls, and Drakes got along? Damia brightened up. She saw a number of important people gathered around Wall Lord Ilvriss.
A Drake with one eye and an artificial leg spoke next.
“Operational security is also important. I am Major Shellc, in charge of the [Soldiers]. We have both a monster danger and a number of irregular Humans who come out and, for lack of a better word, brawl. It’s not a conventional job.”
“Which is why I shall pay for these unexpected contingencies and offer compensation for injuries and accidents, but I want to be up front about all of this. Lady Damia, I do appreciate your hard work, but if you’ve heard of me, I have some requests of you, pending full acceptance of your recruits.”
Wall Lord Ilvriss was precise, clear-spoken, and had everyone’s attention as he laid out expectations and background in a fast manner. He was, in Damia’s eyes, a successful, seasoned [Lord] who could make things happen.
Everything she wanted to be. He eyed her with a hint of a smile, and she smiled.
“Absolutely, Wall Lord. I am here to help! Say the word and I’ll be on it—like—that!”
So saying, she took a step, did a twirl, and raised her fingers. Damia Reinhart gave Wall Lord Ilvriss a pair of finger guns and her biggest smile.
She’d heard from Timbor they did that in The Wandering Inn. The Wall Lord stared at Damia’s finger guns.
Major Shellc bit his tongue. Clan Leader Plisce began to laugh then started choking. One of the Drakes next to Ilvriss rolled his eyes up into his head as he cringed. Damia Reinhart turned red.
Ilvriss turned and coughed-laughed, then smiled at Damia as she lowered her hands.
“I…I have nothing but the utmost confidence in you, Lady Damia. I just remind everyone that House Gemscale is a company, and I hope to deliver the utmost professionalism between all working groups. Thank you.”
Damia smiled until he was done. She went around, shaking hands, and then went back into her tent and hid her head under a pillow again.
 
——
 
Based on just…how he’d met her, Ilvriss doubted Damia was some kind of spy. She wasn’t that incompetent either, according to Welsca.
“She’s asked questions and not objected to me giving her requests, Wall Lord. Despite her, ah, antics.”
“Remind you of anyone?”
“The [Innkeeper] or the Runner?”
Welsca’s face indicated what she thought of a potential Erin or Ryoka-clone, but Ilvriss just chuckled.
“There’s a possibility she’s an excellent spy for her family. Keep an eye on her, but I doubt it. They’re good at acting. But [Spies] tend to want to be impressive. It’s an ego thing.”
Bideting oneself and finger guns either made her a super-spy or an interesting [Lady]. They’d find out which soon. Ilvriss rubbed at his ribs. Welsca put down her notes anxiously. She’d rushed back from Invrisil when she’d heard about the attack.
“Are you still healing, sir?”
“I’m fine. The damn Golem wasn’t shooting to kill. I bet the next one will just break my legs or something.”
Was this hope for peace between Terlands and Salazsar? Or a sign they wanted him to suffer before death? Ilvriss sighed.
“Tell me something good, Welsca. Please. I could use a morale boost. I’ve got upset [Miners]—about the working conditions, no doubt—rogue undead tunneling around me, the damn Terlands, the Lischelles and every other [Rancher] clan, and my thighs hurt. I need a victory.”
All his good mood had evaporated with the anti-Salazsarian press and being shot. He didn’t know how Erin did it. The Drake didn’t have to hunt.
“It’s all worth it, Wall Lord. Even the [Ladies] with the finger…guns.”
“What? I thought that was the best part of my day so far. I nearly died not laughing. I just didn’t want to humiliate the poor girl any further.”
Welsca eyed Ilvriss and shook her head.
“Each to their own, Wall Lord. Here’s your victory: the artifacts were appraised by Master Hedault, Master Grimalkin, and Archmage Valeterisa. They’re not cursed. They are some of the highest-grade artifacts the trio have ever seen. There is nothing in all of Salazsar better than this.”
She placed a pickaxe on his desk, and Wall Lord Ilvriss sat up. He was reminded of what Miner Georgie had found.
Gear from the dead [Miners]. Enchanted, but…Ilvriss picked up the pickaxe. He admired the silver-blue metal he couldn’t place and the visible runes on the haft of the pickaxe. Despite its age, it hadn’t disintegrated or worn down. It felt light, barely a pound, but when he swung it, it had heft.
“Okay, we knew it was probably what we wanted. We still don’t know why there’s a mine around the lost Walled City of Purity. But that’s a bold claim, Welsca. Tune it back a notch, though I appreciate it.”
She gave him a level look and a hint of a smile.
“Wall Lord, I had to fight to keep the [Mages] off this loot. I only made it out because Miss Mrsha and Miss Nanette attacked them with water orbs or something nonsensical. Go ahead and try the pickaxe out. You’re familiar with our Advance Miner gear for infested areas?”
“Yes…”
Ilvriss stood slowly. He cast around, then coughed.
“Isn’t there some stone in Dig Site #1? There’s a huge chunk of granite. Let’s go there and, ah…do we have one of those picks?”
 
——
 
Advance Miner gear usually was the best. Or the kind of gear that Alrric had been issued when he led by example.
The best pickaxes, shovels, and even helmets came from all over Izril’s south. You could buy the best, so Salazsar put together equipment kits; each company had their own brand. It was very nuanced, and Ilvriss himself was rather into it.
“This is a Foreman’s Pick. Pallassian Grade-1 steel. Enchanting is Fissivalian—a Level 30 [Enchanter]’s work. If I’m not wrong, it’s [Protection], [Lightweight], and [Sharpness]. We used to have [Impact], but it blew grit back in the faces of the miners. Oh, and the handle’s Sturdy Oak from Oteslia. Mildly magical on its own. This is a helmet—Yoldenite-made. So that means magicore lining with leather bindings. Protection and cooling enchantments.”
They were some of the best items in Salazsar, and Ilvriss was proud to say that every [Foreman] or Advance Miner got gear of commensurate quality. Obviously, you mixed and matched what you had; pieces wore out, and the best pick would eventually break down from the hard use.
He flipped the pickaxe up and swung it into one of the granite walls. Granite was a hard stone, and Ilvriss didn’t swing it that hard. There was a satisfying crack, and he smiled. Then eyed the crack.
“Weird blue streak in the granite. What’s this stone?”
“Our people identified it as a variant of greywacke, Wall Lord. Annoying, which is why we went past it. Feldspar pockets, see?”
Ilvriss took another swing, harder, sidelong, and grunted as his pickaxe hit the hard seam and rebounded. He’d chunked out a bit more of the seam, but after six swings, he barely crumpled in a small section.
“Damn. No wonder it’s slow going at times. And this is with an enchanted pickaxe! Well, our [Miners] have Skills—one of them could beat me even with a regular steel one, eh? Now, where’s our superior artifact?”
He accepted the other pickaxe, and it was so much lighter that when Ilvriss took it, he nearly slapped himself in the chin. He made a show of inspecting the tip—it wasn’t even that sharp, pickaxes not really needing to be, but still—and then test-swung it.
He was…a tad bit defensive. Obviously, they’d come to dig for just this: artifacts of old. But Naamreles had been the City of Purity, not the City of Digging! Salazsar might have lost a lot, but dead gods damnit, they knew pickaxes!
“Didn’t this thing glow red when Georgie ran into the monsters? I suppose it’s a safety measure—can we copy the enchantments?”
“Not easily, Wall Lord, but Enchanter Hedault said it is a possibility.”
“I suppose he needs one. Well, we could give it to Salazsar too, but then the teleporting rabbit’s really out of the bag, eh?”
If he needed more support, he’d do that, but he wanted to keep this from his peers for as long as possible. Because once they knew, they’d grab.
Was that too Drake of him? They needed this. The world did. Ilvriss had spent months here, and this was only a fraction of the bounty required. So yes, he wanted to find the treasure, damnit, and he’d spread it to whoever needed it, but not some grab-bag with all of his peers trying to hoard this, thank you! He’d take it—and, uh, un-hoard it!
Ilvriss sighed.
“Once we get more, I’ll consider it.”
Welsca hesitated.
“We have more, Wall Lord. Four sets. Not all complete since we think the undead are wearing some of the gear, but pickaxes, helmet, lanterns—even some clothing, though that has deteriorated.”
“We what?”
Ilvriss half-pivoted in his swing. He’d been so concerned about Osthia and the actual attack he’d not paid attention to the artifacts since they had to get them evaluated. His swing was completely off target. Ilvriss swung around, head turning to Welsca—
—and completed a three hundred and sixty degree rotation. The Drake’s head turned as someone made a faint sound. His bad pickaxe swing had hit the granite and greywacke and gone straight through and out the other side.
He had barely felt it. The Wall Lord peered back at the horizontal gash.
“I—that was—hold on now.”
He stared down at the pickaxe. Then swung it again, vertically this time.
He split the hardened seam in the granite wall, cutting through the wall like a man parting grass with a machete. The Wall Lord saw dirt and stone falling to the sides. He swung the pickaxe sideways, got it lodged in the stone as he failed to cut with the pick—yanked it out, and stared at the mess he’d made.
Ilvriss had seen Level 40 [Stonebreaker Miners] at work before. An old Drake had shown him a Skill when he’d been a lad, touring the mines.
[Cut Stone Like Water]. He’d swung his pickaxe like that for all of two hours before needing a rest at his age, due to his arthritis. But that one Drake alone had done the work of multiple teams until he retired.
That—was like this tool Ilvriss held. The Wall Lord shakily glanced around.
“Where’s the Foreman’s Pick? Maybe it’s bad stone. Try—”
One of his people lifted their pick and hit the stone wall, clearly thinking to move it like Ilvriss’—
The pickaxe bounced off and vibrated out of the Drake’s grasp. It fell into the dirt. Ilvriss stared at the Salazsarian-made pickaxe. Then he swung the one he had down at it.
The flash of light kicked Ilvriss off his feet. He landed on his back, with one of his rings shrilling at him, and spoke.
“Okay, cutting another enchanted item was stupid. Did it—”
The Foreman’s Pick was cracked, soot markings around the now disenchanted metal head. It was severed in half. The pickaxe of Naamreles?
Pristine. The Wall Lord lifted it, wide-eyed. And then he said nothing at all. Because with all due respect to his people’s gear, and even his own equipment—
Erin Solstice had given him a sword from one of her [Gardens of Sanctuary], a blade of lightning. He appreciated that trust from her, even if it wasn’t as powerful as…well, one had hoped. It was only a mithril blade that could shoot lightning; slightly better than his old sword. But he had to apologize to her now.
Because Wall Lord Ilvriss was now a pickaxe user. If he’d given this to any Gold-rank team, they’d probably have tossed their weapons and taken this. If he handed it to Yvlon—
Okay, maybe Yvlon would still use her fists. But anyone normal?
If that Golem had come at me and I’d had this, would I have pierced its armor? Maybe not so easily, but—
“Get me, um, get me some ingots. Solid steel. We have to have some for our [Smiths]. For repairs.”
Ilvriss croaked. Someone ran off. There was silence as Welsca inspected the broken Foreman’s Pick.
“It—it could only work on metals and stone, Wall Lord.”
“Oh, naturally.”
He agreed. Of course, it might only be mineable things. Everyone nodded along. Ilvriss went on after a moment.
“And—and it’s a pickaxe. I can’t just walk around with one. It’s too cumbersome, light as it is. I have an image to maintain.”
Nod, nod. Welsca licked her lips.
“I could swing one, Wall Lord. I do have combat classes.”
“Well hold on, Welsca. Let’s not jump to hasty—I mean, it’s not shaped for combat.”
“No, Wall Lord. Hard to block with—well, different ergonomics—”
“Exactly! It’s a damn pick. Plus, it’s just really good at cutting things. No flashy spells attached. My sword—Erin gave it to me—can emit lightning. That’s not nothing.”
“Absolutely, Wall Lord. It’s just a pick. Er…with a secondary enchantment. Wall Lord? Look down.”
Ilvriss was just about to finish talking down the pickaxe to some kind of reasonable level when he stared at his feet. And he realized that in his swinging around at the granite and other rocks, he should have had a bit more resistance.
After all, a pickaxe was still a pickaxe. Cut stone like butter and it still had a narrow profile. You couldn’t use it like a shovel.
But he’d parted the rock too easily. Cut too wide a gap. Where had the excess material gone? Vaporized? What a silly thing to do if it was ore you wanted.
If you were some ancient [Enchanter] of yore, making pickaxes for your people, and you actually cared about them, you’d not do that. You’d make another enchantment instead.
Like, say…some kind of enchantment beyond the scope of modern [Mages]. Something with a simple effect that meant whatever the pickaxe cut through sorted itself.
Granite to granite.
Feldspar to feldspar.
Even particles of dirt.
And it…what, compacted it? Processed it into a solid little brick of…
Ilvriss bent down and picked up a rectangular brick of granite. Then a pale, white mini-brick of feldspar. The mineral was beautiful, devoid of any other kind of rock adhering to it. And oh, to the right—Ilvriss’ claws had to scrabble around.
Then he picked up the tiniest—he grunted. Peered around.
“Welsca?”
“Y-yes, Wall Lord?”
“Get a [Prospector] over here and double-check. I think there’s a tiny bit of gold in this granite. Not worth mining, but maybe there’s a vein.”
“At once, Wall Lord.”
He nodded a few times.
“Right, you do that. I’m just going to pass out over here.”
He leaned the pickaxe down carefully and lay on the ground.
 
——
 
The [Miners] at Dig Site #1 were grumbling about all the new hires they had to train up. The Silverfangs—no one had a problem with the Gnolls! No, certainly not! Just—they had their own style.
Of course, more hands were worth it, but they hoped the Wall Lord remembered who the real employees were. No one was really unhappy. Just upset about the monsters, the brawling—so they vented.
All the bigwigs were here today, and most of the mining was elsewhere, anyways. The mining team assigned to continue probing this area was eventually told to get back to work and check on a higher tunnel that someone thought had gold in it.
Everyone made jokes about the idiot bigwig from their cushy tower-jobs having a ‘hunch’…right up until they saw the tunnel.
“Hey. Wasn’t this a rock wall yesterday?”
There was a huge, almost circular hole going straight ahead for twenty feet. The [Miners] exchanged looks. One felt at the hole in the stone, and yes, there was a bit of gold there. One of them scraped at it incredulously.
“Ancestors, it’s gold. How did they—?”
“I saw them trooping back up with the Wall Lord, no less. Talking about how much their arms hurt. I thought they were joking. Does he have a new Skill or something…?”
“I’ve never heard of him using one. What kind of object made—?”
They got to work, staring at the hole in the wall. When one of the [Miners] thought to ask the [Forewoman] who’d been on duty to make sure the bigwigs didn’t collapse a tunnel on their heads, all the wide-eyed Drake woman said was—
“I think it was new gear or something. They were comparing it against a Foreman’s Pick. I’m not allowed to say more.”
“How good is it?”
The [Forewoman] considered the question.
“I think…however much Wall Lord Ilvriss paid for it, from the Archmage of Izril or whatever, he underpaid. And we’d better hope there’s not much or he’s going to put us all out of work. Or we’re going to add five new floors to Salazsar. This year.”
The [Miners] eyed each other. Then the hole in the dig site. After a moment, one of them picked up a little bar of gold, perfectly rectangular. About eight grams.
One of the bigwigs had forgotten about it. When the team went to turn it in, against some of their instincts, they were told to just keep it.
 
——
 
Ilvriss instantly told everyone to keep silent about the pickaxe and other gear. It had just been his personal adjutants, but the [Forewoman] and his bodyguard had also been there.
Rumors would spread. But he had Welsca assign the Rubirel Guard to the Chest of Holding with the Walled City’s gear inside; it would be anchored to the floor and watched 24/8.
Ancestors. Ancestors.
And all the gear was like that. Not all of it was so—so—flashy. For instance, the lantern was just a bull’s eye lantern, one that apparently had an Everburning Flame inside. Simple. It couldn’t emit a [Fireball].
It just changed colors when exposed to various gases or hazardous materials, apparently. And it could change intensities and thus illuminate an entire tunnel by itself.
And reveal [Invisibility] spells. Wall Lord Ilvriss realized that when he was walking around camp and a giant metal Golem with spindly legs, a long, telescoping head, and huge eye-face appeared over one of the tents. He stared at it. It jerked upright and ran as an alarm was blown.
“Dead gods, another attack, Wall Lord?”
Young Dramm jogged over, pale-faced. Ilvriss shook his head.
“The Terlands are spying on us. Clearly. That thing looked observational—though unsettling.”
“Good thing you have all those artifacts, sir. Been mining to, uh, inspire the grunts?”
“It’s sharing the load, Wall Lord Dramm, and they’re employees. I’m no Alrric, but, er, yes. Just testing some new gear.”
Ilvriss reprimanded the young Drake, and Dramm ducked his head. The Drake boy cast around.
“Er, want us to take your gear, sir?”
“What? No. I’m fine!”
The defensive tone made Dramm step back. Ilvriss and his adjutants glared at him. Dramm nodded.
“Of course, Wall Lord. But isn’t that helmet, uh—”
It was just some miner’s helmet. It appeared a bit worn, and despite being glossy metal, it was far from befitting a Lord of the Walls. But Ilvriss had a pickaxe, a huge one, on his belt, and so did Welsca and two of his employees. They all had those helmets on, and the Drake had a miner’s lantern. Ilvriss adjusted the helmet.
“Er—it’s actually quite comfortable. And it emits cold air. I think I might wear it around camp. You know, safety first.”
Emits cold air? Dramm had to get a helmet like that if they were giving those out to [Miners]. He wiped at his sweaty brows as Ilvriss walked on, looking a bit stupefied. But seeing a huge Golem like that—Dramm shuddered. This job was dangerous. His father had been quite worried about the second Golem attack, and he’d told Dramm to maybe hint to Ilvriss to cut his losses.
All this work, for what? The young Drake shook his head as he watched Ilvriss march off. All they had were a bunch of undead and nothing to show for it besides some damn miner gear. But he supposed Wall Lord Ilvriss couldn’t back out without looking bad. Dramm got that; you had to hard-commit even if it was a mistake. That was real Drakeness.
 
——
 
Wall Lord Ilvriss snapped out of it after a day and a half. He was holding the pickaxe on his lap in his office, tail curled around the safety-lantern of old, when he felt it.
A possessiveness. A need to snap at anyone wanting to take his pickaxe. A desire to tell Welsca to ensure any items found in the mines were his and—
“Ancestors. I’m Hoarding!”
Ilvriss leapt up. He took the helmet off his head, piled the equipment on his desk, and grabbed a speaking stone.
“Welsca? Can you take this to the chest? I’m done.”
“Wall Lord? But your gear—”
Welsca was wearing a helmet, lantern, pickaxe, and other objects he’d let her carry. It made her look stupid, and people had been wondering about it. Ilvriss shook his head. He glanced at the pickaxe and forced himself back from the desk.
“Take it. I know it’s optimal, but I’m—you’re—Hoarding. Can’t you tell?”
Her eyes widened. She recoiled and began to hiss at him, then appeared appalled. Slowly, with great effort, she took the helmet off her head.
“I’m…yes. I am. Ancestors. I’m sorry.”
“Don’t be. I’m—it’s understandable.”
She took the items, and he forced himself not to watch the precious, his valuable—
Hoarding was a Drake phenomenon. It hit most kids growing up. It could last a while; you even had teenagers who went through it. It wasn’t always items. Sometimes, it was things you loved of a different kind. Food, especially if you’d been insecure.
The cutest version was Hoarding people you loved. But even cute turned into possessiveness. Snapping at others. They got it from Dragons.
However, you could be weaned off it. Most Drake parents could find someone who helped talk children out of the habit. You were taught how to recognize you were Hoarding, fight the mentality.
Ilvriss left his tent and went for a walk.
“That is not the attitude of a good Drake. I don’t need it. It’s damn [Miner] gear. It proves we’re on the right track, and there are hundreds of pieces down there, potentially. Enough for one for me—no!”
Some of the people he passed eyed him. Lady Damia strode forwards.
“Wall Lord, can I help—?”
“Hello, Lady Damia, if you could take charge of the Silverfangs with Clan Leader Plisce today? Let’s get them fully involved in our company. I’m giving you full authority on par with Dramm. Test of your abilities and leadership. Thank you!”
He stopped, shook her hand with a big smile, and walked on. That dealt with that. Ilvriss almost ran to the only person who could help.
 
——
 
The Lifted Tail was Thirthoof’s best—and only—brothel. Everyone wanted to be in the Drake-run, alluring establishment. It had class. It had ladies (and men) who didn’t look like they hated being there. It had no drapes and clean beds.
And the other fellow who’d run a business with ladies of the night had quit, especially after having both legs broken and falling out that window like that. Xesci was making a profit, and she felt like she’d convinced a number of Humans not all Drakes should go. Even members of the [Rancher] clans.
She was about to complain to Wall Lord Ilvriss, though, when the Drake came to her. He knocked and, when she called for him to enter, strode in, looking a bit harried.
He felt chagrined, like a boy—not just how he was presenting or acting, but he was actually feeling like a child. Which was fascinating. Xesci could read the feelings of people, if not their hearts or souls, and an adult recapturing childhood, even if this wasn’t the most pleasant feeling, was rare.
“Wall Lord. Something amusing has happened?”
He adjusted his collar, visibly embarrassed.
“Xesci, I’m, uh—I had a Hoarding incident just this morning, actually. I’m coming to you for advice because it’s still ongoing.”
She blinked at him. Ilvriss had run to the only expert he knew in personality. The [Courtesan] coughed.
“Okay. Stop it?”
Her lack of a response instantly had the Wall Lord clarifying.
“No, you see, Xesci, it’s not a regular incident. This is actually in aid of good tidings! Our gear from the mines is amazing! It’s stupendous! It’s Named-rank class, and I was coveting it like I was five.”
“Right. That’s great. Where do I come in here? You’ve stopped. Don’t do it again.”
He hesitated.
“Can’t you do something? Slap it out of me?”

The Wall Lord sat up slowly. The Rubirel Guard stared at Xesci, and she realized their astonishment was genuine. They couldn’t see Zel Shivertail hanging over Ilvriss’ back, an inspiration. Plumbing. You might not care for it. You might not want it spraying water up your nether regions. But the ability to hit a lever and flush a toilet or get hot or cold water on demand?
That…
That was like diamonds in the Cowpat Plains, and the [Mayor] of Thirthoof was up-front.
“We saw your Master Plumber fellow working, and it were like magic, Wall Lord. A few twists and that pipe stuff and you got running water?”
“Well, he is over Level 40. One of the City of Gem’s finest. And I have, uh, a Skill.”
[Adaptive Plumbing]. Master Oidhol had been exceptionally complimentary when he’d heard about it. Apparently, it made the act of joining up the pipes—which was very difficult and arguably one of the hardest parts—very easy.
Mayor Bootsy nodded.
“Any way we might, uh, pay for some? Everyone in town wants one. It’d be gold in your pockets.”

Bidet-diplomacy?

Oh.

Anti-hoarding mentality. Xesci had said he was some kind of Wall Lord with a cape. Well, he wasn’t, damnit. He couldn’t be Zel, he never would be. He was just Ilvriss, [Wall Lord of Corporate Opulence], and he brought bidets when other Drakes brought armies.

Tolveilouka Ve’delina Mer had a barbeque and a snack.
The first meal he’d had in…what, thousands of years? Over ten thousand?
Sometimes, he’d eaten the pests who were attracted to his Master, but they were so boring, and it wasn’t worth rounding them up.
This?
“This is excellent beef, you know. I can see why it’s considered good. Though—have you ever had Salazsarian pork? I bet no one remembers that either. Or Giant’s testicles.”
He spoke to the two dozen Humans sitting cross-legged in the grass. Tolveilouka had built a bonfire and was smoking the meat.
One of the cows was twitching after he’d tossed it on the burning logs. Oh, sure, Tolveilouka had to admit…it wasn’t the most elegant barbeque. You could argue the fear ruined the meat. And agony.
But some people could taste fear, and he?
He sucked off more meat from the bone. Opened his mouth. Began to gnash the bone up. Licked his hand. Grabbed another piece of smoking meat and began to eat.
“Could use some salt. And that ketchup from Liscor. You know, we invented that? We called it tomatus. Wish I’d brought some.”
Or another nice sauce! Maybe they had some? The Humans were trembling.
Tolveilouka was bare-chested. He kept eating nonstop. He had to, because he had a lot of cows to eat. A herd’s worth, really. But he ate so fast it was like he didn’t taste the meat. And the bones—
The sight of a half-Elf eating a cow’s worth of meat was…insane. His stomach was bulging, distended beyond belief but not as much as it should have been. After him eating fourteen cows he should have been far, far larger.
He—the [Ranchers] stared up at him. Tolveilouka glanced around as the cow he’d ‘prepared’ on the fire sizzled.

Tolveilouka seized them, and there was screaming. The rest of the [Ranchers] sat there. Frozen.

Blood and urine and wet bones. He turned, eyes gleaming, and then their horror took on another level. Tolveilouka crouched there. Grinning.
This isn’t even one of my truer forms.

Pulley bars, leg machines—even a moving treadmill animated by gears.
Gears, not magic alone. The Sinew Magus was less-common in the gym these days, but he still put in an appearance at least once a week. Not with Lady Pryde. She got…harassed. After a number of incidents, Grimalkin had agreed it was better to do without, but that knowledge had not made him happy.
Still—he looked happier in some ways. He wasn’t as huge as Nerul remembered him being in the past. Quite imposing still, but slimmer by as much as a fifth. Mobility over pure mass. Possibly more muscled than before, though.
“Diplomat Nerul. What brings you here?”
Nerul walked in, feeling quite out-of-place. He had some pants and a shirt he’d bought, baggy, and he was already sweaty. Nervous. But he was a man on a mission.
“I’m here, Magus Grimalkin, to prevail on you to teach me how to use these blasted contraptions, if I may. We have one in Salazsar, and I’ve done my best, but I confess, I have not had a pleasant time with my diet.”
The Sinew Magus blinked. Some of his apprentices stopped working out as the Drake glanced at Nerul, then gave him a sharper look. Up and down—Grimalkin walked around Nerul.
“Highly fatigued muscles. Mostly legwork…but decent upper body—ah, a tear in your right shoulder.”
Nerul rotated his shoulder.
“I hurt myself with those blasted weights. You can tell?”
“I’ve…levelled a bit. And my own understanding of my speciality has deepened slightly. Is your stomach giving you issues? Stool?”
“I’d love a stool. But if you mean, er, waste. It’s mostly liquid.”
The Drake flushed even more, but Grimalkin was purely analytical, and so were his students, who’d come over.
“Ah. I hadn’t looked into the matter. But it appears that if a person’s stomach is used to one diet, switching over has deleterious effects. Even if it is more healthy, a stomach is apparently used to one kind of food.”
“Really? Damn. I wish I’d known that.”
It made Nerul feel slightly better. The Sinew Magus kept peering at Nerul, then seemed to realize why Nerul was here.
“You’ve come to…train. Diplomat?”
“If you can tell, I suppose it’s a compliment.”
Nerul smiled weakly. He spread his arms.
“I need to get in shape, Sinew Magus. Just enough to, say, hit a man my size harder than he hits me and hold my own. I don’t need to win, but I need to prove a point. It’s diplomatic work.”
“Diplomatic…?”
One of the Dullahans mouthed silently, utterly confused, but Magus Grimalkin asked no more questions. He just put a hand on Nerul’s shoulder, studied him.
“If you have the will, I shall do my best, Diplomat. It will not be easy. How long do you have?”
“Days, ideally. If not ideally, a week or two.”
Again, the wording confused the students, but the Sinew Magus just nodded.
“Crash course, then. Anti-inflammation poultices. Get me Experimental Set #2. You know healing potions don’t work? The idea is to still let muscles perform day-after-day. They’ll be abused, but keeping them from tearing in any excessive way while pushing them provokes dynamic growth. That’s one thing we have over those know-it-all brats!”
He shook a fist at the sky, by which Nerul took to mean Earthers. The [Diplomat] swallowed.
“Wonderful. How painful is this…?”
“Exceptionally! But if you have the will—”
That was the damn question, was it? How far could Nerul push himself in the name of his class? He didn’t know. He’d long passed the days when you could level up and know you were on the right path. But the [Diplomat] had to try.
The next hour saw Grimalkin and his apprentices showing Nerul how to properly work out and formulating the best exercises to build the key muscles Nerul needed. Which meant, sadly, more roadwork.
“I’ve run up and down Salazsar’s damned towers!”
“Good! And you have a foundation, Diplomat! You were already strong, but converting more fat to muscle is our goal! Hm. You really have put in effort. Out of curiosity, have you had any meals in Liscor? The Wandering Inn?”
“A…few.”
“Interesting. I’ll have to check the water again. Do you and Baker Garry ever eat the same meals? It’s probably just a random correlation, not causation, but…five more pushups!”
The problem with Magus Grimalkin was that he was loud. The problem with him was that he knew when you could actually give him another rep. And then he’d insist that despite the evidence of his eyes, he believed you could do another rep.
Nerul grew to hate him and his students over the course of the next hour, where he strained, sweating, chewing on the damn ‘protein’ bars or whatever they were, and gulping the salty liquid that made him think of camel piss. An ‘energy’ drink, apparently.
But he kept straining and kept his whining for when he was really out of energy. Which did come—but the Sinew Magus just stood with a dozen of his students and bellowed.
“Push, [Diplomat]! Push! One more rep!”
“One more rep!”
The students were shouting as Nerul pushed a bar of metal up. Then they had him switch to a new ‘station’—one of them wiped down the metal bar as Nerul left a pool of sweat behind him.
Fun fact: due to the Drake neck spines, Grimalkin had commissioned custom seats for different species. Ones with holes for your tail and neck spines even if you were lying on your back for Drakes, and for Gnolls, anti-stick ones to prevent their fur from catching, and even stations that Dullahans could exercise with only some limbs if they detached them. Garuda-friendly ones with their claws…
A number of Pallassian amateurs were drawn to the sight of a panting Drake swearing at Grimalkin as the [Diplomat] did bench squats. Grimalkin’s now-famous gymnasiums were creating new classes.
The aforementioned [Gym Rat]—and just people who wanted to build muscle. Pallass’ gymnasium was the biggest and best in the world thanks to Grimalkin—only House Ulta could compare, and it was constructing a five-story one. Because Pryde didn’t lose.
In fact, even a Lord Mireden Raithland stopped pressing an enormous amount of weight as four nervous spotters watched him lift and glanced up.
“…Is that the [Diplomat]? What’s going on?”
The half-Giant took some earbuds out of his ears, then snorted.
“Wait, what am I asking? It’s the inn.”
Even so, he watched as the panting Drake stood and did one of the most punishing—yet rewarding—moves.
The squat.
Simple concept. Put a bar on your shoulders, maintain form, and squat. Down. Up. You could even do it without a spotter, if you had a protective bar that would let you fall without crushing yourself if you couldn’t hold the weight.
Everyone squatted. Nerul had never thought it was painful—but if you’d ever done a ‘burpee’, a heinous invention that Grimalkin loved, you’d realize how hellish it was doing the motion.
Let alone with a hundred pounds on your shoulders. His legs were already water, but the Sinew Magus was pushing him beyond his limits.
“You can rest on your way back to Salazsar, Diplomat Nerul! If you can move, I haven’t worked you enough! Come on!”
“I…can’t…”
“You can! Scream if you must. One more rep!”
“One more rep! One more rep!”
The crowd was way too supportive. Highly muscular men—and women—were shouting at Nerul, pumping their fists. It was really hard not to give it a shot.
His stomach hurt. His muscles were cramping. He’d feared falling over, but since Grimalkin would catch him, Nerul tried. He pushed.
Veins bulged under his scales. His face, already crimson, turned a shade darker. He strained as he came down—down—his legs wavered.
“All the way down! Come on! Up! Up! Get up like your life depends on it, Nerul! Push! Push!”
Grimalkin was howling like the training instructor from Rhir. Everyone was yelling, and Nerul thought of Ilvriss.
Push damnit—
He pushed.
He pushed with all his might.
He strained—and then felt it happen. He gasped.
Oh no—
The sound that echoed in the gymnasium, just below the cheering and sudden silence, was low. Deep.
It was like…frblgh. With the last bit being so—familiar to many that they went silent. Nerul’s shaking legs went still a moment. He began to sit down, and Grimalkin caught the bar one-handed.
He had fallen silent. The cheering students had fallen silent. At his station, Lord Mireden Raithland paused. He sniffed the air, glanced up, and muttered.
“Ah. That’s unfortunate.”
Nerul Gemscale sat there as he filled his underpants with what he could only, in the most tactful way possible, describe as his own feces.
When one pushed—especially if they’d been in a coach for a long time with an unfamiliar diet—
Things could come out. In the silence, Magus Grimalkin inhaled, regretted it, and spoke.
“[Cleanse]. Diplomat—”
“I believe that’s my cue. Excuse me.”
Nerul leapt to his feet. He grabbed around. Yanked up a towel, swiped at—looked around.
“Restroom?”
They pointed. He ran. It did not have a bidet. But it did flush, so Nerul watched the pants swirl around in the silence, grimly, until someone knocked and passed him a spare pair. He took them. Finished cleaning his pants and put them in his bag of holding. Excused himself.
It was amazing, really. Nerul checked himself into some temporary apartments and lay down. But he didn’t sleep at once.
He’d done a lot of humiliating things in the name of Salazsar and diplomacy. But umbral throning oneself? That…not even [Diplomats] put that in their arsenal.
 
——
 
The next day, Nerul Gemscale didn’t want to show his face outside. He knew the incident—probably—wasn’t the talk of Pallass.
He knew that. But he also knew that it had to have been the talk of Grimalkin’s Gymnasium. It couldn’t not be.
Presumably, accidents like that did happen. Just not with everyone watching. Even so, Nerul had a workout hoodie on and covering his head, and he breathed in and out for a good eight minutes.
Then?
He pushed the double glass doors open and walked in.
“Sinew Magus. My underwear is enchanted this time. I believe I owe you…one rep?”
Sinew Magus Grimalkin of Pallass turned. Nerul Gemscale’s voice was loud, and everyone regarded him. Several students nearly dropped their weights. Their heads rose. Jaws dropped.
The word ‘gape’ had been employed in regards to expressions many-a-time where The Wandering Inn was concerned. Perhaps too much. The slack-jawed fall of a mouth. The credulous opening by which an Ashfire Bee could fly in and out of your expression—it was too easy to say that.
But today, as Nerul walked into the gymnasium he had just shat himself in—that truly was the expression. Mind-boggled, dumbfounded shock.
Even Sinew Magus Grimalkin’s brows rose. But Nerul Gemscale just nodded at him. His jaw was set so hard his teeth were grinding. He was bright red.
But he had to do this, and he’d just embarrassed himself to the utmost. He might as well see it to the end. No one spoke, so Nerul stomped over to one of the workout machines.
“I think I start with the bench press? If someone can spot me…”
He was sliding himself down, taking deep breaths, hoping they’d stop staring after ten minutes, when Grimalkin broke the silence. The Drake glanced around, eyed Nerul, and then brought his hands together.
The clap of sound was, predictably, large as he was. Nerul jumped. Then he saw Grimalkin do it again.
The Drake did it a third time before Nerul realized he was actually applauding. The slow-clap was not something Erin had brought to this world. But Grimalkin performed it now, and then his Dullahan apprentice joined in. The rest of the students joined as well, and then the other people in the gymnasium joined in, whether they knew what this was actually about or not.
But Grimalkin was just nodding his head up and down. Nerul stared at him, glaring, but the Sinew Magus eyed his students.
They turned back to him, and he cleared his throat. This was an appropriate time, wasn’t it? He got an almost-imperceptible nod from his best student, the Dullahan, Giren. So Grimalkin inhaled, then bellowed.
“TESTICLES.”
Nerul stared at Grimalkin. But the Sinew Magus made a fist and actually did a hop. He punched at the air, then he was striding over.
“THIS IS WHAT I WANT TO SEE. This Drake has more will, more gonads than any of you! This is what I am talking about! Willpower! He could have stayed away. But Diplomat Nerul walked back in, and he is not going to give up! This Drake is going to go the distance! ”
“Alright, Sinew Magus. There’s no need for—”
Nerul began, but the Sinew Magus was clapping again.
“Diplomat, you have my utmost respect—which I do not convey on many beings in this world. If Erin Solstice had a shred of your testicles, she’d have crushed the Bloodtear Pirates’ heads with her bare hands instead of just being mobile enough to dodge them!”
“If she had a shred of any testicles I think she’d be quite unhappy, Sinew Magus—come on now, let’s not go overboard—”
“Double the intensity! I believe this Drake can break our record for day-improvement!”
The Sinew Magus was shouting, and the apprentices were racing for restorative tonics and poultices. Nerul held up his claws.
“Okay, I don’t need to break records—I am riding back tonight. Sinew Magus—hello?”
But he did feel a bit gratified.

Winning the approval of a gymnasium of workout fanatics and going down in history—albeit as a man who’d umbral throned himself and come back in to keep pushing—was nice.
People might not have known about Chief Diplomat Nerul of Salazsar before, for all his fancy titles and rank—but among a certain community, he became a legend. He had…mixed feelings about that.
After passing out after the sixth hour of working out, Diplomat Nerul received the cheers of a gymnasium and was carried to a bed like a hero.
And he heard another voice that made it actually mostly worth it.
 
[Chief Diplomat of Bijou Splendor Level 48!]
[Skill – Bodily Charisma Obtained!]
[Skill – Improved Workout Gains Obtained!]
[Skill – Negotiations: Umbral Curse Obtained!]
 
[Skill – Reputation: Workout Story Obtained!]
