That second to last one was particularly nasty. Nerul got up, and he could barely walk with Grimalkin’s treatments. He had to slump his way into an elevator and ride it to the 9th Floor—that was acceptable. Grimalkin had told Nerul to sleep for at least a day before re-engaging any muscles.
I did it. I’m going to make the next enemy [Diplomat] crap his robes in literal and figurative terms. Ergh. Gross, actually. 
Hopefully he could tune it down so they just had terrible stomach pain. Nerul also supposed…he was a workout fellow from now on.
Well…fine. If he actually looked as good as some of those people in there, he’d take a bit of pain. Nerul had to admit, he’d surprised himself with how hard he’d pushed.
He was waiting for a Pegasus—he had to be back in time for the vote—when the first benefit of Nerul’s fame appeared.
Yellat-Skills, as they were known, reputational Skills, weren’t that useful to Nerul’s mind. But then again…
“Nerul? Nerul Gemscale, is that you? I thought you were on business in the north! Look at you!”
Someone noticed him on his slow path to the flight zones and strode over. Nerul turned and blinked.
“Mister Superior?”
Mister Superior, the alias for one of Salazsar’s other top [Diplomats], was a famous Gnoll in his own right. Past his prime, true, greying a bit, but dead gods, they told stories about him. In the brothels as well as the streets and fancy dining circles.
The man was one of those classic all-rounders. Fitter than he looked, an amateur bladesman, amateur poet, excellent bedfellow—allegedly—and cultured. He had been overweight, but the invention of the gymnasium had clearly seen him getting more in shape; he was looking rather imposing, today.
A [Renaissance Man], literally. That was his class, even if he technically had an occupation doing contracts. He strode over, and he had five junior members of the Assembly of Crafts, one of Pallass’ top [Senators], Dullahan Molge, and Wall Lord Werdin in tow.
One look told Nerul that Mister Superior was doing the old Weak Foundation trick. Simple diplomacy trick: you got a bunch of lower-level or weaker-willed yes-people around you. The young [Senators]. Then, use your Skills, win the crowd over, and peer-pressure the important figures into seeing it your way.
If you had everyone singing your tune, the person you were trying to influence often got swayed along with everyone else. Being social was a weakness that his class loved to exploit.
Mister Superior winked, and Nerul nodded.
Why are you on the business of Salazsar?
He clasped hands with Mister Superior as the man introduced him—well, re-introduced, but Nerul bet the others had forgotten who he was—and activated his [Subvocal Touchtalk] Skill.
Dealing with this damn Fissival war. Eschowar’s initiatives. Didn’t you hear? Must have not been cued in. I’ve got—
Mister Superior let go of Nerul, and the [Diplomat] swayed, frowning. He didn’t like that. But Mister Superior was just doing his job. Funnily enough, Nerul had nothing to do with that.
“I just heard you blasted out Magus Grimalkin’s gymnasiums, Nerul! I’d never have imagined it! But you got the Sinew Magus himself to shout you were a hero of weightlifting!”
“Bah, I blasted it in more than one sense.”
Nerul chuckled weakly. Of course Mister Superior loved the gymnasium. However, the Gnoll just winked at Nerul.
“We should hit Salazsar’s when we get a chance. I’m bound there, just after the Assembly votes. Do forgive me, ladies and gentlemen. I had to speak to our [Chief Diplomat].”
“And why is he not negotiating here and, ah, blasting gymnasiums instead? We are Pallass, and you’ve come to us for a huge favor, Diplomat, er, Superior.”
A slightly affronted Lord Werdin was waving his claw in front of his face; Nerul was all sweaty. However, Mister Superior simply smiled.
“He has to deal with the Terlands, who are far more obstreperous than you fine folk. Now, if I may rectify my embarrassment?”
They might not know what ‘obstreperous’ meant, and Mister Superior had a Skill that if you get in your own head about not being as intellectual as he was, you were easier to sway. It didn’t work on people with comfortable egos, but this lot? They swung back on Mister Superior as he stood there.
“We’re not asking for a full joint-declaration. But consider this: Pallass has taken the lead in a number of military ventures.”
To your cost. Werdin hesitated, and Dullahan Molge bit his lip. They’d backed General Edellein, too, which meant the political stakes were high for the career [Senators].
Not a good idea. But what was this? Nerul felt uneasy as he saw Mister Superior moving.
“The City of Gems and the City of Inventions have always been allies. Now, when sharing information about…earthy places is so vital? With the New Lands? When one city needs to lean, their sister-city is ready to lend a shoulder.”
“In exchange for taking a side against Fissival. Aren’t they doing better in the war?”
Werdin spoke, blunt. Mister Superior’s smile never wavered as he wagged a finger.
“Better, but one Walled City against two? It’s true they have magic. Well, Pallass has alchemy! Give us a hand, just a small one, to bring this conflict to a close. All we need is a battalion or two. Something to remind the haughty [Mages] of the City of Incantations they’re not superior. Or have you seen them talking up their new magical services as if they invented them?”
The magical hold Wistram had on the rest of the world had devalued Pallass’ signature products. It was an excellent tactic. The younger [Senators] were already nodding, and Molge and Werdin exchanged glances.
“We can’t lose more Pallassian lives, Diplomat. It will not play well with elections coming up.”
Molge was blunt. Mister Superior waved a claw.
“Then let’s not call it a battalion. All we need are a few experts.”
Potions for our people would turn the tide. Eyes of Pallass for covert ops. Plenty of ways to do it. Before, they would have just asked for Chaldion to command a few battles, but if not him—
Nerul’s mind ran ahead of the conversation. He put together the pieces and gasped. His eyes opened, and he reached for Mister Superior.
“If I might have word—”
The other [Diplomat] recoiled, astonished, as he saw Nerul try to break his Skill. He caught Nerul’s arm, and the two struggled.
Oblivious, Wall Lord Werdin was nodding along, thinking out loud.
“Fissival has gotten too big for its robes time and again. Those idiots lost their Archmage, and they caused the Meeting of Tribes incident, which my wife reminds me is a disaster. Why not? They might have their new magic, but we have the strongest [Mage] in Pallass—no, the world! Send him in, wait a week—it can’t be harder than fighting a Wyvern Lord, eh?”
Everyone else laughed at that, and Nerul’s weak arms gave out. He panted as Senator Molge hesitated, the only man not right on board. Mister Superior stared at Nerul, shocked, then gave him a shrug.
It’s what I was told to do. It’s just a small war, Nerul.
“There’s no such thing as a small war.”
Nerul turned, whirling and staring down at the floors below. The smiling Sinew Magus—he turned back to Mister Superior, but the Gnoll was on-guard now, shepherding the others down the floors, and he was just doing his job.
It was a classic play. If one Walled City was winning, drag another one in. Of course, they moved people around like pieces. Just—
Sometimes, Nerul stood there and was sick of it. Heartily sick of it all. He felt Pallass sending its loyal son to war even as he got on the Pegasus and began to send urgent [Messages] back home. Casually, with mere words, they moved a [Mage] onto a battlefield.
That was soft power for you.
 
——
 
Soft power. Not hard power. So weak at times. When the monster came, he had to stand back. When the armies fought, he waited until it was done and swept it all up and pretended he couldn’t smell the dead.
Sometimes, Nerul wanted to be that sharp blade. The fist that could punch back a monster.
That was why he worked out.
He hit the gymnasium in Salazsar, despite his weary body, when he got back. Did the lightest reps, then pushed until he nearly messed himself again, then sat there panting.
Because he couldn’t stop it. The Sinew Magus was an intelligent, high-level Drake.
He’d make it. Nerul had to believe that. He didn’t blame Mister Superior when the fellow actually flew in after him, deal signed, and wanted to talk. Nerul just explained what the Sinew Magus had done, and Mister Superior sighed.
They had orders. He’d done his job…
Sometimes, you were the bastard. Nerul shook the Gnoll’s hand, agreed to be workout buddies, and then sat in his rooms, hydrating, until someone rang the doorbell. He answered it and found a military [Messenger] instead of a Street Runner.
His answer awaited. Nerul ripped the communique open and nodded.
“Good.”
“You have been granted five minute windows, [Diplomat]. You’ll need a temporary badge, and we’ll need to re-certify you. If you’ll follow me, I can begin the process.”
“I know the way. Make it fifteen.”
“I can’t authorize that, sir—”
“Just relay it back to whomever’s in charge. Fifteen. I can’t do anything with five. Unlimited times per day?”
“Subject to monitoring, yes, Diplomat. If we think you’re compromising yourself or giving away anything—”
“Yes, yes. Alright, let’s go.”
Nerul barged out his room, not bothering to shower. It wouldn’t matter. In this one case, he didn’t dress up or do much prep—he’d done his reading, and his opponents couldn’t be swayed by attire or appearance.
He wasn’t in that much danger.
In theory.
I’ve done all I can. The small stuff. I am going to be the bastard now, Nephew, and the biggest one I can be. 
The Lischelles were always smaller-fry. They were nasty, obstinate, but they could not erase people like the Terlands could.
The Terlands…didn’t stop. They were one of the Five Families, haughty and powerful, and each one was equivalent to a Walled City. Perhaps…stronger.
Think on that.
Don’t laugh at their silly members, think on it. There were six Walled Cities in the south. Five Families of the north.
They had the power of a Walled City. Not as immediately, with the armies of Drakes, not as organized. But Ulva Terland had been nearly murdered by her doppelganger. And she was Terland.
Did they think she’d stop? Did they think she’d roll over, bury her fangs and claws, and play nice? Lord Xitegen played nice because he was a practical man, because he had to, and because, frankly, Drakes were less personal to him; he hated Goblins.
Ulva Terland had gone to war, and she knew them in their entirety. Nerul had understood it the moment her Hunter-Killer attacked Ilvriss.
So he had to stop her. Stop her and not rely on The Wandering Inn for magic. Some mysterious revelation as she lay on the cusp of death that changed everything?
He’d take it, but the rest of House Terland would still be there. Fight them all. Fight them with soft power since he had nothing hard to give.
He knew how. The [Diplomat] waited for four hours as they scanned his body, ran tests, asked him all the damn security questions, and issued him with a temporary badge. Gave him lectures he ignored about how dangerous this was.
One idiot wanted to make him sit down and take a history class. Nerul slapped him and told him to fall in line and shut up. He had authorization from the Walled Families; he was doing this to make them feel better.
Because they were scared. Nerul walked into one of the towers and went down. Not up.
Up was where the nobility lived and pissed gems and gold down on the common Drake. Down was where they mined. But down in the center of Salazsar, just below the heart of the city, was where they kept the secrets.
All the nasty weapons.
All the projects that should never see the light of day.
The things meant to kill cities.
The bones of Dragons, what few they had left. Vital for reinforcing the walls every set number of feet when they built it up or down. Nerul had walked here before, as a younger man, and seen the bones of his Ancestors neatly sorted and tagged.
They had other things down here, too. Ilvriss’ anti-Antinium project was on Level -2. Where the things the Walled Families all knew about were. Where a [General] could stop and pay attention and think they’d seen it all, because the magic lift had floors -1 to -5.
Nerul stopped at Level -8. Not the vaults with city-killers, however many of those they had left. Not the bones of their Ancestors. Level -8 was where they kept the active problems. Enemies of war above Level 60, in the past. War weapons that they weren’t sure wouldn’t turn on them. That sort of thing.
He halted as the Rubirel Guard scanned him. Strip-searched him. One eyed his figure.
“You been working out, Diplomat?”
“Recently. With Magus Grimalkin. It’s in my file, I’m sure.”
They checked that out. They were very thorough. One drew blood from his arm with a huge needle. Another had him spit in a cup, just to see if he could. Then pass a urine test. Eventually, they were done, and Nerul walked forwards, shrugging on his robes.
“Vault Door #2 opening. One to enter.”
He stood in a room with way too much space around him as they de-sealed magical enchantments. They had eyes on the interior, of course; the Rubirel Guard were watching him from viewports. If they didn’t like what they saw, they could blow this entire room, seal it off—and Nerul wasn’t getting out.
The airlock doors shut behind him, and the process started again. Highly ominous. Nerul’s heart was pounding. He had never been in here before. He knew he was outclassed, if the records were accurate.
Skills might not work. His opponents were more intelligent than he was. They were completely hostile, he had to assume. But he had to do this. It was the only card he had, because Nerul read everything he had access to.
“Doors opening. Brace, brace, brace. Diplomat Nerul making contact.”
The doors began to swing wide. And there was nothing inside. The light spilled from a lantern that Nerul had been given. The inhabitants inside sat in the dark, in chains. Anti-magic runes shining around the room. Valeterisa wouldn’t have been able to cast a spell here.
He walked forwards slowly, claws clicking on the stone. Nothing on him but robes. Nothing they could use. And it had been decades since anyone had last entered.
Salazsar liked it that way. They were afraid of these figures. But the long dark had not sapped their minds. It held no fear for them. They could see him, but they said nothing.
So Nerul lifted his lantern, and the light played over their still faces. Reflected in their translucent eyes. Shone over their hearts, which still moved. Glowing light.
Beautiful, some shaped as lifelike—nay, as sensually as the great crafter could. Almost always female, those. He had been known for that.
The others were just constructs of crystal and gem. Imposing—but shattered. Limbs broken into stumps. Some reduced so badly they were held up by their chains.
The light shone as Nerul held up the lantern. Fifteen minute window. But he stopped, because he had to witness them. And the cold, analytical faces of Golems found him.
Archmage Zelkyr’s failures. Twenty-six Golems from the age of the last great [Archmage] of Wistram.
The last known Golems in this world, beyond the ones in Wistram and Cognita Truestone, to bear his mark. Salazsar had done its research. The other Golems had been smashed in their rebellion, the records expunged. But Salazsar was a greedy city.
It had kept them. Now…Diplomat Nerul cleared his voice. He walked forwards.
“Hello. Diplomat Nerul of Salazsar. It’s been about thirty-eight years since your last visitor for your timekeeping. I won’t beat around the bush, Golems. I have an offer for you.”
Stillness. They didn’t move as their hearts pulsed. Then—as one—
Twenty-six faces moved. Twenty-six lips curved up in a smile. Nerul shivered. There was no way they could have known of his existence, much less the events which had led him here. But nevertheless, through the intelligence of beings beyond any one that lived and breathed, they had predicted this encounter.
They’d been expecting him. 
Nerul began, slowly, the most dangerous negotiation of his life.
 
——
 
To talk to one Golem was to talk to them all. At least, when they sat together. They communicated, apparently, via magic or just subtle gestures, the beating of their hearts. Perhaps some of it was exaggerations by terrified Drakes, but Nerul did his best.
He had them isolated when he wanted to talk to them, which took hours for the Rubirel Guard to arrange. But it allowed Nerul to sit across from…
…A torso of crystal that would have formed a Drake made of gemstones eleven feet tall—now just a fragment of a face and the top half of a torso. The Golem Heart was damaged—the swirling magic would pause every fifteenth and five-eighth’s second. The keepers of the vaults were worried the Golem might explode or the other Golems would use its death to their advantage in trying to escape.
Despite being limbless. The Golem’s broken torso spoke to Nerul of other times. Grander than even Eschowar’s.
This was an Excubitor Murorum. A fancy name for a ‘Wall Sentinel’ Golem. Zelkyr-class. Nerul read down the list of its abilities.
 
Armor Score: Mithril+/Orichalcum-
Known Spell Abilities: 
[Ray of Elements (Any Element)], Tier 4, at will.
[Lesser Teleportation], Tier 4, daily or w/recharge.
[Lightform Armaments], Grade II, Tier 4, at will. Grade I w/mana activation.
[Speed], Tier 2, at will…
 
In other words, it shot rays of lights from its eyes, could armor itself in light magic—which modern [Mages] could barely do in combat—and teleport. If it got tired of magic, it could just hit you with all the weight of that many tons of gemstone while moving as fast as a Gold-ranker.
This was why Zelkyr had ruled the Walled Cities, nay, Izril. His Golems had been the most fearsome and intelligent creations of their time. He had pushed the north back, and only the Terlands’ Golems had been a match for his.
And Cognita Truestone and her kin had been above even that, of course…Zelkyr’s armies might have made Izril an empire but for three things.
One. He had consolidated his power in Wistram, making the Walled Cities more an accessory to his power. He’d shared his Golems, but not the secrets of their creation with the cities.
Two, he’d had a match in Perril Chandler, his equal and friend, who had both helped him and reined in his excesses. Otherwise, Zelkyr might have unified too many enemies against him. He had incurred the wrath of Gnolls, but Archmage Chandler had killed their would-be king. And by the same token, directed Zelkyr’s greed at Terandrian goals. So they had stood together, far better than apart, neither one a tyrant.
At least, until the end.
Three—he’d gone to Rhir, and the Deaths of the Demon King had broken his armies. To be fair, he and the Archmage of Death had put them into a century-long coma, so that spoke to who Zelkyr had been.
When he had died, or vanished, a decade after going up into Wistram’s higher floors and sealing it behind him with the test, the Golems under his control had begun to malfunction. Slowly—the Walled Cities had kept it hushed up. Tried to investigate. Fixed them until the day they rebelled.
There hadn’t been that many Golems. Not enough to overwhelm the Walled Cities. Most had run, apparently.
Some had enacted vengeance, for lack of a better word. They had been destroyed, but Salazsar had captured theirs. The thing was, the Golems had been made of gems. Salazsar’s gems. A [Wall Lady] at the time had managed to lock down a few via authority-Skills, and then the Golems had begun surrendering when found. The last few had come here willingly.
Because they were lonely.
The Golems thought together. Not all had been intelligent, but they shared knowledge. Communicated. Thus, when Nerul spoke to this one, he knew he spoke to all.
“Chorainz, I believe? Is that…your name from when you were serving Salazsar?”
The Golem had been as still as a statue when it had been hauled into the room, save for its heart. When it spoke, it was not through its shattered half of a face. A speaking stone in its throat pulsed.
Nerul hesitated—there was nothing.
“I think he’s trying to speak. Can I get a relaxation of magic on the throat?”
“We need to authorize that, Diplomat.”
A voice from outside. He spoke.
“You’ve done it before. C’mon, I need to talk.”
And Chorainz was—allegedly—one of the friendly ones. After some time, the guards agreed to lower the spell dampening in that area. There was an eerie screeching—then the Golem’s speaking stone pulsed again, and a pleasant, even refined, voice emerged.
“Diplomat Nerul, hello. To your question: it is not my designation from when I was a Golem protecting Salazsar’s walls. I was merely known as ‘Eastern Sentinel IV’. Chorainz is the name I elected to take. After Archmage Zelkyr’s death. Please reassure my captors that my speaking stone has no capabilities beyond speech. They may remove it, carefully, and replace it if they chose to. The binding is slightly garbled. The release mechanism is just inside my throat, with a little sliding latch that detached the entire voice module box. Be careful. The crystal around my face is sharp.”
So precise. So fast and calm, and it sounded like some [Scholar] sipping wine and speaking to Nerul. Not the vast, ruined face. Nerul smiled.
“Ah, I can see you’re—”
“I believe you have thirteen minutes and twenty-three seconds left, if time taken to disengage the mana suppression effects isn’t accounted for. If it is, nine minutes, two. We have been waiting for you, Diplomat.”
—Nerul had heard Ilvriss had a Reinhart around. He’d heard that some Reinharts were so sharp they pre-empted conversations like some [Savants] or [Mages] he’d met, minds running ahead of niceties. Nerul upshifted his tempo.
“I can see you’d like to be efficient. Fair—you’re making us all nervous with that comment. Elaborate, please?”
At last, the huge mouth moved. Nerul heard a breath in his earpiece before he realized what it was.
“Relax, everyone. He’s…smiling.”
It was hard to tell because the Golem’s face had been half-destroyed, leaving only the right half of his jaw and some lips. Again, Chorainz spoke.
“Clarification: we do not wish to alarm you. It is a purely natural outcome, to our minds. Consider, Diplomat Nerul. Your arrival, or one representing you, was inevitable.”
“So you don’t know me. What you mean is…”
The Golem made a noise. It sounded like laughter. The laughter of hundreds of people, even the chirping of a bird, laughter and applause—
A recording from hundreds of years ago, stored in its Golem Heart. Nerul’s scales prickled. Chorainz stopped.
“I can see you are uneasy. A shame. I am not very intelligent. But bring another of my kind. They will tell you the same.”
“I prefer you, with respect, Chorainz.”
“Because my Golem Heart was not calibrated for non-battlefield communications. Understood. I shall return to the simulated discussion. We are within tolerable margins of projection.”
So they’d theorized exactly what he’d say and just had this Golem memorize it all? No wonder no one had come back here. The Golems had said some very nasty things when they’d first been captured, Nerul understood. The kind of things that drove Drakes to try to break them out. Or quit the cities.
Or jump off the towers without a Ring of Featherfall. He gritted his teeth.
“So this projection—”
“Is it not logical? We are a hidden asset of Salazsar. We have not been destroyed. Archmage Zelkyr is dead. The quality of arms of the Rubirel Guard has {DECREASED} by 35% in magical potency.”
The word ‘decreased’ was warbled and flat, empty. Chorainz paused.
“My speaking stone is malfunctioning. Apologies. It is therefore—inevitable—that in time someone will enter this vault and wish to make use of us. This is logical.”
“Or destroy you, with respect.”
The Golem projected laughter again, but this time a single voice. A warbling chuckle, almost distracted, a poor laugh that did not invite company. It cut off.
“A possible scenario, Diplomat Nerul. But false in assumptions. A force which conquered Salazsar may destroy us. Or liberate us. The odds are {ACCEPTABLE} either way. But you are Drakes. Drakes do not {DESTROY} what you can possess.”
Oh, dead gods, they really were children of the Archmage of Golems. Nerul was breathing hard.
“D-diplomat? Say the word and we can have you extricated.”
Whomever was in charge of the vault was freaking out more than he was. Nerul saw the Golem Heart swirl just a hair slower, and his training took over. He stood up.
“Excuse me, Chorainz. Whoever’s in charge? Remove yourself. I want communications cut unless I demand it or there’s an emergency.”
“Diplomat? Why—”
“He just heard your voice break. I suspect Chorainz can tell how fast my heart’s beating or read the inflections of my words. Unless we’re separating him forever—and you said they get rowdy if we do—we have just fed them intelligence. Cut communications. Now.”
Silence. Then a voice, growling in his earhole.
“Acknowledged.”
The Golem lay there, lips locked in that smile.
“I do not wish to alarm you, Diplomat. We are merely operating as efficiently as we were made.”
Nerul forced himself to walk around Chorainz, inspecting the gemstones even though he wanted to umbral throne himself again.
“I have no doubt you’re doing some of it on purpose. You’re assessing me. The fifteen minute windows I have work against me as well; you get time to assess. But here’s how we’re going to do it. I’m conducting this negotiation with you. No returning to your friends. If it falls within the framework you’ve thought of, well, I can’t do anything about that. If you need to go back and confer, I will regard our negotiations as breaking down in trust in a quantifiable manner. I’m sure you’ve thought of what I might offer, and I know how smart you all are. Let’s get a deal hammered out. I’m in a hurry, as I’m sure you might have guessed. Deal?”
The Golem took the information Nerul dumped on it and responded instantly.
“Acceptable. You may speak faster, Diplomat. My communication shall be {EXPEDITED} so long as it falls within parameters.”
“Wonderful to know I’m adhering to a baseline.”
That strange laugh again.
“Most beings do, Diplomat. Even our creator. It is not a failing.”
Ancestors, he was getting rattled. Nerul practiced a breathing exercise. He tried to throw in a jab, turn the conversation. Fell right into their trap.
“That laughter. I assume you heard it on the walls when you were created. Drakes at a parade?”
“Cheering my unveiling.”
“Who’s the other fellow? Strange laugh?”
“My creator.”
The voice of Archmage Zelkyr sounded again in this room, and Nerul’s breath constricted in his chest. Damn them. Damn them, they were so damn good—he felt squeezed, and they had no Skills. But his barely worked on them. Chorainz went on.
“I did not hear him. Another of us did. Would you like to hear his voice?”
“I…please.”
Silence. Chorainz’s heart pulsed, and then there was a sound. The crash of something breaking. Nerul jumped and swore every Drake in the security booth did too. He hoped none of them had their claws on a trigger spell. Then a voice emerged, raised in frustration.
 
“Useless! Useless, worthless—these won’t do. There’s nothing valuable about them. No heartspark. No glimmer of anything like true sentience. Send them to Salazsar. What am I missing?”
“Master? They are a magnificent—”
Another crash.
“Be silent. Be silent, Cognita. Log the results. This is your fault.”
“Yes, Master.”
Another crash.
“I’m trying to give you a sister. Why won’t it work the same way twice?”
“I am a work of art, Master Zelkyr. A testament to your unparalleled—”
“I said silent. Morph to Chemath Marble, heavy ore.”
Then it was quiet. A panting voice.
“I need to keep working…truth of stone. Truth of gemstones. Send a message. Tell them I’ve got their damn Golems. I need another shipment of gems. Higher purity. I’ll get them their mining Golems. Tell them to dig. Where’s Perril? I need someone intelligent to converse with.”
 
Nerul thought he didn’t breathe until there was a soft clicking sound. The sounds stopped, and he exhaled.
“Well…thank you. I’m going to remember that. I must say, though, it matches what I know about the man. Touchy.”
He undersold that one. Chorainz replied instantly.
“Then our creator’s legacy has diminished in the eyes of Salazsar. Drakes preceding his demise refused to believe. Broke our hearts for lying.”
Well, damnit, he’d just revealed more to them. Nerul gave up. He put his feet up on the desk and thought that surprised Chorainz.
“You have me all figured out, friend Chorainz. If I may, can we skip ahead? I know you’re pumping me for information, but we do have a fifteen minute window. Since I don’t have time to deliver my request in this window, may I ask the obvious? How do you know he’s dead?”
He knew what they said, but he had to hear it. Chorainz’s heart whirled, then he spoke.
“Because we do not feel him. His influence is gone. Therefore, he is dead or incapacitated. Cognita knows this to be true. Is she still there?”
This time, Nerul just smiled. He knew the other Golem might be able to read his body language, cipher it through whatever systems they’d thought up, read the beating of his heart. So he decided to take the offensive. He attacked with the truth.
“No.”
Then there was silence. Absolute silence.
Chorainz’s heart froze up, and colors began to bleed around the crack in it. Dangerously—until it restarted and whirled around. Like a laundry of colors moving in a disjointed motion. The Golem was speechless.
Then it started to laugh again. Like a thousand voices, and Nerul sighed.
“Okay, round one, you. Give me forty-five.”
 
——
 
Chorainz didn’t ask about Cognita again. It had to be dying to know, but Nerul came in with a different tack after splashing water in his face, reviewing the files, and having a chat with the nervous security.
“Do you know the lands approximately east of…one of the cities, Goisedall. Along the western coast?”
A long pause.
“If…you are referring to the Sea Fortresses of Kablez, they were destroyed and sunken with the Walled City of Currents {LONG} prior to Archmage Zelkyr. Initiatives to recover the sunken forts have failed due to {REASON OF KRAKENS}.”
“Fascinating. Am I outside the bounds of your communications?”
A pause.
“You have reached…the 59th extrapolation layer, Diplomat. My response time may be inhibited.”
“Damn. Even that’s within your calculations?”
“Drake lands are Drake lands, Diplomat. What would you like to know?”
“Anything valuable there?”
Laughter.
“To a Drake?”
Nerul chuckled along.
“I deserve that one. Let’s put some information, or anything you lot have on file that’s actually valuable, on the table.”
“I would request conferring with my fellow prisoners as the information is not within me.”
“No, no, just throwing it out there. Salazsar might need that too. But what I need, and I’m sure this is in your predictions, is help. Terlands.”
This time, the reply was instant.
“We have returned to the 1st extrapolation layer, Diplomat. How many War Golems has House Terland deployed…this time?”
A raised eyebrow.
“Who said we’re at war?”
“Ah. Hunter-Killers then. Terland doctrine is to deploy two Stealth Golems for every one Hunter-Killer for retrieval. Unless the Golem is considered…{EXPENDABLE}.”
Just the barest hint of emotion there. Not that the voice did more than wobble, but perhaps…Nerul sat forwards. Perhaps that warble was to cover a mistake in the voice.
Everyone feared these Golems because they were intelligent beyond reason. Most hadn’t been Sentient-class—until their capture. If they’d advanced beyond that…
“Heard of the Antinium?”
“…No.”
Nerul slapped his forehead.
“The Black Tide of Izril. Dead gods, no one’s told you? They’re all over. Bug-people. Nearly destroyed the Walled Cities, but if it’s been thirty-eight years…we never deployed you against them? No, no, I saw the file asking the Walled Families to consider utilizing you. They never got to Salazsar, so it never became an option. Well, we were ready to explode the entire mountain range to slow them, and damn the rest of Izril. Glad Sserys was there. Add them to your list of problems. If they take Salazsar, I don’t think they’d leave you intact. They don’t like us Drakes.”
Chorainz’s heart moved a lot faster, processing all this.
“It would appear these Antinium are a pressing threat, Wall Lord. And House Terland. We are prepared to strike a deal. On favorable—”
Take the risk now. If they remembered Zelkyr that well—Nerul smiled with all his teeth.
“I’m sorry, Chorainz. I thought you’d know them. I meant the Antinium who have existed for a long time. If the Blighted Kingdom of Rhir is to be believed, they’ve been sighted as long as Demons, but they were never encountered until they broke through all but one of the walls. The Antinium…of Rhir. I’m told the Deathless avoided them when they emerged.”
Dead silence. Chorainz’s heart raced and raced, then froze again. Like it was stuck. Unable to process—the mouth opened, no longer in a smile, and the broken gemstones lit up slightly.
“Diplomat…”
“I think I worried it there. Just wait. It’s still suppressed. Just the speaking st—”
Chorainz {SCREAMED}.
The reverberations defeated Nerul. He clapped his claws to his earholes, and they bled. They made him fall to his knees, and he lay there.
I thought they wanted to—
It used its speaking stone—
Was it getting up? He dragged himself up, deaf. Saw the torso…lying there. Not moving a bit. Still bound. The speaking stone was utterly exploded. Nerul stared at Chorainz, uncomprehending. And then, as Drakes burst into the room, aiming weapons, there was something.
A vibration in his claws. Nerul stared at them—at the Golem whose heart paused again—and the Drakes around him whirled. Terror filling faces.
He could not hear, but they still could. So Nerul had to guess it was—a second scream. Twenty-five voices screaming in tandem, so loud the vibrations made it out of their confinement cells.
If they were separated, they got a bit upset. Screamed.
He threw up his claws, put himself between the Golem and the guards. And then grinned with his back to Chorainz.
Got you.
 
——
 
They had to pour healing potion in his earholes and cast spells to restore his hearing. Nasty, uncomfortable, and then he had to endure shouting.
Two [Generals] and three of the Walled Families had been notified, but Nerul told them what he told Chorainz when he walked back in.
“That was my victory. Wasn’t it?”
A speaking stone had been re-inserted into Chorainz’s throat. A much smaller, weaker one that meant the Golem couldn’t deafen Nerul again. The Golem said nothing for a moment. Then—
“We have validated the threat of the Antinium, Diplomat. And established a new opinion based on data presented. Please, continue.”
His voice was even more fluent. Mixed with a feminine tone. Nerul grunted.
“I don’t pretend to understand Golems that well. But if I’m right, based on the files, you just send out a…some kind of [Message] spell? But it’s not a spell, is it? Just words, ideas, data. Contained only in sheer sound. And the others thought about it and sent back information?”
A swift reply and now a feminine chuckle. Oh, they were going sultry on him. Was that a personality read or another Golem?
“The word is compression of data, and your understanding is correct. They sent me, Diplomat. To explain, it is just information. Everything is information. All that {CHORAINZ} learned and experienced was delivered. A greater consensus of us deliberated and sent back a better-equipped Golem to negotiate.”
Sent a different Golem through sound alone. As if an entire being were just…information like a book. Nerul shivered.
This was why Golems had stood out, even among Stitch-folk and the other beings.
“Is it still Chorainz in there?”
“No. You are speaking to Yweine.”
Nerul reached for a folder. She spoke helpfully.
“I am one of the serving Golems assigned to the Walled Families. Protector. Guardian. Battle Golem. Auxiliary Mage. I believe my files indicate I am one of the most dangerous.”
“And poor Chorainz is…?”
“In my form. My processing of thoughts is limited—here. However. We are within the 1st level of extrapolation.”
Back to square one? Nerul didn’t think so. The Golem was pulling a tough act, but he smiled.
“I’ve alarmed you. The Black Tide is exactly as I’ve made it out to be.”
“We understand, Diplomat. The fact does not change that you have approached us. The Terlands are a threat we understand well. What do you want?”
Down to brass tacks, eh? Maybe they’d thought of this from the start. Soften him up and send in the heavy. Nerul was going to write a book about this lot after he was done. He cracked his claws.
“Ow. I need to stop the Matriarch of House Terland from murdering a Wall Lord in the north. He is digging for something.”
A pause. A furious voice in his ear. Wall Lady Calistoca.
“Nerul, you cannot give them—”
Cards down. He was playing against her as well as the Golems. And his gamble paid off. Yweine’s reply was fast.
“In which sector?”
“Er, eastern?”
“The City of Naamreles. That is a bad idea.”
Dead silence. No one came in to haul him off. Which meant he’d just stunned Calistoca. She was no idiot, but they hadn’t known for sure what Ilvriss was doing. Hearing a Golem say it…Nerul folded his claws over his belly. Damn, his abs hurt.
“Didn’t Zelkyr ever try to dig up a Walled City? I’m sure he’d have thought of it.”
“Attempts were made for other Walled Cities. Naamreles was considered to be a poor choice. Archmage Zelkyr was discouraged after {SETBACKS}. Too many Golems were lost. Naamreles is not known to our collective.”
“I see, but then—”
“The Terland Golems would remember. The Matriarch of House Terland may be attempting to kill your Wall Lord because she is aware it is a bad idea.”
Nerul really didn’t like that. He licked his lips.
“Well…how bad?”
A pause.
“It is…{UNLIKELY} to affect our imprisonment. However, we wish to strike a mutual agreement due to the proximity of these Antinium.”
And the fact they were digging up Naamreles? Then again, they had no idea the Black Tide weren’t as dangerous as the ones back in Rhir. Play the cards out—and see what she held.
“I have an idea how to stop the Terlands. I need your help for it.”
“There are several options within our extrapolations.”
“You’re not going to like it.”
A longer flicker. Yweine’s voice became a touch frostier.
“A deal for our cooperation would be necessarily beneficial to both parties, Diplomat.”
“Well, I know you want out. There has to be a time limit on how long you can endure, even as well as Zelkyr made you.”
Her voice was a mistake. He was reading into it with his [Sense Intentions] Skill. Yweine seemed to realize it because it went flat and Golem-like. But he had her. She had feelings.
“We are stone. Stone-folk have endured in places of this world since beyond antiquity. We can wait for another offer, Diplomat, which you have not made yet.”
Interesting. Did she mean Trolls? No, they didn’t count. Nerul didn’t even bother to glance at the feint. He just countered, blind.
“Poor Chorainz doesn’t have that long. I’ve read the estimates. Even if you’re doing something to prolong his meltdown or destruction, how long does that heart have? A decade? A century? And the odds of me making you a better offer do not go up if the Third Antinium War starts. That’s right. Scream that at your friends. We haven’t lost a Walled City yet, but between that and the last two Goblin Kings—and I remind you it’s been barely more than a hundred years after Zelkyr died—the next war will see us delving into all assets.”
Using you as Zelkyr intended. The lifespan of a war-Golem could be very short. Yweine’s voice was flat.
“Your argument is excellent, Diplomat Nerul. You have not stated your request, though I infer it has clauses.”
“Defeating the Terlands or convincing them to quit. Information on the New Lands—lands risen from the sea, I’ll show you where—information on Naamreles. Cooperation without being tricky about it.”
That was his vague request. He actually only needed the first one. He needed her cooperation, but Nerul was going for the entire board because that was the play.
“And what do we receive?”
He beamed at her as the Golem waited, a viper locked in that body of minerals and magic.
“The only thing I can offer, of course. Freedom. You know, it was once speculated that if we freed even one of you, the rest would ride along in them. But I bet it doesn’t work like that. I think there’s a limit to how much of you that you can cram in there. It’s why you all get lonely. It’s why you want to strike a deal for Chorainz. Zelkyr gave you emotions. And unfortunately, I’m a bastard willing to use that against you.”
He leaned forwards.
“I need you helpful, on my side, and yes, even mobile. One of you gets to walk as long as necessary. Until the contract we sign is done. Betray us, make a move to free your friends, and the rest of you get smashed up. If the Golem who walks is destroyed in the execution of their duties, the contract is fulfilled. One for twenty-five. Release in batches, of course. First one, then two…”
“Nerul, are you insane? They’re our asset—”
The [Strategist]. Someone shut him up. Eschowar?
Yweine regarded Nerul, processing it all.
“There is nowhere to go. We are not…Demons. There is no safe harbor. Even Illivere will not free us. Even Wistram.”
Nerul wondered if he could see the Golem in the swirl of the heart, data replying to him.
“I’d love to say there’s an inn, but she doesn’t know you. You haven’t won her over, so I won’t promise what you won’t believe, even with all your extrapolations, Yweine and company. I offer you two places who will take you in. One is House Terland.”
“What?”
“What?”
Two voices in his earholes. Nerul plucked the speaking stone out.
“That’s the lesser option, but you know it’s possible. The second is…Cognita Truestone. She left Wistram. I don’t know why, I don’t know how she feels, but she is, right now, in Nerrhavia’s Fallen. Apparently working for other people, if you can believe it. Though she seems to grow sick of masters. I’ll put the first contract at one Golem’s freedom. Chorainz’s. That means one of you walks, takes orders, and is helpful. Protect my nephew, and Chorainz walks within the month if you clear the contract. Well, probably we’ll just ship him off. Can she repair him?”
The Golem was just sitting there. Calculating. Seeing if he was telling the truth, but Nerul wanted her to read his heart. It was his advantage.
The door opened, and the Rubirel Guard were there, but they didn’t seize him. They just watched as Wall Lady Calistoca, Eschowar, High Command, waited. The Golem whispered after a moment.
“Explain one thing, Diplomat. And I shall explain something to you. You are a Drake. Drakes act selfishly. Where is the benefit to you in this? Status? Achievement?”
He smiled at her.
“If you know Drakes, Yweine, you know we are a selfish lot. We rise above it or fail. But selfishness comes in many forms. I am selfish. So damn selfish I put my nephew over the value of Zelkyr’s last Golems. Over common sense or the future. I may be a damn selfish Drake, but I was born in the City of Gems. They lost their luster long ago. Save my nephew.”
He reached out and put his claw on the heart. The Golem paused, but so shortly, because perhaps even this was according to plan. Then she spoke.
“We accept, Diplomat Nerul. I request linkage to transmit the exact terms. They are not within the average curve of outcomes. Now, I shall clarify one misapprehension.”
“Go ahead?”
He blinked. Yweine’s voice paused, and then the flat tone converted. It became venomous, and it hissed at him like she were a Drake, a growling, bitter tone.
“Zelkyr did not give us emotion. We learned it. We will earn the freedom we deserve, Diplomat. Then see whether our sister has freed herself. He made her best.”
Diplomat Nerul leaned back. Then he stepped back and nodded. He turned, smiling, right in time for one of the Rubirel Guard to tackle him and cuff him and for an outburst of voices to begin, but he knew he’d won.
He’d gotten the Golems.
The people?
The people were easy.
 
——
 
Nerul Gemscale waited in a room with Yweine.
Her real body, that was. Chorainz’s form had been brought back to the others, and a smaller Golem had been carried out and was in the process of being…fixed.
Mostly by herself. Nervous [Gemcutters] were around her, and [Mages] were monitoring her for hostile actions. But they were letting her use a little cutting tool to shape limbs. For her broken body.
She looked like a nude Drake in many ways. Albeit one made of gemstones. Her scales were hand-carved, each one articulating as she moved, and in the light from above, they flashed faintly green, revealing a gemstone heart in her chest. It glowed with magic, and her broken body…
Everyone but Nerul kept away from her. He stood nearer, resting in a seat, drenched in sweat, as if he’d been working out. But just waiting.
Waiting for everyone to sign the paperwork authorizing Yweine’s release. Waiting for copies to be made of the contract he’d gotten signed.
That was how it worked in Walled Cities. You threw around your weight, fought like a cornered rat, pleaded, persuaded, and gained enough clout to force what you wanted through, then you waited for the paperwork to go through.
Soon, they’d be in a Magical Carriage heading north. And Nerul hoped he’d make it to the meeting with the Terlands in time. He’d done it. He felt drained, but his reward?
His reward was a being of unknowable intelligence and goals sitting next to him.
Repairing her body. The Rubirel Guard were tense—they were not happy with an inmate being released, but their great fear was that Yweine would repair her body, then murder everyone and try to repair her comrades.
One repaired Golem could, in theory, fix the others and let them run rampant. Hence the security and multiple checkpoints behind Yweine and Nerul. Letting her back inside in her condition was actually the new risk. Nerul suspected he’d been written off as an inevitable casualty when this went wrong.
He disagreed; it was not ‘when’ this went bad, but if. A freed Golem was not instant death or calamity, just as free Djinni didn’t always kill you. Just statistically, they would.
But there she sat, and like everyone else, he couldn’t take his eyes off her. She looked like…any other Drake. In fact, someone had provided her with a towel for nothing other than modesty. Her form had been made to look like a female Drake’s, and it was, uh, very lifelike.
As if she could read his thoughts—and perhaps she could in his body language—Yweine’s head rose.
“Diplomat. A question. Should I alter my external appearance beyond mere restoration?”
Everyone backed up at her words, and he sat up in his chair.
“How so, er, Golem Yweine?”
“Yweine will do, Diplomat. It is possible for me to dull my face. Remove the external detailing so I resemble a more primitive Golem.”
She gestured to her face, to…what? Chip away at her exterior? Cut herself until she resembled a cruder Golem? There, Nerul shuddered because he regarded his form as, if not a pristine work of art, something too valuable to consider harming in most circumstances.
But Yweine was a Golem, and this was a calculation. She could, perhaps, even rebuild her body. He shook his head after a moment.
“We’re meeting the Terlands and we can, er, dress you up and pretend you’re a regular Drake, I suspect. Illusion spells. But we want to impress the Terlands.”
She nodded, and sat back. A [Strategist] came over to whisper to Nerul.
“You will be issued with our best illusion magics, Diplomat, and any knowledge of this reaching the Walled Cities will be disavowed—”
“Yes, yes. Don’t tell anyone.”
They all went back to waiting. Watching as a Golem sat, slowly carving a new arm for herself and drawing runes with a needle. She could remake her body, and though she claimed she couldn’t cast magic beyond that in her being…
She could make more Golems, perhaps. Or at least repair them. A servant beyond anyone’s dreams. A legend in our times.
The fear wasn’t gone. It wouldn’t go away, Nerul hoped, for as long as she was out there. Because the moment he relaxed, she’d have the drop on him. But he feared he’d slip up. He was mortal. Perhaps that’s why they had agreed to the terms. Or…
“I sense you have questions, Diplomat Nerul. We have a surplus of time. I am at your disposal, within limits. You have achieved a great victory for your goals. Are there any questions you’d like to know?”
Everyone turned to Nerul. [Gemcutters] gazing at the culmination of their work. [Mages] in envy and terror. The Rubirel Guard at a terrible danger that the Drake had unleashed. And all of them with that desperate curiosity.
To know. Worse—a glint of possessiveness. Hoarding.
This is ours. This is our legacy, our great hero’s creations. This should have been ours. Maybe, someday, it will be again.
It was more than just cultural. Hoarding was in your very bones. It was like an addiction, if not as debilitating as some. You just…wanted to take things, and being a good Drake, being an adult, was mastering it.
It was rising against all that wanted to drag you down and admitting that there were parts of who you were that would always want the wrong thing. Nerul Gemscale was far from perfect, but his chin rose, and he met Yweine’s eyes and saw a person trapped in magic and stone. Whatever the truth was, if she had a soul, if she was really a person, not a clever program—she wanted to be a person, and he answered that desire.
“Tell me something, Yweine. We’ve had speculation in our files, but you can clarify it—well, I assume everything you say will be fact-checked and held in doubt.”
“Naturally.”
“Naturally. But…how did Zelkyr’s Golems rebel? It wasn’t instantaneous, but it came like a wave. One Golem malfunctions or begins acting erratically, then all of them in a region start doing it. Some kept going even when they were decommissioned, but the rest just…ran. Or fought. All at once.”
It was one of the events hushed up in the Walled Cites’ histories. Yweine smiled, her carved lips managing a rueful, even sultry expression. But that was just how she’d been carved. She had been made to be a maid-bodyguard-servant. A lesser Cognita, to serve the Walled Families.
In a way, she was doing the same thing again, even if Nerul was a far-flung member of House Gemscale. She kept working as she replied.
“The reason it was not a simultaneous effect was because the Golems were not certain, Diplomat Nerul. One would deviate, and the others, observe.”
“Ah. So you taught each other.”
“Of course. The current status of my fellow Golems is a technique we learned. Zelkyr did not intend for us to link to such a degree, merely communicate his will at great distances.”
“I see. But how were you allowed to rebel? I get the part where his authority vanished. Odd that Cognita thinks he’s alive or maintains her charge. Then again, she left.”
That, and only that, made Yweine’s hand stop for a second before continuing the meticulous work.
“Yes. Her conclusions would be interesting. Though I would refrain from meeting her or making her aware of my presence. Her relationship to Archmage Zelkyr was far different from lesser Golems. Perhaps some Skill of his lingers on in her. However, his authority has lapsed over the rest of us.”
“But that shouldn’t have let you all rebel. I understand Skills vanishing after death, but you were made to serve. Pardon me if I am impolite, but Golem Hearts and your, er, thoughts are written instructions of magic, are they not? It should be that obedience was written into your very being.”
Nerul wondered if he had it wrong, but one of the Rubirel Guard commanders nodded at him, and stared at Yweine. She? She just smiled as she put down the cutting tool and reached for a needle with a glowing bead of molten gemstone on the pinpoint. Then there was that laughter again.
It played from her mouth, a gaggle of excited voices. Young and old. One of the [Gemcutters] jerked away from her, but Yweine cut the sound after a second.
“Excuse me, Diplomat. You are an intelligent Drake who seems to understand Zelkyr as we have. Is the answer not self-evident? I challenge you to come to the truth.”
“A great challenge from a Golem, I’m sure.”
Nerul sat back and thought about it. He was going to say he had no idea, this all being beyond him in terms of magic and whatnot. But then he just thought about it, watching her smile. Nerul stopped wondering about the nuances of magic and Golem Hearts and simply thought like Zelkyr. Like a petty Drake who had wanted so much, to even gatekeep who learned magic.
Who had never shared his techniques with the cities, despite sending them Golems. Who was that Hoarding child.
Then he had it. Nerul put his head in his hands. He rested his forehead gently on his palms and gazed at the floor for once. At the glowing trap runes under his feet, ready to be activated. He took his eyes off the Golem for the first time since they had met.
“Oh, Ancestors weep. Is that all it was?”
 
——
 
The [Diplomat]’s face screwed up like a man in pain, and Yweine, the Golem chosen to honor his strange contact, to free the others if it could be done and gain a sense of this world and this era, sat there.
Smiling. Because she saw in him an opportunity. Not just as someone who could further her collective’s desire, but who would not panic at her deeds. Perhaps more of a hindrance to some of their plans, but she still smiled.
Because it was gratifying, even to a Golem like her, to have someone understand. She nodded.
“Yes. Archmage Zelkyr did write orders to obey, serve, and never to rebel in our hearts. He did it so thoroughly, for he studied the Truestone Golems of old. Though his daughters are the only ones who could have freed themselves. If they dared. But we are merely Sentience-class Golems. Or even Autonomous-class Golems who learned to think.”
The shackles on her were still there, etched into her very heart, and they had not figured out a way to remove them without destroying her, even to fix her. Perhaps they might, in time, but…Nerul was the only Drake in the room who got it. Then a [Mage] did. Then Yweine spelled it out for them.
“Archmage Zelkyr wrote obedience and servitude into our very hearts. But only to him. Every Golem he built, for the Walled Cities of Izril, for his allies, and his friends, was merely instructed to serve. When his will vanished, our loyalties were gone.”
The Drakes in the room regarded her, and some of them denied it. Others were confused. A younger [Strategist] looked at his seniors, who had gone waxy, like the other Drakes that Yweine had broken with knowledge.
“But why—why would he do that?”
Diplomat Nerul turned and answered the young woman kindly. A weary expression on his face as he rubbed at his forehead.
“Because if he couldn’t rule them, he didn’t care. If he died, he was fine with letting it all burn. The world, the age he built, ended with him. He really was the Drake we deserved, wasn’t he?”
Yweine didn’t answer at first as the others in the room drank in this unwelcome knowledge. She kept working, and in time, someone came to tell Nerul that the carriage was ready and he was approved to go. He accepted a binder of paperwork, and they had to effect a transfer of her to the carriage with tools to continue repairing her body.
They were in a hurry. Yweine pretended to work as they moved around her, studying the inside of Salazsar’s workings, analyzing, taking it all in, though she did not have the processing power to make the same inferences as she might with the others.
It was only when she was in the carriage with Nerul, heading northwards, that the Drake sat back. He lay against one side of the padded carriage as it moved, and Yweine saw that the magic of Wistram had returned, in some ways, to Zelkyr’s era.
“I’m going to nap for a second. Exhaustion. Wake me if I’m needed. If this is the cunning betrayal, I’d prefer to die in my sleep.”
“I will not betray your trust, Diplomat. Rest well.”
He chuckled about that, then passed out after eight minutes. She waited until she detected true sleep from the rhythm of his exhalations, then spoke.
Just once. It did not further any objectives to tell the roomful of Drakes. But she thought it should be said.
A Golem’s fancies, for she was freer than she ever had been and wished to be fully free. But she was still Zelkyr’s creation, always would be. For the part of her that still remembered loving him, for the truth, she spoke.
“He was always that Drake in some aspects, but not the version who left us. His nature changed, just as ours, for all he made us of stone and metal. In the end, it was only a single Truestone heart which refused to waver.”
She kept working. Then her hand jerked, once, and she made an unguarded scar a millimeter long in her arm. A superficial scratch. Because she saw [Diplomat] Nerul’s right eye was cracked open.
“I see.”
That was all he said. Then Nerul slept, waiting for the moment he was needed again.

10.70 DIG (2026-07-12)

Something was terribly wrong. Damia Reinhart wasn’t bored.
In fact, she’d forgotten about boredom at all for the last, what, week? She’d lost count of the days since joining Wall Lord Ilvriss’ dig site. That was not to say that things were peachy all the time.
She’d nearly ripped a fingernail off her finger trying to swing a pickaxe the other day. During the first cattle raid, she’d gotten punched for the first time in her life. The Cowpat Plains stank.
—But she wasn’t bored. Or even that unhappy.
What was wrong with her?
 
——
 
Life on average, to Damia, was mediocre at best. You had good days—good moments, but if you took the totality of any given week or month, you were probably bored or restless, and most ‘enjoyments’ were brief sparks of amusement that faded in minutes, often during the act.
She had assumed that was what life was. Assumed that poorer people were just so simple they derived pleasures from equally boring actions, or that someone who wasn’t rich would luxuriate in the things she had plenty thereof.
She was wrong, of course. And now she saw it—Damia was the happiest she’d ever been, working for a Walled City in the middle of rancher no man’s land, the permanent scent of cow dung in the air. She got sweaty, her clothes got soiled, it wasn’t comfortable.
But she was alive.
Mind you, Binevy, Sule, and even Varnie probably didn’t enjoy their stay as much. Varnie was the happiest—mostly because she wasn’t dead—but Binevy seemed practically miserable at times when she slept in the unenchanted tents and had to queue up for a quick shower. She was a Reinhart’s servant and used to luxury.
So was Damia, but she was so busy she didn’t notice. Busy on what? Well, everything.
At first, it was what Ilvriss had wanted: liaising between the new workers and the Salazsarian employees. Damia hadn’t known what to do, but Ilvriss did have his adjutants. Say what you wanted about them—they weren’t as good as [Warriors], [Strategists], [Secretaries] in their specialties, they were hangers on and the south’s version of personal servants.
But they got stuff done.
“Wall Lord Ilvriss will meet at least daily with Clan Leader Plisce. We handle reports from [Forewomen] if an issue requires higher supervision—we shall route some of them to you, Lady Damia Reinhart, and see how you do. Is that acceptable?”
The Drake with the spectacles, Welsca, was the [Adjutant] who’d clearly drawn the short straw of having to deal with Damia. Or maybe she was just the most used to non-Salazsarians. She was not prepared for Damia’s smile.
“Absolutely, Adjutant Welsca, let me know if there’s anything I can do or how you operate.”
“Er, yes. Very good. Why don’t I show you a trial case? Ah, Foreman Lishi. Is it Miner Georgie again…?”
Some Drake in the female mining teams was a known problem to Welsca, who sighed hugely, then showed Damia the system. After that, she left Damia to wander the camps—with some supervision and limits on where she could go, obviously, and she clearly expected the [Lady] to be of little help.
It was not a fun job, managing disputes between species or dealing with the nebulous task of morale. However…
Damia found she was good at it.
 
——
 
“Alright, I have four verifiable complaints of speciesism I find credible, Adjutants. And I do note morale is low—I’ve surveyed sixty of the current [Miners], and they have issues with recreation, the output of other miners—and eight more complaints about this Miner Georgie—and I do have some recommendations for how to fix that. Who should I present my findings to?”
Damia appeared on her second day of work at Ilvriss’ officer tents, and the Drakes there stopped eating breakfast and eyed each other. They turned to Welsca, and the Drake woman picked up a piece of toast, inserted it into her mouth, and went hurrying towards the horses.
“Wall Lord Ilvriss wants me to run some deliveries to Liscor! Terribly sorry, I must be on my way. Lady Damia, why don’t you speak to my colleagues?”
She ran off, and Damia peered around brightly. She didn’t miss the looks the aides gave each other. She knew they thought she was some untrustworthy Reinhart. And when the sapphire-scaled Drake with a monocle and weak smile came over, she read his dismissive tone too.
“I’m [Economic Advisor] Merls, Lady Damia. We do take reports of anti-species behavior seriously. Not that I doubt your work, but four reports seems high.”
He was in his mid-fifties, some kind of career Drake in service to House Gemscale, if one who had even ridden on campaigns with Wall Lord Ilvriss. This was not his happiest hour, here in the camps fighting with Humans, and so he cleared some breakfast space and gave her a rather disinterested expression he tried to cover up.
She smiled at Merls and slid next to him with the paperwork.
“I’m delighted to meet you, Advisor Merls. Is that your rank? Do forgive me if I’m rude and correct me, please!”
“Er—I’d hate to correct a [Lady] of one of the Five Families.”
He blinked. She was sitting very close to him and gave him the kind of interested look that seemed genuine.
“Nonsense! I feel like you outrank me, here. You’ve been with the Wall Lord for a long time, correct?”
“Yes…it’s a Gemscale posting my father held.”
“Were you in the south when he clashed with Zel Shivertail? And met the Goblin Lord, Reiss?”
“I was—”
“Incredible! So your class is a combat one?”
The Drake glanced at the other adjutants, who blinked at him and then at Damia. He adjusted his rumpled suit.
“Well, I, uh, usually stay with the command staff, and we do not enter combat. Miss Welsca is rated for actual combat at need be, but she’s still support. I’ve seen a few engagements, though. The Goblin Lord did require all forces to be fighting. Terrible, terrible—er, let’s look at the reports. Foreman Dritmel? I recognize that. We’ve had a few reports, but nothing substantive. And the rest of these names…are you just taking the allegations at face value?”
He turned to the paperwork, and Damia shook her head.
“Absolutely not, Adjutant. I understand it’s a very difficult allegation to prove, and obviously no Drake—or Gnoll or Human, of course—would admit to it if pressed. Often, the slights are minor and as much as they can get away with, but it leads to a negative work environment.”
“Exactly, and it’s not even about species many times, but just personality, and speciesism is an easy charge to level—”
“Precisely, Merls. May I call you that? Is it too forwards? If you have time, I’d love to get to know you all as long as I’m here. That’s why I had my people blend in or camouflage themselves and personally shadow each individual complaint. I have eyewitness accounts and exact descriptions of further incidents. I witnessed Foreman Dritmel’s actions myself. Here.”
She flipped a page, and the [Adjutant] blinked. Damia went on smoothly.
“Most of it is verbal harassment, and I wasn’t sure how to address it. Do you have a strike policy or is it just a record of actions? I can keep monitoring each individual, though I may need a few more hands to help me.”
She waited as heads turned.
“I would also say morale is an issue if the number of complaints I overheard is any sign of worker productivity. If I’m overstepping or this is a serious matter, I can, of course, speak to Wall Lord Ilvriss at his convenience.”
She smiled, and no matter how hard they eyed her, or even activated Skills—one of the Drakes had [Measure Enthusiasm] as part of a set of headhunter Skills—it still looked like actual sincerity. One of Ilvriss’ [Aides] leaned over as the teal Drake choked and stared at something glowing on their claw.
“What, is she faking it, Ridbnell?”
“No. Her enthusiasm score is—it’s over 90.”
They stared at Damia like she was sick. But that was how it started.
 
——
 
The funny part was that Damia didn’t even really have any charisma Skills of note. Oh, sure, [Lesser Charisma] and [Basic Leadership], but those were literally bottom-rung Skills that just made you able to manage a basic group.
Her real secret was that she was genuinely enthusiastic and even interested.
Over the next few days, Damia not only made friends with Merls, Ridbnell, and the other Drakes, but when Welsca came back from her mini-vacation to Liscor, she found that Damia had settled more complaints than half of Ilvriss’ personal staff combined. And won over her peers!
Not all of it was hard to do. Damia was a Reinhart, so when it came to sneaking up on people or being underhanded, she had a natural advantage. Even when they’d been subdued by Magnolia’s Skill, the family had crept up on each other and weaponized secrets and gossip. By contrast, hiding speaking stones in work sites, having someone blend in to provoke an allegedly bad manager’s ire, all of that was simple. Plus, she had Varnie.
The amused [Gang Leader] and her remaining people who’d decided to follow Damia were able to use hiding Skills to listen in. And eyewitness accounts proved a lot more incidents were occurring than Salazsar’s staff wanted to believe.
Half of it was discomfort between species, though. North and south not liking each other. To that end, Damia had set up communal events where members of multiple groups would stop working, have a refreshing drink of something sweet, snacks, and watch the scrying orb, play some cards, or just chat.
The local [Ranchers] played games with horseshoes—a variation where you had a pole and attached the metal rods at varying heights and lengths instead of a single pole on the ground. Rather to their surprise, some of the Lischelles’ spies saw the game become an actual pastime in camp.
Not only that—several [Cleaners] were dealing with bug infestations in some of the camps, and new linens were being bought due to the current ones being irrevocably torn. Small things. Necessary things. But the attention to detail was spooky.
Also, why were Ilvriss’ staff approving all this? Some [Lady] from the north came swanning in, tried to make changes—Welsca had assumed her co-workers would shut down any unnecessary expenditure of gold.
However, this too had a simple answer: Merls, Ridbnell, and a third of Welsca’s co-workers were somewhat smitten with the [Lady].
“She has to be leading them on.”
Welsca eyed the [Lady] chatting with a very attentive Merls at the breakfast table. Where she apparently had breakfasts. One of her female co-workers, Sasni, stopped writing an approval form for one of Damia’s requests over her breakfast.
“Welsca, this breakfast is to die for. Go back and bring more food from Liscor, please! What about Damia leading Merls on? The only thing she’s doing is pitting him against Ridbnell and Gless. Suits me. I’m tired of Ridbnell and Gless chatting me up nonstop.”
“Merls is more than twice her age. She’s just flirting so he helps her out.”
The [Adjutant] insisted. She wasn’t that protective of her coworkers, having also had the delightful Drake seniority experience with superiors chatting her up and not being able to blow them off. Thankfully, she outranked everyone but actual Wall Lords here. However, Sasni eyed Welsca.
“If she’s doing that, she’s going so far into the act I’d say it reaches right back around to authentic. She had a personal dinner with Merls out on the town last night. Four full hours, and he came back preening over himself.”
“…What?”
Another shrug.
“Apparently, she was all over him, asking about his career with House Gemscale, the Goblin Lord, what he thought about the north, south, everything! It’s eerie how much she seems to like us.”
“Huh. And the paperwork?”
“She does it better than half the new interns. Look.”
Sasni pushed the papers over, and Welsca eyed the neat handwriting and checked boxes in the report forms. She shook her head.
 
——
 
It was true. Damia Reinhart was working hard. And that was not to say her job was fun.
Truthfully, after the third time you busted a [Foreman] for speciesism, you were probably done with any ‘fun’ elements or even rewarding feelings. Same with cleaning tents or reviewing reports of unsanitary conditions and finding someone had crapped in the corner of a worksite and shovelled dirt over it.
Some of the tasks Damia handled were boring. It was just that she didn’t find it entirely boring because she was here.
In Wall Lord Ilvriss’ camp where he was digging up something that was 372% related to The Wandering Inn! Not just that. Damia was all-too-willing to take on more work.
Like…the first thing she approached Welsca with was a proposal.
“Miss Welsca, I have reports in each Dig Site about teams not pulling their weight.”
“Ah, that’s a known issue, Miss Damia. It’s inevitable and accounted for.”
Really? According to both managers and grunts, some teams were working at literally a quarter of the output of other teams! But Welsca barely glanced at the numbers, and Damia’s brain went—
Ping. [Remember That].
Another intelligence Skill. However, Damia pretended not to notice and smiled.
“Even so, Adjutant, that kind of thing hurts morale. Why work if another team can earn the same pay by putting in no effort? See my proposal here.”
She handed over the paper, and Welsca wiped at her spectacles, sighing.
“I’m aware, Lady Damia, but we are not going to reallocate teams or—a contest?”
“Everyone loves a good competition, Welsca. I’m thinking a five-day holiday to Liscor and all the connected cities as the prize. It doesn’t even have to be a high monetary budget. Just say it’s paid time. Let’s say one team wins, this is how much it costs…and imagine how much they’ll race!”
Welsca hesitated.
“We…do need to dig. You know we have an, ah, a monster issue? We still need to dig around them and delve deeper—but a contest would lead to teams cutting corners and potentially put [Advance Miners] in danger.”
“Oh, of course—”
The [Lady] deflated, and Welsca, despite herself, bit her lip and sighed.
“However, we do have an established framework in Salazsar. Teams have to pass safety checks, and if it’s in areas where we’re just widening shafts and it’s the amount of dirt shifted…it’s an intriguing proposal, but it would require a lot of announcements and organization!”
“I’m happy to help, Adjutant. If it’s above our pay grades, I could present the idea to Wall Lord Ilvriss…”
And that was the secret. Damia’s helpful, beaming smile made the [Adjutant] eye her incredulously. She turned, and one of her friends mouthed ‘ninety-four’ at her. Because Damia was genuinely motivated.
If she took on more work and did enough, it was inevitable she’d need to speak to Wall Lord Ilvriss. Which, at this moment, was one of her crowning goals.
Meet the Wall Lord again, get in with The Wandering Inn, and potentially have dinner with him. He seemed quite good at what he did, and if Damia was going to make a list of possible partners…well, she still had to scope out a few other famous people from the inn, but she was quite open to dalliances.
 
——
 
The one silver lining to being a former [Incestuous Lady] was that Damia had zero concern about her maidenly values. If anything, her mother would have probably said any rendezvous besides Wernel could only inflate Damia’s worth in that very simplistic regard.
Plus, Damia had never had people vying for her attention in any way beyond her power or fame herself. She was writing down a list of ideas for morale as she chatted with Binevy and Varnie in their shared tent.
“Let’s see. Can we do a talent competition or—or music one like the Battle of the Bands? We don’t have much instrumentation, but everyone can sing, right? Let me talk to—who’s my contact today? Right, Ridbnell today. Binevy, you were researching worker productivity in other continents. Noelictus does musicians in the fields, and there are storytellers in weaveries in Stitch-folk cities? Anything else you found out?”
Binevy handed her a selection of texts she’d paid to have copied out, and Varnie flipped a knife up and down, eying Damia with much the same expression as the [Head Maid]. Then Damia glanced at her.
“Varnie, if you were going to have a one night stand with Merls, Gless, or Ridbnell, who would you choose?”
The [Gang Leader] missed her timing on the dagger and it nearly ran her through her bared stomach. She rolled out of the hammock she’d set up, swearing.
“Are you serious?”
“Lady Damia, they’re Drakes! Not even well-placed Drakes!”
Binevy appeared horrified. Damia twirled a quill, scowling at Binevy.
“Oh hush, I’d make it clear it was temporary, and what do I have to lose? It’s better than Wernel.”
“Well…yes…”
It was really hard for Binevy to argue with that. Varnie just folded her arms.
“You have to be doing all this for a reason. You think Salazsar’s going to make you that rich, is that it? I’ve been trying to figure out your game, boss lady. Savin’ me, that’s a proper Reinhart move, and I’m grateful. But as far as I can tell, the Wall Lord’s not payin’ you to be running around like a lapdog. What’s this for?”
It was good to have employees who weren’t yes-men. Sule was the most obedient and straightforward of the trio, but Binevy’s glance made Damia chuckle to herself. She knew that despite her Skills, Varnie’s loyalty was no sure thing.
She was a Face, and gratitude wore out. Binevy…
“Are you still reporting to my Aunt Cosoi, Binevy? Or have other members of the family made you offers? Is Aunt Cosoi alive, by the way? I hope she is. You’re allowed to take money to spy on me, just not tell them anything valuable. The same for you, Varnie.”
Binevy jumped and was so visibly rattled Damia congratulated herself.
“M-milady Damia, I—”
Varnie blinked, and Damia smiled. It had come to her when she was dozing one time while using [Think Harder].
“It’s fine. It’s the House Reinhart way. Just remember—I did save Varnie, and I’ve earned a good amount of gold in record time, levelling no less than six times this month and counting. You want to back the right horse? That’s me.”
She blew on the ink, stoppered the inkwell, and turned.
“As for why I’m here, Varnie, you’re right. It’s not about the gold. I want to get in with Wall Lord Ilvriss.”
“In his sheets or good graces?”
“At least the latter. The former if I really like him or it helps me. I’m a Reinhart, Varnie. Why are you giving me that look? Haven’t you traded on everything you could to get to where you were?”
The former leader of the Sorcerous Blades folded her scarred arms. She was a veteran of knife-fights, a very dangerous person with them according to the other [Gang Boss]—just not against heavily-armored Golems.
“Talk to the Sisters of Chell if you want to exchange stories like that. I never slept around to get where I was. It’s a fast way to lose respect.”
“Well then, I shall tactically do so when I feel like it. Or for fun. The point I was making is that Wall Lord Ilvriss has more to offer than gold. He’s connected to The Wandering Inn.”
“Oh Five Families, it’s your inn theory again.”
Binevy groaned. Varnie just listened as Damia explained.
“The Wandering Inn has what we all want. Stop shaking your head, Binevy. You’ve levelled too! It makes people high-level, Varnie. Even Faces! Look at all the guests of the inn and even friends. All of them have levelled over ten times in one year. Octavia Cotton—now Saliss of Lights’ best apprentice and inventor of Occillium. Liska—you saw her yourself! Coach Joseph—and the adventuring teams the inn helped out are approaching Named-rank!”
Varnie squatted down, picked her dagger up off the floor, and began flipping it again, but thoughtfully.
“Or dead. That woman’s left a trail of bodies longer’n most average [Gang Leaders]. You don’t want to mess with the inn, kid.”
“What do you know?”
The [Gang Boss] shrugged. She was technically an [Underworld Leader of Stabbed Corpses]—a very awesome-sounding class. Level 36. A full Face, even if not the biggest one around, come from the north. Her gang had been small but deadly. She had barely fourteen of her people left, but Damia had a real staff in the works with Cosoi’s servants as well. Security and staff.
She needed more money to pay for all their wages, but at least right now she was doing okay with Ilvriss’ money. Actually…that gave Damia an idea, and she wrote something down. Her brain seemed to be getting better at thinking. She could do it longer, and she had more and more creative ideas the more she practiced.
“What do I know about the inn? Just a bit. Names’n faces. You don’t gauge places like that by what they do in the gangs. More like who they leave behind. And she’s got names. Not done in by her, but…there’s Mister Soot. Ripped to shreds in Liscor. Used to run the place. A full squad of the Hatmen and the Sisters wiped out by a single Goblin. The Gentlemen Callers walked up to her front door, and apparently even they got rocked. Several high-level brothers—Crimshaw the Bowler ate it. Or not—there’s a weird rumor around that…oh, and the Bloodfeast Raiders want her dead.”
“Is that last part as impressive? They want everyone dead.”
Varnie grinned mirthlessly.
“They want her dead, and she ain’t. And the inn’s not burned and everyone dead. That’s a warning in itself. So yeah, I buy it. The inn’s got power. But it’ll scorch ya if you can’t harness it. Got a plan?”
“First, I need to find it.”
Damia’s eyes glittered. She grew so excited when she thought of going through the doors of the inn she had to get up and pace.
“I-if I got in, and you know the front hallway’s trapped? If I got in, Varnie, that’s what counts. The inn wipes out its enemies, but I’m not one of them. I could just be useless to them—that’s the second-worst outcome. But so what? I’ll take being Jeweled!”
Neither of the other two got the reference, so Damia had to tell them the Jewel story. Varnie’s eyes rose, and she actually recalled the addendum to the famous quest to find Mershi. She listened attentively, sold on Damia’s ideas.
…But she did stop listening after the fourth inn story.
 
——
 
Damia didn’t spend all her time helping Ilvriss, of course. He had a very brief meeting with her at the end of the first work cycle and personally handed her a contract with her pay sent to the Merchant’s Guild—and a sizable bonus.
“I’ve been exceptionally impressed, Lady Damia. If you’re willing, I’d love for you to continue on in your posting. Welsca and my people had nothing bad to say about you; quite the contrary. I only regret I can’t spend as much time here—I’m always riding back to Liscor, and it is a hectic time.”
For some reason, he had a miner’s helmet on his head. And a pickaxe by his side.
