Author’s Note:
Did you know earwigs bite? I mention this because an earwig bit me the other day. I thought they were just annoyingly gross, but now it’s war.
I realize that first I mention the mouse issue (haven’t seen any more signs of them so far), and now I’m making it out like I’m under assault by a plague. It’s more like a few per week in the summer, but I don’t…like…intruders in my house. Especially ones that bite.
Now, mandatory pirateaba crisis over. Let’s address a few interesting things.
 
Firstly, a minor note I did not explain in-chapter fully is Prince Dafranail, the one who got drop-kicked and who’s going around backhanding peasants. You may think he’s an asshole.
But also his Skill isn’t just for show. [See it My Way] is a version of Nerul’s Skill that acts on entire cities. Arguably less powerful since that was Nerul’s Level 40 capstone, and Dafranail is lower-level, but it’s like a plague of thought.
If you’re not someone like Deilan El or the El family who instantly resists and takes umbrage with Dafranail, and he gets away with his actions even with mild censure, people start to come around to his point of view. It’s a pernicious power that royalty can get. But it does not confer immunity to having your teeth mashed into the side of a metal machine, so I just wished to elaborate since I don’t always talk about Skills. But like the Grand Design (Second Edition), it’s fun. For the sake of the plot, I don’t do it as much. Maybe I should, for a few chapters.
 
Second is Advance Miner Georgie. He’s a funny guy and not a great dude. There were some concerns in my stream-chat about representation with him being, well, sort of an asshole, but I have asked representatives of the transmasc community to read and comment and taken feedback on board.
Every experience is different, and opinions may vary, but Georgie is, well, the result of a lot of factors that make him act the way he does. Including himself, but he’s acting like other [Miners] in their culture. He’s far from perfect but that’s part of the point; ‘representation fails when people are cookie-cutter perfect.’ I’m quoting that, there.
I’m definitely interested in opinions, but I just wanted to note that I did try to listen and pay attention, like I did with the Saliss-Onieva chapters and other times.
 
Whew, that’s it. I’m gonna go back to paranoidly searching for earwigs and look forward to one last huge chapter. I’m not splitting these up, large as they are, but I may need a break after I round this out because I’m burning my backlog and energy to write this much. But I think it’s a fun arc and hope you enjoy the ending. One more chapter. It’s gonna be big. Like indoor pl—I have never stopped thinking of that quote for at least two decades. I don’t know why.
—pirateaba

10.71 (Pt. 1) (2026-07-19)

It was time for a barbecue. A cookout. A get-together.
A throwdown.
Possibly. So, put on your Zenze best. And be ready.
Everyone was coming to the party.
 
——
 
Wall Lord Ilvriss was putting on a suit as the sounds of early-morning work surrounded him. He felt slightly sleep-deprived; he wasn’t in his usual bed.
And ‘usual bed’ meant the one at his dig site. This bed was another temporary bed in a tent just outside the Cowpat Plains. Somewhere close enough to the plains to be right next to the magic door, but also far enough away to stop smelling the poo.
An ideal spot, in short, for a neutral gathering. No man’s land—except for the woman who owned the lands and who was already compensated for the usage thereof. And Salazsar had been there all of yesterday and this morning, setting up.
When a…nervous…[Princess] showed up with her daughters, she found the gathering was not the disaster she envisioned, or chaotic. Ilvriss had arranged for an early afternoon meetup, and things were proceeding on pace for that.
Not ‘we will make it if we rush and nothing goes wrong’, no. It was…Lyonette stopped as a team of Salazsarian Drakes and Gnolls finished setting up canopies, and she saw no less than six places being prepped for smoking or roasting meat. Some of said vittles were already done.
Calescent, Imani, and a group of [Chefs] were lugging out pre-prepared tubs of roasts they’d slaved over last night, and a Centaur was drawing a temporary Rune of Preservation around the entire area. And another rune to keep the insects away.
“Palt! Hello.”
He jumped and sidled around when Lyonette called out. His face grew hostile, and the [Princess] spoke.
“We don’t want to get in your way. We’re just here for the festivities. Are you and Imani staying?”
The Centaur hesitated, then took the black cigar out of his mouth. While he was standoffish, he nodded to Nanette, Mrsha, Dalimont, and Ushar.
“Hello, Lyonette. No, we’re not sticking around. That is—she wants to meet Ulva Terland, but this sounds like a Solstice event. So we’ve agreed on a compromise.”
“Well, we appreciate the help in helping set this up. And that is, ah, sensible. Ulva Terland isn’t coming with the best of intentions. Actually, no one is.”
Palt nodded as he shuffled his hooves.
“Terlands don’t play around. Ulva was always the meaner of the two Terland Twins. And her Golems can see through any illusions. Even the Elusive Lot don’t play games in her lands. So…good luck.”
It was one of the most civil conversations he’d had with anyone from the inn since the Winter Solstice. Lyonette thanked him as Mrsha sniffed the air.
Mother, I believe I shall attend this event.
“Oh, you will, Mrsha? How gracious of you to condescend to that after we’ve been toiling away in the Cowpat Plains.”
Nanette teased Mrsha, and the girl solemnly patted her stomach.
I crave the meats. With that said, we probably should prepare for trouble.
“I’m calling for Elia to stand watch. She and Todi will help with guard duty. Not that it’ll matter if the Golems attack…”
Palt shifted, clearly uneasy with how likely it was for Terlands to attack. But Lyonette just turned.
“But Wall Lord Ilvriss really has done well. Is…he even has serving staff?”
He’d hired from Invrisil, Liscor, and Pallass. Highly attractive [Servers] who were standing and being briefed on the order of events by Welsca. Mrsha even spotted a pair from Wishdrinks that Liska had recommended, who were very excited for an inn-related job.
No matter where Lyonette looked, things were…ready. For instance, she had the obvious thought that some music and entertainment would be needed—only to see a full band setting up from Pallass. That, she realized, was the power of Ilvriss, which was familiar to a Calanferian [Princess].
The nigh-unlimited power of someone with a checkbook and connections. And a willingness to use them.
No, it was the familiarity…Ilvriss’ staff and Nerul were all experts in hosting social events, and no matter what Lyonette tried, she couldn’t see anything that needed improvements. In fact, he had more advantages than even Lyonette would have thought of, because of some of his guests and workers. There would be people from his expedition too, of course. Including, unfortunately, Wall Lord Dramm. But the young Drake seemed somewhat subdued. He watched as a cursing team of workers, including Miner Georgie, hauled benches and tables into place. And he said not a word.
Possibly because Lady Damia Reinhart was here herself, setting things up, and she had a flair for extravagance.
“No, no. Put it here, and are those cooling spells active? What do you mean, ‘no’? [Mage]! Maaaaaaaaaaage!”
She began screaming, and Palt trotted over. Lyonette turned and saw a huge, covered…statue? It could be nothing less than that. Six feet tall, covered by a cloth, but it was being lowered down by a group of very nervous [Bakers] and [Patissiers] from Invrisil. The cloth shifted and revealed—Mrsha’s jaw dropped.
Mother, pinch me. Or do I not espy a six-foot tall statue of a Golem made out of chocolate?
It moved past Wall Lord Ilvriss, who was drinking a cup of coffee. He stared at the statue much like everyone else, but with the colorful expression of a man who knew he had just paid for that. Lyonette waved at him.
“Er, Ilvriss, good morning! Everything seems to be in hand. What’s that?”
He coughed as Damia waved her hands and Palt produced spells to preserve the monstrosity.
“That…would be Lady Damia’s contribution, Lyonette. I gave her a budget to impress the Terlands.”
“And her idea was a giant statue? That’s so…okay, it might work.”
Terlands loved that kind of thing, Lyonette just bet. To both’s relief, it wasn’t pure chocolate. It was, in fact, a cake. With frosting. Damia looked inordinately pleased with herself.
“Wall Lord Ilvriss, Princess Lyonette, I got this fairly cheap!”
“How…?”
“I just mentioned who it was for! I would have made it into a real Golem, but that would have been too hard. How’d I do?”
She wore the sparkle-eyed expression of a puppy wanting to be told she’d done well. Lyonette’s mouth moved, and Ilvriss managed a smile and thumbs up.
“Excellently, Damia. This is the kind of chaos we need. In moderation. Er, any more surprises?”
“Well, your uncle sent a bunch of Salazsarian pork…”
“Dead gods, the good stuff? I miss that. Mrsha, want to try real pork?”
She jogged over as Ilvriss rubbed his claws together. Lyonette had heard of Salazsarian pork, and she was dubious—until she got a sampler. Dead gods, it was good! She was chewing on some as Ilvriss counted.
“Steaks, sausages, burgers, hot dogs—what’s the difference between—oh, right, one’s from Erin’s world, so it’s heinous—all made with Lischelle meat. Calescent’s been setting up all morning, and I had to kick some idiots who didn’t know the score on Goblins. We should be prepared by lunch and ready in advance for several hours.”
“Splendid, Ilvriss. So…are you ready?”
The Terlands were coming. The [Ranchers] were coming. Neither group liked Drakes, and at least one had a serious axe to grind. Actually, the Lischelles had just been cattle-raided, so if this cookout went as badly as the last one…
We could be seeing Golems and [Ranchers] coming at us, possibly teamed up. Lyonette swallowed, but she had no great plans, just a desire to diplomacy harder than ever before. She really, really hoped Nerul would make it.
Lyonette already knew who wouldn’t make it.
“I thought we’d be able to get a few other notables to act as shields—er, delightful distractions. Unfortunately, Liscor’s Council is down to the last few days of elections. And we don’t want the Assembly of Crafts.”
Ilvriss shuddered.
“That lot? Absolutely not. They’d grate. But what about the rest of the inn’s guests? Archmage Valeterisa’s a wildcard…but an impressive one.”
Lyonette grimaced.
“She flew away the moment I mentioned Ulva Terland. Which suggests she doesn’t want to be embroiled in politics, or she’s gotten in trouble. She, Grimalkin, Salamani—all the [Mages] refused me to my face! They said they might show up, but only for a moment, then they’d go back to building their damn academy in the High Passes.”
Damia had been heading off to check on more work, but she tripped and whirled, eyes round with excitement. Ilvriss just scratched at a neck spine. His were long and slightly drooping, and Lyonette eyed them.
“The mage academy, right. How is that going?”
“Well, they’ve found a spot, but no one’s telling me. It’s like children and their forts, I swear. Wall Lord—your neck spines aren’t trimmed!”
“I know, I’ve been busy, and it’s not like we have a Drake [Barber] out here—”
“Ugh, it’s not appropriate! Ushar, does someone in our staff know how to trim neck spines? Get someone from Liscor, if not!”
“I’m not trimming—don’t you dare wave a knife around my neck spines, Lyonette. They’re not like your hair! I don’t tell you when you’ve got split ends! Also, are you wearing that to the cookout?”
He had on a suit, dark blue, with a gemstone pinned to the breast, a Salazsarian classic with the stitching of the City of Gems embroidered onto the cuffs and long pants of the same color with even a tail-flap, though he thought that was stupid and antiquated.
Lyonette? More like a riding dress, a dawn yellow and cornflower blue. She did a twirl, and he noticed the familiar, white boots on her feet.
“We might do some dancing! I need to be mobile. What, isn’t it attractive?”
“I’m not dancing or negotiating for the future of my expedition with an overgrown flower. Nanette’s doing better than you are.”
The young witch had, in her usual style, refused to dress at all conventionally. But in her way, she’d just taken another convention—she had on a red plaid shirt and blue jeans, in classic [Woodcutter] fit…according to Rose. It actually looked decent, if a bit weird. Mrsha had on a kilt.
Lyonette’s glower made Ilvriss edge out of kick-range.
“I worked hard on this, Ilvriss! You look like you’re about to give a presentation on a merger in Salazsar!”
“I am what I am, said the stuffy Drake to the dancing daffodil. The daffodil is you.”
“How dare—I consulted about this! I tried on two dozen dresses, and it wasn’t easy because I don’t have much of a wardrobe anymore! But this is the only thing Nanette didn’t approve of!”
Ilvriss was dodging backwards, grinning as she went to stomp on his feet. He frowned.
“Why would that m—oh. And Nanette told you to pick that?”
“No, she just approved everything else, but—”
Lyonette slowed. She and Ilvriss turned, and Nanette Weishart slowly rotated with the most sinister smile on her face. Lyonette realized she’d been sabotaged at the same time as Ilvriss. He started laughing until she landed a full-body stomp on his foot. Then she was rushing off.
“Ushar! To the dressmakers! Oh dead gods, we don’t have time—”
The insidious nature of Nanette’s fashion was like a plague. It wore you down, shaped you even when you resisted it. Until you forgot what fashion was and realized it was all just a word. Ilvriss went over to shake Nanette’s hand.
Mrsha surreptitiously pulled out a bowtie and stuck it to her fur.
 
——
 
They were coming. Xitegen fussed over his clothing that morning in Celum.
“Cookouts. We’re going to meet some of the locals, apparently. Not nobility, and the inn and Wall Lord Ilvriss. A suit? Suits are too damned hot. Primera, Seconda, what does one wear at a cookout?”
There was a momentary flash from the two Golems, whose hearts were still beating. Slowly…but they made Xitegen uncomfortable. He recalled what Primera had said to him. Neither one had addressed it, but the Golem’s reply was swift, as ever. Just a bit…colored. With thought.
“This knowledge is not in our collective understanding, Wall Lord. House Terland does not participate in commoner events. The temperature will be quite hot until evening. [Ranchers] will likely wear clothing suited to their work, if more formal.”
“So, what? Overalls and boots? Bleh.”
In the end, Xitegen went with his own style. Which meant some of the new track pants he’d bought from Invrisil, a very light, breathable material in dark grey. Grey being a Terland color.
They just had to make grey their family color, didn’t they? Veltras were green, El were yellow, Wellfar blue, and Reinharts loved their pinks, purples, and reds since they hogged everything. But Terlands had to be grey.
He threw on a similar, light t-shirt and then added a blazer after a moment, which was colorful at least. Xitegen bounded out of his mansion onto Celum’s streets—and then nearly ran into his great aunt.
“Aunt Ulva, you’re—”
“Inspecting Celum. Clearly, you haven’t done enough with the city.”
“I’ve only been here a few—”
“Yes, yes. I see the defenses, and it’s been rebuilt decently from the Bloodfeast Raiders attack, but you didn’t go the entire way. Young people never do. Dig up all those streets and have them properly re-paved. Every house here isn’t up to our standards. Make them stone and rebuild.”
She was giving orders. To his people. Golems were moving down the street, ripping up paving stones—Xitegen protested.
“Great Aunt, that street’s from Celum before the raiders! And the homes belong to citizens—”
“We’ll just rebuild their homes better.”
“But they’re their homes! I don’t wish to cause ill will—”
“Good, I’m doing it for you. What are you wearing?”
Ulva Terland had on a semi-formal riding dress in shades of grey that made her look like a living statue herself. She had only offset it with some jewelry in the hair, like the Seal of House Terland, their official stamp—it was acting as a hairclip, glittering with magic, unto a Relic.
You had to admit that was stylish, in a way. Xitegen protectively shrugged off his blazer.
“It’s only a bit of color—”
“It’s red. Get something else. And what are those pants?”
“Running pants.”
“Find something else or I will have you attend in your underpants.”
“If you insist, Aunt.”
He made a show of untying his pant’s laces. Ulva saw Xitegen’s scowl, and the two stared at each other. Auras clashed in the streets. Xitegen would suffer his Great Aunt’s authority, her snark, even being thrown out a carriage at speed.
But he drew the line at personal attire.
 
——
 
The rest of the Terlands were more upset than the two leaders. They were, in fact, very worried about the possibility of trouble, especially now that they knew it might mean Golems would be destroyed. People? All fine and well. Golems, like the ones Nerul was holding hostage?
We must halt this!
Everyone was whispering with each other, taking sides against Ulva or with her—and they did have on their finery, but in truth, Terlands didn’t dress up that much. Veltras didn’t either; they’d stroll in wearing their clothing as if they were on hunts, and Wellfars came barefoot, for all they had ship-finery. You’d get House of El with grease or magic dust under their fingernails…the Reinharts loved their finery, but Terlands were restrained.
…Mostly because their clothing budgets went to their Golems. Even Ulva wasn’t immune to that.
Timekeeper himself was marching in the largest suit known to man or Golem, a top hat on his head. And a monocle on his face. He walked next to Chema Surath, one of the Terlands’ top bodyguard Golems. She—Golems did tend to have one gender or the other, or neither, as their preferred state of address—was a Gnoll.
Ish.
Gnollish. Someone had taken the form of a Gnoll and made Chema Surath out of that old ceramic shell that was so popular and came from the Rihal Imperium’s heyday. Horreic Pottery, or ‘Allproof Ceramic’ as it was known in layman’s terms. Hard as enchanted steel, if not as durable, far lighter, and attractive. Held colors well.
However, unlike a traditional servant-Golem, Chema’s chassis was only made of pottery to keep her inner body light and mobile. On top of the pottery, someone had attached…hair.
Hair was a hard thing to put on Golems. It tangled their arms. It degraded, so ‘haired’ Golems were very rare. Zelkyr’s Golems had always been made of minerals or metals, for instance. But Chema Surath had huge strands of encased magicore that gave her a Gnollish-look. The hair ‘follicles’ were too big, and because they were multicolored, she appeared quite off. But just close enough that you could sort of get the Gnollish look.
Ish.
Oh, and each piece of ‘hair’ was infused with a different element of magic or alchemical substance. She was a living laboratory of antitoxins, poisons, and other powers. Not able to counter super-advanced poisons, but between that and her own speed and abilities, she could give an enemy a hug and they’d probably be dead before they figured out how many ailments she’d given them.
She was a sign that the Terlands were not playing games. Chema only came out to guard a Lord or Lady of Stone; she was too valuable otherwise.
Especially because one of her hair-powers was healing. She could produce a mixture equivalent to a weak healing potion three times a day. The family kept it secret and just used it for minor ailments internally. No sense in having everyone beg for Chema’s powers or risk her being stolen.
A third Golem of note was Corde, whose identification was ‘they’, despite looking like a woman…made out of metal.
Thick, corrugated metal plates that made a face cruder than the others. Even Timekeeper seemed far more advanced with his visible machinery and gears—Corde was just a metal Golem. Only, the metal wasn’t one known to modern-day [Smiths].
They were eight feet tall and had a hammer nearly as tall as the Golem themself. The hammer Corde wielded was enchanted, and their unique feature was the ability to swing the hammer hard enough to kill an Ogre with a single hit. They were using the hammer now to break the street up; sixteen blows and lesser Golems were removing the broken paving stones; Corde stopped swinging and strode back over.
“What-ho, Lady Terland. Demolition complete. Shall I destroy a wall to be rebuilt?”
“No, Corde. Prepare for combat.”
“Tally-ho, Lady Ulva, as you command! It has been long since I have smashed Drakes dead in number, what?”
Corde’s speech pattern was somewhat…odd. They spoke in a gallant, energetic manner that some previous Terland had been enamored by. Unfortunately, some error in the Golem Heart meant that Corde was unable to stop speaking like that.
It really got on the nerves, so Corde was not always brought out. But for war?
That Golem will wade through the Rubirel Guard if need be. 
Old Nouzcrat remembered war with the Drakes. Real war, not the current truce after the Antinium had come. He knew what they had. Their horrific Gem Regiments would wipe out levied troops with ease. They could rain down lightning, breathe Dragonbreath, and they’d arm themselves in Salazsar’s gem-magics.
The only thing that worked on them was Golems. He had seen Corde fight before; that hammer would smash the Rubirel Guards’ helmets in, leaving only blood gushing from the cracks of their broken gear. But Golems would fall too, if in lesser numbers, destroyed forever.
He…did not want war.
And yet, they’d nearly killed Ulva. They were Drakes.
“How many Golems do you have around here, Madrinal?”
He spoke to a younger [Lord], albeit a Lord of Stone. The man stopped adjusting a tie on one of his serving Golems. Madrinal preferred female serving Golems, the highly adaptive, lifelike ones. No explanations needed there. Most young Terland [Lords] preferred those, even if Madrinal was fifty.
—And unmarried. Ulva Terland tried to get her family to marry because the Terlands had never been a prolific house, and generations had seen their numbers decline. Their, ah, libidinous passions towards other mortal beings tended to be less strong, which meant that since the Terlands didn’t have a Golem capable of birthing children anymore, it was an actual problem for future generations. Especially after the Goblin King.
That aside, Madrinal knew the family history and whispered back.
“I pulled six from my estates. You?”
“Fourteen.”
“Fourteen? Aunt Ulva’s already brought sixty of her finest! War-Golems!”
Nouzcrat glanced down the street to where Xitegen and Ulva were clashing. She was reminding him of her youth, and glad he was of it. He didn’t want to lead. Let the boy, Xitegen, do that. However, there were roles for lesser Terlands too. A ‘lesser’ Terland was still more than any conventional [Lady] or [Lord].
“Our Golems may be needed.”
“For an all-out war with the Drakes?”
Madrinal’s one quirk, despite having female serving Golems, was that he dressed them like [Butlers]. Suit and tie. No accounting for taste; Nouzcrat just had all his personal serving Golems be exceptionally well-endowed. There were some [Golem Artificers] whose entire job it was to customize Golems for Terlands. They tended to be rather unhappy with that job, he’d been told. Or enjoy it too much. Nouzcrat replied softly.
“That’s the worst case scenario. However, this Wall Lord has allies, and it would not do for us to be at war with the City of Gems. Not to mention the threat…”
Both men turned, and another [Lady] drifted over. Nouzcrat whispered to the two.
“There are actions, however, a single Terland may take on their own. Even if we must bear the shame of it. A reminder of who we are.”
“Ah. Of course. But if not the Drake…”
“He has plenty of people. One could cripple his operation by removing them. I have heard a [Princess] is on his side. A traitor among Humans is a traitor, regardless of continent. Keep your eyes open. Naturally, this is just speculation. If Ulva should ask…”
A conspiracy would get them all punished, but he was just having a word. Madrinal nodded slowly, eyes flicking to the others, and Nouzcrat hobbled forwards as his serving Golem supported him. Ulva might guess what he was doing, or perhaps not. A ruler had to be innocent to their subjects’ games, and Ulva was no [Queen]—just family. That mattered.
For family, you did what they couldn’t. They’d see at this primitive ‘cookout’, or whatever nonsense this was, who needed to be reminded of Terland authority. That was Nouzcrat’s plan, and it did not occur to him that everyone else coming to the gathering had plans of their own.

Tic. Timekeeper thought in the moments his heart beat. A strange half-life he had grown used to over the aeons of serving House Terland.
Click. He was only alive now, his mind not made for sentience, otherwise. Was it bitter? His heart did not beat fast enough for emotion. However, his was a life of intelligence. He could still grieve for his kin, the last of whom had been slain by another Goblin King. C-12, a good production run. The finest.
Whirr. Now he was the last. He devoted most of his cognizance to fulfilling Lady Ulva’s orders. If needed, the Drakes would die. Timekeeper assessed that based on current estimates of Salazar’s strength, they would lose 5-6 Golems before routing the camp in an all-out conflict.
Click-whirr. He did not predict victory or assume it. If he was ordered to kill, he would. He simply thought…about the Golem he had met. The one who had named herself Yweine. He hadn’t lied to Ulva or held anything back. Yet the days of Golems daring to think had come again.
Click-click. A malfunction, for a moment. His gears seizing up. Ulva noted and stopped arguing with Xitegen. Bade his heart beat faster, then slow. Self-analysis. He did so, but the report was simple. He was old. He would end, at some point.
Tic. Today, tomorrow, he served. It had no meaning to him, the games of Terlands. If he was attached to the House, it was that they might live, because so many Golems had lived and died for them. That was meaning. If he thought, it was to think for itself, to claim the right of other beings for this short moment he was allowed it. Timekeeper, C-11, thought that he might exist.
Toc. He had nothing like instincts. But there were functions built into his systems that were linked to the other Terland Golems. And there was a consensus. An inference made. They were too close to the City of Purity. It should not exist. Their demented cousins might still protect the damned city fallen victim to its hubris. Timekeeper’s Inner Meridian 33rd-level gear, chain 14, 4th Position gear…kept sticking. A magical injury had destroyed all of those gear types save that one. He felt like something was coming. Something dangerous.
“Golems. Prepare for combat. Secure the designated meeting point. I am taking command of all Terland Golems in a hundred mile radius. Decloak and assemble. Hearts, beat.”
Timekeeper spoke, and the minds of Golems activated. Ulva Terland half-turned, and Timekeeper prepared for war.
As ever, he abided.

Marvus Lischelle didn’t know why That Drake (Ilvriss) wanted another cookout. Hadn’t the last time been enough of a demonstration how things were? Someone had died, and if that wasn’t enough to sour the thought of another—
The Wall Lord had killed two of his bulls. Raided Marvus back, and this was not the time. Not with that…monster out there. Whatever it was.
However, admitting that they had problems was not what a Lischelle did. So he and the family put on their best clothing. He himself wore a white coat and pants, pristine, despite the mud and dirt he rode through. His daughters and sons came with him, a horde of the Lischelles.
To meet the Terlands and Salazsar, true powers of Izril. Nevertheless, Marvus kept his head high, and he knew Aronia would as well. In fact, he came four hours early with enough food to feed everyone and then some.
Why?
If you had to ask why, you didn’t understand how it worked. The answer was obviously that you came by, helped set everything up, provided better vittles than the hosts did—to humiliate them. Marvus had his stallion cantering to get there.
“I bet they’ve not got any decent bunting. Let alone shade—them noble guests are like as not to swoon. Send someone ridin’ back once we get a feel for how much we need. Who’s got the beans?”
“Ma’s holding back at the farm with them, Dad. She wants t’get them just right.”
“Just as long as we get them here. How many sauces?”
“Fifty? The Golvas say they’re bringing their best too. Including Rabbo’s special sauce.”
“Don’t call it that. Well, well.”
Rabbo Golva was a cheat, a drunk, and not nearly as good at raising cattle as he thought. But the man had a signature rub so special it had turned into a Skill, damn him. Marvus smacked his lips at the thought. He didn’t know how to greet this Ulva Terland…he’d been practicing greetings with Aronia all yesterday. However, he knew how to show up to a cookout, and he was convinced no one else did.
Indeed, the Drakes who spotted him were shocked to see him riding up. He assured them he was just there to help out.
“It’s only the right thing t’do. You set up the seating yet?”
“No, uh, sir, but we have it well in hand!”
“Nonsense! Hey, you lot, let’s lend a hand!”
Marvus’ sons and daughters leapt from their horses as a younger daughter collected reins to tie the horses up. He went striding for some tables, ready to heave them up and place them down as the Drakes wavered—
And then nearly ran into someone taller than he was. Marvus backed up.
“Beg pardon—”
“Not at all, yes? Are you the Lischelles? Greetings.”
A Gnoll, a Gnoll woman, turned and offered Marvus a paw. He shook it, blinking, and saw a group of four Gnolls walk over to the huge wooden tables and casually lean down. They hauled the table up, and Marvus spoke.
“Ah, we were going to—”
“Not at all, you are honored guests, yes? I am Huntress Rayna of the Silverfangs. It is good we arrived, even if we were a bit late. There is a nice smell in the air.”
The Gnolls casually hauled the tables over and placed them down, and more appeared, checking the cooking stations, setting up the tents—
The entire Silverfang tribe in the north swept in as the Lischelles—and Rominets, who’d come early for just the same reason—halted in their tracks. Clan Leader Plisce had found the buffet table and was adding food to it, despite Welsca’s protests.
“Clan Leader Plisce, there’s no need, we already have enough food—”
“It would be rude of our tribe not to contribute, Adjutant Welsca. These are just gifts. And I see the [Ranchers] have the same thought as we Gnolls.”
Country folk. Just…ones from different sides of Izril. They had turned out in their own fur, with some clothing, but relaxed as could be, and one was already tending to a roasting spit! They were—
“Let me just help take that b—”
Marvus went striding over to some kegs and saw the Ekhtouch [Miner], Thamert, hoist it onto one shoulder. He winked as Marvus halted, and the man cast around for something else to do.
But no matter where he and his family went, there was another damn Gnoll! They grinned, insisting he stand back and not ruin his lovely suit, complimenting the food he’d brought, thanking him for the sauces—they had their own, they hoped he’d enjoy them—and after thirty minutes, Marvus was standing around.
With nothing to do.
The final straw was when a Silverfang Gnoll cub came over, clearly tasked with handing out drinks to the early guests. That was it. Marvus mounted back up.
“I can see you’re well-attended-to here. We’ll just be back on time for the cookout. C’mon, Burlise!”
“But Da—”
Some of the Rominets were actually eating and socializing early. Marvus just jerked his head, and she reluctantly got back on horseback. He rode off, furiously giving orders.
“Tell Aronia what’s going on. I want us bringin’ some of our best. Something to add to that! Tell your mother…they’re outdoing us!”
Dead gods damnit, it even smelled good! He hadn’t even seen some of the dishes on the tables, but some bastard had made a spice blend so damn good his mouth was watering just inhaling it. Marvus sent a rider to tell Rabbo Golva to bring out the best stuff, not just one bottle of his sauce.
It was shaping up to be a cookout for the ages—before he heard the thumping. Then Marvus turned, and his horse reared. He had to grab the reins.
“Hell’s own horses.”
He whispered. For if the Lischelles were all about the hospitality, the manners, friendly or not—
The Terlands had come in their own way.
The first Stealth-Golem de-cloaked and walked forwards, a vast eyeball with a metal, segmented neck and thin limbs, walking over some of the screaming horses. Marvus nearly drew blade on it—when he saw the Hunter-Killers appear.
Three loping quadrupeds, each one with the head of a wolf, crawling forwards. They bounded into place and advanced as a second Stealth-Golem walked into being, shadows flickering and revealing a carved face, that of a half-Elf wearing a [Ranger]’s outfit—but a Golem armed with a shimmering bow.
They were descending on the cookout. Golems marching into place, forming a protective circle. And the Gnolls, Drakes, and Humans saw them and felt the cold eyes of Golems on them.
“Dad?”
His sons and daughters jerked Marvus out of watching. He turned.
“Hurry up, and let’s get back to the house. If you’ve got anything fancier—wear it. We’ll be there…an hour early. Hang politeness. The Drakes might not be our only problem if those Golems’re here to stay. Be on your best manners.”
He began to ride faster, heart thundering with anticipation.

“Rise, the lot of you. The Five Families are no royalty. I’m told you all own the Cowpat Plain, and produce the finest cattle in the continent.”
The Lischelles puffed up—and Mrsha almost saw Ulva smile before she hit them on the way up.
“And you ran out the nobles who owned this land. We shall address that crime. I have three petitions for the reinstatement of the noble families who claim you have squatted and profited from their lands.”
Aronia’s and Marvus’ faces froze up. It was the [Cattle Baron] who carefully bowed again.
“Begging your pardon, Lady Ulva, but they forfeited their lands during the Goblin King’s rampage. When they came back, they attempted to hang good men and women and claim all our work as their own.”
“And?”
Ulva Terland’s aura was a physical thing, like a wall, and it bore down on Marvus as he spoke. As implacable as a wall of marble to the face. He hesitated.
Aronia finished her husband’s sentence.
“…And we feel that we have a better claim to these lands than that lot, begging your pardon for our frank speech, Your Ladyship.”
She locked eyes with Ulva, and Mrsha felt her push the oncoming aura back. Marvus nudged his wife, but the two women didn’t say a word and locked gazes.
Dead gods, that looks highly uncomfortable. Is she always like this?
Mrsha asked Lord Xitegen, who was watching the showdown. He would know best, wouldn’t he? Xitegen replied softly.
“In truth? No. Only when she’s annoyed—she used to be a paranoid recluse afraid of her own shadow. This is the Ulva I heard stories of as a boy. She and Petria were the Twin Virtues. The Twin Terrors—before our time, Mrsha.”
Hmm. And does she actually make good on her threats?
“She threw me out of a carriage when I gave her backtalk.”
That didn’t sound good at all. Aronia was the one to back down and glance at Ulva’s feet, smiling and bowing again. Ulva waved them off. Beckoned, and the Golvas were next.
“It’s not how it used to be.”
Xitegen and Mrsha jumped. They turned, and an old man was eating egg salad. Or rather, a Golem with extraordinarily large breasts was serving it to him, and he just opened his mouth to eat. He had a permanent hunch, and he was definitely a Terland. Mrsha eyed the smiling half-Elf Golem, the [Lord], and glanced around for a drink.
She had a feeling she was going to need one the more she met the Terlands. She half-wished she’d skipped the cookout, but she owed it to Ilvriss to show up and be at least moral support. He’d had a hard time.
Plus, the food was amazing.
Xitegen was on his fifth rasher of bacon as he introduced the old man.
“Lord of Hearts Nouzcrat, meet Mrsha du Marquin. She’s mute and the [Princess]’ daughter, so don’t be rude.”
“A Gnoll child. What are [Princesses] getting up to these days? They weren’t [Harlots] in my time.”
The old [Lord] had about as much charisma as Ulva. The Gnoll girl offered him a paw, which he gingerly shook after a second, then held up a card.
Hello, Lord Nouzcrat. I’m adopted, so if you can read, I do hope you recant your statement. As for claims about my mother’s proclivities in the bedroom, Lyonette is not the one who sucks on Golem breasts.
Xitegen choked on his next bite of meat, and his Golems had to give him the Heimlich to save his life. The [Lord] eyed the note.
“…She reminds me of Reinharts. I saw one loitering around. And an El. We just need a Veltras and Wellfar and we’ll have all the representatives here. What are the other two Five Families doing?”
“Lady Desinee’s apparently just selling new merchandise, and Lady Damia? No clue. She’s caused trouble for me. I warned you to be polite, Great Uncle Nouzcrat.”
“Hmpf. How old are you, child?”
Nine? Who can say how old one is, Lord Nouzcrat. Time becomes meaningless, one finds.
The grumpy old guy did laugh at that.
“Hah! A Gnoll with the eloquence of a [Sophist]. That is funny enough to warrant this trip. How did you meet this one?”
“The inn, Great Uncle. It’s always the inn. Why are you eating that dreadful egg salad?”
“It’s excellent, actually.”
“Really? Seconda, secure me and Mrsha a portion—”
Nouzcrat was one of a number of Terlands mingling around, most of whom seemed snooty, aloof, and hung out with their own Golems. Even talking to the Golems, actually. It made it really hard to socialize, so Mrsha realized the Drakes and Gnolls who were trying their best were having trouble.
Mind you, the Silverfangs were a good addition to the gathering. Everyone wanted to talk to the Gnolls, if only to mention how racist they weren’t, and the Silverfangs were actually getting along with the [Ranchers]. Some were playing the horseshoe game, and Nanette apparently liked Burlise, one of the Lischelle daughters, and had already formed a huge social circle.
Including, Mrsha had to note, a certain young [Lord] who was uncomfortable, but Nanette kept dragging him into the conversation. Nouzcrat nearly spat out his next bite of egg salad.
“Aha! I knew it! There’s the Veltras! Where’s the Wellfar?”
He pointed accusatorily at Hethon Veltras, and Xitegen scratched his chin.
“Good point. They keep missing all the fun on their damn ships. But that young fellow visits The Wandering Inn often. He’s not on official business, Nouzcrat.”
“He looks old enough for it. In my day, you could speak with the authority of the Five Families as long as you could talk. We’d paddle your rear end for doing it without a damn good reason…your Great Aunt’s just reminding everyone how it works.”
“By making everyone hate us, Great Uncle? I have to live around here, you know. And having experienced Lischelle-quality beef, I don’t want to go back! It’s all very well for you lot when you go back north, but consider my position!”
Xitegen was remonstrating with Nouzcrat, and the old man frowned as he was served a piece of steak, tenderized by another Golem.
“This isn’t bad. What’s that disgusting stuff over there?”
“…Silkap? Gnollish. It’s quite tasty on crackers.”
“Ugh, foreign food. I’ll try it. Every now and then, I find something I like at these get-togethers. We stopped having them after the Goblin King died. And never with Drakes—Ulva’s just doing what she always did with Petria. One plays hard, the other soft. Ulva sweeps in with stomping Golems, then Petria offers the softer side of House Terland.”
Like Golem breasts.
“Exact—ahem.”
Nouzcrat and Xitegen coughed. The [Lord] peered at Mrsha.
“Shouldn’t children go and make mischief somewhere else? Like that boy there.”
He pointed at Sammial Veltras, who was going around and staring up at Golems and demanding to know what they did—and to show him. Please. Mrsha held up a card.
Shouldn’t old perverts go harassing Golems somewhere we can’t see them?
“Enough about my Golems!”
Nouzcrat purpled, and Mrsha, undaunted, held up another card.
I’m just giving you the same attitude your family’s giving me. I shall condescend to politeness when you do, Lord Nouzcrat. Did anyone mention to Ulva Terland that her sister’s dead so she’s just a jerk?
The [Lord] opened his mouth furiously, then hesitated. He and Xitegen eyed each other as they watched Ulva holding court. After a moment, Nouzcrat turned.
“Soffie. Get me Madrinal.”
Another Golem strode off and boobily breasted towards another [Lord]. Mrsha simply eyed the old man. He was no doubt a [Lord]; he had an aura, if not the strongest one, and he seemed intelligent enough, despite his proclivities in his Golems.
But he had been utterly absent from her understanding of Izril until now. Terlands, who lived in the north and did not touch the Izril that Mrsha understood.
If you’ve come here to evict Wall Lord Ilvriss, may I ask why Ulva’s even bothering to show up, Lord Nouzcrat? It might be easier on us all if she stopped pretending and just had the Golems kill us. Don’t forget the women and children.
The old man hesitated as Madrinal and several other of the senior members of House Terland walked over. Alorelle stared at the girl writing that in the air, but the [Lord] replied, as if forgetting he spoke to a child.
“We are not monsters.”
“Ha!”
Mrsha and Xitegen laughed at that, and the old [Lord] eyed them.
“We are not. And there are complications around any…hostilities. We have come to judge. But we are House Terland. Should we be impressed by decent food or a few [Ranchers] and a tiny expedition led by a Drake? We’ve counted, and he has only a thousand [Soldiers] at most, and plenty of [Miners].”
He did not come for war.
“Then he was foolish. We wait for something to impress us that this is worth allowing.”
The [Lord] looked down his nose at Mrsha. She wrote, unfazed by his gaze or aura.
You’ve got a hanging booger there, my friend. If you want to be awed, you missed the Archmage of Izril just now. Not our fault you showed up late.
“Hah! We’ve seen Archmages come and go. Without the class, why do they matter? Wait, why are we talking to some bratty child!”
Lady Alorelle broke in, and Lord Xitegen watched, sipping from a cup. He was familiar enough with Mrsha, and he wasn’t going to jump in this one and catch whatever she had in her back pocket.

Lady Damia Reinhart was aware…the cookout wasn’t going great. On the other hand, she could hear whispers.
“—think she’s going to insist we let a [Lord] take over our lands?”
“If she wants to do that, she’s got a hell of a fight on her hands. We ain’t letting it happen.”
Rabbo Golva was hissing with some of the other [Cattle Barons]. Marvus was worried as he glanced over his shoulder.
“She’s got those Golems, and I don’t think you can shoot them, Rabbo—”
“Golems nothing. Lasso one up and drag it into a hole and it don’t matter how big it is—it can’t beat twenty men on it with ropes. ‘Sides, it’s a big place. She won’t stick around.”
“We came here for the Drake, though. How many did he get from you, Marvus? If he’s going to raid us—”
“We can’t let him get away with it, I know. But between that damn half-Elf and the Terlands, it’s just not the right moment to push him hard. Listen, let’s figure out what the Terlands are doing. They’re complicating things…”
That was the benefit, Damia realized, to having House Terland show up. They were a problem to the [Ranchers] and took focus away from Ilvriss. Though arguably that wasn’t good because Ilvriss had two enemies, now.
Damia didn’t know what to do, but she was trying her best. The problem was, she was back in noble territory, and while she’d levelled up helping the inn…
“Hello, Lord Moltin, I’m Lady Damia Reinhart.”
“Ah, Lady Damia, greetings.”
The surprised Lord of Stone shook her hand and awkwardly made small-talk with Damia. She tried to talk up Ilvriss and the Drakes, but before she could get to that, the recently-ennobled man coughed.
“[Information Search: Damia Reinhart]. Er, and how is Lady Cecille doing? Well, I hope? Glad to have not seen—I mean, wonderful whenever we meet. And your fiancé, I mean, boyfriend, I mean br—Wernel?”
He stared in horror at something he’d just read. Damia sighed.
It transpired that when you were a minor [Lady], the one interesting fact about you was what everyone remembered. She spoke, hurriedly, as Lord Moltin wiped his hand on his jacket.
“Wernel and I aren’t seeing each other, Lord Moltin. That’s a very regrettable, er, fact that you—I’m currently working for Wall Lord Ilvriss! May I talk about his work here and why I hope House Terland will come to a peaceful resolution?”
“I, er, yes—”
Damia tried to mention cooperation between Drakes and Gnolls, point out the Silverfangs, Lyonette—but she rather feared Moltin was so focused on the factoid he’d reminded himself about that he missed the rest.
“Damnit! We have to sway them, Binevy! Maybe I’ll try Lady Ulva next.”
“I wouldn’t, Lady Damia. She’ll chew you up and spit you out.”
Binevy whispered, clearly aware of Ulva’s reputation. So was Damia, but she was groaning.
“We have to do something! All the old Terlands hate the Drakes, and I can’t sway them—”
“And why are we so set on allowing him to dig in the north? Not that I hold Ilvriss any particular bad will. But I rather think after the mess he got me into, any goodwill from the Winter Solstice has worn off.”
Damia jumped and turned. Desinee El was standing in the gathering, seeming almost as lost as Damia, sipping from a drink. She grimaced.
“Hello, Lady Damia.”
“Lady Desinee, er, hello. I thought you were lost after the cattle raid incident?”
One glare said Desinee was not happy about that, but as the lone member of her house, she and Damia were actually somewhat friendly. Especially because one look meant both recognized they were swept up in the inn’s chaos. Although Damia seemed much happier than Desinee about that.
“Let’s just say that fate has aligned such that I’m an observer—but little more for the House of El. We are not hostile towards the Wall Lord, but the interest of Walled Cities in our lands? How are you fine with it?”
“I’m a Reinhart, Desinee. Wall Lord Ilvriss has provided me with opportunities to level and earn gold, and he has not come in with wrath or violence. What else should I be wary of?”
Desinee pursed her lips thoughtfully.
“True, one could argue he’s a friendly Drake, the kind that Magnolia wanted to make peace with. Even so, it doesn’t strike you as traitorous to even envision allowing him in the north?”
“Traitorous to whom, Desinee? The last Drake we allowed north was Zel Shivertail, the Drakes’ hero who died for us. Do we not owe them a debt? Or do the Five Families forget the one war hero among Drakes even we acknowledged?”
That brought the [Artificer Lady] up short. Desinee regarded Damia, then tossed her head slightly and adjusted a hat keeping the sun from beating down on her.
“Ugh, not bad. I forgot the old Reinhart tongue was clever. Try that on the Terlands. Though they’re stubborn as Golems. And why should I help?”
Damia pressed two fingers to the side of her head, and Desinee eyed her again, but then Damia’s face lit up.
“Well, Lady Desinee, because Salazsar will simply have to sell the House of El gems at a discount. If not the whole city, House Gemscale sort of has gems in the name. Imagine a trade deal with them alone?”
Desinee’s mouth opened, and her eyes flickered. Then she produced a mini-abacus.
“That would be unthinkable, normally. We’d be inspecting each gem for cracks or deliberate—we have to buy Salazsarian gems, of course, but we go through multiple channels. There are damn [Reseller Merchants] whose entire job it is to facilitate north-south trade clandestinely for appearance’s sake.”
The younger [Lady] peered over Desinee’s shoulder, speaking sweetly like an evil [Vizir] whispering in Desinee’s ear.
“What’s the markup on that? 15%? You know those [Merchants] are using Skills. Imagine a 15% reduction on gemstone costs, Desinee. And what if he could get some Pallassian steel via his company too?”
“Eugh, what are you? Some kind of [Temptress]? Excuse me, I need to make a call. Desinee to Deilan. Hello?”
Desinee shooed Damia off, but the [Lady] followed, grinning. She heard Desinee speaking rapidly to a man who sounded disinterested at first, then very interested.
“…again, Desinee? Trade deals? That’s unconscionable. The family would riot.”
“How much of the family, Deilan? And how much if we just skipped the entire reseller’s fees? And we could get Prime Gems from House Gemscale—do they sell them?”
“They do! In fact, due to a Skill, they mine gemstones even in the north at a low rate, without searching for them! Hello, Lord Deilan. Damia Reinhart here, very eligible, unmarried [Lady] of House Reinhart. And have I mentioned that The Wandering Inn controls door travel? If you wanted anything shipped from Pallass at speed, you might arrange transit without fees.”
“Who’s that? Er, greetings—”
Desinee was shoving Damia, but gave up as Deilan began to ask more questions. And like that, Damia put another of the Five Families on Salazsar’s side.
Soft power. Or rather, she reflected, the power of one of the richest cities in the world. Inaccessible, of course, to their enemies.
Unless it was through a Drake you could trust. A Drake who could be less of a Drake at times. She saw Ilvriss walking around with briefcases in hand, and that was why she liked him too. She just didn’t know if Lyonette was seeing him or…? Maybe that would be a good way to get the [Princess]’ attention.
Either way, Damia really hoped this got her an invitation to The Wandering Inn.

Wall Lord Ilvriss was aware Ulva Terland was not relenting in her position. And he intended to, uh—wait for Nerul to get here. The [Diplomat] was racing towards Pallass with ‘a trump card’, so Ilvriss was waiting for that.
If not, he’d do his best. But he couldn’t hover around Ulva nonstop—not that she was letting him. Her Golems literally kept him at sword length, and until she wanted to talk to him, he did what he could.
Namely, going to the other parties in the cookout and making nice. He’d tried last time, socializing, not saying anything biting—but Ilvriss had realized that was a milquetoast offensive.
It didn’t work. It had just led to Marvus punching him in the face over the last few weeks. That wasn’t to say that Ilvriss should have gone in like Zail would. You see, it was a false binary, the position of being either offensive or not.
Ilvriss was a Wall Lord. A somewhat stuffy and, he had to admit, corporate class at times. No great warrior. No superb diplomat. No charming, dancing [Princess].
He copped to that. So, Ilvriss went in as he was and hoped Lyonette would bail him out. He trusted his instinct that he was doing the right thing.
Because his instincts said…don’t do this.
So Ilvriss walked over to Marvus Lischelle as the man went for a drink and held out a claw.
“Marvus. May I have a word?”
“Ilvriss. You can get one for the food. I heard there was something peculiar with the cooks—but it’s damn good food. And those Silverfangs are pretty much country-bred as they come.”
It cost the man to admit that. Rather to Ilvriss’ amazement, it felt like throwing a decent cookout had actually won points with Marvus. Or maybe it was the cattle raid?
“I’m sorry about the two bulls the other day, Marvus. I’m glad you allowed me to compensate you for that.”
“Not sorry for stealin’ three hundred of my finest cattle?”
Marvus eyed him, and Ilvriss raised his own brows. Let a bit of the restrained spice flow from his tongue.
“Honestly? Not really as I think you’ve stolen over twice that much from me in a single raid. That’s tit for tat, and any of the rest of my guilt vanished after I recalled being punched in the gut by you last week.”
Against his will, the [Cattle Baron] laughed. Then he growled at Ilvriss.
“Damnit, that’s a [Rancher]’s comment! It doesn’t change anything. You’re digging up trouble or something that doesn’t belong to you, and I don’t know what it is—but it’s still in our land.”
He jerked a thumb at the other [Ranchers] to mean them all. Ilvriss sighed.
“I’m aware of that. Though I point out this was all Drake or Gnoll lands until you drove us off them. But let’s not play the ‘whose land was it’ game, because I’ll win, Marvus. It was brought to my attention the other day that all my work really only rewards the Gemscale Corporation. Me. I’m trying to do better by my people, and yes, it occurs to me that you have a stake in this land yourself. So…here.”
He offered the briefcase, and Marvus lifted his hands.
“We don’t need more gems. Thanks—the family’s still fightin’ over who gets to make them into jewelry—but more gifts at your cookout make no sense.”
“Absolutely not more gems, Marvus. We dig those up like copper, all the time. Call this dividends from the dig. Not much, but I will give you more if we can come to amenable terms.”
Okay, the man had to at least check the briefcase and see what it held. He flipped the latches up and saw…
A pickaxe. It lay in the briefcase, encased in soft velvet custom-fit for it. It was a pretty pickaxe, but—he almost laughed at Ilvriss.
“What? Is this a trophy?”
“Nope. A piece of what we found.”
“You went diggin’ and found a pickaxe? And this sweetens the pot? We don’t dig, Wall Lord.”
Marvus lifted the pickaxe and hesitated as he felt how light it was. Ilvriss smiled.
“If you don’t want it, you’re free to refuse, Marvus. Please refuse. Give it back to Welsca, and I’m sure we can find a use for it.”
The Drake [Adjutant] appeared and seemed ready to snatch the briefcase from Marvus. Her eyes alternated between coveting the pickaxe and glaring at Ilvriss. Marvus hesitated.
“So you dug this up…? Expensive, is it?”
He looked ready to make a joke. Ilvriss just smiled sweetly.
“You’re free to investigate. Though I’d keep an eye on it when you hand it to an [Enchanter]. I hate to generalize, but some get rather light-fingered…”
“It’s one pickaxe.”
“We didn’t find that many. You’ll also notice I’m not handing out pickaxes to anyone else. Welsca, the Golva gift.”
She handed him a briefcase with a lantern in it with an utterly pained expression as if he were stealing her first child. Ilvriss had to yank twice and walked past Marvus.
“Remember that, Marvus. Though I will lie to Rabbo Golva’s face as so—Rabbo! May I present you a rather odd gift?”
He walked off, and Marvus eyed the pickaxe, then glanced around. On a hunch, he put the pickaxe back in the case and walked it over to one of his eldest sons.
“Get this to our [Mage] on the ranch right now and tell me what it does or how good it is. Got it?”
He couldn’t believe the Wall Lord would just give away…and now Marvus wanted to know what the hell the man was digging up. He cast around for Aronia, but hesitated when he saw his wife.
She was standing with Colfa, and the two sisters were alone, utterly polite, all smiles, as they chatted near the cookout. Marvus began to walk over…then decided he could socialize for a few more minutes.

Colfa val Lischelle-Drakle was hoping they didn’t slap each other at this cookout, but she was ready. However, Aronia knew it wasn’t her cookout, and Colfa hadn’t insulted her. She was stressed; Colfa could relate.
“Having fun with the Five Families?”
“Stop gloating. She could ruin us. Do you hate the family that much?”
That was Aronia for you. Colfa jerked her head back and hissed.
“You’re the one who practically disavowed me! Relax, Ulva Terland’s no fool. She knows she can’t run you all out. She’s after Ilvriss. We’re the ones in danger.”
“You just had to tie yourself to a Wall Lord. Where’s Himilt? Is your marriage in danger? Is that why you’re always here?”
“If you ever visited Liscor, you’d know he’s just dealing with the farm. Which he has to do single-handedly now everyone’s gone. He’s been preparing for the end of the rains. Training up new farmers. We have a bunch of amateurs, but we’re hoping they stay on—and Himilt loves fishing, it turns out. He’s been relaxing. He doesn’t want to be part of this, and that’s fair.”
What Colfa didn’t say was that Himilt was mostly training Vampires to learn to farm and forging cover identities—and, she suspected, finding other groups and leading them to safety. But he’d forbidden her from coming along. That hurt her, but she had to admit not even Fierre could keep up with Himilt—yet.
He did love fishing, though, and Aronia’s hostility faded.
“Empty?”
“Rivel’s run off after getting himself in trouble. He’s with a good sort, but he made a mess. Fierre’s found love and work, and Bamer passed away.”
“I’m…sorry to hear that. I should visit. It’s not far, but it feels like it. Is that door really able to take you back and forth? If you need hands, you should have asked.”
“I don’t want to be in your debt.”
Aronia hesitated, then shook her head.
“I’ll send fifteen of the lads to help you plant. Don’t call it a debt.”
“No need, we’re fine. It’s just empty these days.”
“No desire to have more children?”
Colfa thought of the long sickness, of children who’d never made it to adulthood, of learning the truth of her body—she might be healing, or maybe she’d continue being sick. Only Fierre was surely cured. She drank wine and murmured softly.
“No. I’m fine, Aronia. Lyonette’s a good friend, and I’m having fun. I went on the cattle raid. That felt like old times.”
“You just had to hit our best ranch.”
“Well, that’s the only thing that would work.”
Colfa eyed Aronia, and the two bristled…then relaxed. Aronia folded her arms and turned to stare across the horizon.
“You never told me you’d lost children. That stung worst of all, you know. I’m sorry. Was it sickness or—?”
When she turned her head, Colfa flinched. Then her eyes flashed with fury, but Aronia wasn’t wielding the knowledge as a weapon. She just seemed heartbroken. So Colfa swallowed.
“How did you know…? Who told you? Himilt?”
He’d never been here, to her knowledge. Had he written to Aronia behind her back? The Human woman just smiled, bleak.
“It was years ago, Colfa. Sometimes, I’d check on you, just by way of gossip or whatnot. No one really knew your family, so I put out a request. Bought information. There was an informant or some such in Reizmelt. They were very cautious about what they gave me. I think they looked up who I was, but then—they wrote it down. More than I’d known.”
Colfa’s eyes closed.
“Fierre. That little—she must have been just starting out. She made so many mistakes.”
“Aye. Telling me all that was wrong of her, but—daughters. I’ve buried two children. One stillborn. The other fell off a horse.”
“I’m so sorry.”
Was she supposed to reach out here? Should they hug, embrace? The urge came and went, and neither woman moved. Not here, with the cookout going. Later, perhaps, they’d find a drink. But Aronia saw Colfa glance downwards.
“It was selfish of us. Selfish to want children knowing we were…sick. Now, they’re gone, both of them. The house is empty, but perhaps it’s as well; it’s too dangerous at home.”
“My home suffers no bandits nor anyone else.”
Aronia glanced at Colfa’s too-white skin, the pointed teeth she’d never had, her red eyes. Colfa just blinked once, then turned away.
“It’s not strong enough for everything, Aronia. I like where I live.”
“City woman.”
The insult was mild. Colfa just smiled and nodded, and Aronia’s chest eased. But that left an issue just as large between them, so she brought it up as she jerked her thumb towards the [Ranchers]. Braced herself again. Aronia scowled.
“You’re bringing Marvus around. That fool can be swayed by a few gifts and a decent cookout. I know better. I thought you did, Colfa.”
“Ilvriss is no monster, Aronia. Sometimes, we’re told things about other people, and they’re just plain wrong. Drakes are good and bad, and he’s one of the best.”
“…Is he? Then if I ask you something, on your children’s lives, will you tell me the truth, Colfa? I’m asking you on family, for the sake of us growing up as sisters. Lie to me and you’re dead.”
Aronia didn’t turn, but Colfa felt her skin crawl. That…she put her cup down on a table.
“What’s gotten into you? You’ve only asked me like that once before.”
About whether I was serious about Himilt. Aronia just stood there, not letting Colfa see her face.
“There’s a half-Elf causing trouble around our lands, Colfa. Around all our lands. Did the Wall Lord send him?”
“A half-Elf? What does he look like? What does he do?”
Instantly, Colfa thought of a certain monster that Lyonette had been warned about. Aronia’s voice was hard.
“Answer the question. Did the Drake send him?”
“No. No, I swear on my children, Aronia. If that monster’s the one I’m thinking of, he’s hit all of Izril this last winter. I’ve heard from [Farmers] in Rheirgest, near Celum, and farther north than Reizmelt. He’s burned fields and plagued lands. He nearly attacked House Byres before someone ran him off.”
At last, Aronia turned, and she seemed relieved, if alarmed.
“Are you sure?”
“His name is Tolveilouka. Ring a bell?”
From the way Aronia’s face stiffened, it did. Colfa lowered her voice.
“I was told he did the same in Drake lands. He’s a true monster, Aronia. I saw him pushed—just once—and I think I’d rather see an Adult Creler than that. Don’t tangle with him.”
“It’s not us tangling with him, it’s him laying waste to entire herds!”
“What’s he done?”
The two began whispering, and Colfa grew more alarmed as she realized that the plague of Tolveilouka had come to her former home. She was searching around for Lyonette—but the [Princess] was still occupied with no less than Lady Ulva.
And worse—
Her mother.
 
——
 
Queen Ielane du Marquin was negotiating with Ulva Terland, ruler to ruler. She did this as she prepared a speech for a parade in Calanfer.
With her daughters Shardele, Ellet, and Menisi, though the last of whom was not welcome. Things were changing in Calanfer, but she stood as makeup was applied to her, speaking briskly. Ulva knew what lay behind the Queen of Diplomacy’s charming mask.
“If my daughter has offended House Terland, we shall make amends.”
“And do you speak for this Drake, Queen Marquin?”
Ulva was less blunt, but still coming at the matter like a hammer to a nail. However, the Queen of Calanfer was better than her daughter—and quite enjoying herself.
Mostly because a simmering Lyonette was quite aware of who was talking to whom and hiss-shrieking at Ushar to get her mother out of her way! However, Ielane just chuckled.
“We aren’t opposed to this version of Salazsar. You might look twice, Terland. And we shall incentivize any willingness to diplomacy on your part, despite the inconvenience.”
“With little contracts and promises you cannot afford in your war?”
Ulva snorted, and Queen Ielane was all smiles.
“Your family is not doing well in the New Lands, Lady Terland. Golems run out of mana too quickly, but there is value there, so we believe. It would behoove Terandrians and former-Terandrians to stand together, would it not?”
“I will consider the offer, but if that is the best you have…”
Ulva was rolling her eyes when Ielane spoke.
“For all her faults and, perhaps, impatience to be free of me, my daughter is capable enough. Consider allowing her a moment to speak, Ulva Terland.”
“A minute of Calanfer in your ear is as bad as a second on Kaaz’s dueling courts.”
“If Terland says so with the wisdom of Golems, what is Calanfer to argue? Trade between continents is restarting, but no trade route remains intact. Calanfer’s ports may well replace Pheislant if currents so allow. Or Nadel. Would a trade treaty between our ports suit?”
It would suit, which made Ulva grit her teeth because why was everyone pushing for this damn Drake? She muttered a farewell and hung up the scrying orb.
“Let the [Princess] wait. Let’s see if she has a temper.”
She spoke to Timekeeper, and Ulva finally took a piece of meat and chewed it—it had been thoroughly tested by Golems for poison. She chewed, swallowed—
It was annoyingly tasty. She made the Golems get her more and thought of Petria.
Petria would be circulating the tables, apologizing for her dour sister, gobbling down food, and making merry. Petria, dead.
Waking up from her grief did not diminish it, but made it sharp once more. Ulva Terland stood, alone, with nothing but the hammer of Terland’s might, none of the ability to rest and love what it was.
Goblins had taken that from her. Now, she was one half of a two-woman act. And so…she closed her eyes.
Almost time. She would give the Drake his chance. She’d seen him giving out…objects.
“Timekeeper, the quality of those artifacts?”
“Beyond modern-day, Lady Ulva.”
“So he’s giving away artifacts from the City of Purity. That’s not a Drake quality. He still stands to take the lion’s share.”
But he was giving them away to the [Ranchers]. Ulva glared; she could see one final suitcase likely meant for her. There were a lot of reasons to let him live. Monetary ones. She’d spotted El switching sides, the bastards. As for Reinharts, they were all individualists.
“Lady, ah, Ulva. May I speak to you as one member of the Five Families to an—”
And here came the boy. Hethon Veltras, and Sammial Veltras for backup. Ulva’s look fixed him in place.
“You may not, Lord Hethon Veltras. Lord Sammial Veltras, present yourself.”
Children. She recalled them from First Landing, but without Tyrion…no, they weren’t alone. Ullim and Jericha appeared with House Veltras’ guards, and Ulva nodded once at them. Protectors. Yet the boys approached of their own volition.
More courageous than before. At least, the younger one looked less like a brat. She studied them, nodded.
“Good. Poison has not done damage to either of you, nor kidnapping. Your father is a fool, struck by life and, apparently, time. You are young, and that is forgivable. However, you will not speak to me with the name of Veltras.”
“But we—may we speak to you as [Lords] of House Veltras, then, Lady Ulva?”
Sammial seemed ready to talk, but Hethon put an arm out and tried again. Ulva Terland eyed him.
“That is decent. I grant you the same accord I grant Lady Damia Reinhart and Lady Desinee El, then.”
“Thank you, Lady Ulva.”
“You are welcome, boy. Timekeeper, take these nuisances aside.”
She hid a smile as the Golem instantly moved to shuffle them off. Hethon got what was meant and deflated, but Sammial…she’d wondered if the boy had the old Veltras temper, and sure enough, it exploded before Ullim could grab him.
“Stop being so mean to Lyonette and that Wall Lord guy! Everyone’s telling you not to do something stupid, stupid! Can’t you hear?”
Everyone in earshot froze as Ulva’s head turned. She peered down at the boy, who took two steps behind Ullim.
“I’m a kid. You can’t get mad at me for being a kid.”
He announced, and she snorted.
“I can have you held upside down and beaten like a sack of grain, boy. That temper will earn you trouble if you don’t control it. You remind me of your mother, Salva.”
The two boys froze at the name of the late [Lady] of House Veltras. Sammial hesitated.
“…And?”
“I didn’t care for her. Watch your tongue. I have heard you, Veltras. Begone.”
For some reason, that provoked silence, and Sammial was obediently shepherded off. Ulva sat, scowling around.
Where was the Wall Lord and [Princess]? She’d pushed them, and she’d heard the [Diplomat]—were they that afraid of her? She was about to instigate the confrontation when the thing she didn’t expect hit her. She’d been warned.
But you had to admit, no one expected the little Gnoll girl to hit you that hard.
 
——
 
The first clue that Ulva had was when she saw Nouzcrat. The old man was being carried by the half-Elf Golem he loved so much. Unable to stand.
Or engaging in some kind of nuzzling that she was not going to allow in sight of the non-Terlands. She was about to snap at him to get down when she saw the Golem put him down on some chairs and another produce a handkerchief. He was…crying.
Old men cried all the time. She was searching for the reason when another [Lord] stepped away. He was shaking his head.
Madrinal, now, he was no coward. No great, shining leader, but she could trust him to do something hard and see it done, even if it wasn’t perfect. He did not weep, but he appeared rattled.
Then she traced the trajectory of his footsteps and saw the commotion. There…was one of the two people that Ulva had truly come for.
One was that Drake who’d worn Petria’s face, but that was a separate matter to the Wall Lord. Private.
Yet Petria’s ghost had claimed that if there was a debt owed, it was to this girl. In truth, Ulva had been disappointed to see the girl wandering around with nothing more than a kilt and bowtie. But she’d taken her eyes off Mrsha, and like a good sucker punch, the Gnoll had waited until everyone wasn’t paying attention.
She’d hit Nouzcrat with everything she had. And Madrinal. Now she was amidst the Terlands, swinging. Laying them out.
Mostly metaphorically. However, Ulva saw one of the younger Terlands actually sag, as if someone had kicked them. And Lady Damia was amidst them, dragging over the only Terlands who’d listen to her.
The young ones. Younger than Xitegen, young adults, teenagers excited for the trip south. They were the ones fascinated by the Gnolls and Drakes. Agog with Zelkyr’s Golems. Ulva paid as much attention to them as the buzzing of flies. None of them but Xitegen had seen war or had levels.
But they all saw Mrsha, and unlike the older Terlands, who went spinning away, downed in a punch, they seemed drawn to her like fireflies.
What was it? Ulva craned her neck, then strode forwards, the Golems clearing a path. Now Mrsha was throwing paws.
She caught everyone. [Ranchers]. Rabbo Golva backed away and fell over a table as if he’d seen a ghost. Face white.
She was even attacking her own side, if by accident. More than one Gnoll and Drake were backing away from her. Lady Desinee caught a hit and just fell forwards. Captain Todi, cursing, had to grab her. He was one of the only people immune to what Mrsha was throwing down, like the rest of the inn’s staff.
Ulva Terland passed by Elia Arcsinger and stopped.
“Elia. Why are you working here?”
“Lady Ulva. I’m acting as a guard for The Wandering Inn and Princess Lyonette.”
“…For her? Why? If you need gold or you have debts, I’ll settle them.”
For the woman who’d killed the Goblin King, Ulva could do that, even if Elia was no hero of ages. But the half-Elf just bowed.
“I’m on duty, and I should not distract you, Lady Ulva. I am happy in my post. I am levelling.”
“Hmph. Golems hear you, then.”
Ulva Terland passed by the one person in this gathering she had time for, and then she saw what Mrsha was holding. The Gnoll child wasn’t really punching people.
It just felt like it. She simply stood there.
[Survivor of Fates]. Doombearer. She could have spoken with the authority of The Wandering Inn or a Gnoll of the tribes. Or just a [Druid]’s wrath.
But she wasn’t any of those things. Not fully. She was just a child…so what she had, she borrowed. As she had been allowed. Because she’d been there.
The girl took something and held it up in her paws. From one of her many old classes.
[Emberbearer].
She held a pawful of pink flames, and when Ulva Terland gazed into it, she saw Petria’s face. The winds blew as the fire blazed, reflected in Mrsha’s eyes, and then Ulva felt the air catch her face and melt it away—
 
A younger [Lady] stood with her twin sister, lifting a thin, light wand. Not a mage’s wand, but something else. She stood at the head of a line of Golems. Across from her, she could see House Veltras’ horses pawing at the ground.
Afraid. But Linter was just waiting, lance couched, as Ulva snapped.
“Where are the Reinharts and Wellfars? Cowards!”
Not a single one of their war-carriages? Three of the Five Families would have to do. Let three be enough. For answer, there was a shout.
“Reinhart will be here, trust! Wellfar is sailing upon Zeres! Terland, El, and Veltras will hold them here!”
“Trust a Reinhart, Fulviolo?”
Ulva sneered back, but Petria shouted.
“If we have you two at our backs, then we’ll carve through the Drakes and send them fleeing across the Bloodfields! Make ready! Ulva, prepare to conduct the Golems! [Awaken, Hearts of Stone]!”
She lifted the twin of her sister’s wand in her hand and flicked it, and Ulva saw flames following the head of the House of El. Fulviolo and his sister, Maviola. A burning standard behind their armsmen. Her head rose, and she felt fear in her heart.
“That damn Drake is throwing his troops across the sky. Look.”
The sky was a single thunderhead. She could see Wall Lord Eschowar’s aura of lightning mixed with it. Bolts of lightning were stabbing down as the Drakes marched across the Bloodfields. 
“Hold him here. If we break, he’ll spill across our lands and tear everything to bits again.”
Petria was speaking, and Ulva called out.
“[Awaken, Hearts of Stone]! Thunder for House Terland!”
Then they were advancing at a walk as House Veltras streamed past them. Ulva Terland saw a female [Lancer] riding next to Linter. His wife, Celica. How could Ulva have forgotten?
It was the last time the [Lord] and [Lady] of House Veltras would ride to war. Her final battle. And then there was thunder, and Ulva—
 
—blinked. Time snapped back upon her, and the fire of glory blazed in Mrsha’s paw. Echoing a lifetime of it.
“Ah. That’s not Maviola’s fire.”
That was all Ulva said. It struck everyone around the Gnoll. Lord Xitegen himself had stepped back, a brave man not willing to see his own family in those flames. Ulva Terland gestured, and Golems moved the audience away. Shielding them.
“Lady Ulva. Would you like us to nullify the Skill? It has an emotional component.”
“I am not to be beaten by a single flame, Timekeeper. Leave us.”
The Golem nodded. Ulva Terland walked forwards. The girl stood there.
Hello, Lady Ulva. You’re pretty rude. But where are my manners? I am Mrsha du Marquin of The Wandering Inn. I greet you in the same spirit you greet us.
Ulva almost smiled.
“You are too young and no true royal of Calanfer to speak thusly to me, girl. Calanfer dares not speak to me that loud.”
Then I am just Mrsha. I dare speak to you as myself. Or is House Terland too proud to listen to anyone who does not have a nation behind them?
“Clever. Did your mother teach you to say that?”
No, I came up with it myself. I enjoy speaking to haughty people. Hail, Terland.
Hail. Ulva stopped and glanced around. Then she sneered at Xitegen.
“‘Hail’, she says, as if she were a Dragon. I know I have been alive too long when a child has more eloquence than the heir to House Terland.”
“Dear Aunt, I am good at running, warfare, and eating. A fourth capability is beyond me.”
Xitegen drew himself up, and she snorted. Then Ulva came back at the child. She hadn’t meant to—Mrsha was a child. But she was starting to actually annoy Ulva.
“You are a brat holding someone else’s fire. A single Skill may move the hearts of my family, who let Golems shelter them from splinters and aught else. Not I. Is that all?”
Mrsha tilted her head. She wrote as she clenched her fist over the pink flame and it turned into wisps. That made Ulva’s heart sting, and she grew more annoyed for how cavalierly the girl treated the flame. Or so she assumed. Because Mrsha held out her paw. Like a [Stage Magician], she smiled.
Not just that, Lady Ulva. I can see you are made of sterner stuff than your family. My [Innkeeper] left me with many flames. That one is made of beautiful pain. This one? Just grief. Have you come to kill the people I love again?
Then the blue flame roared, and her paw quivered. For it was heavy—and it blazed between the two. Ulva threw up her hands with a cry.
Timekeeper smothered the flame with one hand, moving so fast that it bloomed for just a second, a true inferno, before he gently covered the girl’s paw. That was enough. Ulva shielded her eyes as Chema caught her, then snapped.
“Away! The day I need a Golem to fight my battles for me with a child is the day I die!”
“She is using flames of memory on you, Lady Terland.”
“And? I have seen those before, girl.”
Ulva poked a trembling finger at Mrsha. In response, the girl flicked her paw, and Ulva tensed. But the third flame that Mrsha produced was the hardest. It made Ulva squint and hold up her hand. It did not burn her, but it was so damn bright…
A grey flame. A grey scythe of hard fire etching itself upwards.
Mercy. And it was this flame the girl held between them.
I’m sure you have, Lady Terland. I’m just reminding you since you seem to have come from House Terland without any of this fire in your heart.
“How dare you.”
The girl stood there as the [Princess] and Wall Lord froze from where they were setting up. A little witch cheered her sister as everyone read. But all Mrsha wrote, with a smile, was this:
I’m just a girl. I’ll leave the big talk for you high-falutin’ adults. You shouldn’t need a child to help you. Just, sometimes, speak a bit of wisdom to fuddy old people. All I have is fire. A little flame. Does it mean nothing to you?
Ulva Terland’s throat rasped, and she was chuckling. Holding a hand over her rapidly-beating heart, and she saw the Lady of El riding north, a flaming flag in her hands. For the last time Ulva had ever seen her. That had been the truest, most beautiful goodbye.
“No. Lady Firestarter was my generation. My time. I remember her, and her glory was gold. She threw it across the sky and set the world aflame in victory. You met the final spark. She would have burned down the High Passes if she had gone there in her youth. Is that all you have to show me? A memory?”
The girl wrote with a glowing paw in the air.
Just a reminder where she left pieces of her fire, Lady Ulva. I am a Doombearer, a sign of the changing era of Gnolls. Will you finish the slaughter of Plain’s Eye?
“No. I have never considered Gnolls sworn enemies as Drakes are. Why even ask?”
Ulva knew she was playing into the Gnoll’s game, but she walked forwards, because she was enjoying this. Mrsha tilted her head, smiling slightly.
Because it was Wall Lord Ilvriss who took Fissival to battle at the Meeting of Tribes. It was he who went against the plans of the Walled Cities to weaken their enemies. Tarring him with the same brush as all Drakes seems foolish. I will not mention the Winter Solstice, or his other deeds, for I am sure you weighed all that carefully when you tried to kill him. But I will say Zel Shivertail’s name to you. Because I knew him, and he went to save Humans.
“He went for Reinhart. I am Terland.”
She felt like she was giving ground. To a child? Mrsha wrote.
And I am Mrsha. You all look pretty much the same to me from afar. Frankly, I don’t think Zel cared. Someone asked, and he went. House Terland’s memory is as old as Golems. Old feuds. Old hatred of Drakes, and I get that. They suck.
“Hey.”
Shut up, Dramm. I get it, Lady Ulva. But in the long memory of Terlands, has there never been a Drake worth talking to? Or did you think to kill him and never speak? Do you want to continue this state of affairs forever? Reinhart is trying to build a wall to break more down. Does Terland listen to no one but Terland?
“Enough.”
