Ulva whispered, and the grey flame of mercy winked out. The tugging at her vanished, but the words did not, and she could remember more than a goldfish. Timekeeper lifted his head as the ticking of his heart extinguished the flames. Mrsha eyed him.
Whoa. Your Golems are cooler than Xitegen’s.
“I resent that.”
The [Lady] and girl ignored the others. Ulva spoke down to Mrsha.
“When one stops selecting Golems based on physical attractiveness, they find the true worth of Golems, girl. You might make for a decent Terland.”
I’m not up for adoption.
“I don’t believe I asked. Enough, though. You’ve made your point. Let adults speak indeed. One last thing.”
Ulva was motioning, turning away, when she swung her head back. Her voice rasped.
“I’m told…I owe you a favor. On behalf of someone else. But I have always paid my sister’s silly debts. If I told you to ask for a wish, would you use it for this?”
Mrsha went still, and no one understood what Ulva meant—but the girl did. And her eyes filled with guilt. She hesitated, then shook her head and wrote.
No. Not for this.
“No? You may not like what I do next. I am not convinced that Drake should stay, even if he might live.”
Ulva whispered, and her family stirred, listening. But the girl just wrote with a faint smile.
I don’t want to sway your decision, Ulva Terland. I’d rather save the favor, if I’m allowed one, for when it really matters. Ilvriss is a big boy. He’ll be fine. I’m just a ridiculously cute little girl. Besides…
Her face fell.
If there’s a favor to be owed, I think we’re quits at best. I didn’t save her. I could have.
That last blow made Ulva nearly fall as she stepped away, but she kept her composure. Turned, with a snort.
“The House of Terland does not need saving by children. Well then. Thank you, on her behalf.”
She walked away before the girl could say something else so casually painful. And Ulva wondered what made a girl write like a Djinni mixed with a little [Sage] and a child all in one.
“Timekeeper? Is she some kind of possessed child? Was she speaking to someone else? Soulsplit? Soulsundered? Something like that?”
She turned, and the Golem regarded Mrsha. It spoke slowly.
“I detect some-thing, Lady Terland. But it is just her, entirely. She is simply a child.”
“A child?”
“Some grow old fast-er than others, Lady Terland.”
“Like Xitegen. Witness her, Timekeeper.”
“Yes, Lady Terland.”
Ulva walked away, unwilling to engage a little girl a fraction of her age of all the beings here. But even despite the wounds she’d taken, she thought—
So it was definitely real. So that was her, and that land waits for me.
What a beautiful thing to know. What a relief.
Thank you.
Behind her, the girl with two souls comingled bowed with all the knowledge of what waited afterwards. Ulva thought she might still fear death, dying. But what came after might be beautiful. That knowledge could change her forever, but for this moment, she waited.
Then it was Lyonette and Ilvriss’ turn. And so the [Lady] observed as the two came to another traditional part of the cookout. She observed them with the memory of Terlands. The memory of Golems—
Who didn’t actually ever remember seeing what came next.
 
——
 
Duke Rhisveri Zessoprical felt bad. So bad he didn’t want to get out of bed and, in a sense, hadn’t.
He was curled up in his rooms as he sent his simulacrum into the world. By now, everyone knew he was ill, and yet he’d dragged himself out here.
He’d made up some kind of excuse and hired a Courier’s boat to insinuate there was a reason for him to be able to attend. Throw in a flying carpet and it was logical he’d have made it all the way here, right?
The [Princess] had not invited him, but he’d heard there was trouble with the Terlands. And Rhisveri was no idiot. Lyonette would mess it up without help, and knowing her, she’d invited the children into the range of a Golem.
He was stumbling around the party as a Golem followed him.
“A magical proxy has appeared. Significant magical grade, just below simulacrum-level. Alert. Alert.”
“What? Shut up. Your face is a simulacrum. I’m a projection, idiot. Who makes simulacrums?”
“A projection has appeared at significant range. Estimating magical levels—”
He slowed, dizzy, feverish, and found a little boy staring up at him. Rhisveri muttered.
“I’m here because of the children. Think of the children.”
He glanced around for the two brats—then Sammial Veltras spoke.
“You’re the guy who stripped Ryoka naked. That’s him, Ullim. And he tried to kill me.”
Everyone turned. Rhisveri froze as he focused on Sammial. And he recalled his sins. He managed to reply, after a moment, as horrified Terlands turned to find the kidnapper of the young Veltras [Lord]—who’d started a war—standing right there.
“I…that was probably a bluff. I don’t recall. Sometimes, you forget they matter. Children. Soldiers. Especially if they’re not yours. Some are always dying. Just not in my kingdom. That’s the goal. I’m sorry.”
Sammial Veltras studied Rhisveri and decided he didn’t need nightmares about the Duke anymore. The huge, floppy, purple talking penis-worm that sometimes appeared in his dreams—he had no idea what that was about since his memories had been altered. But this man wasn’t that scary, sweaty and weird as he was.
Sammy nodded.
“I forgive you. But he doesn’t.”
He pointed, and Rhisveri turned his head right in time for Ullim to punch him off his feet. He went over.
“Not ag—”
Then Ullim and Jericha were kicking him, and he was trying to crawl away. Right before a horrified Lord Nouzcrat called out.
“Stop, stop!”
His Golems separated the Duke of Ailendamus from the furious retainers of House Veltras. Jericha and Ullim hesitated, blocked by Golems. Nouzcrat pointed.
“Let the Golems do it.”
Rhisveri was getting up when one of the Golems punched him. He still got up after that, which was highly disconcerting to anyone who knew how hard he’d been hit. He walked over and leaned on a man, who patted him on the shoulder.
“‘Scuse me, sir. Are you some [Lord] who kidnapped a child and then threatened to kill him?”
“Only once.”
“Right, thank you.”
Nithle Calabie nodded, then threw a [Horsekick Punch] and sent Rhisveri twirling back into a kick from one of the Gnolls.
 
——
 
“What’s going on there? It had better not be a fight. Ser Dalimont, check it out.”
Lyonette was stressing as she and Ilvriss stretched and got ready for their moment. Ilvriss muttered.
“It’s probably just drunk hotheads. That kind of thing happens.”
She glowered as she glanced at the band, who’d been playing a mix of songs on request from people. Mostly classic Izrilian music for the nobility, but one of their number was none other than Songmistress Calla. She got around, and she’d volunteered to lead this band since she could conduct—she could [Summon: Sheet Music] for any song you requested.
Hearing a miniature orchestra riffing on one of the Singer of Terandria’s songs was odd, but Lyonette thought there was something to it. So did Songmistress Calla, but she was preparing for the big moment. Lyonette hissed at Ilvriss.
“We’ve only got a few moments left after this! The cake and then…if we don’t change Ulva’s mind, it’ll be terrible, Ilvriss! We need a united front!”
“I know, but we’re doing this dance because you insisted.”
He hissed back at her as they walked over to a cleared space, and a few heads turned. The Terlands did not look interested, the older ones, at least. And the younger ones were classically shy—
Yes, dancing was customary at formal events, but to the nobility, the cookout didn’t feel like the place for it. The [Ranchers], by contrast, were puzzled and worried. Because they expected noble dancing, and none of them knew any. Thusly, the only group that would think to dance would be the hosts. Lyonette blinked.
“Wh—but it’s your tail on the line!”
“Yes, but you were so insistent—I had to oblige you! Nevermind, what’s done is done. If I die, I’ll just blame you with my dying breath, deal?”
He adjusted his collar as she colored.
“You—you—how dare you humor me! We have priorities, Ilvriss; you could have said!”
Dame Ushar was calling people’s attention to the floor.
“Ladies, Gentlemen, Golems, we have an occasion to dance. I believe Her Highness and Wall Lord Ilvriss will demonstrate, in hopes of unity between north and south and all parties present?”
The Drake rolled his eyes as he stretched.
“Yes, how dare I support my friend? And she’ll definitely let the matter go if I beg my apologies, not hold it over my head forever. Because she’s such a reasonable person.”
“You—you—hold still when I’m stepping on your toes!”
They made for a cute couple. The two stood in front of the hidden cake, and it wasn’t only a certain half-Elf who thought that. But he was just waiting, and no one had spotted him yet.
All eyes were on Lyonette and Ilvriss. Aronia and Marvus had linked up, and they’d been whispering to each other, but they folded their arms.
No one was joining Lyonette or Ilvriss for the dancing. A few of the Gnolls and Drakes might have, but they were wary—they didn’t know the dances either.
If this was meant to be inclusive…Ulva Terland raised her brows and half-turned to Mrsha.
This is what you set up?
Mrsha just shrugged, cheeks full of food. She was done adulting. She and Xitegen were creating the forbidden meat bowl, which involved a piece of every kind of meat stuffed into a bowl and drizzled with three of your top sauces. You cut down one layer and took one huge bite with a fork.
…All of that was background. The crowd were all skeptics, but they were watching as a rather fast beat began to come from the band, who started sweating. A [Violinist] checked her musical sheet and then began to activate a speed skill.
Because they were playing that song. The song that made even Terland nobles blink. It was a country song, a commoner’s song—and it was fast, aggressive.
The song of broken heels and shattered egos.
The hardest dance known to Lischelles.
The one, the only—
The Highstepper.
“They can’t be serious.”
Nithle Calabie recognized the song, and he and his wife turned from kicking Duke Ow Stop That or whatever his name was. They left him behind as Rhisveri crawled away, and they’d heard of the Wall Lord and [Princess] failing the dance.
Anyone their age did without cheating. But they were doing it.
At—this fancy cookout? In front of the Terlands?
Yes. The familiar notes of the Highstepper filled the air, and it was no less fast than anyone remembered. If anything, Songmistress Calla was playing it faster than usual because she had just been told to play it. Not that anyone was crazy enough to dance to the rhythm.
The [Princess] was counting to the beat, bouncing on her toes in her…boots? Aronia choked.
“Those are the boots I gave her! They’ve painted them!”
“Steady. It don’t look that bad. There’s no way they’re trying—are they?”
Marvus was eyeing Ilvriss. You had to practice like a fiend, even with help! There was no way some Wall Lord would do that, would he? Marvus knew the dance because he’d practiced it all his life as a boy. But these two—
Lyonette turned and took Ilvriss’ hand as the crowd watched, murmuring. Skeptical Terlands, whispering [Ranchers], sons and daughters of Salazsar, Silverfangs—and one beat-up Wyrm.
He found an empty spot in the crowd and limped forwards. Then he saw her. Turning her head and smiling nervously up at the purple-scaled Drake who gave her a nod. Then…
“Oh.”
Rhisveri mumbled.
He saw them begin to dance.
 
——
 
The [Princess]’ and Wall Lord’s feet flashed down the aisle of watchers. They were high-stepping, high kicking, a dance that showed off their calves and ankles. Immodest! Unladylike!
To any Calanferian watching, it was unthinkable for a [Princess] to perform a dance like this. Xinthe was recording from under a table, jaw dropped.
And yet—the dance was impressive! Lyonette did a heel turn and skidded left. She and Ilvriss grabbed their belts, and their legs were kicking as they line-danced sideways. So fast that you could barely see their feet move. Then they linked arms and began to step—
“Dead gods! They’re doing it!”
The Lischelles were in uproar. The Terlands were just impressed. They had dancing Golems who couldn’t perform that well.
Seeing someone, anyone, performing an activity at a high level was inspiring. Eye-catching. But the [Princess] and Wall Lord were nobility, de facto; they didn’t have to work hard.
…But they were dancing. Ilvriss’ face was a study of concentration as he let go of Lyonette’s arm and moved into another rhythm of the dance, and his tail swayed along with his legs, so fast it barely touched the ground.
It was the [Princess] who wore a smile on her face and seemed to be laughing, even though a single sound never left her lips. She was breathless, moving from position to position.
They were—they were doing it. Aronia’s mouth was open, and Colfa was clapping to the beat, cheering.
“You can do it, Lyonette! Don’t mess up now!”
Sideways again, moving past the guests, and Marvus heard cheering. From Burlise! She and his family were cheering the Highstepper on! How not?
You cheered anyone who tried it, even if they messed up in three steps. For the daring. For the courage and fun of it. And you bought them a drink…
Just not the Wall Lord and [Princess]. But Marvus watched and saw, across from them, Ulva Terland eying the Highstepper. She was tapping her foot to the beat, amazingly on-rhythm. And he thought to himself—
They’re dancing our dance in front of Terlands and the other Five Families. It was intentional. No one was making the [Princess] and Wall Lord choose that dance. They could have done any Salazsarian or Calanferian dance. But they’d chosen the music that the [Ranchers] knew.
No matter how Marvus turned it around in his head, he couldn’t figure out an angle that didn’t make that somewhat respectful. Learning the Highstepper…
“Aronia?”
“Shush, Marvus.”
“I’m just sayin’, if he’s giving us something worth having—”
“Shush, they’re dancing. Don’t interrupt them now.”
His wife was just watching. No matter how fast the Highstepper went, at the end, when the young woman and Wall Lord turned and clasped hands to bow…they didn’t falter.
Start to finish. Marvus and Aronia began to clap. Then caught themselves, glanced at each other, and folded their hands.
“There’s no way someone can dance well enough to mend this kind of bridge. This isn’t a fairytale.”
“That’s right. And we’re not the villains of a storybook.”
She added, and Marvus nodded. But the cheering continued, and the two saw a breathless Lyonette and Ilvriss shaking hands.
“I’m going to give Burlise an earful after this. Look at her, fawning over a [Princess].”
“Right, because she shouldn’t do that.”
This time Aronia stepped on Marvus’ foot. He protested.
“She is a [Princess] when all’s said and done, Aronia. Admit it, if it weren’t for the fact that she’s against us, you’d be trying to get on her good side. Well, that and Colfa’s with her, and you two haven’t made up.”
“What? Who said that?”
Aronia spun and poked a finger up at him. Marvus raised his hands.
“Er…you did. Colfa’s on the outs.”
“She’s my sister. We might fight, but I’m not having you badmouth her, Marvus!”
He threw up his hands.
“Argh! You two made up and didn’t tell me? Don’t point that finger at me, woman. It’s not my fault for supporting you and not knowing when I need to switch my tune up!”
Aronia’s lips quirked because she had to admit he was right there. She sighed, and they turned to regard the couple—only to realize Lyonette was talking with Burlise and some of the other [Ranchers], breathless. The married couple sidled over and eavesdropped.
“Thank you, thank you, Burlise, isn’t it? I was terrified we’d mess it up. It was one of two dances we were practicing…I’m just embarrassed.”
“Embarrassed about what? That was amazing! Ma and Pa can’t do it better than that!”
The two older Lischelles’ glowers of wrath promised Burlise was going to find herself on some hard chore duty after this. Even if it was true, you didn’t admit it. However, Lyonette just hung her head. She stuck out one of her boots.
“I…used a trick. These boots. I made Aronia’s gift to me into an artifact with a Skill.”
“You did what?”
Aronia jumped into the conversation despite herself, and Lyonette had to explain how she’d made her boots to dance. But she was crestfallen, red-cheeked from her exertions as she nodded at Ilvriss.
“Ilvriss managed to do the dance all on his own! I needed help. There was a time I could’ve done the dance myself, but I can’t anymore. Realizing that was…hard.”
Despite herself, Aronia’s face softened, and she hesitated, then hugged Lyonette with an arm. The [Princess] blinked, but Aronia patted her on the arm.
“Miss Lyonette, everyone cheats at the Highstepper. Marvus? He makes the old Fleethoof Grill. That’s a Skill-food you eat, and it lets you dance right. Rabbo’s wife has dancing socks, don’t you, Aubrie? As for Rabbo, he just drinks—we all need help. I’m mightily impressed you picked it up so fast anyways!”
“Well, we practiced nonstop. It was a bit of an obsession. Even the Five-Step isn’t as bad on the shins! I must have kicked Ilvriss’ legs bloody.”
Lyonette’s confession made everyone smile and relate their own pains when learning the dance. No one liked a genius. And there were some who could pick up the Highstepper within a week or just a single try. Colfa was one of those geniuses, darn her.
But Aronia was calling for a seat.
“Your legs must be killing you. Have a seat. Marvus, you might need to start the Fleethoof Grill. Can’t have our guests thinking we can’t answer to that challenge!”
“Already on it, darling!”
He was indeed manning a grill and preparing the signature blend. A [Chef] with dark skin and an eyepatch was watching him covertly, despite her husband’s attempts to get her to leave.
“Dear, you promised—”
—Background noise. Lyonette was thanking Aronia as she lowered herself onto a stool stiffly. One of the Terland [Ladies] who’d come to ask about the song exclaimed when they saw Lyonette’s sweaty makeup reveal cracked skin.
“What’s that?”
“Argh, my condition—I can dance two more times, but my body still doth protest.”
“I never did ask about that. Is it a sickness?”
“No, just from my class. It’s complicated—”
“You wear it very well. I can’t even tell about the cracking, normally. What kind of makeup do you wear at your age, Lyonette? You look half your age!”
Eni Calabie commented jealously, and Lyonette hesitated.
“Makeup? Mostly, it’s just the cracks…half my age? I should hope not. I’m only nineteen.”
No one here had performed the Winebreath Blaster so far. The oft-overused power, rumored to be the final missing Dragonbreath—was not performed by Aronia now.
She just dropped her cup, and it splashed onto the ground.
“Say what? You—you’re nineteen?”
Burlise had spun around, having nearly crept out of the conversation with her mother and the adults present. Only—Lyonette brushed at her face.
“I don’t look that much older, do I?”
“N—but—your aura and the way you hold yourself! And you have children!”
Everyone whirled to look at Nanette and Mrsha and do some very worried math when Lyonette laughed.
“I didn’t birth them myself! I used to be far more spry, but I got this class just a bit ago…Nanette, do I look old?”
“Yup.”
The witch’s comment hit Lyonette and everyone older than her by proxy. Aronia was aghast. She’d thought Lyonette was at least in her thirties and using illusions or alchemy! The fact that a girl Burlise’s age was negotiating with the Wall Lord…
Then she leaned down.
“Wait, that Wall Lord’s not your age, is he?”
“Ilvriss? No, quite a bit older. Mid-forties? He holds it well, but—”
“My dear, he’s twice your age! You should pick someone else, let alone the fact that he’s a Drake—”
This time, it was Lyonette’s turn to avoid spitting her drink out.
“Ilvriss? We’re not together!”
“You’re not?”
“I’m just helping him out! We only dance together, and he’s a friend of Erin—let me clear this all up.”
Lyonette tried to, but no one was in a position to instantly believe her. The fact that she was nineteen sent Aronia off to have a small crisis. Colfa went over to pat her on the shoulder. Meanwhile, Ilvriss turned with an outraged expression on his face.
“Lyonette, I’m in my thirties, you—you—mathless Human!”
He roared. Lyonette was laughing until Burlise seized her hands.
“You’re my age! I’m actually three years older’n you! How’s that possible? Here I thought my parents were the ones who needed talking to you—”
She was agog. And Lyonette felt older than Burlise! But she grinned as she tapped her boots together.
“I’m just sorry we couldn’t talk, Burlise. This is an important matter—”
“Beating up Drakes and getting beat up? Bah. That’s cow shit on their faces! We’ll never let ‘em live it down, Mom nearly killing you with that slap and you being half her age! And all of them showing off with the Highstepper when that Wall Lord did it cold! He did, right?”
“Unassisted? Yes, and I used to be able to do it…but it’s a hard dance. I can see why everyone cheats. Ilvriss is just gifted.”
Lyonette was trying to downtalk herself, conscious that claiming she could do the Highstepper without magical help when ‘everyone cheated’ was a bad look. However, at her words, Burlise and the other young people gathered around her hesitated. Burlise turned, eyed her mother, then whispered.
“Well, that’s just what they say to make themselves feel better. No one their age can do it. Too heavy, too old, too outta shape. But you think everyone needs help t’do it?”
She stepped back challengingly, and Lyonette remembered a comment Burlise had made at the last cookout. She gave Burlise a sharp look.
“But why didn’t you do it last time…?”
One of the young Golva boys rolled his eyes.
“‘Cause they were busy humiliating you. They don’t let us show off because we can do it better’n they can. You want proof?”
He stuck out his chin, and Lyonette eyed him before standing.
“There’s no doing the Highstepper better. Is there?”
A grin spread over the younger [Ranchers]’ faces. Burlise strode over to the band and tapped Calla on the shoulder.
“Hey, Miss, give the Highstepper some juice and make it faster! You heard the [Princess]! Who’ll dance with me?”
One of the Golva boys she knew strode over, and she took his hand. Then more pairs emerged from the crowd. They lined up, and Lyonette blinked—then she was standing.
“Ilvriss! Ilvriss!”
“What? Oh no. No, Lyonette, we have to deal with Ulva Terland. We don’t have time for—think of my thighs. My thighs—”
He tried to get away, but the [Princess] snagged him. Ilvriss was the oldest dancer on the floor. The younger members of each [Rancher] clan filled the floor, not the heads. When the music picked up—even faster—
Well, half the couples made a mistake and went sprawling or tumbled down with screams or curses, to laughter and cheering.
But the rest kept on dancing around the fallen, and then everyone was clapping. Indeed, at the sight of the Highstepper, there were people asking for a slower version to practice.
The Silverfangs were taken with the dance, even if it looked silly to them. There were brave Drake volunteers, and even, to the surprise of all—Lady Ulva Terland especially—
Terlands.
 
——
 
The dancing of the Drake and [Princess] wasn’t lost on Ulva. Diplomatic and all that. What Calanfer was good at.
It won the [Ranchers]’ approval. Not hers.
So a Drake could dance. So what?
She was determined to be unimpressed and watched the pairs dancing, imagining Petria and her trying it. Ulva sourly ate more meat and then heard cheers, applause—gasps.
A Terland boy was urging a partner onto the dance floor. Not one she knew.
A child, which was to say, someone younger than Xitegen. She didn’t deal with Terland children. They were to be not seen and not heard, and especially not around her. If Petria had lived…
But this boy was familiar to her for two reasons. Mostly—she recognized his serving Golem, who was a dancing-capable model. Able to remove limbs, fashioned after the Dullahans.
Most Golems were made in Human images, but they had a variety of Golem species except for Drakes—given the animosity, Terlands didn’t want Drake Golems, and the ones they had possessed had been used as agents in Drake lands over the ages.
But this Dullahan Golem was a partner to the boy. Bedpartner? It was a dark thought, but that was her family. Ulva asked, and to her surprise, Timekeeper answered in the negative.
“She is Dancer Golem Hidre, Lady Ulva. Assigned to Lord Chovn after his injuries.”
“What—ah. Yes. I recall now.”
A rare accident in Terland lands. Who was that fool who’d been with the boy when he was barely six?
“Bein, yes. One of the branch families. Didn’t he land himself in trouble twice? He was there when this boy lost his arms.”
Freak accident involving one of the mechanical windmills that Golems operated. They’d been playing in the mill when the Golem had begun working, and Chovn had survived—but his limbs had been caught in the gears of the mill.
No potion but a lost miracle would have restored that. So, the boy, who was, what, seventeen? He had Golem arms.
Hidre, the Dancing Golem, had been assigned to him to teach him how to use his limbs. Learning to use a prosthesis was hard. However, it seemed Lord Chovn had recovered well—Ulva blinked as he took the Golem’s hand.
The Dullahan Golem was smiling at him as they joined a slower version of the Highstepper. And he couldn’t have known it, but after seeing it merely twice, the boy started doing the dance with other amateurs and barely missed a step.
He was halfway through it when he twisted the wrong way and went stumbling—his Golem caught him. He laughed, embarrassed, then started as people applauded and cheered.
“He dances well.”
“He is a Level 23 [Fleetfoot Dancer], Lady Ulva.”
Timekeeper could pierce most anti-appraisal spells with his capabilities. Ulva twisted.
“At his age? Then he’s wasted as a [Lord]. Why haven’t I heard of him being trained or sent to study more dances in Nadel?”
“I do not believe anyone has suggested it, Lady Terland.”
“Well…mark it for me to do.”
Even for her, she couldn’t ship the boy off with no regard for his parents or will. But Ulva was annoyed to realize no one, including her, had known he was a [Dancer]. Level 23. He was smiling and thanking his Golem. Her heart was beating, and she was smiling at him.
Slowly, Ulva drank from her cup.
“Timekeeper. That Dancing Golem isn’t equipped for intercourse, is she?”
“No, Lady Terland. She is not.”
“Hmpf. Is she actually smiling at him, there? Or is she just doing her job, heart beating or no?”
“I do not know, Lady Ter-land.”
She glanced at him, and for once, the Golem seemed to be attempting to stay neutral. Ulva’s comment was soft.
“Find me a record of all the times she’s been activated and taken out of storage and how many times she might have…no.”
She cut herself off. Turned away.
“No, Lady Terland?”
“No, Timekeeper. I don’t want to know or guess. If it is, it is. Her heart only beats around me, anyways. We have been fools throughout the ages long enough. Let’s not assume Golems are too.”
Petria would have chased down that thought all the way, but to what end? It just led to tragedy, either way. Time would make tragedy of the story, no matter how beautifully it were told. She knew that. It was Timekeeper’s response that drew Ulva up short.
“Lady Terland. You are correct our hearts only beat to give us wa-king thought by your will. And that we are beings of thought, not emotion. In-correct to assume we do not always see and remember.”
Oh yes, the damnation of Terlands. The reason why their Golems could never, should never be given free will. They remembered everything done to them and around them over these ages. What would they conclude, given the chance? Lady Ulva Terland gazed at the Golem who seemed to be encouraging her [Lord] to try again amongst the cheering.
“It’s a damned stupid story. Why fall in love with a mortal or master?”
“Why do some Golems dream, Lady Terland?”
She turned away, only for a second Terland to join the floor. This one a [Lady] in her thirties. She held out a hand to one of the Silverfang Gnolls, then brushed at her dress.
It was a rather revealing one. Showy in terms of skin. Ulva eyed her bronzed skin, a young woman still in the prime of life, and snorted. Then she saw the two begin to try the Terlands’ answer to the Highstepper.
The 5-Step of Terandrian fame. The Silverfang Gnoll must have been a good dancer—no, wait. According to Timekeeper, he was a [Lucky Miner]. So his mistakes became the right steps, and they were funny enough.
The [Princess] was trying to make Wall Lord Ilvriss join them, but the Drake had sat down and refused to get up, so some Duke attempted to join Lyonette—only for someone to trip him headfirst into a table. The [Princess] ended up dancing with one of her [Knights], and Ulva would have left it at that—except for the [Lady] whirling around to show her dress was ultra-revealing.
In that there was a hole in it, along one of her breasts. And it revealed something glowing. Ulva’s head snapped back around.
“Is that a Golem’s Heart?”
It was! It was beating in the center of the [Lady]’s chest, glowing fast as she danced the 5-Step near-flawlessly. Ulva spun, and Timekeeper spoke.
“Yes, Lady Ulva. That is La-dy Prithna Terland, a member of the branch family. Her serving Golem is there.”
Another shock when Ulva turned her head. She took one look at the Golem with a lifelike face on it and recoiled.
“That’s Drogin. Someone put his face on a Golem?”
“It was his will, Great Aunt. He was dying of magical malady, and he insisted they put his face on a Golem to watch his daughter. Heart failure in the family. You don’t recall?”
Maybe? Ulva remembered Drogin dying, but she snapped at Xitegen, who’d walked over.
“When did that happen?”
She gestured at the heart, and he shrugged.
“The heart? I think hers gave out five years ago. Likely, you didn’t see her because she spent three years having one created that could keep her alive.”
Ulva vaguely recalled being grumpy about the funds for that and hearing the story, but…she eyed the laughing [Lady] hugging the Gnoll as the dance ended.
“Another member of the family with promise, if she survived all that. What’s her level, Timekeeper?”
Then Ulva’s head was turning, seeing her family stepping onto the floor, haughty, but willing to try some of the dances, or just keen on reminding the others they could dance. Terlands dancing with Golems or, more scandalously, non-Golems.
In the center of it all, a [Princess] and that damned Drake. Timekeeper bent over as a drunk-looking man tried to pursue Lyonette.
“That is apparently the Duke of Ailendamus, who is using a magical projection spell to be here, Lady Ulva. He is of approximate danger as a Named-rank adventurer.”
“A high-level spellcaster? Just hit him if he causes trouble. I came here to see the south. I should have looked at my own family first.”
Wearily, Ulva Terland sat. Then she perched on her Dais of Health and beckoned.
“Very well. I can admit when I’m a fool myself, Xitegen.”
“Oh, goodie, Great Aunt. Can I throw you in front of a carriage?”
“Don’t be ridiculous. Send Chovn and Hidre before me.”
So she held court once more. The [Lady] of House Terland rose…and regarded her grey in a mirror. Her austere dress. Then she pulled the hairpin from her hair, and the Seal of House Terland glittered. She handed it to Xitegen and pulled her hair back.
“Hairpin, Xitegen.”
“Er, where…?”
“Dead gods, you truly haven’t ever found someone besides your damn Golems, have you? Change that, boy. Here!”
He stuck it awkwardly in her hair, and it became a ponytail. Ulva Terland touched her clothing and spoke.
“Awaken, hearts of Terlands.”
She drew something from a holster on her inner sleeve. Just a little wand made of mithril, and ran it down across her dress. Then—the grey layers seemed to flake away.
Like stone, revealing color beneath. Until her clothing took on the color of the deep ocean. Ulva whirled the wand over her head, and heads turned. She sighed as the familiar cloak of dark waters, filled with glowing lights, fell on her shoulders.
The Cloak of Submerged Lanterns was her personal attire, just like the dress. She could make most things ‘beat’ or reveal their true nature. Like clothing. If you took it out of the clothing, it turned grey and lifeless. Perfect for making a splash, disguising oneself, or just impressing someone who’d never seen the trick before.
Ulva Terland pointed the conductor’s wand and beckoned to the merry partygoers. She threw back the cloak, and it billowed over the Dress of Night Skies.
“I have made my decision. The Lischelle family shall approach House Terland. So shall each [Rancher] family’s heads. Kneel.”
Her Golems moved forwards until they flanked her—Chema, Timekeeper, Corde, the ancient might of House Terland—and Ulva Terland’s grey eyes broke into pieces and grew colorful. Even her eyes—
 
——
 
Nouzcrat had gone to wash his hands after getting sauce on them. He wasn’t one to dance, and he had missed the commotion. When he saw Ulva standing there, and the wary, nervous [Ranchers] approaching the line of silent Golems, he froze.
“Petria…?”
For a moment, it was her. Not as she had been, but as she would have been if she had lived as long as Ulva. That ponytail. Grey hair revealing faintly red strands. Symbols of their link to Terandrian royalty. And the clothing—
Then Ulva Terland was there again, and Nouzcrat staggered. But he saw her, still. It was not a perfect copy. There had always been impish playfulness, a willingness to push convention that Ulva lacked. But Petria had loved grand moments.
“Lady Terland. If we have offended you, we beg pardon. But we are the families who live here. We will not beg for the lands we have a right to.”
It was Marvus Lischelle who knelt and then glanced up at her. He licked his lips as he stared up at Timekeeper’s graven face, the merciless impassiveness of the other Golems, and the twin War Golems armed with battleaxes.
Ulva Terland just sat on her dais, holding the thin conductor’s wand in her hand. She spoke simply.
“I have been petitioned by House Rumask, House Everight, and House Zigur for the reinstatement of lands that they claim your people stole. They assert you attacked their people and drove them out under fear of death.”
Marvus opened his mouth, and Ulva silenced him with a look and her aura.
“House Everight I object to. Toldos is dead. I do not care if Reinhart claims a descendant has been found. If they did not present themselves to Lord Toldos during his long search, I do not acknowledge them as a Flower of Izril. Damia Reinhart, your family and mine are at odds over this. Ensure your family knows that we do not war.”
Her head turned, and her eyes flashed. Damia held up her hands.
“I disavow everything my family said! Wait, who’s saying—?”
As if she’d heard nothing, Ulva continued, her voice ringing. She knew how to speak, even in an open space.
“I am Terland. It is my will that shapes the north, along with that of the Five Families. We are the gardeners of Izril, and too many have forgotten that. Magnolia Reinhart took it upon herself to prune the weeds as she saw fit. I hold the laws of Izril to simple effect. No one man or woman may claim land that is not a Flower of Izril.”
Uh oh. Lyonette swallowed as she and Ilvriss watched Ulva glance down at the Lischelles. Marvus’ jaw was set, and Ilvriss was reminded of Big Burlap. A bull, but one aware of the danger, just waiting.
Lyonette was watching Aronia, and both she and Colfa knew the woman had a temper. Her eyes were flashing. Ulva Terland had a lot of Golems around her, but Aronia had her left hand, and if it could knock a bull aside…
The [Lady] of House Terland stopped then, with a sense for the dramatic, and took a sip from her cup purely for the show of it. Then she gazed down at Marvus and Aronia.
“After seeing the lands here myself, I do not find the three noble houses’ complaints valid. Each one left these lands when the Goblin King struck. Some to cowardice, others for lack of arms. The reason matters not. None of the houses has the strength to claim their holdings. We do not have enough nobles of Izril. As fortune or fate wills it—I do not need to go through the tediousness of assigning new classes. [Baron] shall do, even if it is [Cattle Baron].”
What was she saying? Everyone but her family was slow to catch on. Nouzcrat had given Ulva an alarmed look and begun to speak, then eyed the [Lady]’s changed appearance and sunk back into place with a sigh. Lyonette’s mouth opened.
“Ilvriss, is she…?”
“I think she just did.”
The Lischelles didn’t get what was meant either. Aronia was bristling like a porcupine, about to spit something back, when she saw Colfa gesticulating frantically with Nanette. The two were doing rapid sign language, waving their hands, trying to say…
All the Lischelles stared at the two dancing about until Mrsha slapped her forehead and wrote in big letters over her head:
She’s making you nobles.
“What?”
Aronia shouted and leapt up. The sentiment was echoed.
“What? Great Aunt, are you mad? They’re manure-shovelling [Ranchers]!”
Alorelle was utterly appalled. The Lady of Stone stepped forwards, and Aronia flushed. Her hand twitched—and Ulva spoke.
“Bodyguard, slap her.”
The personal bodyguard of Lady Alorelle slapped her so hard she twisted around. Ulva eyed the Golem.
“Hmm. That was harder than I expected. Someone’s Golems are not happy with her. Let that be a lesson about something. Rise, Lischelles. You kneel to no one ever again. Next!”
That last snap was purely Ulva. But when she smiled, there was a ghost of Petria Terland in her. The Lischelles were getting to their feet.
“Us? Nobles?”
Marvus seemed like he’d been kicked by Big Burlap. He and his wife were stunned, and Ulva nodded at them.
“Those who tend the land own the land. We are not [Kings] or [Queens] to dole it out. What you take, you keep. The reason Laken Godart is allowed to exist is because he was needed and there was no one who held his lands. But his empire shall endure as long as he is just, and not beyond his lifespan. No heirs. No monarchs on Izril’s soil. That is no saying, but a promise. We’ll get the Serpentine Matriarch eventually. Now, the next family.”
She beckoned impatiently at the Golvas. They were frozen, not sure if this was some huge prank. When they turned to Ilvriss and Lyonette, the two shrugged.
This was new to them as well. Neither Wall Lord nor [Princess] had ever seen noble titles being given out this…liberally! However, Ulva was brisk, and she let each family have their moment.
After the third family, the silence began to break. Applause sounded—by the time she got to the fourth [Rancher] family, their people started cheering. When the last group rose, there was a long silence—then a whoop.
Rabbo Golva slid on his knees across the ground with a drink in hand, and the band began to play as he leapt up and did a jig. Then Marvus swung Aronia around, laughing, and there was dancing, celebrations—
Not all of the [Cattle Barons] were so exuberant. Marvus was overjoyed when the shock faded, but Colfa saw her sister’s face was full of reserve. A weight upon her and trepidation.
Not just her—she recognized Nithle Calabie biting his lip and speaking to Ulva before she bestowed his new rank upon him. She spoke down to him, and he knelt—slowly.
Nobles. Colfa had grown up sneering at the idea of the nobility, knowing them only as greedy thieves who employed thugs by a different name. Now the [Ranchers] were that nobility. To some, it was bitter or as if Ulva had dumped more difficulties on their lap.
But that was one of the Five Families for you, wasn’t it? Ulva noticed Colfa looking at her. She returned the gaze until the Vampiress bowed and ducked her head. And the [Matriarch] of House Terland dismissed her.
I do not have the time nor interest to deal with you, Vampire.
Ulva Terland just sat there as Lyonette and Ilvriss walked over. She didn’t need to beckon them. She just spoke to the air.
“That [Cattle Baroness], Aronia? She appeared ready to kill me. What kind of slap Skill does she have?”
“[Bull’s Slap] or something. It turns bulls.”
Lyonette spoke, and Ulva glanced at her.
“I was speaking to my Golems, not you, [Princess]. Fine. Lady Zanthia teaches [Ladies] how to slap, but not that hard. I’d give good coin to see her and Magnolia Reinhart determine who’s stronger. I was never good at that stupid trick. But it will do. This lot seems sturdy enough. We need new blood. They’ll fill the ranks of the Flowers of Izril well enough. It’s no kindness. When we are called to drive the Witch of Webs back or face the Goblin King, they will be called upon too. If they fail, I will prune them.”
“Is that the way the Five Families do it?”
“I have no doubt my peers and traditionalists will hold me to task. It normally takes a quorum of peers. I am that quorum with my family here. Enough to satisfy any requirements. Moreover, I need less tradition. Golems, witness me.”
She turned, and Timekeeper and all the Golems standing around the party spoke.
“ɪᴛ ɪꜱ ᴡɪᴛɴᴇꜱꜱᴇᴅ.”
That unified, dispassionate voice. Lyonette du Marquin shivered, and she and Ilvriss drew closer. They stood before one of the leaders of the north. Ilvriss wondered if it would have been like this, facing Zail in his prime. But Salazsar was an entire city. A fifth of the Five Families’ will was one [Lady].
Ulva Terland sat on her floating dais and spoke.
“Well? You have your audience. Give me one reason not to have you killed.”
“Has my uncle not been in touch, Lady Terland? I rather hoped he could speak for me.”
She snorted as Ilvriss bowed slightly.
“He gave me reasons the rest of the family would hear. Not I. You are digging for the City of Purity.”
Ilvriss started, and she rolled her eyes.
“That was obvious. The Golems tell me it is folly to unearth. Why should I ignore the voices of stone and let you dig up armageddon? Whatever lies down there, it killed the Drakes there. Do you think you’ve brought enough to stop it?”
That—was a really good point. Lyonette had never gone over what Ilvriss expected to find down there, not really. The Wall Lord took a deep breath.
“With respect, I do think I have some protections, Lady Terland. Your Hunter-Killer might have nearly assassinated me, but I have standing forces. The Rubirel Guard, the Erchirite Spears—”
“Dead and dead if we warred. My Golems say it is too dangerous for them. You are one Drake.”
“I am not alone. I have the backing of the City of Gems.”
Ilvriss was trying to be polite, but Ulva was back to being snappish. She glanced past him.
“You’re no Zail Gemscale. He was a [Swordmaster]. You don’t have his levels. You don’t have an army.”
“I am here because someone must be!”
Ilvriss snapped, and her head swung back down. Lyonette tried to smile and soothe things over.
“What Ilvriss means is—”
“What I mean is that I have The Wandering Inn and a [Princess] on my side! A [Princess] who’s higher-level than most damn monarchs!”
Ilvriss put an arm around Lyonette’s shoulder, and she jumped. She hissed.
“Ilvriss!”
He raised his voice as Ulva lifted one eyebrow.
“A runaway [Princess] is your best asset.”
“A [Princess] who has breached Level 40 before turning twenty. A genius not even Lord Xitegen can match for sheer youth! Or are Level 40 [Princesses] that weak, Lady Terland? I have the Silverfang Tribe, a mandate from General Sserys, and the need to be here. We all do! Zel Shivertail did not die for us to war!”
Ilvriss was not under a [Silence] spell. Lyonette saw heads turning, the music dying down, but the Wall Lord ignored her hands trying to muffle him. He jerked his head around her as she shushed him. Pointed a claw at Ulva.
“I have been respectful as I can be, Lady Ulva! Ancestors witness me, I have a temper and ego, but I have done my utmost to come here tactfully, aware of all the sins of my forebears! But you cannot be blind! Or has Xitegen told you the Winter Solstice was nothing more than a friendly dustup with a few zombies? More is coming! Or has a war in the Meeting of Tribes not shown that? The New Lands rising? The King of Destruction waking would be reason enough to dig!”
“House Terland is not blind, Wall Lord. I am not impressed with the King of Destruction’s little return or the Meeting of Tribes. As for this Winter Solstice, I take my own council. Not that of Walled Cities.”
She was the model of indifference, which Lyonette took to be a calculated move. The Quarass and her mother were experts in the same thing that Ulva was doing. Give nothing away unless you wanted to. She wished she were so good, but she couldn’t be. Nor could Ilvriss; his eyes flashed. Lyonette almost went to stop him, but let him try.
“What about the Goblin King, Lady Ulva Terland?”
That made Ulva stop. When her head rose, mouth opened, Ilvriss cut her off.
“He did return, and it was him. I was not there but I believe it. Anyone who has ever seen him would remember. Do you call that a normal event? Two Goblin Kings in a century. What of the Seamwalkers that Drath and the Iron Vanguard fought? Ask them; one destroyed the Eir Gel island. They’re the reason healing potions can no longer be made. This world is changing, and this is why I dig.”
The murmurs from the Terlands behind Ulva were growing louder. At first, they had sneered or scoffed at Xitegen, echoing Ulva’s attitude and their family’s. But though some might deny these events had happened, Lady Ulva?
No. Not the Goblin King. She met Ilvriss’ eyes and there was a flash of something. A break in her armor. Then her voice cooled down again.
“So the hour has come to awaken more Golems, to rouse the Five Families to action. I am not blind to that. But when a Drake comes to me and says, ‘take my claw, let us stand together’, I go down to our family tombs. And count how many of my predecessors died of being stabbed in the back.”
“I am not my ancestors, Lady Ulva Terland—”
“Hah. We shall see. Your arguments are entertaining, if nothing else, but when a stranger comes to my door shouting for me to take their hand? You do think too much of yourself, Wall Lord of Salazsar. You are not the man who could stop one of the King of Destruction’s vassals, let alone the rest of what you spoke of.”
Ulva Terland was inspecting her fingernails, which Lyonette realized had a very light gloss on them. They, too, had been grey until she activated her Skill. Now she even seemed less old and lined. Ilvriss hesitated, and Lyonette jumped in.
“It’s true that Wall Lord Ilvriss is underprepared for the threat, Lady Ulva. He can’t deny it. He can barely beat those [Ranchers], and that’s partly because he doesn’t want to spill blood, but he’s not ready for a Walled City under our feet.”
Now he was trying to shove her, glaring. But Lyonette went on.
“And—stop shoving—you know what? That’s fine. He is still in the right position and the right time! Already, his subordinates are counter-levelling! That’s why even people like Lady Damia have flocked to his banner! If the Walled Cities were smart, they would have all sent resources and manpower! There might be suffering, but look what the dungeon under Liscor has done for the city! The Golems fear what the City of Purity might be. Golems do not level.”
For a moment, Lyonette thought that the Golem known as Timekeeper nodded fractionally. Ulva’s eyes swung to his face, then she leaned forwards.
“Even were I to accept both explanations, I still object to you, Wall Lord Ilvriss. You are a Drake. If I took that argument, I would just seize your enterprise myself and put Xitegen in charge.”
“Great Aunt, I don’t dig—”
She silenced him with a look. Ilvriss stepped forwards, and Lyonette held her breath. He barked back—
“Go ahead.”
Even Ulva blinked at that. Ilvriss gestured at Xitegen.
“By all means, put Lord Xitegen in charge! I cede it to him. Let’s have a contract. Let the Lord of the Thighs take over the digging work!”
Marvus snorted into his cup at Xitegen’s nickname. Ilvriss’ eyes glittered dangerously.
“Having known Lord Xitegen, I am sure he has ample expertise in running a mining operation. Safety protocols, people for that—I welcome him to do the work. Oh, and to deal with all the flies. They carry diseases, and they need constant killing. Not to mention the cost of this enterprise is destroying me with virtually no yield in this damn soil! And the smell! Do you know what our nose plug budget is? Please take it from me! Let’s see how well the Golems do when they hit their first liquid magicore patch and it drains their Golem Hearts dry!”
Even the Golems were mildly alarmed at this, and Xitegen was making ‘x’ motions at his aunt, but she just sat there. Ilvriss took a breath.
“I’m happy to cede this project. I tell a lie; I’m not happy, but I’ll do it. I’ll even cooperate, but no one asked if I wanted to cooperate. In fairness, I didn’t think to ask. That’s my fault. But you assume I have come to grab. Here.”
He strode forwards, and one of the Golems intercepted him. Ilvriss slammed down a briefcase in Corde’s hands, flipped it open, and gestured.
“Pickaxe! Get it appraised! I’m no fool! Yes, I’m a damned Drake, and we’re greedy, and we can’t give anything away—so what? We’ve been Drakes for aeons and not killed each other because we have laws! Protocols! Ways to enforce collaboration! Do you think I don’t have shareholders?”
He glanced around at everyone. They stared at him, and Ilvriss paused, rubbed at his forehead.
“…You savages don’t know what shareholders are, do you? I refuse to apologize for that comment. Lady Ulva, if you are going to evict me and my people, I insist on at least negotiating. Because this is what we have dug up. And you are no fool.”
He held up a helmet, and it looked ordinary to all those without the senses of a Golem. Ilvriss placed it back down.
“We have struck Truegold in the mines. Leaving it is the biggest waste of all. We know where a fortune is. Is it the will of the Terlands to leave treasure buried? I cannot believe you have survived this long with that mentality.”
He stepped back and realized he’d just been shouting at the woman he’d come to persuade. Ilvriss colored, adjusted his suit, wiped at his sweaty scales, and coughed into a hand.
“…I realize we are historically enemies. But we needn’t repeat the mistakes of our fathers, Lady Terland. I am tired of war, and I have participated in so few. May we speak with earnest cooperation in mind?”
That was all. Lyonette had come up with other levers to use. Arguments based on the magical door or the authority of Pallass and Liscor…but in the end, it was Ulva Terland. She had the power to force things.
The [Lady] just sat there. And, Lyonette realized, she had asked relatively reasonable questions about the dangers of the dig. How anyone could guarantee a Drake from the south could be trusted.
Maybe…she peeked at Ulva Terland, and the [Lady]’s voice was soft.
“The Five Families will never trust a Drake in our lands. I do not. I do not trust Calanfer, either. Trust is not required for profit or else the Reinharts would never have anyone work with them. The final reason I come here is simple. You stopped my heart, and your agent took Petria’s face. But for a miracle, I would have died.”
Gasps from the Terlands, the [Ranchers]. Every eye swung towards Ilvriss and Lyonette, and she opened her mouth. To Lyonette’s intense embarrassment, her first response was purely that of her daughters.
“I—well—you attacked Ilvriss first! Don’t send [Assassins] if you don’t want to be assassinated!”
It was such a bad retort that Dame Ushar covered her face with one hand and tried to pretend she wasn’t Lyonette’s [Knight]. Ilvriss winced.
“That’s Calanferian diplomacy? It was an accident, Lady Ulva. As we fought for our lives? We didn’t think that would occur.”
The [Matriarch] of House Terland glanced from the Human to the Drake.
“…’You did it first’ and ‘it was an accident’ are the best reasons you two could come up with? Is there anyone with a better reason?”
She actually peered past Ilvriss and Lyonette. At Mrsha, who was still trying to work on the Forbidden Bowl—it was Nanette in her lumberjack’s outfit who raised a hand.
“Lady Ulva, if I may?”
“What?”
“What kind of fool tries to manually control a Golem across half the damn continent? Let alone has an aura war against two aura-experts?”
Everyone stepped away from Nanette but Hethon, who took a huge breath and tried to sidle back and put himself between her and the wrath of Ulva Terland. The [Matriarch] sat there, then grinned.
“Girl. You remind me of a [Lady] who gave up her class. Art thou a [Witch]?”
“Without the class, yes!”
Nanette tossed her head proudly and put her hands on her hips. Rabbo Golva nearly leapt into a Golem’s arms as he recoiled from her. Ulva nodded, thoughtful.
“That will do. Golems, dunk her head in a bucket. Don’t drown her. Witches used to send their apprentices to House Terland to learn a lesson. What kind, I’ll never know.”
A Golem went walking towards Nanette, and she wavered.
“Don’t you dare! Don’t you—”
Hethon tried to save Nanette. Ulva Terland just sat back on her dais and sighed. After a moment of gazing up at the sky, she realized Ilvriss and Lyonette were still waiting.
“I have yet to meet the Drake who stole my sister’s face. I will meet with her before I leave.”
“…And the not-inconsiderable threats to my life and that of my people, Lady Terland?”
“We’ll see how this cookout goes, shall we? You’ve earned yourself a reprieve.”
Ulva’s eyes glittered, and she sat back. Lyonette and Ilvriss eyed each other, and Xitegen let a breath out.
Had they actually forced Ulva Terland back? Shakily, Lyonette smiled. Ilvriss turned, saw Nanette screaming as a bucket was filled with water, and smiled.
“I think that we swayed her.”
“Are you sure? Or is she waiting to bring the hammer down?”
They glanced at Ulva, and she sat, beckoning one of her family over next. Lyonette hesitated.
“She’s likely not going to make up her mind on the spot. If we give her a reason to pause, Ilvriss, it buys us a day. Making up your mind isn’t something she’d do lightly.”
“True. And that gives Nerul an opening. Ancestors, I’m sweating arrows over here. What—what next?”
“Er, uh, I’ll buy time with dessert!”
Lyonette rushed over as Nanette emerged from her dunking and was put down. She immediately began kicking the Golem and tried to storm forwards to have it out with Lady Ulva—Mrsha and Xitegen were trying to save her from herself.
And perhaps…
 
——
 
Ulva Terland was holding court, speaking to young Chovn, and letting the boy announce his class to his family. She watched the [Princess] and Wall Lord, annoyed.
Neither one had swept her away. The rest of her family or something, perhaps. But it annoyed Ulva because she had seen better.
Not to say they hadn’t done some things decently. But was Ulva the only one who remembered Fulviolo and Maviola? Linter and Celica, the original love story that had swept Izril before Pellmia had even been a mote in his father’s eye?
One of the few remaining, yes. She exhaled. It was a disservice to compare the two to the Els in their prime, or anyone else. But…well.
This fell into one of the six outcomes she had calculated upon leaving her house. Ulva Terland knew how Golems thought. If she was not as adept…she drummed her fingers on the armrest of her dais.
She would have to inquire further and make sure she was correct. And meet that damned Drake. The face-changer. But she knew. She saw.
 
——
 
There was hope. That was Nerul Gemscale’s only thought when he skidded into the cookout, too late and, perhaps, just in time.
He didn’t greet Lyonette or Ilvriss. He just grabbed the nearest Terland, shook hands, and began throwing Skills.
“Lord Nouzcrat, Diplomat Nerul. Can we resolve this all decently? Lovely Golems, by the way. I’m a posterior-man myself. Can’t beat a good tail.”
“Wha—who are—how dare you—?”
Nouzcrat was ambushed and metaphorically taken into an alleyway and beaten with sticks. Diplomatic sticks. Nerul smiled.
“[Hear Me Out], sir. I realize you don’t like to go against Lady Ulva Terland. But I was the one threatening about the Zelkyr Golems? Ah, you do remember. I just wish to add that old Eschowar’s back in Salazsar.”
“He…he is? That monster’s not dead?”
Nouzcrat turned dead white. Nerul smiled tightly.
“And he’s up to his old tricks. Now, consider that killing Ilvriss gives him full casus belli to invade the north. We both know that Eschowar never needed it. But he needs support from the other Walled Cities, and killing a Wall Lord does that. Think on that. Must run; I’ll be back.”
He left Nouzcrat to sit down and attacked. Like a shark.
“Rabbo Golva! Listen, my man. I know that it’s hard to beat the Lischelles. I, personally, love your steaks. But Marvus there, well, his are the most famous steaks, and I was just in Salazsar trying to order yours, and Administrator Alrric—lovely man, pays for all the Gemscale finances—he asked ‘why not Lischelle beef?’. And you have to admit, they edge you out in prices, if not pure quality.”
To be precise, Alrric had asked, ‘why not Lischelle beef if we have to order some, and why do we want to support Humans in the north when we can get quality meat from our own [Ranchers]?’
But it was enough. The [Primed Talking Point] had Rabbo Golva in a moment.
“Aren’t you that [Diplomat]? See here, Lischelle beef—”
“Beats yours, Rabbo. Not to my palate, but listen: who has a refined palate these days? Not some idiot [Merchant] we’re wining and dining. The wine means he’s not tasting the steak. That’s why the Lischelles have you.”
“I—that’s just your—”
“Unless you had a magical door that cuts all the cost of delivery to Invrisil or Pallass. And Liscor’s got an up-and-coming upper class. Now, I can’t discuss this in the open, but you could undercut every Lischelle delivery by a week and save a fortune on delivery fees. I know the Driver’s Guild and Merchant’s Guild think they’re hot magicore. That door covers four hundred miles. You could beat Marvus with City Runners.”
Rabbo Golva might not get all of what Nerul was dumping on him, but his wife or sons did. They stirred—and so did Marvus Lischelle. The [Cattle Baron] was popping champagne, but the smile faded as one of his sons dashed over. He whirled like a bull scenting trouble.
Nerul finished with two more [Ranchers], then stepped forwards.
And here we go…
“Aren’t you the diplomat I beat out the other day?”
“That was ages ago, Marvus. And you have a damn good punch. I’m not ashamed to say that I’ve lost the spring in my step. But I’ve come back to stop my nephew from losing what brain cells he has left—I like his level of stupidity now. This is my dance, and I insist on having a piece.”
The two men sized each other up as space cleared. They were both big men, and Marvus wrangled cattle. He was a brawler, a strong man—but he realized Nerul had changed.
Despite his efforts, Nerul hadn’t had enough time to make a complete makeover, even with Grimalkin of Pallass’ help. But there was something…sturdier about Nerul. Not just size.
His…thighs? His arms? Everything looked larger, ever so slightly, but the effect made Nerul a bit bigger.
A bit more…
Swole.
And he didn’t back down in front of Marvus, even with the [Cattle Baron] bristling in his face. Nerul flexed one arm, and Lady Damia oohed. She could see his muscles in the definition of the slightly too-tight suit.
“I’d hate to settle this the old-fashioned away, unless that means drinking you under the table, Marvus.”
Ping.
That was the sound of one of his buttons on his suit exploding from the force of his flexing. It pinged off a wineglass and shattered it. Alorelle Terland screamed, but a hand blocked the shards of glass from striking her face.
Her own bodyguard Golem was too slow—but a Drake with a glittering face carved from gemstone smiled as she placed the shards of glass back in Alorelle’s cup.
“My apologies, Lady Terland.”
“Y-you’re—”
Xitegen’s head snapped around, but then it went back to Nerul. The Thigh Lord could appreciate another man with good thighs. Marvus was eying Nerul warily.
“Bit more of a spine in you, eh?”
“I’ve always been spiny, but historically, it’s been supported by less muscle and more fat. The Sinew Magus himself has certified my spine. Now, Marvus. I’m just going to undercut your business with anyone I need to in order to stop the fighting. Alright?”
“I don’t let anyone threaten my family’s way of living, Diplomat.”
“And I don’t let people threaten my nephew or my city.”
The two men squared off. Marvus adjusted his own too well-tailored suit. Nerul popped another button. There was a pause…and Marvus snatched a cup.
“Rabbo Golva’s a crook and a liar. If you’re doing drinks, I’ll bring out the good stuff. Don’t leave me out, y’hear?”
“I wouldn’t dream of it. And may I compliment you on your suit? Marvellous style.”
“You’re not bad yourself. You been working out?”
“At the gymnasium, yes. Splendid for gains or building the core. Which gains and which core, I’m not sure, but there’s a bunch of annoyingly enthusiastic people who will cheer you on even if you crap your pants. Which I did on my first day.”
Marvus began laughing as Nerul began recounting his own legend. Which drew in Rabbo Golva, who wanted to hear the story and know how the Drake appeared so fit and get in on this deal if Marvus was talking—
 
——
 
Ilvriss was rather stunned by Nerul’s appearance. When the [Diplomat] extricated himself—in six minutes—and went moving towards the Terlands like a shark, the Wall Lord caught him.
“Uncle! You’re just in time; we’ve been surviving Ulva Terland, and I think it’s going decently, but—what was that about working out? You wrote me something about that, and what is that Golem?”
He’d spotted Yweine and felt an uneasy flutter in his stomach, but Nerul confused him.
“I thought you were doing all that to beat Marvus’ Skill or how he stopped you last time!”
“Nephew! Gah, you’re sweaty, and I’m starved. I’ve eaten nothing but healthy things—which, delightfully, includes meat at times—but I will feast! Yes, yes, I did it. Hugely embarrassing—I’ll tell you the entire story when lovely ladies aren’t around to laugh at me. And I did manage to take Marvus out. You saw him back off?”
“Yes, but I thought you’d beat him in a fistfight.”
Ilvriss had rather imagined the two throwing down in a bare-knuckles brawl for Nerul to reassert his dominance, and from the disappointed expressions on Nanette’s and Damia’s faces—and several others—they’d been hoping for the same thing. Nerul just sighed and patted Ilvriss gently on the shoulder.
“Nephew…what do you think [Diplomats] are? All that damn effort, stress, and again, Umbral Throning myself in public—was just for that. It’s not about throwing a punch. It’s about not doing it when you can. That’s the entire point of soft power, the lesson some Drakes never learn. The stick needn’t swing for it to remain a stick.”
“…I’ve missed you, Uncle. I could have used your way with words about five minutes ago.”
Ilvriss hugged Nerul, and the [Diplomat] whispered.
“Don’t thank me yet. I’ve landed us in trouble in Salazsar, but it was the only move I had. That Golem with the gemstone face is with us. With you—and trust her like you trust Tessa, or less. I got her out of the Vaults.”
Ilvriss froze. His eyes found Yweine, and he paled.
“Uncle. Are you insane?”
“Only as much as anyone else is these days, Ilvriss. Now be diplomatic.”
“To whom?”
“Her. Charming, charming, Ilvriss! Prove you’re not just some Wall Lord, and believe me, she’s already watching and, dare I say, reading our lips or something clever whenever we’re not activating privacy spells. So—here we go. How mad is Ulva Terland?”
The two Drakes stepped back, and Ilvriss stared at the Golem from Zelkyr’s age. She was greeting the Terlands, and they were dumbstruck. Ulva Terland herself was eying Yweine, and Ilvriss muttered.
“Rude, but not as hostile as I presumed.”
“Interesting. Interesting. Is she pulling the old Good Twin, Bad Twin routine? Hm. She’s lacking Petria, so she’d do it all herself?”
“How the hell did you know…? Is that good or bad?”
Nerul was just eyeing Ulva.
“I’m inclined to think it’s good. If it was worst-case, she’d come in all smiles, then murder you in front of everyone. She still might, but the more time she spends on us, the more I think she’s willing to listen. Ulva Terland hates wasting time on dead men. Let’s coordinate with Yweine before she can divide us. Yweine’s intelligence is beyond ours—in some ways. If we have a chance, it’s with her.”
The two Drakes nodded, and Ilvriss felt a surge of relief. Now they had their heavy-hitter, it was time to finish this dreadful altercation. The Lischelles seemed happy, and maybe he wasn’t wrong in thinking they’d won some respect for the Highstepper and everything else from them.
And Lyonette had the cake. She wheeled it out and called out.
“Everyone? I invite you to have dessert in honor of the Terlands!”
The Golem-statue appeared, and both Drakes winced when they saw it. Nerul sighed.
“A giant Golem as a cake. Somehow, that’s just so typical it’s a cliché. Well, I’m hungry enough for it. And it’s so tacky—”
“Dead gods, what a splendid cake!”
Lord Moltin exclaimed, and the Terlands applauded loudly. The [Diplomat] amended his statement.
“—Which is just what we need. Nice work. Did Lyonette come up with that?”
“No, it’s Lady Damia’s effort. She knows Terlands. Lady Damia, meet Nerul. She’s been nothing but an asset, Nerul.”
She hurried over, beaming.
“Diplomat Nerul, I am so delighted to meet you! I’d love to meet you and Wall Lord Ilvriss formally, if I may, after this—”
“Damia Reinhart! Dead gods, you’ve changed from my reports on you! I’m far too old, young lady, for any flirting!”
“My past? All behind me, Diplomat, no need to bring it up! Ha-ha! Ha!”
“Splendid, my dear. A Reinhart in our corner beats one at our backs with a poisoned dagger, but if you had any insights…lovely cake. I admit, sometimes I don’t go for the low-hanging fruit because I think it’s too banal. How did you get that made up so fast?”
Damia waved an airy hand at the cake as the first slice was carved onto a plate for Lord Moltin.
“Oh, I got it for a song when I went to Invrisil to search for Varnie. Unfortunately, I think she’s run off my money. Ha, hahaha…”
Both Drakes eyed her, and she coughed.
“…Anyways, I was worried, but I found this excellent [Baker] who assured me he’d do it for a song! He was quite the character! Molvedouka, I think his name was. Very funny man. I didn’t know half-Elves grew mustaches.”
Something about that name made a warning bell go off in Ilvriss’ head. But that was nothing to the way the Golems registered the faint conversation they were eavesdropping on—then Timekeeper’s head snapped around, and he began to move.
 
——
 
“A Golem as a cake? Ugh. I can’t count how many Golem-themed foods I’ve had. Just once, I want some originality in life. Fine, get me a slice.”
Ulva Terland was groaning as her family flooded towards the cake. Timekeeper snapped to attention, and she frowned.
“Not instantly. I’m not that hun—”
“Lady Terland. I believe a dangerous individual has infiltrated this gathering or poisoned the cake. You are in critical danger.”
She froze as Timekeeper’s head swivelled, and the Golems around her formed a circle. They were suddenly alert. She spoke.
“The Drakes?”
“No. It may be a coincidence, but a name was overheard that falls into patterns based on an old enemy. Chema, investigate.”
The Gnoll Golem was striding for the cake, and Ulva Terland’s eyes locked on it. She saw the first piece of cake being served onto Lord Moltin’s plate, chocolate, oozing with still-molten brown batter, mixed with green…
Lord Moltin hesitated as he eyed the green strands running from the cake’s interior. Rather odd choice in frosting, he decided. Off-putting. Nevertheless, he’d taken the slice, so he began to lick at a fork—
Chema slapped the fork and plate out of his hands so fast Moltin was licking the air. She thrust him back before he could recoil, and then Ulva saw the green ooze continuing to run from the cake. Then…yellow pus.
The eager partygoers made a sound of disgust and backed away. Lyonette stopped smiling. Her head slowly turned…and the pus that was definitely not frosting splattered onto the ground.
It stank. The smell was so foul that Moltin immediately lost control of his stomach. He vomited, falling onto his hands and knees, and Ulva saw other diners retch. And the pus kept coming…
“How was that in the cake and you didn’t detect it? Poison? It’s too obvious—”
The Golems around her had gone still, she realized. Utterly. Even their Hearts had stopped beating. It was not them who spoke, but Yweine.
The only Golem not linked by the Terlands’ Skills was staring at the cake.
“Intriguing. The plague-like substance does not register as magic or a contaminant to any identification spells despite clearly exhibiting said effects. It is acting as a concealing liquid, akin to neutralized magicore. To what purpose?”
To hide something from a Golem or Salazsar’s eyes, you idiot. Yweine seemed to come to the same conclusion as Ulva did. She shifted, eyes flicking to Wall Lord Ilvriss, Nerul. But before anyone could move, Chema’s circling of the cake-statue came to a halt. She backed up—
A foot kicked the Gnoll Golem in the chest as she tried to dodge, breaking out of the batter. Ulva heard a thump—recoiled in shock—and saw no Chema.
The Golem was gone, just…torn-up ground where she had been standing.
“Chema?”
A hand punched out of the Golem-cake. A figure tore out from the inside, as if birthed by the foul liquids that cascaded down around him. Bits of pus, green ooze, brown filth…and blood. He swept his hair back in a foul spray of liquids, yet it didn’t touch his clothing or skin as he walked out.
He had put on his best clothing. It was a cookout after all.
Tolveilouka had draped himself in the kind of green that reminded Ulva of pond scum. Of a mold, somehow a foul, dirty color at odds with the delicate high-collared coat he wore. It could have belonged to a nobleman with no taste…except for the buttons.
They were tiny, screaming faces made of polished brass. Oh, and Tolveilouka’s boots were filthy black. He strutted forwards, and his shirt looked like writhing maggots. White and yellow over black.
Just cloth. He carried a sword at his side. A single-edged weapon, and his blonde hair was tied back in a long, wide-ended ponytail by two ribbons down his back.
He was the most stylish monster that Ulva Terland had ever seen, and he instantly set off every alarm in the woman’s body. Tolveilouka stepped out of the cake and smiled.
“That’s better. I thought dessert would never come.”
 
——
 
It was all worth it for moments like these. Yes, he had waited for this moment. Yes, he had forced terrified bakers to bake him into this cake. Carefully altered the insides so the Golems wouldn’t detect him until it was breached.
And he had waited through the entire day and cookout for this moment.
Why?
If you had to ask why, you were beyond salvation. The answer was style. There could be no other reason. The only thing that would have made it not worth it was some idiot hitting the cake or running into it.
The other two times Tolveilouka had done this, it had happened, so he was really happy to cross this one off his list. He particularly relished the slack-jawed expression on Lyonette’s face.
She really thought she’d been safe from him. He blew her a kiss as she swayed. Then he turned.
Terland Golems and the [Ranchers]. Oh, and Salazsar. Was it his birthday? Tolveilouka scooped some of the filth he’d secreted onto a slice of cake.
“Wonderful party, Princess. I couldn’t help myself; I made you a dessert.”
He took a huge bite of the mixture, and someone else threw up. Tolveilouka masticated, then threw the slice of cake at a Silverfang Gnoll.
Someone blocked the cake, cursing. Ser Dalimont dropped his shield instantly—Tolveilouka was disappointed.
He would have loved to see what that cake piece would have given the Silverfang. Damn Golems. They’d stopped the others from eating the cake.
“Well then. Shall we get this cookout started?”
No one was speaking. Shock. Tolveilouka sighed as he stretched, luxuriating in the moment. Yessir, you had to have fun in life.
He credited Erin Solstice with it, really. His Goddess, indeed, his muse. Just when he’d thought life had nothing left to offer, here he found new joy in mundane things. After all…
He was helping. The theory was simple. The Wall Lord’s dig was in jeopardy. How did you unite such horrible enemies? Give them the biggest one of all to unite against.
Or just kill them all. Tolveilouka was on the fence about it. He figured he’d wing it.
 
——
 
Thump.
That was the sound Chema made as she hit the ground in the distance. How long had she been airborne…?
“Lady Ulva. Golem Chema has been rendered unable to serve. Threat identified. The Putrid One’s minions walk again. Warning. WARNING. ALL GOLEMS OF HOUSE TERLAND, TO ARMS. TOLVEILOUKA THE WRETCHED IS STILL ALIVE. LOCK DOWN HOUSE TERLAND.”
Timekeeper was first to speak. And when he did—his voice boomed. It echoed.
 
——
 
It echoed across House Terland. Golems in the field froze about their tasks. Citizens of House Terland and the nobles of their house jumped as the Golems swung their heads down.
The Light of the North, the giant Golem who acted as a lighthouse, moved its eyes from the seas. It looked south, and Timekeeper’s distant orders came to it. Minutes too late. Too slow.
“The Putrid One’s greatest servant is threatening the Head of House Terland. Golems, march! The plague cannot be allowed to sweep the world a fifth time.”
The Golems of the North stirred. Conferred—and then the Light of the North took a step. It ripped free from the ancient masonry of the tower it was built into.
Below, the city of First Landing that had overgrown its initial boundaries rang with alarm. Mortals gazed up as the lighthouse broke and the tallest Golem they had ever seen emerged. It was huge, even rough, simple arms and legs for a Golem meant to stand forever. A statue with glowing eyes.
It took one slow, creaking step. Then another. Across the streets, southwards. An alarm was ringing in the Light of the North’s head. One it had heard time and again.
The Putrid One. It remembered…and knew that from the Mansion of Stone, Golems were emerging.
Unsealing the doors of their own vaults. Marching past terrified nobles and storming down the streets. The vast Golems who tilled the fields. The most powerful serving Golems still active.
The ones who were needed.
Step. Step.
The Light of the North’s heart did not thunder. There was no [Lady] of House Terland to order it to beat.
But that was needed. It walked, and there was no hope for the ancient Golem. Only certainty.
When it met the Putrid One’s servant, the ruler of House Terland would need to order its heart to beat. Or it would be destroyed.
The Golem took another step as alarm bells began to ring. It had heard the commands from afar, and it took time for Golems to scream across the continent. It would be too slow when it arrived, of course. It always was.
It might be too slow already. Too late.
The Golems marched upon a foe they remembered from an age when they had resided on Terandria’s shores. The younger Golems did not know why.
They…
Were lucky.
 
——
 
“Tolveilouka Ve’delina Mer.”
Ilvriss had heard the name before. Heard Lyonette tell him about it and how she’d defeated him, and Duke Rhisveri, like an Erin story. Like Facestealer, a great foe laid low by cunning.
Defeated?
He should have asked more. But Lyonette had been confident…and perhaps she hadn’t known. Erin had dealt with this monster, but even she had only—Timekeeper’s voice was measured, even now, but fast.
His heart was beating so fast the words were perfectly-articulated.
“Tolveilouka Ve’delina Mer is a half-Elf from the age of the Putrid One. His nature pre-dates the Creler Wars by numerous ages. He is the greatest creation of the Putrid One, whose name has been damned to history. Combat capabilities are well above that of Named-rank adventurers of the modern era. He has slain Dragons in single combat. Lady Ulva Terland, you and House Terland are in danger. Please retreat. Immediately.”
That was what this thing was? Ilvriss felt his scales crawling. He was sure every [Dangersense] was blaring out of control, but they should have been screaming the moment that damn fake cake arrived.
“Oh no. This is all my fault. My…”
Damia was horrified. But this thing…seemed to know how to cheat every safeguard and Skill. No—he.
He was still a half-Elf. And a monster. Tolveilouka was listening, nodding in approval.
“I love Golems. They remember things properly. I recognize you, Golem. So, the old Gearboxes are still ticking away, eh?”
“Tolveilouka the Wretched. House Terland will destroy you. Desist in your actions or perish, yon fellow.”
Corde spoke. Tolveilouka eyed them.
“You have a funny way of speaking, Golem. I like it. It reminds me of the era I slept in. You think you Golems can halt me? I’ve been watching you all afternoon. So this is why House Terland left Levicus, eh? In decline. Sad, really. But even Golems break. Like toys. Your family cried so loudly when I broke their favorite ones. Like children.”
His teeth, when he bared them, were sharp. Unsettlingly so, even to a Drake.
“I miss that. Shall we dance?”
He stepped forwards, and Corde swung down their hammer. It was a fast, precise blow. They smashed the enchanted hammer against Tolveilouka’s shoulder. There was a ringing impact. The ground deformed under his feet.
His body didn’t shift. Tolveilouka eyed the hammer resting on his shoulder.
“…See?”
Corde stepped back, resetting their stance, and Tolveilouka chuckled. He glanced around, and Marvus Lischelle paled.
“You’re here. You monster.”
“Why, Marvus! Thank you for the meal, y’ken. I’ve been right pleased by all your mighty generosity!”
Tolveilouka hooked his thumbs in his belt and swaggered over, mocking the man’s tone. He leered at Aronia.
“Is this your wife? She looks good enough to eat.”
Marvus raised a fist and hesitated. Tolveilouka ignoring the hammer blow was one thing. And the stench from the cake…Marvus’ instincts were warring with his brain. But he had to do something—
There was an oath. Rabbo Golva swung up a shortsword and pointed it at Tolveilouka.
“You’ve murdered good men ‘n women and cattle! We’re going t—”
Tolveilouka slapped the tip of the shortsword off with a hand. It spun into Rabbo’s temple and lodged there. He fell, clawing at the blade with a cry.
Marvus froze. Eyes locked on Rabbo. Tolveilouka peered down.
“Huh, I missed the brain. That’s so fascinating—it almost never isn’t critical. Actually, I once hit a pickaxe into a man’s head. Got half his lobe, and he just walked off. Saw him two months later, and he was doing sort of well. Pickaxe piece still lodged in there. Even my master was fascinated and wanted to keep him alive, but he tripped running away from us, and that was pretty much it.”
He sighed. Then turned.
“Where was I? Oh, right. Thanking you for your hospitality. And the Terlands. And this lovely Wall Lord, and you, [Princess]. I have room enough for everyone.”
He leered around. Ilvriss saw Lyonette jerk.
“I—I thought you were dealt with. How are you here?”
“Oh, you mean that cute trick you used to try to save your inn? Princess, Princess. I’m Tolveilouka Ve’delina Mer. Nothing and no one is safe from me. I swore to drown Izril in the dead and plagues. And I shall. That [Innkeeper] gave killing me her best shot, I’ll admit…but no one was helping her, and now she’s out of the way, it’s time to feast.”
