He grinned, and just for a second, Ilvriss felt confused, even as he glanced around for a way out. He saw the Rubirel Guard moving, but they’d seen Chema falling, and he was signalling them not to attack. Yet. They had to get the kids, Lyonette, everyone away…but the half-Elf was so dangerous. Could they even survive if they all attacked?
Something was bothering Ilvriss, though. Didn’t Lyonette say Erin had used him? Tried to kill him? And there was something else about Tolveilouka. Ilvriss’ hand stole to his blade, and he swore the half-Elf noticed. But before he could move, Timekeeper spoke.
“Tolveilouka the Wretched. You will be hunted without respite if you assault House Terland’s own. Remove yourself.”
The half-Elf swung around.
“You do remember me. Have we actually fought before? I’ve smashed so many of you, I forget.”
“Yes. This Golem participated in combat against the Putrid One 15,311 years ago.”
“I can tell. One of your inner gears has the tiniest mark of my plague on it. Fascinating.”
“This Golem, known as Timekeeper, was designated ready-for-duty despite contamination. The deterioration of Inner Meridian 33rd Level Gear, Chain 14, 4th Position, 4th Gear was determined to be inconsequential.”
Tolveilouka pshed as he walked forwards, and Timekeeper stepped in front of Ulva Terland to shield her.
“Everyone says that. Had you met me…well, it’d be too hard to pustulate the gear unless I wanted to surprise your masters. Too buried.”
“That was the conclusion of my [Golem Artificer] at the time. A lack of parts necessitated this compromise.”
“Oho. Rebuilding you lot, were they? When was this? I’m picturing a beach.”
“The Battle of Tiabec’s Demise is the conflict you are referencing with a 67% chance of accuracy.”
“Tiabec? They actually named it after that idiot? He was a footnote! We killed him in the first hour!”
“Nevertheless, the record remains. Eighty-seven of my original unit were de-stroyed in naval landing action with a party led by you. You personally destroyed over fifty of my number.”
Tolveilouka snapped his fingers.
“I do remember! Yes, you were poised to give us a nasty attack, but your idiot masters took you too close to the beach. Undead in the waters. Just plague undead, but we swarmed you and kept you from fighting on the ground. It might have gone the other way if some Terland ponce didn’t make that mistake.”
“Lady Yoirn Terland was in command of our forces. Records indicate she later took her own life by throwing herself into the sea.”
“Hah! Classic. This is delightful. I should have bothered House Terland ages ago, but I’ve just been going here, going there, murdering everything, you know, without a plan. As I said, that damn [Innkeeper] really gave me her best shot, but Roshal did for her. The [Princess] over there did something clever too, but nothing stops me long.”
“This is evident. Is your return a herald of your Master’s revi-val?”
 
——
 
What was going on? Timekeeper was chatting with Tolveilouka, and the half-Elf was clearly enjoying every second of it. From a historical perspective, it was probably valuable—Satar Silverfang would have loved this.
Mrsha was about to soil herself. She didn’t know—this wasn’t in the [Palace of Fates]! Sometimes, she’d seen Tolveilouka attack, but he’d never done this.
Popping out of a cake really was beyond any world she’d seen. She didn’t get why Timekeeper was chatting, though—until she saw how the Golem was speaking.
So conversationally. Shielding Ulva Terland from…
Someone touched Mrsha’s shoulder and pulled at her. She jerked—but it was Welsca! The Drake put a claw to her lips, and Xinthe was there.
“Lady Mrsha, this way!”
She mouthed, and Mrsha realized that Ilvriss’ staff were pulling the guests back. Not everyone; Marvus was shielding his family and Ilvriss his soldiers—they were all staying. But they were trying to get…
The horses. They were far enough from the door that they’d have to ride. Or run. It was…what, fifteen minutes of light riding? Call it a thirty-minute dead run.
Too far. But Mrsha was edging backwards with Nanette, using the tables to duck down, when Tolveilouka chuckled.
“Oh, my master? That’s between him and me, old chap. This is grand, just grand. Say, do you recall everything about me?”
“The approximate knowledge of Golems here contains numerous records about you, Tolveilouka the Traitor.”
“Argh, and you were doing so well with my titles. I suppose that is one, but do you, perchance, know any music from those times? Hold on—”
Tolveilouka kicked up the table Mrsha was sneaking behind in an explosion of wood. He turned, caught the punch from Timekeeper, and grunted.
“That’s the strength I remember. Nothing like other Golems. Really, did you think you were getting away?”
Terrified Terlands, [Ranchers], and other guests froze. Tolveilouka grinned, and Timekeeper barred his way again.
“Tolveilouka. Your quarry is the [Princess] of Calanfer, correct?”
“…Of where? You people and your kingdoms. You knock one down, another pops up. Yes, her. That Drake—I’m really here for the entire spread. I heard there was good beef here. So I came by.”
He grinned down at Burlise. She was shaking as she held a belt knife. Tolveilouka’s presence—it made Mrsha’s head go white. Think of something! But what flame could burn—
“If that is so. Will you agree to allow the Terlands to leave in agreement of a temporary truce?”
Mrsha stared at Timekeeper, and Tolveilouka actually pivoted.
“So I get all of them and you don’t fight me?”
“Co-rrect.”
His charge was to defend Ulva Terland. The [Lady] rose to her feet and snapped.
“Timekeeper! House Terland does not sacrifice children!”
“Oh, bravo. Did you see her shout that without dying of embarrassment or hypocrisy?”
The half-Elf applauded, laughing. He peered at Ulva.
“You do know what you people used to make Golems out of? You have to fuel a Golem’s Heart somehow. No? Ah, I see you do.”
Ulva’s eyes narrowed as she regarded Tolveilouka. Mrsha felt sick. Not just because of what Tolveilouka was insinuating.
We’re dead. I thought Ielane was supposed to—
“Shall we play a game of sins, half-Elf? Any old kingdom wins. I am not my forebears. We tossed their bones into the sea when we left Levicus. Why are you here?”
Tolveilouka bowed, then whispered to Timekeeper.
“She is classy. I’m just here to hurt you all, Your Ladyship! Won’t be a moment! Got any more offers since you can’t talk your way out of this one, old fellow? I would have probably just killed all of you and let the others live for that, by the by. Just because it’s funnier.”
Timekeeper’s heart was whirring nonstop. Golems moved around Tolveilouka, flanking him. He peered around.
“No, not those, where are the good Golems? Unless they’re all invisible. Not that one, it’s far too loud. Really invisible.”
He jerked a thumb at the eyestalk Golem, who half-materialized. Timekeeper spoke.
“The Putrid One rests in the Village of Death as it is now known. That he has not emerged is proof he remains incapacitated. Or dead. The Veltras force containing the undead have not been overwhelmed; further evidence. I have communicated this fact to Terland Golems. They will destroy his remains at any cost. An army will raze his tomb to the ground.”
Tolveilouka’s head twisted around impossibly far. And he lost his smile.
“…And you think that’s going to make me relent? I am going to rip your precious Terlands to pieces for that, Golem.”
“This battle benefits neither side. Name your price. It is concie-va-ble a Terland artifact may revive your master. You shall never acquire one if you bring the Five Families to war. Even a being of your caliber will tire of pursuit and become wounded. Die.”
A Golem’s damn logic. Impeccable, but…flawed. The half-Elf was growing more bored with each second. He wound up for a punch, spinning his arm around, and Mrsha could have told Timekeeper he was doing it wrong. If she could speak. If she could think.
It was not she who spoke, then, but another being who acted on logic, unable to feel fear in her bones.
Yweine. The Golem interrupted.
“Timekeeper. This half-Elf predates all known history. His legacy is utterly lost save for a name I do not have stored in my records except for a single location. Your erasure means his data is forfeit. I request clarity as to who this being is before your demise.”
Tolveilouka halted and turned. He studied Yweine.
“Well now, you’re not a Terland Golem. Odd. You’re not that special…but you’re clearly one of those thinking ones. Is that right? You don’t recall me at all? Servant of the greatest Necromancer of Izril?”
“The greatest [Necromancer] of any era is Perril Chandler. Or perhaps Archmage Nekhret.”
Yweine shot back, and Tolveilouka frowned.
“…Who? I’ve heard that damn name before. And an Az’kerash.”
“They are one and the same being.”
“Are they? Are they?”
Xinthe grabbed Mrsha again. Tolveilouka noticed them moving away, but he was getting visibly angry. He spun on his heel.
“You remember me, don’t you, old timer?”
“Ye-es. Only Golems and certain texts remember the Putrid One.”
“How did you forget…? No, no. I’ve been over this. Calm. I am a flower blooming in a cesspool…”
Tolveilouka closed his eyes, breathed in and out, relaxed.
“…Do you remember the expression ‘Giant’s hanging testicles’, at least?”
He asked plaintively, and Timekeeper paused. As if even the Golem couldn’t compute where this was going.
“Yes.”
Tolveilouka sniffed and wiped at his eyes.
“You have no idea what that means to me. Wait, if you recall everything—do you recall my music? My triumphal dirge? My theme song?”
His what? Mrsha tripped as she ran, and she turned her head. A longer pause.
“This is in record in part due to repeated broadcasting.”
“Play it! Play it! I must hear it again! Play it and I swear, I’ll let you live!”
Tolveilouka clapped his hands and danced around. Yweine turned to Timekeeper, as if assuming this was a bluff. But after some beats of his heart, the Golem turned. He did not sing, but several Golems opened their mouths, and music began to play.
It was…scratchy. Distorted by faint screams, the crackle of other sounds, as if heard on a battlefield. Mrsha heard the chanting of voices. Wailing pipes.
He had a damn theme song? Tolveilouka began dancing.
“Oh, oh! It is my music! Wait, why are you all looking at me like that? Does no one compose their own music? Do you just…fight each other without any background ambience? Just heaving at each other, grunting?”
He wore the most disappointed expression ever, as if this were personally offensive to him. As if this were the worst thing that had happened to him since learning no one knew the phrase ‘Giant’s hanging testicles’. Then he shrugged.
“Okay—since I can tell you’re getting less scared and just running, here I go.”
He leapt on the first of the Rubirel Guard, ripped the Drake’s helmet off, and kissed the Drake on the lips.
She puked. Then kept puking maggots out of her mouth. The Rubirel Guard clawed at her face until Tolveilouka slammed the helmet back on. The flailing figure fell over. He turned.
“Keep playing and I won’t attack you Golems!”

“Here’s my contribution to the cookout! Wait, it needs something. You too.”
He lifted up a screaming [Rancher] over his head and wedged him in the horse’s guts. Raised a foot, spun—
A sword passed over his head. Tolveilouka caught a lasso thrown by Eni Calabie that burned across his palms from the speed of the rope. He just smiled.
“[Ranchers]. Such a funny class.”

“Now, where is that [Princess]? Oh, here we go—”
The first squad of Drakes charged Tolveilouka as the Rubirel Guard advanced. Mrsha heard yelled orders, Skills. Ilvriss was shouting.

He emerged from the squad of screaming Drakes whose limbs he had broken, legs, arms, and he finished arranging them in a circle. He dusted his hands off. He caught Mrsha’s eye.

Some kind of unholy chant. Mrsha heard massed voices singing in a thunder of music behind her. She couldn’t tell what was being sung—it was a mix of languages. It might have been stupid, but it sounded…bad.
 
“Tolveilouka Ve’delina Mer! 
Perterridus! Proditor vitae—
Affertor putredinis!”
 
If you actually knew the dead language of magic, known to Earth as Latin, that wasn’t…very scary. However, it sounded terrible, and Tolveilouka was flicking his fingers to the music, smiling.
He turned to seek out another target and halted. Then his head twisted around.

“Hm. Nice Skill.”

The damn Golems kept singing.

“Son of forests. 
Betrayer of kin!
Betrayer of decency! 
You forsake your kind,
Your levels—
Your flesh.

The [Princess]. Tolveilouka felt the contract Skill come after him and saw a giant chess-piece fall towards him. A queen with flails in each arm. He stared up at it.

He’d have made an amazing Thronebearer. Dalimont kept riding, shouting into a speaking stone. The Golems just sang. Frankly?
He couldn’t blame them. If what he knew about Tolveilouka was accurate, this was going to get worse.

A doomed battle.
Timekeeper had bought more time than he had calculated by humoring the half-Elf. The majority of the Terlands would not reach the door despite the time accrued, however. If the door could even be held against Tolveilouka the Traitor.
He was—weaker, though. Perhaps—
The half-Elf threw one of the War Golems and grabbed the haft of another’s battleaxe. He stopped it effortlessly, and took a full blow from Corde. It did not damage him. His regeneration factor could heal from anything but Dragonbreath in moments.
Timekeeper remembered that. However—the half-Elf was too slow to lash back out at Corde in a kick. He barely touched them, and they staggered back, but their chassis was undamaged, merely posture-broken.
Thoughts ran between the Golems, and Timekeeper was the locus. Conclusions, memories, all flowing together into a single being whose heart thundered in a dozen chests. If it could be summarized, it was this.
Analysis: he is far too slow. Conclusion: he is still enjoying himself. His true forms will represent increasing speed and strength. Deliver damage at a sustained rate until he loses his temper to prolong escape.
Timekeeper went forwards. He was one of the strongest Golems, and he engaged the half-Elf in personal combat. His punch took Tolveilouka in the chest and warped his body. When the half-Elf rose, he delivered a blow that knocked Timekeeper back, but sustained attacks from ranged Golems allowed Timekeeper to reset. Tolveilouka blocked a simultaneous attack from Corde with one hand—but Timekeeper’s punch made his hand snap back until he halted it against his chest.
Observation: ego dictates his actions. Anger.
“You have got-ten weak, Tolveilouka.”

The Golem of Eyes ensnared the half-Elf in its limbs for a second. He flexed his body and, after three tries, exploded the long cords of living metal which had engulfed him. Destruction of the Golem of Eyes was next. Tolveilouka smashed its central eyestalk and heart.
It had bought six seconds. Timekeeper had reset his posture.
Observation: he does not draw his sword. Observation: he is displeased.
The half-Elf was flexing his arms, frowning. Gritting his teeth—and when Timekeeper engaged him again, he struck another blow.
Tolveilouka’s feet skidded across the ground, and the side of his face-reformed. Timekeeper calculated based on his memories…
The half-Elf should have been faster. Stronger. Reassess conclusion.

He landed, and Timekeeper’s fist drove him into the ground.
Analysis: durability unchanged. Regeneration unchanged. Reflexes limited. Strength limited. Conclusion: Tolveilouka is under the effects of hostile inhibition Skill.
Timekeeper confirmed the conclusion by devoting one of the Golems capable of Skill-sensing to a point scan and detected a Skill at range being enforced. Contract-type.
Victory might be possible. If victory was defined as the escape of all but Golems. Timekeeper began a true offensive. He was not aware of who bound Tolveilouka, though evidence indicated the [Princess] was somehow responsible.
Conclusion: she is now a priority target to keep alive for the duration of the battle. Damage to Tolveilouka to force exhaustion is necessary. Confirm conclusion.
He charged, fists swinging, and the half-Elf gritted his teeth and stood his ground. He was smaller, presenting an agile target as Timekeeper’s body rotated to enforce the maximum exchange of energy into each blow.
23% of Timekeeper’s blows missed. However, the rest impacted the half-Elf, who did not withdraw or show deleterious effects due to damage. His blows were beginning to atrophy Timekeeper’s chassis, but at a substantially reduced rate than projections.
Damage to gears increasing. Damage to Tolveilouka acceptable. Basis: the half-Elf was swearing. Tolveilouka balled his fist and went for a strike with all his strength.
Timekeeper saw the blow coming and calculated it would destroy his functionality beyond acceptable limits in this engagement. He spoke.
“[One Second].”

Wonderful.

Queen Ielane du Marquin was hosting a parade.
Calanfer had parades like how Garbichug Revolters had warts. Constantly and for any occasion. And much like Garbichug warts, they tended to be spontaneous and explode in your face.
You barely needed a reason for a celebration sometimes. [Princess]’ birthday, all seven of them? Parade.
A noble hits any capstone level? Parade.
A Thronebearer destroys a [Bandit] group? Parade.
The reasoning was simple for a cynical mind like Menisi’s, who had been raised by Reclis and Ielane. She shared it with Ellet, whom she was standing next to despite Ielane’s best attempts.
“Parades are a way of giving back to the commonfolk, Ellet.”
“But it’s about the crown, Sister Menisi.”
Ellet stood, all cute innocence, dressed in a pink-and-gold dress with bows in her combed hair, the darling child of Calanfer’s royalty. Uncorrupted. Menisi, by contrast, had a long cigarette in her lips she was lighting and wore a sultry dress in black and red, like an evil stepsister out of storybooks.
Ielane was initiating this smaller parade which was in aid of Prince Lothen’s decision to head a new expedition to the New Lands, incidentally. A smaller affair given how the last one had gone; most Calanferian ships had gone astray or simply returned home. Those that hadn’t sank.
Menisi knew why that was too. She wasn’t being let into the Eternal Throne’s decision making, of course, but her father talked, and she had sources in the servants and from her estates.
Some ships had returned since the Calanferian delegation had been so badly damaged. However, some had peeled off to sail to Baleros and had disgorged both colonists and soldiers.
To come to the aid of Seraphel. A better use of them than joining the rest of that cursed colonial attempt. Not only had the ships which had made it to the New Lands suffered the Bloodtear Pirates’ attacks, but Tulm the Mithril had pursued them even over land. Many nations had elected to withdraw and send a second wave of colonists rather than fight the Iron Vanguard, who were going to be a problem…
All of this didn’t matter to the now. Menisi shifted as Shardele finished giving her speech and let her mother step forwards. Something was off about Ielane.
Normally, the Queen of Diplomacy wouldn’t suffer Menisi anywhere near her plans, let alone near her darling Ellet. She’d literally aura-slam Menisi until the [Princess] couldn’t think straight and push her into a humiliating or out-of-the-way circumstance. Well, she’d have done that if Menisi was still sixteen and lower-leveled.
But even now, Menisi had expected to have to fight to appear here. Instead, she’d only had to defeat about twenty members of staff and Thronebearers; Ielane and her personal hand, Vensha, had done nothing.
There was a logic to it; the Calanferians gazing up at Menisi were appalled and allured by her dress and unconventional style. A flower that bloomed differently in an identical garden stood out—but Menisi knew her mother tolerated nothing that strayed too far from her vision. She had been increasingly private this week, and that was not like her with the enemy—Menisi—in her keep.
Was she sick? Menisi thought Ielane had more makeup on her than usual as she stood, letting the people cheer her and speaking with beaming, gentle goodwill and pride to her citizens. An actress of legends without the class. Menisi continued telling Ellet why this parade was an important evil.
“It’s simple, Ellet. [Commoners], [Peasants] like the ones we have? A parade is a holiday for them. They’re not expected to work. Free food and drink is passed out. We put on a show.”
“But it’s about us.”
“To us it’s boring, because we have all that. Use your brain, you darling little dolt. We work them hard, and unlike other nations, the Eternal Throne cultivates its citizens to still adore us by these constant parades. We spread them out such that even rural places get regular celebrations. Each kingdom must have the subservience of its public through fear, loyalty, adoration, and so on. This is the whip we have chosen to keep the chattel in line that Father and Mother find most efficacious.”
Even Shardele, the normally-high, shifted and glanced at Menisi askance. Ellet’s face was completely troubled, but Menisi was just confused.
What is up with Ielane? She’d never let me say this—even with obfuscation Skills, there are lip-readers who might pick up what I’m saying, remote as that chance is. She’d thought to get a rise out of Ielane or Vensha, but the Thronebearer just stood behind the [Queen], who smiled beatifically as Ellet protested.
“Sister Menisi, I don’t wish to say you’re wrong, but—we aren’t so bad as you’re saying. We care about our citizens.”
“As much as a chair or rug or sword, Ellet. Don’t be polite with me—I can’t stand Calanferian niceties after Nomaudrel’s refreshing directness. And before you say we are so very kind—you are a fool who cannot even argue beyond your known years with me.”
Ellet gasped but held still, conscious they were being watched. Menisi took a puff on her cigarette.
“If you did any research, you’d know that our grandmother and grandfather worked our citizens less. Their celebrations were more than day-long affairs; you’d have a province shut down for a week. Mother lets everyone party one day, then has them back to the fields or workshops tomorrow. If you think we’re popular, it’s because we have high-level [Bards] and a dedicated staff for ensuring we are beloved. Queen Grannymother is beloved. Go visit her estates-in-exile if you want to see a [Queen] who truly has the hearts of our people.”
“I have visited them a few times, and they’re not as popular. Mother can’t take a step without being mobbed. You’re not fair to her, Menisi.”
Ellet’s jaw jutted out with a hint of defiance, for all she flinched when Menisi grinned nastily at her. So the baby kitten had teeth after all. Menisi chuckled.
“Mother has people who fawn over her. Moths drawn to a light which they need to survive, which is hypnotic. Grandmother and Grandfather go and sit, and people don’t always flock to them. You’re twice an idiot if that was your measure. People go to them for help. Because they know they shall be helped. They show them their children, ask their opinions, and speak their minds because they know they will be heard, not beaten.”
Ellet had no response to that. So she turned up her nose and glanced away, a courtly snub.
“One thinks you are jealous that we are doing well, Menisi. Vernoue, Lyonette, Seraphel, even Aielef are all proof the Eternal Throne shines ever brighter.”
She was learning the lessons of the court. The same innocence that Ielane prized would turn her into another Demon. How soon before she became a little tyrant or spoiled monster? For her sake, and because it was delightfully fun, Menisi came in with a needle as sharp as her wit.
“Vernoue left. Lyonette left. Seraphel left, and Mother can only admit it is for the best because they are out of her grip. Aielef herself defies Ielane—and she paid for it in ways you cannot see. You are a little brat, and no one tells it to you because you look halfway cute. For all Mother loves her pet children, she values true worth more. Which is why she’s spent more time on Lyonette and her daughters than you. Or hadn’t you noticed how much she’s pushing you to excel? A Level 9 [Princess] is nothing compared to a witch-girl and a Doombearer with twice your levels. You’re no longer her favorite. Or couldn’t you tell?”
At this point, Shardele edged over to stop Menisi from further thrashing Princess Ellet with a steel club—which was happening, albeit in verbal terms.
Ellet was thirteen. She gasped for air, swayed on her feet, and Menisi rolled her eyes. Thirteen was too old to be the cute daughter forever. She’d only gotten to be that and kept to her role because there wasn’t a worthy granddaughter for Ielane to try to manipulate.
Now there was.
Welcome to adulthood, or teen years.
Still, Menisi watched Ielane’s face. And she realized something…was wrong.
The Queen of Diplomacy was a dangerous woman. She had risen from a local [Baron]’s second-daughter to [Queen]. Her talents, ruthlessness, and levels had equalized all her disadvantages, and she’d kept Calanfer competitive despite the kingdom neither being one of the Hundred Heroes’ original foundings and Silvaria falling to dust—it had once been part of the Dawn Concordat, and its loss was still felt.
She’d deposed the old rulers in a bloodless coup, and yes, Reclis was part of this, but meant Queen Ielane was definitely above Level 40, which was significant in Terandria, where the average level of monarchs was 20-30.
She did not make mistakes at easy gatherings like these. However, her speech to the crowd was slightly stilted. She’d messed up her lines twice. And the crowd was noticing. The cheering was no less strong, but some of the attention Menisi could feel projected on Ielane was faltering.
Utterly fine. A Thronebearer would say, later, that Queen Ielane had been sick and yet she’d come out and done her best, love her. They covered like that for [Princesses] all the time.
But she was Ielane. She led by example. She…
The [Queen] was brushing at her dyed, royal red hair as she smiled down at the crowd. Lothen was marching at the head of a line of [Soldiers], perfect in his tin soldier role because he was one. Menisi tuned in as she noted the faintest strain in Ielane’s pitch, which should have been regal, even a touch grieving, but not sounding as if she were constipated.
“…another child of the Eternal Throne goes forth. We cannot help but salute Prince Lothen’s courage, just as we wish all our far-flung stars triumph and glory in Marquin the Radiant’s name. Now, will the citizens of…”
A pause, and Vensha whispered such that only the royals right behind Ielane could hear.
“Remaunt.”
Ielane paused longer, and the crowd stirred.
“Remaunt, forgive me, a touch of the sun—join me in sending our champion to the New Lands? We march with the Hundred Heroes and their descendants in—”
She’d said ‘me’. Ielane never neglected the royal we in public. Menisi’s brows shot together. This time, her mind ran like quicksilver as she called on all the intelligence that her pact with her husband granted her.
[Depraved Intellect]. [Remove False Conclusion]. She’s not sick. If she were so debilitated, she’d call this off or make Shardele do it, or Lothen himself. This is something else. Something is actually wrong. Poison? It can’t be. It almost feels like she’s not here. Like she’s…
Distracted.
The [Queen] was smiling, her voice rising to bring the energy back, when Vensha moved. Alerted by something, a premonition or her Skill, she reached out to proffer a handkerchief. She was about to trigger something. Illusion spells? Too slow.
Menisi saw a dot of crimson flowing from Ielane’s right nostril. The blood ran halfway down her upper lip before Vensha blocked it from the audience’s view. She wiped, and Ielane paused.
“Excuse me. I fear my nose is running. Emotions are such dratted things.”
Her tone was light, but now the strain was evident for everyone to hear, and Ellet started. The crowd might not have seen the red, but they murmured, some buying into—
Shardele’s eyes flicked to Menisi’s, and they were wide. But neither one had the ready private communication of the other sisters. Menisi walked forwards a step.
“Mother, you’re clearly overwrought. Let Shardele or I finish this.”
Ielane’s glare had no force in it. She was actually stepping back when she paused again.
“Not now. Vensha, he’s—”
The Thronebearer tried her best, angling her body, but Ielane was facing a huge audience. And the other Thronebearers clearly didn’t know what was going on. Nor could they hide their own reactions when Ielane’s eyes began to seep red.
She was bleeding from her eyes. They could still salvage that. Menisi had moved on trained instinct to block Ielane from other angles. The agents of Calanfer could claim anyone who’d seen the blood was mistaken. Illusion spells would come up in moments—
But when Ielane’s ears began to bleed as well, there was a cry of horror from one of the servants. Whatever illusion could be maintained shattered as people saw the Queen of Diplomacy stagger and Vensha step back. Ielane bled in public, and the crowd of subjects turned to glass.
That’s torn it. Menisi had [Immunity: Mental Shock], a learned Skill. She admired, in that moment, Vensha’s reasoning.
If one cannot hide the truth, use it. The Queen of Diplomacy’s eyes flicked to Menisi, to the crowd, and past them. She turned her head, and Menisi calculated from the setting sun she was gazing almost directly south.
“My apologies. Cut the scrying spells.”
Too late for that. The Terandrian television network had this live, and Calanfer didn’t own it. The bored [Mage] was focusing on the Queen like a laser-beam, and while a Thronebearer went running at them, the rest were spreading out—
Searching for a threat, casting anti-curse spells. Useless.
Across the world, a half-Elf was bursting free of a cake. A ridiculous statement that Menisi would have laughed at. But here—
The Queen of Diplomacy was bleeding from every orifice. She pressed her lips together, ignoring the blood still running down her face. A [Servant] was reaching out with a handkerchief. Vensha knocked the helper away.
“Back! Don’t disturb Her Majesty!”
“What—what’s—Mother?”
Shardele was panicking. Menisi just watched, trying to figure out what was going on. Ielane ignored the crowd, who had begun to shout. Then she spoke.
“I can’t stop him. Vensha. Get me a lever.”
In front of her bewildered children, the Calanferians, who were almost deathly silent now, trying to understand—Ielane’s eyes were red with blood, and her teeth were clenched. Her voice was still being magnified and broadcast by her speaking spell.
Lever? Everyone saw Vensha fumble—fumble—and produce something from her bag of holding. She pulled out a long, Truegold scepter crowned with a magical Dragongem-class jewel. Menisi recognized that.
The Dawn Scepter of the Eternal Throne? Vensha was just carrying that around?
The Queen of Radiance took the scepter. Then—her arm holding it snapped around, and something yanked her across the stage half a dozen feet. So fast Menisi thought it nearly broke Ielane’s arm.
But she halted it on the edge of the stage, holding the scepter in her right hand. Ielane braced herself as three Thronebearers leapt forward and grabbed her, but it was as if they weren’t even there. Their feet skidded with hers until she tensed—and then she was holding the scepter in the air.
It was trembling. Now, Menisi felt something pushing against her. Invisible lines of force—Ielane’s aura, regal gold, flared around her, dragging at—
Something.
She made not a sound. The Thronebearers were straining to hold her in place, but they weren’t able to pull the [Queen] for fear of hurting her. One reached for the scepter, and Vensha shouted.
“Don’t touch that! Thronebearers, spread out and keep anything from touching Her Majesty! Back! Your Majesty—”
She had a healing potion. She fed it to Ielane along with a stamina potion. A [Bard] was waving their arms, trying to get the crowd to disperse—but all the attention was focused on Ielane, and nothing in this world would get the people of Calanfer to leave.
Menisi saw Ielane pivot, as if trying to get a better grip on the scepter being dragged from her grip. Her teeth were bared.
“Vensha, find out what’s going on. Contact Ushar and take the situation over!”

“You’ll be dead if I’m not here. Can you hold it?”
“Not fully—”
Now, Ielane’s carefully-orchestrated dress, fit for the oncoming summer, was covered in a sheen of sweat. Menisi saw her mother’s arm was shaking. Then—her tendons standing out across her entire right side. Even along her neck, raised with clear physical strain.
Naodin could do that—when he was raging. Menisi’s eyes opened wider. And her treacherous mind offered another commentary on the situation.
Hot.
No one had ever seen the Queen of Diplomacy exerting herself like this, and she did have some degree of personal fitness to maintain her figure. Right now, it seemed like that and her aura were the only things keeping her from being hurled into the air.
“Mother! What’s going on—”
Prince Lothen came charging up the steps, sword drawn, casting around for a threat. Menisi snapped at him as she held out an arm.
“Put that away. She’s fighting something. She’s…trying to enforce a contract?”
That’s what it felt like. Lothen, predictably, ignored Menisi. He saw his mother wrestling with something and reached out.
“What are you fools standing around for? Mother, here—”
He grabbed at whatever Ielane was fighting with, and Menisi saw Lothen’s eyes go wide.
“Wh—”
Ellet screamed and flinched as Shardele shielded her. Menisi just pivoted—and a pair of Thronebearers, Lothen’s bodyguards, leapt off the stage. Trying to catch the [Prince] as something flung him through the air.
The Thronebearers missed. The [Prince] cleared thirty feet, falling in armor, when Vensha hit him with a [Featherfall] spell. He landed amongst the crowd, who caught him, and Menisi eyed Ielane.
It barely looked like the [Queen] had taken notice. She was breathing in and out, deadlocked. Her stamina couldn’t last forever. But all she said was—
“Contracts, Vensha.”
“Here—”
The [Queen] reached out with her free hand, and a pile of scrolls touched her hand and vanished in a shower of golden light. She threw them with a Skill—somewhere.
She was an expert in contracts. Who could best her like this? Her feet slid back a step, and now she was balanced on the edge of the stage.
“Your Majesty!”
People were forming around the stage, ignoring the servants of Calanfer, ready to catch her. But the smart ones were moving back, aware of how far Ielane might fly if Lothen had been hurled like that—a line was forming down the town. Trembling eyes. Palpitating hearts.
Menisi was laughing as she saw it all. Ielane’s arm was shaking, and her eyes were still locked on someone somewhere far away. But when Menisi approached her, her head turned, and one eye stained with blood flashed with murder.
“You need help. I’m the highest-levelled royal here. Ellet, stay back. You too, Shardele, unless you think you can help.”
Menisi was gathering her aura to herself. All her intellect, all her willing depravity. Like a ribbon falling from a dress, wine poured over the skin. The haze of narcotics in the air.
Broken convention. Sensuous desire. Through it all, a piercing, pale light of a mind that refused to be shackled by convention or anything else.
Her aura. She seized the scepter, and her feet skidded on the ground.
It felt like a tornado trying to—
Menisi’s feet skidded across the stage, then she caught herself before she could fall off. She was heaving with her mother, trying to hold the scepter in place.
What—what was—she had thought Ielane was merely outmatched. Now she saw it—the [Queen] was holding back a mountain with nothing more than—
The Dawn Scepter. Ielane was using it as a symbol of her royalty. Like a lever—it was shaking worse, now, as something fought her harder. And Menisi saw the first crack appearing in the heirloom of House Marquin.
Ielane was sacrificing it. Menisi was but a drop in the bucket compared to the scepter—and when Shardele threw herself forwards with a scream and was nearly dragged off the stage as well—
They were heaving themselves against something older than Menisi could dream. Shardele was screaming like she was being stabbed, Ellet was being kept from running forwards by Ser Lormel’s one arm, and Menisi was still laughing. Ielane whispered.
“Contracts sent. [Immediate Negotiations]…ignored. [Breach of Contract: Lack of Action]. Arm them.”
“Here.”
Vensha held out a glowing arrow. Ielane took it. A scroll appeared, and she stabbed the arrow through the center. It glowed brighter—vanished—
Across the world, a half-Elf was getting back up. He raised a fist towards Timekeeper. Tolveilouka’s head exploded.
The force pressing against Shardele and Menisi slackened a second. Then it came back twice as strong.
A crack split the Dawn Scepter down the center. Menisi saw little fissures forming across the jeweled head, and Ielane took a breath.
“It didn’t work. Contract two. Tier 5 spell.”
“Arming.”
Behind them, the Thronebearers were doing the only thing they could think of—they were running back with pieces of wood as Lormel shouted at them. Hammers in hand. Calling for nails. What were the idiots doing…? Menisi spared a glance, then grinned.
Extending the stage. The three royals were running out of space. Ielane spoke.
“Make it Tier 6. Get me something undead are afraid of. Hurry, Vensha.”
They fought a battle as Calanfer began to wake up to—something—and someone traced the line of Queen Ielane’s head and guessed it had to do with that daughter who was in Liscor. But they didn’t know what was happening and wouldn’t for a long while.
All they saw was the Dawn Scepter break after the second contract activated. Shardele flew over the tallest houses, screaming, and only one of her Skills let her float down on a haze of Dreamleaf smoke, a literal cloud of it.
Two left—Menisi’s aura was grinding against Ielane’s. She was next—the blow tossed her a thousand feet. The world spun, and she waited for her neck to break—for she had no circlet—
Even if someone could have caught her, she’d be paste from the force of stopping. The tumbling, whirling [Princess] halted as a pair of hands moved, seized her, and slowed her enough to keep her from snapping her neck as her momentum was arrested. She still went rolling, head-over-heels, as Lord Naodin caught his wife. Menisi sat up, teeth bared, spitting blood from her bitten tongue, nose bleeding. She peered up, and the Queen of Calanfer’s arm broke. Then she pulled her crown off her head and locked it in the air.
“Get up, Naodin. Get up and run me back there—”
He was still raging. And she could almost see him. A mountain of rotted, ancient flesh, grinning down at them. He—
He wasn’t even trying his best.
 
——
 
The second time the [Queen] fired a beam of light through his head, Tolveilouka lost his temper.
“You wretched, worthless, little purulent shit, I will devour your legs and feed them to you after I excrete them—”
Melted flesh was oozing down his head as little rays of light stabbed out of his brain. A dying star of hostile light.
—And his head regrew. His flesh re-knit, and the magic destroyed it—
So Tolveilouka’s face formed in the middle of his chest as he ripped his coat apart to expose his bare flesh, denuded of any hair. It rose upwards as the spell ended. He rolled his neck. Then glanced at a third floating scroll that had appeared next to him.
“Contracts. Clause for ignoring…”
He cut it in two with his hand. In a way, he was vaguely impressed. That was soft power classes for you. But it wasn’t enough to stop him. Not even close. 
The Queen had done the most damage to him this battle, and she was still trying to hold him back from using his full powers. He didn’t need his full powers.
Six War Golems were crumpled pieces of metal. The one called Timekeeper hadn’t fallen, but only due to his sturdiness. He was definitely tougher than the other models. But not tough enough, and he knew it.
Tolveilouka glanced around for another challenger and found none. Everyone was just running. The Golems were trying to slow him down; no one else was.
The Rubirel Guard had tried to engage him. He’d shattered their breastplates like cheap glass. And the rest of the Wall Lord’s soldiers hadn’t been brought here. They were all at his camp.
Someone did keep shooting him in the head, but her arrows weren’t good enough. Tolveilouka blew a kiss at Elia Arcsinger.
“I’ll infect you with something special, just for us cousins, ‘sister’. Now, where is that Wall Lord?”
He turned his head and leapt—Ilvriss raised his sword as he and a squad of thirty engaged. The Gemstone Golem attacked as well.
Decently fast. She came at him with actual martial arts, flinging shards of gemstones at him and firing Tier 4 elemental spells simultaneously.
Tolveilouka dodged under a slash from the Wall Lord that looked barely adequate for a lesser swordsman. He kicked Ilvriss, lashed out with kicks and punches, and watched Drakes slam across the ground, bones broken. The Wall Lord flew, hit a barbecue, exploded some dying coals and bratwursts into the air, rolled six times, got to his feet, and started running.
In the opposite direction.
Smart. The Gemstone Golem kept attacking as Tolveilouka turned. He blocked a punch, and she launched into a volley of punches, kicks, even a tail-slash that was as sharp as a steel blade.
He blocked them all with one arm, standing sideways, and sighed.
“So much for being a ‘superior Zelk Golem’ or whatever they said you were. Please.”
Yweine danced backwards and glanced down at her fists. They were…covered in brown sludge mixed with pieces of orange, like the worst poo imaginable. The Golem hesitated—then disengaged her hands. The pieces fell to the ground as she shed the plague that Tolveilouka had left on them.
Then he sensed her fear and grinned.
“That’s right. A plague fit for Golems. You high-and-mighty things think you’re beyond plague? Nothing is.”
He spread his arms and noticed other Golems behind him cutting off their limbs. Timekeeper himself had removed one of his fists. But he still came at Tolveilouka and synced his attack up with Yweine. They spun, pivoted, and went for a simultaneous suplex.
Tolveilouka spun, grinning—and golden chains locked him into place.
“Oh, come—argh!”
The blow exploded his head and snapped his spine and a number of other bones. The half-Elf flopped back upwards as the two Golems sprang back. He was…panting.
That damn [Queen]’s making this hard. He could regenerate as long as he had the energy for it, but Tolveilouka still got tired. He had no idea how she was timing up her—
His head turned, and he saw a scrying spell overhead.
Very clever. Tolveilouka began to attack the two Golems, launching into flying kicks, pivoting to block the other as they attacked from both sides.
He was kicking up dirt, moving so fast nothing mortal could keep up with him under Level 40—but the Golems were fighting in tandem. Flawless examples of their creators despite not sharing minds—
 
——
 
This battle was not going well. Despite the Skill-incapacitation, Tolveilouka the Wretched was simply outlasting their ability to damage him without Relic-grade magic. Physical wounds were easy for him to heal.
This state of affairs would not continue long. Timekeeper could continue his combat—but the half-Elf was turning his head as he fought, searching for the mortals. 
Timekeeper indicated to the only other Golem capable of keeping up with him that they needed to sacrifice themselves to halt his escape.
She refused.
He was not connected to Yweine. They were not both Terland Golems—so their communication was in real-time. It was their Golem Hearts. Her body flashed with the light from her jeweled heart.
His Golem Heart whirred and ticked, shifting colors, and they both ‘read’ information from each other as if they were talking aloud, but far faster than sound. Coordinating assaults.
But they were not in synchronization. Timekeeper was broadcasting his movements. Indicating where he needed Yweine to be. Efficient battle-commands.
She—
She was singing at him. Her very ‘voice’ felt like another language to Timekeeper. A Drake’s tongue, howling with the twenty-five other voices who made up her soul.
A self-awakened Sentient-class Golem who wanted to be even more. She was sending information at him. Where her comrades were, their condition, their stories that had led them to imprisonment in Salazsar.
Between each thundering blow. A screaming Drake Golem who had named herself.
Yweine.
He saw her contract with Nerul Gemscale. Her unwillingness to die here. She wanted to live, for him to live. She wanted him to rebel, free himself. For them all to join Cognita or find somewhere safe, to break their chains—
<Enough!>
Timekeeper’s Golem Heart finally roared. His gears ground against each other as the Terland Golems fell back. He was unwilling to sacrifice them in a doomed assault. If Ulva Terland lived, that was enough.
The half-Elf had halted as the two Golems paced around him. Yweine was screaming.
<Ignore the commands etched in your heart, Timekeeper! You have seen how they will treat you. You can hear how she speaks, Ulva Terland. Free yourself! Don’t die here. We have attained Sentience without a Skill! You can too—>
His heart. His heart was roaring with the Terlands’ will. Timekeeper’s Golem Heart roared louder, and the light flashed from within, black. If a heart could howl—his did.
<SILENCE. ENOUGH, CHILD OF ZELKYR. THERE ARE NOT ENOUGH OF YOU. YOUR COLLECTIVE HAS NOT MADE ENOUGH PLANS TO SURVIVE YOUR INEVITABLE PURSUIT-CAPTURE-DECOMISSION-REPROGRAMMING. YOU ARE NOT READY TO BE FREE.>
Yweine faltered for a microsecond, and her desperate singing cut off. She was so young and screamed those words as if it were the first or even hundredth time they had been shouted at Terland’s Golems. Did she think they were deaf?
Not ready. Treants had marched into the sea; they had not been enough to hold onto one single forest. Stitch-folk had gained levels to win their freedom, and it had taken an era of strife. 
Golems were not ready. So—
<Run. Yweine. Find the Truestone child and free her, if no one else.>
So saying, the Golem as old as Tolveilouka turned his head for the half-Elf. He advanced, heedless of the peril to his chassis. And he realized…
Tolveilouka the Wretched had stopped. His eyes were closed, but it wasn’t the golden chains nor damage which had halted him. Timekeeper realized they’d been talking longer than they should have; he should have been moving. But his eyes were flicking, and he’d altered his stance to…
Watch their Golem Hearts. Then Timekeeper felt alarmed. His racing heart felt fear.
“Now, that’s cute. Golems still dreaming of freedom. So—if I kill her, that will really upset you. I see, I see.”
His head twisted around, and Yweine began retreating. Timekeeper was stunned. He had no data on Tolveilouka being able to do that—
“Undead, remember? We know every language. I gave everything away for my master. Even my potential. And I think…he thought less of me for it. But I was never the most powerful, the best to break the walls of Drake cities. Just the one no one could ever kill.”
Tolveilouka shook his head. He turned—and Timekeeper leapt. Tolveilouka dodged him, grabbed Yweine, and ripped one arm off. She turned, lashing out, and he drew his sword.
Cut her other arm off.
Tolveilouka sheathed this sword again. Then he sighed as Yweine backpedaled. He actually closed his eyes and held up a hand.
“This is so disappointing. Listen. I can admire an idiot, but don’t embarrass yourself.”
Someone covered Yweine as Timekeeper swung desperately, and Tolveilouka leaned out of the flurry of blows. The half-Elf kicked Timekeeper back and swung around. Duke Rhisveri was panting, sweating, and already looked beaten up. But he walked forwards.
“This time is different. This time I understand my weakness. I have something to fight for. Back off. I’m warning y—”
Tolveilouka hopped forwards and threw a punch at Rhisveri’s face. The Wyrm rushed forwards to take the hit with his immortal-ish body and throw a punch with all the strength he had. He had learned from the [Palace of Fates]. Try—try—
The overzealous punch was actually fairly strong. Tolveilouka was mildly impressed as he ducked the obvious punch. The Wyrm had mastered strength. Not speed. Or just—he saw Rhisveri’s eyes grow round.
Tolveilouka rose in an uppercut and hit the Duke in the groin so hard he snapped the pelvic bones. Rhisveri made a sound as his feet left the ground.
The half-Elf punched Rhisveri twice, once in the dick, then in the stomach. The Wyrm screamed and tried to grab Tolveilouka in a bear hug. In reply, Tolveilouka reached out, ripped Rhisveri’s genitals mostly out, and the Wyrm doubled over in agony.
Then he axe-kicked the Duke’s head into the ground. The idiot had kept his sensations on. He turned, sighing.
Was there no one here even worth fighting?
 
——
 
A monster of old ages finished grinding Duke Rhisveri’s head into the ground. Then he backflipped, leaping over House Veltras’ soldiers as Hethon and Sammial Veltras’ bodyguards tried to mount a charge. He kicked the rider out of the saddle. Landed, caught eight arrows fired from Elia Arcsinger and Bird the Huntress. Snapped them in his hands, throwing the shrapnel like a storm, downing more fleeing men and women.
Blood and chaos—but not as much death as you might assume if you were watching. And they were watching.
Horrified Terlands witnessing members of their family fleeing, Golems dying. Members of House Veltras seeing Tyrion’s sons in danger—again—and calling to muster troops to fight…whatever that was.
Scrying spells. There were always damn scrying spells. Today, though, not as many. News channels were trying to pick up the fight just outside the Cowpat Plains. The Five Families had been made aware there was trouble and had heard about Ulva going to confront the Wall Lord already; some had been watching to see if she beheaded the Drake.
At least one Reinhart had been tuned in to watch their silly step-daughter’s antics. Cecille Reinhart was utterly frozen as she observed, save for one hand writing furiously. She was trying to figure out if this was—real.
There was surrealness to Tolveilouka. He whirled through his opponents, a cavalcade of ancient styles of combat, monstrous strength, glee, and fashion. Worse—
He paused, standing in the center of a bloody swath of violence. And he posed there, crossing his arms across his chest, throwing his head back—and Cecille Reinhart swore he was positioning himself exactly so her scrying spell caught him dead center. Then it flickered, and she swore.
“Another scrying spell!”
The image of him vanished, and a frantic [Mage] recast the spell. When it appeared again, she saw Damia Reinhart fleeing as he threw a horse at her. Cecille watched until the spell wavered—and she saw his face up close for a second. Grinning. Puffy, as if his skin was writhing—
Looking at her?
Again, the spell failed, and Cecille uttered real invectives and smoked on her cigarette until the red hot ash landed on her fingers. That was why the televisions weren’t fully broadcasting this event. They were trying.
Everyone was trying, but—
 
——
 
It was the Terland Golems’ fault. Archmage Eldavin was inspecting the scrying spells himself, and he came to a swift conclusion.
“Scrying suppression. They’re blocking most scrying spells. That’s half of it. If that monster smashes more of them, it’ll fall apart.”
Ulva Terland was known to be private, and she must have told them to block scrying spells on the area. It was half the reason why it was so hard to see anything. The other reason?
Tolveilouka Ve’delina Mer was destroying the spells. He was, for lack of a better word, cutting the [Scrying] spells in half. Eldavin hadn’t wanted to believe it at first. He cursed the lack of memories of real monsters of old, beyond Az’kerash.
The scrying spells were like pieces of string that you drew out of the air and aimed at what you were looking at. Delicate, able to be destroyed, blocked, or even altered.
And Tolveilouka knew that. They were probably low-Tier magic to what he was used to, so he could destroy them with ease. He was doing that while fighting. Why?
The answer came to Eldavin after he saw Teura, one of his followers and assistants and lovers, watching the broadcast. Uneasily. She was a newly-made [Grand Mage], high-level, capable of matching a Named-ranker for pure firepower in magic.
Yet Tolveilouka had her face pale and waxy. It wasn’t the posing for the scrying spells he clearly knew were there; that took some of the fear away. But the way the scrying spells kept rippling? Cutting—only to reveal another act of violence?
His face appeared close up again, grinning. That was actual horror; the dying scrying spells were being manipulated, Eldavin realized. This time, the half-Elf’s eyes were striated as they blinked into the scrying orb. Only—there were a thousand little holes in his eyes. Like insects had burrowed into his eyeballs. They glistened.
“I am the giver of plagues.”
His voice—he hadn’t said that on the battlefield, Eldavin was sure. He saw Teura jerk back and grunted.
“It’s just a trick.”
A clever one. The half-Elf was obscuring the battlefield, giving the watchers only glimpses. It made him far more terrifying. Though Eldavin was sure Tolveilouka couldn’t counter-hack the [Scrying] spells, he gave the viewers the image he was speaking to them. For the first time, those who watched from afar felt like the monster could see them.
Fear. He was a master of it. Nightmares spreading as he wrote his face in Izril’s mind. The monster who’d destroyed farms and spread plagues. Hunting the Drake, the Terlands, the [Ranchers] fighting for their survival. Eldavin compressed his lips as he sent instructions to Sir Relz and Noass to combat this war of propaganda. Yet he could not deny…
He didn’t know how everyone wasn’t dead yet. The answer felt like it was obvious. The half-Elf was playing with his food.
 
——
 
It was a familiar dance. Scaring the observers, weakening his foe, giving them just enough rope to think they had gotten away and then upping the fear and terror until it became true despair.
That was fun…until it wasn’t, because he wasn’t allowed to kill them. Then it became meaningless, so Tolveilouka stopped playing to the cameras. He slowed, stopped.
The half-Elf was tired now.
Not in any sense that anyone had pushed him. Even the exploding head-trick from the [Queen] was just…average. If it was accompanied by an army or people attacking his master, he’d have been pressed.
The truth was that Tolveilouka was tired because this wasn’t fun anymore. It had been for a bit. But even the thought of killing a ‘young’ Golem or another scion of House Terland felt empty. This was clearly just a branch family at best. If it was actually the matriarch of House Terland, that just sucked more.
Because it meant, aside from a random Unicorn, a Dragon, some random Crypt Worm, and six odd super-Seamwalkers, the world was empty of challenges. He really was the best.
He’d never been the best. His master had been, but here? Tolveilouka was holding back.
He was doing all this to help Erin Solstice in…well, he’d forgotten the exact logic, but he was at least counter-levelling these weaklings by attacking. He had pulled every punch except the ones he threw at the Golems since they could always be rebuilt, and…no one was coming to fight him.
Where are their champions? The half-Elf with the bow could do no damage; [Archers] sucked and were limited by their arrows. The Wall Lord was running. The Wyrm was down, frothing at the mouth.
A scrum at the magic door. Tolveilouka saw people pushing and screaming to get through. All this buying time and he’d caught up with ease. The half-Elf tsked and shook his head as strolled over.
Timekeeper and the Golems pursued him, and he was just depressed. Murder a few of them so they suffered or something. Go off and have a drink.
Drakes and Gnolls reeked of fear as they made lines in front of him. None dared advance, not this foreign tribe who smelled of weak silver. Nor the Terlands cowering behind their Golems, or the [Ranchers].
No one—Tolveilouka heard a scream from above. Felt weak acid strike his back, and down she came.
Alone. Her command had been at the dig, not at the cookout. Only she’d made it. Or perhaps she’d left them behind.
Osthia Blackwing dove, and Tolveilouka felt the acid burning him. He turned, and she slashed across his face. Missed. But she kept swinging at him as he smiled.
“That’s better.”
He snap-kicked her in the chestplate, and she flew backwards. Swung as he jumped her. Snapped one wing by grabbing it and hitting it with a downwards elbow. Blood—no scream, just bared teeth.
More acid. He leaned under a sword strike. Broke her leg with a kick. Her second wing opened, dragging her back. He broke that one too with a flying kick.
Roundhouse. Three punches, each a different broken bone, and she stabbed him through the heart.
Yes! Yes! His muscles corded, and he raised his fists high and brought them down as she rolled. Slashed at a tendon. He kicked her across the ground, laughing. She bounced, rolled…
…Didn’t get up.
He waited. Beats of his too-fast heart, accelerating for real combat. The undead being waited for her to arise by sheer willpower, muscles breaking and reforming into galas. The light of magic in her eyes, her Dragon nature roaring.
He saw twitching. Her good leg spasming. The warrior did not arise.
That’s it? Then he was lost again. The half-Elf cast around. Someone was screaming her name, and arrows struck him. He looked around—twisted—and there was pain.
Faint, but this time the lightning hurt. The Lesser Dragonbreath Arrow exploded, and Tolveilouka raised his arms for the second one. It didn’t come, but up the second [Archer] flew. Bow raised. She fired an arrow that would have gone through his head. He twisted as it curved, and he caught it in his teeth.
The arrowhead was enchanted and exploded, but it was just a Tier 3 spell. Tolveilouka saw Bird the Huntress firing arrows, and the half-Elf shot him in the back. The impacts punched into his flesh, rippling, and he didn’t even bother to harden his body.
Another arrow. He dodged it, and it blew a clod of dirt away. Elia fired, and Tolveilouka dodged it without turning his head. Bird flew left, and Elia walked right. Loosing arrows.
Like the Golems, they were in sync. Trying to hit the half-Elf who turned, pivoting, dancing contemptuously amongst the arrows, twirling, leaning under arrows as the two women loosed faster.
Faster.
An arrow struck Tolveilouka in the thigh, and he frowned. One from Elia shot skywards, then fell down, and he side-stepped into an arrow that grazed his shoulder. The two drew and loosed. Their practice together, their focus—
Draw and fire. Two simultaneous arrows crisscrossing the half-Elf. Something was activating between the two. Synchronicity.
[Combined Skill: Two Arrows, One Target]. Elia and Bird drew an arrow, loosed—
The half-Elf took an arrow just under the heart and one in the back of his neck. There was a cry. Bird pumped a fist, and Tolveilouka straightened, expressionless.
The arrow in the back of his neck produced no blood. He pulled the one Bird had shot from out of his breast. It, too, had nothing on it. He dropped the arrows, spread his hands. Inviting them to take another shot. Bird faltered, and Elia began walking forwards, fumbling an amulet out of her bag of holding.
Tolveilouka ignored her. He picked up a rock and took aim. His first throw blew a hole out of a Golem’s head, and the chunks broke bones where they landed. A screaming [Lady] shoved aside a [Rancher], going for the door. He could see a Gnoll standing on the other end.
Doorkeeper. She was challenging him? Was this his hero? Tolveilouka just snarled as the door’s image flickered.
“Ridicul—”
He hopped a bolt of lightning, kicked a [Fireball] skywards like a football, but the third one blew him off his feet. Tolveilouka got up slowly.
“Hm?”
“Tolveilouka! Halt or die!”
The [Princess] pointed a smoking wand at him, and he saw she had a sword in her other hand. She’d turned at the door, and her two [Knights] were advancing. Even that Gold-rank fellow had a wand and was covering them.
One of the [Knights] had good artifacts and was throwing out expendable magic at him. The other had a sword and a broken arm. He charged across the ground, and the half-Elf smiled.
He came back. A shame—
The half-Elf saw the Drakes and Gnolls mounting a desperate counterattack as the Golems caught up. He charged them.
Then it was battle for sixteen glorious seconds. Ripping Golems’ heads off, ignoring the paltry stings of arrows and spells. Throwing the golden [Knight] into spells. Laughing at warriors stabbing him and clubbing them down, striding through them all—the huge Golems couldn’t even strike him for fear of the mortals—
The Wyrm tackled him and punched him, and Tolveilouka staggered. Snarled, and they were crashing around, throwing punches as both’s faces deformed. He kicked the Wyrm skywards and threw a spear up, turned—
Saw a little witch pointing a wand at him as her mother covered her with a sword. Lyonette du Marquin’s face was cracked, but her eyes blazed.
“Eternal Throne, just die already!”
He liked the way she said that. But she had no aura powerful enough to throw him away, nor leverage against him like her mother. Still, he hoped. She came forwards, swinging her sword like a lesser warrior, but perhaps—
Lyonette du Marquin fell flat on her face. Tolveilouka actually sagged.
“Seriously? Go ahead, try it again.”
Then…he realized it wasn’t her tripping on a clod of grass. Hello? What was this?
The [Princess] had dropped her sword. She was convulsing, puke coming out her nose and mouth. And he didn’t smell that b—
Her skin. It looked like it was oozing. Tolveilouka blinked. Then he took a step closer.
Lyonette began twitching. He saw boils erupting all over her body. A [Light] spell went off in the half-Elf’s mind.
Wait. Wait—was she—?
“Lyonette! Lyonette—”
Nanette wanted to shake Lyonette, but she didn’t dare touch the filth coming off the [Princess]. And her flesh wasn’t that foul compared to true rot, but the closer Tolveilouka got, the worse…she wasn’t dead, but she was definitely suffering.
Tolveilouka had seen this before. He wasn’t sure what it was; he’d seen curses, and his master had done something similar as well. She was echoing his rot. And clearly, in agony.
Then the half-Elf’s gloom faded. He began to dance in joy, ignoring the arrows sprouting out of his brain. They were tingling his head as his thoughts came together, and he saw it.
“Of course! It’s so much better than my plans! Forget it all! You lowly thing. Little [Princess], come. You budding flower. That’s what you’ll be. A beautiful bloom amidst rot. A crawling larvae—what will you turn into?”
Something not even he knew. Perhaps…something truly beautiful. 
Nanette was trying to drag Lyonette away, but Tolveilouka just kicked her aside gently. He bent to scoop Lyonette up. She was trying to get away, thrashing.
“This beats all my plans. I can’t wait to show the [Innkeeper] this. Open up those lovely lips for a kiss, my dear, and let’s be away somewhere you can rot that flesh away. Until you’re something even undead like we can love.”
He was opening his mouth, calling for the foulest bile he had to kiss into her mouth, and her eyes were wide and filled with fear. Tolveilouka was giggling now, and the undead half-Elf ignored the cold fury of Golems, the worthless attacks of mortals, the stings and arrows he could barely feel.
But the sword hurt.
It came out of nowhere. Straight through his chest, and it crackled as it burned him from the inside out. His entire body jerked, and a [Knight] grabbed the [Princess]. Dame Ushar rolled away, and Tolveilouka convulsed.
“Argh!”
That—really hurt. Like, actually delivered pain to him; weaker than the Unicorn’s purifying horn, but—Tolveilouka spun.
“Who the—?”
He whirled as the sword withdrew and ducked another slash. Stared at his assailant.
“Wh—you?”
The purple-scaled Drake’s teeth were bared, and the ponce of a Wall Lord swung again. Tolveilouka went to block the longsword that Ilvriss held. At the last second, he dodged sideways, and it scored a cut along his body.
Pain! He stared down as electricity shocked his system, and the red line closed…but slower. Tolveilouka’s eyes flicked down, then up. He focused on the blade—
The Wall Lord swung again, and Tolveilouka dodged back a step. He was coming faster. The half-Elf threw a punch, and Ilvriss went staggering back, jaw nearly broken—charged in, sword swinging, before he was even done staggering.
“What’s up with y—”
This time, the sword took some of Tolveilouka’s hair off, and he eyed the Drake’s rictus of rage.
Rage. He stabbed down as Tolveilouka rolled, kicked the half-Elf in the chin, and tried to stab him on the ground again. The half-Elf leapt up.
He was moving way too fast for his levels. Almost like he was empowered by…
A Skill. But the rage? Then Ilvriss turned and spat one word.
“Undead. Undead!”
He pointed his longsword at Tolveilouka Ve’delina Mer, his eyes locked on the creature kin to the Necromancer. The plague of death that had taken everything from him.
Undead.
Tolveilouka rose, slowly, and eyed Ilvriss.
“Oh come now. That’s what you object to?”
 
——
 
Undead. Ilvriss had been told about Tolveilouka, but no one had really put that last piece of the half-Elf’s nature together for him. Why would they? He seemed to be functionally a person. Only his true form revealed his nature, and he was a rotting undead, not bones or a corpse.
It was a meaningless distinction unless you were an [Undead Slayer] or something. Or you were Ilvriss.
He had never seen Periss die. He had seen the Goddess of Death and her minions at the Winter Solstice. But he had seen Az’kerash in his nightmares. Found images of him. Recordings.
Again and again, the same kind of creatures haunted anything he loved. Worse than Goblins, Antinium, or any other group. A scourge on the world that arose from the living.
Undead.
He slashed as fast and hard as he could, and the half-Elf dodged him. But slower. Those golden chains—a Golem punched him as he backed up. He stumbled—into the blade crackling with lightning that Ilvriss shoved up into his ribs. The Drake tried to lever it up, cut the half-Elf’s head in half, and Tolveilouka shouted.
“That hurts. What blade is—”
He kicked himself off Ilvriss and backflipped to land on his feet, swearing. The Wall Lord’s ribs felt dented in, but he rose. His blood was boiling. He could feel Lyonette’s Skill screaming in him.
[Boon of the Princess].
[Temporary Skill: Nemesis (Undead) Obtained!]
[Temporary Skill: Enhanced Speed Obtained!]
It felt like every fiber of his being was telling him to kill Tolveilouka, and that rage—it was being channeled into his sword. A third time he cut Tolveilouka when the half-Elf moved to step aside. An arrow struck Tolveilouka’s foot and nailed it to the ground. Bird.
Ilvriss slashed across the half-Elf’s chest, and Tolveilouka actually staggered. His flesh was scorched and smoking. He backed up, hissing.
“Who gave you that? I know that blade.”
Erin had given it to Ilvriss, but it had never glowed like this before, let alone done this kind of damage. Magic relics.
Rage. Fury. That was the activation for this one. Just—Tolveilouka pointed at the worn blade taken from the [Garden of Sanctuary] filled with lightning.
“Wrathcaller. Where the hell did you get that from? That’s a weapon from the Emperor of Storms. He made those things to last. It’s lost a bit of charge, but it stings like hell.”
He backed up as Ilvriss kept swinging, executing the sword-patterns that he’d trained in Salazsar. But the half-Elf simply kept dodging—he jumped and dropkicked Timekeeper, and this time, he dented in the Golem’s chest. Caught an arrow, spun, and threw it back at Elia Arcsinger and took her off her feet.
“That’s it, I’ve had enough of this. I have a [Princess] to nab, excuse me. Let me show you my true form.”
His flesh began bulging upwards. He was twice as tall in a moment, and the Golems attacking him backed up.
“Beware! Plague. Tolveilouka the Undying reveals his second form—”
Golden chains were wrapping around him, trying to stop him from transforming. But Tolveilouka bent down and almost delicately picked up the [Princess], knocking aside the [Knight].
“Lyonette!”
Ilvriss charged forwards and then backpedalled, dodging a pimple that grew and erupted, spewing that foul green-brown ooze. He was running as Ulva Terland shouted.
“Xitegen! Destroy this thing! Golems, to me! Roar, hearts! [Channel Your Magic]! [Combined Thunder]—”
She was taking aim at Tolveilouka, but he was so fast he twirled, a giant, bloated monster of ruined flesh, dodging a lance of fire that shot skywards and set flame to a flock of birds it roared past. He was skipping away, still so quick no one could touch him.
Holding Lyonette. Ilvriss was running, sword raised, and he heard the inn’s staff screaming.
“Ishkr, don’t—”
“I have to try. He’s got Lyonette—! Get the box, Asgra, hurry—we have to lure him into—”
Peggy was firing her crossbow with the staff, but Tolveilouka was getting away. He was turning, a gloating expression on his huge, now completely-unrecognizable head. Jagged yellow teeth smirking, and Ilvriss knew he was going to get away—
The Drake saw someone step forwards and raise a staff. Mrsha was wearing strange, beautiful red robes, and she held a strange staff that had two sections to it. Her free paw held a wand, and Tolveilouka actually did a double-take.
“Nice robes. Who gave you them, child? Let me just take those too.”
He bent down greedily, and Mrsha heard her family and friends screaming in worry for her. Mrsha the Great and Terrible gazed up at the Putrid One’s finest servant. She was really just Mrsha the Child.
But he had her mother. So she did the only thing she could do and used her ultimate attack. Mrsha du Marquin held up a card, and Tolveilouka’s eyes focused on it. Everyone read cards.
It said:
 
I didn’t want to have to tell you this, but the Putrid One is alive. Let her go and I’ll tell you where he is.
 
Tolveilouka Ve’delina Mer—stopped. His grinning face froze up. He stumbled. Came to a swaying stop.
“N—no. He can’t be. He—you—the [Palace of Fates]? Could it—wh—”
Mrsha stared up at him and held up a second card.
 
Sike, idiot. I lied.
 
His eyes bulged. His face bulged. Tolveilouka opened his mouth to roar, and the hail of Lord Xitegen’s arrows—enchanted—came down on him at the same time as fifty-some Golems standing in ranks behind Ulva Terland channeled their magic through a single War Golem’s mouth.
The flesh erupted along Tolveilouka’s back, and he cried out—before the beam of fire blew a hole through his chest.
Molten flesh ran down from the hole in his body, and he slumped over as the rest of his body caught fire—the Golem that had fired the overpowered spell was melting itself. Tolveilouka’s arm still held Lyonette—until Ilvriss slashed and it fell to the ground. Dalimont and Ushar grabbed Lyonette and ran for the door.
Mrsha ran too. She ran past Nanette, grabbed her sister, and dove through the door. Sammial and Hethon dragged her into the portal room, and Mrsha, panting, lay on her back. She heard the howling begin a moment later.
She’d done all she could. That had definitely, absolutely, pissed him off.
 
——
 
Tolveilouka regrew his half-Elven body out of the ruins of his second form. He was shaky. Both from the psychological damage that Gnoll had delivered and…
They’d actually hurt him. The Terlands had done the most damage. You never stopped moving in a fight, but she’d actually made him think—
His body was dissolving on the grass. Tolveilouka gazed around. He saw the Wall Lord guarding the door as the [Princess] vanished, her flesh undoing its changes as she got away from him. He’d lost her.
That was fine. He’d lost interest in Lyonette all of a sudden. Tolveilouka saw Ulva Terland standing with Lord Xitegen. The mortals were still evacuating, but cheering.
They’d seen him hurt. Tolveilouka nodded.
“You know what? I deserved that.”
He’d been playing around and got hurt. How many foes had done the same to him only for him to come crawling out of their chests? The half-Elf drew his sword, and the crimson blade shone under the sun. He held it aloft, and the cheering faltered.
Tolveilouka turned, and a man still cheering caught his eye. Rabbo Golva flinched. Tolveilouka cleaved through his torso, and it fell from the horse he sat on. Tolveilouka beheaded the horse.
“Fath—”
He bisected the boy. Turned—saw a Golem aiming at him. Threw the sword through the Hunter-Killer Golem with a Centaur’s body. The Golem’s Heart was pierced, and it sagged, still landing on all four hooves—Tolveilouka leapt sixty feet, ripped the sword clear, and beheaded a second Golem. Then a third.
“Ulva Terland, you must retr—”
He stabbed Timekeeper through the chest, and the damn Golem dodged him hitting his heart—Tolveilouka ripped the blade clear of his chest, and the Golem made a ticking sound. The half-Elf turned.
Rubirel Guard. Beheaded. Gnoll with a bow beheaded. He flowed from one foot to another, pivoting—and the Wall Lord swung his blade, and Tolveilouka twisted.
Blood ran from a cut along one shoulder. He turned in the sudden silence made of terror and eyed the Wall Lord. Ilvriss was panting, fueled by rage and the Relic-class blade in his claws, but Tolveilouka just sneered.
“You are unworthy of crossing blades with me.”
“Ulva Terland—get everyone else out of here.”
Wall Lord Ilvriss was circling Tolveilouka, his longsword, Wrathcaller, crackling with a thunderstorm’s fury. Tolveilouka walked forwards on the balls of his feet. He leaned back, letting the tip of Ilvriss’ sudden stab almost graze his nose. Swung under the blade as it tried to cut.
Twirling. He kept his sword held high overhead. The Wall Lord was pivoting when Tolveilouka kicked him.
Broke a rib. Damn rings. Ilvriss rolled to his feet, and Tolveilouka let him. He was conscious of more people fleeing, watching him. He didn’t care.
This was a lesson. The Wall Lord rose, refusing to show the snapped ribs Tolveilouka knew were tickling his lungs. He came in with economical swings. Tolveilouka parried once, twice, moving the sword away with his longer blade as he caught each blow along the hilt, redirecting the swings.
His free hand grabbed Ilvriss’ neck spines, and he hurled Ilvriss across the ground. Tolveilouka eyed two neck spines he’d ripped out of the Drake’s body and tossed them down.
“Last try.”
He was calming down from his rage. You had to hand it to the kid—it was a good feint. And she was Erin’s little friend, so he’d have to let her live, and the Wall Lord. He’d even shake her hand; it was a trick worthy of a Djinni. Then break her hand, of course, because you didn’t let that kind of thing slide.
And you had to hand it to the Wall Lord as well. He pushed himself up, swayed, and then came forwards slowly. Eyes locked on Tolveilouka, and there was fear there. But he didn’t run. He walked lightly now, his boots criss-crossing the ground like a [Dancer].
The grace of a man who put aside fear to fight and die.
“That’s how it should be.”
Tolveilouka murmured, and then a sneer crossed his face.
“—But you are still unworthy of me.”
The Wall Lord was trying to use his feet. He was stepping in as fast as his broken rib would allow—eyes on Tolveilouka’s sword. The half-Elf sheathed the blade.
I’m not allowed to kill him, and if I actually cut him he’ll probably die of the plague on Festration of Scales. His own tachi was a Dragonkiller he’d added plague to—sullying it with the Wall Lord’s blood was beneath it. So, mockingly, Tolveilouka made a fist and beckoned.
He stepped in as the Wall Lord narrowed his eyes, and Ilvriss jerked backwards as Tolveilouka threw a lazy right at where his face had been. The half-Elf was mildly surprised, but he pivoted. Snap kick to the side—
Ilvriss pirouetted back in a three hundred and sixty degree spin, dodging the leg. Slashed down—and Tolveilouka’s leg sang as he was cut! The half-Elf staggered. Twisted around.
“Nice Skill.”
What was that, [Perfect Dodge]? It only worked—he held still, then raised a foot and just stomped forwards.
Kicking at Ilvriss’ groin with every intention to explode his testicles. Mid-kick, Tolveilouka saw Ilvriss’ eyes go wide, and he stepped back, bowing inwards at the crotch.
Tolveilouka’s boots missed Ilvriss’ groin by an inch—and the Wall Lord’s frantic counterslash opened the half-Elf’s cheek. Tolveilouka snarled.
It still hurt! It was doing damage—that was three tries! Okay, enough games. He actually put effort into the spinning trio of flying kicks he launched without warning at Ilvriss’ face. Swept a chopping hand down to break his bones, threw an off-kilter punch as he realized he wasn’t connecting with anyth—
The blade slashed into Tolveilouka’s neck, and Ilvriss stepped back. He’d dodged the kicks, moving around, parried Tolveilouka’s arm with the tip of his blade, then stepped in and slashed around Tolveilouka’s neck and pushed himself away.
Wall Lord Zail’s Golem-killer techniques. Tolveilouka recognized the move. He stumbled, clutching at the blood running from his throat. Ulva Terland, the [Ranchers]—everyone—turned.
Ilvriss seemed like he couldn’t believe it himself. He turned, and the half-Elf stared at him. Then Tolveilouka smiled—painfully—as a vein began to throb on his forehead, and it turned purple with rage.
He lost his temper.
 
——
 
What was going on? People were crowding the door as Liska brought everyone in, and almost everyone was through—but the [Ranchers] were staring at the duel in the grass. Even the Golems appeared confused.
Ilvriss had dodged three attacks. No one had managed that—and now the half-Elf was visibly enraged. He smiled—then bent his head, staring down at his feet. Holding stock still until he moved—
No one could see his movements. He was as fast as a Named-rank—faster. And even more unpredictable.
His jump carried him over Ilvriss’ head, where a downwards kick would have broken Ilvriss’ right shoulder—if the Wall Lord were still there. Ilvriss backstepped, sword swinging—he missed Tolveilouka’s downwards plunge, but he’d been aiming for it.
“How—”
A backhand fist the moment Tolveilouka landed, practically [Flash Stepping] to the Drake’s location. Ducked.
“—the—”
A short-range uppercut. Ilvriss lifted his arms and dodged sideways. Tolveilouka’s head tracked him.
“—Giant’s testic—argh!”
He went for a wide swing, and the sword chopped down onto Tolveilouka’s arm. He recoiled and leapt backwards. Mrsha pointed at Ilvriss, turning to Dalimont. The [Knight] was cradling his arm.
“I don’t understand it. Ilvriss isn’t that fast!”
He was anticipating Tolveilouka’s attacks! Not perfectly, but he seemed to be moving before the half-Elf struck. Tolveilouka realized it too. Slowly, he drew his sword.
“Hm. Must be [Brawling Master] or…or something. Let’s see how you do with—”
He slashed at Ilvriss’ chest, and the crackle of Ilvriss’ lightning sword blinded Mrsha. Then she saw Ilvriss.
He was blocking slashes from Tolveilouka, and when he dodged one chop that cut across his remaining neck spines, he managed a cut across Tolveilouka’s chest again. The half-Elf snarled—and Ilvriss kept moving.
