He leaned out of the way of the blade, knocked it aside, leaned the other way out of a kick—and kept wobbling his torso.
Ilvriss was backstepping, but there was a weird rhythm to his steps. When Tolveilouka halted to stare at him with the same expression as the others—Mrsha saw Ilvriss keep moving.
He was—
Was he—dancing?
Yes, he was! He was pivoting across the soil, tracing the steps of a Terandrian waltz. The same kind he’d practiced with Lyonette. No—it was even more familiar. Mrsha knew it in a moment.
That’s Erin’s dance! Only, it wasn’t perfectly according to the steps. Ilvriss’ tail kept wagging across the dirt, and Tolveilouka watched it, seeming hypnotized. Then he lifted his sword—
He came forwards in a [Fencer]’s lunge, stabbing, and Ilvriss slashed across his guts. He had been dodging the lunge before the tachi moved. He backed up—and he was definitely dancing.
“You—damn—”
Tolveilouka went chasing after him. He got Ilvriss’ sword buried in his guts and screamed before twisting his torso. Ilvriss had to let go of his blade, and Tolveilouka punched, kicked, slashed—all of them misses. The Drake danced in, and Ilvriss ripped his sword out of the stomach and kept dancing.
And now he was doing the Highstepper. The half-Elf’s eyes bulged, but Mrsha was suddenly cheering. The Wall Lord was focused, sweating bullets—and when Tolveilouka charged him, sword swinging, he got in two cuts and jumped back.
He’s seeing the future!
She wrote to Dalimont. The [Knight] stared at her, wide-eyed, then at the Wall Lord. That was the only explanation for it. Tolveilouka was leaping, slashing across the ground, each lunge carrying him a dozen feet or more, but Ilvriss was stepping out of the way, even leaning under one blade-sweep.
Not perfectly. He ate a close-range punch he was too slow to dodge. Stumbled on some dirt and had to block a slash that sent him skidding—but he seemed to see what was coming.
His eyes were wide, sweat rolling down his forehead into them, but he dared not blink. Then Mrsha saw what Erin had been trying to teach. What she herself might not have learned yet.
Her magic, silly dance with its steps that you’d mess up. A dance where you had to anticipate your partner’s moves and yet never could until you learned the magic at the heart of it.
The [Dance of Foresight].
Both men were moving faster now. Tolveilouka was attacking in wide arcs, face disbelieving.
“It can’t be. You—those were rare even in my—argh! A magical dance?”
He knew what was going on. But Ilvriss kept stabbing him, and the half-Elf was panting. He looked around and saw the Golems arrayed against him. Saw hostile magics in the air, starting to track him.
But he refused to back down.
“Two can play that game, you damn amateur. How’s it go?”
He began to move his feet across the ground in a complicated rhythm, clearly concentr—
Ilvriss’ sword beheaded Tolveilouka as his footwork began to become ominous and sharp, and the half-Elf’s body splayed across the ground. The Wall Lord stabbed him eight times before the head reattached to the body. Mrsha was shouting silently, and Nanette was screaming.
“Kill him, Ilvriss!”
The Wall Lord was panting for air. He had to keep moving, Mrsha realized, or the [Dance of Foresight] was going to wear off. But the half-Elf was breathing in and out too. Sweat beaded Tolveilouka’s skin.
“Argh! Stop dancing, you ridiculous—”
He came in, wildly swinging, trying to foil Ilvriss’ foresight by the sheer speed and volume of attacks. But he’d forgotten that this was no gentleman’s duel. Ilvriss was backing up when a Golem holding a scythe hit Tolveilouka. His body began to reattach after it bisected him, bloody strings knitting together—Ilvriss slashed, and Elia Arcsinger spoke.
“[Line-Ending Inferno].”
Flames exploded around her. She screamed as her amulet protected her from the flames for all of five seconds—then erupted. She went rolling across the grass, but Tolveilouka had been hit by all the flames. He was a fireball, now.
“You—you—”
Golems firing spells at him or darting in. Yweine swung her head, and her neck spines fired off her body like darts. Ilvriss drove his blade into Tolveilouka’s heart, twisting it, and the half-Elf staggered. He kicked off, slashing, attacking the Golems, backswinging, leaping around wildly, bouncing like a grasshopper.
“Aaaaaaaaaaaaaaargh—enough—enough—”
He kept slashing, striking Golems randomly, the ground, cleaving left, right, rolling as the fires ate his flesh, and he couldn’t get them off, swinging at the Drake dodging left, right, bouncing around Ilvriss, staring at the red blood on his sword—
“—huh.”
The wildly leaping half-Elf stopped, and Ilvriss stopped dancing. He staggered, and Mrsha stopped cheering. She saw a huge line of red running down Ilvriss’ sword-arm. His clothing fell away and revealed a deep cut, down to his bloody bones. He staggered, kept himself upright on his sword, but his feet had stopped moving.
Cut.
Tolveilouka inspected his blade, then turned and eyed the Wall Lord. Just for a second, Mrsha thought—
He hadn’t meant to do that. The flames on Tolveilouka finally went out, and the burnt, smoking half-Elf eyed Ilvriss. Then the Golems and the sky.
A bolt of red lightning crackled down, and Tolveilouka split it with his sword.
“Ah, the good Duke. You know what? I think I’m done. Er—see you. Lovely cookout. There’s that famous hospitality I’ve heard about. So…adieu!”
He sheathed his sword, cast around, then went sprinting away. Ulva Terland, holding her conductor’s wand and charging up another combined attack, blinked. Another lightning bolt crackled downwards, then a glowing meteor.
The half-Elf began weaving in a serpentine motion, running northwards, audibly swearing until he was a dot on the horizon. Then…
He was gone.
Mrsha didn’t believe it. He’d just—left? She’d gotten the feeling Tolveilouka was messing with them, but he’d actually seemed nervous at the end there. Had they done enough damage…?
She caught Dalimont’s eye, and he shouted.
“Victory! Everyone, through the door before he comes back and heals!”
That moved Ulva Terland. She pointed, shouting, and Golems picked up anyone who’d been hurt and unable to leave. More people began streaming through the door as Liska cursed.
“More mana stones! I’m charging it up—”
Chaos, a babble of voices. Mrsha saw Wall Lord Ilvriss smile, disbelieving.
“Lyonette. Is Lyonette—?”
He pushed himself up off his sword, took two steps towards the door, and she saw Wrathcaller lose its magical lightning effect. Then Ilvriss touched at his right arm.
“It’s pulsing.”
He collapsed, and then Mrsha was howling an alarm as Welsca turned in horror, and [Soldiers] finally reached them from Ilvriss’ camp. Lyonette woke up and demanded the [Box of Incontinuity] to end this.
But it was too late.
Too late…
 
——
 
Tolveilouka kept running, and the magical spells didn’t stop targeting him for two damn hours. He had to find a cave and literally dig past some magicore before the tracking stopped.
That had come from multiple senders. The Terlands, the Duke…a lot of people wanted him dead.
He was not a happy undead monstrosity.
He hurt. He actually had taken a lot of damage in that battle! He was tired, his skin was burnt, he felt electrocuted, and there were cuts that refused to heal even if his flesh had joined up.
Damn swords, damn self-immolating half-Elves, damn Terlands—damn dances!
He’d done his job, though. Right? The half-Elf dug down deeper into the earth, where he could heal. Oozing like a rotten pustule downwards, wishing he’d gotten the [Princess]. He’d done good, right?
He’d cut the Wall Lord with his sword. That…hadn’t been the plan. 
It was fine! Tolveilouka uncomfortably squirmed down a bit more, like a repugnant slug. It was just his right arm. You—you know what? Magical limbs made you look far better, and losing a limb was normal.
It was worth, what, two levels? If you thought about it like that, he’d actually done the Wall Lord a huge favor. Two levels.
They’d definitely cut it off in time, right? No one was stupid enough to try and save it. How important was…? He was only a Lord of Salazsar. Not critical to Erin Solstice’s plans, and she probably didn’t even know about him, being in Baleros.
He’d…you know what? He’d just take a look around that Drake’s dig site. See if he could help out discreetly. Ensure things went smoothly or—or maybe he could go kill one of Erin Solstice’s enemies. She didn’t have to find out about this one.
…Dragons’ dangling dongs, this had not gone well. He really was out of shape himself if a bunch of low-level nobodies had actually chased him off.
The half-Elf sank deeper until he ran into a nest of glowing orange eggs. And weird little bugs which tried to eat him. He began to snack on the eggs, too gloomy to even do much torturing.
What an embarrassing day. To make it worse? That night he had a stomach-ache from eating the ‘Crelers’ or whatever they were called.
And that was about it.
 
——
 
Calidus Reinhart watched the television broadcast finally end, after the presenters had pieced together all the scattered footage into something close to a recap, and experienced two moments of surreality. A novelty, for him.
The first one was seeing a half-Elf taking on all of House Terland, transforming into a super-undead monster, and witnessing a [Princess], a little girl, and Ulva Terland going after it like they were Named-rank adventurers.
He was bleary-eyed, stubble on his chin, grease from the takeout he’d ordered still on his bare chest hair, and he had a wedgie from sitting in a weird posture. Calidus Reinhart hadn’t slept.
Who slept after seeing a throwdown like that? Let alone the cookout and—and—he was still pacing around.
“I could have been there. I’m a Reinhart. I can weasel my way anywhere—Damia. Cousin Damia? Tolveilouka Ve’delina Mer.”
The very name was so pretentious it made him worried anyone could say something like that with a straight face. That was old might. And—he turned to some of the other [Assassins] he’d summoned for the watch party.
Some were out of excitement and were either sleeping or had vanished. Zeomtoril had passed out with a bottle of wine spilling onto his lap. Calidus had been drinking water. He hadn’t wanted to get distracted.
It had happened before his very eyes. He kept giving orders.
“Every Rank—no, every other Rank is to enlist in this digging operation, even if it collapses tomorrow. I want agents in Salazsar. Hang the risk! And by ‘every other’, I mean 50% of the Ranks in the region. Send more.”
He wished he had hundreds now, not just dozens. Something was there, he was sure of it. Calidus was trying to decide if they could spare two Faces—and he was still thinking out loud.
“Going after that half-Elf sounds incredibly stupid. Maybe he’s got to die, but if his master’s in that village, destroying the tomb is just going to get that fellow walking around kicking our heads in, and I don’t believe anyone can survive an assassination attempt if he’s pissed. What did that kid write?”
Mrsha? He had a thousand questions to ask Selys and was only upset she hadn’t attended his watch-party. Now, Calidus turned. And his second surreal moment was this: he had a connection to that crazy battle. One he was employing, no less.
“Calidus to Guildmistress Shivertail.”
She didn’t answer unless—he heard an annoyed voice after two seconds.
“Calidus, I’m working. If this is stupid—”
“Present yourself in my mansion as fast as you can make it. There was a huge event just now. The scrying spells weren’t complete, but it’s going to spread. Some of your people and House Terland just threw down with a monster that makes Named-rank threats appear cute.”
“—The Wandering Inn? What did those idiots—is anyone dead?”
“Just a Drake and possibly anyone else caught by plague. So potentially no, if they’re quarantining.”
He meant it to be reassuring, but the intake of breath—Selys responded after a moment.
“I’m there in five.”
It sounded like she began running the moment she said that. Calidus put down the stone. Turned to Losmere.
“Investigate her again, more thoroughly. One of you, show her everything. I’m going to either nap or think. Don’t bother me, either way.”
He sat back down. Closed his eyes, and therein made a mistake. Calidus Reinhart was shaking with adrenaline, fascinated, mind engaged with the possibilities. He saw Lyonette, Ilvriss, and the strange web around the Cowpat Plains, but his error was that of a neophyte.
He thought it was over. He gave little thought to anything coming next, because, like everyone else, he thought that was it. Battle over. Later, he’d think of himself as a complete fool for that moment. But now, Calidus just thought of that blade. It had cut the Wall Lord.
He was waiting for a tally of the dead, and while everyone waited, they counted casualties.
 
——
 
Fallout afterwards.
Once the panic was done, casualties and wounded assessed, there came time to actually think, not react.
‘It was a mercifully low amount of casualties.’ After hearing that one too many times, Ulva Terland decreed that the next person who said that or a variation thereof would be beaten black and blue.
It turned out to be the [Mayor] of Invrisil who said that next, and he hadn’t been warned. Ulva didn’t care.
It was obvious the half-Elf had been holding back. To what end, she didn’t know. But when he had lost his temper, he had killed with ease. She might have almost thought he was trying to help that [Princess] or the inn, ludicrous as the thought was—he had killed no one, just broken bones until he’d lost his temper, and one could argue…
But no. Ulva’s skin still crawled at the sight of the [Princess] reacting to Tolveilouka’s presence and his attempts to carry her off. He was a murderous, ancient undead monstrosity of plague—and a rapist. What he had intended to do to that girl, Ulva didn’t want to imagine.
And the Wall Lord…she had offered the services of her Golems with healing capabilities, though all were damaged, and let his people tend to him. No one was stupid enough to give him a healing potion, and he’d shown he had some bite.
The rest? The rest was just snapping at people.
“I want that thing tracked and dead. No excuses! Do not move the Light of the North back! Raze the Village of the Dead.”
That place? It ended. She was calling on all the Five Families to form an army and hire the Named-ranks in the north to destroy it. Not just them.
Ailendamus, which that Duke had belonged to, was aware of the situation. So was Levicus; the old home to the Terlands had some of their records, and it had known the Putrid One, evidently.
Numerous nations were, in fact, calling her after learning of his attack. Some had actually helped, like Calanfer. Apparently, Ielane had been live on television helping hold the Putrid One’s servant back.
Ulva owed Ielane that; she hadn’t thought the Queen of Diplomacy was so powerful.
The other nations? They went through the gamut of asking, ‘who is Tolveilouka, are you well?’
Then, ‘why didn’t you kill him? Wait, who is the Putrid One? Is he like Az’kerash or something?’
Presumably after some research and a [Historian] had shit themselves and come running after finding the right texts, ‘dead gods, the Putrid One’s greatest servant? Please kill him, please don’t let him come near us.’
And so on. She was coordinating it, the hunt for this half-Elf, and putting together pieces.
“Burnt farms. Plagues. He has been sabotaging Izril for half a year! Damn those Horns of Hammerad!”
They’d woken a true terror, and she wanted to blame them, but the truth was that someone should have ended that Village of the Dead by fire. Only the fear that the Putrid One might be awoken kept her from just ordering someone to use a Tier 7 spell and hit the place.
She would be busy. The Terlands were in shock, and she ordered [Thought Healers] or Golems of the same kind to treat them. Some were more resilient; she took notice of some of the younger Terlands, including Prithna, the [Lady] with a Golem’s Heart, asking what would be done about Tolveilouka.
Bravery in the face of terror. Good. Ulva Terland forgot to actually check on her family; they were alive, most of them, and that was all. But she was reminded of her duties to them when someone came to get her.
“Great Aunt? The family would like you to join them.”
It was that boy with the Dullahan servant. Lord Chovn. The boy bowed as Ulva snapped at him, one of the Golems transcribing a reply to one of Wellfar’s [Lords of the Sea].
“What? I have no time to hold anyone’s hand. We are alive, and if Lord Rithav is lucky, he will be cured of the sickness. No visitors. I am sending for more Golems.”
I have much to do. Why are you bothering me? Her glower made the boy hesitate, but he glanced at his Golem, then bowed.
“I know. We know, Great Aunt. But the Golems. The half-Elf killed so many. Please…won’t you witness them?”
The fury in Ulva’s chest abated. She stopped, put aside her scrolls, and stood from her Dais of Health.
“…Where?”
 
——
 
They had collected all the pieces they could find in the manor. Terlands, working like common [Laborers]—but they’d refused help. Insisted on combing the ground with their own bare hands—then gloves when someone had insisted—because they did not trust anyone else to handle the Golem pieces.
No one but the Terlands and their staff knew how. Some Golem pieces could contaminate the ground or were dangerous. So, then Terlands had carried them to the mansion they had in Invrisil. The beautiful marble flooring was covered with dirt and oil and pieces of broken metal.
And they lay there.
The Golems. The true casualties of Tolveilouka’s assault had been them. Most fittingly, but even Ulva Terland halted when she saw how many were destroyed. Nearly a hundred. Ripped apart. Hearts shattered, some cut in twain.
Her family was weeping. They were a selfish lot. They prized stone over flesh, but in this, they were like historians, curators of a great museum that came to life. They had been entrusted with creations of bygone eras, and they were broken. Less, now.
“Timekeeper.”
He stood there, a sentinel, his chest damaged, his gears whirring off-sync. Regarding his fallen comrades, and she knew that he ‘liked’ her in that he served without issue. Golems could just become less effective, the smart ones, at least. A Djinni would rebel as best they could, manipulate you, defy you as people.
A Golem rebelled by breaking. A tool that no longer worked. But Timekeeper had served faithfully as long as she and Petria had known him when they had first chosen him from the deepest vaults.
She wondered what he really thought of her. He was witness to the many destroyed Golems, an impassive figure as Terlands knelt in their ruined clothing and mourned. She spoke to him, because she could not share her family’s raw emotions.
“Is this what you serve House Terland for across the ages, Timekeeper? What, twenty thousand years? Speak truthfully. Please.”
His head turned, and she saw old Nouzcrat’s head rise. Tears streaking his face. His silly personal Golems—broken to protect him from shrapnel. Chovn stood next to his dancing Golem, and Ulva was glad the boy hadn’t lost a true companion. But every Golem here…
“No, Lady Terland.”
The whirring in Timekeeper’s heart accelerated so he could respond. Some of the Terlands glanced up. The Golem stood there, his metal face impassive.
“There is no gain to be had from tears. On-ly levels for Terland. We are broken.”
“Then we shall mourn and level. Terlands, say farewell to our long companions, our protectors, servants, friends, and lovers. All the things we wish of stone—and shall never have in truth. Yet stone was loyal. Metal moved to shield us. Bear witness.”
Ulva was no grand speaker for these moments. It was Petria who would have spoken as if to move the Golems to tears. Yet still, Ulva knelt. She came before a Golem she recognized, whose body was oozing. Someone had set up magical barriers—but Chema, the Gnoll Golem, was losing the magical ‘fur’ that had made her up. She was almost completely intact, but her heart—
The half-Elf had broken her heart in a single blow.
“Chema. You were a true treasure of our house. I am sorry.”
The empty-eyed Golem lay there. Ulva Terland heard more sobbing, and she felt a pang. Then there was only one Terland on his feet. He walked into the mansion slowly.
Lord Xitegen Terland had run to Celum to muster his Golems. To set his city to wariness. A good [Lord]. When he saw the destroyed Golems, his breath caught, and he walked forwards. He stood there.
“Boy. Kneel.”
For the first time, Ulva thought it was he who was disrespectful to the Golems, not the other way around. But the [Lord] just gazed around the mansion.
“I didn’t even know we had this mansion. We have too many properties, Great Aunt. Never used. How many people or Golems do we employ who keep empty houses? Well and so; this one will serve as a storehouse.”
She laughed at him softly.
“Xitegen. Tomorrow, I will have the Golem pieces taken back to the Mansion of Stone for repurposing and salvage. Let them repair other broken Golems. I will not make a museum for them, even these ones who died for us. Golems are a tool. I will not glorify them. Even if they deserve it.”
Timekeeper bowed his head, but he was watching Xitegen. The [Golem-Lord of Enduring Dignity] smiled.
“Great Aunt Ulva Terland, you have named me your heir. So for once, I insist. Many of these Golems may be truly dead. But I insist on my chance, first.”
To do what, repair them? Even if they could salvage Golem Hearts and install them in ancient bodies, they wouldn’t be the same. Ulva almost snarled at Xitegen to kneel when she saw him bend down.
Over Chema. His fingers brushed the chest and the broken heart. It was almost intact; the Terlands had found every piece of her and even fitted them back into place. But the magic was gone; the glass cracked.
That was enough. Xitegen whispered.
“This is a gift I wrested from the Goblin King. From the inn, in a way. There is always a devastating price, but this…be it so selfish, it is mine. [Revive Golem].”
Ulva Terland’s eyes opened wide. She heard a gasp—and then she saw Xitegen concentrating. His palm was laid across Chema’s chest, and it was cut on the sharp edges of her heart. He bled, but he held his hand there, and it felt like there was a glow about him.
His aura? Something else? It swirled…and condensed. Like magic itself were becoming a drop of water which fell. Xitegen exhaled—and there was a flash of light. Soft as the birth of a star.
Then…he stepped back, and Ulva saw pale green lights glowing. In Chema’s eyes.
The Golem slowly sat up, and the oozing liquids swirled up and became her fur once more. She reached down, touched her chest, and her Golem Heart shone.
Someone made a sound. Not Ulva. She was speechless. Chema paused, as if uncertain, then stood in a single motion. She touched her heart again. Then turned to Lord Xitegen and bowed.
“Lord Terland. My functionality is intact. What is my designation and task?”
She didn’t know her own name? For a moment, Ulva saw Xitegen’s face grow somber, but then a voice spoke.
“Gone. Re-link, Chema. Your record is preserved.”
Timekeeper spoke; no one else was capable of it. Chema turned, and her eyes flickered as he sent information to her. Then she nodded just…stood there. Waiting for orders.
“Golem Chema is restored, Lord Xitegen. Awaiting your commands.”
“Xitegen. What Skill—”
“It only works once a month, Great Aunt. We had enough destroyed Golems from the battle with the Titan that I didn’t share it. I didn’t know if it worked on beings of Chema’s quality. Well…it will take years.”
Xitegen turned and gazed around. Nearly a hundred Golems. At one a month? And Ulva knew of many Golems who lay in the Mansion of Stone. Who had malfunctioned in less visible ways. Or were waiting to be disassembled. Or just…
She was thinking of them all, suddenly. And wondering, if Xitegen levelled—would the Skill come faster? He stood as his family rose from their knees. Staring.
The Golems were looking at him too. Ulva Terland finally managed words.
“You are the fitting heir of House Terland, Xitegen. If any doubt it for his youth, his opinions, speak of this moment. Level, Xitegen Terland. You have the Skill that our house has always longed for. Petria and I were only gifted different arts.”
He nodded at her, humble. She stepped back as the family flooded forwards to embrace Chema, who gently patted them like children.
“Chema. Go to Lord Ilvriss and heal him if you are able.”
“Yes, Lady Terland.”
Already, she was needed. Ulva ignored the protests; the Drake was wounded. They had time, now, to celebrate Chema. She stepped back and turned.
“Timekeeper. Is that what you serve for?”
“Yes, Lady Ter-land. The power of those who level allows us to en-dure. I would be rust if not for this bond. Sym-bi-o-tic.”
The Golem did not smile as she stood with him, but she saw, then, a reason for him to tolerate his long service. Perhaps he was just waiting for a day when one of the Terlands could command his heart to awaken and beat until he was truly a person.
Perhaps that Terland had come. Ulva let her eyes rest on Xitegen, but he was not merely accepting congratulations. He strode towards her, and there was a focus to him.
“I have Celum on alert and have marshalled my Golems for the hunt, or the half-Elf’s vengeance. First the damn Titan, then the Goblin King, and now this. I don’t actually believe The Wandering Inn is cursed, Great Aunt…”
“Don’t be stupid. It’s just like the Adventurer’s Haven. It attracts powerful people and enemies. Enough. Go heal, eat, let the family celebrate you, and come to me with any suggestions. I’ll be in Invrisil until I sort this out.”
She returned to her study and let herself be relieved, just for a moment. But since that was not a natural state of being for Ulva, eventually, she got back to work. She was angry at herself, at the monsters of old, and wondering if that Drake would live. She’d just been persuaded to give him a chance and some idiot had the effrontery to kill him? What a waste of her time if he died.
Since she refused to say a good word about Drakes, that was how she thought of it. When she did fall asleep on her Dais of Health and Timekeeper, slowly repairing himself with the help of other Golems, draped a blanket over her, Ulva Terland levelled for the first time in a long while.
Almost everyone did, really.
 
——
 
Every single person who had encountered Tolveilouka levelled. The only exceptions were people who levelled twice, three times, or five times. Or who were waiting for Level 50.
Or who were dead, Golems, or Rhisveri.
Some gained classes like [Survivor].
Some gained conditions like [Terror of Rot]. Or [Resurgent Trauma: Crippling Fear].
One person gained [Idolizer of Monstrosities] as a class. A rare class that the Grand Design of Isthekenous hadn’t assigned for the last three ages and was a bit of a red letter moment—for it. That person was not Damia Reinhart.
Everyone obtained levels, because they had met a true monstrosity, even if he hadn’t been ‘seriously’ trying to murder them, Tolveilouka was quite capable of murdering by accident, as he had done when he lost his temper. The grieving Golva family were proof of that, as well as the other dead. But the levels came, a paltry reward, perhaps, for a brush with that monster.
Nevertheless, they were aware that one day, the differential in power might be equalized.
The first person to level was Lyonette du Marquin as she had passed out due to the effects of Tolveilouka’s rot.
 
[The Cracked Princess, Keeper of the Inn Level 42!]
[Skill Change: Imperial Aura → Aura of Radiance Obtained!]
 
[Conditions Met: Crippled Reflexes Removed!]
 
She did not receive the Skill for the dance. But Lyonette didn’t care. She was on her feet as soon as she realized the battle was over.
Concerned for…
Ilvriss.
Welsca had rushed him back to the dig camp against everyone’s protests. She’d left Osthia behind to be healed by Healer Demerra herself, but Lyonette didn’t understand why—until the Erchirite Spears had literally fired a lightning bolt to keep Ishkr from chasing after them. Welsca’s voice rasped across the speaking stone.
“Wall Lord Ilvriss is under quarantine! I…I have isolated myself and everyone who escorted him to camp. The Rubirel Guard are showing no signs of illness. I wish to inform you, Diplomat Nerul, that I am feeling unwell. Major Shellc has already evacuated the camp and is holding the workers at Dig Sites A, B, and C. All those injured by Tolveilouka are in separate tents, being tended to by those of us still able to move. I have refused volunteers.”
Lyonette’s blood ran cold. She realized that number included several [Ranchers] and even one of the Terlands. Ulva had sent Golems to monitor the sick, but had informed Lyonette, coolly, that they would be bathed in flames and isolated until they were absolutely declared clean.
The Putrid One had apparently made rot so foul it corroded stone and Golems. And Ilvriss had been cut by his blade.
“The Wall Lord is semi-lucid and still mobile, perhaps due to his levels. He has not slept…he is attempting to treat his wounds. I have been informed amputation is likely the only outcome. We will attempt it after receiving instruction from the Last Light of Baleros when she can…can…participate. Tell us how.”
They moved to the [World’s Eye Theatre], and Lyonette saw Welsca was already stumbling around. Visibly sweating.
“You weren’t struck, were you?”
“No. Sickness. Wall Lord Ilvriss’ blood got on me. Burn everything that half-Elf touched.”
The [Adjutant] mumbled. A Golem had to pick her up. Lyonette wanted to go to Ilvriss, but Welsca shouted at her.
“The sickness may transmit via even sight!”
“Don’t be ridiculous, Welsca! That’s not how sickness works. Does it?”
Lyonette wavered, and after sending Ishkr, Ulva Terland tersely sent him back with a reply that ‘yes, some sicknesses of the Putrid One’s caliber do that. Unlikely this is one of them. Don’t risk it. I’m burning everything with a Golem.’
Better to have half your bones broken than a single cut to have touched Ilvriss’ arm. Lyonette herself went to be screened additional times, but Healer Demerra, wearing a weird full-body suit, declared Lyonette healthy.
[Resonant Flesh] merely…resonated. If Lyonette had ingested whatever Tolveilouka had been producing or stayed in his presence for an hour, it might have become permanent. She was safe.
Ilvriss? Lyonette hugged her daughters, scolding and praising them, and wept as she waited. A beat-up Rhisveri came to apologize, as if he’d done anything wrong, and they sat together.
After some time, it occurred to Lyonette that her mother might have been hurt. She hesitated, but called Ielane. When she stepped into the palace—her mother was too warded for Lyonette to find her—Princess Menisi spotted her. She was the only [Princess] without a circlet, and so she could speak to Lyonette.
“Hello there, little sister. You look ravishing.”
“M-Menisi. Hello.”
Lyonette wasn’t in the mood for anything, and Menisi herself had two wads of cotton stuffed up her nose.
“Oh, don’t worry about the look. We’re all little war heroes for fighting that thing. The kingdom’s abuzz. Father’s beside himself. He didn’t know what Mother was up to, did you know?”
“I…I thought it was working.”
The 2nd Princess chuckled.
“Doubtless, Mother did too. Don’t beat yourself up. She spun it into a victory.”
“How?”
“Why, she had it all broadcast. It was a risk, but now she looks like a hero, holding off a monster with sheer grit. I suppose if her head had exploded it would galvanize Calanferians—or traumatize them. Just when I thought I admired her, she manages to make herself a tool of the crown. So. How the hell did you keep him off you last time?”
Her elder sister pressed, but when Lyonette just mumbled she was relieved Ielane was well, Menisi told Nanette to take care of her. Then they sat together.
The only thing that broke the stillness in the inn was Lady Damia. They found her crying in a corner of the inn. She had gotten her wish, come to The Wandering Inn—and found the truth behind the legend, even if she had been warned. Seeing Ilvriss being carried away…Damia blamed herself for the cake.
Nanette, Lyonette, Mrsha, and the staff did their best to cheer up Damia and reassure her that it would have gone down that way regardless of the cake. That helped, but after a while, there was nothing more to do. Then they were just…
Waiting.
It was a long night.
The first to level was Lyonette du Marquin.
The last was Wall Lord Ilvriss.
 
——
 
Ilvriss still felt like he was dancing.
It was a pleasant way to die.
And he suspected he was dying. He hadn’t fallen asleep after collapsing. Just lain there and known there was something in his veins. He’d thought, ‘well, shit.’
Not exactly heroic, but it was honest.
There was an irony to it. He’d been ready to die when he’d tried to dance, on a hunch it might help him hit Tolveilouka. He’d been ready to die to stop Lyonette from being abducted when he dueled the half-Elf.
Now, having been cut and Tolveilouka having run, Ilvriss wanted to live.
But the plague was boiling him from the inside. He didn’t want to cut off his arm. He’d refused—twice—when a sicker and sicker Welsca had tried.
Not because he thought she was wrong. Rather…Ilvriss was concerned it was too late.
His entire body was twisting up in pain. Here was the thing: if he could have been saved by amputation, Ilvriss felt like it would have had to have been in the minutes after he’d been cut at most. How fast did a magical plague run? It had already gotten Welsca. It had gone into his blood, and now he was sick.
So he’d refused, twice, and lain there as a Dullahan who called herself The Last Light inspected him.
“Can you press against your sinuses? Your lymph nodes in your armpits? Now your groin?”
“Same pain. They’re all bulging.”
“Bulging?”
He showed her. No embarrassment to be had even when he pulled his pants down. It appeared very bad. His purple scales had swelled up, revealing flesh underneath. Ilvriss was no expert on what Drakes looked like de-scaled, but he was pretty sure yellow veins weren’t part of normal skin tones.
The Dullahan glanced down at her notes and then up at him.
“I’ve never seen that before. I regret to tell you that I believe your conclusion is correct, Wall Lord. The pathogen has spread through your system.”
“I see. Please tell Welsca that. Is she…as bad?”
“I believe she is experiencing earlier stages of your affliction, Wall Lord. Now, I am sending you Occillium, which counters most bacterial infections, and I am authorizing you to take ten times the normal dose. I have also prevailed upon Healer Demerra and Invrisil’s Healer Basine to send you every poultice and cure they have at similar doses. I am going to walk you through each step when they arrive. I want you to take the cures and report any change in your condition.”
“Just…take them?”
“Ideally with thirty-minute gaps to see if they have any effects. There may be side-effects from the interactions between medications. Given your level and the severity of this ailment, I believe it is necessary.”
She paused.
“Understand, Wall Lord, that I am not sure any of these medications will work. However, I do not expect you to survive two days. Your temperature is already in excess of survivable range for most Humans.”
She didn’t expect him to survive a single day. And that meant everyone else in camp…
The healthiest person was the Rubirel Guard who’d been puking maggots. She was the healthiest…Geneva had her moved to the furthest tents because she was worried the guard would catch what Ilvriss and the others had.
It was so funny he was laughing when the Golem ran into camp with the medications. Then Ilvriss began taking them.
But…there were signs it wasn’t going well. Big sign number one? Geneva wanted Ilvriss to inject the penicillin stuff as a liquid. Since Demerra didn’t know how, she apparently made a paste out of the raw mold and just had people eat that.
Ilvriss was gamely pulling the mold out of the jars and putting it in a bowl to mash up when he noticed something. He slowly held up the blue-green mold.
“Doctor.”
She was wearing a suit, just in case even looking at him could…the Last Light gazed at Ilvriss’ claws. Her features were still, like a Dullahan’s, but he saw her eyes close a second.
“Ah. I see. Can you…repeat the process with another jar? Put gloves on to avoid touching it?”
The Occillium had turned black. It was shrivelled up, and Ilvriss smiled grimly. He went to the other jar. Breathed on it as he worked.
It died too.
 
——
 
Water was nice. It just hurt on the way down. He was burning up, taking the medications, sipping water.
Thinking of what he’d done wrong.
He had listened to Sserys. Maybe that was his fault. Who listened to that guy? Sserys hadn’t been known to be perfect. Look at his last battle. Classic overcommitment.
He thought too much of people, that Drake. Ilvriss had tried…
I should have just gone to the inn. Stayed with Erin Solstice and never left. Especially at the end of the battle. I should have been there, and even if I was in Baleros now…
I’d just be some Drake. She needed the Wall Lord to do something, and I did my best. I’m just not my father. I’m not Zel. I’m not her.
Really, he felt guilty about Lyonette. She was going to blame herself for this. Sometimes, you ran into a monster and you died.
He’d wondered if it would ever be his turn. Just—just—
“I wish it wasn’t that guy. He’s so damn silly.”
The Wall Lord was in his tents. He’d torn the place apart, searching for anything. Something to help cure himself. Welsca was down—sick.
He’d been told Osthia was going to be just fine.
That was great. Ilvriss had refused a speaking stone from Lyonette. He didn’t want to…you could be damn silly about final words and all that. Same for Zail. They kept calling him, but he had gone down fighting.
He was just worried he’d start crying and asking Lyonette, or his father, for a miracle. He didn’t want to leave them like that.
This was peaceful. Ilvriss just wished Welsca hadn’t come with him.
“How’s it go? Lyonette said you just…put your claws together and pray. Someone said you pray to levels the other day. Silly fellow. Here I go: I’d like to not die. Very much. Thank you.”
Ilvriss felt like he was at a board meeting, trying to argue his case before a superior. He was all fuzzy, but he did his best.
“I can be better. I can do more. I thought we were making it. I really did. I messed up, sure. But I thought I did okay with the pickaxes. Even Georgie. I hope he finds work. I should write a reference letter to Alrric about the situation. Excuse me.”
He penned something down and broke off his prayer. Then someone knocked at his tent door.
“Wall Lord Ilvriss. I am Golem Chema.”
“Hello again, Chema.”
She hadn’t helped him, but the damaged Golem was in charge of the others assigned to him. He rasped up at her.
“You—you remind me of my first nursemaid. I’m told I had sexual fantasies about her or something.”
“This is often expressed to me, Wall Lord. I am designed to be maternal.”
“Well, I don’t want to have sex with you. Just so you know. What’s up?”
The Golem spoke as the Wall Lord tried to smile.
“An Antinium [Priest] has arrived at the camp. They have been sent from the Free Hive of Liscor with a sample of ‘Antinium curative substance’ and they wish to use their ‘Miracles’ <DESIGNATION UNKNOWN> to cure the sick. Will you allow it? Your orders are to—”
“Of course. Yes, yes! Send them to Welsca first!”
Ilvriss surged upright. Relief shot through his veins. Chema nodded, departed, and Ilvriss turned. Put his hands together.
“I’m very thankful. I’ll…um—dedicate a statue? Pray six times a day? Is this a rewards-based thing or something?”
Faith. He sat there, fidgeting, drinking water, and wondering if he was getting better as he took another medication. He was impatient, feeling like hours were passing when it was just minutes. He was just about to ask Chema if the Antinium could see him—he knew there were others sick—when the Golem returned.
“Wall Lord. I have a report.”
“Great! Yes, send him in—what report?”
“The Antinium [Priest] has declared their healing btiqk ineffective. As are their ‘prayers’. They are now ill and being quarantined.”
Ilvriss gazed at her. Chema bowed and left.
 
——
 
Faith worked miracles. But how much faith for how much of a miracle? Perhaps if they were higher-level, if they had more faith…
Pawn was in Khelt.
And perhaps a certain half-Elf, on encountering Antinium resilience, had upped his plagues a bit.
Ilvriss was lying against a table, waiting for the inn to send…something. Something from the [Gardens of Sanctuary]. Or—or Erin had something in her room or a contact. He’d told the Last Light about it.
He thought he had. He’d drank, eaten, slathered himself with all the cures. He felt worse. It had just been optimism.
He was lying there when the tent flaps opened and someone cursed.
“Tree rot.”
“Get out. Sick.”
Ilvriss muttered. Someone hauled him up, despite his protests, and put him in a chair. Even put a pillow beside his head.
“Didn’t they cut off your arm? Those idiots—!”
“Didn’t do it in the minutes…”
“They didn’t cut it off instantly? Kraken’s multiple cloacae—what is with you people? Argh!”
It…dawned on Ilvriss that whomever this was, this wasn’t one of his people. He gazed up, fuzzily, then tried to get a sword. The half-Elf just pushed him back into his seat. Then he poured himself a drink of water.
“Not even ice. You people really are primitives. Want some?”
Ilvriss flailed at him, and Tolveilouka sighed. He pulled up a seat, then put his feet up. He appeared disheveled, dirty, and he kept patting his stomach.
“Sorry. Indigestion. I ate some weird eggs, and I keep excreting bits and pieces of them instead of digesting everything. Pretty tough monsters. I think they wanted to hatch inside me or something. Mostly, they make my stomach queasy.”
“You—you—just kill me.”
That was it. He was dead. Tolveilouka eyed him. Then he sat back in his chair.
“She’s going to kill me. How, uh, how likeable are you to Erin Solstice, scale of one to ten?”
Ilvriss was dreaming. This could not be reality, even for her. Tolveilouka went on after a second.
“It wasn’t supposed to go this way, you know. I was helping you. You know, common enemy? I trashed the [Ranchers] a bit, ate some cows…I just, uh, lost my temper with the dance. Nice footwork, you know. It’s hard to pull off a magical dance in a fight.”
Ilvriss tried to strangle him. He ended up flopping onto Tolveilouka’s chest, and the half-Elf laughed as he put Ilvriss back in his seat.
“Ooh, so forwards. You know, that’s the interesting bit. I’ve been watching you and that little miner. So progressive. Drakes hate that sort of thing. Always have. The City of Purity was bad about that—but they were bad about everything. No one liked them. I was there when they died, but, if you can believe this, it wasn’t even our doing. They killed themselves.”
“If…you’re going to help…cure us.”
That was all Ilvriss breathed. He’d take it. His heart lurched. If this was a Solstice miracle and the plague monster was on his side, he’d have something to say to Erin Solstice.
Thanks. And how the hell—?
Tolveilouka appeared uncomfortable. He smoothed his hair, poured Ilvriss a cup of water, and went pacing around before staring out of Ilvriss’ tent. And that way, Ilvriss knew the answer before the half-Elf spoke.
“Here’s the thing. I make things. I can see things. I can grow…well, I didn’t use a lot of my powers in the fight, but I have them. It’s usually not as effective as punching or stabbing someone. Just more amusing. But my master made me to be undying, a vessel for plagues. I never really learned the, uh, control part. If it’s just magical and I’ve made it, sure, all under my control. But once it starts living in your veins I can only negotiate a bit. I mean, sure, I could pause the effects in you, but we both know that’s a waste of our time.”
Tolveilouka leaned on a wall, and stared at nothing.
“My master could command sickness perfectly, of course. He always thought of me as a failure.”
Ilvriss just stared at him. The half-Elf spun.
“Listen! It makes sense! Plagues, even magical ones, are alive. I’m a level-less undead! How am I supposed to…? What you do is create something nasty and throw it out there. You can’t pull it back. So, uh—let’s see your medications. I reckon I can whip up a good mixture.”
Ilvriss stared at him. Then croaked.
“[Alchemy] tent.”
He had to find a damn map of the camp and mentioned Chema—the half-Elf ducked out. He came back a minute later.
“Okay, excellent. Lovely directions. Got a good look at that Golem. Here’s the thing…when I say ‘alchemy’, do you hear ‘barrel scrapings and apprentice reagents’ in your delirium? Got any Unicorn horn? Phoenix feathers? Kraken anything? C’mon, I know there’s at least one Dragon around. The stool of a Silver Dragon? I reckon I could maybe find that Unicorn and snap his horn off…”
Ilvriss started laughing. He couldn’t help it. His death was here, trying to fix the problem, and Ilvriss was going to die. Tolveilouka paced around, then sat again.
“Okay. Okay—we can fix this. Here’s the plan: I’ll just go down there and see what’s in the City of Purity. If we’re lucky, it’s now inert.”
“And there’s healing down there?”
Tolveilouka snapped his fingers.
“That would be nice. If I find some, I’ll bring it back. I, uh, reckon you’ve got about four hours. Tops. Once the tingling becomes super bad, you’ll start squishing. Then I’d grab a wand and blow your head off. Hmm. I’d better make sure this tent is airtight. Don’t need that spreading in a cloud. Same with the other tents. They’ve all got it.”
He got up and bustled around. Then he poked his head back in.
“Oh, what I meant was that we’ll get that city found. Big win for Drakes. I’ll make sure that [Princess] gets a bunch of the good stuff. Listen—you did great for your species.”
Ilvriss said nothing. He really, really wanted Tolveilouka to go away. The half-Elf seemed to sense it.
“Listen. I really was trying to help. It just turns out that I’m not much of a team player. Maybe that’s why my master didn’t come back. Not much to live for.”
He stood there, and Ilvriss just stared at the half-Elf making Ilvriss’ death all about him. Tolveilouka coughed.
“Right. Sorry. If it helps—”
“Get out.”
He left. And then…
Well, Ilvriss felt tingling. He started laughing, then. And crying. Because he heard the voice, now.
It whispered across Izril. To Ulva Terland, who looked up in her study, then went back to work. To Lord Xitegen, who halted in eating at a restaurant and found a glass. To Damia, Cecille, and every Reinhart.
To every noble of the north, the voice spoke:
 
<Heroic Quest – Keep Him Alive: Wall Lord Ilvriss!>
<Conditions failed. Quest cancelled.>
 
Then he knew. And he hoped, only—that the [Innkeeper] didn’t find out for a while.
 
——
 
Ilvriss’ will broke. He called Lyonette.
He heard the speaking stone pick up, and he spoke.
“Ilvriss…?”
“Lyonette, is there something in the [Gardens of Sanctuary]? Some—some—he was on our side, but he messed up. But I bet that means she had something to use against him. A cure. In her rooms. Can you—”
He heard a sob.
Just once, muffled, then she tried to say something.
He hung up the speaking stone. Smashed it, with one claw, shaking. So ashamed because he had heard how desperate he was.
Lyonette, I don’t blame you.
He wrote that down on a piece of paper.
Realized how that sounded and was trying to burn it. Gave up and tried to eat it.
No saliva.
He was lying on the ground of his tent, laughing. He had been in denial until Tolveilouka had come along. He hadn’t thought this was…it.
Not for him.
Not with his death waiting in Az’kerash.
“Periss.”
He hadn’t thought of her this entire time. Just Lyonette and other people. Ilvriss felt guilty, then not.
He’d see her soon. Then she could scold him.
Or was her ghost not…
Erin had said there was a place after death.
Ilvriss hoped there was. He was afraid of being alone.
He was afraid of nothing being the end.
 
——
 
He was trying…
To find something.
Something. He was knocking papers around. Swinging the last pickaxe from the City of Purity to open locks and drawers and pull himself up.
Because he wanted to live. Because he didn’t want that to be how Lyonette heard he’d died. Begging her for…
I want to live. I want to fall in love and live for decades before I go. I’m sorry, Periss. 
If I couldn’t do that—I wanted to avenge you.
Instead, he was dying in a shit-smelling camp at the hands of a half-Elf who hadn’t even meant to kill him. Ilvriss swung the pickaxe again and again, destroying his orderly world. He only stopped when he saw something glittering.
He’d hit…a pile of gifts meant for the [Ranchers] and Terlands. The Wall Lord gazed down and saw the gift-briefcases that were all the rage in Salazsar. This one was glittering, cut by the pickaxe that had left a neat rectangle of leather on the ground.
Inside was something he knew. He stopped, then bent down, laughing.
“A toll for the great beyond. Fitting.”
He didn’t really say the words. Just thought them as his lips moved soundlessly. What he’d found was…the quintessential treasure of his kind. That which his Ancestors and Salazsar coveted.
Gemstones.
The magical gemstones he’d given to Marvus. A fortune in magic, not just pretty gems. Ilvriss picked out two.
You put coins on eyes, didn’t you? Gems would suit a greedy Wall Lord.
Then he went to lie down.
He was tired.
 
——
 
He couldn’t lie down right. His lungs felt like they were filling up with something. And—this was why people used coins—the gems were uncomfortable.
They dug into his eyes, which felt…squishy. He was tingling. Rotting. The Wall Lord tried to hold them, but his claws were sweaty. He put them under his pillow in his uncomfortable travel-bed.
“Ow.”
He rolled his head, trying to find somewhere to sleep. It was like…you know when you were tired and you had been up far too long, but you couldn’t sleep because you were so tired? And you just knew that when your body finally let you, you’d rest forever?
That was how it felt. Only, the thing keeping him up was life.
Still fighting.
He was proud of himself for that. But he was so uncomfortable, and he didn’t—Ilvriss rolled over—
There wasn’t a way out. So he’d just like to rest, please. He’d tried.
He had tried.
Ilvriss turned over as he felt a haze pulling him away and heard a sound.
Crack.
His head rose muzzily, and he cursed.
“Oh come on.”
He knew what it was. When he pulled his pillow aside, he saw the magical gemstone had turned to powder. The magic was actually visible, swirling up like fine dust. Ilvriss coughed, waved it away. Then sighed.
Turned out the entire batch of gift gemstones was actually flawed somehow. He owed Marvus an apology. Magical hazard, that. Terrible. Someone else could deal with it.
Ilvriss put his head down on top of the cracked gemstone, and the other one cracked too. He just lay there. Until he realized that the gemstone fragments digging into his forehead was the most uncomfortable way to die.
It took him six tries to get up and swipe the gemstone fragments off his bed. Highly hazardous, that. Any magical gemstone above Cirozine-quality breaking was a minor disaster. They had such unpredictable effects…
His scales were tingling on his head, and he’d doubtless absorbed something magical that might give him a permanent health condition. Since that was probably all of forty minutes left, Ilvriss’ main concern was the pieces of gem that had decided to bury themselves in his forehead.
His flesh was definitely getting weaker. Scales too. Ilvriss staggered up and found the vanity. He stared at the pieces of gemstone embedded in his forehead.
“Ow.”
What a failure. Couldn’t even die right. Ilvriss picked at the gemstone shards where blood was oozing around them. They hurt.
Like actually hurt. His blood was thick and red, and they were stuck in there damn hard. Ilvriss gritted his teeth—then reached into his mouth.
Pulled out a tooth with some gum stuck to it.
“And that’s it, folks.”
He whispered in his head. His body was sagging, now. His claws scraped listlessly at the gems in his forehead. Maybe just lie down and die? His brain whispered that to him.
But they hurt. They legitimately hurt, those shards, and everything else was tingling.
Like…
Ilvriss spat blood out of his mouth; it was replacing saliva. It was yellow and red. The wrong color of red. He stared at the drool and noticed he was bleeding the same revolting mixture.
Don’t want it going downwind, Tolveilouka had said. So why…
Why…?
Why was the blood coming from his temples red? Ilvriss stared at it fuzzily. A part of his mind had a thought.
Gemstones.
Gemstone magic.
Magic…magic was powerful. Raw.
Took on flavors. Elemental. Something.
Magicore for absorbing.
Maybe—
Raw magic purity? Unicorn magic. Phoenix feather magic. No big magic in alchemists for Tolveilouka.
Magic.
One last thought made the Drake waver. His bed was calling him. But he glanced in the mirror, and though his flesh was sagging, though he had changed and forsaken so much, he was still Ilvriss.
Ilvriss.
Gemscale.
 
——
 
He was scrabbling at the briefcases. Clawing at them. Putting them in his mouth and biting them with his teeth, even as they shifted around. Swallowed one whole.
Break them. Ilvriss had the pickaxe, and he was tapping them. Each time he missed, he felt like that was the end. But then he’d break one. Pour it over his scales—and it seemed like they were sticking to his scales, or maybe that was how much he was rotting.
He had a lot of briefcases. He was a Wall Lord of money. The Drake broke more. More, until he lay under a covering of broken, glittering gems. And magic…he felt magic in the air, a thrum in his blood and bones.
It was louder than the tingling. It reminded him of that [Innkeeper] he loved.
Not like Periss. But like someone who reminded a boy what dreams were like. It felt like her [Immortal Moments], her greatest Skill. A grasping towards unknowable wonders.
Brushing eternity.
Because he could find no more gemstones in his blurry vision, because the tingling had stopped for a moment, and because that was a fine feeling to die with, if this was the last thing he’d ever know, the Drake lay down and went to sleep at last.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
[Class Change: Wall Lord of Corporate Opulence → Wall…]
[Skill…]
…
But that wouldn’t really help, would it?
 
[Conditions Met: Drake → Oldblood of Gems Species!]
[Condition: Body – Breath of Jewels Obtained!]
[Condition: Body – Oldblood Wings Obtained!]
[Condition: Body – Scales of Opulence Obtained!]
[Condition: Body – Fortune’s Scent Obtained!]
[Condition: Body – Greater Resistance: Sickness Obtained!]
 
Now…
[Class Change: Wall Lord of Corporate Opulence → Wall—]
 
——
 
Ilvriss pushed himself up.
He rose before the voice continued, and his body responded to his will. He heaved himself up and felt something on his back. Like a cloak, only lighter, and they flexed. He could see.
The world had stopped spinning. He felt…wonderful.
Alive.
But he was running. Running, scattering the briefcases, picking out the remaining gems as if they were all aglow—he could even smell how many there were left intact.
Running out of his tent. A Golem walking the camp, Chema, jerked when she saw him. Recoiled in pure alarm and fright.
“Wall Lord?”
He threw open the tent flaps to Welsca’s tent. She was lying there, breath rasping, stained rags covered in that filthy blood lying next to her, a cooling compress on her head. He staggered over to her.
“Welsca. Welsca…gemstones. Where are the others? We need—”
He began smashing them in his palms. Sprinkling them down on her. She stirred.
“Ilvriss…?”
He kept smashing gemstones. He didn’t know how many she needed. A fortune. How much time did she have?
“Hang on, Welsca. We’re going to make it. For once, we brought our own miracles. Just hang on.”
“Yes, Wall Lord.”
The tent flaps opened. Someone spoke.
“Wall Lord, what is—”
“Gemstones!”
He turned, and Chema jumped again. The Drake shouted.
“Get me every gemstone above—no, every gemstone! Fill them with magic! Buy them from Invrisil, Pallass—get them, now! Hurry! Run!”
She ran. And then Welsca was blinking up at Ilvriss.
Did her flesh look more stable? Was it working? Would it be instantaneous? Or slower, since she might not level up when she slept?
She lay there as he tried to explain.
“There’s a way to cure the plague, Welsca. Just magic. Magic. You might die…but don’t. I’m going to cure you, understand? You and everyone else I can.”
“It’s a fortune, Wall Lord. Can’t afford it.”
“Shut up about money. Just hang on, okay?”
“Okay. You look different, Ilvriss.”
He felt different. Ilvriss had no mirror. He just cradled Welsca in his arms.
“Not bad, I hope? It beats dying.”
“No. You look like I imagined a Wall Lord should look like when I was small.”
“Oh. Good? Welsca? You’re not asleep, are you?”
“No.”
“Keep talking to me, then. Just hang on.”
“Okay, Ilvriss.”
He knelt there until the tent burst back open, and there was a babble from a speaking stone. And he began to smash more gems and give orders. But he waited until he saw Welsca’s scales begin to glow. Then he glanced away, respectfully. When he rose…
He breathed out. And his breath glittered in the air. Like broken gemstones. Like magic.
It was in him, now.
A piece of wonders. Like Erin.
 
——
 
Seven.
Seven. Five Drakes and one Gnoll from the Silverfang tribe. Two of the Rubirel Guard, Ilvriss, Welsca, a [Soldier], the [Lucky Miner] from the Silverfang tribe—and the Antinium [Priest].
That was how many made it. Eight died, succumbing to the plague too fast, including one of the Terland [Lords].
Ilvriss didn’t know if the Human could have been saved. He would have paid for it all, though the cost to transform was placed at about 63,000 gold pieces. Per person, excluding the Antinium [Priest], who managed to fight off the sickness themselves. Whether that was biology or prayer—the other species had been only saved by magic and gold.
It was bitter.
It was something that only a Wall Lord could do.
It was wondrous—and a secret, because Ilvriss pictured people giving themselves mana poisoning or all his peers just wasting fortunes to do this. Because he felt like it was not something to be done because you were rich. Perhaps the catalyst was a need to change, not just the magic.
If so, it was earned, by each and every person. But not a one was alike.
Ilvriss kept flexing his new wings. It was like having new muscles on his back, and he knew his scales were…sparkly. The people who saw him, Drakes especially, would just stand and stare, or stutter.
However, his was the only transformation into an Oldblood of Gems—or whatever his subspecies was. The others were different.
Welsca Crimsonscale’s coloration had only deepened and now took on a bit of orange and even deeper ruby. She had wings—but the breath that came from her lungs was hot, like a furnace was in her chest. He’d feared she was still dying when she woke up, but the fever was instead just permanent for her.
She had become an Oldblood of Flames. The other Drakes had each taken on different elements; one had become an Oldblood of Winds, the first Ilvriss had ever seen. And the Silverfang Gnoll was just—strange.
He had a silver streak down his neck and back, and he seemed no bigger; if anything, he might have shrunk. But he appeared more compact, and the biggest changes were his claws and eyes.
They glowed. From brown, his irises had taken on a silver hue, a crescent of silver in the brown, and his claws were now pale white. Could every species become magical? Had Ilvriss found something truly important? And if so, why had it been lost? Or was it just that risky?
He didn’t know. These were questions for later.
Ilvriss was alive. Cured of plague, and after the bodies were burned and the most thorough screening he could think of, he rode to The Wandering Inn. Not flew; he had no idea how, really. Though he felt like he could make himself lighter.
But he rode, then walked through the magic door—and a [Princess] tackled him in a hug, then stood back and stared at him.
“Ilvriss? You look—gorgeous.”
“I’m not sure if that’s a compliment.”
His scales were still largely purple, but they’d taken on variance, the kind he’d only ever seen in a few Drakes, like Rafaema or Onieva come to think of it. A slight patterning where the scales changed colors. In places, Ilvriss’ scales had turned pearlescent. In others, they simply glittered. Like jewels.
He had highlights around his eyes, and his tail had some kind of pattern too, though it was hard to get a great look at it. It didn’t matter. If he’d turned poop-brown, he’d have been happy to be alive.
Ilvriss was swaying on his feet. He’d not slept more than, like, five seconds, but he let Mrsha hug him too and tried to explain it without giving away the secret.
“It was just luck. We, um—there’s something you need to know, Lyonette. Privately.”
Tolveilouka’s admission. Suddenly, Ilvriss had a hundred problems. Dying not being one of them, he felt great. He was hugging Lyonette, and she was beaming, and he just—kissed her on the cheek. Then apologized.
“I’m so sorry, that was entirely inappropriate—”
Damia skidded to a halt, her tearstained face turning into awe and delight. Just in time for Lyonette to blink, turn, and kiss Ilvriss on the lips.
Everyone turned, stopped, and gaped. The two broke apart right away, and Lyonette coughed.
“That was just—I’m so relieved. I thought—”
“Right—”
The two stared at each other as Mrsha slapped her forehead with a paw. Ilvriss had no idea what to say, but ‘I didn’t mean that’ felt like a bad move, even if he sort of felt like—
Then, through the [Door of Portals] that Liska was holding open for Welsca, he heard and felt the faintest tremor. And a sound.
It sounded suspiciously like ‘boom’. But faint.
Slowly, everyone turned to the door, and Welsca’s head rotated.
“Wall Lord? That came from the expedition’s—”
Ilvriss had never been more grateful for the inn’s signature brand of chaos. He turned and began running with Lyonette without a word.
 
 
 
 
Author’s Note:
I finished the arc, and it’s a long one. But as you might haven noticed—the final chapter is in two parts.
That’s just how long it is. 90,000 words before edits, I believe. And because it’s so dang long, I had to split it, on this cliffhanger.
It fits.
But here’s my plan: I’m going to try and release the 2nd part on Tuesday. I’ll take that entire day to edit so it might be late, but if I can, I’ll release it then. No promises, but that’s because the chapter’s done.
Then I’ll take my monthly break. That way we both win; you get the chapter early and I get to rest a bit longer.
Once it’s out, I’d love feedback on how it felt to have a longer arc without moving perspectives. It’s always longer than I planned but we hit a bunch of plotlines here. And this was actually feedback from the [Palace of Fates] survey. I did my best, and like Ilvriss, sometimes you’re a fool while doing it.
But sometimes you do the right, amazing thing. And even our silly, purple-scaled Wall Lord who once got clocked with a frying pan can become a shiny new Drake. I hope you enjoy how the chapter has gone and how it ends.
(Also Tolveilouka is really funny to write.)
That’s all from me!

10.71 (Pt. 2) (2026-07-22)

(The author is on break until August 8th! I’m signing those bookplates and travelling, so wish me luck! Seriously, I don’t want to get COVID again, it sucks. Enjoy your early chapter!)
 
 
A bit earlier.
Tolveilouka was reflecting on his actions. He was. He’d even gone through the mines that were mostly unguarded now. All the Drakes and Gnolls were above, bedding down, and upset.
Because, uh, their Wall Lord was dying. Which was his fault. So Tolveilouka was really thinking about it.
That Ilvriss. Upstanding fellow, really. Low-level, but he’d activated Wrathcaller, and he’d done a magical dance in combat.
Great prospects.
Shame how it went down. You had to respect your foes after they bit the dust. Why, even Yderigrisel had been…adequate…
You had to admire the fellow’s tenacity. That was Tolveilouka’s problem, really. Not being a team player. He’d do better.
Mind you, he’d probably burned all the bridges around here, but maybe there was another group he could ally with? Be a friend.
Buy a drink, talk about the weather. Was that what friends did? Or was it—order around his minions in a rage, howl his anger to the sky, then grab Tolveilouka and proceed to violently lovemake until some new atrocity occurred to his master—?
Damn, I like the other option a lot more. But since Erin’s not very good at that, I have to change with the age.
He was reformed, that was the point. In fact, he was so reformed that when Tolveilouka found the undead hiding in the bottom of the mine, he ignored their requests for him to take over the death of the living and smashed them up.
“Listen, it’s nothing personal. It’s just—you’re mostly bones, and I’m plagues. We don’t mix. We’re cousins at best.”
That done, he scratched his head.
“Weird mine.”
It was all caved in on one end. He shrugged and began excavating it. Then, after an hour, he made a sound.
“Aha! It is the City of Purity. Smells worse, but I’d know that obsessively clean look anywhere. Eugh. Not a microwhatsit in sight.”
Too pure. But he’d carved his way into it. Which was odd because this place had clearly been buried by the miners. Tolveilouka scratched his head.
“…Miners? No, that makes no sense. Oh, they were escaping. Duh.”
Probably ran out of air or food. He began walking around and whistled.
“Light spells still active. Dead gods, this might actually make Erin forget all about that other business. This place is loaded. Wait, do they still have those old Sets of Immaculacy? Even I’d wear one of them.”
You know what? This was all working out for the best. Tolveilouka would just nip down there, maybe open one or two of their vaults—pick out a few items for himself—then deliver some stuff to that [Princess]. Everyone won!
He was just strolling forwards when he had a thought, and he got to one of the obsessively-clean streets.
It’s been a long, long time. And they were buried. There’s no chance the doom of Naamreles is still active, right? Not after all this time, no matter how well they made the stuff. If it were, they’d already have attacked and noticed me.
That was the last thing he needed. They’d managed to push back even the Putrid One, which was why Ilvriss had wanted this place to begin with. But since he wasn’t under attack…Tolveilouka wiped at his forehead.
One good turn. Which meant all the real Relics were his to h—
He got four more paces when the alarm began to sound. The half-Elf froze, and a thought occurred to him.
If the Emperor of Storms’ weapons are still good after all this time, then Naamreles, which is younger, might be—
There was, suddenly, more light. Harsh light. Magical light.
The half-Elf glanced up.
“Treant’s nutsacks. Are they…bigger than before?”
They were shouting, of course. Those old words. Tolveilouka swallowed, suddenly no longer confident. A bunch of children and Golems was one thing, but this lot hurt—
He raised his fists, began growing in size—and the [Queen] cut him off. Tolveilouka swore.
“Nononono—you idiot! This is bad, really—”
The first guardian of Naamreles came at him, and Tolveilouka snarled.
“Fine then! Bone and nail it is! I am Tolveilouka Ve’delina Mer! Come and die, already-dead city! Come and—”
 
——
 
Twenty-four minutes later he was running up from the mines, collapsing the tunnels behind him. Unfortunately, they were digging. He ran, trying to regenerate the holes in his body.
Dead gods damnit, that hurts so much! Tolveilouka was panting as he ran for his life. Literally, if they surrounded him. That was a lot of—
Okay, no one panic, how far could they get without their masters? Probably only a few hundred miles. Maybe a thousand. Not my problem! How far away is the inn? I just need to get back and heal and—
He ran faster. He heard the alarm now, through his feet, and they were coming. Worse—
They’d recognized him, and they were not happy.
 
——
 
Captain Osthia Blackwing had discharged herself from Healer Demerra’s to get to Dig Site B. Well, okay, she’d signalled for the Sisters of Chell to carry her.
She had to be there if—
If Ilvriss—
She’d continue the fight without him. She didn’t know how, but she lay there as the Sisters paced around, swore, argued, and asked her if she needed anything.
The camp was silent. No one wanted to do anything, but as morning came, someone did shout everyone up.
“Alright, up! Let’s get to it!”
Foreman Rolx was shouting as Osthia heard swearing. She hobbled onto her one good foot, using Boyd for support, and emerged to see Advance Miner Georgie arguing. All the [Miners] were standing around.
“What the hell are we working for? Wall Lord Ilvriss might be dead—”
The Gnoll growled back.
“It beats you all standing around picking fights and drinking. C’mon. Let’s kill the undead and just…finish the job. We owe him that.”
It got people moving and kept them from stewing in their juices. Georgie didn’t argue, just grabbed his magical pickaxe and trooped past Osthia. He glanced at her.
“Hey. Um…”
He trailed off. Captain Osthia saluted him.
“It was our fault in being too lax.”
“You weren’t even there, right? Those Rubirel Guard, those…”
Georgie trailed off. He stared at the Rubirel Guard. They weren’t at their posts. Some had taken off their helmets. Others were just sitting.
Osthia spoke, not unkindly, to everyone listening in.
“It was a monster. The Wall Lord did his duty. He saved lives. He didn’t run.”
“I know. I wish he had. I wish someone ran because I’m damn well sick of losing all the people we need.”
The Advance Miner spat bitterly, and no one, not Mining Leader Maiss, nor Dramm, argued. Osthia stood there as Georgie walked down into Dig Site B, shoving a helmet onto his head.
“Let’s move some damn dirt.”
Everyone moved down the steps. Georgie did see a half-Elf dashing up the stairs, swearing, but he just assumed it was some new hire who’d gotten lost. Idiot didn’t have any safety gear on. He’d mention that to a supervisor if he saw the fool again.
 
——
 
Advance Miner Georgie’s team was assigned to the mining tunnels. For whatever reason, despite their inefficiencies, Maiss and the miners had been handpicked by Shellc for the risky excavation work.
They had good nerves, even if Georgie was doing most of the work, boring a careful tunnel into the rock. Rubirel Guards breathing down his back and [Soldiers] on duty, but Georgie felt off.
Not just because no one knew if Ilvriss was alive…he stopped swinging his pickaxe after barely seven minutes, taking the stub of a cigar out of his mouth.
“Something’s wrong.”
“Undead ambush, Advance Miner?”
Whatever they thought about him, the Rubirel Guard and [Soldiers] respected an Advance Miner’s intuition and tensed. But Georgie just put one earhole to a piece of stone, frowning. Checked his pickaxe.
“No. The opposite. They must not be down this tunnel.”
“This is where they were last sighted. Major Shellc wants an explanation.”
The speaking stone crackled to life, and Georgie had to explain it best he could.
“It’s intuition and the pickaxe, er, Major. I got [Itchy Scales].”
“We have a cream for that, Advance Miner. Unless that was actually a Skill?”
“Skill. It’s like [Dangersense], Major. Only, it’s more like it just goes off whenever I know I’m in a tricky spot. More reliable, but it never tells me when it’s gonna go bad. I have to know there’s something bad—and the pickaxe. It’s a different color today.”
“It’s not red. The warning magic—”
One of the Rubirel Guard glanced down and blinked. The pickaxe appeared…sort of blue-bronze-ish. Not red. As in—Georgie explained.
“It only turns red when there are monsters nearby, yeah. So they’re not even in the area.”
It was just a hunch, and he was no [Enchanter], but his intuition was often right. The Rubirel Guard hesitated.
“Maybe they escaped? Damn, sir, if they found an exit—”
“I’ll put our people on it. Get us in there, Advance Miner, and we’ll pick the trail up. We can locate most undead’s mana signatures.”
“Yessir.”
Georgie breached into the mining tunnels and shuddered at the familiar dead air scent, the faint odor of bone dust and…undeath. But he was right. No undead. He held back as [Soldiers] did their soldiering things.
Maiss’ team enlarged the tunnel, and Georgie waited until someone called him forwards.
“Tunnels are empty! Advance Miner—I need you to look at something.”
“Hells—okay.”
He jogged forwards, ready to run, but his pickaxe wasn’t giving any warnings. Georgie headed down the mining tunnels…then down another diagonal shaft and felt that odd prickling again. They were all just going down in one direction. No exploratory shafts beyond avoiding sheer rock, and even then he bet the old [Miners]’ pickaxes would have cut most of it easily.
The [Miners] had been going straight down, nearabouts. Or—as it had occurred to him more than once—
Up.
But there were no bodies, just the uniform support beams, the paved ground—and—he stopped.
The undead.
To be precise, what was left of them. Two [Captains] were standing in front of a mangled pile of flesh upon which a deformed skull had been placed, so many holes in it that Georgie doubted it would reanimate on its own in a hurry. The rest of the flesh seemed…ripped up.
Bones mangled, and the entire blob squished together. But not in a Wailing Pit kind of way, more like a hamburger with bones.
“Major, are you seeing this?”
“Get ready to evac right now, Captain. Captain Shieldscale’s been apprised—get Advance Miner Georgie’s opinion and prepare to fall back.”
“The hell did that?”
Georgie whispered, and someone, Advisor Merls, spoke crisply.
“We don’t know, but these match the remaining undead we were tracking down. Ignore them, Advance Miner. What’s this?”
Georgie’s head pivoted, and his mouth opened. Because beyond the undead was…a tunnel. It sloped downwards and crumbling dirt and rock and a lack of support pillars made him instantly nervous. He backed up.
“The hell’s that? That’s not their mine.”
Anyone could see that. The neat, obsessive mine of the dead [Miners] versus this—he took one look at it.
“Looks like a mole or some kind of tunneling monster. Big. Big. Only, it’s not even dug well. Most digging monsters know how to not collapse shit on them. [Sense Structural Integrity] says that’ll collapse fast if the earth so much as trembles.”
“So we’re looking at a monster big enough and strong enough to take down that many undead—who dug up into the mines? Wonderful. You hearing us, Major Shellc?”
Merls grumbled, glaring at Georgie, but not in an anti-Turnscale way; more like a ‘you have given me more bad news’ way that was iconic to all executives. Major Shellc replied, loud and clear.
“We’ll operate like that’s the case. I’m lifting the speaking stone lockdown. Full communications. Advance Miner, good work. Unless you can identify anything, fall back with your team after giving us entryways. And I want only three openings. Fortify each, and permanent overwatch. Advisor, get me a sensor spell to run down there and pull back once it’s deployed.”
Neat and tidy. Salazsarian mining protocols. Georgie was already stomping away, wiping sweat from his brows in relief, when he heard the faintest of sounds from below him. A tremor. Then…
An alarm.
It sounded like the alarms Salazsar would ring during tests, the big ones. City-wide ‘mine breach’ alarms for gas, monsters, or war.
Only, these weren’t the clarion calls from Salazsar’s towers. These were deep, almost like voices. Low voices, singing single notes, and then higher-pitched ones.
It was almost like music. A call to alarm—and a song. The instant he felt it, Georgie began running.
“It’s below us! Run, run!”
He got twenty feet, saw Merls turning his head, the rest of the [Soldiers] spinning around or frowning, raising their weapons. The idiots—
“Run! It’s coming from below!”
They didn’t have his instincts! Soldiers and their—Merls whirled and cupped an earhole.
“Below us? Those sound like—”
“Figure it out later! Run! Run!”
It was Major Shellc who barked.
“Full retreat! You heard him! Go!”
Only then did the damn idiots lurch into motion. Georgie wavered another moment longer despite his instincts. Because he saw one of the squad leaders glancing around and realized they didn’t know how to get out—despite the mine being so obvious to him.
Non-miners had no sense of space or direction underground. The Drake waved.
“This way! Move! Move!”
They began running, but slowly. The Rubirel Guard formed the rearguard, shouting, and the squads moved back as a unit. Great for fighting, slow when the mine was collapsing—which it wasn’t.
He didn’t know.
All Georgie knew was that the alarms were getting louder with each passing second. From a faint murmur, they started to fill the air. By the time five minutes had passed, and he was screaming at the Rubirel Guard to run faster, it was filling the tunnels.
Ten minutes and they were at the breach he’d dug. And it was so loud he thought it might begin tremoring…
Full evacuation. Major Shellc was ordering it, and Georgie saw [Miners] streaming upwards as he reached the breach. Second problem.
He’d been too slow to run.
Georgie blamed Ilvriss, really. He’d hesitated for that one crucial moment. Maybe he’d bought into the Wall Lord’s talk about a future, thought he owed Ilvriss something.
The time it took to lead the [Soldiers] up instead of leaving them to find their own way…it wasn’t long, but it meant that everyone else had heard him shouting. So [Miners] were evacuating—and filling the tunnels.
They were moving fast, but there were only so many ways to go. When you were at the back, closest to the alarms blaring louder—
Georgie stood there, watching as people shoved. Team Leader Maiss was shouting.
“Move it! Move it! Don’t shove—”
He was keeping his head, like Foreman Rolx, who was standing on some scaffolding, directing the teams upwards. And still…no one knew what was coming. The Rubirel Guard were six strong.
They formed a line in the beautiful tunnel of old, holding halberds, facing the darkness. Behind them, Advisor Merls had a wand aimed down the corridor, and the [Soldiers] were waiting. Just…
“Get out of here, Maiss!”
Georgie was hollering at the Drake. Maiss, his recently-healed jaw Georgie had broken, was wavering as a gap opened. He hesitated, and his eyes locked with Georgie’s.
“They’re coming. Two minutes till contact.”
How did he know…? Skill. But which one? Then Maiss turned, and his team were heading up. Georgie was estimating how many people were in front of him. Now the regular [Soldiers] were retreating, and Merls was hesitating.
“Rubirel Captain—Advance Miner—”
“Get out of here. I run fast, and I have an enchanted pickaxe. Advance Miners and heavies in the front.”
The [Advisor] hesitated a moment more, then spun on his heel. Georgie glanced at the scrum of bodies, then lifted his pickaxe and turned back around. One of the Rubirel Guard’s backed up from the breach and halted next to him, chestplate rising and falling rapidly.
“We hold the breach into the mining tunnels until we have a clear shot at retreat. Advance Miner, stand behind us.”
“Don’t get in the way of my pickaxe. I can throw it once, and it’ll kill anything. Pretty sure.”
A moment of hesitation, then they formed a wedge. Three on either side, with a gap down the center, slanted inwards there.
