Four hundred angry cattle defecated, distracting one of the Purifiers. Desinee clung to Big Burlap’s back as arrows fell around them. Then her heart was pounding.
I knew I was mad. But the world was mad after the Winter Solstice. Because it was so ordinary. Here—right here makes a dreadful kind of sense.
Aunt Maviola?
Desinee stared ahead and saw a flash of red hair and a burning banner. Then she raised the Kaalblade high.
“House of El!”
She watched Big Burlap run onto a sword the glowing Drakes drew. Then hit a second rank of braced Drakes. Then crash through the third—and they realized the angry bull wasn’t stopping for mere flesh wounds. Desinee swung her Kaalblade wildly, screaming.
 
——
 
Once again, for the first time since the Sacrifice of Roses, a battlefield saw multiple [Ladies] advancing into enemy lines. A screaming, terrified [Lady] of the House of El. A Terland [Lady] with a Golem heart roaring like the rest.
And Lady Damia Reinhart. She was swinging the Kaalglaive, screaming, as Varnie and her people fought around her.
Her job was simple. There was a Purifier lumbering towards Salazsar’s forces. If even one reached the Drakes, it would crush and kill them. Damia’s mind told her the simple equation: the Purifier had to be stopped.
If she popped it, the waste would distract the others. The only problem was reaching it.
There were glowing Drakes everywhere, and Varnie was a whirlwind of blades, stabbing through faces, swearing nonstop. Damia’s mind was shrieking something at her, but she had meant it.
Level or die. There was only one way a weak [Lady] could be useful, and it was this:
“[Bridge the Gap]!”
She was close enough—a ramp opened and forced the glowing [Soldiers] apart. Damia rode up the ramp with Desinee’s screaming mare and saw a huge, clawed foot stomping past her. She swung the glowing Kaalglaive at it.
Missed.
Her third wild swing saw the cumbersome, poorly-designed Kaalglaive’s tip slash across the Purifier’s leg. Damia saw the magic deforming around the tip of the glowing blade. Then something black bulged from inside the Purifier—
This time, it popped like a giant zit, pus blasting out the leg. It knocked the light-soldiers down, and they began crying for more Purifiers. Above Damia, the giant glowing Drake form wobbled. It tried to hold its structure, but then it started to destabilize. Before it could ‘bend’, it just—shattered. Into a million fragments of light.
Damia Reinhart caught her breath. She gazed up and saw a being more magical than she had ever laid eyes on vanishing, claw holding a blade that vanished and turned to fragments of light.
In the distance, the fighting Drakes and Gnolls and Humans were shouting. Cheering her? Damia Reinhart hefted the Kaalglaive higher with trembling arms.
She actually had done it. Even she couldn’t believe it. And she wondered…
Was this her Level 20 capstone deed?
Or even more?
A new class?
Her heart thrilled. She almost laughed—then turned around. And all she saw around her were glowing Drakes. No gang.
Just…Varnie, panting, as she stopped her whirlwind of knives Skill. Damia’s mind told her that maybe Salazsar was cheering her. But right now they were also telling her to get out of…
She turned her horse. The mare collapsed onto her forelegs. Damia tried to urge the creature up, startled, then saw glowing arrows standing out along the mare’s head. She fell onto the ground.
“Up. C’mon—damnit, it worked, but it was stupid as hell—”
Varnie heaved Damia up and threw a dagger into a Drake’s eye. Damia whispered to her.
“Your gang, Varnie. I’m so sorry—”
The [Gang Leader] eyed her and leapt forwards. Slashed a Drake’s head off, backstepped, knifed a Drake without looking with a backwards jab of her daggers. Pulled something out and tossed it.
Explosion of smoke. She activated a Skill and stood in a cleared section of ground, balanced on the balls of her feet. Smiling.
“Them? They’re not all dead. They just ran for it ‘fore we got this far in. Whaddya expect? You hired criminals, remember? I’m just surprised the idiots followed me in. Dumb as rocks. It worked, though. You just didn’t think of an escape route, did you?”
Damia’s silence was enough. Varnie checked her corners, drawing her daggers.
“Why are you here, then?”
The [Gang Leader] grinned.
“I’m Varnie the Bloodletter. I’d rather be dead than a Face who ran from a debt. Stay behind me or we won’t make it. Shame there’s no bodies to hide behind.”
The smoke was clearing. Damia swung the Kaalglaive around wildly and wondered when the charge would run out. It’d kill any Drake soldier until then, but they were surrounded—
 
——
 
Damia’s destruction of the Purifier did not go unmissed. Everyone saw it—it was just that there was no one able to save her.
Ulva Terland was ordering her Golems forwards, but they had been fighting a flanking action, not doing a suicide charge. Bird and Elia were sniping down soldiers around Varnie and Damia, but…
Lord Gorthes eyed the Drakes and didn’t see any Oldblood Fliers anywhere near the fighting. Drakes liked fairly static formations, anyways. He leaned on the driver’s seat of his reinforced carriage and sighed.
“That’s your daughter alright, Cecille. Dumb as you. Goes charging in for a wagging tail and gets in over her head.”
“Gorthes. Be silent.”
Was that emotion in her tone? Gorthes grinned into the scrying orb and bit a lump of chewing tobacco. He eyed the Unmarked Coach, but the driver wasn’t doing shit. So Gorthes regarded the carriages of his best bullyboys and sighed. Then he lifted the scrying orb and spoke into it.
“This is Gorthes to the family. Is that Damia still sleeping with her brother? Werbel or whatever his name is?”
Silence. Some of the other Reinharts shrugged. Tourois Reinhart took a gulp of wine.
“I swear I saw that boy porking a [Maid] the other day. Not that it means much. In the damn garden.”
“She’s stopped.”
Cecille was pale-cheeked as she stared at the spot where the smoke was clearing. Gorthes nodded. He checked his chewed fingernails.
“Anyone got a good reason she should be dead? She murder too many people? Too much of a headache? Sleep with, I dunno, children?”
Silence. Which, when you got to it, was like a room full of applause in House Reinhart. No one ever said good things about the family. But if they had nothing overly bad to say…Lord Gorthes sighed.
“Damnit. Alright—on me!”
He grabbed the reins, then just drew a bullwhip and cracked it overhead. The stallion team moved into action. Behind Gorthes, he heard his minions, the sycophants and idiots he had for servants, hesitate.
“Lord Gorthes—”
They followed him. Although when they saw what he was driving at, they hesitated again. But Gorthes’ blood was up. He put the reins of the carriage in his teeth, gritting them so hard they nearly cracked. He swore he saw that damn driver of the Unmarked Coach staring at him out of the corner of his eye.
Gorthes spat out the reins long enough to bellow over his shoulder.
“Hey, you! Look at a real driver.”
Then he was roaring. The two carriages behind him were wavering, the [Drivers]’ faces white. The thugs he’d recruited were panicking.
“Lord Gorthes—we’re going be—”
“[Shut Up And Obey]!”
The [Brute of a Lord] roared. He saw the Drake light-soldiers turning. They paused, perhaps not sure how you attacked a carriage. A problem House Reinhart’s many enemies had faced over the years. Unless you had a pike wall, the horses, terrified of the bullwhip but mostly the multi-ton vehicle on their asses, wouldn’t slow.
Even if you got them, then you just had an out-of-control carriage reinforced with steel and magic—Gorthes was laughing.
A [Lord] laying around him with a bullwhip as he drove into the glowing Drakes. He kicked, got a slash on his enchanted clothing, swung a club into a face as he urged the horses forwards—
In his carriage, his servants were swinging their weapons. But the cowardly pukes were panicking. Gorthes saw one of the carriages pulling away.
“Traitorous cowards! [No One Double Crosses Me]!”
The [Driver] was turning his carriage away when Gorthes’ Skill hit him full-force. Literally; it was like the [Lord] wound up for the heaviest punch he could make and hit the man with it. The [Driver] reeled, insensible, and the carriage skidded into a wing of the [Soldiers].
Good enough as a distraction. The second carriage bogged down, and the panicked servants leapt out, trying to make a break for it.
Gorthes’ carriage went onwards. He felt the Drakes trying to grab him. But his eyes were on the smoke. One of the stallions went down, screaming, a glowing spear in its guts.
“[Cut It Loose]! Where—there!”
Gorthes saw a flash of blades. He bent down, leaning across the driver’s seat, and yanked something up.
A Kaalglaive, energy spent. He hauled Damia up, and she screamed, flailing, thinking he was a Drake. He punched her, dragged her over his lap, and then cracked the bullwhip again.
“Get us out of here, you damn nags!”
The stallions were screaming. They heaved, and the carriage moved as Varnie whirled, did a double-take, and leapt for the carriage. But the Drakes were clinging to the sides of the carriage.
“Lord Gorthes, we can’t get free! We’re too h—aaaaaaaaaaah!”
Gorthes grabbed the [Servant] who was screaming and heaved the man over the side of the carriage.
“[Die Before Me]!”
The Human projectile hit the Drakes trying to climb on board, and Gorthes felt the carriage moving. He shouted.
“I’ll promote ya if you live!”
Then he felt them accelerating. Lady Damia raised her head woozily.
“Uncle Gorthes? What the—”
Gorthes ignored her, cracking his whip at the horses, at the Drakes. It was only when he felt his carriage reaching a critical momentum and knew the Drakes couldn’t stop him before they burst free that he began laughing.
He threw back his head and roared with laughter, leaving bloody carnage behind him—even if most of it was magical light-soldiers. A full Reinhart. He grinned down at Damia as blood ran into one eye from a cut on his head; he had two arrows in one arm, and he didn’t even seem like he felt them.
“Always have a way out, you worthless little shit. Now you owe me.”
Gorthes just guffawed louder at Damia’s open-mouthed expression of astonishment. He loved it when he collected big favors.
 
——
 
They were—all fighting.
House of El. House Terland. Even House Reinhart.
Calidus was laughing so hard he had tears in his eyes. Clapping. Cheering even for Uncle Gorthes’ iconic madness. He’d never been prouder, truly.
Selys was searching for her friends, for Wall Lord Ilvriss. But Calidus just rose to his feet.
“He sees it. So does Damia. Are you all blind?”
The Faces of his Guild sat around him. Faces and Ranks. They were in the Assassin’s Guild. Selys was trembling, trying to be composed.
“Calidus, I—we need to assist. Strategically—if that is the Walled City—”
“Let them all die and collect on it after they’ve weakened the city.”
He nodded. Selys’ face turned stricken, then blank as she clenched her claws. But the [Lord]’s calm face burst into another maniac grin.
“That’s what my Grandfather would do. Because it’s the logical move in a world where no one trusts anyone and where allies are just that of convenience. The logic of someone who is unloved and loveless.”
Her eyes widened, and he turned. Calidus calmly lifted a speaking stone to his lips.
“This is the Guildmaster of the Assassin’s Guild to every Rank in the area. Undercover or not—you have full permission to attack the City of Purity’s forces. Do not attack or hinder Wall Lord Ilvriss or allied forces.”
He lowered the speaking stone and turned, beaming around at Losmere and the others.
“That goes for anyone who wants to participate, here as well. Don’t worry, I’m sure the fighting will last long enough for a carriage ride.”
Full permission? The Ranks and Faces eyed Calidus with as much skepticism as Selys. They looked, pointedly, at the giant Purifier shooting beams of light out its mouth before one of the Golem volleys ripped it apart.
But Calidus just chuckled. Then doubled over with mirth. Then ripped his shirt open because he liked the move. His belly flopped out as he breathed in and out.
“Do you not…see it? The City of Purity? And this is our chance! Rehabilitate our image! Put it out there, now, that the real Assassin’s Guild is defending the Five Families, as it’s always done! Levels! I bet Salazsar’s posting an all-call bounty for that Wall Lord! Get in touch with their Assassin’s Guild and demand a bounty!”
“Lord Calidus, you want our members to fight light-constructs from another era?”
Losmere was trying to do her cool, professional—Calidus seized her shoulders. Then scooped her up in his arms. She froze up, then tried to get free. He beamed at her, dropped her, and she landed on her feet like an angry cat. He shouted.
“Are you [Assassins] or not? I thought [Assassin] meant you killed things! Not just fleshy, blood-filled mortals! Here is the challenge of a lifetime with the rewards to match, and this is why your Guild died. Cowards stay behind! To every single Rank out there—the one that kills a Purifier is a Face! My oath on it!”
The Ranks froze up. Selys saw one of them, Slashface, push herself up from a table despite her healing injuries. Selys almost grabbed for her, but Calidus seized her shoulder. He glanced around in the silence.
“Well? Go!”
Two dozen Ranks were on their feet at once. One leapt out a window; another vaulted the table. And Calidus turned to the scrying orb, then hesitated.
“Ah, probably a little delay. Perfect. Well then…[Ascertain Consent]. Miss Selys? Would you mind it greatly if I swept you into an impassioned kiss?”
She blinked at him. Calidus Reinhart beamed at her. His eyes flickered—then he swept an arm around her and kissed her on the mouth. He was still beaming when she elbowed him in the stomach and slapped him.
“Someone get me a drink and a recording of this.”
Then he sat back down and leaned forwards. Because he couldn’t wait to see how this ended.
 
——
 
The news broke in Salazsar nearly two hours after the battle started. To be fair, there were people who’d seen it the moment the City of Purity’s alarms had been going off.
Alrric didn’t know if he’d blinked. He was sitting in his office, just watching, paws gripping his desk. He’d lost track of Ilvriss several times.
But now—he was aware the City of Gems was finding out. Of course they were.
Wall Lord Brilm’s son was there, and if there was a soul within screaming distance who hadn’t heard Brilm—of course, Eschowar and the smarter lot might have wanted to keep this private.
It was too late.
The funny thing was that it wasn’t on the news. Citizens of Salazsar were being told by word of mouth. Racing to get scrying orbs. But every time one of them tried to send a [Message] to Pallass News Network or Wistram to ask why the hell they weren’t covering this—nothing happened.
Only a bit concerning, that. Alrric filed that away for later. And he suspected—well, think about it.
All of House Terland was either engaged in the fighting or watching. They didn’t want anyone to know if their precious Golems died. Reinharts? Not big on sharing information.
The House of El was the only group who’d give anything away, and they might be glued to their scrying orbs like Alrric. If The Wandering Inn wasn’t shouting the news, then the only major city that could see this was Salazsar.
Salazsar was watching their Wall Lord fight. Ilvriss, the same Drake who’d been dragged in their own newspapers and the court of public opinion, the Drake who’d done the Right Thing at the Meeting of Tribes.
…His shouting at Periss still rattled Alrric. So he really had been in love. And…Alrric gazed downwards and saw.
Colonel Maiss was still holding the front lines. He was fighting side-by-side with Maisy, the Rubirel Guard having lost her damaged helmet, and the two were clearing the light-soldiers around them.
Roaring orders. Blood was running down Maiss’ rather impressively clenched jaw, and Maisy was hoisting a struggling Drake over her head with her halberd before she flung the enemy soldier off her.
“They’re fighting like Named-rank adventurers. We employ them? For how much?”
Alrric was checking on how much you had to pay someone to fight like that. He’d always complained about salaries, even if he was a big proponent of paying [Miners] better—but how much did you put on that?
Two hours of fighting. It felt like you couldn’t manage ten minutes, but Salazsar’s forces were used to fighting, or mining, for long bursts. They were rotating troops off the front, but the front lines still engaging with the light-soldiers were furiously battling for their lives.
See—there was Lady Damia waving her Kaalglaive from well behind enemy lines, exhorting the troops. Silverfangs had united under Elia Arcsinger and Salazsar’s [Archers] and were volleying into any exposed area nonstop.
There was a clearing in the fighting as Alrric saw someone standing at the fore of the battle. Alrric leaned forwards.
“Ilvriss?”
There he was. The Wall Lord came into view as he appeared on a giant scrying mirror in the main plazas of Salazsar.
His father, his administrator, his mother, his friends saw the Wall Lord. He was remarkably unhurt despite the fighting. A single cut marred his prismatic…purple…
What had happened to his scales? The Drake turned, and his eyes gleamed like the very gemstones his city was named after. His scales were still purple, but they had changed, taking on the colors of an opal. And his wings…
 
——
 
Helessia Gemscale couldn’t breathe. [Healers] rushed into her rooms, but she was pointing. And when they tried to turn the scrying orb off, she fought them.
She was gazing at his wings. They fluttered open as the Drake ran. So changed, but she would always recognize her son.
Wings.
It wasn’t…like he was the only Oldblood Drake anyone had ever seen. There were plenty, but—
 
——
 
In the City of Gems, Drakes were seeing the Wall Lord’s image being shone higher. On the sides of the towers. Someone had rigged up a projection spell, and citizens were pointing. Asking what was going on. Gnolls, Drakes, and a few other species, yes.
But it was the Drakes who went stumbling. Some nearly walked off catwalks or into traffic. They would look up, recognize Ilvriss, see those wings, and their minds would shut off.
For a moment, they’d be children again. Reading stories of Dragons and their ancestors of old. Seeing those Drakes flying with Dragons and dreaming of it.
Wings. How? How had he…?
To them, it was as important as seeing that Archmage fly. A dream that they’d forgotten they had, recaptured. Like seeing the Flying Gnoll of Pallass.
A million pairs of eyes followed the Wall Lord, and he was still running, larger than life, as his forces fought glowing Drakes. As if they’d come straight out of the storybooks into reality.
If they had been able to call the New Lands, the Meeting of Tribes, return of the King of Destruction, the ghosts—everything—anomalies, craziness, but within the keeping of this time, this was the final blow. Men and women and children going to their ordinary jobs working for the companies gazed up and wondered if this was the era of fantasies.
And if so—
What were they doing here? 
Still, Ilvriss ran.
 
——
 
The Son of Salazsar was shouting.
“Hold the line! Don’t give up on me now! I’m not laying your pay slip on a grave! Do you know how much a funeral and pension costs?”
—He was still doing it too. If anything, his voice seemed more confident. He spun, and Alrric saw he had on a crimson cloak. Was it enchanted? The Drake wasn’t holding a sword, but he strode past the fighting [Soldiers], a squad of battered Rubirel Guard following him.
He was peering around, gauging the fighting. Alrric was sure that one of the other leaders, like Major Shellc, was directing the actual battle from behind the scenes, but Ilvriss was on the front. He ducked an arrow, cursing, and Alrric heard some pithy language.
“—gargling ballsacks of a Oliphant—”
He’d never heard Ilvriss swear like that. To be fair, Alrric had never seen the Wall Lord fighting up close. Practicing swordplay, or as a tiny image at the Meeting of Tribes, yes. But this?
Was Ilvriss mad? One arrow while his rings were recharging and he was dead. But it was working. He went striding down the line again, then spotted something.
A knot in the fighting. Another group had plunged too far in and refused to pull back. Only, this time, it wasn’t a hairbrained charge by a young Human [Lady].
No, happily, it was Wall Lord Dramm who had rushed forwards with his entourage, thinking to press an attack. From above, his section looked like a bulging ball of shrinking bodies; he was being enveloped.
The young idiot was making it worse because he kept shouting the same ironic phrase used by dead Drakes.
“Drakes don’t run! Hold! Hold, damnit! Drakes don’t—”
“That idiot!”
Alrric thought he was about to see a dead young Wall Lord. Ilvriss seemed to believe so too. He froze, pointing, and the Rubirel Guard tried to advance, but they’d be too slow. Dramm was swinging his sword wildly, and the light-soldiers were closing in. So the Wall Lord looked around—up—and then sighed.
He flung the cloak back to let his wings unfurl with a snap, then leapt. One of the Rubirel Guard tried to grab his legs, but it was too late. The Wall Lord flew up—and fell.
Straight into the middle of the fighting. He snapped his wings open as he landed and sent allies and enemies stumbling back. Dramm whirled.
“Wall Lord! Wh—”
Ilvriss strode over, headbutted Dramm, and shoved the dizzy young Wall Lord back at his people.
“Get him out of here! You idiots—retreat! Enough of quoting Sserys! Real Drakes run when they have to! And fight when—”
A sword nearly pierced his stomach. Ilvriss whirled, and it then became clear that his saving Dramm meant the entire area of fighting was collapsing.
On him. Light-soldiers advanced, and Ilvriss didn’t have—
Where was his sword? He dodged another sword, then grabbed an arm. Alrric saw Ilvriss pivot—then he performed a shoulder throw.
The light-Drake went flying over Dramm’s head as the dizzy Wall Lord sat up. Ilvriss pivoted, kicked another light-soldier in the ground, and when that didn’t work, swept a leg. He backhanded another version of Vnariss, and then he was boxing, punching.
And still shouting.
“We are more than one damn Drake! Look at the folly of Naamreles! We are Salazsar—if I fall, keep fighting! Drakes, Gnolls, Humans—with me!”
He sounded a bit like that young [Lady] from House Reinhart. Only, Wall Lord Ilvriss was under attack as he said all this. A slash cut across his armor. He staggered as an arrow hit him from behind and went down—had he locked legs with another of the light-soldiers to trip the Drake up?
—He came up after four heart-stopping seconds and threw another light-Gnoll. He was throwing them into each other, and the Rubirel Guard finally cut forwards. But the Wall Lord wasn’t done.
He wiped blood running down his cheek from his face as one of the versions of Vnariss got an opening. But it stopped and ran that eerie light over Ilvriss’ body.
They’d largely given up on scanning, but maybe the Wall Lord’s clear Oldblood ancestry had provoked the scan.
The copy of Vnariss spoke.
“Analysis: 50% genetic viability.”
Even it seemed confused a moment before Ilvriss drew a dagger and threw it through the Drake’s eye, and it vanished. He swept his cloak off his shoulders; it was clearly getting tangled. The Drake turned.
“Oldblood doesn’t matter. This is where that line of thinking ends. With me. With me!”
Then he inhaled—and Alrric saw him exhale something that glittered and burst. The light-soldiers threw up their shields, but something coated their armor, their ‘skin’, and hardened.
Crystals. It weighed down the light-constructs, some to immobility, and Ilvriss exhaled again. Only then did he cough and turn.
His tail swished on the grass as he lifted a fist. He practically sauntered back behind the lines. Alrric was a very happily-married Gnoll with a loving wife.
But he had to stare at Ilvriss’ tail, and he wasn’t sure if he’d ever seen tail-movements that suggestive on—more than one citizen of Salazsar experienced a moment of worrying confusion before putting it down to a trick of the light.
Certainly, the Wall Lord didn’t stop there. He rested one knee on a crate of ammunition, speaking to one of the [Archers], and his armor and pants outlined his body until someone blocked the shot. Possibly for his dignity, although dead gods, what did the Wall Lord have to be ashamed of?
Eye-catching. A presence larger than life. Captivating in his new form, in leadership and presence and—
Ulva Terland stood apart from Ilvriss, a forgotten heroine conducting Golems to war, eying the rising son of Salazsar. Across from them, a giant bull covered in wounds was deigning to let Lady Desinee clean his cuts—though Naamreles’ weapons left virtually no chance of infection—and the [Rancher]-lords and ladies fought for their lands.
Magic being plucked from fallen constructs’ hands. Levels gained by every person fighting. And more—more coming to give battle.
 
——
 
It was the only thing she could do.
Mrsha du Marquin was not stupid enough to join the fighting with the robes of Warmage Thresk or his staff.
She just…walked into a building after climbing a good-sized hill. Stopping to listen to the clamor outside. Moved slowly, despite the need.
She found him inside, for once, though she hadn’t thought to. But when the man turned from tending to the glowing, green flame, Mrsha stood there.
Almost ashamed. She didn’t want to do this. Not to them—but it was why they had been formed.
He would have wanted her to tell him.
“Mrsha? What’s going on?”
Dame Ushar said nothing as Mrsha handed Grandmaster Normen of the Order of Solstice a card. He read it, asked a few questions—and then his burned features firmed. He took something from the inner keep of the Order of Solstice, a single lantern glowing with green fire, and Mrsha wiped at her eyes.
The [Grandmaster] noticed and bent to hug her. And she didn’t tell him his stupid armor pinched her fur terribly. When Normen rose, he smiled once.
“We’re not ready. But we will never be. And we’re more ready than last time.”
So saying, he strode out of the Celestial Keep, still being built, and called out. Gnolls, Antinium, Drakes, Humans, and a half-Troll girl looked up. They listened—then, when Normen pointed, they began to run.
Antinium [Squires]. Over two hundred of them. Gnolls like Dekava Silverfang, holding yet-unlit lanterns. Waiting for their flame.
Armored—streaming for the [Portal Door] held open by a grim Liska.
Reinforcements.
Mrsha stood there as the remaining [Knights] that Normen had left to hold the keep should none return tried to go back to practicing, then ran to find a scrying orb. Then, heavily, she returned to the inn to see how it ended.
 
——
 
The Order of Solstice joined the fighting at the five-hour mark. The initial assault from the light-brigades had slowed, but with alarming regularity, Dig Site B spat out another group.
The Purifiers were almost completely entrenched around Dig Site B and the town of Thirthoof, engaged in a perpetual cycle of cleanup and explosion. Filth-elementals were rising as the Purifiers concentrated the waste, then detonated, unable to contain that much sewage. It was also pulling off some of the light-brigades who engaged the muck-monsters, but the rest kept attacking Salazsar’s position.
They ran into Golems launching spells, a rain of arrows from Lord Xitegen and the [Ranchers], flaming [Knights], Silverfang Gnolls, Salazsarian heavy armor troopers, the occasional pickaxe, and at least one bull too angry to die.
…It couldn’t last. Major Shellc had made a prediction.
“We can operate for three more hours at most before we begin to buckle. The moment we begin taking excessive casualties, the effect will snowball, and we’ll be overrun. Either we get help from Pallass or some other force or we’re dead. Lady Ulva’s reinforcement Golems will not make it in time.”
The faster Golems might, but not enough to turn the tides. Nor was the [Major] hopeless; he saw this entire affair as the opening salvo of a true battle, if not war.
They needed time. They needed to regroup, analyze which strategies were working, dig in, cooperate, and heal.
They would not have it. The power of Naamreles was to overwhelm and not quit. If they had space, hundreds of miles, it was conceivable they might wipe enough troops to get that time. Not with the City of Purity on top of them.
Yet the Drake was cool. Calm, even. He delivered this strategic assessment to Salazsar, and he was sure their High Command was counting which [Strategists] had figured this out and had viable solutions.
Major Shellc let the bigwigs, higher-ups, and brass confer and then ignored whatever they were going to say. Because, of course—
He’d come up with this analysis in the first twenty minutes of fighting. He had simply reaffirmed his hypothesis with actual observations and data. Now, the Drake raised a separate speaking stone to his mouth.
“Wall Lord, I trust you heard all that. We must slow the City of Purity.”
“Understood, Major Shellc. We are in position. We will begin the operation—now. Going mana-quiet unless we are compromised or need long-range Skills. Wish us luck.”
Major Shellc nodded tightly. Wall Lord Ilvriss’ voice was terse and a bit echo-y. But Shellc kept his posture, leaning on his war desk, not giving the enemy any signs he’d just said or done anything significant. They were probably dumb constructs, but they were adapting tactics. Slightly.
He went back to directing the battle, eying the Wall Lord who was still encouraging the troops from the front. Ilvriss didn’t seem to tire as he held a shield up awkwardly. He was dynamic, with the right thing to say to every soldier, captivating his city and everyone else with his charisma. Oh, and he had that stupid cloak back on.
 
——
 
Wall Lord Ilvriss sneezed, then cursed as more dirt cascaded down around him. He was covered in it, and how not?
Five hours, more or less, of sneaking across the Cowpat Plains—literally crawling through cowpats in his armor—and then digging. He was covered in filth and would have liked nothing less than for a Purifier to clean him up.
But since running into one of those would botch this entire mission, he just stifled another sneeze.
“Damn. I forgot to ask if Xesci’s doing alright.”
He hoped she hadn’t gotten hurt, playing ‘him’. She’d volunteered, saying only she could do it. And it made sense to Ilvriss, because he had to be here.
This mission was going to win or lose the battle as much as holding the line up there. He had ten of the Rubirel Guard, three [Mages]—and Captain Osthia’s squad. All volunteers.
The Drake herself had somehow weaseled her damn way onto this mission despite having probably broken twenty or more bones. She’d insisted—and when he’d told her she was too hurt, she’d flown off and gotten Magus Grimalkin to cast [Restoration] on her.
Changing tactics. Even a healing potion couldn’t have done that. He and the other [Mages] were providing magical fire support, but Ilvriss had requested they save their mana for [Restoration] spells if possible.
He just hoped there’d be enough of them left to heal. He leaned against one wall and regarded his command squad.
“You heard Shellc. This has to be done. Now, to repeat the plan so we all understand it: we are to collapse the entrance tunnels to the City of Purity and everything else. The old mining shafts will be a problem given how they were reinforced, but if we can just tremor enough dirt, it’ll buy us time. Days, or if we’re lucky, the constructs will just forget we’re up here. Once the collapse starts, anyone trapped down there is dead. So we move fast, but we cannot hesitate. Understand?”
Everyone nodded. They’d dug down around Dig Site B to get to the mining shafts. Slow, stealthy mining while they heard the fighting above. Anxiety-producing. But they’d had to go slow to avoid detection.
Shellc had tried to collapse the mine shafts, but he’d only had time for a single spell. The magicore had absorbed the spell, and while it had slowed the light-forces, they’d just cleared the tunnels near the surface.
However…they had only one path of egress to the surface, via Naamreles’ ancient mineshafts. Collapse those and the security systems might not know where the ‘enemy’ was any more. Or they’d lose cohesion or, at very least, have to dig up through countless tonnes of dirt. The only problem would be collapsing the mineshaft and not dying.
Hence the tense Drakes and Gnolls, Rubirel Guard, Advance Miners, and Ilvriss. The Wall Lord checked his armor and sword. It sparked as he willed fury into it.
I am not going to die here. Especially not before I clear up that kiss with Lyonette.
It might be a stupid reason, but it worked for him. There was only one commenter. Advance Miner Georgie just had to say something.
“Listen, Wall Lord, I can see why I’m here. You need the best man for the job. Which is me.”
He ignored the other seven [Advance Miners] glaring at him. Georgie hefted his enchanted pickaxe on one shoulder as he gritted a fresh cigar between his teeth.
“—But why’re you here? We don’t risk the executives on this kinda thing. Sure you can’t get Magus Grimalkin?”
“Shut it, Georgie.”
Someone began, but Ilvriss held up a claw. He smiled at Georgie and got a gritted smile in return. They nodded at each other.
“Three reasons, Georgie. One, I have the levels and Skills to boost you all. [Opulence Guard], my Skill, will let us tank attacks when we’re noticed. Second—I have a magic sword that can kill constructs and, I hope, even Purifiers. Third, I’m not going to ask you to commit to a mission of this danger without doing the same.”
“Hmf. Sure. What if you’re that fake Ilvriss?”
Georgie grunted, but Ilvriss just smiled. As everyone braced for Georgie to breach into the mining tunnels, he whispered back.
“There’s only one way to tell us apart, Georgie. One Ilvriss can breathe magical Dragonbreath, use his wings, and is, I daresay, a charismatic, captivating Wall Lord.”
“Uh huh. And what makes the other one unique?”
Georgie tapped the wall, and it collapsed. The tunnel was aglow with marching light-soldiers coming up. Someone cursed—but Osthia’s squad was already charging forwards. One of the Rubirel Guard unrolled the Tier 5 scrolls, and Ilvriss began to run, heart pumping. He passed by Georgie as the [Advance Miner] threw his pickaxe through the first rank of surprised light-constructs. Then Ilvriss was shaking his hips right to left. Waggling his tail.
He ignored the look Georgie was giving him.
“This Ilvriss can dance.”
In hindsight, he really wished that sounded better.
 
——
 
Major Shellc saw the Drakes made of glowing magic visibly slow, and Shellc swore they grew…fuzzy.
Did that mean they were being projected upwards after all, like the Archmage of Izril was speculating? He hoped so, because it had turned a desperate holding action into a battle that could be won. He began broadcasting the news, of course.
“A strike force has collapsed the tunnels leading into Naamreles! The enemy is out of reinforcements! Hold the line and we have them!”
He heard cheering, but the reason Shellc was being so loud was because victory was no surefire thing. The [Major] was sweating.
This was going to come down to the wire. The dirt-fortress that Salazsar had constructed was under siege from three cardinal directions. If it was breached, or their other allies lost their nerve, he’d have to call for a full retreat.
The light-forces of Naamreles were a bog of glowing limbs throwing themselves at Salazsar’s walls. They were like that joke you told about the heathen barbarous enemies of your nation: they attacked you en masse with little strategy, marching into your killzones.
The problem was it worked if you had so many bodies you could flood the area. Worse—he put them at Level 15 [Soldiers] in quality unless they combined or activated more advanced magics—which they could do.
But the light-soldiers resisted magic. A [Fireball] would cook a regular squad of troops or leave them so disoriented and hurt they were functionally mincemeat. Hit a squad of Naamreles’ forces and the ones not blown to bits would get up and keep fighting.
The true danger was like Shellc’s studies of the Antinium; if the light-soldiers surrounded you, anyone but someone in plate armor was dead. And they pushed.
“Our western flank is folding! Do not let them encircle us! Ranchers, give me a skirmishing line, there! [Form Battle Line]!”
Shellc was engaged in a brutal clash along Salazsar’s dirt-fortress; his entire objective was to keep the elements of the light-forces from encircling Salazsar’s position. As long as he kept their rear open, they could rotate soldiers out for healing and keep ammunition stocked.
The moment they were encircled, they died. The enemy seemed to know this, despite not having a living leader, and were advancing again. They were slowed by Shellc’s only tools. The [Ranchers], who rode and shot arrows from horseback. A skirmishing line of irregulars who could maneuver and fire.
Their angry cattle could provide a flanking charge as well, but the animals had no real direction. Lady Desinee could direct them, but then they’d be butchered unless he gave them an escape route.
Suboptimal, and he had no healing potions. However, Shellc’s other tool was the Golems under House Terland. And Ulva Terland was a seasoned commander.
The light-Gnolls armed with bows were beginning to shower the [Ranchers] with their light-arrows when a trio of Golems moved forwards and screened the [Ranchers] with glowing barrier spells. Then one rolled forwards—it had wheels instead of feet—aimed its odd body upwards, and began launching arrows nonstop.
One of Xitegen’s personal Golems. Mobile artillery that spat arrows at the archers. That allowed the whooping [Ranchers] to rain down arrows on the advancing Drakes, but in response, the Drakes just projected those damn shields above their heads.
Cue Battle Golems, who smashed into them. The light-soldiers began to swarm the steel Golems—then pivoted, a hair too late. Cattle charge from the left flank; Rubirel Guard leading an advance from Salazsar’s fortifications.
Grind them down. The light soldiers didn’t stop, of course. They kept pouring into the pincer attack, and they’d eventually overwhelm the other groups and force a victory. Now that their numbers were limited, maybe Shellc could wear them down, but he had no fallback point from Salazsar’s fortress.
So they had to break the lines here. The [Swordgrace Major]’s eyes glinted as he saw the western flank bunching up. Thousands of the light-soldiers pushing to advance…
“Now! Major Shellc, requesting bombardment spells! On my position! Fire for effect!”
A [Scrying Mage] standing next to him flashed the sea of enemy soldiers up, and Shellc waited. He stared upwards, and this was the part that made his guts churn.
“Come on. Come on…”
He didn’t know who he was speaking to. Truly. Shellc prayed for magic from the skies like a man dying of thirst prayed for rain. And then he saw the air twist. A gigantic spell circle appeared in the sky, and he breathed out. Three of them.
Spells came down.
A tornado, two bolts of [Grand Lightning]—and a hail of magical arrows. They merged together, and winds hurled bodies of light-Drakes skywards. Some survived, despite the magical arrows raining down everywhere—Shellc cursed and ducked his head down.
“Beware of enemy soldiers landing around you! To anyone watching—no wind spells! Don’t hurl the enemy around! Reinforcements coming from the north!”
He pointed out another wave of reinforcements, hoping they were one of the last ones. And he gazed up at the skies again.
 
——
 
Major Shellc’s image of the enemy soldiers he needed dead were playing on scrying spells in other kingdoms, as was his commentary. Demanding fire support.
The effrontery of this Drake. [Kings] and [Queens] glared at him. Then asked their [Mages] how many spells they had. Demanded to know if Wistram was…
They were watching, of course. There were jamming spells everywhere. Terland Golems? Naamreles’ magic in the Purifiers?
Whatever it was, the battles were flashes of images. You’d get fifteen seconds of one particular area, then the scrying spells would fizzle out, go dark, and the [Mages] would need another coordinate. Major Shellc was getting around that by sending [Magic Pictures] with coordinates.
It wasn’t their war. In truth, the Five Families were probably sending the most magic. But even distant nations in Terandria were watching.
Naamreles. A name they had in their history books. The name provoked the same unsettling nervousness, the tension that had not left the hearts and bowels of the mighty since the Winter Solstice. Or even before that.
Once more, kingdoms tried to throw magic and Skills across the world. But they had spent their magics again and again—instead of one-time scrolls, it was linked [Mages] firing Tier 5 spells off, using all their magic to contribute a single spell to the battlefield. And the Drake was demanding dozens of such spells. But no nations wanted to spend their artifacts.
Ailendamus had hurled two dozen spells in the battle already. All products of their linked [Mages]. A sign they truly could influence the world. Lesser nations? One.
But Ailendamus had ample reason; occasionally, someone could see a Human man fighting at the front of Salazsar’s forces. Not in the vanguard around Ilvriss, directly facing the buried City of Purity, but holding down the eastern flank.
Virtually unsupported. He was two dozen feet in front of the spear walls and trenches, fighting with his clothing akimbo, surrounded by light-soldiers. At first, you thought he was being sent to die—until he threw a punch and sent the enemy around him scattering like dandelion seeds blown by the wind. He was throwing spells too.
So was the Archmage of Izril. She and several [Mages], including the Mage Runner, Salamani, and Magus Grimalkin, were launching spells skywards into the Drakes. There were fires blooming around one section of the battlefield as well; the Knights of Solstice were burning down the light-soldiers, refusing to yield before the forces trying to overwhelm the eastern flank and get around the defenders.
Lines in the sand. Magic from above. But reinforcements?
Not many of them. They kept coming from Celum, yes. Golems marching from the Terland’s holdings, even running south at such speed they made it to the battlefield. [Assassins]—yes, [Assassins], including one who managed to behead a Purifier as it lumbered down on the Drakes.
But where was Pallass? Where were the other forces?
Too slow to react. Too unaware; there was no 2nd Army to mobilize, and 1st Army had standing orders to guard the City of Inventions. [Wyvern Riders] were flying from Salazsar and Manus, but they would take too long.
They’d have to teleport in, if that was even possible, and there was only one force in the world who could do that, or at least, advertised they could.
Wistram Academy had tried it twice. The Archmage of Memories had clearly thought to prove that Wistram was everywhere, and with the Archmage of Izril fighting for her life, he had sent a strikeforce. The ‘Super Soldiers’ armored in enchanted platemail who could fly and [Battlemages]—a squad of thirty.
Enough, by his calculations, to make an impact. What Eldavin hadn’t considered was that Naamreles was a city whose magic was as advanced as his. They knew about teleporting [Mages].
The first squad had appeared inside the largest formation of light-soldiers. Only the [Barrier] spells on the [Mages] had saved them, and even then, half had been dead by the time they fought their way out. Even the Super Soldiers’ magical armor hadn’t saved them from a Purifier. They’d practically retreated off the battlefield, and the Archmage of Memories had tried a second force.
No one but Wistram knew a second attempt had been made. Eldavin still wasn’t sure where they’d gone. So he waited, pacing and cursing, determined not to look worse as shaken [Mages] asked about their friends.
The half-Elf ignored them. He was calculating which nations were sending magic so he could advertise Wistram’s services to them. Make it clear everyone needed long-ranged magic. That these events were only going to continue. Advertising. But he wasn’t sure who was going to win as he saw the western attack finally break.
The forces of Naamreles was making a push down the center now. Climbing over each other to just break that center line. Were they going to make it?
Did he want them to make it? The half-Elf didn’t know. His stomach hurt, but he watched as his advanced scrying spells finally broke through the interference. And he saw a man running to break the column of light-soldiers flooding forwards.
Just a man everyone knew.
 
——
 
It was a light war. Lord Xitegen Terland meant that sort of as a pun, but it was also true.
Dangerous as the Purifiers were, and the light-soldiers of ancient Naamreles, his heart had been pumping harder at the Winter Solstice. Against the Goblin King.
He still had nightmares about that crimson gaze. He still saw the Mortemdefieir Titan in his dreams, and that was why it was hard to be around his family.
They asked him if it was real. If it had happened. The people of Celum were humbler and did not know the north’s splendor. But they believed. And so did Lord Xitegen Terland.
He was younger than he looked, he knew. Most people didn’t believe he wasn’t a decade older, at least. It might have been his levels or stature. Or, more likely, the long siege that had cost him his entire family. It had aged him, the [Healers] said, more than merely physically. He’d had grey in his hair before he was even twenty. Lines that only deepened with the years.
So what? He was alive. Alive, when his parents and household had starved. After the soldiers and staff had starved, then eaten the dead. When one wondered why Lord Xitegen Terland was so high level, so relatively young—
That was why.
He was one of, perhaps, four people in this world to have charged the Goblin King twice. The second was Saliss of Lights. The third was a farmer named Himilt who Lord Xitegen suspected was a ‘Vampire’ that had the north so unsettled. The [Lord] was no fool; it became obvious, despite Erin Solstice’s trick, and rather, in spite of it. The last was Elia Arcsinger.
The Vampire Hunters would know that the val Lischelle-Drakles were Vampires after they had broken every Golem in House Terland, tortured him to death, and animated his corpse since he assumed undead had no concept of honor. A man who had fought the Goblin King twice should not be treated as less than a hero, unless he betrayed all trust—and he should be given all trust.
Now, Lord Xitegen had experienced a lot of unpleasant things since then. Having to team up with Goblins against the Titan. The half-Elf, Tolveilouka, Wall Lord Ilvriss being in the north—
He did not like these things. He did not trust the Drakes or the inn, and this was all Ilvriss’ fault, in a sense. The high point had been the excellent cookout. Xitegen thought of all these things…and he would continue thinking about them when he returned to his mansion, poured himself a light brandy, and sat with a charcuterie board and considered what it meant, what was good and wrong and his part in it all.
But as the light-arrows rained down around him, the [Lord] of House Terland just gazed up. The [Golem-Lord of Enduring Dignity]. Level 49. And he felt it was incredible to be living in these times.
He did not think he entirely deserved his levels. But he had challenged the Goblin King twice. Seen a dead goddess bringing a hundred thousand Draugr to life. Yes, it was a lighter war, despite the desperation. They could always retreat.
So…to speed up his too-calm heart, Xitegen went jogging forwards. He heard someone shout at him, but he had never liked following orders. Even Ulva’s.
His thick thighs carried him across the ground as his running outfit caught the falling lights. A glossier material, light, breathable—he took off his coat. He was wearing running shoes, of course. They just looked vaguely like a nobleman’s since he’d had them polished black.
Ryoka Griffin had once told him he had good running form. Arms moving in sync with his legs; when one rose, the opposite arm rose with it. His hands made blades as he held his fingers straight out, pumping, eyes fixed on the middle distance, over the heads of the soldiers.
“Hold the line! Hold until the tunnels are collapsed—”
Some Drake was telling everyone they were sapping the tunnels, or it might have been done. An end to these reinforcements—but in answer, the light-legions were mounting an offensive. The Purifiers were still gorging themselves and exploding like pimples of rot and ruination.
How beautifully abhorrent. The ground smelled like crap, but Xitegen had good purchase on it, even if he kicked up a bit of soil. When he turned his head and heard the thumping, he saw Controller Lectara running behind him.
A good woman who was piloting a Golem made for that purpose. Armor encased her, and despite the huge weight of the metal frame around her, which turned her into a giant in plate armor like a War Walker, she was running. Sprinting thanks to her new Skills. She’d levelled up well.
What?
Oh…she was calling his name. Xitegen Terland glanced down and realized the ground was moving under his feet at commendable speed.
I’m faster. He slowed and realized that Primera and Seconda were with him, as ever. But the foot-soldiers and Golems were further back. So he turned and jogged in a curve as light arrows hit the ground behind him. Faster. Faster—until his heart was singing.
[Run, Like My Beating Heart].
Such a fanciful Skill for a man of his dignity. But he had to run, didn’t you see? He did not necessarily like being on the side of Drakes. Or playing into this alliance. Or letting his brave people and Golems die here.
But she was there. Standing with the wind blowing in her hair, firing arrows down at the nearest Purifier, next to the Antinium.
Elia Arcsinger.
He hadn’t been wrong about her. She’d just forgotten who she was. All the trust in the world. The Named-rank adventurer was loosing arrows into the mass of soldiers coming at Salazsar’s forces. They were set—but they needed help. So, Xitegen caught his forces.
“With me!”
“[Follow the Standard]! [Raise the Banner of House Terland]!”
Lectara cried, and her armor projected the crest of House Terland over her head. How lovely. Xitegen thought the Golems who saw it moved faster—and he heard Primera’s heart singing.
I’m sorry. He peered at his bodyguard Golem and had so many questions. Then Xitegen ran on the guilt, his queries. The sight of Elia Arcsinger.
Arrows. Some Gnoll copied ten thousand times had seen his forces moving. They were sending more arrows raining down. Even—a light-ballista?
He saw something streaking towards him and ran left. His forces thundered left with him, and the ground exploded in showers of dirt. Now, his arms and legs were pumping. He remembered running at the Goblin King like this. If this wasn’t all a dream he was having as he lay upon the battlements, a child—
To make sure he wasn’t dreaming, he forced more energy into his legs and arms until he was gasping. Until the ground was truly blurring—then he saw the light-Drakes turning. Pivoting as a wing saw his forces coming. Xitegen was running across them. The light-Drakes spun, spears lowered to block his charge—but he just jogged past the spears. Refused to run into a damn line of pikes. He pointed one finger right.
“[Again, Again, and Ever Again]—”
His famous Skill. Shields appeared in the soldiers’ hands, and they raised them skywards. They’d seen his trick. Lovely adaptation. Xitegen stared into the eyes of a long-dead Drake who smiled at him. And Xitegen thought he could hear his weary soul asking for relief.
“[Covering Fire]! [Point-Blank Volley].”
Little holes in the air opened next to Xitegen—and then the arrows loosed. Not from above, but horizontally. A point-blank barrage. Piercing arrows, too.
Upgrades.
The light-soldiers jerked as the arrows hit them. Xitegen kept running as the lines of Drakes began to vanish—then they dropped their shields. So he rained arrows on them from above.
“House Terland, with me!”
He was still running, circling the Drakes, who had to slow and block his formation. But then Controller Lectara fired a [Ray of Incineration] as she ran. Golems unloaded spells as they moved, and Primera tossed a [Greater Force Orb] into the light-Drakes’ formation.
“Lord Terland! Purifier!”
Another one had approached the battlefield. Xitegen gazed up, and he remembered the Hag Queens of Aklat Vunn. He hadn’t been able to challenge them. If he had been the same level…
He was jogging at it when it vanished. Exploded in a shower of muck. Xitegen shielded his face at the smell, then looked down.
“Ah. You.”
So that was where the real Lord Ilvriss was. He had emerged from behind the light-soldiers. Which indicated that they were cut off from reinforcements if the [Major] shouting in Xitegen’s ears was any indication.
Some [Miner] had thrown a pickaxe through the Purifier. That, unfortunately, had just attracted every light-soldiers’ attention, and the Wall Lord was running from more arrows. And spellcasters.
That was really unpleasant to see; another light-Drake, female, with robes, conjuring what looked like [Fireballs] made out of yellow light. It was so unpleasant, in fact, that Lord Xitegen ran into her formation.
“[Full Momentum Kick].”
He saw her turn, and his foot hurt, but the blow blew apart her barriers and the light-mage. The copies of her went down as Primera ripped one’s head off, and his forces were on top of—
“Fall back! Fall back!”
Then they were gone again. And Xitegen was running at the Wall Lord. They locked gazes, and Ilvriss shouted.
“Lord Xitegen—”
“With me! We have to divide them or they’ll overrun us!”
The light-soldiers were getting distracted. Their push against the Salazsar wall was faltering. That was all they needed to do. Divide and conquer. Leave strategy to [Strategists].
It was just that Xitegen’s forces from Celum were maybe a thousand men and Golems because Liska had been able to send no more. They were dead the moment they were surrounded. And here came the light cavalry. Xitegen saw their lances dipping. He swore, out of the corner of his eyes, he saw Ilvriss dance-running next to him.
“Objectively hilarious.”
“Leave the [Riders]! We need to charge the center; they’re going to combine into mini-purifiers and attack!”
That might break the Salazsarian defenders. Xitegen didn’t trust Ilvriss’ precognition that much. But when he turned, eying the center of the light-soldiers’ mass—he saw air glow before the Golem leapt.
Yweine landed, swinging a sword made of magic through the light-Drakes riding horses with long, scaled tails and who looked lizard-like. When they tried to lance her, she turned, pointed a hand forwards, and each claw on her talon rocketed off her hands and fired into the enemy around her.
Then the claw tips detonated. She swung around, and before the rest of the lances could touch her, they exploded in a shower of lightning. Xitegen raised his hand, squinting, and another man was running forwards.
Nerul Gemscale was no born runner. But he led the charge of the Erchirite Spears.
“Nephew! Get out of here!”
Every Erchirite Spear of Salazsar was present—a full battalion of a thousand. Disguised [Miners]—Xitegen saw Ilvriss shouting.
“Uncle, you get out of here! Don’t be a fool—”
“Wall Lord, we are escorting you out of danger. Do not resist.”
Yweine strode forwards, and Xitegen would have loved to talk to her as well. However, Ilvriss was pointing.
“They’re combining! We have to attack! Major Shellc!”
Sure enough, the Drakes were stepping back from the fighting. Walking towards each other, smiling, and forming glowing orbs of light. The orbs were getting bigger, and the first one disgorged a Drake that was twelve feet tall.
Light-soldiers able to break the enemy lines and fight Golems on equal footing. Xitegen hit one with arrows and watched the light implode.
“I concur. Gentlemen—if we nobly charge the foe, we may stop the worst of the casualties and all die. Since there are two Wall Lords here and one of me, I consider it a worthwhile trade. Shall we? Or shall we bravely pretend we were better than doing the right thing?”
Nerul hesitated. He looked to Yweine, whose eyes flickered. A Golem with a spark of light behind them.
“The action is tactically sound. However, I shall escort you and the Wall Lord back—”
She didn’t want to die. Xitegen smiled. He regarded Primera and Seconda and wondered if they wanted to run. But he was a bad man; he didn’t ask.
“I’m with you, Lord Xitegen. Let’s go. Georgie, fall back with the non-combatants.”
Ilvriss snapped at the Drake who’d thrown the pickaxe, and the fellow hesitated. Before anyone could make up their minds, there was a voice.
“You don’t know how to charge the foe, boy. You do it like a drunken [Sailor]. You, Drakes. And you damn cow-riding fools, with me.”
Xitegen turned, and if he had thought his heart leapt to see Elia Arcsinger, it truly beat now. For there she was.
Ulva Terland appeared terribly afraid. She was sitting on her Dais of Health. But she was making it fly forwards as she carried the conductor’s wand. Timekeeper and all her personal Golems were with her—and to the right? Marvus and Aronia Lischelle. He was trying to get his wife to leave, but the [Ranchers] were with him. Even some of the bulls too angry to quit.
“Great Aunt, House Terland cannot afford to lose both its leaders.”
“Quiet, boy. You sound like a coward, and we are many things, but not cowards. Ranchers of the Plains, to me!”
Ulva shouted, and Marvus rode forwards, breathless.
“They’re turnin’ into super-Drakes. If we run into them and can’t get out—”
“Then we die. Or we cut through. Don’t stop or turn. Trust me. I will lead the charge.”
Ulva Terland pointed.
“Wall Lord, you and your spears fire left. Xitegen, behind me. [Ranchers], fire right and do not stop. The Golems will fight; keep moving until we clear the other side!”
She paused, and no one argued with her, though even Xitegen had questions. Ulva turned her head, then shifted around in her seat.
“There’s no Petria. It’s the first battle I’ve faced without her.”
She breathed out, and for a moment, he feared she’d crumble. But then Ulva Terland just gazed down.
“You are no Petria. But I have no other choice. With me. Hearts of Golems, thunder! House Terland, forwards! Create a breach!”
The [Matriarch] of House Terland pointed, and the air split as the first Golem unleashed a beam of flames. Timekeeper followed as her dais sped up, and there was a second—everything froze, and the Golems smashed through the first rank of light-soldiers. Then the second.
She’d gone in so fast even Xitegen was running to catch up. Wall Lord Ilvriss and Nerul Gemscale were running to the left, and Marvus Lischelle was swearing a storm on the right. For a moment, they caught each other’s eyes.
Ilvriss, Nerul, Xitegen, Marvus—all of them approaching that next step or who had begun the climb. Nerul and Xitegen locked eyes and felt it.
It was calling to them. Something beyond anything they knew. Their next level.
It was she who led them forwards, that glorious heroine of House Terland he had always remembered. Ulva Terland pointed.
“Five Families, follow! Forwards, you Golems of flesh and bone! [Awaken, Hearts of Izril].”
His heart—! Xitegen felt himself speeding up as it thundered, louder and more furiously than he had ever known. He was running, sending arrows flying left and right—and he saw green flames bursting along Salazsar’s lines.
The Order of Solstice. Salazsar was counter-charging. But Ulva—
The giant light-soldiers were forming. Trying to halt the advance. It was stalling. Timekeeper slammed into a giant Drake and was fighting, punching. The other Terland Golems grappled with their foe.
“The Doom of Naamreles will end.”
“To the Matriarch.”
“Bear witness.”
Voices without inflection that still conveyed something. A Steel Wargolem bringing down a bladed elbow into a light-soldier’s head. A Golem shaped like a Gnoll stumbling as a warhammer was brought down on its shoulder.
A desperate [Rancher] lassoing one of the light-soldiers, pulling it back to keep it from mincing one of the Erchirite Spears. Xitegen kept running, seeing it all. And then he saw Ulva Terland’s dais go crashing down.
“Great Aunt—”
A light-soldier had knocked it down. Xitegen was charging at it as Ulva arose, blood running down from her forehead. She pointed the conductor’s wand up, fearlessly, waving it like she were still hearing a song.
“[To Me, Servants of My Proud House].”
She spoke, and the light-soldier thrust down at her. But it hit Lord Xitegen, and he landed on the ground as the spear overloaded his protection charms. Seared his flesh and bones.
I’ll live.
He was trying to get up, to grab Ulva Terland, when he wondered where those helpful Golems were. He didn’t see a lovely reinforcement. The giant light-soldier was glancing around for some, too. It turned—and looked up.
And up.
And up—until the largest Golem in all of Izril, the Light of the North, struck the ground with a fist. The earth quaked. Then it paused.
“LA-DY TER-LAND. ARE Y-OU WE-LL—”
It spoke, and Ulva Terland shouted.
“Light of the North, destroy every light-soldier!”
The Golem paused as light-soldiers milled around it, attacking its gigantic frame. It ignored them and regarded a Purifier, which stared up at the Golem. The great Golem opened its mouth, and Xitegen jerked his head away.
The beam of light blew a hole through the Purifier and two more. Then the Light of the North rose and was sweeping its arms around. Smashing Drakes flat.
“Keep moving! Out the other side!”
Ulva Terland’s words made the [Ranchers], Drakes, and even lesser Golems and men and women remember they were in the middle of battle. She rose and sat on the only vehicle she had left: Timekeeper’s shoulders. She pointed, and Xitegen began running again. Until they breached the other side.
Even then, the fighting didn’t end. But the light-soldiers were dwindling. Xitegen kept running until the last glowing form had vanished, and the Purifiers began flickering out as the Light of the North walked towards them.
It was not over, of course. But he did stop and drink some water Seconda handed him. Then…he saw the [Princess] running to hug Ilvriss and wondered who that Duke was, the one from Ailendamus.
He’d sworn he’d seen the fellow punching out an entire company of Drakes bare-handed. But the Lord of House Terland just decided to ask questions later. He did the only thing one did.
He made sure the wounded, Golems and people, were being seen to. Walked over to greet Elia Arcsinger. Made sure Farmer Himilt’s wife was well as she and her sister embraced and went about the difficult task of tending to the wounded and dead.
Then he went to check on his aunt.
 
——
 
That night, the television networks picked up on a story they weren’t really sure how to relate.
Er…armies of light-constructs attack in the Cowpat Plains! Which is really the name of the place! A Walled City dug up beneath our very feet, but halted, if temporarily, by an alliance of Salazsar, House Terland, [Ranchers], and—is someone smoking Dreamleaf?
It was already a crazy story, but one you could get behind—if you’d seen it. And surely someone had recorded it, but the copies were strangely hard to get ahold of.
None were coming from Salazsar despite eyewitnesses swearing up and down that they’d seen them. When someone had offered to sell Pallass News Network a copy, the bill had come to Sir Relz’s desk.
70,000 gold pieces to the care of House Reinhart. For half the recording.
He…was almost tempted to pay for it after having to sit in front of a camera and try to get answers. No one in the region was answering, and it wasn’t like the place was replete with Mage’s Guilds!
And someone was blocking scrying spells to the entire region. Which was fine. Just send a [Mage] from Pallass to the spot, right?
…Only the [Doorgnoll] claimed there wasn’t an exit point there. The [Mages] insisted she was lying, but she refused to open the door, and Sir Relz just gave up and hired a Magical Carriage instead.
When he finally got a [Mage] over there, the carriage never got to the site of the fighting. Instead, it was stopped by a [Lady] and a patrol of Golems.
The [Lady] had a glowing Golem’s Heart, and she introduced herself as Prithna Terland and informed Wistram News Network that the area was off-limits.
“By the authority of House Terland, this region has been sealed off.”
“But we’re the news—”
A Golem swung down a giant sword, and the news team backed up. The young woman smiled sweetly at them. Her heart…pulsed, and Sir Relz saw her gaze into the scrying orb.
“Please speak to Lady Ulva Terland or a representative of House Terland.”
“Miss, that is to say, Lady Prithna, we are Wistram News Network and representatives of Pallass.”
Her face never changed.
“And we are House Terland. Cross this line and you will be neutralized. By Golems.”
So that meant Sir Relz had to interview eyewitnesses raving about Drakes made of light appearing everywhere. A very entertaining Mayor Bootsy gave the best account, but when she said she was going back, she undercut the danger.
“Wait, back?”
“‘Sright, fancy newsman. It’s my home. Plus, I reckon there’s more call for us. Them Terlands are settlin’ down, and the damn Salazsarians are digging. Reckon we’ll bill ‘em for trauma and insist on walls, but I smell a fortune. And if there’s new boots down there, Mayor Bootsy will be wearing them!”
“Down where?”
She developed a twinkle-eyed smile and spat through a gap in her teeth.
“Can’t say.”

No one wanted to say. Even the miners who’d fled just got shifty-eyed and said ‘terrible thing, nearly died, but I guess I’ll be back to work. For the, uh, incentives.’
Naturally, everyone smelled a rat. But when the other Five Families politely inquired about the situation—did House Terland need help? Happy to send a few Named-ranks or a regiment, what’s with our lighthouse walking off—they ran into Ulva Terland.
Ulva Terland ignored everyone except for Deilan El and Magnolia Reinhart. She gave those two some time as they were heads of their families, but steadfastly refused to let anyone approach, even nobles.
The few who tried were sent back with a salve for the bumps on their heads. And spanked backsides. When an outraged conclave of Wellfar’s Admiralty demanded answers, her rejoinder was simple.
“If we need help, I’ll ask for it. We have it under control. I didn’t see you lot down there.”
“Down where? Lady Ulva, what is going on?”
And have you dug up a Walled City? The Wellfars were all glancing at each other. But the ones old enough to know Ulva Terland, the Ulva Terland of old, had a sinking feeling in their stomach. Ulva just grunted.
“I’m sure someone will have explanations at some point. I have to go.”
Golems were striding around behind her, their hearts beating. That told the Wellfars something. When one caught sight of Wall Lord Ilvriss running across the plains and hugging a little white Gnoll and swinging her around, then hugging a [Princess] and an Antinium—well, they did check their drinks for Dreamleaf too.
One of the oldest of Wellfar’s [Lords] raised a hand. Captain Adamaze looked Ulva in the eyes.
“Ulva. Tell me one thing. Was what we heard the Golems saying real? If it is a Walled City—really?”
His voice cracked with disbelief. The Admiralty leaned forwards, and Ulva Terland considered the question. Then she leaned forwards too, and her face of stone seemed to come alive.
“It was as real as the Winter Solstice.”
She cut the call on that. Belatedly, House Wellfar realized it might be further out of the loop than it wanted to be.

The deal was simple. Not that there was a written deal; Nerul was working on it, but it’d be the work of months, if not longer.
But Ilvriss had hopes. Now they’d found the City of Purity. All they had to do was, uh, re-dig it out.
They’d buried it pretty damn well with the Advance Miners’ help, but the [Miners] speculated that it was only a matter of time before the constructs got out, with that many of them. Even if they didn’t know how to dig for shit.
By the time they emerged, Salazsar would have real Gem Regiments ready for combat and specialized weaponry. Ilvriss was calling in everything he could, and the Sons and Daughters of the Wall had unanimously voted to send him reinforcements.
Even if they were hopping mad about the other unofficial part of the deal. Which was that whatever House Terland, the [Ranchers], or any of the interested parties found, they kept.
Oh, there might be a division of spoils, shares of the items, but more than one [Soldier] was swinging around a looted blade this night—as Enchanter Hedault politely screamed at them not to do that before he’d appraised them.
Keep what you take. Ilvriss had told them it was the only thing that kept Ulva Terland from killing them all.
Frankly, he wasn’t sure she wouldn’t try something, but the [Matriarch] seemed willing to admit that the City of Purity might be too hard for House Terland to take on alone. So, she, Marvus, and Ilvriss were going to sit down and come up with a plan of action.
For conquering the City of Purity.
No adventurers—unless they were hired. No games or infighting. They went in, they grabbed treasure, they walked out.
It’d probably go bad, but Ilvriss had seen the City of Purity. He sat, sipping a juice drink.
“It’s very…shiny.”
Lyonette just stared at him. Ilvriss ignored her poking him until it hurt too much.
“Ow, ow, stop that! Oh, fine. It’s all reflective surfaces or so it seems. Nothing to, ah, prove purity than seeing one’s reflection in the mirror. It’s actually so damn dazzling that the look we got at it was blinding—but Osthia got inside a building. She says the windows are tinted so you don’t get blinded inside. Predictably, she and her squad looted the place. Even their cups are enchanted.”
Everyone was hanging on his words. Ilvriss saw Georgie bragging about being the [Advance Miner] to all the other miners, who were giving him the time of day despite his personality. Lady Damia was still being tossed up and down by people cheering her—he winced as she finally threw up.
And he laughed. He laughed and sat there, feeling relieved, feeling a great battle ahead of him and risk—dead gods, the risk!—but relieved.
The city was real. Even if it hadn’t been—he glanced at his boots, and they twitched a bit. Lyonette noticed.
“I suppose you’ll have less time, what with all the action here.”
She sighed wistfully, and Ilvriss coughed.
“Actually. It might be pretty slow. We’re not going to risk a breach like that again. There might be a lot of periods of entire boredom. Followed by heart-stopping terror.”
“Oh? How so? Now that you know it’s there…”
She raised her brows, and he clarified.
“Now that we know it’s there, it’ll send waves of soldiers at us nonstop—if we go in the way the security systems remember. But if we find other points and send in Stealth Golems or [Rogues]…we have even more digging to do. It looked like a lot of the city had collapsed, and there’s all those damn filth-monsters. They’ll keep turning into trouble, so we do have to actually deal with the waste at some point.”
It turned out that after all that digging, they needed to do more digging! He sighed. At least they had a framework, and Lady Ulva Terland had Golems. Dead gods, Ilvriss loved Golems.
He was still eyeing Yweine. She had introduced herself, and he’d barely screamed at Nerul about the crazy deal, but Ilvriss had it on his calendar to do sometime this week. For now, he just sat back and laughed.
“Okay, okay. Let’s not talk about all that right now. Who wants a souvenir?”
Nanette Weishart was beaming as Mrsha pinched her nose; the place stank even worse now that the true origin of the smell that had plagued her had come up. Lyonette sighed.
“Ilvriss, come on. I have a hundred thousand questions, and I know you must be exhausted—but your Oldblood form? How does it feel to have wings? And—wait, souvenirs?”
Ilvriss modestly put one hand behind his back and felt at his bag of holding.
“I can see you’re not interested, Lyonette. But as Osthia’s people reminded me, whenever you visit a new city, you take souvenirs. I suppose I’ll let Nanette have the first pick.”
“Wall Lord, thank you so m—”
Nanette put her hands out, and Mrsha and Lyonette shoved her aside. They began to fight as Ilvriss peered around for Hedault. He waved at Bird, who was smiling as she waved back. The inn, triumph, and dead gods, no one he loved had died.
Except Merls. Ilvriss’ head bowed, but then he smiled and put the grief aside. He stood—and wondered, selfishly, what he’d get when he levelled.
He was a Drake, despite everything.

People were signing up for Wall Lord Ilvriss’ company, banging on the doors, asking if they could join up.
He was the talk of Salazsar. A hero who had challenged Sserys’ cursed words. Who’d fought his way through the enemy.
A Wall Lord, the very image of one.
And he had even grown wings. Become an Oldblood. There was a certain kind of traditionalist Drake who read a lot into that.
Wall Lord Zail might have been considered one of those Drakes, but he’d never really cared about Oldblood. The rest? Yes.
He was trembling in his rooms. He’d left Eschowar to scheme with the others. For once, he’d not been in the mood.
Everyone put it down to him being overwrought with relief that his son was alive after all that. And Zail was glad.
However…
His shaking wasn’t from that. It was from nerves. He’d watched the recording of the scrying spells—Salazsar was intercepting the others, and they’d leak eventually, but to his knowledge, this was the only recording of this particular incident and scene.
It wasn’t hard to see why; this scrying spell had been just before Ulva Terland had blocked all scrying spells, and most people had stopped watching after the battle was well and truly over. Zail, who had wanted to see all angles, had kept watching the footage until this had crossed his path.
Nearly three hours after all the fighting had ended, when the real Ilvriss had emerged and the [Princess] had run over to him with the white Gnoll girl, he’d been hugging people, trying to talk to Major Shellc, nothing to really see.
The Wall Lord was grinning, and it was really him; Zail had wondered if the fake Ilvriss was his son, but his son wasn’t good at fistfighting, let alone throws, and he would never have gone into a battle without his sword.
It was just one moment that not even the [Strategists] had paid attention to, yawning as they let Zail inspect the recording. They hadn’t seen him appropriate the memory crystal. So…it might be only he’d seen this.
Zail paused the recording again in his private scrying orb, which he’d been assured by the [Wardmistress] that no one could tap into. He saw the scene play out, rewound it, stopped it.
“There.”
It might be that this was the fake Ilvriss. Somehow. Or—no, he doubted it was faked, but maybe? Would someone have been that subtle? Ulva Terland? It wasn’t beyond her, but surely she’d have made it more obvious. The answer was more likely that it was real. But then…
Wall Lord Zail stared at the frozen image of Ilvriss, who had turned and was hugging an emerald Antinium with wings, beaming with delight.
Bird the Huntress. He was embracing her—just for a moment—before he went to high-five the others. An unguarded moment of…
An Antinium.
Zail vividly recalled Ilvriss being in his study, talking to him the day after Bird the Hunter had appeared on Pallass’ walls. They’d talked. About Bird and the Antinium, and that had led to…
Everything.
Zail rewound the clip. Played it. Stopped it. Went frame-by-frame until he’d burned it into his memory. Then, silently, he got up.
With his reclaimed strength of youth, he crushed the crystal and swept it into the fireplace and mixed it with ash. Then he went to sit.
Sit and think.
