Who else, then, but the man whose potions armed Torreb the Undefeated and have been used by the King of Destruction and other champions of Chandrar?”
His voice was carrying, loud, and Pisces groaned as he saw Yisame’s head turn. Eyes fell on them, and Master Therel was trying to make a scene, clearly. Since there were about six such events a day at least, many elected to go on chattering, but people turned. Pisces began shovelling food into his mouth.
Like hell he was going to deal with whatever came next on an empty stomach. Ceria was rising, an impish smile on her face, and he hoped she didn’t cause trouble. But rather to everyone’s surprise, before Therel could get to them, someone stepped forwards.
“Aye, the Horns of Hammerad and great adventurers should use the services of a master of alchemy! A pity, then, you chose to speak up. I doubt the Silver Killer is looking for a Love Potion. Are you trying to sell her polish for her arms? A Potion of Warmth for the Ice Squirrel? Your best works fit Silver-rankers, Therel!”
The [Alchemist] spun on his heels, face clouding with fury.
“Who dares insult my work—ah. Apprentice Shedrel. Cowering behind your master’s reputation. What, is the great Alchemist of Ten Thousand Trivialities too afraid to face me in person?”
A knife appeared in one of his hands, and he pointed it at the younger Stitch-man, who stood wearing a more ornamental version of Octavia’s clothing. His vest was festooned with pockets which held glowing bottles, and he had on glass goggles on his head. There was even a small pack on one shoulder, clearly there more for the appearance of it; he looked like what you imagined if you thought of Saliss and never met the Drake.
A battle-alchemist, a travelling concocter of magic. Therel, by contrast, was closer to a nobleman in tall boots and a stylish red coat that swept around him. But it was Apprentice Shedrel—who was a full [Alchemist], Pisces guessed, at least Level 30—who sneered back.
“My master, Alchemist Patsiuda, for you Horns of Hammerad, is the Alchemist of Ten Thousand Creations, the best [Alchemist] in Nerrhavia’s Fallen and, dare I claim it, the world! Her creations serve adventurers far and wide. Nor would I stain the floors of the Court of Silks with your blood, which would not be useful in the simplest tonic.”
“I take your words and challenge you to put them against me. My alchemy has melted more than one challenger to dust, and your master is nothing but a rank amateur who was begging at my doorstep a decade past. I turned her away for being a waste of talent!”
Therel motioned with the dagger, and Shedrel sneered more as he yanked a vial out of a holster on his right arm. He raised it.
“My master is in her prime and only avoided your tutelage because she had better uses of her time than jumping into your bed like every apprentice! Such as surpassing you, Therel. Look. Here I hold one of her creations: the Elixir of Gorgon’s Form.”
He uncorked it with one thumb and drank it—and his form shifted. Pisces blinked, and a Gorgon rose over Therel, scales flashing. His clothing fell to the ground, and Ceria whistled.
“Whoa. I’ve seen Saliss do that, but that’s top-tier alchemy.”
“Alchemist Patsiuda is considered the best. She has dozens of apprentices. Therel…”
Delitandra’s voice was a bit too loud. Therel flushed.
“You think a simple polymorph potion makes you dangerous, boy? Let us dance.”
He seemed ready to fight, and Pisces recalled that [Alchemists] were known to fight in the very streets. Octavia had talked about going over to beat another [Alchemist]’s brains out for a slight; he’d thought it was hyperbole.
Not so. But Shedrel flicked a second vial into his clawed hands and hissed.
“I would hate to kill you before Her Majesty’s eyes. But if I must—here is a Vial of Molten Snakes my master herself brewed. Liquid lava that hunts. It can kill any three Manticores you name before it expires. And what do you have, Therel? A Potion of Burning Rays? It won’t even scratch my scales.”
It was faint, but Pisces thought he saw Therel lick his lips. Colth agreed. He whispered.
“Lot of magic in that vial. This apprentice came to play. And Gorgons are resistant to spells. He came with a counter.”
There was some kind of rhythm to this, though. It wasn’t a pure street fight, Pisces realized. The murmuring voices died down as music rose. The court musicians were playing? Therel strutted right, circling the Gorgon. He brushed at his robes. And his voice took on a different cadence. Faster? He spoke past Shedrel, to the crowd as much as the apprentice.
“Boy—you aren’t the first, you won’t be the last. I’ll melt you in the time it takes to wipe my ass. I’ve seen the best, and your master isn’t even close—do you know how I know? She isn’t here. She’s sent you and a bag full of tricks. How rich. You’re nothing in my eyes. Not a surprise. You don’t have a chance, so I will let you walk away. Go home, boy, find the other no-namers, second-rates, and play. Not here, not in Tyrant’s Rest. You stand before me, Therel the Incandescent, best of the best.”
He whirled the dagger around his fingers, and the one vial became five, held between his fingers, each a different color and type, and he was nodding to the right and left, a confident smile on his face. Pisces—blinked.
Was that poetry? It was close, and he saw Delitandra and the Heromakers nodding along. A murmur of approval rose, but everyone was clearly waiting for Shedrel. The Gorgon had listened impassively to Therel, and now he lowered the vial in his hands. Tossed them down to murmurs. Therel wavered, and tensed—but he hesitated, and then Shedrel replied.
“Old man. It makes me sad to see you here, all filled with fear. Do you think my master’s hidden away? She’s just too busy, sad to say. Busy making alchemy for all the adventurers who’ve come to call. Who’s at your shop? No one at all. Not [Beggars] on the streets. No mistresses between your sheets—and oh, your poetry puts every courtesan I know to sleep. You’re washed and out of date. You’ve come here for attention—too little, too late. If you want me to put your sad reputation to rest? I can. But don’t do that. Don’t play to be the best. You’re not. For your sake, old man, walk away. Live, tail between your legs, another day. Go pretend you’ve got another camel to chase. That’s my piety towards the old. I rest my case.”
He bowed, then held up his claws as he slithered about, showing everyone he had no vials. He didn’t need any. Therel’s face reddened, and when Shedrel turned to face him, it went silent. Dead silent.
He’s going to throw and fight. Or…Pisces was tensed. He didn’t know if the next thing he’d see would be explosions until there was a pounding sound. The throne.
Neither Yisame nor her interpreter spoke, but a lesser member of her circle.
“Her Imperial Majesty is not inclined to see one of Nerrhavia Fallen’s finest [Alchemists] melted upon her courts. If the [Alchemists] declaim they are the finest, let them provide their services to the brave adventurers here.”
Instantly, both [Alchemists] bowed, and there was a sigh. A relaxation.
No duel. Instead, Shedrel shed his form and emerged, a nude Stitch-man who stood behind a towel, dressing himself swiftly as people came over to applaud him or ask about his vials. Therel stepped away, throwing his head back to laugh in Shedrel’s direction, then to speak to someone he knew, slapping a back, acting confident. But Pisces eyed the larger crowd around Shedrel and knew who’d won that.
Colth agreed.
“Bad look. The moment the apprentice faced down Therel, he lost. Even if he won, he just beat his opponent’s apprentice, and if he had fought for his life, that would prove he was weak. Plus, Shedrel had him dead to rights. Yisame saved him from losing face. He might have even signalled someone he needed a favor.”
“I liked that. What was that? The speaking-poetry.”
Yvlon was tilting her head, more intrigued by the wordplay. Delitandra smiled.
“Verbal sparring before the knives fly. Common in Nerrhavia’s Fallen. You’ve truly never heard the like?”
“I have. It’s rapping. Or close enough.”
Elena was familiar with it, of course. Earthers seemed to have an example of everything. Pisces just waited for either [Alchemist] to approach, but they were playing to their bases.
“Do we not get free samples of alchemy?”
He was disappointed when Delitandra favored him with a shake of the head.
“It would make it seem as if Therel were scurrying over to us, and Shedrel would very much like us to come to him. There are other adventurers in the room; they will go secure their favor first.”
“But free potions—”
“We can just buy them, Sniffmaster Pisces.”
“But free, Colth.”
The [Supporter] patted Pisces on the shoulder. Pisces knew that his team had money, but he hated the idea of wasting potions. Magic was free, and once you used a potion, that was it. He was mostly familiar with mana, healing, and stamina potions. Did they need alchemy? He knew Colth would take them if no one else, and Ksmvr loved alchemy.
But not every adventurer subscribed to Pisces’ model of fiscal responsibility. In fact, a team practically charged Shedrel, shoving people aside, and he met them with open arms.
“Ah, the redoubtable Conquerors of Rameid! What brings the northern giants of Gold-rank adventuring so far south?”
Ceria’s head turned, and Yvlon closed her eyes. Then a loud voice cut over the babble.
“Why, we were invited, of course. We heard a fellow Gold-rank team were making a splash, and we thought we’d show them what real Chandrarian adventuring was like.”
“Ah. And there’s the competition. I blame you for this, Yvlon.”
Ceria stuck a fork into a burrito and began to munch. Yvlon herself sighed. Pisces eyed her.
“You know them?”
The Conquerors of Rameid were a four-person team who were mixed Stitch-folk and Human. Yvlon shrugged.
“They were in Medain, and I don’t think they took to me. Perric used them to get us to go back to the capital. Apparently, they conquered Medain’s biggest dungeon? How did they get here?”
“Doubtless, someone’s decided to counter Yisame’s new pet adventuring team with their own. They’re not the only adventurers in the room. Heads up. They’re going to start something. Yvlon, don’t play into their games.”
Raava, the Stitch-woman who was speaking, was clearly the captain of the Conquerors. She was haggling for Shedrel’s potion and glancing at the Horns.
Rather to her displeasure, all the Horns were eating. Pisces watched as Therel slunk around the room, searching for other adventurers. There were clearly a few allowed in the Court of Silks, but Therel definitely was on the outs.
“I wonder what Saliss would say about all of these [Alchemists]. He studied here.”
“Think he ever did that poetry-duelling?”
Ceria smiled, trying to imagine it. Pisces shuddered.
“If he did, I pity the fools who went up against him. No wonder he’s so good at dodging. So what’s this about Yisame’s quest?”
“Oh, that. She’s going to tell us she put up a request in the Adventurer’s Guild. As a <Quest>, no less.”
He brightened up immediately.
“Aha! A <Quest>? We haven’t done one of those in a while! All of ours were rather fraught too; a lower-stakes one would be welcome indeed. Excellent! Elena, do you want to come with us?”
“Uh…how deadly is it? I can definitely stay in the palace, and if there are monsters anywhere around, with respect, I don’t really want to risk it. I’ve been in danger, but I don’t exactly have the Skills or reflexes to survive if things get bad.”
“See? That’s sensible. That’s why I like her.”
Colth pointed at Elena and handed some sauce over. Delitandra cleared her throat.
“We are able to both record your deeds and hold our own, Adventurer Colth—”
“You’re not invited.”
“Ah.”
Out of the corner of his eyes, Pisces saw Alchemist Therel moving around the room, greeting people he knew, trying to engage the more powerful people in conversation. He didn’t seem to have much luck, or they just didn’t need his alchemy. Which—fair. You didn’t need alchemy all the time, especially given how much it probably cost.
Therel stopped just once, though, as a huge trailing mass of robes swept out of the Court of Silks. The Mage of Falling Skies had no time, it appeared, for anything here. Everyone got out of his way, but he halted, just once.
Nodded to Therel, who turned, spoke to him with a weak half-smile. The Mage of Falling Skies moved on, and Therel kept circulating. That was all Pisces noted.
Well, that and every adventurer in the room not really liking his team. The Conquerors of Rameid were extolling their exploits and mentioning how a certain team was wanted back in Medain, only saved from wrath because they were the High King’s brides.
Yvlon seemed to have genuinely not heard a word they said…she was poking at a fried scorpion with more nerves than Pisces had seen in her the entire trip, and Ceria kept daring her to take a bite. But then Ceria glanced around.
“Hey, another Gold-rank team. There. See that trio? What’ve we done to them?”
A trio of adventurers were being fêted at another table, if less grandly than the Horns. Pisces turned and saw three Humans looking his way. Two were quite tanned; the third had naturally dark skin. Two young men, one young woman. One of the two young men had dark black hair dyed white, like a slash across his hair; the other was blonde and eating with a will. It was the young woman who was glaring. She had on robes, and Pisces identified her as a [Mage].
“Beats me. More competition? I don’t recognize them.”
Colth squinted, and Ceria got up.
“Let me see if I can tweak the Conquerors’ noses. I’m gonna play nice. Anyone want to say hi?”
Colth, Yvlon, and Pisces got up at once. They walked towards them as Ceria bounded over.
“Another Gold-rank team! Hello! I’m Captain Ceria of the Horns of Hammerad, and you are?”
The other adventurers got up—except the young woman, who folded her arms and glared. The one with blonde hair held out a hand, and Pisces noted he had a [Warrior]’s build. Muscled, in short. Though he had on far lighter armor than Pisces would have thought. A light shirt and pants, showing bare legs and arms instead of Colth’s all-leather gear.
“Oh, er, hello. We’re the Wildcards. A Gold-rank team, like yours. We just got made Gold-ranks, actually. We were invited to the capital, and it’s our first time in the exalted Court of Silks. I’m Leo, and this is Kusal. And Lareceina—Lareceina, say hello.”
He nudged the scowling [Mage], but she refused to even get up when Ceria shook her teammates’ hands.
“I’m not shaking hands with a murderer. I will greet the rest of you. Colthei the Supporter, Yvlon Byres, the Silver Killer, Pisces the Bane.”
She nodded at them, and two of the Horns flushed at their silly names. Leo nudged Lareceina.
“Come on, Lareceina—they’re famous. From Izril?”
“And who’d I murder?”
Ceria wanted to know. Lareceina’s eyes flashed.
“The Champion of Monarchs? And the Master of the Coliseum! I’m surprised you all haven’t been assassinated yet. We can’t be too friendly with them, Leonardo. They’re part of the Queen’s faction, and she’s a cold-blooded killer.”
“Hey. I prefer ‘adventurer’. It’s a catchall term.”
Ceria’s voice was mild and untroubled in the face of the hostility. Pisces cleared his throat.
“We appear to have gotten off on the wrong foot. We just wished to greet fellow Gold-rankers. We haven’t met any in Chandrar before.”
Leo and Kusal were flustered, and Leo nudged Lareceina with his elbow.
“Absolutely. We don’t want to start anything. Lareceina, chill.”
“Well, we just wanted to say hi, but if your teammate doesn’t want to talk, maybe after she’s calmed down? I only murdered the guy yesterday. And he was gonna come for us.”
Ceria decided to disengage and motioned her team back. The Wildcards sat, but Lareceina called out.
“Watch your backs. No, that’s not a threat from me, Kusal. You cannot just go around murdering—”
They started arguing, and Pisces shook his head.
“Oh delightful Captain of mine, does it ever occur to you that we don’t have many friends among other adventurers?”
“We don’t know many teams, Pisces. But yeah…and the ones we do know are dead or on another continent. Fine. I take responsibility for that one. See anyone else who won’t jump down our throats?”
Ceria was casting around for another team they could at least say hi to. Pisces thought he saw other Gold-rankers, but it might have been they were bodyguards or just…independent. They were making their way back to their table when Colth’s head turned.
“Conquerors coming up. Yvlon—”
He flanked her as Pisces took her other side. The Silver Killer protested.
“I’m not going to murder them. They can’t be as annoying as Perric. Ceria, show them Perric’s crown.”
“Oh, good idea!”
Then Pisces and Colth were grabbing at Ceria as Raava stalked forwards with a crowd clearly hoping for more drama. He grabbed for Ceria, sneezed—and then whirled. So did Colth. Yvlon stopped walking towards Raava with her hand outstretched. She and Ceria turned and stared right with the rest of their team.
Pisces’ nose seemed to be acting as a detector of levels or things he found important. Which he wasn’t sure he liked. But unlike Beton—or the Mage of Falling Skies, who’d hidden his presence—this time, Pisces felt like something was physically attracting his attention.
Like gravity magic. When his eyes alighted on the figure who had just entered the Court of Silks, it felt like an explosion going off on his head. It was like a song.
“Who’s—that?”
Ceria rubbed her eyes and laughed, but her eyes flicked towards Pisces, Colth, and Yvlon, and the [Silversteel Armsmistress] began walking.
“She’s strong.”
“I think—I know her too. So the rumors were true. Heads up. That’s a monster, no matter how she looks.”
The Conquerors of Rameid saw the Horns instantly pivot and walk past them. And correspondingly—the Heromakers of Hraace leaned out of their booth and leapt up. Which made Elena glance up, and the attention that focused on the newcomer reflected off her. Interested people turned and grew disappointed instantly.
The smarter ones, like Prince Zenol, knew better than to judge by appearances. And when he peered around, Barelle the Bard smiled, just once, opened a little book, and produced a quill.
A strange adventurer had come to the Court of Silks, even by their standards. Because she didn’t look right.
It was like a midwife or mother had put on somewhat-damaged chainmail over enchanted leather armor and paid for the biggest club she could carry. It was nearly as tall as she was, and she rested it on the ground as she surveyed the room. That was the contradiction.
Everything in Pisces said she was high-level and dangerous. But she appeared almost homely. Her clothes? Cotton, he thought, and she could have been a Human mother in Liscor but for her equipment.
“Who is that?”
Colth didn’t need to answer. The [Herald], who announced people to the Court of Silks, was surprised by the sudden hush in the usually raucous room that ignored him. He cleared his throat, then spoke.
“Presenting, the Gold-rank adventurer! The only woman to attain Gold-rank the moment she became an adventurer in three decades since Mars the Illusionist herself—the daughter of Chandrar’s greatest [Warrior]! Itkisa!”
Torreb’s daughter? As in Torreb the Undefeated? Ceria’s eyes slid to Colth.
“Isn’t he dead? At Pomle?”
“That’s right. His daughter. I heard a rumor she was strong. Of all his offspring, though, she never adventured. Never made a name for herself, and he has sons who’ve become Gold-rankers and [Generals]. But she—”
“She’s Level 40, isn’t she?”
Pisces saw the woman’s head turning, and Itkisa paused to bow to the throne. Then she nodded at Barelle and got a nod back. She was poised, despite the disappointed murmurs. A lot of the Court of Silks just saw her appearance, but Pisces remembered how blown away everyone, even Yvlon, had been at the celebrations.
The Court of Silks might not have been celebrating, but all this attention struck Itkisa, and she just stood there. When someone offered her a drink, she waved it away. Ceria squinted at the woman, confused.
“Her gear…it sucks. That’s a lot of damaged equipment. I don’t think that club has anything beyond a basic protection spell on it. Wasn’t Torreb rich?”
Colth scratched at his chin.
“He had a lot of offspring. She might not have gotten much. Where’s his famous club?”
Delitandra leaned over, eyes alight with interest as she also studied Itkisa.
“Vanished, the rumor goes. Along with his body. She was there when he died. They said Torreb died rather than fight the Strongest of Pomle. Well, well.”
The Horns of Hammerad saw Itkisa step forwards, after a moment, and greet Alchemist Therel, who had found her with a smile and, Pisces noted with jealousy, a free potion. She smiled at him and seemed to know him. Following his example, people who had known Torreb chose to greet the woman.
“So that’s the competition. Think someone called her up to make a point?”
Ceria glanced around airily, then chose to go back to her seat. Yvlon hesitated.
“Aren’t you going to greet her?”
“Nah. I think she doesn’t like us. She seems like she’s spoiling for a fight.”
She does? Pisces eyed the calm woman who’d only glanced their way once, but Colth grunted.
“She is, isn’t she? Maybe she thinks she’ll make a name for herself if she punches Yvlon. I’d do it if I wanted attention.”
“Colth, some may call me the Silver Killer, but the truth is I’m hardly so famous—”
Laughter. The Horns sat back down as Elena listened to an explanation of who Itkisa was.
“Wow, so she’s got to be one of the older adventurers.”
“You get some like Typhenous, but it’s true she’s past the age most would retire.”
“What a queen. I respect that.”
Elena said the oddest things, but Pisces just sat back. Indeed, the [Herald] was calling out all the teams in the room now. Reminding the Court of Silks how many adventuring teams there were in case someone wanted their services.
“—the Conquerors of Rameid, known for taking on the dungeon of Rameid, the Carpetriders of Thistob, mourning two of their own lost in a terrible crash, the Singing Stingers of Scaied, and, an achievement among any adventurers, a team who has earned the recognition of Rhir! Hell’s Wardens!”
Raava and her team stopped waving around and developed a scowl. Ceria beamed at Raava, and Pisces blushed and groaned.
“Does it really make that much of a difference?”
“Adult Crelers are Adult Crelers, Pisces. Even Gold-rankers hesitate when they appear, and we’ve all killed one. It’s how you know a real adventurer, even among Golds.”
Colthei’s voice was a bit too carrying and loud, and he definitely did that on purpose. Pisces peered around. Ceria and Colth were not above needling the Conquerors, and Yvlon just did it accidentally.
“I’m sure the other Gold-rank teams could do the same, Colth. Most of them.”
They rose to their feet as people applauded the famous title and deed. Pisces saw Ceria waving, blowing kisses, and then a confused sound. The clapping slowed—then there was laughter, cheering, and Pisces blinked. Because a second team had gotten to their feet and seemed as surprised as him. Even the [Queen] appeared shocked as she peered from behind her veil.
The Horns of the Hammerad were standing—and so were Wildcard. The [Herald] continued shouting.
“Two teams have achieved this great title! The Horns of Hammerad, Gold-rank adventurers and a Named-rank adventurer who hail from distant Izril, and Wildcard, a team newly elevated to Gold-rank for their slaying of an adult Creler! They also mourn their late comrade Adventurer Justine, fallen in battle against the scourge of Rhir! Hell’s Wardens!”
Pisces stared at the trio, who gave his team a second look. They sat, and Pisces nodded at the trio. They’d lost a teammate? After a moment, they nodded back, and Colth cracked his fingers.
“Not bad. At least one team has guts. So—which teams are going to try and get in our way for this big quest?”
Pisces sighed and remembered Beton’s warning.
The tangle of politics had begun. In his adventures, no less.
 
——
 
Queen Yisame always enjoyed seeing the Horns in her palace. She just wished she could be with them, not on her throne, listening in via its powerful spells.
Then again, she might be so tongue-tied as to not say anything. The position of the reader, the observer, the fan of the Horns was to let them act as they willed and just be part of the audience.
That was what she told herself as she held court, paying some interest to the machinations going on around her, but listening into the Horns, thinking up story beats for her next literary work. She’d been published four times so far, and her credibility as a [Writer] was rising. Heartslayi, damn her, was still more popular, but there was a lot of appeal to Sandquen’s ‘realistic storytelling of the Horns of Hammerad’. That was a review she’d framed in her secret rooms.
Of course, Etrikah would have lectured her about balancing things, but Yisame was happy. She was allowed to be happy, and so what if the Horns caused trouble?
They’d arguably helped her more than not by killing one of her rivals and backing Zenol. Adventurers were a different kind of game in Nerrhavia’s Fallen. By backing the Horns, Yisame benefited when they did well, and she suffered a bit less for their foibles; everyone knew adventurers were crazy.
That didn’t mean all was perfect, though. What the Horns didn’t realize was that there was a substantive group in the Court of Silks who were unhappy today, as they had been yesterday and all week.
That would be the, ah, ah, members of the court who had a personal attendant or bodyguard who had been instructed to refrain from entering the Court of Silks with their usual entourage. Or the palace.
[Slaves]. Yisame had personally told her Chamberlain of the Palace to move them away from any conceivable wing that the Horns—especially Pisces—might venture into. Similarly, she had made it clear through lesser channels what was not acceptable in the Court of Silks at this moment.
It wasn’t a royal proclamation. That was far too obvious for this. She just instructed the Voice, who said it in the hearing of servants, who reported it to their masters, and word spread in subtle ways such that few, if any, in the Court of Silks turned up with a personal [Slave].
Naturally, they weren’t happy about that, but Pisces’ reputation as the Bane of Roshal helped. No one wanted to risk an accident. As for the rest? Yisame wanted him to be comfortable, so what were a few favors to her team?
They had done so well at the Coliseum. An adventure worthy of them. She couldn’t wait to see how the Tomb went. True, it was more political than their regular adventures, but it would be a useful boon for them to act, and the other teams…
Yisame actually had Itkisa, Torreb’s daughter, approach her and introduce herself. She said nothing of course; her Voice greeted the woman distantly, as befit a mere Gold-rank adventurer. Yisame tried to see some of the legend of Torreb in Itkisa, but the woman was distressingly plain, and she didn’t have Torreb’s famous club. Ah, well…it was hard for anyone to match the Horns save maybe a Named-rank team.
She did get a thrill when they approached her throne and Ceria accepted her quest on behalf of them. Yisame tried not to show Yvlon any signs of favor, but it was hard—she smiled, wondering if they were enjoying themselves here, in the heart of Nerrhavia Fallen’s luxuries. She hadn’t heard of them availing themselves of any of the more exotic luxuries one could ask for, but perhaps they just had no interest in that.
The Adamantium Bathhouse did get tiring after you’d seen it a few times, and she didn’t care for the menagerie much herself, even with the new magical beasts. Going to the library—there was an adventuring team after her heart. Far better than the Fall of Nerrhavia’s, that eyesore of a hallway a hundred thousand paces long.
 
——
 
The pronouncement of Queen Yisame telling the Horns to take on a quest and the rest of the palace was a bit more tiresome after that, and without great note to Pisces. He could have too much of fame and attention, so the Adventurer’s Guild was the only highlight to him.
Tyrant’s Rest had a proper Adventurer’s Guild on par with Invrisil’s. Bigger, Pisces dared say, though he had never seen First Landing’s.
It was massive, and so many teams were inside who wanted to talk to the Horns he promptly cast [Invisibility]. Unfortunately, that had [Mages] coming up to him.
The worst part was that many were friendly, if wary.
“Bane, a word? I don’t own [Slaves]—”
What a curious way to greet him. But Pisces realized the teams were different from Invrisil’s in one huge way: none of them cared he was a [Necromancer]. Unlike the memorable Captain Todi and their brief stint in Invrisil, he ended up shaking hands with several [Mages].
“You’re an [Illusionist]? Truly?”
A Stitch-girl who wore a [Fool]’s outfit juggled knives which were all fake.
“That’s right. My entire method is baiting monsters into traps while my team skewers them. I can’t imagine fighting and casting. How do you manage it?”
“Er…practice?”
“Truly? Most battle-casters can’t use a weapon. They have to be [Spellblades]!”
Pisces hesitated. When you mentioned it…he shrugged.
“I was raised as a child to keep focus while dueling. I had to practice to use magic and the sword.”
His father had certainly beaten it into him, and Feren, the highest-level [Necromancer] Pisces had known, had taught him to cast and fight. Another [Mage] who had graduated from the Academy of a Hundred Thousand Tomes sighed.
“Interesting. I do some fighting, but only after I use my mana. [Summoner]. I’d love to pit my spirits against your undead. There are plenty of [Summoners] in Chandrar; I know some [Necromancers], but it fell out of style after Az’kerash. Plus, cloth is harder to animate than other bodies.”
Fell out of style. Pisces swallowed his disbelief.
“I might not have time for that depending on how long we’re here—but why summoning?”
The [Summoner]’s name was Asmal. He showed Pisces a set of amber crystal preserving pieces. A bit of a sword, a tooth—Pisces had seen Revi’s gear, and he was familiar with it.
“Naturally, naturally. Summoning relies on pieces of what we want to revive. We need the whole corpse, though, then we take a piece and bind it. It works less well on continents where things rot or mold. But in Chandrar, one can die and become dessicated. And Stitch-folk leave lifethread behind, which is a catalyst.”
“Ah. Quite understandable. What do you prefer? I, er, favor Skeleton Champions these days, and a warbear. We have a Frostmarrow Behemoth, but the mana cost is intensive—”
Asmal had a fascinating array of monsters and even an ‘ancestral spirit’, who used a sword and shield. But he confessed it wasn’t much.
“Two Giant Scorpions and a Silver-ranker fighter that can’t hold off Gold-rank threats. If the Sandworm fails, I’m in trouble. I’d sell my right arm for a good summon.”
He flexed his arm, which was a dusky, even purplish hue. This limb was apparently tuned for fighting; it was made of a strange cloth that turned translucent in the sunlight! Indoors, it was only partially visible. Pisces imagined it’d be hard to see a blow coming, though you could see what Asmal held.
“Lovely cloth. Er, I’ve never thought of Stitch-folk changing their cloth like that. I know a [Summoner], Revi, who has a giant Shield Spider.”
Asmal’s eyes lit up with envy.
“How big? What a catch! If she got the body right away…summons degrade over time. Which is why even a Named-rank’s body might only turn into a Gold-rank’s spirit. But you can summon them forever as long as your crystal isn’t damaged, which is the benefit. Yes, this arm was an investment. Nightmare wool. I had the thought to make my entire body out of it; I’d have to go naked or enchant my clothing to be invisible, but I spent a fortune on this arm!”
He heaved a huge sigh.
“I was investing for another limb, but then Tiqr fell. It comes from there. No more to be had. That’s the problem with adventuring, especially abroad. You need specialized limbs and cloth. Your friend probably doesn’t want to risk having a limb that she can’t repair or maintain.”
“Revi is sensible. So the war with Tiqr has led to shortages?”
Grimaces from the Stitch-folk adventurers around him.
“Too many damn wars. We’re not soldiers, and some of the fools who went to fight Tiqr at the start never came back. Fighting Grand Oliphants is madness. Now we’re wanted for the wars in the north—fat chance against the King of Destruction! Same for Pomle and their [Martial Artists], Illivere’s Golems, or Tiqr. As for the eastern wars…”
“What eastern wars?”
Pisces had utterly forgotten how many conflicts Nerrhavia’s Fallen was invested in. One of the Silver-rankers scoffed.
“Some incident at the Meeting of Tribes. An [Ambassador] with a camel’s asshair for brains slew another. Now the only direction we’re not at war with is the south, and that’s just because there’s nothing there to fight but the sea!”
Everyone laughed. When Pisces asked if anyone was concerned about the number of wars, he got very neutral shrugs.
“We have more armies than sand, Bane. They’ll push the borders, win wars—then give up after enough of our armies strike them. The only true foe is the King of Destruction and—”
The [Summoner] hesitated.
“—He will be defeated like any other foe, of course.”
Well, that was politics. Ceria had to march in to drag Pisces out of the only fun conversation he’d ever had with teams he didn’t know to show him the board.
“Pisces, look at this! Why’d we have to be adventurers before this, huh?”
He regarded the board on the Adventurer’s Guild, and his jaw dropped. Pisces was immediately upset. Mostly because…being an adventurer had never looked more fun. Because, upon the board, each one glowing, the text literally shining different colors?
Were <Quests>.
 
<Rare Quest — Slay a Raging Manticore!>
<Basic Quest — From Githe the [Butcher]: A Prime Cut of Meat!>
<Rare Quest — Undead Horde! Bounties for Skulls! (Do not turn in literal skulls).>
<Rare Quest — Kidnapped: Hithcombe! Rescue him from the [Bandits]!>
<Basic Quest — Escort Duty to the Border!>
 
The rest of the world may have forgotten <Quests> or absorbed them into the cultural zeitgeist, but adventurers?
Adventurers were always doing this job, only now, there was a framework to reward people. Not just reward; the random items and extra experience from <Quests> was a lure. A siren’s song, and Pisces instantly regretted not taking on some casual quests.
Colth dragged him back to reality, though.
“According to the local adventurers, most <Quests> are just ordinary with a few surprises. You don’t get much from a rare quest, other than a nifty trinket or low-grade artifact if you’re lucky. But it also depends on the poster, apparently.”
Yvlon was standing alone; no one wanted to be near the Silver Killer, but her head turned from studying the board.
“Really? How so, Colth?”
His eyes twinkled with great interest.
“Why, a good <Quest> poster has Skills, Yvlon! Larra was complaining about not levelling or having any since she splits her Skills between magic and innkeeping. You can get extra rewards if you have a high-level [Guildmaster] or [Innkeeper]. That’s why Queen Yisame had the quest posted here instead of doing it herself. See?”
Pride of place on the board was a huge, recently-posted quest, and Pisces stared up at it. The other teams were blatantly envious, because it was clearly marked for the Horns. And this one made Pisces’ heart beat.
 
<Heroic Quest — Secure the Tomb of Yad’thuv!>
Limits: The Horns of Hammerad.
By order of Her Majesty, Queen Yisame of Nerrhavia’s Fallen, hear and obey! The Tomb of Yad’thuv has been uncovered, an ancient resting-place of Stitch-folk. This hallowed ground is, no doubt, filled with restless undead, guardian spirits, and traps.
Enter, but do not slay the guardians carelessly; secure the Lifethread of each fallen warrior and ensure the tombs are kept safe. For the ancient warriors of old may become great warriors in service to Nerrhavia Fallen’s [Summoners].
Quest Reward: The favor of Queen Yisame, 12,000 gold pieces, experience in <Adventuring> classes, one lesser artifact of the vaults in Tyrant’s Rest.
Capital’s Reward (Bonus): An item of the Tomb of Yad’thuv.
 
Ceria was the first to finish reading and exclaimed.
“Dead gods! That last part—is that from Yisame?”
A woman leaned over the counter and spoke.
“It is none other than my Skill, Horns of Hammerad. I am Zamielle, [Royal Guildmistress], and my Skill allows me to append greater rewards on suitable quests. By the will of Her Majesty, I have done so. It is a rich reward, is it not?”
An artifact from the vaults and an item of old? Pisces licked his lips and noticed the other teams glancing at him. This was definitely favoritism. But Colth was just rubbing his hands.
“This is a good quest. Not only is it good, old-fashioned dungeon-diving, but we have lots of experience.”
“We do?”
The Horns had actually done Liscor’s dungeon and Albez, and Colth pointed out that some teams had no experience with that, like the Silver Swords. Moreover, as Ceria called for one of Wistram’s Magical Carriages to begin the journey now, he gave more reasons this quest had been posted.
“Summoned spirits are powerful. Even if they degrade over time, the odds are a tomb like that held Named-ranks. Which turn into Gold-rank spirits in life. If we’re lucky, they were already preserved before their death.”
“What? So they processed their dead but sealed them up?”
Ceria frowned, and Colth nodded as the carriage got moving. Yvlon waved at several Bronze-ranks who’d painted their arms silver then almost slammed the door shut—she had fans. The carriage slowed because plenty of people had gathered outside to mob the Horns, but they got moving as guards cleared the streets. The magical carriage effortlessly navigated traffic and then left the city, moving faster and faster. Inside, the seats were comfortable, the air cooled.
The Horns were riding off to adventure, albeit not on their chariot but in comfort. Pisces felt a bit like Deniusth and the Named-ranks. The chariot was a lot of fun, if bumpy, but this was faster. Colth kept explaining to the others.
“Yes, Stitch-folk would have known someone wanted the remains. But you seal a tomb up like that as, well, insurance. Especially if you don’t want current [Summoners] running around and getting too powerful. It’s also emotional. Imagine someone using your dead friends or heroes.”
Pisces sombered. There was a core of necromancy to summoning. He nodded, and Yvlon got it.
“Ah, and because it was just found, everyone wants it. So Yisame has us grabbing it. What’re the odds another team was hired to also grab the stuff?”
Colth’s eyes glinted.
“Almost 100%. But they would never admit to wanting to steal what belongs to the crown. Still, that means we’ll have Gold-rank teams running in there unofficially. We’ll have the high ground there, but they’ll be paid to get what we’re after.”
“Even if accidents happen. Great. Adventurer on adventurer violence.”
Pisces finished, but he was the only one who seemed terribly unhappy. Colth was just calculating, and Yvlon grunted.
“If they’re a good team, they won’t take the contract or we can talk them down. I don’t like it, but it also lets us go travelling. We might visit the Mad Ones. According to the map, we’re headed eastwards.”
Where Bearig and at least some of my friends are. It was a big nation, but Pisces’ heart leapt. Colth nodded, eyes flicking to Pisces.
“We’ll take a long trip, even if the dungeon’s simple. Let’s focus on the dungeon first, ey, Pisces?”
“Of course. Undead…it’s always undead, isn’t it? I could probably slay most of them by snapping their necks. Unless they’re Skeleton Lords.”
Ceria flexed her skeletal hand, grinning.
“And the circlet’s good for anti-trap duty. The real danger’s other teams. How d’you want to tackle them? Colth? You’re the expert. Darn, I wish I had some of those spellbooks from the academy! Well, maybe I can learn a spell or two on the ride. It’ll take time, even in this carriage.”
Pisces and Yvlon exchanged looks for a second, but he was relieved; they were away from the academy, on an adventure, and closer to his own goals. He settled back as Colth began to plan.
 
——
 
It took thirty-eight minutes for Colth to come up with a plan and everyone to agree. Which left, uh…two days for transit.
It turned out the tomb was far away, and fast as magical carriages were, Nerrhavia’s Fallen was vast. So the travel was boring.
Here was the thing: the chariot was more fun because even if bugs sometimes hit you in the face and it bumped, you felt in the world. From behind the magical glass of the carriage? Sounds were muted, and it was too loud if you rolled down the windows because of the speed they were going.
Nor could the Horns slow; Colth was pretty sure any teams who’d gone from the capital would have taken this very conveyance, which meant they had to go full speed. After all, another team looting the tomb wouldn’t be instantaneous, but half a day’s march would be disastrous.
Thusly, Pisces got to see Nerrhavia’s Fallen’s roads, and that was a dry, dusty sight. In places, they were beautiful roads kept by Djinni; in others, literal dirt and sand with tracks. He pointed out where the roads the King of Destruction had built across Chandrar via Drevish met roads that the Immortal Tyrant had laid until Ceria hit him with a comment.
“Pisces, all your roads appear the same to me.”
Whereupon he sulked and read the book he’d checked out until Ceria started whistling. Colth produced some cards, but he bet like a literal Demon; he was used to the Haven, who were cardsharks. Only Ceria could keep up with him.
What did one do to cut the boredom? The same thing everyone else did, these days.
They watched television.
“Next. Next. Next.”
“Stop flipping through channels, Springwalker. That one looked—”
“It’s Chandrarian propaganda. See the logo on the side? Wonders of Nerrhavia’s Fallen. Oh wait, we’re on it. It’s me stealing books! Okay, bored. Next.”
…Even finding a good channel was hard. Pisces put away his book because he felt mildly nauseous. He was, in fact, carriage-sick while trying to read. Nor did the Horns want to dwell on their popularity in Nerrhavia’s Fallen.
Colth was squinting at a complimentary booklet in the carriage.
“Eugh, it’s like someone ate on top of this. Disgusting. Hold on, let me file a complaint.”
There was a magical survey form, and he began writing on that. Pisces sighed.
“Let’s just watch something. Channel 2!”
“Drassi’s not on it all the time, Pisces. Plus, it’s boring today.”
“⅕ stars. There. Sent. It says here they have ‘on demand movies’. Movies. What kind of word is that?”
“Earther term.”
Yvlon and Pisces chorused. Colth scowled.
“You can’t say that about everything.”
“You can if it’s from Wistram. I’ve seen them at the inn. Erin’s got them. What are Wistram movies?”
“Recordings of famous events. Oho. The Players of Celum! Darn, no Elisial. Just the classics they did in Liscor. There’s tours of kingdoms—all propaganda, I bet. And—oh, the Ksmvr of Chandrar documentary.”
“Let’s watch that!”
Ceria brightened up at once. Yvlon shifted.
“I’ve already seen it.”
“You have? When?”
“The moment I got back to Izril and he told us what happened. You didn’t?”
“I heard it firsthand from Ksmvr.”
“He downplays everything, Pisces. It’s good.”
“Well, let’s watch it again—”
“I’ve seen it six times, Ceria. Isn’t there anything else?”
Pisces tapped his fingers together as Ceria threw up her hands.
“What about a historical documentary, perchance? Some retelling of the Creler Wars or, more interestingly, a city or nation?”
“Pass.”
Colth was interested, but the two female teammates overruled Pisces. Colth patted him on the shoulder.
“Okay, wait. According to this, there’s a chatroom that Wistram has. You can talk to other people. There’s even one dedicated to finding newsworthy events. I think I heard there was some fellow in First Landing who had a class dedicated to watching the television.”
“And they call me lazy—aha! Here it is!”
Ceria hunted around and hit something on the side of the scrying orb installed into the center of the carriage. A blue screen with scrolling white text appeared, and Pisces blinked at an advanced [Message] spell.
They never taught us that at Wistram. Ceria began scrolling through the chatrooms.
“Huh, this could be fun to mess with. I wonder if we can get anyone to believe it’s us. Wait…#television-1. Looks like there are…1,903 people inside. Whoa.”
“Anything worth watching?”
She was rapidly scrolling up and down, eyes flickering.
“Heh, is your super-viewer named ‘Molen’, Colth? Everyone’s deferring to him. Lord of the Couch, they’re calling him. Pretty funny. I’m definitely going to mess around with this place.”
“Rings a bell. There’s a Lord Molen Terland.”
Colth had an eidetic memory for people and places like that. Ceria hmmed.
“He’s talking about us! Classic Horns? Do we have a reputation? Am I predictable? Weird, he’s telling everyone to tune into one of the Terandrian channels. The one from Ailendamus? He’s not being complimentary, but he says it’s a ‘must-watch’ for Horns fans. Hold on, let me see if it’s on the scrying orb.”
She began changing channels as Yvlon squinted at the messages and seemed appalled.
“Someone wants to lick my metal foot?”
She edged back from the message box, and Colth chuckled.
“Ah, fans. You get used to it. You wouldn’t believe what kind of offers Mihaela got around her feet. A rather common fetish.”
“Colth, do you ever think we don’t need to know things?”
Pisces folded his fingers together, and the [Supporter] gave him a huge smile.
“I share the curse of knowledge, Pisces. I could hit you with something truly painful to hear.”
His smile dared Pisces to take him up on it. The [Necromancer] thought and carefully sat back.
“…No.”
A flashing [Message] lit up the text box as Yvlon stared in horror at the words, and she jerked. Then read more.
“Wait a second. This is a mass alert. Jaw of Zeikhal sighted? A juvenile one—”
Colth sat upright.
“That’s like an Adult Creler or natural disaster. They must be warning everyone to take cover. Near us?”
“No, it’s a ways away, but close enough…we’ll go well clear of it. They’re calling all adventuring teams. Do we go?”
Yvlon glanced around as if that were the foregone conclusion, and Pisces was nodding, but Colth threw up a hand.
“Wait. If we do that, the other teams will loot the tomb. There are plenty of teams in Chandrar.”
“But it’s a Named-rank monster—”
“Juvenile, Yvlon. Nerrhavia’s Fallen has its armies. It might even be a trick. I’d do that—well, I’d call it an Adult Creler. Either way, we’re on a mission from the crown.”
Yvlon might have protested, but she saw Ceria shaking her head, and Pisces admitted Colth had a point. He sat back, and Colth smiled brightly before noticing the other two’s discontent. He hesitated—and then Ceria crowed.
“Got it! Let’s see what—oh shit.”
The scrying orb finally stopped on a new television channel called ‘The Glorious Report’, which was clearly Ailendamus; Pisces saw the familiar sigil in the corner with the lancearrows and ‘his’ kingdom’s crest.
Well, he was long gone from Ailendamus, and he had never thought of himself as a proud citizen beyond being born there. His father had wandered from place to place, and Ailendamus held nothing but regrets for Pisces. The only person who had survived his childhood and that blaze was Ama and, apparently, Feren.
Still, he wondered what was so important about his team on this channel? Pisces saw someone, clearly a reporter of some kind from Ailendamus, doing one of those interviews where the person being interviewed was in a smaller box.
Screen-in-screen. The [News Anchor] was smiling, and a picture of Pisces was present, hair all a-tangle, leaping into the Coliseum of Monarchs. Pisces turned beet red as Ceria began to hammer on the scrying orb. Him? They were broadcasting his face?
Of course, his name was out there because of the bounty that Montressa had put on his head. They had records. Pisces was about to tell Ceria to turn the orb off—he didn’t need to hear the Kingdom of Glass and Glory claiming him—when there was a voice.
“Disgraceful.”
The one word jerked Pisces upright. It was familiar. Pisces couldn’t have forgotten that voice, though he had not heard it for…
It was acerbic. Even grating. There was no sneer in it; it was precise in that each word was carefully enunciated, like the edge of a blade. Everything about that man was like that. But despite that, there was the sense that the speaker regarded everything as lacking. Including himself.
The excited [News Anchor] hesitated.
“Excuse me? This would be the, ah, aforementioned [Necromancer] and duelist who is believed to be a Silver-bell duelist, Pisces Jealnet. Of Ailendamus, though the Kingdom of Glass and Glory does not recognize his class, naturally. Yet his considerable abilities and fame—you disapprove, sir? Of your son?”
Then the image of Pisces was replaced by a man’s face, and Pisces’ hand leapt to his side. Because there he was.
Padurn Jealnet looked like Pisces, though the [Necromancer] was loath to admit it. But to his teammates, who had frozen, it was obvious.
His hair was a similar shade of brown, though a touch darker, and unlike Pisces’ untidy mop, Padurn’s hair was combed straight. And he was, disconcertingly, thicker than Pisces, if still fairly lithe. A [Duelist]’s fighting trim. He wore a leather guard on his non-dominant arm, and he stood with a simple rapier in hand. A silver bell hung from it, and his face was…stern.
Unsmiling. Creased from the scowls which were too common. Pisces knew that Padurn’s hands would be callused from holding the rapier. His eyes were dark brown and would only light up when he was angry or, so rarely, happy.
His father. The man was unchanged. After all this time—
“Pisces? Turn the scrying orb off, Ceria.”
Colth reminded Pisces he had stopped breathing. The [Necromancer] let out his breath in a rush, but stopped Ceria.
“No. I have to see…”
Padurn Jealnet interrupted Pisces, as ever, despite being a world apart. He addressed the [News Anchor] with a half-bow, precise as a razor. The Fencer’s Bow. He had names for every move. You inclined yourself to a 68° angle. Keeping your weight on your toes to move out of the bow at any moment—
Never show any openings, boy, even in courtesy.
That voice. It was all coming back to Pisces. A blow across the shoulders from the training stick. That expression of uncomprehending disappointment.
Flesh burning. Smoke in his lungs.
“Naturally, I disavow his class, Anchor Jormen. I consider my son’s actions a personal disgrace. Were it in my power, I would personally drag him back to face judgement.”
The man had a little box floating under him for identification.
Padurn Jealnet, Silver-bell [Duelist]. Ailendamus.
“I, ah, but he is your son and a Gold-rank adventurer considered to be on the cusp of Named-rank. The most famous [Necromancer] living, sir. And an acclaimed fencer in his own right. This is Padurn Jealnet, father of Pisces Jealnet, to any new viewers…”
The poor [News Anchor] hadn’t expected this. The number of the Horns of Hammerad’s parents that you could interview were pretty small. Ksmvr of Chandrar had no parents or it was the Free Queen—unacceptable. Ceria Springwalker’s parents? Deceased. Colth the Supporter, mysteriously, had no records on family, and it was presumed they were dead. As for Yvlon Byres, the man kept advertising Byres silversteel—so naturally, the most mysterious of the Horns, Pisces, was a shoe-in, right?
Unfortunately, no one had actually thought to consider Padurn’s character. He was simultaneously uncharismatic, but captivatingly grating. He shifted, posture immaculate, and shook his head.
“My son ran away from his home years ago to join the Academy of Mages. They, clearly, did not know about his previous misdeeds. I had already disowned him and disavowed any knowledge of his deeds. Clearly, he has learned nothing in the time since.”
“…But he is a Gold-rank adventurer, Duelist Jealnet?”
“Fencer.”
“Pardon?”
Padurn gestured to his rapier, obviously unaware of the title hovering below him.
“I consider myself a fencer. A duelist is a challenger, roaming and pursuing mastery of the blade through combat. A fencer practices to refine their techniques. I have chosen a sedentary life, although my current occupation allows me for more travel. Therefore, I am a fencer.”
“You pedantic bastard. Nitpicking as ever.”
Pisces muttered under his breath. Yvlon glanced at him, opened her mouth, and shut it. The [News Anchor] tried again.
“Er, [Back on Topic], if you please, Fencer. I do apologize. Your son demonstrated incredible talent in the Coliseum of Monarchs. And we have numerous examples of his swordplay. The Village of the Dead, his raid on a [Slaver] caravan—”
Padurn shifted and grew more pained, as if the sight of Pisces in any kind of heroic moment went against all he knew to be true. He replied swiftly. That was the thing about him. You might think you could flummox the idiot with his hardheaded, stubborn ways, but he was fast verbally, on his feet and with the damn rapier.
“I have observed all these recordings. My comment stands: he has not improved since I taught him. If anything, regressed. His form is off. In the first instance, he shifts from foot to foot on the sands, unable to balance any cut. Here—”
He pointed as Pisces wobbled in the image of him fighting two [Slaver Guards] at once. The image froze as the [News Anchor] pointed, and Padurn gestured.
“His arms and body are completely out of sync. He has no follow-through on his cut, which is what follows.”
Sure enough, Pisces slashed lightly across a face, and there was a spray of blood. Padurn turned his head.
“He relies on that spell, [Flash Step], without any nuance and magic to overcome his numerous shortcomings. I did not teach him that, nor do I hold his swordsmanship on any pedestal.”
Pisces was grinding his teeth. The worst part about Padurn was that he was correct. Those were bad cuts. Though the [News Anchor] was clearly on Pisces’ side and coughed.
“It was a rather hectic battle, Fencer Padurn.”
“I’m sure that is what he would say as his excuse. A true duelist—and he has met at least two, the Maestro in the Trial of Blades and the King of Duels—shows no weakness.”
“So…you have nothing to say about your son, sir? Is he not deserving of the silver bell he carries?”
The slightly waspish tone of the [News Anchor] did get through to Padurn. Once more, he shifted and grew uncomfortable. His hand touched his rapier’s hilt.
“I did not state that. Pisces Jealnet bested a silver-bell duelist in combat, albeit by ambush and with magic. However it was done, the precedent stands. A silver bell is a mark of competency. It is not the golden bell, which itself is controversial. He is far from worthy of a true fencer’s regard.”
“Ah, the silver bell. We were curious about it; he appears to carry a silverish bell, but not a standard one. But can you certify that Adventurer Pisces deserves the bell, sir?”
“Yes.”
“Did you witness the duel between him and a Silver-bell duelist? The Fencer’s Guild of Terandria cannot ratify it.”
More discomfort. Pisces did smile then, darkly. Padurn paused.
“I did. The individual he bested was myself, before his flight from Terandria.”
“He bested you? Before he went to Wistram?”
The [News Anchor], uncomfortable or not, realized he had a story here. Padurn shifted once more.
“He did. I was unprepared for his use of magic, and it was an ambush; I have no excuse. It does not change my analysis, as a pure fencer. Neither he, nor I, have reached any adequate level of bladesmanship.”
His eyes were boring into Pisces, and the young man wanted to jump into the scrying orb and take Padurn on. Though he had never dared without that ambush. And he’d only done it with rage and luck—
The broadcast continued as the Horns watched. Padurn Jealnet was a [Fencer]. Not the best. Far from the best given he had no golden bell and had always aspired to it. But he was a silver-belled duelist and, Pisces scowled as they saw him preparing to do demonstrations—
He hadn’t lost his edge. He hadn’t changed as much over the years, but when he drew that rapier, Pisces still knew he was behind the man.
Not with magic. With magic, Pisces could bet on himself. With artifacts—but with that mastery of the sword? If it was nostalgic to him, a bitter quill, it was illuminating to everyone else.
 
——
 
The Arbiter Queen, Jecaina, had nearly spat out her breakfast when she’d seen Padurn on the scrying orb. When he’d started to insult Pisces, she’d hoped the [Necromancer] couldn’t see this, and her ire had risen.
She was worried about Khelt and Fetohep, who wasn’t responding to her requests to talk, and her father was preparing to raid Medain again. The television was, then, an unhappy but welcome distraction.
The problem with hating Padurn was…she watched as another [Duelist] with a silver bell demonstrated Padurn’s training and techniques. She observed a graceful lunge at Padurn’s chest and how he backstepped, showcasing a classic guard against the dangerous move unique to rapiers.
“Damnit. He’s better than I am.”
“Who is?”
Raelt of Jecrass wandered into the dining room, eating a banana from the royal gardens. He took one look at the scrying orb and, without missing a beat, grunted.
“Silver-bell? He’s good. Better than you, yes.”
She glared at him, and Raelt hesitated.
“Er…who is he? Very interesting. It’s like watching a Training Golem fight. Dead gods, he looks as strict as can be. I can’t imagine he’s much fun to talk to. I wonder if I ever met him as a lad? Funny, he looks like Pisces.”
It said something that the King of Duels could read that much in the form of Padurn Jealnet. It also said something that he had focused entirely on the swordplay and not the name hovering under Padurn on the broadcast. Jecaina pointed, and Raelt swallowed.
“Oh. Huh. He and Pisces don’t fight the same at all.”
It was true. Padurn was demonstrating a relatively perfect display of fencing, albeit so hidebound and standard it would bore Jecaina to tears. But Pisces had been far more adaptive. You could see the basis of Padurn in Pisces’ form; he favored a fast-moving footwork that gave him a lot of range and only closed in for decisive blows. Pisces had taken that further with [Flash Step], staying mobile, but diverged in other ways.
Like someone who hated to fight like the man who’d taught him. The problem was—Raelt muttered.
“He’s better than Pisces too. At least in pure form.”
Jecaina threw an unpeeled orange at him, and Raelt seemed hurt.
“The blade doesn’t lie, Jecaina.”
“No, but you can be slightly nicer to the adventurer we like!”
“I swear I’ve met him before. Maybe we fought. You fight a lot of silver-bells who want to level. Hmm. Ah, well, he’s levelled since then, clearly. Watch this next bit.”
Padurn was standing sidelong, as fencers did, presenting the narrowest angle for his opponent to attack. He stared away from the other duelist, who circled him—then lunged, stabbing. Padurn’s hand blurred and swatted down the stab.
Instantly, the other [Duelist] backed up and hesitated. Then they came at Padurn, fast. [Flurry of Strikes], Jecaina guessed. Six blows in quick succession.
One, two, three, four—
Padurn knocked all four blows down with economical moves. Then Jecaina cursed and saw the other [Duelist] falter. Because Padurn?
He’d closed his eyes.
 
——
 
That was…new. Pisces had never seen that trick before, and it gave him a nasty feeling down his spine. When Padurn turned, he just confirmed it.
“My Skill is called [Automatic Parry]. Any mundane strike or blow within my ability to deflect will be.”
“That sounds quite—powerful, sir.”
“It is average for a Silver-belled duelist. It has most use when my attention wavers or I am taken from odd angles, which I should not be. It is a Skill no true [Fencer] needs. Clearly, I was awarded it after my disgraceful duel with my son.”
Padurn’s inability to take a compliment was a superpower. He went on commenting, having demonstrated his actual talents.
“What separates Pisces, myself, and any true duelist from that of one who holds a golden bell is simple: technique. He covers up his numerous shortcomings with magic. It cannot replace the fact that he has no ability to wound a foe of suitable talent or parry a sufficiently Skill-based strike.”
He didn’t know about [Jovelyn’s Parry]. But Pisces still glowered because once again—the [News Anchor] coughed.
“Without magic, you mean.”
“If he truly had any talent with the blade, he would not need magic.”
“But you yourself are no gold-bell duelist, sir?”
“My comments to him apply to myself, of course. Were he to assail the King of Duels with sword alone, he would never leave a scratch. The same for myself. Nor can he block a cut. If the Adventurer’s Guild certifies him as a Named-rank adventurer, I can only conclude it is a grave oversight and an insult to any true master of the blade. The next step, the next stage of mastery is not something a mere copycat can equal. It would be apparent if he were that.”
Padurn was clearly about to expound on every way in which Pisces had failed to learn anything when the scrying orb turned off. Pisces jerked.
“Hey!”
“Okay, what about Ksmvr of Chandrar?”
Ceria turned the orb to the movies as Yvlon nodded. Colth patted Pisces on the shoulder.
“Parents. Your swordsmanship is just fine, Pisces.”
“I am not worried about—change it back, Ceria. That man. He’s clearly sold out his principles. What happened to ‘eschewing fame for the art of the blade’? He’s barely improved. So what if my form isn’t perfect? You can’t perform any magical blade arts after a decade of study!”
Pisces was stabbing a finger at the scrying orb as his team tried to calm him down. His blood was boiling. Especially when he read in the chatroom that Padurn Jealnet had been invited to the royal capital as a sword trainer. Pisces threw his hands up.
“He’ll ruin everyone for the blade! That’s because I’m the famous one! He’s got no originality! He’s a snivelling yes-man who thinks the law is the law because someone wrote it down with a shiny quill! That pathetic, self-serving, unoriginal—”
He caught himself, staring at Padurn, and for a moment, the Trial of Shields flashed before Pisces’ eyes. He had won that due to his magic, inspiration, a feat he could not replicate.
Could Padurn have beaten the hologram Drake with a sword? Pisces doubted it. But he took no satisfaction there. He glanced down at the bell on his sword and whispered.
“We’re both unworthy.”
And he was a [Duelist], now. Just like his father. Pisces glowered at the scrying orb.
The next step. He wished he knew what that idiot meant. Yvlon patted Pisces on the shoulder.
“I’m sorry, Pisces. I have my own problems with my father. And my mother, in some ways. Just differently. Being raised by a single man like that—no wonder you ran from home.”
He blinked at her. Untensed slightly.
“Single? Padurn’s not a widower. My mother, Enica, is alive, unless anything’s changed.”
She hesitated as Ceria blinked.
“Oh? How bad is she?”
“She’s fine. What she sees in him, I’ll never know.”
Pisces sat back, sighing. He glanced around.
“What? She’s not the problem. He is.”
 
——
 
Enica Jealnet was no Padurn, that was true. But Pisces’ memory, which was over a decade out of date by now, wasn’t perfect.
Then again, he had only known his mother as a son, a child.
The Court of Masks had different opinions on the Jealnet family, all five of them. Which would have astounded Pisces on multiple levels. Firstly, that the distant and powerful center of the realm had any knowledge of him when he had grown up in obscurity, raised in a provincial lord’s employment.
Secondly…five?
Well, his siblings were eight and two, respectively. Pisces had no knowledge of them, having never returned or made contact with his family, and wasn’t that interesting?
He was interesting, and sort of a puzzle for the likes of Baron Regalius, Lady Demizine, or the other high-ranking nobles who spent their time advancing the cause of the realm, gossiping about Duke Rhisveri, and arguing in the Court of Masks.
Because, well…Pisces Jealnet was one of the most famous adventurers in the world right now. That wasn’t a subject for debate; a [Regional Bard] had conducted a survey, and Minister Sophridel had confirmed that in terms of name-recognition, he beat half of the world’s Named-rank adventurers.
Obviously, having a famous adventurer who came from your country was a boon. Ailendamus had long wanted for a big representative, and the reason they didn’t have one was a bit of that old ironic hindsight; when they’d conducted a review, it had transpired that all their talent that normally went into the adventurers who made it big…had been recruited as promising [Knights], [Mages], and so on.
You could do too well in mobilizing your young population. Thusly, Ailendamus would have loved their own adventurer to make figurines out of and to advertise their nation. Pisces would have been looking at a substantial deal to represent the Kingdom of Glass and Glory already except for the, uh, [Necromancer] thing.
That was why Padurn Jealnet had been on television. It wasn’t hostile! Not quite. It was Ailendamus feeling their way around him as an issue.
Embracing a [Necromancer] was unthinkable in a post-Az’kerash world, but he had been dead for a decade. And adventurers were their own breed…but it still would have been a hard sell.
On the other hand, Pisces Jealnet wasn’t the wretched sort of fellow you sometimes got in high-level adventurers. He was, by all accounts the Court of Masks could find of him, rather brave. Selfless in battle.
…But he was a [Necromancer].
“Damn! But for his class and we’d be printing stories in Tales of Adventure and Woe already! We don’t have anyone half as appealing in our Gold-rankers.”
Regalius was groaning as he eyed Enica and the rather surly Padurn Jealnet, who were quite overwhelmed by their visit to the Court of Masks. Well, Enica was. She seemed to be a pleasant woman, minding her children, who were tongue-tied, bowing despite being assured they should not.
Interesting…Regalius knew a bit of swordplay himself, and so he’d watched Padurn’s broadcast with several winces. The man had no charisma, but Regalius could recognize how good he was with a sword.
Even so, he muttered to Lady Demizine out of the corner of his mouth.
“I’m not recommending him to teach anyone in the palace, though. And I will defend that to His Majesty myself!”
General Bathnir, the retired, white-haired man who also associated with Regalius’ group, grunted in agreement.
“There are trainers who inspire and those who crush motivation, and that man is the latter. The one thing I find good about him is that he’s grating on anyone he talks to. Equal opportunity condescension.”
The [Baron] swallowed his wine with a grimace.
“Dead gods, is that the best we can say of him? Someone else, say something nice!”
“His wife is quite pleasant.”
Yietha murmured, and Regalius eyed Enica again. It was true; Enica Jealnet was not what you might think of her. She was no shrinking violet like he had assumed the surly Padurn might marry. She was actually…fairly athletic. She was long-legged, fit enough to have strode about the palace all day with two kids, and seemed ready to run a footrace.
Regalius suspected that anyone whom Padurn Jealnet married had to at least keep up with the man’s personal training journey. She even used a fencing foil quite well, though she had no silver bell. She was sociable, kinder than her husband, and yet Regalius shook his head.
“She is pleasant, Yietha. I just…did anyone notice she never brought up her son, unprompted, once? She never asked me how he was doing or for more tales of him. There is a rift deeper than the Kraken’s Trench between father and son, but the mother has her husband’s side. And from meeting and listening to that man for five minutes—I am somewhat inclined to wonder if Pisces Jealnet’s crimes as listed are accurate.”
The other nobles turned to Regalius. Strong words. Shocking words that called into question the judicial system and the authority of the local [Lord]—but no one took him to task instantly. General Bathnir put aside his wineglass, frowning.
“I think House Shoel has opened an investigation, Baron Regalius. I reviewed the case myself. On its face, the situation was simple. [Necromancers] were found in a cabal. Their sentence was perhaps overzealous, but they had raised numerous undead.”
“Some were children.”
Lady Demizine’s comment. Regalius found the wine had soured, and he nodded.
“Let’s wait for Shoel’s report. But if the question is whether or not to embrace our notable adventurer…he is a [Necromancer]. He is a criminal. But his father does not exactly add to his indictments. Preliminary surveys are in from Minister Sophridel, and it appears our nation is not exactly against Adventurer Pisces. Fencer Padurn’s broadcast may have actually added to his popularity.”
“How surprising. Do we allow the man a segment to demonstrate his abilities? We did bring him all this way out here.”
Everyone turned to Regalius, who had a lot of authority in the areas of entertainment under Minister Sophridel. Regalius smiled as he watched the Jealnet family.
“Of course. It may be Padurn wins over the courts or public. But if he fails, perhaps that’s an argument to embrace Adventurer Pisces after all.”
“Regalius, Regalius, the scandal—”
“Is it a scandal, Lord Cobilet? How many monarchs or nobles know of Pisces Jealnet? If we have one [Prince] who’s not from Ailendamus express support for him in a public comment…”
Regalius was thinking out loud. Then he thought of Noelictus and stopped. His brother had made war against the Kingdom of Shade, which harbored undead in its borders, for over a decade. It still…Regalius let the other talk for a moment, staring into his winecup.
Nevertheless. Digneral, his brother, had never searched for popularity or the benefits of being liked. Perhaps he should have. All Regalius knew was that there was another angle to embracing Pisces’ reputation. Whether or not anyone here said it…Pisces the Scourge had been made slave of Roshal. Embracing him would put their kingdom against Roshal, if only in some small way.
But upon small things did national policy sometimes turn. And Regalius? He took a longer drink from his goblet and thought Padurn uncharming His Majesty and everyone else might not be the worst thing. It was just a small play from a man who had some opinions on [Slaves]. He only wondered if his peers shared his opinion.
That was all, though, for the Court of Masks. Pisces was just one issue; far less consequential than the funny old Duke, who was becoming more of a character every day, or the war or—
But they did watch when his team got up to their shenanigans. The results of a single Gold-rank team’s actions reached across the world. The only question was: what would they do next?
 
——
 
The Tomb of Yad’thuv was no crypt buried in the side of a hill. That was only Pisces, Ceria, and Yvlon’s memory that played tricks on them.
This one was a hole in the ground. Sand formed the dunes that provoked the memory, and they had no grass covering them; this empty ground had been uncovered by a chance gust of wind. But for that and you would never know the tomb lay here.
Arid, inhospitable land all around, the uninviting façade of a series of low-hanging cliffs, and ground so hard as to be rocky, despite technically being made up of sand.
The only vegetation here were cacti. This area lay inland of the coast, so Pisces thought no one could have lived in this region. However, they had passed at least one small community of Hemp-folk who lived by raising small herds and growing Yellats and cacti.
They were, then, surprisingly beautiful when you passed a cultivated cactus and saw it adorned with flowers that alchemists prized, blooming towards the sky, as Hemp-folk cut the blooms and gave the cacti little cups of water.
Flowers amidst the wilderness, and at the tomb? What always popped up: lookie-loos, people hoping to sell tools to adventurers, thieves, and lower-ranked teams. And the people who lived here. Again, Hemp-folk who stood well back from the actual tomb.
Possibly because the adventurers hired to clear it were already there.
“Shit, they’re already here! They must have taken off last night or at dawn!”
Despite Colth using Skills to boost their carriage, Pisces saw no less than four other Wistram Carriages at a standstill, and his heart leapt.
Other Gold-ranker teams really had been hired to undercut Yisame’s authority. This truly wasn’t Izril. Because they were also fighting.
Even as their carriage sped forwards, Ceria enlarged an image of the tomb’s entrance. Pisces saw at least eight people battling; there was the flash of a [Fireball]—a Garuda leapt out of the explosion, trailing smoke. They hurled something down, and a dual-colored flash of green and blue engulfed a team. But when it cleared, their barrier spells had kept the group protected. The Garuda linked up with five more fliers, and they dove straight into the exposed stairway.
“[Sycophantic Identification]. That team—those are the Jade Garudas. Fuck. That’s Named-rank. I’m counting the Singing Stingers of Scaiid on the ground—and the Roving Spearmasters, there! Gold-ranks! And another carriage is coming in. That means one more team’s lurking around, at least. Two, if the Garudas flew instead of rode.”
“Three Gold-rank teams and a Named-rank one? How valuable is this damn tomb?”
Yvlon’s voice was incredulous. Ceria grinned.
“More like—how much do they want to humiliate us and, by proxy, Yisame? Named-rankers are not within your plan, Colth. Retreat or circle?”
“They’re in the tombs, and they’re fliers. If we drop on them inside, I’ll give it to us. The moment they get out, they can just teleport or fly off. We can’t let an adventurer escape with the summoning materials. We need to secure the entrance. Your ice walls can probably hold even a Gold-rank team, right, Ceria?”
“If I reinforce them? For a while, yeah, unless they’ve got a Yvlon or a powerful Skill. But then, all the other teams are on our ass.”
Colth was thinking out loud.
“Then we wall the front. Get in, wall, take on any teams inside, and get out. Our advantage is being sanctioned. Scrying spells are already being deployed on this tomb. No adventuring team wants to make an enemy of the crown. Once Yisame’s people start shouting at them, they have a narrow window to pretend they didn’t hear. We just need to cut off their window of opportunity. I think the plan’s a go. Advance on that tomb and wall up. Pisces, you and I will deploy temporary spells, but Ceria has to use her magic.”
Specialization. At this point in time, Pisces’ [Bone Wall] spells were incomparable to Ceria’s ice magic. They had finally begun to diversify in abilities such that he couldn’t keep up with her. He nodded, but his heart was pounding.
“Colth, they’re going for the kill. Look—”
The Roving Spearmasters were fighting the Singing Stingers of Scaiid, and there were just three Stitch-folk with spears. But from the way the team of eight, the Stingers, kept back, each of the [Spearmasters] was like Relc. One opened up with a lunging stab that took one of the Stingers through the chest. The spearmaster hoisted the screaming Gold-ranker adventurer up into the air and flicked them off the spear.
Blood. The Stingers replied with a volley of spells and arrows that blew the ground apart; the [Spearmaster] was lying flat on their back when the air cleared. But some of the magic arced up, rebounding from the offensive, and landed near the civilians.
A bolt of green; it left six figures lying on the ground. They began to wriggle around, and Pisces saw more people fleeing backwards, towards the Hemp-folk who had stayed well clear.
Colth grimaced.
“Sloppy idiots—they’re not going as lethal as they can be, but only because they’re largely Stitch-folk. It’s a fight to the death if we start killing them.”
“And we’re doing this?”
Once again—Pisces felt like he was the person standing still while everyone else was preparing to move. Yvlon was flexing her hands, glancing around for a target. Ceria’s eyes were narrowed as she chanted spells. Colth turned to Pisces.
“We can’t fail the crown, Pisces. Like Yvlon said, if they were entirely upstanding teams, they wouldn’t be here. Don’t kill them; it’s not like the coliseum, Ceria.”
“Hey, I’m amoral, not stupid, Colth. Ready? Pisces?”
They looked at him, and he reached for his rapier. He didn’t want to do this. Can’t we just talk? They were looting a tomb of Stitch-folk. It felt different from Liscor’s crypts for some reason. Pisces frowned. What was telling him that? Instinct?
His class?
The [Necromancer of Reclaimed Grandeur] felt at the back of his neck, then saw his team waiting on him.
“I’m with you, of course. Always.”
Yvlon smiled at him. Then her eyes swung to the battle, and he thought he heard her heartbeat pick up. Did the adventurers down there hear it?
Or was it just their [Dangersenses]? Then he saw a second carriage appear on their right, and Colth swore.
“Gold-rank team! It’s the Conquerors—”
The Conquerors of Rameid rammed the Horns’ carriage with their own, and then Pisces was fighting. No longer thinking. He wished that was less of a relief.
 
——
 
The Conquerors had spotted the Horns and been dogging them the moment they left Tyrant’s Rest. Now, Raava swung the carriage into their team with a shout.
“Horns! Now we sett—”
Their carriage bounced off the Horn’s magical carriage from Wistram, and an alert began to sound.
“Collision detected. Slowing to ascertain damages and contacting your Wistram representative. Please hold.”
“No! Damned thing—what was that?”
The Ultimate Supporter’s green hair poked out of the side of his carriage. He flashed them a smile with no actual mirth in it.
[Veteran’s Ramguard]. Their carriage kept moving. The Conquerors kicked at the magical control box and tried to open the doors—which had just locked.
“For your safety, please do not exit the vehicle. Please hold—this is Magus Rievan. Let me just see what the problem is, esteemed g—what the hell?”
The [Mage] whose face had appeared on the scrying orb did a double-take as Lorllemdrom shouted at him.
“Open the carriage or get us moving!”
“Is this a dungeon? Hold on, you can’t use our carriages to ram—it’s against our code of conduct!”
The [Mage] was staring around. Iptiv kicked the doors.
“Get us out of here! Get us—”
“Watch out!”
Orsenor shouted, and Raava stopped trying to bail out one of the windows. She’d broken the magical glass with her pickaxe only to see someone leaning out of the other carriage.
Ceria Springwalker. The Ice Squirrel beamed.
“Hey, Raava! I owe you some of these! [Ice Lances]!”
“Dead gods!”
The first lance of ice slammed into the carriage, and alarms started blaring. Magus Rievan panicked, waving his arms.
“Stop! Stop attacking the carriage! This is Wistram Academy’s property—”
“Get out the other side! Hurry!”
One of the Conquerors slashed through the magical doors, and they leapt out, but used the carriage as cover; Ceria was bombarding it with more spells. Raava was poking her head out from the right side.
“We have to break clear and get into the tomb! Orsenor, give me a [Dustcloud Bomb]—”
“More magic!”
