Lorllemdrom, their [Mage], warned the Conquerors and they took cover. However—the second spell wasn’t a direct attack. Instead, Raava yelped and then stared down at her armor. There was frost on it.
“She’s lowering the temperature! Get clear!”
“She’ll snipe us—”
Iptiv tried to dash free and nearly ate an arrow. Colthei the Supporter had a bead on them, and he was keeping them pinned. But that meant the Ice Squirrel was still casting.
[Snap Freeze]. As the Conquerors felt the numbing cold eating at them, there was wind. And snow. Then—
[Whiteout Blizzard]. They were immersed in freezing winds, shouting. Raava leapt out of cover, and an [Icy Lance] slammed into her. But for her magical chestplate and she would have been killed; her team dragged her behind the carriage.
 
——
 
“Conquerors locked down!”
Ceria grinned as she saw the four heat signatures of the Conquerors staying put. Then she switched targets.
They were right on top of the two Gold-ranker teams, the Singing Stingers of Scaiid and the Roving Spearmasters. Both teams saw theirs coming, of course, and pivoted.
“The Horns! Damn the other teams—we need to be done before the palace blacklists us!”
That was the leader of the Stingers, who were advancing, seven-strong. The two Spearmasters called out.
“Truce?”
“You took out Marid! Never!”
That was all they got before the Wistram Carriage nearly ran over one of the Spearmasters. The Stitch-man leapt aside, and there was a voice from the inside.
“Pedestrian collision detected. Informing a representative of—”
The carriage didn’t slow, but did a U-turn and tried to run the [Spearmaster] over again. He stabbed desperately, but his enchanted spear didn’t penetrate the reinforced magical sides of the carriage. Then there was a voice.
“This is Magus Rievan, please h—are you running that man over? Stop! How are you controlling—”
Colth, again. [Commandeer Vehicle]. [Bandit] Skills. He swung the carriage around, spraying dirt, then someone launched from the side.
The Stingers were making for the tomb as the two Spearmasters dodged the carriage. Then they saw someone hit the ground and come running at them. Their [Captain] turned.
“Threadmakers. The Silver Killer! Drop her!”
They spun as the Silver Killer of Izril ran at them. She was—fast. The Stingers still managed two volleys.
Two [Lightning Bolts], an enchanted arrow, and a throwing disc—all hit her dead on. She burst out of the first volley, and they saw her skin was grey.
[Aspect of Iron]. She ignored the damage, and she was grinning—
“Hold her at the barriers! Ready—”
An arrow hit her in the cheek. Glanced off. One of the [Swordsmen] in the Stingers put a hand on their blade.
Wait—
She hit their barrier spells, and the barriers went out. The Stingers weren’t expecting that. They saw Yvlon Byres go through the barriers, and only the [Warriors] had a moment to react.
“[Quadruple Slash]—”
The [Swordsman] hit her. Three times; she blocked one of his slashes with an arm. But despite his enchanted mithril sword—all his blows bounced off something. Her skin. The prismatic barrier of their [Mage]’s magic was on her skin—
She shoulder-charged into him, and a fist met his sword. It compressed his sword back against his chest, and the [Swordsman] twisted—bounced off two of his teammates. He was trying to get up when her metal arms just—exploded into spikes.
 
——
 
The two Roving Spearmasters saw the entire team of the Stingers vanish in a giant porcupine of silver metal. Instantly, they spread out. One of them kept dodging the magical carriage, which was trying to run him over.
Colth was in the driver’s seat, and Ceria leapt off the carriage next, skating on a ramp of ice. She was covering her friend; the Stingers were trying to fight Yvlon as she punched through them at close-range. When they backed up, Ceria blasted them from behind.
“Disgraceful.”
The Captain of the Roving Spearmasters planted his spear on the ground. Three Gold-rank teams against one? He prepared a Skill. [Inferno Javelin]. Aiming at the Ice Squirrel. Barriers or not…
He had a half-second to notice the sand moving slightly before the invisible blade slashed at his chest. Nevertheless, the Captain parried Pisces the Bane’s cut. He cursed, whirling his spear around in a [Deflection Pattern].
Four strikes—one got through and cut across his chainmail armor, but that was all. The [Spearmaster] returned with two jabs. He saw the sand moving.
“Your teammate is down. The other one is fighting Colth, a Named-ranker. I would retreat, Captain.”
“We are [Spearmasters]. Face me openly, duelist. Let us see which is better. Silver bell or [Spearmaster].”
The Stitch-man motioned, and to his surprise and gratification, Pisces did appear. The [Necromancer] hesitated, and he raised his rapier. But that strange bell he carried—Captain Rashoy glanced at it.
That’s not silver, like the television said. He lowered his stance, preparing to sweep in. But the [Necromancer] just lifted his rapier.
“I regret to say, Captain, I have no time for a duel. Forgive me. Then retreat. My teammates are all more dangerous than me.”
What did that mean? The [Captain] was running forwards for a [Low Sweep] Skill followed by a Spear Art. But he aborted the charge—pivoted—
The arrow hit him, and only his helmet saved him. Even so, his head rang—but the man was blocking something else. A heavy swing—he stumbled. Then had to leap back away from—
He leapt back into a blade, which slashed across his chainmail. Then he felt bony hands on him. But he saw nothing. Just twisting sand—
The [Invisibility] spell broke, and six Skeleton Champions appeared. They’d gotten the drop on him! The [Archer] took aim as Pisces saluted the man.
“Apologies. I am a [Necromancer] more than a [Duelist].”
Then he [Flash Stepped] away. The [Captain] swung his spear through one of the Skeleton Champions’ heads, but the rest came at him.
[Undead: Bonerattler Charge]. He ate his first real wound as the one with the greatsword drove the blade into him and nearly broke a rib.
“Calpit!”
He shouted for his teammate—and didn’t see the other [Spearmaster]. The final member of his team had tried to take the driver of the magical carriage out.
Colthei the Supporter drove past Captain Rashoy. He had a bloody blade in hand. He leapt off the carriage, and it skidded to a stop. Someone was being dragged behind it. Rashoy saw his teammate—Calpit was missing an arm and still struggling to free himself from the rope that the [Supporter] had used to drag him across the ground.
“Fall back! Grab Miha!”
He swung at the Skeleton Champions, who were pulling back, five strong, towards the tomb. Rashoy deflected an arrow and heard a scream of fury.
The Conquerors of Rameid emerged, frostbitten and furious, and the Stingers were scrambling away from the Silver Killer, five standing. A flying carpet descended, and three teams of Silver and Gold-rankers leapt down, shouting.
But the Horns had reached the tomb’s entrance. Rashoy saw the [Necromancer] turn back as the Ice Squirrel and Silver Killer joined his position. The [Supporter] was using the entrance as cover, firing arrows at the other teams. For a second, Rashoy locked eyes with Pisces the Bane.
He’s no slaughterer of men like the rumors say. He even appeared guilty. Rashoy lifted his spear. The [Necromancer] could have done far worse during that surprise attack. Then Rashoy fell back, running to get his fallen teammate.
Rashoy was a Level 35 [Spearmaster of Sand’s Flare]. After today, Rashoy hoped it was Level 36; that would be the one consolation prize from this disaster of an attempt. He consoled himself with two things.
Firstly, his team had only gotten cut up but not wounded beyond some good cloth and stitching. Second? He peered over his shoulder.
“Gold-rankers. Hah.”
“Damned Adventurer’s Guild.”
Calpit agreed, hunting around his for his arm. They were all over Level 40 or Rashoy would eat his damn spear.
The other teams were bearing down on the tomb’s entrance as the Horns regrouped. There was a pause; one of the Conquerors fired a glowing arrow, and it exploded as a Skeleton Champion threw itself in the way of the projectile. Then…
The Frostmarrow Behemoth roared its way skywards. Ice and ivory funneling upwards from the two [Mages] who held hands, a glowing blue flame in the eyes of the largest—and first—bear that Rashoy had ever seen. It turned, and the Conquerors of Rameid slowed and began backpedalling.
The Frostmarrow Behemoth charged, roaring like an earthquake given voice. Then the Horns of Hammerad vanished inside. The Roving Spearmasters retreated towards their carriage, shaking their heads.
“Let the Jade Garudas try them. Or those other two teams. Let’s get out of here and find a [Mage].”
“To do what?”
“See if they’ll pay us to do an interview.”
 
——
 
The Horns made it to the Tomb of Yad’thuv by virtue of superior gear and strategy, mostly. Colth had reasoned that since no one knew how Yvlon’s ring worked, any team using conventional barrier spells would be easy pickings.
Moreover, Pisces and Ceria were experts at locking down the enemy—even if the two of them didn’t actually do that as much, their classes were perfect for delaying actions. Colth had been most worried about Pisces getting hurt or Ceria growing overconfident, but her takedown of the Conquerors with his help? Textbook.
Even the Haven’s crowd would admit she’s got Named-rank instincts there. Three spells to take the Conquerors out of the fight long enough for them to secure a position. The last trick had been the magical carriage, obviously.
Far too useful. Archmage Amerys had demonstrated how they worked, and having a vehicle that was a lesser version of Magnolia Reinhart’s carriage was hard for anyone to beat, even a Gold-rank team.
We’ll have to watch out for someone doing that to us. Though Colth had already speculated that if he deployed an obstacle, he might be able to flip one coming at them.
They made it to the tomb’s entrance, and Colth reviewed their state. No major wounds on anyone in the party. Yvlon had taken some hits, but she was using her second ring to heal herself. Magic expenditure was moderate with Ceria, but she was guzzling a mana potion.
Pisces had lost all but three Skeleton Champions, but had enough bones to remake two. [Ice Walls] were now deployed, and with Ceria’s [Glaciersheet Ice], they’d have plenty of time before a Gold-rank team broke through—once they dealt with the Frostmarrow Behemoth.
“Alright, let’s push. Ceria, how much mana are we working with? Can you cast [Summon Frost Elemental]?”
She flicked her eyes to him, still grinning with the adrenaline.
“Sure! How many do you need?”
“Can you do…four without needing a mana potion? And use the Crown of Medain?”
“If I draw on the circlet’s magic, sure. Just flood the corridors?”
He had his bow in his hands and was scanning down the tomb. Colth saw old murals and text on the walls, beautifully preserved. He wished he had time to read it; the creators of this tomb had clearly recorded the history of the place. Perhaps even the names and levels of the dead. But he focused.
“That’s right. We don’t have time to search for traps beyond quick checks. Send them forwards. If they vanish, let us know. And tell us when your ice walls come under attack.”
“Aye aye, Captain Colth. Everyone good?”
“That was crazy. We just rushed three Gold-rank teams.”
Pisces was wiping at his brows, but Yvlon only grunted.
“They were easier than I thought. I was worried when they tagged me with spells. The Stingers fell back without engaging me hard.”
Well, you probably outlevel all of them by ten levels, and you ran at them with Galas-muscle. And they saw your last fight. 
Colth didn’t say that, obviously. Better if the Horns continued behaving like underdogs. He just smiled as Ceria conjured four beings made of frozen ice. Tall, angular; the Frost Elementals strode forwards, shedding vapor, and Pisces pointed.
“Skeletons, advance and…engage? Don’t kill adventurers. Any defenders of the tombs—yes. Don’t kill anyone living.”
The Skeleton Champions let the Frost Elementals go forwards, then the creatures summoned by the Crown of Medain. Smaller, snarling jackals made of light, a green bird with huge claws—eleven Silver-ranker monsters.
Nothing fancy. All together, the summoned monsters would probably only delay a Gold-rank team, but it was a damn horde. Colth smiled wider.
This team of mine has so much utility. He loved it. Normally, you had to pay for this kind of firepower if you were with Eldertuin or Viecel, or you traded all your offensive capability for magic or being all-rounders like Larracel.
But with Yvlon and Pisces, Colth actually had a strong frontline too. Their only weakness was a lack of [Rogues], and he filled that gap.
“Okay, I suspect two teams are down here—one’s Named-rank. The Jade Garudas are respected, but fliers. They favor magical attacks with their speed. Hit-and-run tactics. I think they’re some kind of magical Garuda subspecies? They’re overconfident or desperate. They shouldn’t have entered the tomb, but waited to pick off anyone coming out. My guess is they think they can blitz the tomb and get out. They might be able to cut through Ceria’s [Ice Walls], so our goal is to negotiate or neutralize.”
“Think they’ll be willing to talk?”
The Horns strode down the corridors, which were actually well-lit. Little balls of [Light] had illuminated on sconces, revealing the old sandstone corridors and sarcophagi lining the walls. Colth glanced at them.
“Hard to say. I’ll get a read on their personalities and communicate it to you, Ceria. Remember: they’re a Named-rank team, so they’re sharp. But I’m a Named-ranker. If they recognize me they’ll think twice before assuming they can overpower us. Also, we can rely on Fetohep’s friendship.”
“What about Yisame? Ow. There goes one of my aspects. One left.”
Yvlon was scratching at a chunk taken out of her cheek. As her [Aspect of Iron] faded, it became a bloody gash; she grimaced. Colth sighed.
“It’s just politics with Yisame. Fetohep, though…he’s a petty [King], and a powerful one. I heard he reached out to them.”
“Colth…do you ever stop coming up with weird facts?”
“I just listen to gossip, Pisces. Now, note the light spells. Inbuilt from the tomb’s creation, not placed by the first team who got in. That means the magic is still good. I reckon the other teams dealt with traps or guardians. It also means our loot’s here. So no adventurers get past us without turning out their bags of holding. Well, I’ll check them anyways. They can hide loot anywhere.”
“Like up your butt. Yvlon style.”
“I swallowed my loot, Ceria.”
“It all comes out one way, Yvlon. You ever had to deal with that, Colth?”
He sighed.
“Too many times. It’s worse when it gets stuck.”
Pisces groaned.
“Colth…can we just be professional?”
“That’s as professional as Named-rankers get. Okay…silence spells. Keep chatter low.”
The Horns advanced. Colth saw the corridor of the honored dead sloped downwards, and his hope was that the tomb was just one long, long corridor. That’d make it a real easy killzone.
Sadly, it was not. Everyone had to be cute. Happily, though, when they reached the first intersection, someone had actually chiseled a map onto the tomb. Colth chuckled.
“I love helpful architects. Nice. Okay, three passages but just three wings. We have a chokepoint here. The northern wing is largest…I’d bet that’s where our treasure is, just based on general vibes.”
The writing on the walls was in the common tongue, telling Colth this wasn’t too old or made by unexpected groups. It was Pisces who hmmed and read as Ceria directed the summoned creatures to split. She sent the Ice Elementals forwards, the Medain minions right, and let the Skeleton Champions go left. The [Necromancer] eyed the writings.
“It says ‘Skein of Yad’thuv’ is the western wing. Whereas the right reads, ‘Threads of the Guiders’. But the northern tomb is simply, ‘Legacy of Thuv’s Reed-folk’. Fascinating. From this, I infer that the left corridor isn’t what we need. Stitch-folk might put just a lifethread in a pot.”
“Mass-graves, then. Low-level. ‘Threads of the Guiders’ means the ruling class? They might be valuable, but probably are lower-level. Treasure might go there.”
Ceria commented, and Colth concurred.
“Wall the left side and north? The north sounds like our destination, mind you. ‘Legacy’ indicates that they intended this place to be found, and their champions sound like a legacy.”
Pisces sniffed at everyone stealing his thunder, but nodded. Yvlon just raised a hand.
“Reed-folk? Why are they called that? This is a high-level tomb, right?”
“Maybe they were all made with reeds if this place had water during their time, Yvlon.”
“I know, but can you even make reeds into cloth? Is…is that comfortable?”
The question genuinely gave the Horns pause. Colth knew you could make cloth out of most plant or animal fibers, but he hesitated.
“You’re right, it sounds closer to Hemp-style cloth. But magical reeds? Or maybe that’s how their civilization evolved? Let’s speculate later.”
They were about to head down the right corridor when Pisces held up a hand.
“Contact! One of my Skeleton Champions went down; the rest are fighting.”
Colth nodded.
“I’ll go first with my armor’s advanced invisibility if I need to. Yvlon, don’t let them get at Ceria. If we need to, just [Ice Wall] and fall back, but try not to cut me off if they detect me?”
Pisces nodded and lifted a glowing finger. Yvlon strode forwards as Ceria covered her with a wand, and Colth kept low next to her, bow aimed. They heard fighting ahead of them.
“—dodge]! They’re damned fast!”
“Someone’s coming! I can sense their footfalls! Living! Hey, help us—”
“They’re the ones summoning the undead, jackal-brained asses! Hold! Hold, we wish to parlay!”
The most authoritative voice came from ahead, and Colth decided not to use his armor’s powers—yet. They’d need time to recharge. Instead, he peered down the sloping corridors and, as they descended, saw Pisces’ remaining two skeletal champions fighting a group of six.
Well, some of the six. It was a mix of species. Three were wounded, one quite badly burnt. The other three adventurers were…Gold-rankers? Colth didn’t recognize the team, but the wounded ones felt weaker.
Golds and some Silvers? Not unheard of, but it was stupid for this. He called down as he aimed at the leader, who was actually one of the Fox Beastkin.
“Horns of Hammerad! And you are?”
“Nerrhavia’s bones, it’s them. We are the Adventurers of Nerrhavia’s Fallen! Pull back these undead! We wish to negotiate!”
“What a name. I should have called myself Ceria, the Cold Half-Elf.”
Ceria muttered sotto voce at the others. Yvlon snorted, but Pisces was already calling the Skeleton Champions off. Colth would have preferred them to stay at melee range, but he just called down.
“You’re interfering in the business of Queen Yisame, Adventurers!”
“We took on a job, same as you. It’s not personal. Listen…you.”
“Colth, the Supporter.”
He sighed and the Fox Beastkin squinted.
“We don’t want to quarrel with the Bane or Silver Killer, alright? Nor are we carrying treasure; the other team already did for us. We would have left but for the teams above. Let us pass, and we’ll go. Agreed?”
Colth turned to Ceria, and she tapped the circlet.
“I don’t think they’re lying. Hey, Captain You! You guys come up one-by-one, and we’ll have Colth search you and then let you leave, agreed? There’s walls of ice up, so I’ll have to let you out.”
Muttering from below. The adventurers didn’t like that.
“Why one by one?”
“So you don’t try and pull a fast one. We’re not going to kill you. You can watch us, but that’s the deal.”
“Do you have any assurances?”
“Swear on a truth spell.”
“We don’t have any.”
Colth was pursing his lips, thinking of a solution, when Yvlon called out.
“I swear by my arms. Silver and steel be my witness, let my arms fall off if I lie. I’m from House Byres of Izril; upon my class, I promise. And Pisces will swear by his broken chains. Agreed?”
The Adventurers muttered to each other, but Colth raised his brows.
“Pretty good, Yvlon.”
“They like poetic stuff.”
Sure enough, the Adventurers called back.
“Agreed! Swear!”
Pisces and Yvlon gave their words, and the adventurers came up, though they actually had to help some of their wounded party members. They were badly hurt indeed; all of them had magical damage, and the worst off was a Garuda whose feathers were scorched to her skin.
“Damn, you don’t have healing potions?”
Colth actually had to stop checking them for loot and pull out a burn salve. The Garuda twitched when he applied it, but he thought it wasn’t critical. Just bad. The Captain, whose name was Fetriv, only grunted as he watched his team moving past the Horns.
“Not for that. The teams you want all went straight. We heard a second team fly past.”
“The Jade Garudas. So the first team got you? How many, and what did they do?”
Intelligence was key. Fetriv just scowled.
“We were here first! We set out while you were all napping—but they had summoned Stitch-folk we had to fight past. Damn them. It was all a test; the summoning crystals are waiting to be claimed—once you slay the guardians.”
Interesting. Colth was sorry to miss the actual dungeoning portion.
“Let me guess, the other team let you do all the hard work then came at you from behind?”
He was surprised when Fetriv shook his head.
“No! They must have had a Skill or cloaked themselves; the summoned warriors didn’t attack them! We tried to fight, but their [Mage] just hit us with…something. It wasn’t a [Fireball]. We had barriers up, but she detonated the spell, and the other two forced us to retreat down here. Then you all showed up.”
Hmm. Well, it was good enough. Colth nodded.
“You’re cleared—except for this.”
He reached down and plucked something from the wounded Garuda’s side. The Adventurers stirred, and one protested.
“H-hey—”
“You put whatever you grabbed in here.”
The bag of holding had soot all over it, but it wasn’t actually damaged; they’d just made it look like it was. Colth emptied it into his bag of holding.
“It probably wasn’t what was needed for your assignment, anyways. And we’re not going to sort it. Clear out, deal? The Jade Garudas are up ahead, and it’s going to be Named-rank fighting with that other team. Which one was it?”
For answer, Fetriv shrugged.
“One of the ones at the damn banquet. Fine! Open the walls and we’re quits. Thanks for not murdering us and reanimating us, Bane. Good thing we never bought a Slave Adventurer.”
He commented to his teammates, then saw Colth and Pisces staring at him. The team of mixed adventurers beat a hasty retreat, and Colth muttered.
“Ceria?”
“Opening a gap in my ice walls. They’ll squeeze through. I’ll re-wall the main corridor. Summons found nothing on the left side. Maybe keep them there in case a team’s in hiding? But I say let’s push the north.”
Good instincts, good leadership. Colth didn’t object, and the Horns saw the other team running as Ceria raised an [Ice Wall]. But she didn’t get it up entirely before she whirled.
“North—”
There was a muted squawk—then the scream of something hot hitting Ceria’s [Ice Walls] that had blocked the northern wing off. Colth saw white-hot light behind the wall and snapped.
“Yvlon, forwards! Let’s flank ‘em, left and right!”
Ceria dove to the left and raised an [Ice Wall] at chest height to crouch behind. Pisces copied her as Yvlon and the skeletons planted themselves in the ground. Colth saw something burn through Ceria’s ice walls, fast.
“Jade Garudas. Let’s get—”
A hole appeared, and he fired a [Lob Shot] through the gap as soon as the steam revealed one. Just an arrow with a Potion of Blast attached. That was a lovetap in Named-rank terms.
However—the Garuda who barrelled through the gap came out fast, in a horizontal dive, caught the arrow in one claw, and tossed it back at Colth. He aborted the [Remote Detonation] Skill, kicked the arrow down the corridor—
“We’re retreating. Stop or we fight.”
The Garuda had brilliant magical feathers—and a cracked beak and scorch marks all over his armor. Colth hesitated, and Ceria threw up a hand.
“Swear to it or I’ll wall your team off.”
“I swear. We’ve been bested. Damn these walls!”
Colth waited for the nod, and Ceria lowered the [Ice Walls]. Instantly, three more Garuda flew over and carried one of their teammates out.
No burn marks here. Colth eyed the fallen Garuda and asked the obvious.
“Who got you? And how?”
“Some new team. Lack of air, the damn Stitch-folk summons—and whatever the hell weapon their Captain is using! They’re set up down there. We can’t maneuver. We’re out.”
The Jade Garudas were clearly a cautious team, for all the risks they’d taken. Like any Named-rank who’d lived long enough, they’d seen something they didn’t like and bailed out. Colth checked them for loot, then turned to Ceria.
“They’re clear.”
“Opening this wall. What team? Stitch-folk?”
The Captain of the Jade Garudas had magical talons still radiating heat. He grimaced at them.
“I thought they were your friends. Humans. None of them look Chandrarian. I’d say ‘best of luck’, but I’d rather you all failed right now.”
He flapped through the second ice wall, and the Horns glanced at each other. So, one team had held down a weaker Gold-rank team and a Named-rank one? True, the Jade Garudas were out of their element, but that set alarms ringing in Colth’s head.
“Sounds like one team’s actually in position. I don’t know how they got the Stitch-folk on their side. Might be they can suborn summons? Or they just activated the crystals. Let’s move up.”
“Should we negotiate?”
Pisces was licking his lips. Ceria laughed softly.
“For what? Half the loot? They’ve got everything, and all they have to do is break out or beat down every team who comes in here. That’s going to be hard; I can tell someone’s hitting my ice walls at the entrance. Probably too scared to squeeze their way in. They’re trying fire magic, though, which is as good as pissing on it.”
“Let’s call it twenty minutes before anyone gets past both ice walls?”
Colth guessed, and Ceria shrugged.
“Double that if—no, wait, something’s taking chunks out. Must be Raava and her pickaxe, but I’ll solidify. Twenty, yeah.”
“Then send the Ice Elementals and Skeleton Champions forwards and advance. I think we use your [Ice Walls] and let you hang back; Yvlon charges, I go invisible, and Pisces sniffs.”
“Good plan.”
“I do what?”
“Go long-ranged, unless you can get past their defenses. You’re squishy; Yvlon and I aren’t. You only have 89 Health Points, Pisces. It says so right on your character sheet. I’ll show you when we get out of here.”
“Damn, that’s only a bit more than mine. Pisces does have the Stalker underarmor, but Colth’s right that we can’t take careless hits. Okay, team. One more group to spank. I’m pretty sure that’s Wildcard down there. Time to give them a real reason to hate us.”
The Horns advanced past the ice wall the Jade Garudas had melted through. Yvlon was smiling faintly, but saying nothing. Tensed. Pisces was pretending to sniff, but his rapier was drawn, and he was staring down, following his Skeleton Champions. Ceria just smiled, eyes flicking from Pisces to Colth to Yvlon…
The Ultimate Supporter was calm. Smiling—he sent a Skill on the summoned minions.
“[Summons: Enhanced Movement]. Any cont—”
Boom. The Horns felt it up ahead. Yvlon started running, and Ceria called out.
“That’s one Ice Elemental d—two. Damn, they’re not supposed to be that weak!”
“Pull them back! We’ll send them with the Champions!”
Ceria tried, but there was a second explosion. She called one up the hallway, and Colth saw it sloping downwards.
Nice, long tunnel…with scorch marks on the bottom. He held up a hand.
“Hold on, I sense—”
“Something on the ground. Walls. Magic. That must be trap spells.”
“Taking them out.”
Colth fired an arrow at one. He swore he hit whatever it was; some little object, he thought. The size of his thumb? Good magic. But the arrow did nothing, so he grunted.
“[Piercing Shot].”
The shockwave blasted up the corridor, and he blinked.
“That wasn’t fire, but air. What the hell was—”
The other magical signatures vanished abruptly as Ceria hit another with an [Ice Spike] and unleashed a torrent of electricity. She called out.
“Looks like the [Mage] has pulled back their mana. Not sure what that spell was. The Circlet’s never seen it before.”
Well, I don’t like that. But you could hide the effects of a spell with a Skill. Pisces just frowned.
“Weird mana. I almost thought I recognized—”
“Hey up there! We’ve got the treasure of Yad’thuv! It’s over! Let us out peacefully and we’ll share a bit of it; if not, you’ll have no chance! Deal?”
A voice from below, loud, male, and reasonably confident. The Horns stopped. Ceria muttered.
“Circlet recognizes that voice as the Wildcards. Hey, Leonardo, Kusal, Lareceina! There are a bunch of angry Gold-rank teams behind us, and we’re all on the same side! You’re interfering with [Queen] Yisame’s own quest! How about we settle this without violence? You give us the stuff, we don’t stab you. Deal?”
There was a faint curse from below. Colth was moving down slowly. The damn slope meant he couldn’t see the corridor below, but it seemed to straighten out. Which meant the Horns were descending a ramp while whomever was there had a straight view of them.
Killzone. He hated cracking one, but if he could see what they had…
“The [Queen] isn’t the only person who put a request up for the Tomb, Captain Ceria! We beat a Named-rank team just now, and the summons are on our side! They’re stronger than you want to tangle with, on my word! Let’s call it 75-25?”
“…Sure, we’ll take 75! Listen, you don’t want to be on the Palace’s bad side. Steal from the crown and get killed in your sleep. We’ve got a real Named-ranker on our side.”
Ceria shouted back. Colth squatted down.
<Colth to team. I think I see barricades. Steel. The kind you deploy from bags of holding. Glowing figures behind…but it’s just three of them.>
Not the worst killzone. In fact, only two of Wildcard seemed to be armed. Saying that, though, an arrow cracked off the stone, and Colth leapt up. Then there was a female voice.
“That was one of the summons. Don’t try to sneak down here. There are only four of you, Captain Ceria. The [Queen] is not the deserving party of the Tomb’s legacy.”
That must be Lareceina, the [Mage] who didn’t like Ceria. The half-Elf exhaled.
“Okay then, nothing personal. Colth?”
He walked back up.
“I’m not sure what they’ve got, but the Stitch-folk have bows and wands. Yvlon could rush them, but I don’t like risking that. If you [Ice Wall] and we dive behind it, then it’s a shooting war.”
“Send the Ice Elementals forwards and have Pisces summon more? Snipe them down until we can rush?”
“I don’t have a bow.”
Yvlon complained as Colth deliberated with Ceria. Pisces scratched at the back of his neck.
“All I have is [Shatterbolt] and [Deathbolt]. I don’t want to use either—”
“Break the left barricade with [Shatterbolt], Pisces. They’ll survive one [Deathbolt]. Just do summons. We can send one wave, and if we don’t like what we see, fall back, use mana potions, try again? Just don’t leave cover. I’ll use an [Arrowguard] Skill. Yvlon, I have a spare crossbow and some alchemical weapons.”
“See, this is what we need to buy alchemy for. For when Yvlon’s useless.”
Light voices from Ceria and Colth. Yvlon was crouched, and Pisces was motioning the Skeleton Champions forward, animating his Warbear. Then there was a shout from below.
“Horns—we really don’t want to hurt you. Back off. Last warning.”
The Horns of Hammerad didn’t answer. So, below, the team of three tensed. They were coming. That terrifying team. Who, in their right minds, wanted to fight the Horns of Hammerad?
 
——
 
It was like you could feel them. Auras or something. The coldest [Mage] in the world. A strange, quiet figure, filled with silent, respectful death. And the crawling thunder of a heart beating.
The Silver Killer.
They had seen her in the Coliseum of Monarchs, hadn’t they? And everyone had seen the other broadcasts. Ksmvr of Chandrar. Pisces the Bane…the Village of the Dead.
“Damn. We’re so dead. I wanted them to like us.”
“They’re not good people, Kusal.”
“They’ll kill us. Are we sure we’re doing this, Leo?”
The team of three were new to Gold-rank. They’d only gotten certified after the Adult Creler. Adventurer’s Guilds didn’t like what they didn’t understand, and the trio didn’t have regular classes. Their leader, Leonardo, was far from fearless. But he just stared up the corridor.
“I think we have to try. We’re adventurers. We promised our clients.”
Lareceina nodded, rubbing her fingers together. She was casting. Readying herself…and she knew at least one of the [Mages] above outclassed her. Wistram. She had never had formal training. But her only comment was—
“We have the moral high ground. We have to try.”
Kusal was their [Rogue], if not in class, then how he operated.
“They have the literal high ground. If the Silver Killer jumps us—I’ll try.”
Leonardo nodded.
“Watch out for the one called Colth. He’s supposed to be the real Named-ranker. I’ll do my thing. But we have to attack them first. Everyone ready?”
They nodded, and Leo paused. Then took a breath.
“…I wish Justine was here.”
With her, they would have been fearless. Well, more fearless. But their front line, their stalwart warrior—Wildcard stopped for a second. They would have traded all their levels from the Adult Creler for her.
“They’re casting. We have to go.”
Lareceina spoke and produced her magic. It looked like…a marble. It grew as she poured her mana into it. Fire, swirling around and condensing. Like a [Fireball], but different. Kusal nodded as Leo pulled out his secret weapon. Not the sword he carried, but the real tool he had made, the only thing he was good with. But before that—they stood together.
A group huddle. Leo swung an arm around Kusal’s shoulders, and the young man from Sri Lanka put his arms around Lareceina’s shoulders. She grimaced and held the ball of fire in her palm. She had more little marbles floating around her hand. They winked and glowed. Leo muttered.
“Here we go. [Combined Skill: Ready, Set, Serve].”
He walked backwards, and Lareceina turned. She lobbed the orb of fire at Kusal, and the [Rogue] fielded it with his gloved hands. Straight at Leo. The orb spun through the air—and he hit it.
He jumped up, and the tennis racket, a wooden frame and strings, hit the orb of fire. It compressed as he connected with it.
[Racket: Bounce Magic]. [Ricochet Strike]. [Ball: Acceleration]. 
The [Tennis Champion] hit the ball down, aiming it for the end of the corridor, and saw it flash across the ground. And bounce—
He heard a voice.
“Incom—”
Then the orb exploded. The backdraft of flames echoed down the corridor, and Leo landed. Lareceina had cast a spell so his ears didn’t ring, so he heard voices.
“—hell was that? Wall spells and—”
A second ball flicked towards him. Same height; Leo wondered if the Horns had spread out. So he hit the ball at the walls instead of the ground. Bounce it up in a zig-zag—
This time, it was made of lightning. The boom made dust fall from the ceiling. There was a shift. One of the summoned Stitch-folk warriors was gazing at him.
“Sorry.”
That was all Leo said. Then the third ‘tennis ball’ flicked into the air. He struck it again, sending it up the tunnel at a new angle. This was the plan they’d come up with when they’d been briefed on the tomb. Lareceina’s magic and their unique classes…
The Horns would have to come down. The third orb was made of something green, and it burst without a sound as he hit it and shot it up. So, Leo was waiting, racket raised, sweat coating the leather grip.
Come on. Come on—

Pisces had no idea what was happening. His ears were ringing, and only Yvlon had saved him from the third orb. It had exploded into a shower of leaves or something—so sharp and fast that they had cut his cheek open. But Yvlon had tackled him. Now, she threw him up the corridor.
“Get back! The walls—”
“They’re not working!”
[Ice Wall]. Ceria’s trick. It was raised, but the second orb had bounced over it. Colth was swearing.

Sound.

Ingenious. How many did she have? She was like Saliss, but magic. Could he do that? The [Necromancer] had to abandon his [Bone Walls] and used [Flash Step] to dodge away. The two people who wanted to negotiate least were Colth and Lareceina. Probably because they weren’t the ones in mortal danger.
Pisces quite appreciated Captain Leo’s words. Because he was pretty sure he could dispel whatever was in Lareceina’s orb. It really was just…compressed mana. He’d never seen a compression spell like this, though.
Compress magic? It wasn’t something Wistram [Mages] thought of. Why bother? The spell itself was simple, though he felt like Lareceina had put a ‘lock’ on it. The equivalent of tying a bit of string into a knot. Not hard to figure out—just hard to dispel in a firefight.
His issue was that he wasn’t sure if dispelling it would release the magic. And he didn’t want to try it at the moment.
Yvlon? She was just eying the orbs of lightning, and she and he had the same thought. If she had her [Aspect of Silver], it might work, but without it? Yvlon wasn’t that tough.

Their employers? Ceria frowned.

“Fifty-fifty.”

I’m not going to be one of those people! Stalker’s underarmor might reduce some of the blasts, but his flesh beneath wouldn’t survive those detonations. Yvlon might, but Pisces was glaring at Ceria. However, the [Cryomancer] was in full bluff mode. Lareceina’s eyes flickered to Leo.

Ah, of course.
 
<Heroic Quest — The Tomb of Yad’thuv Failed.>
 
It didn’t hit him like a blow. He just exhaled, sniffed, sneezed, and wiped at his hair.
He couldn’t really remember the last time his team had lost.
It didn’t feel great.

Some days you won, some days you lost. Some weeks, some years, even. It was the mark of a seasoned warrior, or person, to recognize that losses, setbacks, were inevitable and not rage or despair entirely at them.
Nuvityn, King of Myths, wasn’t sure if that applied to [Kings]. Because, so often, a good man was not the same as a good ruler.
Perhaps they should be, but what should be was not what was.
For instance, he was sailing to hold an [Innkeeper] and her inn to trial. Whether it was right or wrong—his son was dead. As [King], as father, he would have a reckoning for that.
His army of ten thousand of Erribathe’s famous warriors, Prildor, Tserre, and much of his royal council suited for campaigning were a force to set even the Five Families to alarm. Nuvityn had written ahead, of course, using the power of diplomats to assure the Five Families he was coming not to upset their authority, but to go south.
The Walled Cities he would see about, but he intended to visit Izril and see what had changed. Visit the inn and deliver judgement, right or wrong—and then continue onwards. To the New Lands? To Baleros to find the [Innkeeper]?
That was the plan. There had been hiccups on the way. Not even bad ones; the fact that his company now had a [Princess] of Calanfer in it was not entirely bad. Nuvityn did not love Calanfer at this moment, but Princess Vernoue was youthful, earnest. A refreshingly young voice in love with stories.
And she might even crack the mystery that was Magus Tserre, whom Nuvityn regarded as a [Mage] as legendary as Archmage Eldavin. For she had once been an Archmage herself.
Yes, things had been decent when he had set sail on The Gathering Light, one of Pheislant’s largest trading vessels, to Izril. It, along with several other trade ships, had been paid to carry his army across the changed sea routes to First Landing.
Nuvityn had been hoping for a Treant or some wonders at sea. Perhaps even a [Pirate] attack, but sadly, his days had been largely without event. Oh, there had been dolphins, that magical storm in the distance, ships, even Drowned Folk, who had risen to talk and trade with his famous army, but nothing extraordinary. So he had bided his time. He knew how long sea trips were.
…Which was why after two weeks, he had begun wondering how badly the sea currents were changed between Terandria and Izril. The [Captain] was a good man, Level 37. But despite his speed Skills, the winds and currents just didn’t have them seeing land. Nuvityn had accepted the man’s hospitalities and spent the time talking with Prildor and Tserre when she emerged, catching them up on recent events.
That had taken a week before he noticed his crew going to ask [Sailors] what was going on. Then Nuvityn had sensed… a problem.
Even becalmed, three weeks from the southwestern edge of Terandria to First Landing was too long. And yet, Captain Giltreder swore the winds were good and that he’d found the right currents. Yet when he deployed his spyglass and checked the stars—everything must be muddled because he could neither see shore nor figure out their location.
“It looks as if we’re only two days from First Landing. But I do not see it. And…this makes no sense, Your Majesty.”
After two days, the [Captain] showed the King of Myths his chart. It was a neat progression from Pheislant’s capital harbor to First Landing…and then onto Izril’s shores. They should have been at Invrisil by now. Nuvityn stared at the map.
“And you are sure, sir?”
There were numerous cross outs and question marks. Captain Giltreder was sweating.
“Your Majesty, I have read the position of the stars and my best [Storm Sailors] swear that they feel us going the right way—but it makes no sense! And sire—”
He looked around and lowered his voice.
“When I check the winds, and currents, I think they are too strong.”
“Due to the magical storm? Could that have thrown us off?”
“Entirely possibly, and I cast myself upon your mercy, Your Majesty. But I mean that in the sense of other ships. That Drowned Folk ship we saw—when it caught the wind, I had thought it were blowing slightly crosswise to ours, and far slower. We have had…good wind for a week now. And the current appears becalmed at times, but I feel as though we are moving faster than I think. Yet it appears still.”
For proof veritas of this, Nuvityn went to the bow and saw the waters did indeed seem calm with little wind. Yet…Captain Giltreder motioned, and, covertly, one of his [Sailors] tossed something down.
A…bucket. It splashed, then jerked out of the woman’s hands. Silently, the King of Myths spoke.
“Why covertly?”
“Because when we lower it normally, sire, it dips into the water and comes out unlike that.”
Nuvityn didn’t like the way Captain Giltreder was speaking. Nor the sudden suspicion in the back of his mind. He recalled his own feelings.
I can sense the auras of distant people, and I swear I had felt the Five Families’, though they are not royals. The same when I beheld the other great events of note. Yet I do not sense them from the right…places…
Strange. If you had a ship that appeared to be moving at a decently high-level [Captain]’s will, yet had oddities with the observable wind and stars and waters beneath you—what could muddle even the wits of a [Storm Sailor]? Only a great foe, perhaps. A Skill? A magical storm of passing weirdness?
Or maybe…
 
——
 
Magus Tserre had her rocking chair and sat in her cottage, which had folded up and sat down on the deck of The Gathering Light. Vernoue, her apprentice that Tserre had still not really acknowledged, was balancing on one foot on the rocking ship and casting spells.
“Focus, Princess. Cast one hundred spells in the hour or we’ll have to come up with a punishment for tonight.”
“I’m…not…quitting, Magus Tserre! So can you please stop trying to make me?”
Vernoue appeared distinctly seasick, but she was keeping with the magic. Tserre saw Nuvityn and his people approaching and sighed, closing her book.
“Whyever would you think I was doing that? I’m simply bringing you up to an acceptable focus. You and I have limited time. So enjoy the training we used to give [Mages] who were about to be sent to Rhir.”
Vernoue made a whimpering sound, but she turned as Nuvityn called out.
“Magus Tserre, good morning.”
“A fine day to you, King of Myths.”
She replied blandly, and everyone stared at her. Not really welcomingly. Even Nuvityn’s face was clouded.
“Is it, Magus? I have just spoken to my people, and I am troubled by some reports.”
“Oh, what might those be? I am, of course, at your service.”
He grunted.
“So you claim. Yet, Magus, it appears the interference from the magical storm still lingers. Scrying spells do not work on us.”
“Such storms are beyond any [Archmage] in power. Even Level 80 [Druids] would barely match such awe inspiring magic, Your Majesty.”
“Fair enough. Yet we are three weeks at sea when we should have been one at the longest.”
“Perhaps we are catching new currents changed by these New Lands, or the storm sent us to sea, Your Majesty. It is hard to navigate the open ocean.”
Indeed, the blue-green water around them was impossible to use to place where they were; a [Sailor]’s nightmare. Tserre pointed up.
“Without scrying spells, I suggest using the stars.”
“Which is what the good [Captains] have done. Strangely, they have not led us to shore. It almost appears, Magus, as if something odd is happening to our vessel.”
She sipped from a teacup as Vernoue stopped balancing on one foot. Now, even the 5th Princess of Calanfer was staring at Magus Tserre. But the old half-Elf’s face didn’t move one whit.
“Disturbing, Your Majesty. Should I look into the issue?”
It was Prildor who sighed.
“Tserre…”
“Yes, Prildor? I require some kind of word aside from my name.”
The half-Elf stared blandly at her two chickens until Nuvityn spoke.
“Magus Tserre. Would you kindly drop whatever illusions you are casting? I order it by the Kingdom of Myths. An authority you may not well recognize. But by our pact—I would consider it the bare minimum to keep trust.”
His eyes glinted as he folded his arms. Voreca, Miihey, Andromeda, the leaders of Erribathe’s warriors all gazed at Tserre. She just sipped from her teacup and glanced off the portside bow.
“Oh, very well.”
She didn’t snap her fingers or tap her cane or…one second, the waters behind her were bright, clear, and calm. The next?
Rain hit Vernoue in the face. Rain—and she saw land. Dry land. Arid. Yellowed, not the greens she had expected, or First Landing’s harbor she recalled from being a girl. The geography was the wrong color. Yellow and…
Sandy.
Sand, which as some people might observe, got everywhere. But which was also more endemic, more common, to a certain continent than, say, Izril. The rain hit Captain Giltreder in the face, and he blinked at the distant shoreline. Only visible thanks to extreme magical magnification spells. Perhaps still days from the ships reaching shore. But they were here instead of…
Giltreder keeled over backwards onto the deck. Nuvityn’s head turned, slowly, and then he stared at the city in the distance. It had a harbor, yes. Even ships. But…Tserre spoke.
“I believe rations are getting low, given our numbers and the unexpected voyage. Perhaps we should put ashore, Your Majesty?”
“Tserre. Where—is this?”
Prildor choked, and King Nuvityn stared at the distant flags. He eyed the crowns united under one larger one, the dry ground, and then turned his head.
Tserre sat there as the port city of Medain drifted past them. She smiled behind the teacup she raised to her mouth, and only Vernoue, open-mouthed in horror, saw her expression.
“Incredibly, we appear to be closer to Ceria than I thought. We might as well ask about her.”
Then, it occurred to the King of Myths that he might have erred, prevailing on an ancient mage of old. Magus Tserre had appeared entirely reasonable, willing to put his desires before her own pressing obligations.
He really should have remembered what old damn [Mages] were like.

10.73 H (2026-08-15)
