“Compression fracture, two places. Idiot.”
“Nasty. Pisces, go help the poor bugger out.”
The Horns were getting out of the carriage and stretching, and Pisces did indeed stride over and hear the wail of a woman’s voice.
“Help! My legs! You damn fools, help!”
She was screaming at two people standing on the wall above and clearly not willing to jump down and break their legs. Pisces cast [Featherfall] and hopped down…he saw a woman clutching at her legs.
“Excuse me, I am a [Necromancer]. I can heal—”
The woman stopped screaming, did a double take when she saw him, and raised her hands.
“B-Bane Pisces? I don’t own slaves! I thank you, but if you just help me—”
She had a dagger out, but not for him. He realized she was sawing at her broken legs, despite the pain. She was trying to remove the stitching—
Right, Stitch-folk rules. Bemused, he took the dagger, gingerly severed the strings, and her legs became cloth the moment they were cut. Cloth with broken white fabric sticking out from the brown ‘skin’, he saw.
The woman, who it turned out was a [Trader], had new legs she pulled out and sewed on in a trice. There was some blood on her clothing, and she was clearly shaken.
“Nerrhavia’s bones, that hurt! My best legs too! Agh, and to embarrass myself in front of a famous adventurer no less! I thank you, sir. If I were Human, I’d need your magic. One wonders how anyone does without cloth for flesh.”
She stood, and he had to own, he was impressed.
“Stitch-folk bodies are certainly far more adaptable and easy to repair than Human ones, Miss?”
She bowed.
“Trader Hexata, Bane! And if you need for knickknacks, curios, interesting items, I will go across Nerrhavia’s Fallen for my clients! And if my two idiotic brothers would deign to come down and introduce themselves?”
They had a ladder by now and tumbled down it. Hexata and her two older brothers were a funny trio. Not the most well-to-do. Scrappy in a vaguely Octavia way, Pisces decided. They were much taken with him and chatted openly.
“You say Stitch-folk bodies are all that much better, Scourge, but our limbs fray and wear down a hundred times faster than yours. We need to restuff or repair an arm in but a month whereas your flesh heals.”
“Constant repair vs a permanent body. Tradeoffs; I do understand. Even so, one of my teammates nearly lost her arms to infection. When I think of that—”
Pisces recounted Yvlon’s battle with her infected arms as Hexata, Grulive, and Xomet listened with rapt interest. Hexata stared at Yvlon herself as the Silver Killer landed on the ground next to Colth; he’d leapt down easily, and she landed on her metal foot which extended to stab the ground then arrest her fall. Ceria just slid down a ramp with the Heromakers.
“So you too have come to visit the Mad Ones then, Scourge? For any one purpose or just to see what they have cooked up this month? If I can introduce you to any—I visit them often to see what they make. And if you need anything…”
Pisces thought it might be good to have a contact like Hexata. He was taking her card when Colth swept over.
“Pisces! We’re meeting the Mad Ones—hello, excuse us. Pisces, c’mon.”
“I was just meeting Trader Hexata here—”
Pisces reached for her card as she proffered it to him with a desperate smile, but Colth moved such that he blocked her and didn’t seem to see the card. He hurried Pisces away, and Hexata sighed as Pisces twisted.
“Colth, what are—at least say hello—”
“Pisces, don’t waste your time, and therefore ours, with the small fries. She’s a Level 20 [Trader] who doesn’t even know how to get a rope. I get you like being in that Silver-ranker mentality but we don’t have time for that. Even Yvlon’s figured out who she is now.”
Pisces stared at Colth, rather offended. The [Ultimate Supporter] saw his glance and grimaced.
“Oh, now you’re all upset.”
“I just don’t think it’s fair to write off anyone for being low-level—”
“Listen, Pisces. I get it. I had the same thought, but after the ten thousandth person you meet who’s earnest, excited, and just needs a tiny bit of your time, some gold, or a favor—it gets old. You’re famous. That girl who was so excited she wanted you to sign her breasts? You’re going to meet a lot of people with that energy, and I’m warning you—it’ll burn you out. Even Eld got that, and he was a literal [Beet Farmer]. I’m trying to preserve your youthful charm.”
Pisces understood Colth’s point on some level. But he couldn’t help but snap back.
“Wouldn’t it be better if you let me wear out such feelings on my own?”
Colth glanced at him, and Delitandra half turned from where the Horns were talking to a gaggle of odd-looking people.
“Maybe. But it sucks seeing someone make the same mistakes, Pisces. Perhaps that was an earnest young [Trader] who just wanted to strike a deal. But the first one who takes your money or tries to sell you under the river—we’re trying to keep your innocence. Dead gods, is this how Larra and the others felt about me?”
Colth just shook his head, sighing. Pisces didn’t know what to say to that, so he sniffed and met another group of the King of Destruction’s famous vassals.
The Mad Ones.
 
——
 
A question for you. Flos Reimarch, King of Destruction. Famed for ruling all of Chandrar and having countless mighty vassals who had as-yet not joined him.
Like the Monks of Sottheim or the Loquea Dree. Each one whose capabilities were such that they put other forces to flight. Yet in his conquests, his battles with nations to re-establish his empire, he had betimes bemoaned his lack of good, standing forces.
Wished the Rustängmarder were with him, for instance. Or Amerys. Or…the Mad Ones.
Out of all of his vassals, not once had the King of Destruction invoked groups such as the Monks of Sottheim except maybe in a passing comment about high-level staff fighters or experts in childrearing. Yet he had spoken of the Mad Ones a hundred times more than other groups.
Why? It occurred to Pisces to question why his team had been asked about the subject, and that curiosity had taken them to the place where Nerrhavia’s Fallen had begrudgingly allowed the famous group to settle. He understood they were, well, eccentrics.
[Alchemists], [Inventors], [Mechanics]—crafters who had formed a kind of commune, but who were so unpredictable, so prone to making things explode, that even regular [Alchemists] wouldn’t hang out with them.
His guess would be that they’d be like Octavia after three nights without sleep, or mini-Salisses. Full of that energetic chaos, unable to sit still. He was…sort of right?
They had a lot of energy, and once you got past the relatively deserted area around the walls, you ran into tents. Some freestanding buildings, but mostly tents. Clearly pitched a long time ago; people had altered them to stitch two together, formed a walkway between another, and there was patching indicating where holes had been made.
For instance, one wooden building appeared, well, cheap. Not bad, but Pisces suspected it had holes, and the wood wasn’t all one type of board. It was clearly cobbled together from scrap; he’d associate it with a poor district in old Celum.
But one wall was made of steel or some metal, a huge, vaguely round splash of material that looked like the wood in texture and was clearly tough; pockmarks indicated impacts against it. The entire building was a microcosm of the Mad Ones’ camp.
Improvisation, chaos, a lack of great funding, and occasionally something crazy you had to glance twice at. The inhabitants of each building had the same vibe.
Most were dirty. Sand blew over their compound with some regularity, and if not that, then the fumes from other alchemical works or just grease and dust created a second layer of skin on them. They were a bunch of species—though Stitch-folk and Human predominated—and wore overalls or vests with lots of pockets for tools. But where they diverged from the quintessential mad genius look was the magic.
A lot of them were spellcasters. Pisces saw more varieties of spell schools and magic he’d never conceived of across the camp in a single minute than he’d seen in all of Wistram.
Weird magic too. Like…he saw someone bending a strand of fire magic in a complete circle with a wand. Then tying a knot in it. Utterly free-form—and the fiery knot blew up in a miniature explosion, but the young [Mage] had already taken cover behind a bench. He popped up and chewed on a biscuit, mildly singed.
“Damn, it keeps blowing up like that. But I need a knot here, or something close. Anyone know knitting or needlework?”
He called out, and a few others turned. One raised a hand, but didn’t come over; the Garuda was forging something at an anvil.
“I do, but what’s the project?”
“I want to shape raw magical threads together.”
“In a tapestry or something?”
The Garuda leaned out of his open-air forge, growing interested as he pushed some goggles up. A few more of the other crafters glanced over, visibly interested, but the young man shook his head.
“No, I’m thinking more like a statue. Or an art piece, but not linked up like a tapestry. I’m trying to make a spell that’s beautiful. Any takers?”
The Garuda shook his head and slapped his goggles back down without a word. The other crafters went back to work, and the young man sighed. He went back to his task and formed another circle in the air. Added a different kind of twist in the fiery thread, prepared to dive…and when the strands didn’t detonate, added another circle with a pleased look.
Pisces had never seen someone free-cast like that. Holding magic in the air was hard as hell. He stared as the young man kept working. Two circles now, and he was adding more magic around it, giving it contouring, details. He was, in fact…
Making a pair of breasts. Pisces stared at the floating magical ‘artwork’ as a passing Mad One scowled at the image. But the young man kept working with the dogged persistence of someone who believed that a fire-spell in the image of a naked young lady was a worthwhile addition to the world.
“I love these guys.”
Ceria Springwalker was grinning from ear to ear as she took in the camp. Their guide was a Stitch-man in his mid-fifties. He had some white hair and was bald except for a frizz of hair like a halo around his head. And from the grease stains on his fingers, he was more of a mechanical sort. His name was Otevious, and he had served the King of Destruction himself.
“This is all the freeform stuff, guests. Don’t mind them. The better, more structured projects with funding are more interior. Anything’s a project out here. You get silly ideas from the younger lot like this all the time. ‘Is my Potion of Excellent Sensations working? I need fifteen lovely ladies to volunteer for me!’”
He shook his head at the foolishness of youth. Yvlon gazed at the panoply of people working around her. Something exploded, and she reacted instantly, making a shield out of her arms. She blocked a tiny, glowing piece of metal that had nearly gone through Ceria’s nose. The half-Elf recoiled. Pisces himself hadn’t reacted fast enough.
Otevious had leaned out of the way of the shrapnel.
“Right, that reminds me. Barriers up, guests? Unless you’re a [Warrior], of course. I think we have some rings…nope, we either used the last bunch up or tried upgrading them. If you’re killed by something exploding, that’s the risk you take. Even Flos knew that. Sorry, I’m all over today. Who are you again?”
Refreshingly, he had no idea who they were. Ceria held out a hand.
“Ceria, Horns of Hammerad?”
“You sound like adventurers.”
“Er, yes. Gold-rank? We conquered the Village of the Dead? Reached the Crossroads of Izril? That’s Yvlon, the Silver Killer. Killed the Champion of Monarchs?”
Otevious blinked at Ceria, then put on a disingenuous smile.
“Charmed, I’m sure! The Champion of Monarchs you say? Never liked…her. If we need any silver killed or crossroads found, I’m sure we’ll call on you two!”
That took the wind neatly out of Ceria’s sails, and Pisces hid a smile. Otevious led them onwards.
“No offense, truly. But we don’t, uh, pay attention to current events as much. Unless it catches our eye. We have one of those things everyone yammers about in camp. Scrying orbs, right. Television? Weird name. Someone new to our camps was familiar with it, but the nomenclature felt wrong to me. Wistram wouldn’t name it that. Um…oh, right, it’s from another world.”
This time, all the Horns glanced at him, and Otevious smacked his forehead.
“The entire Earth wing of studies. Too much damn funding for all that. Was that why you were here? You said Flos sent you.”
“We’re here on behalf of a number of prospective clients, sir. May I ask if we can help by providing our unique skillsets? I’m a [Supporter], and we have a high-level [Necromancer], [Cryomancer], and a [Warrior] with living metal arms!”
Colth leapt in, clearly trying to ingratiate himself with Otevious. He obviously thought this would arouse the man’s passions, but Otevious glanced over the Horns and shrugged.
“How long are you here for?”
“Er, we could be here a day or two—”
“Pass. I’m out of [Eureka Moments] for the month, and unless you find someone who wants to gamble on a breakthrough in a day, you won’t find much interest. Again, no offense, but if you’re not going to put in at least four months’ time, using someone with high-level anything is pointless. You’ll be gone soon, and then we’re back to square one.”
What an interesting perspective. It made sense, but that took Colth out of the running as he recalibrated. Pisces and Yvlon got nudges to go humiliate themselves, and so Pisces thought and tried next.
“We are here at the request of His Majesty of Reim and the Quarass, asking for you to relocate your camps to their nations, Inventor Otevious. Naturally, I imagine this is a tricky political matter, and we do not wish to endanger your camp. Is there a governing body here we should speak to? We have made no promises other than to carry the requests.”
Even if the Quarass had a good incentive for Colth to help her. Otevious blinked at Pisces and then scratched at his head.
“Governing body? Sure, there’s the Funding Committee. But we’ve fielded both monarchs’ requests for, what, nearly two years now? Ten for the Quarass, I think. Flos came back and wanted us to join him, which has some appeal, but then we’re at war, and he always wants the weapons. Other things too, and the funding was appealing, but…I think we’re just going to let him come to us.”
“Er, pardon?”
Otevious waved his hands around.
“Tell him what we told—wait, we never hired a Courier did we? Oops, no wonder he’s mad. Right, well, this is perfect. Tell him that we’re delighted he’s back, we’d love to take his gold—when he conquers this section of Nerrhavia’s Fallen, we’ll get right back to it! If he had any big projects in mind, we’ll get a few concepts running. How’s that?”
Pisces’ mouth stayed open, and he stepped back. Once he conquers…Ceria raised one finger to her temple, a grin of delight on her face. Colth grabbed it.
“Er, Master Otevious. You’re willing to work for the King of Destruction? What about Germina?”
“Oh, sure. The Quarass is a wonderful collaborator if you can get her to sit still on anything. It’s like asking a Djinni for hints; she’ll get you ahead, but it’s bad to rely on her. We’re down for both.”
“Which one?”
“Whichever gets here. Or offers us a lot of gold to move. Actually—if the Quarass could pick us up with a Djinni? Lift the entire camp up and just move it around? We had a prototype regarding that. Hey, Yerelia! Guests! Where’s your prototype concept for the House-mover?”
They entered the inner camp where there were better buildings with actual enchanted walls and fewer people. A woman stepped out from working on a complex series of magical objects floating in a glass aquarium. Some spell was sucking the light out so they moved in a black void. She lifted something off her face—odd monoculars over both eyes with multiple colored lenses which could flip into place to magnify her vision.
Yerelia was another Stitch-woman, albeit one with one hand which was a Gnollish paw, the other being a tentacle that split into five digits, like fingers. She also had digitigrade legs and walked out in a fashion Pisces found fascinating—and wondered if it was cumbersome. The Horns stared as the woman called out.
“That old thing? Buried in my files; we got rid of the actual prototype, remember? What’s with the guests? Nice magic on them. Recruits? Hired help? Did the committee finally pay for a good [Mage]?”
“Nope. Just lookers.”
“Damn.”
“They might send us all to Germina or Reim, though. Got a preference on which one?”
The woman leaned on a curious object that looked like some kind of wrench married to a needle; it was altering magic around it, Pisces realized. And it had a strand of magic in it? He peered at it as Ceria squinted.
“Um…I’ll take…Germina. Probably. They have better finger foods. And poisons.”
“Poisons, I forgot! Put my vote in for poisons too. If you’re taking votes when you abduct or transport us, that is.”
Otevious snapped his fingers and turned to the Horns. Ceria’s smile seemed forced this time.
“Er, you don’t mind if we put sacks over all your heads and cart you north?”
The two [Inventors] stared at her. Otevious scratched at his chin.
“I’d hope it was faster and a bit more elegant than that. But we’re hardly going to fight adventurers who kill silver, are we? Just make sure you have us disarm all the active experiments of a certain type or they might explode when you take us. Even in Chests of Holding. Oh, and you’re bringing our experiments, right?”
He seemed actually worried there, and a few more crafters came over, mostly in their later years. Pisces presumed these were the ones who could duck or knew how not to explode themselves.
“Still working on your Earth projects, Yerelia? How’s it going? Who’re the lookers?”
“Adventurers. They’re going to kidnap us to Germina or Reim—they haven’t decided yet.”
“Damn, I was working on a project—did they say when?”
The Horns were treated to several stares, and Colth opened his mouth only for a woman holding a canister of what might have been magicore to open it and check on something.
“Can I persuade you to wait until Beithday? I’ve got a few projects I’d love to finish up if we’re getting kidnapped again. Want to try this one?”
She offered the canteen around, and everyone instantly refused. Pisces hesitated long enough for her to shove it in his face, and it turned out to be not magicore but…soup.
Soup with at least some magic in it. He eyed it, and Pisces, who had stared down at Erin’s magical cooking, feared to imbibe whatever this was. It had a sludgy quality to it. If colors could melt…the woman sighed and took a bite of whatever it was. Instantly, she spat it out.
“I’ve poisoned myself. Let me know about the kidnapping when we get that sorted.”
She walked off. Colth was trying to clarify.
“We’re not kidnapping anyone. We’re just asking on behalf of Their Majesties—”
“Didn’t we tell Flos we were waiting to be conquered?”
“We forgot to pay the Courier, remember? We had them doing exercises instead before they got mad and left.”
“Right, damn. No wonder he sent this lot. Are they threatening to kill us if we don’t go?”
“Not yet…”
Ceria was laughing too hard to do anything. Colth had the colorful expression of a man trying to up his weirdness levels to keep up. Pisces was just hesitating and wondering if Erin would have fit in or been blown away by them. Even the Heromakers were clearly not sure what to do.
They trained heroes, not dealt with madfolk. In the face of all this, every head turned to Yvlon Byres.
The Silver Killer of Izril, who had been yawning a bit. Pisces thought the camps were fascinating, if obscure, but he supposed Yvlon had no appreciation for it. Ksmvr would have loved this. She blinked at him, hesitated as Colth and Ceria nudged her, and sighed when she realized it was her turn.
Without much faith in herself, she lifted a hand.
“Hello, my name is Yvlon Byres. Some may call me the Silver Killer of Izril, but the truth is, I’m hardly so dangerous. I got my name fighting in the Coliseum of Monarchs in Chandrar, and my team has fought everything from Adult Crelers to monsters in dungeons like the Ruins of Albez.”
She held out a hand, and Pisces’ eyes rolled up into his head. But the inventors turned, eyed her, and Otevious shook her hand.
“Splendid introduction. What rank of adventurer?”
“Er, Gold.”
“Thank you. I’m Otevious, [Inventor of Mechanical Genius]. Some may call me the Madman of Oletto, but the truth is I didn’t kill that many people. I got my name exploding three buildings, but casualties were minimal.”
Another hand from Yerelia.
“Pleased to meet you too. Yerelia, [Engineer of Magic’s Grasp], on the Funding Committee. Some may call me Yerla, but that was a nickname when I was a child. I don’t think I’ve killed anyone except monsters, and half of those were accidental.”
Yvlon’s face grew more colorful as the others shook her hand. The rest of her team was clutching at their sides. Pisces was shaking in agony, trying not to laugh, and Colth was crying.
Yvlon appeared ready to kneecap the lot of them, but she bared her teeth and then glanced around the camp.
“Very delighted, I’m sure. Before we figure out about, um, kidnapping, which I don’t think we’re doing, may I ask about this funding I keep hearing about? Are the Mad Ones in need of financing? We do have a bit of gold, and if you had anything to sell, we’d be interested.”
The inventors paused a second and Otevious squinted at Yvlon.
“Gold-rank adventurers don’t tend to have that much. What’s your budget, a thousand gold pieces?”
“Er…we could spend more than that, I think?”
Yvlon glanced at Pisces, and he tried to recall how much the Horns actually had in the Merchant’s Guild. That, it transpired, was enough for one of the other Mad Ones to eye them.
“[Investor Appraisal].”
He looked the Horns up and down, then ran off. The other Mad Ones turned—saw the Garuda tear into a tent, and come running out with one of his inventions. Otevious’ eyes brightened, and Yerelia rubbed her hands together.
As it so happened, Yvlon had said the magic words.
Funding. Instantly, two dozen more Mad Ones emerged from their workplaces to welcome their favorite guests!
Paying customers. Pisces blinked, then saw Yvlon smile smugly and put her hands on her hips. The rest of the Horns half-glared at her as the Silver Killer met their eyes. Then Yvlon yawned again.
 
——
 
“It’s all about funding. No one has much gold, and if we have any, it’s either spent on necessities or it goes to the Funding Committee.”
Yerelia was a lot more willing to spend time with the Horns after realizing they might give the Mad Ones gold. It was remarkably straightforwards; the Mad Ones didn’t care for fame or levels if it didn’t help them.
But gold was gold. The reason they liked the Horns was, well, because the Horns were easy marks.
“You’re not lookers, you’re spenders. Very important difference there. We get [Traders]—”
“Ah, like Miss Hexata?”
Pisces was standing there with Yvlon as Yerelia worked on whatever strange Earth-creation she was about. She was delicately maneuvering magical strands together in the weird tank, which was actually a fishtank she’d converted into this project. Ceria and Colth were meeting with a lot more people, trying to figure out who was in charge.
Good luck to them; Pisces doubted there was anything for either one to make sense of in terms of actual leadership. Even Ceria’s circlet would be flummoxed by this place because it was a well and true commune.
Having been part of one himself, he knew how it worked. Some people were in charge, of course, but the rest? Chaos. Yerelia was as good as anyone to talk to since she was on this Funding Committee, and Yvlon was so out of her depth she was sticking by Pisces out of pure desperation.
The unlucky [Trader] was known to the Mad Ones by name at least; Yerelia glanced up.
“You know Hexata?”
“We just met. She broke her legs jumping into the compound—”
“Oh, the walls. Yes, they make them higher each time something blows up or escapes. We’ve had to move eight times. But Nerrhavia’s Fallen gives us a budget. We spend it, so we always need more gold.”
“Why would Nerrhavia’s Fallen give you a budget? My impression was that you were considered terrible nuisances. Yisame said you were a stain on any nation you came across.”
Yvlon interrupted, and Pisces winced at the blunt statement, even by her standards, but Yvlon clearly had the lay of the land here. Yerelia just smiled.
“That is the position any monarch would take, but we have our uses. There was some kind of plague of those damn beetles. Oresects? It annoyed us so much everyone stopped working on our projects to figure out what the Great Sage had made and create a cheaper solution.”
Yvlon and Pisces stared. The Mad Ones were responsible for ending the Oresect plague? Yerelia just nodded absently.
“Not by creating the mixture that kills the bugs, of course. That was already done. We just devoted time to taking one of the ingredients—Kalaab seeds—and finding a cheaper solution. That’s all we needed to do. That’s how you win wars. Against bugs, people. Economize the cure. Well, if that didn’t work, we were going to create a Rustshredder spell, but it would have been less effective.”
—There it was. Just for a second, Pisces saw something. He hesitated, and Yvlon’s head rose like a woman who had just seen a threat. For a moment—they eyed each other.
“So you do understand war, Miss Yerelia? You served Flos?”
The [Engineer] glanced up again.
“Of course I did. All the older members did. It was good for levels, but we died fast too once the [Assassins] realized who made his weapons. If we’re not keen on joining him, it’s simply because all his inventions go one way. Nor did we find something meaningful in what we made, by and large. Because most of it was just war.”
“Like what?”
Pisces didn’t know the legacy of the Mad Ones well, so Yerelia just thought a moment, before snapping her gloved fingers.
“What might you know? Ah, the Tripvine Bag, for example. The same one I trust you have used, or at least, seen as an adventurer.”
It took Pisces a moment to realize what she meant, then he stared.
“Your people invented the modern Tripvine Bag?”
“A more effective version of it, yes. Tottenval’s seeds were hugely effective, but it was in how they were packed and organized. A shame; when he was alive, they were practically a sidearm in every [Soldier]’s arsenal. Terrifying to fight, I’m told. Astounding tactics came of his plants; any cavalry charge turned into dead animals. You could tie down a formation and just ignore them or shoot them dead while your forces advanced. That was worth making—to some. I wasn’t responsible for more than the bag and configuration. I’m no [Mage], you see.”
Yerelia recounted this all distantly. Pisces blinked. He stared at the tool she was using and protested.
“But you’re using magic right now! This entire creation—”
Little orbs were hanging in the pitch blackness, made out of magic, and it was so adept he couldn’t see the details of the delicate mana weaving. But Yerelia just smiled, and here her eyes did light up. She tapped the monoculars on her face.
“Ah, but that’s because I’m using this tool. I invented it myself. I can neither see nor use magic, Adventurer Pisces. I was born without the talent. But I have always wanted to make magic, so these lenses let me see it. This tool lets me manipulate magic very carefully.”
“But these are spells! You can make a spell with—”
Pisces had heard of expert [Mages] using their fingers to adjust magic. Never someone creating a spell from ambient magic. He watched Yerelia tease another strand out of the air, and she nodded.
“Yes. It’s not fast nor simple. Even now, I can injure myself greatly, so there is no mass appeal for this device. I didn’t argue my case hard in front of the Funding Committee, but they’ve seen the value of it.”
“Giving a non-[Mage] the ability to see and manipulate magic isn’t worth money? How does this committee work?”
Yvlon was incredulous, but Yerelia laughed.
“I can see why His Majesty took an interest in you. Let me see if you can understand how we think. Outsiders seldom do. Yes, my creation is valuable—to me. Yes, it is revolutionary—again, to me. But consider that it only gives me the abilities of any Level 5 [Mage]. Is there a benefit in making more? Yes…but is it worth spending the time, the resources, to refine this process? To make something that will be used across the world? For now—no. When this tool can do what a [Mage] cannot do easily, then it will be ready.”
She held up the curious grabbing device that held magic like thread, and Pisces thought he saw it. It was not a lack of passion; it was in Yerelia’s eyes, her evident pride in her work. But it was a kind of ruthless efficiency.
I am not yet ready to change the world with this. And the way she had spoken of the Tripvine Bag…that was the quality of Mad Ones that set them apart from a casual [Mad Genius], Pisces realized. They understood the difference between the glorious bang and something that would change the world.
The woman went on, casual.
“I was part of the teams that worked on alchemical items, as I hadn’t finished this design. Not all of what we made is still in use, of course; the designs change and alter, but I am proud of it. Potions of Blast, healing potion bottles—”
“Wait, wait, you made all of that?”
Yvlon was in disbelief, but again, she was mistaking the woman. The [Engineer] snorted again.
“Of course not! We just created the version that was most effective. You see? We experimented to make lower-cost versions of each formula, altered designs for the King of Destruction’s army. You know how you can smash a healing potion on someone? Who do you think made it so the glass shatters yet won’t break from sitting on it?”
She tapped her chest and grinned. Then she went on, sighing.
“Spells too. So much basic spellcraft like making a Rune of Cooling last another week—you come from Pallass, yes? Some of our designs they used on their ballistae. It was damned hard to get ahold of samples, but then we churned them out! The Drakes were always so confused at how we made them, but once you actually break one down…well, it’s teaching a generation to think without the need for Skills. Their Engineering Guild is a fine asset; if we’d worked with them, we’d have had the Flying Gnoll in the air a decade ago!”
That was the fearsome power of the Mad Ones, Pisces realized. Their hands were so subtle in how it had changed the world. On a hunch, he asked, and she grinned at him.
“No, not spell scrolls. The blend of papyrus or parchment used for it was long set before us. But His Majesty did need plenty, so we set up fields and tools to make more. Most of it still lies in Belchan; doubtless, he needs for more [Mages], but he will not ever need parchment again, unless those idiots burnt down all the workshops.”
Monsters of efficiency. That was the Mad Ones’ power. Mind you—they didn’t dislike the glorious bangs, either. Yerelia was chuckling as she recounted some other stories for the two Horns.
“And yes, sometimes he just wanted something to explode, so we’d all take a break and design five different spells or explosives for him! Then he’d have it hurled by a trebuchet, or Takhatres’ people would drop it on the enemy. Ah, those were sights indeed. Flos had too much money. We grew spoiled under his rule. We’d make something that exploded or a living magicore serpent that he’d unleash on his foes. True, it’d crater a hole through an enchanted wall, but it was never worth the cost, you see? It scared his foes, but this is better.”
This humble community at the edge of Nerrhavia’s Fallen? She nodded in response to Pisces’ words.
“Yes. Oh, we need more gold, but we are making things that can be scaled up, that are needed. Things not meant for war or combat alone—there were some ways in which they served more than that, but it drew too much focus. With too much gold, we make one-shot marvels, and that’s fun for a moment. They will not reach Terandria’s shores. Knowledge will. So this is my project. It has no commercial value, but it came with our understanding of Earth, so I have the funding for it for now.”
She hung another orb in the aquarium, and now Pisces and Yvlon focused on it. They peered at the floating ball of red with white clouds spinning through it.
“What is this, Engineer?”
“A planet. A simulation of interstellar bodies; I’m trying to approximate the exact gravity and flow of stars in this other world. Purely so we have a baseline to measure with. Some of the ideas these children come up with are fantastical, but we cannot tell if we’re making what they want too well or if their rules are different. Gravity, for instance. They claim it’s the same as their home, but they also claim their world is three times smaller than ours. Something is off—we want to know what. A shame we don’t have a map of our world, but, well…would you like to see how they’re supposed to orbit the sun?”
Yerelia pointed, and Pisces and Yvlon stared at each other. Their mouths opened.
The who now?
 
——
 
A young woman was standing behind a glowing barrier as Otevious worked on his projects, which included more magic than Yerelia’s had. He was peering at a canister of something that everyone was staying away from, using metal arms to manipulate it as he took the lid off.
“So, for the sake of our guests, you are telling me that the key to advanced pyrotechnic heat is not more magic. At least, in your world it is not. The secret that Dwarves hold over us in their Dwarfsteel is a more fundamental reaction. More fundamental than even alchemy—which we shall separate from ‘chemistry’ as two differing fields. One uses magic. The other…the most natural forces. Elemental.”
“Elements, yes, sir. And this might work because it’s not one exact combination—”
“It’s the reaction that matters. That goes against some alchemical truths that hold that it is usually one set of combinations that are incredibly difficult to replicate. Magic refuses to be put in a neat equation, often. But this? Once lit, this will create an extreme—what’s the word?”
“Exothermic reaction, sir. B-but it’s just a theory! A game theory, even! I don’t remember how it works—”
Otevious had a visor over his face, and he snapped it down with a maniacal grin.
“It’s a nice theory. Let’s test it. Three, two, one—”
He lit something. Whatever it was, it took a second to ignite the mixture of reddish dust that Colth and Ceria were peering at, but then there was a flare. An explosion of light, and Pisces saw the canister turn red-hot.
Something was burning in the center of it. Burning, and it did not go out despite not having…a flame? It was so damn hot that Pisces saw it melting the metal canister. Yvlon shifted, eying the metal, and stared.
“That’s no fire I’ve ever seen. Is it magic…?”
“It’s not magic.”
Colth responded quietly. The burning mixture tilted outwards as Otevious used his metal claws to tilt the mixture onto a variety of substances. Most of which the burning metal ate through—fast.
“It’s working! It’s wooooorking!”
He was shouting in delight. A crowd of Mad Ones were all watching, nodding—not cheering, but watching. And the young woman whispered.
“Thermite.”
“Non-magical thermite. Alchemists can produce the same reaction, but we did it without. No fire crystals. No salamander skins. I’m calling this—victory for replicable materials from Earth. Victory for their elemental table—I’m requesting money for a [Mage] capable of casting memory spells.”
One of the other Mad Ones was shouting as people took notes. Colth interrupted quietly.
“Victory for modern warfare?”
Otevious was lecturing the other Mad Ones about this compound. Which apparently, refused to go out when smothered. In fact, water would just make everything explode if you tried to pour it on this stuff. Pisces shivered as he imagined that being thrown on them. But to his surprise, the [Inventor] just turned and shook his head.
“It’s a finicky combination, Adventurer Colthei. If we can make a flask of it that detonates, I imagine it’ll scare Stitch-folk. Might be used to intimidate the poor Hemp-folk. I’ll vote against manufacturing it if that’s the only use-case. But even if we made it—and cheap—so what?”
He pointed at Pisces.
“I knew I remembered you lot somewhere. Liscor, yes? We were trying to buy that acid stuff. Don’t you get it from a fly over there?”
Pisces jumped.
“We do, sir, but—”
Otevious was taking apart the thermite, removing the unburnt material to stop the burning reaction as the young woman peeked over.
“I was going to breed some, but no one would transport the things. And a [Druid] we consulted said it might ‘spread across habitats and wipe out natural populations’. Bah. That’s acid in a jar at almost no cost. This is an expensive blend of metals you need to grind up. No comparison.”
In his books, acid beat thermite. At least in the case of throwing it in people’s faces. However, Otevious grunted.
“The real use for this isn’t pure violence. I’m thinking…if you slap a simple illusion over this? It’s a non-magical powder that melts locks, and the Acid Fly acid cannot do that. A [Rogue]’s friend. I want to test this on enchanted locks. Tell the Funding Committee that if we make a workable vial-sized prototype, we’ll have money coming in from every [Rogue] in the world.”
In a minute, he’d talked himself out of making a weapon of war and instead pivoted to a way to rob vaults. There it was again; Colth wore a genuinely unsettled expression as he tried to peer at the recipe list. He met Pisces’ eyes and nodded.
These people are actually dangerous. Pisces realized the occasional bang and noise from the exterior of the Mad One’s commune was a false illusion. The real danger was here.
“Alright, young lady, we’ve earned our funding for today. Let’s get some food, and you write up that report. Then we’ll chat about the uses of this stuff from your world.”
Otevious let his apprentice go, and Pisces saw the Earther dash off. He had to ask.
“Where did she come from?”
“Oh, we found her. That’s Botane. It was…a year ago? My, how time flies. Come, come, prospective clients. Let me offer you some food.”
The man led the way to some tables, and Yerelia had seen Yvlon too. They sat the Horns down and presented them with some actually quite good food.
…That someone had run from the city. And which also cost—Pisces nearly spat out his bite of pita bread filled with savory meat when Yvlon whispered the price in his ear.
“Eighty gold coins?”
The two inventors beamed at him.
“Nothing but the finest for our guests.”
They were charging the Horns for their food at insane markups! They really just wanted money, didn’t they? Otevious didn’t deny it either as he chuckled.
“All of this costs gold, guests. Plenty of it! Even if I were to make my rogue’s favorite device, I’ll give 70% of the profits to the Funding Committee.”
“They take your profits?”
Yvlon was aghast by the worst-sounding deal in the world, but again, the old Stitch-man just chuckled.
“We don’t care about personal wealth. Far better that I have anything I earn taken away so it can be allocated. No one gets all of what they want unless they have something truly, truly revolutionary. But by combining forces, we can all keep this going. Another plate?”
Pisces wisely refused a second helping, but he felt like this trip was illuminating if nothing else. Even Flos Reimarch hadn’t been as interesting as this group. Overwhelming, yes, but he felt like the Mad Ones were making things that would truly change the world. Colth was the skeptical one.
“May I ask how you met Miss Botane, Inventors? One doesn’t just find…Earthers. Larra never found one, and her inn moves.”
“Larracel the Haven doesn’t seem interested in people who aren’t above Level 40 or rich, Colth.”
Pisces returned softly, and Colth hesitated and bit his tongue before nodding.
“But the free bread—argh, but I don’t believe an Earther just pops into your camp. Did she seek you out?”
The [Engineer], Yerelia, was unabashedly eating the food the Horns had just paid for. She frowned.
“I think it was the scrying orbs, remember, Otevious?”
He snapped his fingers.
“It was. It was right when Wistram began mass-producing them. A few of the younger members of camp had them. Why not? Then someone—I think it was Addy?—noticed the spell was easily reversible. We didn’t like that. Cue us smashing over three dozen of the damn things and repurposing the crystal. But that got us paying attention, and we noticed weird scrying spells. Who made the sensor net?”
For a second, Yerelia stopped eating.
“Thomos.”
“Ah.”
Otevious pushed back his plate after a second. Then he swallowed and turned to the Horns.
“He built a rather impressive scrying spell detection network. It ‘caught’ spells and backtraced them. We saw who was sending and what they were searching at. We were all rather fired up about Wistram, you see. That’s when we noticed young folk getting grabbed. Botane was the fourth girl, and she was close enough that we rode out and nabbed her before anyone else did. Well, we did it with two other groups.”
Someone had been searching for Earthers? Pisces was astounded.
“How many do you have? May we meet them? We know someone—”
Colth nudged him hard, and Pisces kicked back, scowling. The secret was out! But Otevious just shook his head.
“Botane’s the only one who remains. The rest left. Or died. Whoever was after the Earthers sent [Assassins]. We suspect it was Roshal or someone connected to them. They destroyed Thomos’ scry-catcher, killed him, killed a number of our camp.”
Pisces lost his appetite abruptly. He sat there as Yerelia nodded. Both of the Mad Ones glanced across the camp towards where a gap might have been…? Someone had replaced whatever had been lost, and only they saw it.
“If it was Roshal, they wouldn’t have stopped until they got their quarry. So it wasn’t them.”
Colth’s voice had an edge to it despite his pleasant smile. But here was the last mistake he made. Otevious gave him a blank glance.
“It might have been them. We are not speculating more than we have, and the matter rests for now. It is not forgotten, Adventurer, but we are well aware of the risks of taking on a nation as we are. If the King of Destruction finds us, we will discuss it with him. Along with any other grudges we might have.”
Then he looked dangerous despite the sweat on his silly bald pate and simple inventor’s clothing. Colth frowned.
“But Roshal does not relent, sir. Believe me, they want Earthers. They wouldn’t stop at a hundred [Assassins]. They have endless Ranks.”
Yerelia pulled a plate over and took another pita sandwich and bit into it.
“So they do, young man. But even they run out of Faces. After the eleventh one we killed, they stopped. We are the Mad Ones of Chandrar. If they throw an artillery spell at us, we throw one back.”
Ah. So that was why they existed. Pisces wondered what kind of weapons the world’s greatest group of inventors had stored away. He shifted, and it was Yvlon, the Silver Killer, who sat up from where she might have been napping during the story. He frowned at her, but she gave the others a sleepy smile and said—
“On that topic, if you have anything we can use, we’ll buy it from you. At a fairer price than lunch.”
The two inventors grinned. They’d been hoping she’d say that.
 
——
 
Ceria caught up with Pisces after the second hour of being in the Mad Ones’ camp. He was essentially being given the run of their inner area. He could walk over, and one of the Mad Ones would put aside what they were doing—assuming they could—and pull out whatever they had that he thought he’d like.
More than one was open to making something for him, but then you were talking budget, timeframe, expectations…Ceria walked over and leaned on his shoulder.
“Pisces, I’m ready to go.”
He turned to her.
“Ceria, this is the most incredible camp we’ve ever been to! You haven’t even asked about all the things they’ve made, surely—”
She rolled her eyes.
“Yeah, yeah. It’s amazing, they’re smart, I can see why everyone wants them. But there’s not going to be anything for us. Colth, yes. Yvlon? Maaaaybe, but I doubt it.”
“They’ve invented amazing things, Ceria—”
She peered at him, then shrugged.
“Okay, sure. I’m gonna nap like Yvlon. Let me know when you’ve worked it out.”
So saying, Ceria wandered off to find a place to snooze, and Pisces stood there and was unaccountably stung.
That implied he was missing something. That implied she thought with her circlet she’d figured out—why not just tell him?
Dissonance, again, with his team. He would have loved nothing more than to go around, the four of them, inspecting each item and arguing whether they needed it. But his team wasn’t together.
Ceria was cocooning herself in ice magic to avoid potential accidents, snoozing in the street. Colth was running from inventor to inventor, trying to figure out what to buy with his funds. And Yvlon?
“Come now, Yvlon. This is fun! Let’s go around.”
She tried, he could tell. But she was leaning on him, and she was heavy.
“Sorry, Pisces. I didn’t get good sleep last night, I think. I’m exhausted. It is fun, it is.”
After their late night of discussing the raid, Pisces could admit he wasn’t the freshest, but he tried to put some energy into both of them.
“They have everything from weapons to homemade spells.”
“Ksmvr would love it here. Please don’t buy a home-made spell.”
That, uh, was the thing. Anything the Mad Ones made was usually a prototype, and they were fairly good about warning you that user-injury was likely if you used a spell or invention. Or…bomb.
 
——
 
Botane was helping do sales. Apparently, the young Earther had been inducted into the Mad Ones’ senior membership as a kind of roving apprentice. She was advertising to Trader Hexata, Colth, and a few other clients and exasperating one of the Mad Ones.
“And here we have an attempt at a Djinni’s magical makeup, madam and sirs, which was made of gaseous magicore infused with—”
“It’s a bomb. It explodes in a cloud, and no one knows what it does.”
The group edged back from the container made of, alarmingly, wood. The Mad One in question, Adda the Alchemist, glared.
“It’s a beautiful experiment even the Djinni admired, Botane! Ignore her. Here we have another attempt at the cumulus Djinni’s body—”
“It’s also a bomb. This one has 20% more magic in it.”
Botane indicated the item, and Colth checked his money pouch. And whispered.
“[Check Integrity]…pass on that.”
Everyone instantly passed on the second canister, and Adda put it carefully into a reinforced chest. Then put that chest in a second chest. Then loaded it into a vault in a trolley. The vault was made of steel, Pisces couldn’t help but note, and enchanted. When she lowered the entire contraption into the ground, he decided to step back.
“Very well, very well, how about one of my best flasks? Perfect for a—”
“It fills the tunnel with a long line of clouds which explode. It was another version of the Djinni bomb.”
Colth did bid on that one. He began haggling with the others as Adda pulled Botane aside.
“Young woman, I appreciate your help, but please, stop characterizing all my inventions in such simple terms!”
“If it blows up, Alchemist, it’s a bomb. They’re going to buy your works.”
“Yes, but the Djinnis loved the attempts! They said so!”
“They said it was ‘hilarious’ to get you to make more, Alchemist. Look, they’re going to buy them! Excuse me, if you like that—”
Pisces would have loved to talk to her; she had a few scars he could see, but he wasn’t sure if she’d gotten them from here or just…coming to this place. However, he was distracted because while he was not in the market for…bombs…the Mad Ones knew he had gold.
And they were a-hunting.
“Necromancer! Silver Killer! I have just the item for you. Are you tired of fighting crowds? Would you like to walk into a room and obliterate everything? This is a lovely, lovely experiment in dimensional magic that sucked in a lot of wires and a few people that I could part ways with! Now, I imagine that once you unleash this, it will let the wires out at high speed.”
Pisces eyed the orb he was being offered, and here was the thing: he didn’t want to hold the contained ball of wires.
In fact, he didn’t want to be anywhere near a compressed orb of what he was told was five hundred feet of steel wire compressed into about a baseball’s worth of space. He didn’t think it would go well in a bag of holding, and he was not sleeping in the same building with that around.
When he said that to the [Enchanter], the man was very understanding.
“Absolutely, absolutely. I would have definitely said that putting it in a bag of holding would be an amazing way to murder yourself. I assumed you wouldn’t do that. How stupid do you think the average person is…? Hold on, let me get a piece of paper to write that down.”
He hurried off, and Yvlon sat down on the ground. Pisces nudged her.
“Yvlon, are you playing into your Silver Killer role? Did you not break out into a sweat at the sight of that thing?”
“What? No, I got it’d kill us, Pisces. I’m just…I’m sorry, I really need a nap. I’m gonna lie down on Ceria.”
She got up, and he hung his head glumly. Was it that boring…? No, he thought she was genuinely tired. But what did Ceria mean? That ball of compressed space was definitely Named-rank gear. Transport and safety issues aside, he couldn’t name anyone who wouldn’t fear that thing.
The answer came to him with the next prospective seller: Otevious himself. He walked over with an object in his hands.
“This may interest you, Necromancer. I’m told you do something with the rapier? Any [Rogue] crossover, perchance?”
“I do use [Invisibility], but I’m afraid not, sir. Colth is our generalist.”
Otevious hmmed.
“A shame. Well, let me pitch you on this. I was a Gold-ranker myself as a lad. I did a bit of the old dungeon raiding, and I dabbled in smithing, magic—I’m not a huge fan of alchemy, but I’ve gotten into the chemistry stuff.”
He was a genius. Someone who made things for the joy of it as much as chasing after value. And what he’d made was…
At first, Pisces took it to be a stylish cigar case. It was made of wood, long and thin, and the real clue was the image of a cigar on it. It also said Cigar Case, which Pisces felt was slightly redundant. Otevious even slid open the case to reveal space for exactly, uh, one cigar.
Pisces was about to ask what kind of cigar it was in the spirit of things when the [Inventor] flicked his wrist and a piece of metal snapped outwards. It locked into place with a click as two other sections unfolded and locked into place.
In a moment, the man was holding a shortsword with an actual edge. Pisces stared at the composite, folding sword Otevious had made and resisted the urge to applaud wildly. The Mad One smiled at the expression on Pisces’ face.
“I did the same thing with other weaponry. But daggers are so concealable—a rapier is a long, flexible piece of metal. Very difficult, but if we made part of the blade telescoping—this is a prototype. Would you like to see my concept for a personal rapier?”
 
——
 
An unfolding sword. Pisces stared at a bunch of roughs on a piece of canvas that showed exactly how each piece could unfold and fit together to form a rapier. It would, when assembled, compress into a block of metal about as long as his hand.
It seemed insane, but Otevious was confident it could be done.
“The trick will be a magical alloy. Not too magical or it would defeat the purpose of a backup weapon. But with it you’d have a blade you could smuggle into a room. Now, the flick-action should result in the full blade. It might not be the sturdiest, but—”
A sharp rapier when no one thought you had one? Even in battle, you could surprise a foe! Pisces was like a kid looking at magical toys.
“That—that does seem useful, Master Otevious, and I would be in Chandrar for a while longer. How much would one—?”
“Five thousand gold pieces.”
Five thousand!? Then again, Pisces caught himself, he could pay for that. And this was the most interesting blade he’d ever seen. True, the handle wasn’t that impressive since it had to unfold, but when he heard that, Otevious had an idea.
“What if the handle were a mesh guard that expanded when you flicked it? I’d have to prototype it, but that’s intriguing…and I was going to make it just a piece of metal, but if you had a good cover for the item? A flute? I could potentially try to find space to make it a case—”
A custom-made unfoldable rapier. Not in a cigar case, but Pisces was rubbing his hands together.
“This—I think I may have room in my budget to commission this, Master Otevious. You see, I do not have a rapier of sufficient quality myself. This is what I am working with—”
When he showed the man the bone-metal rapier, Otevious was very interested and lifted it, remarking upon how Pisces had married ivory and steel to create a working balance.
“You say you reforged it in the middle of a battle?”
He frowned as Pisces nodded.
“I’ve been practicing spells to remake my blade in case that should happen again. [Bone Rapier]—if I have the ivory.”
He cast the spell he’d improvised, and a rapier made of bone grew from his bag of holding. It was slightly off when he held it up; a bit unbalanced. And [Flame Rapier] was good, but as Pisces had learned in his duel, dangerous to use on a foe who didn’t care for the flames. But with the metal one—
When the [Inventor] saw Pisces conjuring both rapiers, his interest and excitement in his unfoldable rapier project vanished. Pisces didn’t understand at first and thought the rapiers were just too showy or unimpressive. But the man took his unfoldable shortsword prototype, then pulled the concepts of the rapier off the drawing easel and laid them aside. He smiled.
“Well, that’s a shame. But if there’s anything else I have…?”
“I’m sorry, Master Otevious? I thought we were coming to a deal.”
Pisces was confused, but the [Inventor] just nodded to his designs.
“I can see you’re well served with improvised weaponry. I should have expected no less from a [Necromancer].”
“But your unfoldable rapier was a masterwork of metallurgy! I’d gladly pay for it!”
The style! Yet Otevious waved it off.
“It is nice. But if it’s just for vanity, pardon me if I don’t waste our time on it. That’s the problem with making weapons, you see? His Majesty was always complimentary, but…it’s just hard.”
He sat on his messy workbench, and Pisces felt a tingle on the back of his neck. Ceria’s words came back to him.
“I’m sorry, Master Otevious, I fear I’ve offended your sensibilities. I don’t follow.”
The Mad One glanced up and smiled. He explained, kindly, to Pisces what the issue was.
“I take no offense, and it’s nothing you’ve said. It’s just magic, young man. Magic is our enemy, for all we use it. It is damned hard to beat. Here, let me show you an example.”
He hunted around his workspace and then came up with a shortsword, a simple one enchanted with a cutting spell.
“A good testing benchmark. This is a simple blade, the kind any Level 20 [Enchanter] and [Blacksmith] who pour some energy into their work can make. It is…difficult to surpass. You have seen our numerous creations, many of which are deadly. Most of which cannot be mass-replicated. A benchmark we use in our camps for weapons is: is it better than a [Fireball]?”
Pisces blinked. A [Fireball]? A Tier 3 spell most [Mages] could cast…he saw Otevious gesture at the folding blade.
“That would be the work of a month. Custom prototyping, advanced metals—all for what? A blade that springs to hand when you could cast [Bone Rapier] and produce one nearly as fine in a moment. There is no point to my invention, Necromancer. In the same way, this shortsword…there is nothing I can do, from a mechanical sense, to best it. A simple cutting spell and it is sharper, more deadly than most blades. Oh, I could make a spring-loaded blade that does more damage—for single swing. But I am defeated again.”
By magic. Pisces sat down as the Mad One flipped the blade up and caught it by the hilt. He glared at the enchanted shortsword, then shrugged.
“We live in a world where magic exceeds science. Except for maybe the weapons of Earth…which I do not feel like creating as of yet. And even then, can they beat the true foe, the one that humbles us all?”
“What would that be, Master Otevious?”
The Mad Ones had magic. Otevious seemed to enjoy more mechanical projects, but Pisces had seen any number of magical creations here too. But the man just waggled his finger in Pisces’ face.
“The real foe is not just magic. I thought it was, but in truth, it is simply…rarity. Or as I put it, levels. Earth is delightful because it is not as convenient as our world, you see.”
He folded his hands together, and Pisces frowned at him.
“I don’t follow. They have achieved a higher level of technology in some ways—but they lack magic.”
Otevious nodded.
“They also lack rarity and levels. That darling girl tells me they have made weapons that erase cities. I told her we made the same. She told me hers can destroy an island. Hers could pollute a thousand miles and leave it dead. I told her we sank the Continent of Glass. Damned nations with a single spell.”
The City of Shields in the Crossroads had been destroyed when they threw a volcano at it. After turning all metal to…Pisces shivered, and Otevious nodded again.
“The difference is, Necromancer Pisces, one world does this with fundamental elements, however rare. They can mass-manufacture what they want within limits because it is a formula. Here? It is a Level 80 [Archmage]. And that is why we win and lose. That is why my sword is useless. Because on Earth, Dwarfsteel is a top-tier metal. Here? If I were to want to improve it, I’d hire someone to dig for Adamantium or better. Or find a [Smith] with [Forge of the Supreme Temperance] or some such…”
Ah, and there it was. Pisces finally got it. Otevious patted him on the shoulder, not resigned or even upset, but just…realistic. Brutally so.
“In a sense, we Mad Ones are mad because we are challenging the true rulers of creation: levels. We lose, time and time again. Your [Bone Rapier] spell has bested my invention. Well done, I applaud you on your levels, young man. I shall do better.”
Pisces twisted as Otevious put the show-weapon aside. He tried to protest, offer the man a flower because he did have great appreciation for all this.
“Master Otevious, I truly do think your blade design is inspired. An [Assassin] might make great use of it—”
“Or simply gain a Skill that lets them hide a blade. I would look into a mithril rapier, young man. Or an enchanted one. There is no point to mine, made of simple metal, because you cannot enchant sections of metal the same way. Perhaps if I made a blade with the help of a Level 50 [Enchanter], such that each segment were pure mithril and enchanted with runecraft so there was no magical interference on each part…”
Otevious sat back, speculating, then glanced up at Pisces and grinned.
“…But it would just be one. And take too much time, you see? Come, come, let’s see if anyone else has something worth you buying.”
He chivvied Pisces up, not actually that down, but then Pisces saw what Ceria’s intelligence had already led her to understand.
Aside from, well, a one-time explosive, Pisces and Ceria were [Mages]. They cast magic, and the Mad Ones were in a race against them. What they had…Pisces gazed at a spring-loaded axe hanging on Otevious’ wall.
“Does that work, Master Otevious?”
“Oh, splendidly. You hit something with it and the compressed springs explode outwards. It could down a man in plate. But it might shatter your hand, and the springs require a tool to compress again.”
The man beamed with self-evident pride for the creation he had worked so hard on. Both he and Pisces knew that aside from maybe Colth, no one would ever use it. And Colth…probably just once. It hurt Pisces’ chest a bit, because there was something in this place that made him wish it were more respected.
What the [Necromancer] didn’t realize, of course, was that he was no gifted liar. The Mad Ones had seen royalty, adventurers, the desperate, all come for their treasures. He was an unguarded fellow, for all that he was. They saw his dismay and appreciated that, of all the Horns.
Mind you, they did wish he’d spend more.
 
——
 
The problem, in the end, was that Pisces had not enough time in the Mad Ones’ camp and the mentality Colth had lectured him on.
He still spent like a Silver-ranker, which was to say, not at all. Whenever someone quoted him anything above a hundred gold pieces, he winced. Several thousand and he just didn’t have the ability to buy it.
Even useful things! The Mad Ones had magical items on sale. Not everything, not private projects, but one gamely showed him a series of enchanted pots.
“These are designed to eat magical interference and still maintain holding. How it works is that it’ll start to vibrate—then crack as you exceed your interference. You can use them as Bags of Holding or as ways to survive your equipment detonating. Store it until you have that issue.”
They were a set of six, each one designed to break in such a way that they vented the magical dissonance and bought you time to transport gear—or just made your bag of holding sixteen times larger. It was splendid, and Pisces saw the use case for them.
…He didn’t spend thirteen thousand gold pieces on them. He could have. Pisces had estimated he could spend forty-six thousand gold pieces on—on something. But when he tried to make himself buy these useful items he might well need if they found magical loot or just to carry things—
Thirteen thousand gold pieces? When it would break? After twenty minutes, the Mad One sighed. That was the problem they faced.
Trader Hexata was perusing the shops and making deals too—Pisces saw her, but she couldn’t have afforded the pots nor found a buyer. So the Mad Ones needed either something cheap and mass-producible or a big spender.
Pisces was not that kind of person. He hemmed, hawed, appreciated their work, and spent nothing, and they would have begun chasing him away, politely, for the sin of getting their hopes up but for that other annoying thing about him—he wasn’t a complete idiot.
“So this crossbow auto-cranks itself with each shot?”
“Partially. The impact reloads it slightly, but you crank the entire thing back anyways—it’s designed for someone who can use [Power Shot] or overload it. In theory, it would almost perfectly reload without magic. Which then lets you enchant it with something else instead of a reloading spell. I’ve had two Hunters from Noelictus ask about it, but the perfect buyer…”
A somewhat brusque [Tinkerer] knew Pisces wasn’t going to buy it, but she did have to show off. She was going to pointedly suggest he go to another of her associates when he murmured.
“Fascinating. You know, I had a similar design in a skeleton I made.”
“Really?”
She raised a brow, and Otevious, who had been about to go back to his workshop, half-turned. They weren’t entirely dismissive, but Pisces hesitated.
“I—it wasn’t so adept. A friend dared me to innovate, you see. And they couldn’t reload since I never figured out how to have them self-crank the crossbows or reach around inside. Too much fine control when I mass-animated them.”
“So you created a mass-animatable skeleton with a crossbow mechanism inside? Uh huh. And you’re Level 60? An honor.”
She took off a glove to shake his hand, revealing a lot of scars from accidents with wires, and he raised his hands.
“No, no! I was entirely inept, you see? My teacher at the time also speculated it was a waste of complexity because you’d be able to animate less. I—drat—let me just show you. Animate Skeleton Chestburster!”
It took him a second to remember how, but when a skeleton with the ribcage configured to blow up did arise, the two Mad Ones blinked, and then the [Tinkerer] was leaning forwards.
“Wait, this is a hurling design. Very simple, but—”
“Careful, it’ll snap and explode in your—”
Pisces grew alarmed, but she instantly disarmed the mechanism by pulling the bone that would snap outwards and spray bone shrapnel. Then Otevious was peering in as well.
“I’ve seen Goblins build similar weapons. Simple use of compressed force…but that’s the necromantic challenge, isn’t it? You can create an entire crossbow out of bone, Calice. I once saw a [Necromancer] do it in a single spell.”
“Impressive.”
“Yes, but it’s such a headache he couldn’t do it twice, and it costs more mana. This is a good mix between efficiency and complexity! Hey, Poetr, you like undead? Come see this!”
Pisces puffed up a bit as they called other Mad Ones over to see. Right up until Calice made a comment.
“I doubt it aims well, though. And the force won’t take out anyone in armor. Plenty of room to adapt; is this the first trial? How many iterations did you go through?”
“I, ah—well, this one worked, and I’ve barely used them in combat—”
Their looks of appreciation became ones of sardonic exasperation instantly. Pisces lifted his hands.
“It wasn’t a viable concept, and I have Skeleton Champions!”
“Well, if you kept it here, it wasn’t viable. Far be it from me to tell a [Necromancer] his business. How many undead have you created that are new? I’d love to see them.”
“Well, ah, new—”
Poetr slapped his forehead.
“Oh dead gods, he’s an Az’kerash [Necromancer]. Mass-summoner. No offense, I’m sure it works well, but he was a very uninventive spellcaster, historically speaking. You know?”
Pisces tried to protest, but he’d thought the same thing himself. Even so—
“He was one of the two most powerful Archmages of the time, though, sir! And a master duelist and—”
“Oh, no, I’d never deny that. Have you studied his life? I have a lot of proscribed accounts of his battle prowess, and as a duelist, he was supreme. As a creator…I think it was Terandrian sensibilities. When I compare that to the [Necromancer] who invented the Crypt Lords…”
“Er, someone invented Crypt Lords?”
They smiled as Poetr insisted Pisces have a cup of tea with him and began to talk undead, even if not all of them were experts. Some had fought undead, and Calice had once come up with the concept of a skeleton bound to an oversized crank-crossbow which would revolutionize loading speeds—Noelictus hadn’t wanted to buy or trial her designs.
They chatted more with him, because one had to, of course. There was a mind behind that poor adventurer’s brain of his, and it was the duty of the Mad Ones to engage it. Unfortunately, it meant they lost the chance to upsell more stuff onto him, but sacrifices had to be made.
 
——
 
When Colth found his team, he was flushed from running around buying things. Ceria was eating overpriced food, Pisces was not really reading his spellbook, and Yvlon was asleep.
“I’m finished buying items. Did you get anything?”
“Nope.”
The other three Horns’ complete lack of purchases made Colth scowl. He nudged Yvlon with a foot. She was dead asleep on the ground.
“Come on, we have to at least see if we can convince the Mad Ones to move to Reim.”
“They clearly don’t wish to, Colth. Unless we can secure transport, it seems pointless. I’d try moving them to Germina, but assuming we cannot get them to leave, where are we bound next?”
Pisces glanced up, and Colth hesitated.
“Well, pending Her Majesty wanting us to make up for our debacle, we could roam some of the eastern cities. Search for Pisces’ friends.”
Pisces sat up a bit. Bearig, Merr, Eloque—his heart began to beat faster. Ceria glanced at him and stopped shovelling loaded fries into her mouth.
“Sounds good. Let’s get going. I say we skip even talking to them. They’re crazy, but boring crazy after all. Hey, Yvlon. Yvlon, c’mon, we’re going.”
She nudged Yvlon again, and the woman didn’t wake up. Ceria and Colth tried before Ceria smirked, then reached over.
She shot a snowball into Yvlon’s face, and the [Armsmistress] came up swinging.
“CERIA—”
She spluttered, lurched two steps after Ceria, then sat down. And yawned. Colth frowned at her.
“C’mon, Yvlon. What’s with you?”
“I don’t…know. I’m just really tired. Are we leaving yet? Did anyone explode?”
“Not for lack of trying. C’mon.”
Pisces got up, a bit disconsolate. The Horns were walking out of the camp, and Otevious and the others hadn’t come to see them off. They’d done their business, and Pisces didn’t see Trader Hexata.
There was something off about the entire trip, he decided. It just wasn’t fun. He didn’t know what had changed. Even going to Invrisil or camping outside the walls hadn’t been always mindblowing, but there had been an enjoyable component that was lacking here.
Part of it was Ceria, Colth doing things his way, or Yvlon being tired but the team just wasn’t…together. He knew the others were feeling the same way, at least, Ceria and Colth did. He was making plans.
“Okay, let’s head for an eastern city. We might as well put Delitandra’s group to work. We’ll get some actual progress done on our goals.”
“Yeah, and we could do some strategizing in the carriage. You know, how to fight together and not get wiped out? Even fight some monsters.”
Pisces was reminded of something as they approached the walls and realized they didn’t have a ladder. Ceria obligingly began to make some ice stairs, and he did the same. They stared at each other’s ramps, and Pisces began to de-animate his only for Ceria to do it first.
“Bone before ice, especially stairs.”
“Er, thank you, Ceria. I was going to ask, but I forgot—Delitandra, what about that Jaw of Zeikhal? Did anyone end up stopping it?”
Delitandra and the Heromakers had been observing the Horns and taking notes. Possibly, they dovetailed with Pisces’ feeling, because Delitandra leapt forwards.
“Ah, to that, Pisces, I do know it was ended. So do not fear for commonfolk.”
He did relax at that; it had hurt his conscience. She strode up the stairs with him.
“In fact, the one who took out the Jaw was one of the adventurers you met in Tyrant’s Rest. It was none other than Itkisa herself.”
“Torreb’s daughter? She took it out by herself?”
Pisces was surprised. A single adventurer had taken out a Jaw of Zeikhal? Even a young one—Torreb had been famous for killing one in single combat. There was someone who clearly wanted to capitalize on her father’s myth. Or perhaps, reforge it anew. He rubbed at his chin.
“If we assume all the teams we met were hired to go against us in some capacity, then it follows that she might have been hired to fight us as well.”
He climbed the walls separating the Mad Ones from the rest of the world and stopped. A sleepy Yvlon walked into his back and nearly fell down the stairs. Colth had to push her back up. She complained.
“Pisces—”
Then she heard a voice, and her head snapped up. Pisces stared down the wall at a figure who stood outside the Mad One’s commune. The wind blew at her cloak, and she still, even now, looked too different from what he felt she should be.
Like a mother despite the chainmail she wore and the oversized club planted in the dirt. Itkisa, the newly-made Gold-rank adventurer, lifted the club one-handed, and it was as tall as she was. She pointed it at Pisces.
“I was hired to defeat your team, Horns of Hammerad. I thought, from the stories of you, that you’d fight the Jaw over the Tomb. My mistake. Shall we?”
Pisces stared at her. She smiled at him, and he felt a crawl down his back. Ceria was mouthing at him.
Stall. Colth was swearing as he reached for a bow.
“Hey, Itkisa! Are you sure you know what you’re doing? There’s four of us and—”
He was calling out in a loud, confident voice when Pisces saw the woman tense. She crouched, and he shouted.
“Watch out—”
She leapt, and he [Flash Stepped] off the walls. Yvlon blinked up as the woman fell to earth, club swinging. Pisces half-turned, drawing his r—
Itkisa hit the walls, and they exploded. Dirt rained down. The ground shook—was it still shaking? Pisces stumbled and saw a figure rising from the hole she’d cleaved in the compound’s defenses. She turned, and he swallowed.
Aw, hells. Then the second adventurer battle in as many days began.
 
——
 
She just didn’t look right. And she knew that too.
Itkisa wasn’t even the right…species. Torreb had been Stitch-folk. His body had been thread and cloth so scarred and pitted by war it had made him look like the Hemp-folk. But no one had ever asked him his thread.
He had transcended social norms. He had been the greatest [Warrior] of Chandrar, perhaps the world. The unstoppable force that armies feared. Whom even Mars the Illusionist had not eclipsed.
Her father. Itkisa knew Torreb better than anyone else in the world. His wives had not outlived him or stayed with him, for Torreb was exactly as people had known him: unpredictable, unshackled by rules, prone to violence or whimsy. He could have passed from this world into the next like that whirlwind, shifting things around by his passage, but for one thing.
Her. Itkisa’s mother had claimed a Skill from him.
[Inheritance: My Father’s Strength]. A simple Skill. A brave Skill for a mother to leave a child. He’d killed her for it, even though it hadn’t taken anything from him. Torreb had just hated the fact that someone else had gained what he had earned himself. As if that were cheating. Perhaps it was. Even now, she didn’t know how to use his strength. He had never taught her. He’d kept her by his side for a lifetime, terrified she’d grow up and kill him in the way of brutal succession, like they were animals.
To be fair, she had killed him at the end. Just not the way he’d expected.
Well, she’d waited decades to find out who she was. And yes, she looked like a mother despite never having borne children. She wasn’t a lithe figure nor scarred by battle. She was thickset, stomach wrapped with a colorful band of red cloth one of her half-sisters had given her. One of the few not fighting over Torreb’s wealth. Her armor a mix of cheap chainmail, battered and scavenged for she had no coins; he had left her nothing. Leather under it that she might move around freely. No potions, no magical items. Just a single club.
One woman versus four storied adventurers, one a Named-ranker. The world’s most famous team, arguably. Itkisa fell like a comet, and only someone like her would know why she smiled.
Smiled like a girl, alive for the first day in so long.
A shard of ice grazed her cheek and tore her bronze skin open. The half-Elf would have shot Itkisa through the cheek but for her moving her head. So fast. Deadly—
But she saw them. The [Supporter] raising a bow, then switching as he observed how fast she was coming down, dropping it and drawing his blades. The yawning [Armsmistress] who didn’t react, blinking upwards and her pupils dilating.
All a moment. Then Itkisa struck the ground with the force contained in her body. Like a child hammered the earth. Not too hard. She could split the club if she swung it too hard, despite the magic on it.
It wasn’t even a Skill. Just—
Impact. Dirt heaved upwards in a column around her, and she shielded her face with her free arm. For a second, she was blinded by her own att—
Dodge. The second spell came through the dirt, an [Ice Lance] that would have hit her in the chest. Flawless aim, as fast as an arrow. If she was just Torreb’s strength, she would have been dead.
But she was a [Warrior] in her own right, and it was still slower than a cup that Torreb hurled when drunk. Itkisa punched the [Ice Lance] and grimaced.
Pain. A cold shock as it exploded. Her flesh wasn’t as tough as she needed it to be. Like the King of Destruction, the only man Torreb had thought might win an arm-wrestling competition with him. She knew the [Supporter] and [Armsmistress] were here, so Itkisa did as Torreb had done.
She swung her club again. And the dirt, a second spell—everything in her reach vanished.
 
——
 
The explosion of Itkisa landing was followed by a second one in moments. Pisces had no idea what was going on; he’d taken cover reflexively. Then he saw a spray of what he thought was Ceria’s ice magic—but in fragments?
Then the wind hurled shrapnel at him. Three impacts on his chest; he grunted and sat down. His underarmor saved him, but what…
Dirt.
Dirt and stones. Hurled by her swing. When Pisces got up, she was swirling that club around. One-handed, laughing.
The Horns were all running for it. Yvlon was stumbling away as Colth dove and rolled out of the way of Itkisa’s strike. Ceria was hiding behind three [Ice Walls], firing [Ice Lances] at Itkisa. But the woman was alternating between dodging, punching, and swinging through the magic.
“Incredible.”
Pisces aimed a finger at Itkisa’s back and hesitated. Again, this all felt wrong. She was a fellow adventurer. Why were they fighting…?
But she was terrifyingly strong. Strong in a way that instantly spoke to him of a Named-ranker. That strength…Pisces shouted.
“Itkisa, stop! We don’t want to fight with you!”
[Deathbolt]. It shot at her, and she turned, saw it coming, and went to punch the magic with her free hand. Then block it with her club. Her face twisted with uncertainty. Then she sidestepped, cursing.
—She walked straight into an explosion. One of Colth’s flasks hit her and blew up. He followed it with a charge, and Itkisa leapt clear of the blast. Her skin was bloodied and charred, but she had some kind of toughness Skill or she’d be dead. She snarled.
“Pisces! Flank her with Colth at range! I’m going to chill her!”
Ceria shouted, and the air around Itkisa grew cold. She was backing up, and Colth was keeping out of range of her swinging club. It was longer than she was tall but she swung it as fast as Pisces could swing a shortsword! He couldn’t get close—so he flipped something else at her face.
Acid flask. This time, she went to catch it, and it exploded in midair. Colth’s Skill—it showered her in steaming acid, and Pisces cried out at the same time as Itkisa.
Before the acid could coat her fully, Itkisa did something Pisces had never seen before. She had a traveller’s cloak on her shoulders. She didn’t reach for a potion; instead she grabbed her cloak and swung it around her.
She snapped the cloak, and the gust of wind snapped all the acid off her skin. The spray of it hit Colth, and he leapt back, shouting.
“Dead gods—”
Could you do that? Manifestly, but Itkisa was panting. Sweat and some acid on her skin froze over, and she glanced at Ceria.
“So this is…how did he say to do it again?”
She was muttering. Colth had sheathed his shortswords and was juggling an assortment of alchemical weapons. He gave her a sinister smile.
“Surrender or you’re not going to survive the next attack. You have thirty seconds before you’re a block of ice or a new corpse for Pisces to use.”
Itkisa met his eyes, her orange irises flashing in anger. For answer, she tightened the grip on her club. Colth backstepped fast—but he missed the woman’s next trick. Itkisa had dug one of her sandals into the ground. Pisces shouted.
“Colth! Watch out—”
Itkisa kicked sand at Colth. Another simple trick unless you were so strong—
It looked like an attack spell. Sand and dirt nearly hit the [Ultimate Supporter], who dodged with a Skill. He came up, eyes wide, and Itkisa—
Kicked again. Colth vanished in a spray, and she pointed.
“You.”
Ceria was aiming a wand at Itkisa, concentrating hard. She saw the woman draw back one hand and blinked.
“No w—”
The club smashed through two of Ceria’s [Ice Walls] and nearly took the third one out. The shockwave still slammed Ceria down. She lay there, gasping for air, when she saw Itkisa leaping at her. One fist drawn back to punch through the spells…
