Yvlon hit Itkisa before the woman landed. The two collided with a sound like ringing metal, and then they were punching, rolling—before a blow tossed Yvlon back onto her feet, and Itkisa rolled upright. She had a bloodied nose. Yvlon had a dent in her face.
But her body was metal. [Aspect of Iron]. She shook her head, and her face re-formed as she raised her fists. Sluggishly. Pisces appeared behind Itkisa, shouting.
“Enough! We don’t have a quarrel with you!”
She twisted around, and four Skeleton Champions rushed at her. To stop her, not—she punched through one’s face and tore through another with a fist so fast the third and fourth were stumbling when she kicked through both of them. Pisces ducked a flying piece of bone, but he had a finger aimed at her. Again, she hesitated and went to k—
He nearly stepped away, but she stopped. Why? He realized he was standing in the ruined wall; the Mad Ones’ camp was behind them. She pivoted, and the spray of dirt missed the camp—he had already stepped away from the gap as well.
For a second, they hesitated, and Pisces wavered as Itkisa frowned at him.
“Pisces—just [Deathbolt] her three times. She can survive it.”
Ceria croaked as she crawled up and conjured an [Icy Floor] spell. The half-Elf tried to skate away as Itkisa swivelled. She angled herself to face both Yvlon and Pisces at the same time.
Barehanded—she was lifting a palm towards Pisces, a fist towards Yvlon. Martial arts? She seemed warier of Pisces than Yvlon for reasons he didn’t understand until she spoke.
“It’s harder than I thought. Fighting other adventurers. My father always feared monsters over men. But he faced the greatest of monsters. Hitting someone like that—”
Ceria was skating away at speed, eschewing static defenses. She fired another [Ice Lance] at Itkisa’s face. Itkisa pivoted—grabbed the [Ice Lance], and threw it.
Completely wide. It went flying into the distance as Pisces and Yvlon stared at it. But they had never seen someone grab a spell and throw it back. He widened his eyes at Yvlon.
Do I cover you? He wasn’t about to go in close against that woman, even bare-handed. Yvlon…yawned at him. Then gritted her teeth.
“Something’s wrong. Itkisa, why are we fighting?”
“For glory. You are the most famous team in Chandrar. How else am I to make my name?”
Itkisa re-pivoted to them and kicked again—Ceria ran into a second storm of dirt and coughed. The woman’s eyes darted right, left, and Pisces croaked.
“I have no desire to kill you.”
She focused on him and smiled—then her eyes grew round in alarm. She whirled with a cry, and Colth stabbed into her from the side. [Greater Invisibility]! She was quick—he got in two slashes, but her punch sent him skidding across the ground. Pisces fired a [Deathbolt] into Itkisa’s legs. She dodged the second one, staggering. Yvlon—
—Had missed her opening. She stumbled forwards. Itkisa was cursing. She reached into her bag of holding as she searched around for her weapon, but it was far out of reach.
“To the death, then?”
Colth and Pisces hesitated as Ceria shouted.
“[Dangersense]! Get back!”
The woman was checking her bleeding body and damaged armor. She ruefully shook her head.
“A team is better than a woman alone. Magic. [Rogues]. Though you’re not much of a team. Ksmvr of Chandrar was more frightening.”
“We’re more than enough for you. Back off.”
Yvlon Byres was walking at Itkisa, swaying. Pisces was moving left, invisible, and he saw Colth crouching as he snuck up on Itkisa’s back. Ceria was casting as Itkisa peered around, tensing—and then she focused on the Silver Killer.
Something was very wrong with Yvlon. She wasn’t running at Itkisa, and her eyes were unfocused. She took two more steps, silver hands clenched, then…yawned. Her eyes rolled up in her head, and Itkisa halted, hand still in her bag of holding.
“Ah. You’ve already fallen prey to the empire’s games.”
She regarded Yvlon, then turned away from the woman. Almost sympathetically, she looked straight at Pisces—and Yvlon fell forwards on her face.
“Yvlon?”
Pisces stared, and Colth shouted.
“Poison—no, it was the damn kiss! Get her out of here, Ceria—”
He charged Itkisa as Pisces took aim. He didn’t want to [Deathbolt] her again, and she was staring at him.
She doesn’t know how my magic works or if she can block it. She was going to come for him. He prepared to [Flash Step] and then heard Ceria shout again.
“[Dangersense]! Oh tree rot—[Fortress of the Ice Q—]”
He heard a whistling sound, glanced up, and saw something falling at him. Itkisa and Colth gazed upwards, and she bent and heaved the ground upwards as Colth leapt and covered Yvlon with his body.
“[Emergency Shield]—”
Then the falling ballista bolt split into eighteen separate shards which Pisces realized were individual arrows bound together in a single—
 
——
 
The explosion was still ringing in his ears. He got up and began to [Flash Step] around in a circle.
Dizzy, but he’d get killed if he stayed still. [Invisibility]—he couldn’t concentrate on the spell. Dust everywhere. He ran into someone in the cloud.
Ceria nearly shot an [Ice Lance] through his face. She was covered in dirt, but there was a shell of ice over her body. She mouthed at him. He blinked at her, and she slapped his head.
“[—store Hearing]! Take cover behind my barrier spells!”
She’d raised a glowing barrier. When had she learned to cast…? Pisces looked around as his head cleared and saw Yvlon and Colth. He’d dragged her behind a metal barrier he’d set up, and Itkisa was shaking her head. But she hadn’t fired…
The five brawling adventurers all turned, and they remembered where they were fighting. The wall around the Mad Ones’ camp was broken in where Itkisa had hit it, and a few tents were downed from Ceria’s magic or Itkisa kicking around dirt. But there was still a crowd of the Mad Ones.
And—Pisces felt compelled to focus on this—
Adelaide. She was sitting on some kind of weird contraption. It looked sort of like Bird’s ballista…if you’d attached the ballista to something that reminded Pisces of Pallass’ elevators. It was like an extending stand that put her twenty feet straight in the air. From this mobile platform, she’d fired a single bolt which had exploded on their position.
The entire contraption was noisily reloading, and Pisces saw another Mad One aiming a five-tubed something at him. He had no [Dangersense], but he put up his hands slowly.
Yerelia had a simple megaphone. She shouted into it.
“Adventurers! If you keep fighting near our camp, we will kill you. Take it elsewhere.”
Four Gold-rankers and a Named-ranker looked at each other. They eyed the Mad Ones. Colth slowly raised his hands, and Itkisa took her free hand out of her bag of holding. She raised her hands as well as Ceria muttered.
“Okay, maybe we should have bought their stuff. But that wasn’t for sale! You gonna fight when we go for round two? Colth and I can’t take her out alone, Pisces.”
“I’m not killing her.”
She stared at him as the Mad Ones made vague shooing motions. Some were shouting at the adventurers to drop some gold before they left. Ceria exhaled a plume of frost.
“Listen, Pisces, we have to work together.”
“She’s not a monster.”
They stared at each other as Itkisa walked over to grab her club. Ceria felt at her head and grimaced as she pulled the circlet off. She dusted her robes off, and they saw Colth levering the unconscious Yvlon up. Awkwardly, Pisces walked away from the Mad Ones’ camp after dropping a few hundred gold pieces onto the sand; no one else had done that. Ceria vanished, and Colth was moving towards the magical carriage.
He stuffed Yvlon into it, and Pisces found himself walking next to Itkisa. She glanced at him as he hesitated. But both peered at the Mad Ones’ camp—
“Further away! At least a mile!”
Neither he nor Itkisa were willing to break the treaty, so she nodded at him.
“Your choice, Adventurer Pisces.”
“To do what, fight to the death? If the three of us battle you, it won’t be bloodless even if you win.”
“Or your team could fall back and ride away in the carriage. I am here for the glory of chasing the Horns away, as I was employed to do.”
“What? You want us to flee?”
She smiled at him as she rubbed at her bleeding cheek.
“It would advantage you, with your warrior gone. And it benefits me greatly. Somehow, though—”
Her eyes flicked to Colth, who had turned from the carriage to favor her with a sinister smile. Then she stared at an empty patch of air to the side.
“—I doubt your teammates will be so reasonable.”
Ceria re-materialized with a curse. She could cast [Invisibility]? Pisces stared at her as she called over her shoulder.
“She’s aura-sensing, Colth. Either that or a tremorsense. Pisces, get over here before she takes you hostage.”
“I’m negotiating. We could fall back, Ceria.”
“Fall back? It’s three versus one, and she’s no Torreb.”
That made Itkisa twitch. Her eyes narrowed at Ceria, and Pisces actually put an arm out to block her. He stared at his offending arm. So did she. Then Pisces addressed Itkisa.
“Did you have to attack us to begin with? To my knowledge, we have never quarrelled, Itkisa. I was actually hoping to talk civilly; you met Orjin of Pomle, and your father was a famous adventurer. I would hate to maim or kill each other.”
A flicker of guilt crossed Itkisa’s face. She brushed at her black hair that she’d tied back in a ponytail, then shook her head.
“It is hard to be Torreb’s child. I am grabbing for what you have plenty of, Adventurer Pisces. Fame must truly taste like water to you if you don’t see how much circles you. Perhaps I was too hasty to judge you. For all they call you the Bane of Roshal. Or Scourge. Which is it?”
“Neither. I’ve barely killed any [Slavers]. I…I think someone is using my face.”
She regarded him as they walked away from the Mad Ones’ camp. Ceria and Colth were following to their right and left, clearly communicating as they eyed Itkisa and counted their distance from the camp. But the woman just smiled at Pisces.
“Titles are not things we choose, Pisces. I am Itkisa, Torreb’s Daughter. The Scourge of Roshal is a fine title, to my mind. If you feel it is undeserving, or wish to rise to it, prove it. But I do not think a boring pretender would draw blade on the King of Destruction.”
He blinked down at her; he was taller than she was. But she had seemed like she was towering over him a moment ago. Pisces came to a halt in the dirt, and she gripped the club tighter at once.
“We are not a mile from the Mad Ones’ camp, and I think if anyone could measure, it would be them.”
“I am not going to fight you, Itkisa. I would prefer we part without violence.”
He crossed his arms, sheathing the rapier at his side. She eyed him as Ceria and Colth halted. Itkisa pursed her lips and dug one foot into the earth with ease. She peered down at her sandals; she’d ripped the toe off the one she’d been using to kick dirt at Colth and Ceria.
She must wear out clothing and gear with how strong she is. No wonder she wanted gold and fame if she couldn’t afford it yet. Itkisa glanced up at Pisces.
“If you were to retreat for the sake of my reputation—”
“Hell no! Pisces, we’ll just kneecap her! Get over here!”
Colth shouted. Pisces scowled at him. Itkisa sighed.
“If we agreed on terms—”
Then she pivoted at the same time as Pisces leapt back from her. Itkisa raised her club, then sighed and lowered it. Ceria waved her arms frantically, shouting.
“We’re too close to the Mad Ones! Stop, stop—oh hey, that’s our side. Or not—hells!”
She went skating away, but belatedly—something hit her, and she tangled in it, cursing. Pisces saw the net covering the Ice Squirrel, and Itkisa lifted a club and blocked another thrown at her. But there were more, and ropes were flying from…
Chariots? One missed Pisces, and he began [Flash Stepping] away. He remembered the war in Pomle—and these were the same damn chariots! He saw Silk [Chariot Riders], whooping as they shot forwards. Carrying the flags of Nerrhavia’s Fallen and shouting…
“All will put down their blades! In the name of Queen Yisame—you are all under the authority of the crown! Do not resist, Torreb’s Daughter, Horns of Hammerad!”
They tried to net Itkisa again, but she swung her club and sent the nets flying. However, she did halt as more drew flaming arrows and aimed at her. They were trying to net Colth as well—he was dodging back towards the carriage. The lead [Rider] screamed.
“Her Majesty’s wrath on any adventurer who fights us! You are to be escorted back to the capital—now! Cease fighting, all of you! Where are…?”
Itkisa had lowered her club, though she kept tearing nets off her. She was sighing, and the chariot riders were circling the adventurers.
Nets. They didn’t look like much but when they landed on her, Itkisa growled, and had to rip at the bright, colorful threads. She heaved—and nearly ripped her own skin off as she cursed.
“What the—”
They were tough! Little stones made of jade carved with runes were attached to the nets to weigh them down, and each one was sewn out of some kind of magical thread. Tearing one apart took a lot of her strength, and she wasn’t the only one.
Colth had slashed two in midair only to find his blades barely cut the thread as well. And when you were caught—
“Hells, it’s anti-magic!”
Ceria was trying to cast a spell, but she was covered partially by two, and she wasn’t able to even cast [Ice Spike]. She was wriggling, though, trying to get out from under—
“By Nerrhavia’s Fallen, you will obey! Hoist the Banner of the Dark Queen!”
The charioteers saw the three Gold-rankers bristling, and one of them unfurled something. A black standard caught the air, and Itkisa gazed up—
A flash of darkness fell over the world. A fell wind blew; the carrion-eaters were pecking at the dead. A fortress loomed, and from it, bones littered the ground. Itkisa felt her chest heaving with panic. She stumbled back—
Fell to a knee—
The woman blinked and pushed herself up. This time, the effort cracked the earth, and not from the weight of more nets. The standard blowing in the wind was physical force. It flattened everything around the charioteers, who were immune. She rasped.
“That’s the standard of the Immortal Tyrant!”
She recognized it. Her father had told her about this when he had inspired her with tales of adventure. One of the proscribed relics of the old era. It had utterly flattened Ceria Springwalker; the half-Elf was lying spread-eagled on the ground, trying to breathe. Itkisa could stand only because of her strength. And Colthei…
He had been crawling towards the carriage with Yvlon Byres in it, but the [Charioteers] had already secured it. One had swung a spear, delicately, and sheared the door clean off. It was screaming about ‘property damage to Wistram’ as they emerged, carrying the Silver Killer, who was still unconscious.
That spear cut Wistram’s magic like it was butter. Itkisa had watched Archmage Valeterisa duelling Archmage Amerys, and the Drake [Spearmaster]’s weapon that Amerys had shattered was not so fine.
This was a full Nerrhavia’s Fallen Silk detachment. Wealth beyond measure. All for the Horns? She gritted her teeth, but then raised her hand as well. There was no mistaking that standard.
Colth had put up his hands as well, scowling. The duo who had gotten to the carriage shouted at their leader.
“We have the Silver Killer! She’s asleep!”
That was a huge relief; the Stitch-woman in charge wiped her forehead. Unpredictable adventurers…she counted.
“That leaves the Ice Squirrel and Scourge. Damn, they’ve vanished. [See Invisibility]!”
She raised a feathered mask shaped like an owl to her face that she’d brought for just this purpose and peered around. It took a second before she saw a crouching half-Elf trying to scuttle into the Mad Ones’ camp.
“There!”
Ceria reappeared and swore before half a dozen nets hit her. The chariot leader rubbed at her neck; it had been a long ride in the damn heat for this.
“Horns of Hammerad, Adventurer Itkisa, we are on the Queen’s mission! Do not resist, I ask it in sanity’s name. Who else? Do we pick up Wildcard?”
She consulted her list. The [Queen]’s words had been to return the Horns and any adventurer team brawling with them. The other Gold-rank team wasn’t here, so the [Chariot Leader] decided to leave them off the list. A subordinate riding in her chariot leaned over as they aimed a flaming arrow at Itkisa.
“What of the Heromakers with the Horns?”
“Bah. They’ll follow as their kind does. Alright…where’s the Scourge?”
She’d been searching around for Pisces, and a few of the other chariots had produced their own anti-invisibility artifacts. Your casual [Invisibility] spell did not work on the Chariots of Tussah, who were an all-Silk group that had more gold than one could dream of.
Not that they wanted to tangle with the Horns or Torreb’s daughter. The [Chariot Leader] was hoping the Scourge of Roshal didn’t know about her family’s [Slaves]—surely, he was a reasonable man and less prone to violence than the Silver Killer, who ate ears like one ate dates?
He was still a Gold-rank adventurer, and they numbered over two hundred across fifty chariots. No ordinary team could face that many, and no [Mage] escaped their eyes.
…So where was he? The woman peered around, then snapped.
“He can’t have gone far. Anti-illusion magic. Is this artifact dead?”
The chariots split up, circling the area. Some Stitch-folk even leapt down to search on the ground. They would have entered the Mad Ones’ camp, but the insane lot appeared, and they were armed—the remaining Horns and Itkisa were shepherded towards the magical carriage. Then Itkisa was given a separate one for fear of violence.
After twenty minutes, the charioteers were stumped. And the adventurers were getting more antsy, as were the Mad Ones. Fearful of more violence, they decided to head back towards the capital. But the irate [Queen]’s representatives echoed the same question the charioteers were asking themselves.
How did you manage to lose one of the Horns of Hammerad? Everyone knew Adventurer Pisces could cast lower-level illusions and [Invisibility], so the Chariots of Tussah had brought plenty of artifacts to locate him. But he was—gone.
Did he know a magic unknown to them? The Mad Ones swore they were not harboring him. The embarrassed [Chariot Leader] rode back the long road to Nerrhavia’s Fallen capital, sweating and cursing adventurers in general. All this for the Queen’s favorites. Well, she did get an autograph from the Ice Squirrel, which cheered her up. But she wondered where Adventurer Pisces had gone.

10.74 H (2026-08-23)

Pisces to Ceria: Are we hiding or securing Yvlon and fleeing?
Pisces to Ceria: Hello? Do you need a distraction?
Pisces to Ceria: I can’t tell what’s going on. I presume you’ve all vanished; I can hear them searching around me.
Pisces to Ceria: Reducing spellcasting in case they’re using [Detect Magic].
Pisces to Ceria: I think they’re gone. Where are you?
Ceria to Pisces: Hey, you’re a genius, idiot. They got all of us. How the heck did you escape? Will be out of range soon—head back to Tyrant’s Rest.
Pisces to Ceria: Clarification?
 
He never received a response. Which made him think their personal, secret communication spell from Wistram was out of range. Pisces eventually did emerge from his hiding place. He sat up with a gasp, and the sand covering him fell away.
Quite a lot of it, actually. He’d buried himself in the sand to avoid them spotting him. He had it in his hair, in his robes.
“What do you mean they got you all?”
He’d assumed they were hiding in case it wasn’t Yisame’s people after all. Or just because they didn’t want to obey—Pisces looked around and saw the Mad Ones’ camp in the distance. No chariots.
No magical Wistram carriage.
Nothing.
“…Tree rot.”
It sounded awkward when he said it. He got up, shaking sand out of his robes, and stood.
How did he escape the charioteers when Colth and Ceria failed to? Well, he knew how he’d done it, but he’d assumed Colth with his nigh-infinite Skills and Ceria’s magic…Pisces felt his stomach sink.
Now he had to go back by himself? He’d been so sure—
He rubbed at his face. Once again, it seemed to him that his team was out-of-sync with each other. He’d just assumed…
Here was the trick. As Pisces gloomily began walking back to the Mad Ones’ camp, he did congratulate himself on his new levels of artifice. He, Ceria, and Colth all had access to some form of [Invisibility], clearly. But the charioteers had been ready for them, and Pisces had known the instant that mask appeared they’d see him.
He was hardly a strong illusionist, so he couldn’t disguise himself with magic that way. Which left another trick: burying oneself in the sand. Classic to Chandrar, he’d read.
However, any fool could intuit that. The [Charioteers] weren’t stupid. They’d begun casting [Detect Life] spells—even [Detect Death] once they’d realized he was hiding. Pisces, covered in the sand as they rolled around him, had panicked, then come up with an interesting idea.
He was a [Necromancer]. He’d show up on a [Detect Life] spell, but what if he projected death magic such that he looked a bit more dead than usual? Not enough to register as undead, but just enough to ‘cloak’ his signature.
It had been a fun challenge to balance his magical essence, and he’d assumed Ceria’s circlet would do that for her, and Colth would use his helm. Then they’d link up, get Yvlon once she woke up, and…
…And it turned out he’d been way too clever. Pisces scuffed at the dirt.
“Do I rent a Wistram carriage? Maybe the Heromakers of Hraace can help me. What is ailing Yvlon?”
She’d just keeled over in battle. And she’d been yawning all day…
Ever since that kiss in the parade. Colth had said that. But he’d also ruled out poison at that instant, so what…?
A lot of questions, and not a lot of answers. However, Pisces did at least make it to the Mad Ones’ camp, and they didn’t murder him.
Indeed, some of the Mad Ones were trying to invent new shovels or ways to repair the wall. When they saw him, a few jumped.
“Dead gods, where were you? We were searching with the charioteers, and no one found you, Adventurer!”
That did cheer Pisces up a bit. He sniffed, sneezed because he had sand in his nose, and coughed.
“I appear to have done my job, ah, too well. They’ve all left, haven’t they?”
“A good thirty minutes ago. Hold on, let me get Yerelia—”
 
——
 
The Mad One was hugely amused to see Pisces. When he told her how he’d evaded them, she laughed.
“How inventive! That makes me want to look into spells that could deal with this unique case. You’re on par with a Level 30 [Rogue]; fools upon the Silks for thinking they could bring a few artifacts to catch you. Well—unless you want to buy anything, we’ll call it even. You paid us enough for the food and dropped enough gold to make up for the wall. I’m glad I didn’t kill you all with that round. Did you like how it spread out?”
“It was utterly terrifying, Inventor Yerelia. May I apologize for my, ah, team?”
She eyed him as she stopped laughing.
“Now I know you’re no Chandrarian adventurer. That sort of thing is part and parcel around here. Adventurers brawl and kill each other; now I’m glad I didn’t fire a second shot. Be on your way, then.”
No ill will nor questions. Pisces hesitated. He cast around.
“Er…thank you.”
Did he just go back to the city or something? He awkwardly walked off as the sand blew around him. This was so uncomfortable.
He hadn’t been by himself for a while. This was the first time he’d been alone since coming to Chandrar, really. Certainly in Nerrhavia’s Fallen.
It felt odd. And guiltily, Pisces realized—a bit freeing.
 
——
 
Too freeing, Pisces knew, when he got to the mansion where he and the Horns had been staying. When he entered, he nearly scared a team of Cotton-folk [Cleaners] to death. They stammered that his entourage had left twenty minutes ago. He realized the Heromakers of Hraace were gone too.
Delitandra and the others had heard the Horns were going back to the capital and done the obvious thing. He groaned.
Alone.
It wasn’t like he was unused to the feeling. He had been alone for years after Wistram, and before that as well. But of late…Pisces had to think back to the Horns’ last few adventures.
Ever since Chandrar, they’d been together. Even if he’d gone out by himself, the team had been, well, a team. From going south to the Meeting of Tribes to the Crossroads, they’d stuck by each others’ sides. Colth had joined them and until the battle at sea…
Even after, he’d been in Colth’s company. Or if they’d been split up like at Jecrass, he’d been talking with Jecaina. The closest to alone he’d gotten was, what, being in Hraace and sitting in a pool with Nawalishifra?
Or the five minutes he’d followed the coliseum master while Yvlon was fighting? Truly, Pisces hadn’t been by himself for ages. He wished he didn’t feel like it was a relief.
“But why is it a relief, per se?”
The [Necromancer] went for a walk in the city, which was named Halqued, apparently. Funny, he hadn’t even known where the Mad Ones lived by name. That was how fast his team had zoomed across Nerrhavia’s Fallen.
True, they were busy. But would it kill them to at least stop and appreciate the local cuisine or customs? Pisces Jealnet was the sort of fellow who would make it a point to stop at every museum in a city he came across. Of course, his team was not that sort; Yvlon did it out of obligation, but only Ksmvr really appreciated history. Ceria and Colth were more the types to hit up the local market or go out and see the nightlife…he had no idea what Vofea was like.
Which was fine. Pisces could enjoy himself plenty at a restaurant, and he imagined Ceria would be a hoot, perhaps even a holler, in any museum. She could appreciate such things.
Funny. He just couldn’t imagine it all working out right now. Because, as he had observed, his team was fractured. Their teamwork was shot, and it was…
“It’s not all because of Ksmvr, is it?”
The young man stood in the local museum of Halqued, inspecting, well, pottery and old relics as the Stitch-folk eyed him. He knew he stood out because of his dusty robes, his fair skin, and probably the rapier on his side. He couldn’t help it; he had no place to change clothes, and Elena wasn’t around to put on makeup.
Pisces half-concentrated on the displays, which were fascinating. But he was just thinking to himself.
Maybe they were laying too much of the blame on Ksmvr not being here. Maybe…even if the Antinium were here, they’d still be like this. In which case, better that Ksmvr weren’t here because he’d be worrying himself sick.
Nor was it all Ceria’s fault. True, she was one of the issues with the circlet, but Colth was being sort of, well, an adventurer. The kind that existed at The Adventurer’s Haven, not The Wandering Inn. Yvlon was Yvlon—Pisces felt like he and she were on the same page.
He hoped she was okay. What had happened to her? He bent over a faded bit of pottery where little figures made of different pieces of cloth were joining hands. Not the most…intricate of designs. An amateur potter’s work, but fascinating.
At least, he thought so. The museum was fairly empty, and it wasn’t a rich place; no enchantments on the cases or cooling runes in the air. But authentic pottery from ages past! Museums weren’t big in Izril; you tended to get less memorabilia because Drakes would use anything worthwhile or hoarded the rest. But Chandrar was known as one of the ‘oldest’ continents because of all the buried kingdoms. Arid climates preserved things wonderfully, you see.
However, some people had no taste. Pisces heard a loud, and slightly exasperated, voice down the hallway.
“Look, I love pottery—no, I’m lying. I don’t love pottery. I’d rather use a chamberpot than look at this stuff for another hour. Can we go?”
Pisces closed his eyes. He could just imagine Ceria saying that or trying to use one of these pots for said purpose. Was it her new [Trickster] class? Was she that much less like the Ceria he had met after so long?
Yes and no. She’d gotten crazier. Had fame done that? Their travels? Was he different? He gazed at his reflection in the glass and thought he looked the same. But he had a brand on his chest. He had been a [Slave]…he carried a rapier again. He was an adventurer, not a lost [Necromancer].
Yes, I am different. In mostly better ways, I hope. Pisces thought of Erin. He wondered if she would be proud of his latest adventurers. He hoped she was alright. Wherever she was. The imposter in Baleros…
His hand was gripping his rapier’s hilt. Pisces let go as a wide-eyed Stitch-girl hurried past him, staring at her. He smiled; she began to run.
I am an armed stranger in these lands with a reputation for being a murderer. I should be more discreet. Can I buy some skin-paint and…no, that’s a terrible idea without Elena. But maybe some different clothing? 
He could dye his hair? Pisces had an image of Lyonette going around with black hair and snorted, then sighed. He doubted it would work on Stitch-folk given how adept they were at changing appearances. Then he heard the second voice.
“I vote to leave. My feet hurt, and I have [Lightfoot].”
A third, impatient voice argued with the two male ones.
“We agreed to do my thing today!”
“It’s been two hours, Lare.”
“But it’s so fascinating—how can you not see it?”
“It’s pottery.”
“Broken pottery. Listen, what if Kusal and I just met up with you later? Lare, c’mon—”
“Shit, she’s getting mad, Leo.”
“No, I’m not. I’m just upset you’re changing the rules we agreed to.”
“C’mon, Lare—”
A trio of Humans were coming down the corridor. Pisces, by now, had identified them by their names. He was unlikely to forget them so soon. He debated leaving—but he didn’t need to fight the trio of adventurers, did he?
Wildcard, the Gold-ranked team of Earthers, halted when they saw the young man standing there. Instantly, Leonardo reached for his tennis racket, and Kusal pivoted.
“Pukka, it’s them—”
“Hold on, hold on, we’re not fighting!”
Leonardo put out an arm, and the third member of their team, Lareceina the [Mage], put a hand to her belt. Where she kept the glowing orbs…Pisces held up a hand.
“I’m by myself, and we’re not adventuring. Truce?”
He maybe shouldn’t have said he was alone, but it worked. Wildcard relaxed, and Leo nodded.
“Truce. Hey—did your team go fighting the Mad Ones or something north of here? Everyone was talking about it.”
News spread fast. Pisces grimaced.
“It was Itkisa, though the Mad Ones did participate.”
“Torreb’s daughter? Wow, your team fights nonstop.”
The slightly accented common came from Kusal, their [Rogue]. He glanced at Lareceina, who was glowering and looking around. Likely for Ceria. The Horns had not left a good impression. Pisces exhaled.
“We would prefer not to. I, ah, apologize for my teammate’s actions earlier today, Adventurer Lareceina.”
“You didn’t harass me. I accept on behalf of your team, not Ceria Springwalker.”
Lareceina folded her arms and instantly got a nudge from Kusal and Leonardo. She glared at them harder.
“What? I accepted his apology.”
Her captain sighed at her.
“C’mon, Lare, play nice—sorry, Pisces. She’s, uh, stubborn. No harm, no foul. Sorry about the Tomb—it was a quest for both sides.”
He shifted from sandaled foot to foot warily, but Pisces waved this off too.
“We didn’t realize there was a group with an actual claim on the Tomb. If we had known, I doubt my team would have taken the contract. I would have objected to robbing the Hemp of their ancestral spirits. I assume they did receive the summons?”
Again, Wildcard seemed surprised by his response, and Lareceina raised her brows as Kusal nodded.
“We got them to the Hemp. Did you get in trouble for not doing your job?”
“Not to any great degree. We’ll see. I simply appreciate that no one was hurt badly. The same with Itkisa. She is a rather…fearsome woman.”
“Is she strong? Everyone says she’s strong.”
Pisces found himself standing with the Gold-rankers in the now-empty corridor. He indicated his sorry state of apparel.
“She was strong enough to break a wall with a single swing, and her method of attack was swinging her club—or just kicking the ground hard enough to make it explode.”
The Earthers had a fine appreciation of how strong that was. Kusal began nudging Leonardo.
“Told you. She’s one of your, uh, what’s it called? Dragonball people.”
“Saiyans. Shut up, Kusal.”
“All we have to do is find a magical girl too, like the transforming Gnoll. For Justine.”
A grin from the [Rogue], then it faltered, and all three of them glanced down, and Pisces was reminded. He coughed.
“Ah. That would be the teammate of yours who passed away?”
“We fought an Adult Creler, yeah. Just last month.”
“My condolences. I’m…very sorry to hear that. I also lost friends fighting an Adult Creler.”
They blinked at him, and it was like a strange connection. Lareceina stopped fiddling with her belt and focused on him. Leonardo’s head rose.
“That’s right, you’re also Hell’s Wardens. You—was it one Adult Creler, or more?”
“Just one. Though one is…too much. And thousands of small ones.”
“Thousands? How did you survive? We barely had sixty, and they—it—the entire village was nearly wiped out.”
Kusal stared at Pisces, so the [Necromancer] had to clarify.
“There were over a dozen Silver-ranking teams present. My team was one of many, and we all nearly died. It was luck we managed to defeat it—we even had [Mages] from Wistram, and we barely won. Barely. How did you…?”
A pause, but the words spilled out of Lareceina as she fiddled with her belt. She had those compressed marbles of mana, Pisces realized, and she was rotating them around in her fingers. Playing with them like, well, marbles. He glanced at them as she spoke.
“It was immune to my magic. Leonardo and Justine engaged it while I killed the smaller Crelers. She—cracked the armor, and Kusal delivered the final blow. But it got her. Even with her Skills, it bit her almost in half, and there was no healing her. If I’d known more magic…”
Tears in her eyes. She blinked them away, and Kusal squeezed her shoulder. Leonardo stared at his feet, and Pisces’ own eyes stung a bit.
“I’m sorry. I saw many good adventurers die. Captain Stan, friends—it was a close run thing with my team as well. My magic was useless. Even a fine [Mage] couldn’t even harm it with his best spells.”
It was easier to say that after Isceil was dead. Leonardo smiled, then held out a hand.
“Well, one less Adult Creler in the world is a good thing. Can we be friends? Or at least, not enemies?”
“Of course.”
Pisces shook his hand and got a firm grip. He then shook Kusal’s and got a cautious one; Lare’s was like a wet noodle, and she let go fast. Each member of Wildcard was different.
Leonardo had the palest skin, and Kusal was—Drathian would have been Pisces’ guess, or Balerosian. Darker skinned, but different from Chandrarian natives, he felt. His accent was like none that Pisces had ever heard, and Lareceina was black-skinned and shortest. Leonardo was taller than Pisces and Kusal shorter and slimmest of the lot.
[Warrior], [Mage], [Rogue]. But an odd variant on the archetype if that made sense.
For instance, Leonardo had that tennis racket on his hip, and his armor—sporty cloth—was far too light compared to Yvlon’s. Kusal was armored heavier with metal incorporated into leather and lots of pockets built into his armor, containing gadgets like the strange weapon he’d used on Yvlon.
Lareceina wore a long-sleeved tunic and skirt with a twist; Pisces glanced down and realized there was metal underneath her skirt. An armored skirt? He’d never seen the like.
Their gear was substantially worse than his team’s, at least by the quality of Stalker’s armor. Nevertheless, he knew their levels were at least competitive with his team’s, and he could tell they were eying him too; Lareceina pointed.
“That rapier. It’s magic, but it’s not enchanted. May I see it?”
“Of course. Er—”
Pisces looked around, but the [Curator] of the museum had fled. No one else was near, so he showed them his bone-metal rapier. Leonardo exclaimed over it.
“That’s so cool.”
“Heavy metal.”
Kusal agreed. Lareceina just frowned.
“It’s the ivory that was fused to the steel. There’s trace magic in it probably because it’s bone you used, but it’s not enchanted. An ordinary rapier would be just as good, or better.”
“Lare, be nice!”
Another nudge. This time, she jabbed Leonardo in the side with two fingers so hard he yelped. Pisces wasn’t offended though.
“That’s entirely true, Miss Lareceina. It was improvised after I broke it in battle—I could very well upgrade it. I just haven’t found a good replacement.”
Rapiers were not exactly big in Chandrar, so the market for enchanted rapiers wasn’t high. Plus, he liked this weapon. Lareceina nodded, unsmiling.
“Don’t call me Miss, please. Lareceina is fine.”
“I’m sorry about her.”
Leonardo whispered and got another poke. Pisces smiled.
“I’m not offended, Captain. Did I hear you talking about—what was that word? Saiyans? Dragon’s…balls?”
This time, the man flushed so red it went up to his ears, and Kusal and Lareceina cackled at his expense.
“That’s, uh, a story. Just a story—Justine loved transforming heroes. Magical girls. Which is, um—it’s when someone has a weapon and transforms. There’s this Named-ranker who does it!”
“You mean Lehra Ruinstrider? I have met her, and she does do that.”
“She does?”
Instantly the other two Wildcards stopped laughing, and Pisces described the iconic Lehra.
“So she has to say that each time? That’s hilariously stupid.”
Kusal laughed, and Leonardo’s eyes lit up.
“Just like home.”
Here was the moment Pisces had waited for. He glanced at the three members of Wildcard and coughed.
“Ah, which nation would that be? I presume you are all from different countries. Spain, perhaps? Er, Poland? Canada?”
He threw out the names he’d heard mentioned a few times, and he was rewarded with stunned looks. Kusal instantly backed up a step, face wary, but Lareceina interrupted.
“He knows about Earth. I told you his team knew. It was that [Innkeeper] who contacted us. Erin Solstice. They stay at her inn. It was obvious.”
She appeared so smug that Leonardo and Kusal lost their stunned expressions and rolled their eyes. Pisces? He smiled wider.
 
——
 
“I’m from Portugal, Kusal’s from Sri Lanka, and Lareceina’s from Trinidad. So was Justine. We all found each other in the first month we were in Nerrhavia’s Fallen.”
“So you all, independently, became adventurers?”
Pisces had never heard other Earthers talk about their first days in this world. Leonardo smiled ruefully.
“Hardly. Lareceina found work in the Mage’s Guild. Kusal was scavenging for a living, and I got everyone’s attention by teaching people tennis and doing tricks. It’s a game from home, and it’s the only thing I can do. Justine was the adventurer who got us together.”
“He’s not just good at tennis, he was a champion back home.”
Lareceina interrupted, and Leo grew more embarrassed and waved a hand.
“I’m just a challengers champion. I won once by luck—”
“He’s one of the best in the world. Just not the top player. No one in this world can beat him.”
Pisces believed that, having met Erin who also ‘wasn’t the best’ and was able to play with Niers Astoragon himself regularly. He was telling them about his team, though they’d all apparently seen Ksmvr’s famous Chandrarian documentary. And they knew of the Horns from the Village of the Dead Raid. It was all very embarrassing, but this was convivial. Fun, even.
“I observed that in many Earthers, they tend to have a talent in one field or another. Does that hold true with you?”
Wildcard eyed each other, and Kusal raised a hand.
“I won an award for robotics. I made, eh, how do you say it?”
He whispered to the others and came up with the closest analogy for Pisces.
“Like making Golems that run on electricity. They fight to the death in this little arena, and mine was the best. I also made this.”
He pulled out the long tube-like device he’d hit Yvlon with and hit a button. The zap of electricity made Pisces recoil, and Leo swore.
“That’s a stun gun. Don’t touch the ends!”
“What does it do?”
“Zap people. Kusal had one on him, and he altered it.”
Kusal let Pisces examine it; it was a weird casing of some substance he called ‘plastic’ that had been taken apart then melted back together. The [Rogue of Tricks] had even added a telescoping handle of wood painted black.
“I had two. This is my Double Stun Gun. It has all the safeties taken off, and it can stop even a Manticore. I don’t know how the Silver Killer didn’t fall over when I hit her with it. I even have [Electronics: Triple Charge] and more Skills!”
His class had apparently advanced to let him perform all kinds of weird attacks. Ksmvr would have loved Kusal; the young man was able to carry two bags of holding, and one was filled with stuff to toss at an enemy.
Including just…a twelve hundred-pound piece of stone. A true boulder that only Kushal’s Skills let his bag of holding carry. He solemnly patted it.
“That’s how we killed the Adult Creler. I had to get Lareceina to boost me, and I just hit it with this.”
Dead gods, they might have been lucky not to fight him in the open. Leo’s weapon of choice made more sense to Pisces; the tennis racket was upgraded as well, but his entire ability revolved around the sport he played.
“I can block arrows with this and reflect almost anything as long as I’m strong enough. It’s pretty silly in combat, but we have that combination Skill.”
“The one where you hurl those orbs at us? It was very potent.”
The captain was pleased and ducked his head.
“Well, we had to work on a really good team attack together or we’d have been dead when we took on our first dungeon way back when. Justine used to be part of it…what’s your team attack?”
He changed subjects hurriedly as their fallen teammate kept popping up, but Pisces hesitated.
“Us? We don’t, ah, have one. We tend to just attack.”
It had never occurred to him to practice some kind of combination attack, but that was twice now a foe had needed one; first Bograms, then the Coliseum of Monarchs. Leo hesitated, but Lareceina broke in.
“I’m a [Magus of Compression]. You’re a [Mage] who studied at Wistram, correct? Will you discuss magic with me? I haven’t had a proper education; I’m self-taught. I’d like to, if we’re being friendly. I still dislike your Captain, Ceria, and I think breaking into the Coliseum of Monarchs was dangerous and against Nerrhavia’s Fallen’s laws.”
She was quite insistent on that point. Leo winced, but Pisces had really wanted to ask about her magic. She offered him one of the marbles she’d used to such deadly effect. He gingerly, gingerly took it.
“This is…just compressed mana after all?”
It was an insane technique. Lareceina built up mana, then gave it an element and put it in the orbs she carried on her belt and in a small sack. He could imagine doing it, and there was some genius to it; she could store mana instead of having only what was in her mana well in a fight.
It was also highly potent as he’d learned, and she could use it in all kinds of tricks like traps or letting Leonardo hit the marbles at a foe. Except Pisces had to point out two things.
“If the compression spell failed in any way, it would explode, and if all the ones on your belt detonated—”
The museum would be gone. His skin itched just being near her. And he wondered how good those compression spells were.
From the way Leonardo and Kusal shifted, they were aware of this fact and uneasy themselves, but Lareceina simply frowned.
“I’m aware of that. I’ve altered the compression spells so they just vent magic if they’re damaged. The possibility of explosion remains, but my class gave me Skills to mitigate the risk and compress more mana.”
“There’s still a risk that someone like Ceria could remotely dispel the bindings.”
“Maybe. That’s why I want consultation on how to prevent that.”
“Of course, I think I know some of that—it’s akin to tying a knot on a spell. But, ah, may I ask how you’re doing it?”
It was still crazy magic to Pisces. Because…none of this was a spell. It was literally just mana-shaping, and it reminded him of the Mad Ones’ camp. Lareceina’s answer was to sigh.
“I had to teach myself magic. I had no spellbooks, and the Mage’s Guild only taught me basic spells to help out, so I experimented with mana flows. I was told it was stupid and that spells were the only acceptable way to cast magic. Do you agree with that?”
“I would be a fool to ascribe to that philosophy. Many [Mages] are hidebound—this would never have been accepted at Wistram, but it clearly works. I just…”
Pisces could imagine making a mana orb of death magic. He gave it a try now and condensed the mana around a finger. He could easily do that, and Kusal shivered and moved back from the odd, clammy feeling around Pisces. Death magic wasn’t cold—it just felt that way because your body started to stop working around it. But Pisces only managed a vague orb of death.
Nothing compressed. Let alone binding it…he began to sweat as Lareceina nodded.
“That’s how you do it. My first orbs were Tier 0 in force. You simply lock it into place after that. You can hold it, but it’s a strain…you have to create a containment sphere around it in your head.”
“I…understand. But it’s so damned finicky!”
Magic did not want to compress. It wanted to go to natural sources of itself. Like how death mana concentrated around dead bodies. It was not happy about just existing in a cheerful orb. Lareceina nodded.
“My orbs deplete. I have a Skill—[Mana: Reduced Drain], but I still need to upkeep them. Actually, until recently I spent a lot of mana upkeeping them, but it’s worth the effort. There. Now, just close the circuit. See?”
She demonstrated and compressed fire magic in on itself, and Pisces saw her locking it down, creating a perfect sphere by which it could not escape. The problem was—you had to mentally hold a sphere in your head and cut off each point it wanted to escape from. You had to also account for the variance in elemental types! Fire magic didn’t behave like, say, water magic. Ice magic would freeze over and become inert…
“Whoa, so this is really tough magic? Lare, how do you do all that?”
Leo and Kusal realized their companion was a bit more magically adept than they’d known as Pisces struggled to figure out her technique. She smiled.
“It’s my special power. Autism.”
Kusal spat out some water all over a display and laughed at her until she went to poke him again. Pisces just gave up on his death orb; it was going to take a lot of practice if he wanted to master this trick, and he was considering it.
“I’m not familiar with the word. What is this…?”
“It means my mental processes are wired a bit differently than normal. I sometimes overfocus on things. I don’t like being touched.”
“And she’s not a fan of breaking rules, which is why she hates your Captain. And because she rubbed Lare’s hair.”
Leo put in. Pisces scratched at his head.
“Intriguing. I’ve met a number of [Mages] who fit that descriptor.”
He wondered if Master Hedault qualified under that. Or Watch Captain Zevara given how much she was a stickler for rules…
“I take it this gives you some advantage in magic?”
Lareceina hesitated, then shook her head.
“Um, not really. It’s just a joke.”
Pisces decided not to press her because she looked a bit embarrassed, now. He nodded.
“I see. Then may I just ask how you came to this style of magic? It’s so novel, compressing mana.”
“Well, I just…experimented. When I saw a [Fireball], I wondered how it was cast since I didn’t know the spell. I learned, later, it was ‘woven flames’, but I thought I could make a version just based on compressing heat.”
“Ah, that’s actually an older style of [Fireball] that fell out of fashion. The modern spell is more explosive and harder to dispel or prematurely detonate.”
Lareceina’s eyes lit up.
“That’s what I was told! But I still thought it was worth a shot. If you could compress even just water into a thin jet, you’d create something that cuts through steel. I knew that, and the Siren of Savere does it. So when I started experimenting…”
They got to talking more as Leo and Kusal tried to keep up with the magical discourse. Pisces wondered if it was Lareceina’s background from Earth, but it was so refreshing. Lareceina didn’t understand any rules of magic–so she had tried anything she wanted and found what worked. She spoke like someone who might have written the Djinni’s spellbook. Magic without needing a spell for everything.
She really was self-taught, and Pisces knew he had been considered something of a genius for his magical acumen, but he really was astonished by her lack of grounding in any formal training. They were discussing magic and realized that a lot of advanced topics were a mystery to both of them.
“Linked magic is really hard. I keep trying since I can store different mana types in orbs, but I can’t make them work aside from elemental reactions.”
“I doubt any modern [Mage] except maybe Valeterisa or Eldavin could do the same. Ceria can, but it’s her circlet which enables the feat. It’s quite powerful—we do have a combined spell, actually. Frostmarrow Behemoth.”
“We saw that! It was awesome!”
Kusal loved the giant undead Frostmarrow Behemoth which he termed ‘heavy metal’, and Pisces was reminded that not all Earthers feared necromancy. Lareceina was insistent, though.
“I want to learn combination magic. Is that the term for it? Mixing elements and spells together. That’s how my spellcasting improves to the next level. There are many ways, clearly. That one is mine. Compression magic will only go so far. But if I create combined spells…”
“I am also trying to break through the ceiling of my magical studies. I have a spellbook, actually, which has some fascinating magical shaping tips…”
He was all set to even break out his Djinni spellbook, but to his perplexment, Lareceina turned.
“If you have time, I’d like to read it. However, I have thirty minutes left at the museum, and I’m not done looking around.”
“Oh come on.”
Leo and Kusal had already been dying to leave, and Lareceina’s insistence on finishing her museum tour instead of chatting with another Gold-ranker who knew other Earthers nearly made them drag her off. Unfortunately, she had an ally in none other than Pisces.
“I was fascinated by this museum myself. For such antiquities, it’s rather underfunded.”
“This is interesting to you?”
Kusal had a variety of electronics he’d altered, and he was opening one up to tune it; he had even made some primitive batteries with Lareceina’s help. He had zero interest in pottery, as did Leonardo. However, Pisces was only too happy to explain as an amateur historian.
“Yes, actually. This isn’t just pottery, but pottery that dates back to the Immortal Empire of Nerrhavia. Highly controversial in many places, but it does reflect a period of Stitch-folk power that even Nerrhavia’s Fallen couldn’t equal. And a different society. See how all the Stitch-folk here are represented equally? They aren’t based on the same Hemp, Cotton, Silk caste system. I was just reading a book on that, actually.”
One of the enduring ironies from the time of the Immortal Tyrant was that Stitch-folk had won freedom from her, but created a system where the most numerous cloth type was distinctly subservient to the rest. Not that Pisces was going to vouchsafe that anywhere Stitch-folk could hear…
Leonardo and Kusal grew more interested as Pisces pointed this out. The two Humans saw Pisces point out a map that even showed that this particular city had endured since the Immortal Tyrant’s era; many modern buildings were built on the foundations of old ones worn away.
“The reason such mundane pottery exists when magic itself wore out in the intervening periods is twofold. Firstly, magic would have been used until the items broke. Secondly, when magic fades, it does tend to damage what the enchantment was bound to. So you get some mundane, simple pieces of pottery that are the only relics of truly ancient eras.”
“Huh, that’s actually pretty interesting. Lare, why didn’t you say anything about that?”
Her expression was so utterly outraged when she turned that Leo and Kusal decided to beat a hasty retreat and find lunch. That left her and Pisces standing together in dead silence. A bit awkwardly now…Pisces wondered if Lareceina was potentially bad at conversation. She did break the silence abruptly.
“I maintain my position that we were in the right both morally and legally, despite the crown’s actions at the Tomb of Yad’thuv, Adventurer Pisces.”
“Er, Pisces will do, Lareceina. And I quite understand.”
She nodded, abruptly.
“I also don’t like the actions of Yvlon Byres or Ceria Springwalker. There are customs and rules in Nerrhavia’s Fallen your team ignores to their peril. You will provoke hostile responses, such as Yvlon has already encountered.”
That made Pisces turn.
“You know what happened to her?”
She hesitated.
“I…suspect she was poisoned or something was done to her when she was kissed in that parade. You didn’t see it, nor did anyone else, but the girl who kissed Yvlon went away, and some people helped her lie down. She appeared to fall asleep or pass out moments afterwards, and they spirited her away.”
Pisces really didn’t like that. He hoped Yisame’s people could help—and he coughed.
“I understand, Lareceina. Yvlon is a bit of a rulebreaker, but her friends had been improperly accused and were in mortal peril.”
She frowned at him.
“I wasn’t referring to that. I am going to be more precise: I objected to the killing of the Champion of Monarchs in cold blood after he surrendered. There is a cultural precedent for Yvlon Byres’ actions, especially if her friends were accused and she had been challenged as well. The murder was where your captain crossed the line.”
That was harder for Pisces to argue with. He closed his mouth hard. Ceria had murdered Lenxiol, and it was true he might have come back for vengeance…but they hadn’t discussed it. He wasn’t sure he could let Ceria just be besmirched by Lareceina without some pushback, so he replied after a moment, gently.
“This is fair. But my team also attacked [Slavers] of Roshal, unprovoked. And I am the famous Scourge of Roshal. Do you hold a grudge against me?”
The [Mage] went very still as she peered at an old illustration of the Immortal Tyrant’s city in her time, and then she turned. She spoke as she met Pisces’ eyes.
“My understanding is that you were illegally taken as a [Slave]. By that logic, all your actions were that of an innocent person held under false pretenses. There is no legal system in Chandrar that can hold Roshal to account; nothing you did was wrong.”
He felt relieved at that, but she took a hurried breath before he could reply and held up a finger urgently.
“Furthermore—there are some laws and cultural norms in Chandrar that go against universal rights and basic morality. Which I do not respect.”
She peered around, and he felt a curious emanation from her. A pulse—her way of scanning for detection spells? She leaned forwards and whispered to him in the empty corridor.
“But I am also aware of how dangerous and how far such an institution’s authority spreads. For the sake of my team, I do not interfere with such rules because we will not survive being made targets. You might. But I would be very careful how much you do and leave quickly if you go further.”
Lareceina whispered in his ear then stepped back abruptly. She went back to studying the illustration, and after a moment, Pisces saw the [Curator] peek at them then hurry off. He stood there and took her warning seriously. There it was again, that shadow he could sometimes ignore, but never forget was in this nation, in this continent.
Roshal.
“Have you ever thought about leaving Chandrar?”
She half-turned.
“Perhaps. But Justine died here. Our reputations are built here. We will see the world, but we have just reached Gold-rank. We are not ready. Your team proved that. Someday, I will go to Wistram, to the Walled Cities, to Rhir, and see it all. But not before I make sure I won’t lose my teammates. They’re all I have.”
She glanced back down at the displays. Pisces nodded to her.
“I understand that quite well.”
“Then we understand each other. Good. You do know I don’t hold you in contempt.”
“I believed that was the case, but thank you for clarifying.”
“Good.”
After a moment Lareceina looked up and added.
“I can never tell what people understand. Language is so imprecise; even when it seems like I’m speaking clearly, mistakes seem to occur. I wish you’d met Justine. She was our captain before she died. She should have survived.”
He didn’t know what to say to that. After a moment, Pisces fished around in his bag of holding and handed her a handkerchief so she could wipe her tears. It transpired that Lareceina didn’t trust anyone else’s handkerchiefs, which was very fair. And he did have to mention an unfortunate fact he’d learned about [Cleanse]…
But it was a good meeting to have, truly.
 
——
 
Pisces felt like it was worth being left behind just for that one meeting. Mending the bridge with Wildcard felt right. Moreover, the team was a highly interesting one who might be valuable allies.
Certainly, they seemed trustworthy and knew Nerrhavia’s Fallen a lot better than Pisces himself did. When Leo and Kusal came back with some skewers of meat, they even had news Pisces had wanted to find out.
“Oh, you’re a famous name on the borders. Not a month goes by without ‘the Scourge of Roshal’ striking a [Slaver] caravan. They don’t normally report strikes this far inland, but it happens. It’s sort of common knowledge that Roshal will call any attack an attack by you, but people say they’ve seen you.”
Pisces stopped chewing on the meat skewer outside the museum. He looked up sharply.
“Truly? I had wanted to, ah, investigate that.”
Lareceina’s face was utterly smooth and gave nothing away, but Kusal raised his brows.
“Well, if you go further east…there’s [Rebels] who free [Slaves]. But Roshal and Nerrhavia’s Fallen send hunting parties after them. Or even Djinni.”
“Against people?”
“They don’t do it against normal people, but [Bandits] and the like are free game. You, uh—we saw you taking down that caravan on the scrying orb. That was pretty m—”
Lareceina stomped on Kusal’s foot, and his eyes watered up as she turned to Pisces.
“Utterly lawless, which my team is against, Scourge. I trust you will behave yourself under the laws, unlike your team.”
He would have taken some offense to that—Leonardo frowned at Lareceina—but for the conversation they’d just had. Pisces smiled blandly at Lareceina.
“I would hate to make an enemy of Wildcard twice! Perhaps I’ll just collect locations…”
It wasn’t like he could set out that far even with a magical carriage. He’d have to get information on a few places, go to the capital, persuade the others to come all the way back…well, it would only be a day or two of that dratted carriage. Pisces sighed.
“Well, uh, we’re going to the Mad Ones’ camp to see if they have anything Kusal wants to buy. Do you want to come with us…?”
Pisces rather suspected he’d worn out his welcome there and said so, and Wildcard waved as they departed. He would have liked to talk more, but Pisces realized it was already midday—he’d need to charter a magical carriage.
 
——
 
If the Mage’s Guild even had one around here. Another issue that Pisces realized might be more of a problem, especially when he entered and was told there was none in fifty miles of the city.
“I’m terribly sorry, Adventurer, but between the one chartered for Adventurer Itkisa by order of the Crown and others in use—there is one reserved for the team of Wildcard, but we have no more.”
“May I request one from further abroad, then?”
“Absolutely, sir! Please inform the crown we are working to accommodate you at full speed, but it is a matter for the academy, not—”
The very nervous [Receptionist] quoted him as having to wait three hours and twelve minutes, which was reasonable, all things considered. Just…
Pisces wished he’d asked for the carriage before the museum because he’d just passed all the time he cared to, and now he was bored. He had even had lunch.
“Drat.”
He was only mildly put out by the situation. Pisces reflected that now would be a splendid time to read his book and do some studying in peace. He had to think on the last two engagements as well.
Even if I wasn’t fighting to kill, I did let down the others. Lareceina’s magic is quite useful. I doubt I could store death mana so easily, but perhaps…?
He was hunting around for a nice place to sit and read. Such places seemed to be attached to cafes though, and he didn’t see a lovely park, the kind of which he’d expect in Izrilian cities.
Oh, there was a fountain, a plaza—all too full of people who started to stare at the odd Izrilian Human or, worse, recognize him. Probably from Yvlon’s actions—or the Tomb of Yad’thuv—or his father being on television.
Even now, the man made Pisces’ life worse. But who should appear on the streets as Pisces was wandering than another familiar face!
“Adventurer Pisces?”
He blinked at the trio of Stitch-folk setting up their wagon and smiled.
“Trader…Hexata! Good to see you again. I trust you weren’t, ah, hurt by the fighting?”
She gave him a wide-eyed look.
“We saw you fighting Itkisa, then the Mad Ones firing at you. Truly, the actions of real Gold-rankers! I would not wish to take up your time—weren’t you carried back to Tyrant’s Rest?”
He had to explain his situation, and outmaneuvering the charioteers impressed Hexata more. Pisces felt bad about how Colth had rushed him off, but Hexata waved it all away.
“If you’d like to rest, Adventurer, may I offer my wagon for shade?”
She and her brothers had a little table and chair that Pisces thought would be splendid—and secluded—and he accepted, buying a snack of some sweet jerky to eat while he read.
…He was not a fan of sweet jerky. But he left it on the table as he went back to reading. He could skip lessons in the spellbook if he wanted to. He was still on Lighted Arrow, believe it or not, because there was so much supplemental material.
How to upscale the magic. How to make it spin or track. Weight, density—he felt like the book was trying to politely ground him in all the magic theory he didn’t have, but Pisces did sort of need to advance. So he tried to look up a more advanced spell. The book flickered as it did the same trick as when he’d first opened it.
A spell flashed across his mind; burning motes of fire hanging in the air, not flames as he knew them but…swirls in the air? Purple? He saw a woman with nine tails waving behind her, a fox’s features. Beastkin? Something else? She pointed, and the strange flames flashed past her.
Do you understand this?
He did not. Not the nature of the fire, nor how it was held—so the book’s pages flipped. Another one appeared.
A struggling figure in the deeps of the sea. Drowning, dying. Lungs bursting. Pisces could feel the terrifying pain, and he knew it from when he and Colth had—but magic glowed, and the lungs inflated with air. A spell for breathing water.
Do you understand this?
He did—but he didn’t need the spell. He needed…what did he need? An attack? Something like necromancy, perhaps?
The pages flickered again.
The green land was dying. A stain was spreading from the clawed hand pressed to the earth. The Drake had put his palm down, and now the wave of death was killing it all. Plants, soil, animals—
No. Pisces recoiled from the magic. Not that. Too indiscriminate. The pages flickered—
 
——
 
Was he being picky? After nine spells, Pisces had to take a break. He’d gone from spell to spell and hadn’t found one—yet—he could devote time to. The book had showed him spells he’d been trying to classify as if they were traditional magic. He’d cribbed some notes and his thoughts.
 
[Fox Fire]?
[Breathe Water]. No—[Create Breathable Air]—no, [Create Oxygen], yes, that was what it was!
[Ritual: Death Wave].
[Animate Bone Ogre]. He could do [Skeletal Champion], and he needed something more immediate for combat.
[Summon Animated Bone Axe]? A floating, hacking axe was appealing, but it seemed to require concentration.
[Death Orb]. A higher-grade version of [Deathbolt]? Again, not quite like the spell and fairly powerful—the example had it animating a corpse pile and attacking an oncoming Troll, but it looked slow.
[Flash Phoenix]? Okay, he didn’t know what this was. A more powerful version of Ceria’s [Firefly] spell that looked very fast, but he wasn’t sure about the pyromancy…
[River of Bone Water]. Again, he didn’t know what you’d call it, but it looked like a wave of putrid water filled with bones and death magic. Highly effective against crowds, but what if his opponents jumped?
[Flock of the Carrion Crow]. Blood magic where you slit your veins and red ravens flew up and killed everything, very fast, very efficiently—Pisces sort of suspected the book had been getting annoyed with him at this point.
 
The problem was…Pisces glanced down at the Djinni’s spellbook as he massaged his aching temples and came to a reluctant conclusion.
“I don’t believe this book is replete with death magic.”
A common problem. Sort of ironic given it had belonged to the Putrid One, but if this really was a book that Djinni had written, as Azam had claimed…he’d never heard of a Djinni whose entire thing was death magic.
It wasn’t like he had to know death magic, but he was specialized in it! Plus, Pisces appreciated a big spell, but he kept thinking of all the fast foes he’d fought. He needed a quick, heavy-hitting spell useful against Level 40+ foes…
“I might as well wish for [Flight] while I’m at it.”
He grumbled. In truth, [Deathbolt] might do…but was he going to be like Ceria? Just throwing out her signature spell nonstop? What about his rapier? He did want to be able to fight in melee range. Maybe binding that [Light Spear] spell to his rapier tip was the way to go after all.
Then again, Lareceina’s method of throwing magic arguably beat even Ceria. She could flick those marbles as fast as her thumbs, and she had a slingshot and her teammates. It was almost like Saliss’ attacks.
So powerful. Pisces paged through the book, thinking idly about how it was a tad bit unfair Lareceina’s spells were so useful. Was compression magic the route to success? True, she perceived a hard limit on her powers without training, which was why she was into combining magic…
The book’s pages flickered. Pisces jumped—then stared at the page. And this time, the spell wasn’t—
A [Druid] was sitting under a tree, next to a Unicorn, who was resting with one eye open. Apprentice? Master? The [Druid] was in his fifties, hair unshorn, covered in moss, and his clothing made of bark and natural elements. He was the apprentice, then. 
He sat cross-legged, holding his hands together over something he was working on. It came from every leaf and bit of dew around him. From himself, condensing. Magic, forming the foundation of a spell he might cast or just store. More and more until it exceeded the mana he could store in his person, until it became visible. He was concentrating, not sweating because this was not a sprint, but a slow work. Refining it—you had to refine it and make it deeper, until it was like a jewel—
Pisces blinked, and there it was. The book’s pages flipped before him as he seized on the same technique Lareceina had taught herself. Compression magic?
No, refining mana. Gathering it. Storing it. Yes, that was worth something. He had never wondered about the quality of his mana. Did he have good mana? Suddenly he had questions, and the book obliged him. The pages moved and moved and—
Pisces saw the book’s pages stop flickering. Trader Hexata and her brothers, who had been peeking at him from around their caravan, saw him stop on a page glowing with mystical spell knowledge. He stared at it. Then flipped the cover of the book up, and the little mirror-thing blinded one of the brothers as it caught the sun peeking through the shade of the wagon. Pisces stared at his page. Checked the book again.
He was on…Page 2. He put his palms together and pressed them against his lips. After a few moments, Pisces began reading with a sigh.
 
——
 
Okay, maybe he should have just read the book from the start, but he’d assumed it had known what it was doing when it assigned him magic. It…had…started him at Lighted Arrow. Worse, this introduction to magic was, uh—
Sort of easy to get. Pisces quickly realized you could intensify mana, and the book even gave him a primer on how to condense it, Lareceina-style. Only, instead of holding it in your hand and having to manually contain it…
After six minutes of scribbling on the table with a bit of sand, Pisces swore. He stared at the book. He stared at the containment circle and death mana inside. It wasn’t forming a sphere, but it was condensing without any real strain. The spell circle had a hard limit based on the materials, and if the sand shifted, it’d instantly unleash the magic, but…
He put his head down on the table so hard the sand shifted, and the death magic released with the sound of a Grand Elephant farting. He colored as people walking down the street turned; Hexata was hawking to people entering the city of Halqued.
“Perhaps I need to find Wildcard.”
If he showed Lareceina this, the team might let him hitch a ride back to Tyrant’s Rest if they were headed that way. He thought she was pretty advanced, but she could scribe a container and make a super-orb with this technique. Plus, he felt like it was time for his own carriage to arrive…though, what was this about refining mana?
“You can make a crucible and there’s higher tiers of mana? If I were to make some…put it into a [Fireball]? Ah, wait, you can literally overload a poorly made matrix. So the very spell you cast can be a poor container. Is—what grade of container do I use for spells?”
Reading was fun, especially reading and studying magic. Pisces had never asked these questions of himself before! He was drawn back to the book like a fly to honey. He’d go find Wildcards in…five minutes. One more page.
By that logic, Pisces might have spent the next five days in his seat but for a sound which eventually broke through his concentration. At first, he didn’t register it, despite the high-pitched shouting, until there was a cry desperate enough that he heard it.
“—turer! Scourge! Adventurer Pisces!”
He looked up. And there, standing behind a camel hitched to a post, was someone calling his name. He blinked and saw a familiar sight he hadn’t seen often in this faraway land.
Scales. A Drake girl was standing in a line of dusty figures. Her hands were tied together with a bit of rope, but her feet were not; she was too small, and presumably, it was too easy to catch her even if she got free of the simple tie to the slave-line. Besides—a metal collar was around her neck, and the line of men, women, and children were already marked.
[Slaves].
Pisces dropped the book. He stared as the Drake girl shouted again.
“Adventurer! Over here!”
She was dancing in line, and it was she who’d been shouting. At him. The other [Slaves] were staring at him or at the ground. Some were looking anywhere but him, but all were watching him, even out of the corner of their eyes.
“What—”
But he knew as he arose from his seat. He knew in a moment what this was—it was just that it had not hit him in the face so directly. No, he’d seen this.
As the Horns had moved across Chandrar, he’d seen [Slavers]. When they’d gone north to Hraace, and he’d seen them in Tyrant’s Rest. But he’d been with Gazi and the soldiers of Reim, or there had been no time.
The last time had been with Yvlon, and she’d distracted him. Everyone had. Or tried to keep him away from this reminder. Yisame had done so well, but she was not here.
[Slaves]. It was a caravan headed to market, and they had stopped by Hexata’s stall as the owners went to do something. If there were [Guards], they’d relaxed or were at the gates; they were inside the city. Who’d rob them here? None of them had seen the [Necromancer] sitting there; who would think to look for him when the Horns of Hammerad were known to be headed back to Tyrant’s Rest?
But the girl had. Now, she danced from foot to foot as he stood, color drained from his skin.
“Adventurer, Adventurer Pisces! Over here!”
He didn’t hear anything. Pisces saw the girl, and she was a Drake.
Kidnapped? Or did someone sell her? [Slavers] were banned across most of Izril, but—
He was in the city’s limits. Try to free her and the local Watch and Nerrhavia’s Fallen itself would be on him. Yisame might be [Queen], but this was a bad idea.
Roshal’s hand was everywhere, and they had [Assassins]. The girl was probably, what, nine? Mrsha’s age. She’d never get anywhere in a foreign land. Were the collars death-spelled?
…They looked like location and durability enchantments. But he had no idea how to cut them. If he—
“Scourge, Scourge, stop!”
Someone tackled him. He was halfway across the street when Trader Hexata and one of her older brothers slammed into Pisces. He went sprawling and nearly stabbed them.
“What are you—”
“Stop! Stop, Scourge—you are within the city, and the Golden Hordes will be on you in moments. There is already a garrison of soldiers who were here to tamp down on Hemps—a thousand will be on you in no time. You cannot attack. Even the Queen cannot shield you from this!”
The [Trader] was babbling in his ears. Pisces saw her brother let go of him, fast. Both were pale as well, sweating—
“I wasn’t going to—I was just—”
He sat up. Hexata scrambled up.
“Scourge—”
“I know.”
He knew that. But they flinched back from him, and the girl…Pisces saw her dancing in place. Someone had put a hand over her mouth. A Gnoll? He was watching Pisces.
“I—hello.”
What did you say to someone like that? Pisces stopped, and the Gnoll let go as the girl cried out.
“Adventurer Pisces, here I am! Help, help! No one’s here!”
She gazed up at him, eyes huge and earnest, and he stared at her. At the Gnoll, who whispered.
“Lleta, be silent. If they see you—”
“He’s going to let us go! Everyone knows! He’ll kill the [Slavers], right, Verg?”
The Gnoll man said nothing. He had—slashes on his fur. Black stripes that seemed not like normal fur, but some kind of dye? His fur was brown like Krshia’s, but he was thinner. Pisces’ ears…he rubbed them.
“What are a Drake girl and Gnoll doing in here? Izril doesn’t allow [Slavers].”
He said that, but remembered that caravan he and Colth had found. There was a derisive laugh at Pisces words. Just one, down the line. Pisces saw another Drake standing there. He turned his head away when Pisces peered at him, but it was the Gnoll who replied.
“Not in most Drake cities, no. But they sail the coasts. We came by harbor, from Zeres.”
“From Zeres? But—”
“The City of Waves allows [Slavers]. Just not business. That’s changing.”
So much was contained in these words that Hexata and the other Stitch-folk now watching couldn’t pick up on. Pisces and Verg traded looks, and the Drake girl interrupted.
“Adventurer Pisces, you’re the Gold-ranker who went to Albez, right? Here.”
She tried to twist and hold out her wrists. Verg closed his eyes.
“Lleta, he can’t do anything.”
“But he’s the Scourge. The television said. They beat up everyone for watching it.”
The girl informed Pisces as he stood there. And now there was something wrong with Pisces. Perhaps he was the one poisoned, not Yvlon, because he was in pain.
Not nausea, but a kind of agony that was eating him out from the inside. It made him want to scream, and it was clawing at him as he whispered.
“How did you get here? You two?”
Her face twisted up, and the Drake girl fell still. Then spoke.
“They said my parents owed a lot of money, and—and there was a mistake because Mom said it’d all be fixed, but then someone came and took me. And I told them all it was a mistake, including the Watch, and the [Guardsman] said he’d fix it, but then they took us and—”
She started gulping, then went silent. She didn’t cry. She just stared up at him, and he had to turn to Verg. The Gnoll’s reply was easier. He nodded at his stripes.
“I was bought from Drake prison cells. Not that they would have dared sell me if I had been in my tribe. I was Weatherfur.”
“Outcast?”
“For murder, yes. I was with the main tribe when we heard what had happened in the Great Plains. I disagreed with Torishi’s choice during the Meeting of Tribes and fought against my kin. It went to blood. I was exiled, then got into trouble in a Drake city for petty crimes. Funny. It all seems petty, now. Pointless.”
He stared up, at the sky, and the entire story of the man’s life to here was spelled out to Pisces. A single, crimson trail that snaked into Izril’s cities. Where it could, and then it brought them across the sea to this vast kingdom.
Roshal.
Now there was a crowd. Some of the [Guards] standing at the gates were glancing over, and Stitch-folk were lined up—but far away. Watching Pisces. Fear in their eyes, or perhaps an expectation, but most were just afraid.
They knew him. Hexata and her brothers were the only ones who dared stand close.
“Scourge…mark me, for I hold no chains, and I respect your team and wish you no ill will. Should you free them, you are a dead man within ten minutes. Even if you gained the gates, where would you go? If you had horses? They would ride you down within the hour. If you escaped them, their blades would be in your back by night.”
She was, of course, right. He had no idea where they were on a map, and crossing this vast nation—even if you got to sea, you’d need a crew who could outrun Roshal’s ships, and they were everywhere. You couldn’t hide. You’d have to take their collars off and know where…
Verg nodded.
“She’s right. Leave us, Adventurer.”
“But, Verg—”
“Tell the girl to shut up or we’ll all be whipped for it, again. Not her since she’s too young, but I’d prefer not to be lashed bloody before we get to the auctions.”
A caustic voice in line. A Drake who met Pisces’ gaze. He jerked his head.
“Interested in life stories? I’m a failed [Merchant]. There. Now, kindly, begone.”
“I’m sorry.”
Pisces felt like he was dreaming. That moment of surreality where he walked and almost saw himself from above. Yet he was also aware of each passing second. The thrumming of his heart. He stood there, and Hexata’s reasoning matched his mind perfectly.
Yet the girl was waiting. Mrsha’s age. She whispered.
“Please?”
“Necromancer—”
Verg was motioning him back; someone was hurrying through the crowd, shouting for them to make way. Pisces saw [Guards] coming from the gates. Some had bows, and they were aiming them down. Not quite at him. He looked up, and one flinched back and made a sign on her chest.
What were they afraid of? He wasn’t sure, and glanced around. Then he felt an arm on his shoulders.
“Hey, Pisces, c’mon! I think we owe you a drink.”
Someone strong finally shifted him; Hexata and her two brothers lurched as Leo pulled Pisces back. The [Tennis Champion] was grinning with all his teeth.
Wildcard? They’d returned, and Pisces saw Lareceina, Kusal—the [Rogue] grabbed his other arm.
“Let’s get him out of here. Hey, move it!”
“Adventurer! Wait! Wait!”
Lleta was shouting, trying to twist free of the ropes. Verg was holding her, but she was kicking him, screaming. Pisces saw Lareceina between him and—Leonardo was swearing.
“Fuck, Kusal, pull—”
“He’s strong—”
He was just standing there. Then came a sweating figure, who pushed through the crowd, wearing a turban, travelling clothes with that symbol burned onto them. And Pisces stared.
A Drake.
The [Slave Merchant] cast around, and when he saw Pisces, he recoiled. [Slave Guards] rushed forwards, studying him, and there was shouting.
