“Back, back! Protect us by the authority of Nerrhavia’s Fallen!”
“No one is to draw blades! There is no affront! None!”
The Watch Captain was shouting, waving his hands as he looked around. Eyes flicking to Pisces. But he just heard Lleta shouting.
“Adventurer! Wait! You’re a Gold-rank adventurer! Come back! Please?”
He wanted to say something. Then Lareceina blocked his view, and they finally pulled him off his feet and then—
He woke up. But like his memory of Igheriz, of those days—
The nightmare was simply reality.
 
——
 
Pisces Jealnet didn’t kill anyone. There was no incident that need involve the Watch or the garrison, and even Roshal’s merchants agreed it was best put behind all present.
The [Watch Captain], [Garrison Commander], and the [Mayor] all appeared to say that. Though it was Hexata and Leo that did the talking. Pisces only sat there.
For a moment. He didn’t talk. He just…
Re-articulated everything they were telling him. Of course there was no way to rescue them. Suicide. His team would be in jeopardy. It was one thing to join the fighting out in the straits—another to participate here.
Lareceina pointed it out at increasing volume to Kusal.
“This city is Nerrhavia’s Fallen. Not the wilds. His team are independent adventurers, and he can claim justifiably he was falsely imprisoned. Here is where the crown’s authority lies. If he draws blade unprovoked in this city, it is a blade drawn against Queen Yisame and her kingdom. If it were outside the city—”
“God damnit, Lare!”
They split up, both of them red-faced, and Pisces went over the conversation again, as if Ceria were talking with him. It was, of course, correct. Colth would say the same thing. We cannot save them all.
Eventually, he did get up. It was evening, and Wildcard were arguing whether they should leave via magical carriage to get to Tyrant’s Rest now or later.
“I’m going for a walk.”
They all turned to him, and he clarified.
“Just around the city. I’m not going to the…I’m quite aware, thank you, of the situation. There’s no further trouble?”
Leo, Kusal, and Lareceina glanced at each other and shook their heads.
“None.”
Pisces walked out of the rooms they’d rented. He didn’t know where Hexata and her brothers had gone, but it was late. The sun was setting on the city, and it was orange, casting long, lurid shadows.
Like sins. His shadow stretched behind him as the [Necromancer] saw people in the inn turn and stop talking. His name felt like it had been whispered throughout until they saw him. Then the voices died, and there was only silence.
In the street, people stopped and turned to him. Eyes filled with fear, incomprehension, or worse, a painful expectation.
He could meet no eyes. He couldn’t stand the gazes.
So he vanished.
 
——
 
Lareceina de Verteuil was correct. She had studied Nerrhavia’s Fallen and grown to know it for the year plus that she and her team had been here. They knew it too.
But despite her pointing out that fact, Kusal and Leo didn’t want to hear it. In the end, Leo told her to ‘drop it because you’re not helping, even if you are right’. Which made her so angry she stormed out of the inn.
Someone had to believe in rules. Being Gold-ranked didn’t mean you had an excuse to break laws. She, at least, was a respected Gold-ranker now.
Even if the Ice Squirrel was more popular despite being chaotic, a murderer, and rude. That annoyed Lareceina. But today had also been upsetting on multiple fronts.
In times such as these…she glanced around the streets filled with gossip, the Horns of Hammerad’s name being everywhere.
Their fight with Itkisa and their visit to the Mad Ones, their deeds, had utterly eclipsed Wildcard’s. True, the events at the Tomb of Yad’thuv had been covered up as part of their agreement, but that was fame.
She stared around as she projected mana from her body, like a pulse-wave, then condensed more in her hand. Like she stored feelings, bottling them up and compressing them.
She made the ‘mana marbles’ constantly, replenishing her stocks, concentrating the ones she had, and it gave her clarity. In such moments, Lareceina would prefer to be left alone.
—Which is why she found it intolerable for Leo and Kusal to follow her.
“I want to be left alone right now.”
“C’mon, Lare. Don’t—”
Her glare made Leo throw up his hands, but he did follow her as she walked to her destination. Which made them all the more upset.
“I’m going to hit her. What the—”
That was followed by some Sinhala swearing, but Lareceina was smiling.
“Hello, I am a Gold-rank adventurer and [Mage] inquiring about your services. May I ask if this is the only ‘stock’ you have in today?”
The person in charge of the Slaver’s Guild in the city was a Stitch-woman, Cotton, skin done up beautifully. She appeared a bit—shaken.
Everyone did. Word from the encounter on the streets had the more resplendent members in the Guild muttering and keeping to the backrooms, while prospective buyers were thin. Even so, there was traffic.
People coming to sell and buy. Though this place was not where you sold—they had a less luxurious lounge than this for that transaction.
The word ‘adventurer’ made the woman tense and everyone glance around, but Lareceina clarified.
“I am part of Wildcard, who battled the Horns of Hammerad, an adventurer in good repute with all Guilds.”
Leo gave the woman an unconvincing smile; Kusal hadn’t entered. But the woman brightened up and checked something via a magical ledger.
“Adventurer Lareceina, of course! I see you’re not a member here, but you do have a very good record with other Guilds—hello! Are you here to buy or sell?”
She was suddenly very friendly, and Lareceina got plenty of smiles and nods around the room, which made her predisposed to think she was welcomed here. She smiled back.
“Just to browse. Do you have anyone capable of acting as a Slave Adventurer?”
“Oh, no one like that—it’s a highly qualified role, but we could have a catalogue written up for you? There would be a delivery fee—our current roster is being written up.”
Lareceina nodded.
“That’s very reasonable. Hm. In that case, I’d just like to look around.”
“Absolutely, Miss! Let me issue you with a little token if you’d like to sit and have refreshments; a sign of goodwill. And if you’d choose to register with us, we would upgrade your membership—”
At this point, Leonardo’s foot was pressing down on Lareceina’s toes so painfully she shifted. But she accepted the little badges and promised to give them back once she left. Lareceina began to walk towards the VIP guest area when she had a thought and walked back to the counter.
“Excuse me, I have another question if I may? I don’t know if we can buy now, because we’re moving. But I am curious—we might be in the area. Do you have any more caravans coming to the city?”
The [Receptionist] had to check, humming as Lareceina waited patiently.
“A number—this is a decent stop along the Leashed Trails—it goes all the way to Lailight Scintillation itself, you know. East to west, across all of Chandrar.”
“Could I ask you to give me a copy of them? In case I wanted to wait for one or two. I’m trying to convince my team—do you have any attractive female [Slaves]? Garudas?”
Another smile, and the [Receptionist] laughed as she whispered to Lareceina.
“For you or your team?”
“My [Captain].”
“Well, I suppose since you are a prospective Gold-card member—we use ranks like your Adventurer’s Guild, but we go above Gold-ranks. Give me five minutes?”
It took less time than that for the [Receptionist] to get a list printed for Lareceina. Well, a [Slave] actually did the scribing onto a copy of a map, and there was no fee. So Lareceina left a gold-coin as a tip. At this point, Leo almost dragged her out of the Guild, and she protested they hadn’t looked around, to which he told her they had to go to get on the magical carriage.
When they left the Guild, Kusal appeared and spoke.
“I can’t find Pisces, but he’s not here. What did she do in there?”
“She was asking about buying—c’mon.”
They almost dragged her off. Lareceina shifted.
“Don’t grab me. Look at this.”
She flourished the little piece of paper at them. It was amazing work and spoke to Roshal’s wealth.
Not only did they have a map of the ‘Leashed Trails’, which highlighted their caravans’ travel routes across cities of this region of the kingdom, but they could make copies and they’d annotated them with each caravan. Which meant they regularly checked in and monitored their people.
It was highly impressive, and the Merchant’s Guild might not have such impressive data. Kusal stared at Lareceina.
“Leo, I’m going to punch her.”
“Cool it, Kusal. Lare, we’re not happy right now. So let’s all go back to the inn or get in the carriage and find Pisces—”
“Let’s rent two carriages, and she can ride in the other or walk back.”
They bickered in the street. Lareceina glowered at Kusal and offered him the catalogue. He tried to rip it up—she flicked a miniature gravity marble into his chest and knocked him down. Leo put Kusal in a headlock and then grabbed the map.
He crumpled it up and tossed it aside. Lareceina turned around, crossed her arms, and spoke as she stared down the street.
“Leo, I am very unhappy with you at this moment. I would like to go now.”
“Fine by me.”
They stormed off and found the magical carriage waiting for them at the inn. Adventurer Pisces still hadn’t appeared, and since he had his own magical carriage, they got in theirs. Lareceina insisted they take a specific route through the city on their way out.
“Okay, Lare. Explain exactly what that was before one of us starts shouting—”
“Shush.”
Leo made a sound, but Lareceina stared out the one-way glass of the Wistram Carriage. They were in the street right outside the Slaver’s Guild, and she stared, and Kusal nearly shouted—then saw the finger she’d put to her lips.
They had put a cloth over the scrying orb in the center of the carriage, but it was reasonable to assume that Wistram could still hear through it, potentially. Lareceina had asked, and the ability to cast a spell that let them see through cloth via the scrying orb was remote; she’d gotten some and sewn a lead lining into it anyways just in case.
Leo and Kusal stared into the street. They were right where they’d had the fight. Lareceina peered down, and there was nothing there.
Of course, the ball of paper might have moved with the wind or been swept up. But if you followed a magical signature you’d attached to it…
She saw nothing. So the carriage rolled on after a moment, and then her team sat back. And they were no longer angry.
Language was so imprecise. Lareceina hated it. So she sat back and began to flex her fingers. Her fingertips glowed in the gathering darkness, leaving little trails.
Just light magic. Words, if you squinted at the aftertrails. Wildcard sat in silence as they drove off, and that was that. They were respectable adventurers. Unlike the Horns of Hammerad.
That was, for the moment, how you had to be.
 
——
 
The magical carriage rolled away, and Pisces wondered if Wildcard had been inside of it. He suspected they had been, but he didn’t drop his [Invisibility] spell.
Perhaps they knew he was there, the Slaver’s Guild. They had magic too, but he didn’t approach. In the end, he walked off, tucking a piece of paper into his bag of holding.
He was late for his magical carriage back to Tyrant’s Rest, but the [Mage] on duty told him there would be no fee. Pisces thanked him, then got in it.
“Welcome, guest. Please state your destination and enjoy Wistram’s Carriage Services! Please note our updated policy about use in situations of conflict—”
Pisces ignored the familiar voice of Mage Rievan speaking and spoke.
“Tyrant’s Rest, palace.”
“Please enjoy our complimentary—”
He ignored the scrying orb, then opened a window. The city moved past him as the magical carriage navigated the now-dark streets at slow speed, heading towards the nearest gate.
 
——
 
The [Guards] at the gates didn’t exactly like the annoying Wistram Carriages, which would loudly request entry and priority passage at increasing volumes, or the fact that they weren’t allowed to always search them.
Wistram was negotiating with each nation for this kind of access, but in this case, they were glad to see the carriage go. For everyone knew it held the Bane, and the sooner he was out of the city…
Disagree, agree with him—his name was famous, and his team, perhaps rightfully so, the talk of Chandrar and the world. But an honest or dishonest Stitch-person did not long to see the legend of the [Necromancer], Pisces, told in their city.
By the Threadmakers, no. So each tensed spine straightened as the carriage left, pausing only before the gates to be waved past all those in line, and even the Watch Captain on duty was said to have gone to the nearest [Stitchmistress] to have her spine and shoulders replaced, so knotted were they.
The carriage sped out into the darkness, glowing faintly blue, made of magic and light and carrying a legend off, and leaving only this city to smaller stories, like the Mad Ones. Funny to now think of them as the lesser of great tales, but theirs was a contained thing, unlike the match which might blaze brightly, then fade away just as quick.
Who were they to say? Let it only be a story, then, for all to brag about or speak of when drinks were spilled. They had seen a legend, but not any more than that. Lucky, then! Ah, yes…
 
——
 
Trader Hexata was shaken herself from the events of the day. She thought it was worth something in coin; spinning the tale of her brief encounter with the Horns would attract some customers, surely, and the Mad Ones always had curios.
Still, had it not twisted at the heartstrings to see that girl begging to be freed? For a second, she had thought…well, her brothers had remonstrated with her on her madness, but she had truly liked Necromancer Pisces. At first, she had thought him so much more mild than his reputation.
But at the end, there…
Well, all things were mended with thread and time. She was packing up her caravan; they’d leave at dawn for new cities and profits. She was wondering if she could sell the table and chairs where Pisces had sat—a shame they were not marked, but if she got it certified on truth spell?
As the magical carriage rolled towards the gates, perhaps only Trader Hexata, cleaning her caravan, saw the dust swirl oddly in the street next to the open window. For a second, the carriage slowed, then a bright voice spoke from within.
“Window closing. Please note, Wistram is not responsible for passengers l—”
The [Trader] straightened. Perhaps that had only been her mishearing or a trick of the wind. Likely, likely…but the [Guards] waved the carriage through, and who could see through the glass that did not reveal the occupants?
Of course, it would be silly of her to think otherwise. A fool’s madness, perhaps.
“Brothers? Mind the wagon. I’m just going for a walk…”
“At this hour? Sister, is your head stuffed with wool? Here, wait a second—you’ll have a [Brigand] or [Footpad] on you—”
Her eldest brother peered up from the wagon and leapt down, but Hexata was walking towards the gates. The [Guards] let her out but warned her the gates would close within the hour, and she walked further.
Further, as the dust swirled across the ground. Then her eyes narrowed. They passed beyond the sight of the gates as the terrain changed slightly, leading them over a slope. And then the wind blew a storm of dust across her, and she shielded her face.
“Sister! Have you taken leave of your—”
Grulive followed her at a run, cursing, with Xomet behind. They halted in their tracks as the wind died down, and the [Trader] sighed.
There he was.
Pisces Jealnet was walking across the ground. He had found a hood and bought it, and the cloak hid his iconic white robes. Even if the wind had revealed him in sight of the walls, what of it?
It was dark, and at a distance, he looked like any other traveller or vagrant. Only one who had been standing right there…
He turned as she called out.
“Adventurer. I meant every warning. You are a famous Gold-rank adventurer, and if I do not mistake your level, it is over 40. But Nerrhavia’s Fallen eats such individuals up. Our greatest [Mage] is one that not even Archmage Amerys challenges. Our coliseums made the likes of Mars. You are one man, and the nation of Roshal is vast.”
He turned back, and his face was calm. So oddly calm, not like he was reading his spellbook. She had stolen glances at him, wondering if he might look up and their eyes meet. Though he had charmed the Arbiter Queen, it was said, and she was a humble [Trader]—
But he had been so engrossed in reading, smiling, musing, eyes glowing with a passion that she had just watched him for hours. Nor was it the calmness of the man who had come to meet the Mad Ones, peaceable, in good humor with his team for all he might grimace or quibble at times.
This was a different man, unlike the one she’d wrestled on the street. Just…
Confident. Yes, that was the word. A confidence she had known a few times when she had the perfect deal, when she knew herself to be poised and all things seemed to be balanced. Not luck, but surety. Nor was he utterly happy, but he was sure. Now, he bowed, a [Duelist]’s graceful motion.
“Trader Hexata. Thank you for your help in all the ways you have aided me today. I hope you will aid me in one last way by keeping our encounter private.”
She didn’t say anything; her throat was tight, so it was her eldest brother, Grulive, who croaked.
“That—you have our word on it, by coin and honest means, Adventurer. May we never take a copper if we lie. But you have no team.”
They pointed this reasonable thing out, and he nodded like it was meaningful. But then Pisces just brushed at his hair and looked around. His shoulders seemed to lighten at their very words.
“Yes. That’s true. I would prefer their company, but some things…I have always aspired to be a good teammate, you see. I have been a poor friend and led my first team astray by my presence. I would hate to bring them more trouble, even if I hope they’d support me.”
He stopped a moment and smiled at something only he could see.
“Surely, they would. This, though, is something I can do. In my spare time. I’ll find my team in a moment. I’m just…restless.”
Then he turned, as if that said it all rather than left a thousand thousand words unspoken, and walked away. Darkness claimed him in moments, or perhaps he became invisible again. It left Hexata and her brothers to stand there until they knew the gates would close and had to turn. But it lingered in their ears, each and every one. And they said nothing as they returned to their wagon or over their late repast, but it was in their eyes. An echo unsaid.
In my spare time. Restless.
They were not grand words, but Hexata approached the sleepy [Barmaid] at night and paid for a week’s worth of rooms on instinct. Then she went to her rooms and tossed and turned for so many hours that a weary guest below her had to bang on the door and demand she be quiet. But she could not sleep.
Hexata waited—not knowing when or where. But knowing nonetheless. Like a team of Gold-rank adventurers headed back to Tyrant’s Rest. As a girl cried herself to sleep in cells—
Six people in this world could not sleep.
They waited.
 
——
 
Pisces Jealnet awoke after a satisfactory five hours of sleep. He needed his rest, and he rolled out of his bedroll. He’d created a little bone bivouac, but failed to account for the winds. They’d blown sand all over him until he’d had to enclose himself entirely in the improvised tent. For air, he’d built a breathing tube.
He’d still been buried and realized this location had to border the Great Desert. The Glass Straits too; it was a famous natural road across Chandrar and part of these Leashed Trails. Exactly the place you’d put the Mad Ones in case something blew up too big.
Sparse cover meant it was harder for [Bandits] to lie in wait, he supposed. Plus, his knowledge of history and the town’s museum had said that the roads that the Immortal Tyrant had built intersected with the ones the King of Destruction had laid down the eastern coast. Ideal for caravans.
Getting out of bed was Pisces’ first challenge and surprisingly hard. He nearly buried himself trying to get out of the sand. Then he slapped his forehead.
“I am such a fool. Out of practice. Arise.”
Bones flew up out of his breathing tube, then formed Skeleton Champions who began to dig with their bare hands. Then bone shovels. Pisces finally excavated himself and shook his head.
In a way, he felt like a sleepwalker, much like the King of Destruction had been said to be. He felt more focused today. Hraace, even the coliseum, felt like another man’s memories.
Pisces was no smarter today, but he was aware when he was being a fool. And he could not be—so he regarded the Skeleton Champions, who were currently naked.
He’d have to armor them up with Colth’s gear. Several had ‘perished’ at sea, and Pisces had not thoroughly replaced their armor and weapons.
“I should have done that the moment we reached land.”
Bones too. He had Nekhret’s bones, but if he had more space in his bag of holding, he could double his supply, and it was a finite resource. Gargoyle bones…Ama was right.
Pisces got moving as he ate the sweet jerky that Hexata had sold him. And again, he caught himself.
He had been moving with [Flash Step], trying to time each footfall so he was able to run with the spell. It was making good progress, but Pisces felt too noticeable; he couldn’t keep up [Invisibility] and [Flash Step]. Plus, each cast burned magic, however efficient the spell was.
So he stopped and thought. He needed transport…this was a vast region. But he had no handy camel like Ksmvr had claimed he’d had, his arch nemesis Spitty. But…
“Is it here? Please let me have taken it, not Colth. Aha.”
Pisces smiled when he pulled an object out of his bag of holding. He truly didn’t make use of his gifts, but this, at least…
The curious saddle lay on the ground as Pisces animated a horse, and he had to adjust the bones, but the saddle made for undead horses from the King of Duels himself had been created for just this purpose.
Then he was riding. And the undead horse…he poured death mana into it until the blue eyes were glowing bright.
Pisces cast an illusion on himself and the horse. At a distance, they seemed like an ordinary horse and rider. It’d fall apart the moment someone got close since he was no great caster, but he didn’t take the main roads. He was reading the map that Lareceina’s team had tossed aside, doing calculations.
The nearest caravan would be…it was a lot of guesswork, but Pisces had other advantages. He galloped over to a section of the road after a few minutes, tossed something down, and moved off the road again. He then found another stretch of road about twenty miles north and did the same. If he saw anyone on the path, he’d either get off his horse and jog over, pretending to be a traveller, or wait until they were gone. Or just toss down the object and let it make its way over.
He lost three of his undead mice to casualties; two were snatched up by birds who mistook them for actual mice. The last ran into something from underground; a scorpion or snake he bet. But the rest surveyed the road.
The more he tossed down, the more he had to concentrate, of course. Pisces had always felt Ivery and Bearbones, the Skeleton Lord and Skeleton Warbear duo, as distant foci he had to ‘upkeep’ with mana, but they had been largely self-sufficient.
Now, each mouse plus the skeleton horse was a little amount of death magic he had to expend—and he was counting how much he had. He did have a [Ashen Mana Well], but he wished he was stocked up on mana potions; he only had six.
Ceria’s circlet or Lareceina’s stored magic would be invaluable. But he had been lax. Lazy. So Pisces did what he could.
He went to the bathroom in the sand, and his second crisis was a lack of toilet paper. That one was highly distressing. In the end, Pisces, cursing, had to cut up some spare clothing and use the strips…
“Colth and Ksmvr always had the supply.”
Highly embarrassing. He’d need his own. At least he’d had a sleeping bag. But one had to do one’s business. Ahem. Pisces buried the waste, then finished his work.
The Skeleton Champions stared accusingly at Pisces as he assembled them. He’d forgotten to make them turn around. They felt weirdly judgemental, and he hoped this wasn’t a Toren scenario. Or maybe it was just how he’d react.
He had them put on the rest of his gear; they seemed to fight for gear such that instead of three or four fully-geared ones, he ended up with all of them having a piece of armor, but none of them being fully kitted out.
A bit…well, less impressive. Some didn’t even have weapons, so he made weapons out of bone for them.
Pisces recalled Colth’s comments in the Meeting of Tribes and made sure that each Skeleton Champion had a weapon that Pisces had at least basic competency with. All rapiers seemed like a bad idea; they needed to mix weaponry.
He also had a choice to make at this moment when he reviewed his remaining bones and remembered—there had been two Manticores in the Coliseum of Monarchs. He briefly toyed with animating a full Manticore…but ruled it out for two reasons.
Firstly—he didn’t know how they were assembled. He’d have to puzzle together their anatomy, and that took time he didn’t have. He could get one working in a day or two, but he’d have to make sure they moved right—you could swift-animate the bones, and they’d more or less work, but you ‘strengthened’ undead so they swung harder and were more durable at the joints.
The difference between a Skeleton Knight and a mere skeleton. Instead, he re-purposed the bones and added three Skeleton Champions, spreading out the Manticore’s bones across the rest.
That gave him eleven who looked markedly more sturdy, if a bit lopsided due to having to fit Manticore bones in their frames. Hulking. They stared ahead, eyes glowing…then shuffled around as Pisces went to pee again.
He couldn’t help it. He was nervous. But then Pisces led the Skeleton Champions over to a patch of ground and let them work. He sat on the flattest section of the ground; on an ancient block of stone cracked in a few places, but forty paces by forty paces across.
And here was history. The Immortal Tyrant’s roads. Many places had been covered by dirt or broken at the edges, but these roads had endured long past her laws. He stared up at the sky, and it was blue. The air was dry, hot, even, but his white robes held the heat off, and he drank water sparingly. Cast a little cooling spell.
Pisces took this moment to reflect. He appreciated what Hexata had done for him, and Wildcard. He wished them well, and he knew he was selfish. He made trouble for his team, even if he’d tried often to be…
“A better person. But I suppose I am selfish. I wonder if I would recognize myself. The Pisces who came from Ailendamus.”
Would he be impressed? Uncomprehending of how his road had taken him so far? Proud? Pisces wondered what Ceria would say. He tried to predict the future. There were plenty of dire outcomes. Outcomes that stemmed from his actions. If they came and his team suffered…
“Taking responsibility isn’t enough. I never took responsibility for Wistram. How could I? I can only hope it doesn’t come to that. Utterly selfish.”
But he kept sitting there and thought of her. He didn’t think of her every day. But that refrain was always in his mind at moments like this.
Because you’re better than they are. Was he? It was the doubt that kept him guessing. Trying. But—he was putting their chances of getting to Ksmvr and her in jeopardy, he knew. Yet he still couldn’t get up and leave.
He had no profound insights as he sat there in silence, with only the undead for company, and they didn’t talk much in Pisces’ experience. Just that odd sense of calm.
At last, he saw movement and half-stood. But then he sat back with a sigh.
“Silly me.”
The figure that came pounding the road was the most common sight in the wilds. Reassuring, somehow. A Runner.
Down the road he came, feet pounding the pavement. Bare feet, Pisces noted; the swearing Stitch-man did a double-take when he saw Pisces.
“Here, are you hurt? Lost?”
He looked around for an ambush before hurrying over. Perhaps the fellow was snake-bit or delirious? But Pisces just waved at him.
“Just resting.”
“Well, get up if you’re in the path of a cart or they’re like to run you over! Got any deliveries? I’m bound for Halqued, then beyond!”
Something about the young man sitting there was vaguely familiar, but the City Runner was hopping from foot to foot, and Pisces saw.
“Are you alright? Your feet—”
“I’m trying to run like the Wind Runner! Argh! But however she does it, it is not on the sunbaked sands of Chandrar, or may my stitching rot and fall out! If I gain the class, may it all be worth it! I’m sorry, I cannot stay.”
“No, no, best of luck!”
Pisces shouted after the City Runner, who went pounding off across the road, cursing. Pisces shook his head, smiling. Ryoka Griffin, truly an inspiration.
That actually cheered him up, so he was lying on his back, gazing at the sky empty of clouds, when he felt the faint rumble and sat up. Ah.
There they were. He stretched and was glad he’d used the bathroom. As it so happened, something reached Pisces at that moment. Fate? Funny coincidence? Then again, it was about, what, ten in the morning? Right when a half-Elf might rise after a long day.
A [Message] spell.
 
Ceria, Exalted Captain: Hey, are you almost back yet? Yisame mentioned some kind of fracas, but we’ll sort it out later. Yvlon’s sick. Magical sleeping sickness. Pretty nasty. What’s your estimated time of arrival-thing on the carriage? (It’s a display on the scrying orb.)
 
He blinked at the sky. Then raised a finger to his temples.
 
Pisces: With apologies, Ceria, I might be a bit late.
 
Then he waited.
 
——
 
The caravan was known as the Blessed Chains of Hotq. Their owner wasn’t Hotq; he’d retired two decades back, and his best apprentice, Slave Merchant Throsa, had succeeded him. They were known for throwing open their covered wagons to pour thick, black tea in cups for any visitors.
Fine hospitality, and finer flesh. But only when they had visitors. Right now, Throsa was pushing everyone to more speed. Horses strained as they moved at a fast clip, and the [Guards] were thinking of making the merchandise get out and run to reduce weight.
That would soil them a bit for the markets, and they were a day out from their next stop, but they were also cautious of going too fast. The reason Throsa was so upset was because of her Skill.
[Forewarned Attack]. A useful Skill for a woman in her business. She did not know where or exactly when, only that one was coming in the next few days. Sometimes, the attack never came; the Skill was imprecise, but let you know if the possibility arose.
If they got to the city and unloaded some of their merchandise, she’d be happier. She could add more [Guards] for the next leg of the journey, even hire adventurers or mercenaries. That let her cut losses and sacrifice wagons if it was a monster attack…
Her nightmare, which was unspoken, was that it was the [Rebels], but they were far east of here according to the Guild’s networks, and she paid her dues for knowledge, damnit! But perhaps it was that name that had come down the road with oncoming traffic.
It was a forbidden name in her caravan; she insisted the scrying orb be turned off and had petitioned every notable in the cities she had visited to see it her way. Such actions, such deeds against Roshal, who was so rich and an ally of Nerrhavia’s Fallen—!
But she had it on good authority that he’d gone to the capital, so it was [Bandits] she feared. Throsa had a spyglass out as she rode on one of her wagons and kept peering at the sky. She had it in her head that the attack would be from the sky. A Garuda flight of raiders. The damned pests might try to carry off a prize slave if they knew it was her wagon, despite the weight…
But her caravan was no small one, for all it prized quality over quantity. She had no less than six holding wagons and three-score [Slave Guards]. A score was twenty. It was a good rule of thumb to carry one [Guard] per every eight [Slaves]. You could go up to twenty, but only a fool exceeded that.
Sixty [Guards], some of whom were above Level 30, and herself. More than enough for the short transit between cities in this section of the Leashed Trails. If she were to go across the Glass Straits, she’d double or triple the guard…
They were barely ten miles from the city. With all her scanning around, she actually missed the figure sitting on the road until he stood. Even then…Throsa didn’t register him until there was a call from the lead [Slave Guards] riding.
“Exalted Merchant, ahead of us…”
Something about the woman’s tone was caught between amusement and uncertainty. Like someone assuming a prank was being played on her, if only her mind. Because…it was a joke, right?
Throsa’s spyglass fixed on the Human who was standing in front of the caravan. She heard a few voices shouting.
“You on the road! You’re finally awake, eh? Out of the way before we run you over!”
“We’re of Roshal! We’ll ride you down for impeding us or take you as merchandise!”
That came from another [Guard]—it was mostly just a threat. Throsa nearly snapped at him to mind his tongue; it was frowned upon to remind people how many tricks Roshal had. Then again, there was the prestige of—
Her gaze slowly swung back to the young man. He was just standing there as the wind blew his white robes and hair. Just…a Human.
His skin was not as fair as all that; he had a slight sunburn, actually. And he was shaking his head. The images she had seen on bounty posters had him on horseback, in motion. Surrounded by others. Even with breasts—his was a face that every man or woman on these trails knew.
But this one…there was something about him that fit more than the others. As if…
It was him. Her tongue locked in her mouth before she could stutter.
“S-stop! [Caravan, Halt]!”
The horses screamed, and the riders of each wagon cried out as the animals and the riders were forced to slow. Glowing chains of authority whipped between Throsa and even her guards. Her will. Her burgeoning aura, a sign of her promise.
“Exalted Merchant, what—”
“That—”
She pointed, and her [Head of Chattel Guarding] turned. He stared across the road, and then his eyes widened. He turned his head right and left.
“Ambush? But there are no dunes—they ride over dunes or out of cover—or the sandstorms from the [Bandit Lady]—”
“It’s him. Get—get the—”
She was drawing a wand with shaky hands. It could kill even a Gold-ranker in a single shot, or so the [Mage] in Lailight Scintillation had claimed. [Scaied Venombolt]—it had never failed in killing anyone she’d struck. With her other hand, she drew a magical dagger that could extend and stab through a foe in a moment, like a lance.
The [Guards] had gone silent. Half were pointing, glancing at their fellows to grin and say, ‘look at this mistake I have made’. The others, like their leader, were protesting.
“We had word he was going to—”
“Get the wagons in a circle!”
She shouted. Her Skills. She was frozen up, but she knew her trade. But there was no [Rebel] wave riding at them. No sandstorm. Just…
Pisces Jealnet. He moved at last. He was walking forwards. Now, she saw him reach for something at his side. Part of her had wondered if this was a dream, hoped it would be.
But when she saw that curious rapier, Throsa knew. It was metal and bone, two gleaming colors. And a little bell hung from it; her spyglass picked it out. He was striding, now. Long-legged, moving faster. She shouted.
“[All To Arms: Protect the Merchandise]! [Caravan: Pricklethorn Flesh]—”
Her defensive Skills. The [Head of Chattel Guarding] was still denying it. Throsa didn’t see anyone else. He was one man. One versus sixty—
A Gold-rank adventurer. Scourge. Bane of—
Then the sand moved next to the road. Ahead of Pisces, Throsa heard a cry.
“Ambush! Ambush—”
Someone’s Skill went off belatedly. Giving them, what, ten seconds? A low-level fool’s Skill, which was sometimes all that you needed—
Bows sang as the [Guards] fired, some reflexively, others with Skills like [Opening Shot]. But even the ones that landed just…
A Skeleton Champion dug itself out of the earth where it had been waiting and caught an arrow. It shook dirt and sand off its body as it lifted a greatsword. Eleven undead figures rose, like a ghastly honor-guard. Then they were running. Bones clattering as they charged the caravan—and now a cry was going up from the [Slavers]. Horror, fear.
“Necromancer! Undead! It’s him!”
They took aim at the [Necromancer], but he was running. Running…and he vanished as the first arrows loosed. One of his steps took him a dozen paces forwards.
[Flash Step]. And his second step just as far—
He was running, vanishing and reappearing across the ground so fast Throsa could barely track him. Curving, dodging arrows and spells. But coming at the caravan—
Then she pulled her head behind her enchanted wagon’s fabric. For she had seen his finger rise. There was light filtering through the thin canopy of her wagon. Shouting voices. Throsa shivered—then saw the light flicker out as something passed by her wagon’s walls.
Silence, for a moment. Then a figure fell from their saddle. They landed with a dull thump on the ground. A quiet voice. Someone calling out for a friend, a comrade.
Then—the scream of horses. A cry of agony as a Skeleton Champion shot a mortal woman in the stomach. The clash of metal on metal—
Chaos and battle. Throsa waited by the driver’s seat, hands shaking and sweating. She closed her eyes. Battle she knew; she had faced this before. But this time—
This time, she could hear them. Curse them. She’d brand them all for this. She’d make them scream. But it didn’t stop them.
The [Slaves] in the wagons.
They were laughing.
 
——
 
His first [Deathbolt] took a [Slave Guard] out of the saddle. Then he was amidst them. No time to circle; there were too many. His Skeleton Champions hit the caravan a moment later, and he was fighting up.
They were all mounted. It wasn’t an advantage; they were trying to form a circle with the wagons, and if they’d split up and rode, he’d have been attacked from all angles.
Instead, they were at the mercy of their horses. Pisces spoke.
“[Flashbang].”
The explosion of sound and light sent horses rearing. The [Guards] clung to their saddles or fell off. One tumbled to the ground, crying out as she broke an arm. She looked up, and Pisces stared down into terrified, blue eyes. A Human’s face. She opened her mouth.
“P—”
He drove the rapier through her mouth. Turned and pointed. [Flame Swathe]. It coated a Stitch-man, but the flames didn’t take on his skin at first. Pisces kept his finger pointing for six seconds. Eight…
Too slow. The screaming figure was writhing as their horses galloped away, and the others were getting up. One was already on his feet. A Skill—he hadn’t attacked. Fear? He raised a shield.
Pisces’s [Shatterbolt] hit the shield. The unenchanted metal exploded, and the [Guard]’s flesh-and-blood arm cracked. Blood ran out of the broken skin, and he screamed, clutching at the bone.
Pisces beheaded him, then saw another [Guard] riding. He stabbed through a chest, wrenched the blade out, and heard a scream. Still alive—
A Skeleton Champion brought down a shortsword into the [Guard]’s guts. It turned, caught a blow from one of the mounted [Guards] on a shield—Pisces spoke again.
“[Flashbang].”
If it worked once—the horses went stampeding away this time. And the others were taking cover behind the wagons. Trying to stop the Skeleton Champions—
But the eleven had come in swinging so hard that the one with the greatsword had nearly cut a [Guard] in half, chainmail or not. Their blows were as heavy as Yvlon’s—for two or three swings. Then they grew weaker.
[Bonerattler Charge]. It was enough—there weren’t that many. The guards on horseback were racing around, trying to aim. Where was he…?
Gone. The [Necromancer] had vanished. The Skeleton Champions were pressing against the wagons, fighting individually. But where…?
The circle of wagons had [Guards] on the inside, screaming for enchanted munitions, for help against the champions—but some were fighting near the wagons holding the [Slaves].
“Get out! Get out and fight or die! Merchant, the kill-collars! Stop laughing! Stop—”
Six of them were trying to yank out the [Slaves] of one wagon and arm them. One of the [Guards] glanced around and saw the dust rising in the air swirl. She turned.
“Behind—”
Pisces stabbed her through the eye. Five [Guards] were in front of him. Two on the ground, one climbing into the wagon, two inside. He stepped back.
[Quick Reset]. Then lunged forwards in a fencer’s attack. Just like his father had shown him.
But the impact of his rapier punching through cheek and bone…Padurn had never described that. He didn’t know it. The second [Slaver] went down. Pisces saw the third moving, swinging a shield up—
His rapier sprayed blood, gore, and brain across the face as he withdrew it and slashed across the throat. So fast that the Stitch-man reached up and choked on his own blood as he tried to inhale. And Pisces’ rapier was already hamstringing the fourth [Slaver], who fell, screaming. Then Pisces ran him through.
All of this in the span of three seconds. He moved faster than they could dream, a blur.
[Manacharged Reflexes]. The two [Guards] in the wagon cried out, and one shouted.
“[Quick Stab]!”
A fast blow to Pisces as he was turning from the fourth [Slaver]. His blade came up.
[Flash Parry]. The other [Guard] lifted a bow, fired. Pisces stepped left, and the arrow punched into the dirt. His [Flash Step] carried him back, and the [Slaver] with a bow fumbled for an arrow.
He dropped it, and it clattered to the floor. He reached for another as his companion with the sword backed up.
“Jotec, help! Draw your blade and h—”
The terrified archer saw Pisces’ blade rise. It seemed to glow as he swept the blade up in a stab. The swordsman shouted.
“[Deft G—]”
He did block the blow, but his sword wasn’t strong enough. Pisces’ Skill punched upwards. His rapier extended and ran the Stitch-man through the chest.
[Rising Spearthrust]. The [Slaver Archer] was fumbling for a dropped arrow on the ground as the body of his comrade rose, then fell back, blood coating the wagon’s floor. Then he looked down. Five dead guards—the [Necromancer] was standing there.
“Help—”
The other wagons where his comrades were fighting hadn’t even seen. One of them turned their head and saw Pisces at last. They stared. The [Archer] backed up—the [Necromancer] was pointing at him.
He ran into something. Bodies. The [Slaves] were all bunched up inside. There was an impact on his back. Then he was stumbling forwards.
They’d kicked him. Kicked—he went over the wagon’s edge, screaming. Pisces stabbed up as the final [Guard] came down. Then he heaved the body off his rapier.
“Behind us! He is inside the—”
The [Necromancer] rose, blood coating his white robes and sword. But he shook the blood off his enchanted robes, and his blade gleamed as he stepped backwards. He strode away, [Flash Stepping] out of the circle of wagons before the [Guards] could surround him. He had only said one word to the six dead men and women. A whisper.
“Arise.”
The dead man he had impaled opened his eyes. They glowed. Slowly, he got up as the other [Guards] rushed past him. They thought he’d made it. One turned—and the zombie grabbed a shoulder. Opened his mouth wide, unhinging his jaw, and bit—
 
——
 
He felt like he was too slow. Pisces emerged from the brief skirmish in the wagons and was aware that every second, the [Guards] would overwhelm his Skeleton Champions. Six were damaged. Two down.
How many of the [Guards] were left…? He spotted the ones on horses circling and firing arrows. Pisces’ instinct was to attack them, but then he realized they were switching weapons.
Arrows were useless on Skeleton Champions without Skills or magic. He was panting. Did he have magic for [Invisibility]…?
Not in quick succession. He leaned against a wagon, then saw the riders charge the Skeleton Champions from behind. One was clubbing down at the Skeleton Champion who had a rapier—Pisces charged.
[Flash Step] three times, then—he stabbed up into a stomach, wrenched the blade around, and heaved it out. Not dead, but the Skeleton Champion dragged the screaming figure down. The other [Riders]—Pisces didn’t want to kill the horses, but he slashed their legs. They kicked, screaming, and one bucked a [Rider]. He saw a Skeleton Champion seize the [Rider] and grapple on the ground.
“[Deathbolt]. [Deathbolt].”
Mana running lower. Skills—he had used a lot of them. Pisces spoke.
“Keep them boxed in. Archer, don’t let the ones with bows shoot me.”
The Skeleton Champion with a bow began loosing arrows rapidly, forcing the [Slavers] to keep their heads down. Pisces saw the remaining riders turning to scatter. Eight.
They fled, and he ran them down. No spells save for [Flash Step]. Just his sword. If they turned, they left an opening while they were presenting their sides to him to stab, when the horse was at its slowest. If they gave him no opening, he cut the horse on the legs, and the animal would try to kick or buck its rider and give him that opening.
Three went down, and he took his first wound. An arrow punching through his guard and striking him on the chest.
His underarmor meant he barely felt it.
I might be dead without armor. If it hit me in the face—foolish. He turned, and the remaining five…
Were running. Pisces chased them down. He could beat the horses, and they’d all tried to go for the road to the city. By the time they thought to split up…
Half his Skeleton Champions were down. Pisces was panting as he drank a mana potion. He was running, now. And he saw…
Most of the [Slavers] were dead. Barely a dozen were left, clinging to a carriage they were trying to get moving. One was running, trying to jump on it, when a spear ran him through. Pisces glanced around. Were there any…?
The six Skeleton Champions charged, but the wagon was picking up speed; the wheels were enchanted. One of the [Guards] took an arrow to the chest and fell off the roof. Another was thrown off the roof at a Skeleton Champion, sacrificed to slow it down. Pisces saw the pair of stallions running and whispered.
“Sorry.”
He exploded a [Flashbang] in their faces; they reared, cut the leads as they halted, trying to tear free of their tethers. Then he swung himself up—
The dagger nearly shot through his face. Pisces recoiled as a woman slashed at him, screaming. The [Slavers] were fighting as their leader came out. Pisces [Flash Stepped] back. There was a moment when both pointed at each other.
[Deathbolt].
“Die!”
His [Deathbolt] hit the wall of the wagon, and she recoiled; her spell would have gone through his chest but for his [Flash Step]. Pisces took aim again—she fired wildly from inside the carriage, and he, panting, missed his second shot; it must have gone over her head.
He was standing on the balls of his feet, tensed, prepared to lunge forwards and leap into the wagon. But that dagger. [Invisibility]? Could she see him? She’d feel him on the floorboards of the wagon or see him moving if he got too close. [Acid Orb] the entire thing? What spell was—
He was locked on the wagon when it jostled, and he leapt sideways. But no spell came from inside—there was a scream, a flash of muddy brown light. Then…silence.
Pisces wavered. Then a Skeleton Champion pushed the wagon’s curtains aside. It had two daggers in its hands. Bloodied. It pushed the [Merchant]’s corpse out and onto the ground, then its head swivelled. Searching for foes. It leapt down and strode towards the other wagons. And then—and then—
He realized all the [Slavers] were dead.
 
——
 
In the aftermath, as the adrenaline left Pisces’ body and he felt shaky and emptier, he did come to his senses and count his mistakes.
A number of them. The first was not properly ambushing the caravan. He’d just thought…
If the skeletons had emerged around the caravan, they’d have been in a better position. Even with the anti-ambush Skill—no, he should have known they’d had that.
Second, he should have never attacked the [Merchant] at the end. He’d nearly gotten himself killed when his Skeleton Champions had been able to deal with her. Whatever that spell was, it looked highly poisonous and had scarred the ground black.
Third was not taking her out at the start. She had been the leader, and her Skills had empowered the caravan. In fact, she had killed two Skeleton Champions herself; holes in their skulls showed where that dagger of hers had punched through their bones, and another had a fully-melted ribcage. If she’d had a wand suited for killing undead instead of people, she might have torn through the lot.
Fourth, his aim…he was sure there were more mistakes, but Pisces realized he was distracted. He drank more water. Poured some over his face. Then got to work.
“Grab the dead Skeleton Champions. Get all the bodies you can. No—load them up into the wagons. Grab the horses if they’re around. Get them moving off the road, now!”
Dispose of the evidence. It was lucky no one had come down the road. Perhaps they had…perhaps the [Slavers] had sent a distress call. He had to move fast.
Pisces didn’t know this part. He went to the dead Stitch-woman and searched her corpse. What he was looking for he didn’t know. Keys? He knew some [Slavers] could kill their [Slaves] with a spell. If it was keyed to her survival…
His heart began to pound in horror. But then he heard faint laughter from the wagons. He didn’t find keys on the woman. So where…?
At his instruction, the Skeleton Champions collecting bodies searched, and one finally jangled something. One of the [Guards] had a keyring. Actually, several did.
Pisces snatched one and swung into the wagons. They were already moving as terrified horses trotted away from the skeletons herding them and making vague shooing motions. For a moment, when he pulled the coverings back, there was silence. He stared into the darkness and saw faces squinting at him. Blinded by the light…uncertain. Afraid—
Until they saw him. Then he heard a sigh and saw a mix of Humans, Stitch-folk, a pair of Garudas blinking up at him. Some recoiled. Flinching back from the man covered in blood and gore. Others just smiled politely.
“Ah, there he is. Don’t wake me from my dream another moment, please, friends.”
A Stitch-man spoke up, leaning back against the tiny bench where he was jammed shoulder-to-shoulder with the others. They were chained to the benches. Unable to move more than a foot from the berths. Pisces wavered.
He didn’t know what to say. It was the nearest [Slave] who spoke next. A Garuda with brown feathers that turned slowly to orange lifted his head. He gazed up and rasped with a throat parched for moisture.
“Bane of Roshal. Are we free?”
As if he knew Pisces. As if this moment hadn’t been luck, improvisation, an arrow’s trajectory from Pisces’ death. He spoke the words with such trust. Pisces stared at him, and for a moment, he was sitting there.
In chains, staring up at a falling rainbow. Hearing a booming voice in his ears as the Death of Chains turned the dark night into magic and freedom.
He was not Czautha’qshe. He had no grand words. He had failed so many on his journey here. But…Pisces fumbled for the keyring, then handed the Garuda it. The man almost dropped the keyring and saw Pisces fish out another copy.
“Yes. Hurry. Free yourselves and then the others. Never let yourselves be chained again.”
It was such a damned silly thing to say. They were not even out of chains, but he said it, because the words were hot in his chest. Hotter than the brand on his skin.
Someone had to say them.
The Garuda tried to sort the keys, but his wing-talons were shaky. Pisces found the right key first. He slotted it into the lock, and it clicked. He yanked the manacles off and realized there was another set for the Garuda’s wrists.
The same key fit both locks. The heavy iron fell, and the Garuda stood. He spread his wings—then glanced at the keys. Fumbled to find the same one Pisces did as the [Necromancer] turned to the next person in line. A Stitch-woman who was crying. Silently—
The wagon had gone so quiet. Like people trying not to wake up. Waiting…Pisces realized that the wagon was so full.
How many bodies were crammed in here? He’d counted at least five other wagons—he began to call for the Skeleton Champions, but realized they might not know how this worked.
“I’ll free someone in the other wagons. Just keep unlocking—I’m sorry, I’ll be back.”
The Garuda half-turned as he strode for the wagon’s lip. He blinked at Pisces, then spoke.
“You returned to Chandrar and freed us. Some claim yours is just a face that [Rebels] wear. But you’re him. The first one called the Bane of Roshal. The actual [Necromancer].”
“Yes. I am.”
Pisces spoke to the Garuda, and it did feel like the two men were in a dream. One reliving his, the other…but the Garuda felt at his wrists, at the bruised flesh under his feathers, then peered up at the sky.
“Are you sure?”
What a question to ask. But they all regarded the filthy adventurer covered in blood. It had splashed his skin, but slid off his robes enchanted for cleanliness. He was covered in sweat and grime, but his robes were pristine. Just like the rapier. The Bell of Challenges didn’t ring as it swung from the rapier’s hilt. Pisces turned and nodded.
“My friend…the [Slave] who was chained up next to me was a Garuda. Cawe. It’s not just because you’re a Garuda. I wish I had been able to free her. You’re all free. I just can’t kill them all, so you’ll have to run. I’m sorry. I’ll try my best.”
Then he leapt out of the wagon. The [Slaves] regarded each other. The promise hung in the air.
I’ll try my best.
Then…the freed [Slave] turned the key and listened to it click. He waited until he’d unlatched every single chain—and they were leaving the wagon. Crying out. Weeping. Asking what happened next. Afraid or relieved or…the Garuda just walked to the edge of the wagon and looked up.
Then he spread his wings and flew into the blue sky.
 
——
 
The first caravan was hard. Hard in how it was fought, but hardest in saying goodbye. Pisces was a flurry of motion the moment he realized they were on a time limit.
“Roshal checks its caravans. This one was nearly at the city. Grab the horses. Grab every weapon you can, and—I don’t know which way to go.”
Then he felt like a murderer, for he had no escape route planned. He’d been so focused on this—but the Garuda whom he’d freed first had a thought.
“The Ekhot Straits. No one lives there. Or perhaps the Devilt Foothills. Even a city, should we get far enough.”
“They’ll ask if we are escaped [Slaves] at the gates—”
“Only on entry. And if you were taken before they reached a full Guild, you won’t be on the registers, perhaps. If we leave Nerrhavia’s Fallen, only Roshal will have us on lists.”
“Those are too far. We’ll never make it—”
That despairing comment came from a Stitch-man. But a chorus of voices silenced him.
“We must try. At worst, we split up after this. If we pose as travellers, with clothing, coin—”
There was a chance. But for the moment, the irony was that the [Slaves] had to get in the same wagons they had been freed from.
No longer chained, but they had no other conveyance. Pisces ordered his skeletons to strip the [Slavers]. The work was simple; he scavenged armor and weapons off the dead for the Skeleton Champions to re-arm.
Not the best gear. He took several enchanted swords off the Skeleton Champions and handed them to the freed [Slaves]. They needed them more.
“Divide it amongst yourselves. Coin—the [Merchant] had some, surely.”
“Her chest. It’s trapped. But I saw how she used the key.”
One of the other [Slaves] volunteered. Pisces saw the Garuda standing on the wagon.
“If you fly, you can keep away from pursuers. Split up if you must; I don’t know if they’ll scry you…”
“Perhaps, but there are Skills and scrolls against it. You’re warded from scrying?”
Pisces had a ring that Ceria had insisted the team get, but the thought of each [Slave] being hunted down—
“I’m sorry. I don’t have anything else prepared.”
It was the tenth time he said it, and the Garuda smiled down at him.
“You freed us.”
“Won’t you come with us, Scourge? If you did and brought us to the straits or to your people—”
One of the former [Slaves] began, but Pisces was glancing over his shoulder. He hesitated, and his face twisted up, but he shook his head.
“I can’t. I am so sorry, but—I have to go.”
He was staring at something only he could see. One of his mice…the [Slaves] saw him point.
“Another caravan is headed towards the city.”
It took them a moment to realize what he meant. Then they all sat forwards.
“You mean to strike Roshal again?”
Pisces turned and realized they had no notion of his plans. He gestured, aimlessly, as the Skeleton Champions finished repairing themselves. More bodies were arising, now. Naked, mostly. Eyes glowing. Zombies. A few Ghouls.
“I cannot free the [Slaves] in the city.”
Again, the massed people glanced at each other to try and divine what he meant. One spoke.
“…Halqued?”
“Yes.”
Lareceina was right. Hexata was correct. In that city, Yisame’s people kept law and order. An attack on the city was an attack on her. Outside the city…
There were no witnesses. And if there were, so what? The Scourge of Roshal wore Pisces’ face. Everyone knew that, but Pisces was also sure it was a face that Bearig had adopted. A way to disguise the [Rebels].
The ‘Scourge’ has simply hit another caravan. That was the flimsiest pretext he had, but…it was a madman’s plan. Pisces half-turned.
“I have to go to intercept it. If you need other places to go, north…east would be good. Though help would be at least a hundred miles away, likely more. Tiqr is even further, and I do not know this region. Again, I’m…”
A skeleton horse was rising as the undead began to move. First shuffling steps—then he pointed, and the zombies began to jog. Then run, arms pumping, organs glistening. The [Slaves] saw him turning, and then there was a feeling.
Not just them. Not just one act and desperation. If he meant more—
“They’d send out riders after us instantly. Scry us and post bounties on each one. But hundreds? Thousands?”
“He’s mad. Mad as they say. Was it just one of him versus every [Guard] and Throsa herself?”
Whispers. The Garuda saw Pisces getting on the horse with the curious saddle. He called out.
“Scourge!”
Pisces turned, and the Garuda lifted a wing-arm.
“Luck. If I return to Qualvekkaras, I will speak your name and Cawe’s to the winds themselves. Or any Garuda I meet.”
The [Necromancer] called back.
“Your name. What is it?”
“Josiever.”
The connected gaze lingered as Pisces began to ride. Then it broke. When he turned and rode ahead, he didn’t look back, at least, not until he was a distant speck. As if he were ashamed, perhaps. Embarrassed.
Free, in a moment. The [Slaves] gazed down at the blood in the wagons. Their captors ran, a shambling horde, dead—and there might have been that anger. Hot and bright for the way it was too easy.
Like a Djinni coming down a minute too late to break chains so easily. After so long, for some of them. Too easy. Why had no one done it?
Then they turned and saw him riding now, a speck. Just one man. No Djinni of Demons, no legend.
“I’ll try my best.”
Gooseflesh rose on Josiever’s arms, under his feathers. He spread his wings and leapt into the air, hesitating until he realized those chains were gone.
Never again. Then he was flying up—up—every cell in his body screaming in relief. But craning his head to see that figure moving. And if he had a regret…
It was that Pisces hadn’t asked Josiever to join him. But then, the Garuda wondered…who could keep up with the Bane of Roshal? The original had come back to Chandrar, and now he was free of his team, of his obligations. He had been a fine figure on the scrying orb, in the palace; they had all seen broadcasts of him despite their master’s dislike of him.
Now, though…
He appeared truly passionate.
 
——
 
His plan was insane. It was only working right now because they didn’t know what he was doing. The element of surprise was going to run out by the second caravan—let alone the third.
But they were on the roads. Unless they turned around—and even if they did—it was hard to hide that many people. Going off-road was nigh-impossible unless the [Slavers] had enchanted wheels. They’d run into monsters or just get lost.
And he had a map detailing where each one was. He just needed to kill them all. Hundreds of [Slave Guards]…
Yes, a madman’s plan. But Pisces had to do it. If he did, no one could buy or sell that girl. There was no…ending to this that went well. He knew that too. It didn’t matter.
He rode, and the horde of undead he’d summoned was the first, the largest—when he looked back and saw them running after him, he had an image in his head.
Feren. Gewilena. Ama. His first coven of [Necromancers], cheering a group of zombies led by a Ghoul. He saw in the undead the same horde attacking Liscor and Erin’s inn.
All the evils of my class. Then he blinked and saw the dead [Slavers]. He didn’t know what Erin would say. But he knew what he needed.
He had never summoned a horde of undead and controlled them himself. It was…unsettlingly easy. And alarming. Pisces didn’t have individual control over the undead. That was the worrying part. They might well revert back to their natural instincts and attack anything living. Twice, when he stopped to orient himself, he saw a zombie try to dig up a snake or something in the ground. But Pisces could easily correct one undead.
It was like a herd of sheep. He could move them around in a mass. And then just send them at, well, a target. Terrifyingly dangerous.
He kept a firm grip on the Skeleton Champions. They were now fully armored and armed, albeit with unenchanted gear. Pisces wished he’d kept some enchanted weapons—but the [Slaves] needed them.
Do without. Now that he had sixty-odd undead, he had a fighting force, albeit a naked one to back up the Skeleton Champions. But Pisces had a problem. He considered it as he rode; the undead horse didn’t need to slow, and it rode flawlessly for him.
I need to hit the other caravan fast. If I can ambush them the same way, I will, but word may have spread. I’ll see. I wish I could intercept spells like Az’kerash did for me. 
Either way, he’d flood forwards with the zombies and Ghouls—let the Skeleton Champions pick out targets. Go for the leadership and high-level [Guards]. He’d also play it safer; one blow to the head and he was dead.
He should have gotten a damn helmet. Personal barrier spells like Yvlon’s ring! He’d keep invisible and minimize risk.
That was the benefit of the undead horde as well; Pisces realized they were generating death-mana. He was recharging rapidly.
[Drain Death Mana]. He tried it on a zombie, and it collapsed and actually turned to ash as he yanked out enough mana for a half-dozen [Deathbolts]. From one zombie?
The rest seemed to run faster in response. Not from fear; the death magic was invigorating them. So Pisces might be able to cast even more spells, despite having used a mana potion in the previous battle. And his Skills would have recharged…
His problem was singular. He could adjust his strategy. Plan on the fly when he saw the second caravan’s numbers and disposition, though he was no Colth—but he had a crippling weakness.
“Aim.”
During the last battle, Pisces had missed several spells. Especially at the final moment when he’d been duelling the [Caravan Leader]. Deathbolt was a Tier 4 spell; it wasn’t as costly as some, but he couldn’t afford to miss with it.
The problem was that Pisces was no Ceria Springwalker, who’d been trained for the better part of a year by a known sharpshooter spellcaster, Illphres. He remembered laughing at her having to get up daily to practice shooting targets by the surf.
Now Pisces would have given anything for that practice. He was a decent shot when stationary, but when moving? Ceria was an actual deadeye given how little she missed.
Pisces flexed his left hand’s finger. Could he correct that aim somehow? He tried. He reduced the mana in his finger and conjured a spell he’d deemed useless for the first battle.
Lighted Arrow. Not [Light Arrow], but the freeform casting version of it. Functionally the same spell, but customizable. In this case, he reduced the amount of light magic in it to almost nothing. He kept it bright, fast—and fired it from his finger.
It shot into the dirt and didn’t even shift the sand. Pisces wondered if it could kill a fly. Well, perfect. He fired five and guessed it was five per one [Light Arrow], already a Tier 1 spell.
Perfect; he could breathe and almost regenerate mana faster. He rode and began shooting the arrow nonstop at everything he could see.
Rocks, cacti, a bounding rabbit, more rocks—his Skeleton Champions—
Pisces started shooting one of his Skeleton Champions in the skull nonstop, or trying to. It kept pace with his horse, so it was actually the best target. He ignored its reproachful stare and cursed after about ten minutes of practice.
“This isn’t ideal.”
He was missing about 60% of the time! The skeleton horse wasn’t that smooth, but at even twenty paces, Pisces had terrible aim. True, they were both moving targets…but Pisces quickly realized the issue wasn’t just his aim. It was more technical still.
There were a lot of good reasons for Pisces to free-cast with his bare hands. It was adaptive, surprised foes, he was used to it—but the reason Ceria favored a wand was because it was a non-flexible rod. Even if not all wands were straight, she knew exactly how long it was and the trajectory it formed.
Pisces had a finger. He liked his forefinger, he thought he knew it well, but it was a finger.
Each section of bone moved with his muscles. If he pointed it straight, it would vary slightly in position each time he did it, despite his best efforts. If he were some kind of supreme…[Monk] he might be able to control it so finely, but that variance meant that he was inevitably going to miss.
Especially when a slight wavering would lead to a lot of error over distance. Pisces hunted around.
“Where is it? Delitandra just had me practicing with…aha!”
He finally yanked out the wand that was a replacement for Mrsha’s favorite chew toy and tried some spellcasting with it. His aim improved…but Pisces felt weird holding it. And he still missed three in ten shots. Nor was it calibrated to amplify death magic, just a cheaper wand some [Mage] in the Coliseum of Monarchs had owned.
He didn’t have time for this. By his calculations, he was already halfway towards intercepting the second caravan. Pisces cursed. But for the Heromakers of Hraace—! If ever he needed Delitandra to come running over with a suggestion, it was now.
Defeat spurs one towards training. She was right about that, only his motivation was failing to do what he had to. Pisces’ mind raced.
How do I correct my aim? If I miss, I could hit a [Slave]. I don’t know how to curve my magic, even if I thought I could correct a [Deathbolt] mid-flight. Colth could do it if he were here…
Think, fool! He closed his eyes and tried to remember the other [Mages] he’d seen. Eldavin came back to him. He’d told Pisces to concentrate his magic, and he’d been right. But he’d had superb casting.
Montressa hadn’t been that accurate, nor Palt, to his memory. The [Illusionist] had preferred to just fill the air with [Light Arrows]. Courier Salamani did the same thing. It was hard to make sure a spell landed on target; that was why other kinds of magic like [Fireball] were so appealing. Pisces’ aim with his rapier was a million times better at range, but he couldn’t rely on it.
…Or could he? Pisces remembered he could bind spells to the tip of the rapier. He imagined him shooting spells with the rapier as an extended wand. It almost sounded viable to him until he remembered the point of his free hand was to do the casting.
“It has to be free-handed. So how…?”
He thought of another [Mage] and hesitated. Wait a second. Viceria had great aim from practicing with Wailant, allegedly naked. Larracel used homing spells, but you know who didn’t have great aim?
Archmage Valeterisa. And she was a seasoned Wistram duelist. In fact, in fact, he recalled Montressa talking about her famous trip to Fissival with Valeterisa. Dead gods, he’d seen her casting magic. Not her fighting, but there was that recording of that Mage Lord Ascoden…using a spell Valeterisa had invented.
[Valeterisa’s Overly Complicated Seekers]. Pisces had heard it maligned as difficult, but the Drake had used it to fire off a lot of spells at targets even hiding behind walls. The problem was…it was very hard to cast. It had a windup time, which meant you couldn’t use it in a fight.
Also, he didn’t know the spell, and he wasn’t going to learn it in less than an hour on horseback without a spellbook teaching it. However, the concept stuck with him.
Valeterisa’s spell isn’t an attack spell. You can’t hurt anyone with it. It’s light magic that bounces around until it finds what you want. Like a guide. Now, he didn’t know it, but a thought occurred to him as he eyed the Skeleton Champion he’d used as target practice.
It was the faintest bit sooty on its forehead where he’d hit it with the weak Lighted Arrow spell. But Pisces didn’t even feel the strain of hitting it, what, three hundred times? He could alter the Lighted Arrow spell as much as he wanted.
It was not a useful spell in a life-or-death fight. Unless he could fire about fifty in one go, [Deathbolt] was far, far stronger. Even at ‘max strength’, Pisces’ Lighted Arrow was pretty much like Ceria putting a wooden box on her hand and punching you as hard as she could in the face with it. Surprisingly painful, but compared to, say, [Deathbolt]…no.
But he could alter the spell. What if…Pisces aimed his finger back at the Skeleton Champion. It sighed. He shot it in the head with a glowing arrow of light.
Yeah, yeah. Doesn’t h—
“[Deathbolt].”
Pisces shot the Skeleton Champion through the head, and its green eyes blazed. It actually sped up like it was under a [Speed] spell for a second, then slowed down. It gave him a second look as the other Skeleton Champions’ jaws dropped.
Do me, do me! They saw Pisces eye his finger, then smile.
 
——
 
Five more [Deathbolts] later, three Skeleton Champions were happy. Pisces…not.
“It’s still not working.”
His idea was simple—fire a guiding arrow to see where his [Deathbolt] was going to land, then follow it up when he saw the ‘guide’ arrow land.
It was a good idea, right?
Wrong. In the time it took for him to fire the guide-arrow, his target could still move or he could shift. The [Necromancer] was almost about to give up on the concept—he had to prepare for battle. Then he had one more thought.
Hm. Here was a question for you: his spell. Lighted Arrow. Why did it have to be…an arrow? A projectile?
For the purposes of being an arrow, sure, it was essential to compress the mana and fire it out. A ray spell was far more mana-intensive and required shaping of magic he wasn’t up to in his book. But if he just projected light-mana constantly, narrowed the focal point from his finger…
He’d seen Ryoka Griffin cast a variant of this spell herself. She had made the [Flashlight] and [Flashbang] spells with her own rudimentary knowledge of magic that he still used in combat. Lareceina had been self-taught, and she was more deadly than most Wistram [Mages] he could name.
There was no spell for what Pisces wanted. It was a Tier 0 magic…he concentrated, frowning. Just enough to see by. Reduce the force to zero. Yes, otherwise he’d burn out all the mana trying to make the projection solid…
Something flashed from the tip of his finger. He blinked at it—then pointed. The Skeleton Champions eyed their master’s new magic.
They didn’t get it. They might have Pisces’ [Duelist Instincts], but all they saw was…a thin ray of light. The width of a piece of chalk, really. Then even thinner. It shot from Pisces’ finger, straight as, well, a beam.
He pointed it at the ground. Shone it on a Skeleton Champion’s forehead.
For reasons they didn’t get, he started laughing. Laughing like a madman. Then he combed his hair, and his face still had some dried blood on it. His eyes focused, and they felt it too.
A kind of…sharpness. Like the blades they carried. He hadn’t felt this sharp except when he’d called them to kill those other [Slavers]. Except at sea.
They liked it. Because Pisces took this spell, which Lareceina might have invented if she’d needed to—something Earthers would come up with because their world had done it all, seen it all, invented every damn thing—
And then he improved it again because he needed to.
 
——
 
The second caravan was known as ‘The Speedy Servant’. It was less…trendy than the Blessed Chains. Not as high-class. Nor did it have fancy, painted wagons to carry its slaves.
Their master had them march along in lines. Why bother pampering them when they needed to get toughened up? It increased their [Slave] class. To that end, Master Khormez actually gave them ropes and connected them only by the manacled hands. They had to run, and if one tripped, it was a damned problem.
Naturally, that meant more risk. But he chained them up at night, and to prevent problems, he ran with a far heavier guard than the Blessed Chains’ caravan had.
About a hundred [Guards] to watch what could be up to a thousand [Slaves] when times were flush.
Times were not that flush, and he had only six hundred, despite having gone all the way to the coast and back. Khormez was highly annoyed, but one of the kingdoms he liked to frequent, Alka dez Vrent, a former Terandrian colony gone to ruin and corruption, wasn’t open for business.
It was a poor nation with a lax monarchy and governance, ideal for him to pick up deals and mass-cargo. However, word was that Alka dez Vrent was no longer safe. It had a new ruler no one dared speak of, who murdered everyone who crossed him.
Even [Slavers], potentially. The Guild had marked it as a no-go zone while they investigated and saw what the new rules were. So Khormez had lost profits.
First that, then the sightings of the Scourge on the eastern edge of Nerrhavia’s Fallen, so he’d avoided that—then the actual Horns of Hammerad flying in on a damn carpet! He’d almost spit blood when he heard they were ahead of him, but other adventurers had chased them off.
He’d light incense for Wildcard and Torreb’s daughter at the Guild, see if he didn’t! Even if he was a notorious [Skinflint Slavemaster]—what was good for business mattered. What had Khormez’s teeth on edge was a [Message] he’d received from the Guild.
At cost. They had burnt up one of his [Message] scrolls, and they never apologized, even when it was just an update about weather or traffic. But he tolerated it because this had been an update.
The Blessed Chains hadn’t appeared at their destination, the same city he was bound for. He forgot the name; it was a Hemp-forsaken place, this run. Were the Mad Ones around here? Bah, he would just unload whatever was profitable, take whatever wasn’t broken, and head on.
That was how he made a living. But the Guild monitored every caravan and their business. Often, they pried too much, but if the Blessed Chains hadn’t made it…?
Perhaps they’d thrown an axle. Perhaps they’d found someone and were doing business. But perhaps it was trouble. The Guild had sent someone to check it out. So Khormez was wary.
He didn’t have a Skill to detect attacks. But his [Guards] were used to fights. Khormez himself was a big man whose whip was coated with venom that could put any man down. He liked to let new [Slaves] think they had an advantage, unchain them, then hit them with the whip. Once he had them pliable, he chose his favorites among the lot. In time, he’d upgrade his caravan. He didn’t see the need to stop making the [Slaves] run, but if he had a Djinni—the Guild sold them at extortionate rates, but they’d go cheaper if you were high-ranking or had a patron.
Then he’d be a true Master of Roshal.
Khormez rode his tired camel, head on a swivel. Foot traffic was clearing out as they passed a crossroads. He took note of such things…this was a trade road. But suddenly, even single riders weren’t appearing on the road ahead of him.
That often meant trouble. Khormez spat and snapped at a guard.
“Look sharp. Someone ride ahead and figure out why no one’s about!”
They rode ahead and, after a few tense minutes, came galloping back.
“Master Khormez—I caught a man on horseback. Here, here!”
He was tugging a fellow over. The reluctant rider protested.
“I have to be going—”
“Just tell him what you told me!”
The Stitch-man pointed over his shoulder.
“There’s a damned horde of undead coming this way! Dozens of zombies! Everyone ahead is moving away from it! You’ll want to ride fast; I got around it, but you won’t! There’s Ghouls amongst them!”
Khormez’s skin tingled, and he shuddered.
“Damned undead! First the Oresects, now this! What good is Nerrhavia’s Fallen if it can’t even upkeep the trade roads?”
The man was a native of the kingdom and frowned mightily, so Khormez adopted an insincere smile.
“That is…I am sure the Golden Hordes will deal with it. In time.”
Perhaps that was the reason for the Blessed Chain’s delay. Khormez halted the caravan as the rider nodded at him and rode on fast.
A few dozen undead versus his guards weren’t that dangerous…though Ghouls would be threats. But each hurt guard was money from his pocket, let alone the helpless merchandise.
“We’ll head down the road. Find some other fools and travel together; if we need to, they’ll bear the brunt of the fighting. The local garrison should sally out to deal with them. We’re close enough.”
The [Guards] were all in agreement. They were turning the [Slaves] when Khormez was struck by two thoughts.
One—the Guild hadn’t harassed him about undead on the road. They always did for the slightest monster attacks, even Sand Slimes. Perhaps the horde had just appeared.
Perhaps, but wasn’t a certain [Necromancer] said to have been around here? He had left, though…the Guild had sent him a message to that effect. 
But that was two oddities. Khormez didn’t fear the so-called Scourge of Roshal. He’d had it on good authority from other [Slavers] who’d run into the legend that it was just a face the [Rebels] sewed onto their leaders to instill fear. Though the real man…
Khormez felt his shoulders prickle, hard. He hunched his body up, glancing around, and saw, suddenly, how empty this road was.
Utterly.
It made sense from one direction…but someone should have outridden Khormez’s slower caravan from behind. Yet that [Rider] was first to come down the road from the other direction.
Why, then, was his caravan alone? It was almost as if…something was scaring traffic away from behind Khormez. Like, say, the sighting of more undead.
Ping! Khormez jumped and slapped a hand to his side. Another disposable [Message] scroll. He’d save a fortune if he invested in a permanent one, not bled for each expendable—
He read the note slowly.
 
Guild Update: Monster sightings. Skeletons sighted on the road behind The Speedy Servant. Numbers reported as less than a dozen. Potentially armed. Updates forthcoming; the local garrison has been alerted.
