Behind. Skeletons. Khormez’s head snapped up. He wheeled his horse around, stood up in the stirrups, and began to bellow.
“All hear me and obey! Prepare to ride north at speed! We are cutting through the undead and reaching the city! Lash the slaves; they will run or suffer! [Run, Worthless Slaves]!”
His guards began to protest. Khormez pointed down the road, trying to explain his sudden intuition.
“It’s an ambush! I th—”
He swore he saw something flash at him in the fading light. Khormez blinked, twist—
The [Deathbolt] hit him in the chest. He went white. Swayed in his saddle, and his vision greyed out. The [Guards] stared at him. They half-turned.
“Spell—that was a sp—”
He felt like throwing up. Khormez was falling. He felt his heart stopping. And then…he saw it. He looked down at his chest as he began to topple over.
Oh.
There was a beam of light on his chest. A beautiful, pale one of a color he had no words for. Why had he not—
The second [Deathbolt] hit him, and the [Slave Master] struck the ground. Then, when he rose, already a Ghoul, he could see it clearly.
 
——
 
The final aspect to Pisces’ laser-trick was this: death magic. A beam of light was noticeable. Anyone who saw it on them would guess what Pisces was doing. So…why let them see it? He’d practically heard Colth muttering that.
Pisces couldn’t make a light he couldn’t see; Ksmvr might have been able to. But he’d given it some thought and realized there was a way to create a light most people couldn’t see if they weren’t [Mages].
Magic. And if you were going to go that far, why not death magic, which was a unique element few non-[Necromancers] were familiar with?
He’d still had to wait for the man he assumed was the leader to stop moving. The [Deathbolt] wasn’t as fast as he wanted it to be; it was actually slower than Ceria’s [Ice Lance], even. But it was now…very accurate.
Though the [Deathbolt]’s speed was an issue. Which meant the [Slavers] still could avoid the projectile. He’d work on making it invisible and faster—later.
“Charge. Skeleton Champions—wait for the zombies to hit them before entering the fray.”
Pisces whispered. He was lying on his stomach on a dune, and he watched the battle begin without exposing himself instantly. This time…he used strategy.
The [Slavers] were already panicking with the death of their leader. No sooner had they hacked down the newly-animated Ghoul than the zombies and Ghouls appeared. And they were outnumbered by the hundred-some [Guards], who had Skills and weapons.
The zombies were naked. But here was a factor the [Slavers] hadn’t been prepared for:
The zombies were running.
Most people didn’t know zombies ran. It took more death mana—or the presence of a Crypt Lord—to make them sprint. Pisces didn’t work with flesh-based undead normally.
He made an exception. The zombies ran at the [Slavers], who again tried to form a defensive formation around the [Slaves]. Pisces directed the onslaught from above as he watched the Skeleton Champions running towards the rear.
“Ghouls—the riders. Don’t kill the horses, spook them.”
He made the zombies split; instead of coming in a rough wedge towards the center of the living, which they wanted to do, they began to encircle the [Slavers]. They were just there to get in the way. A [Rider] trying to break around the horde was watching the running zombies and never saw the tensed figure until the Ghoul jumped and took them off the saddle. Then the Skeleton Champions moved into the fighting.
That’s when the [Slavers] started dying.
Pisces’ Skeleton Champions had never been made to fight multiple foes at once. His Skill was [Undead: Duelist Instincts]. They were specialized at one-on-one combat where even a Level 30 [Warrior] might sweat to see one coming at them.
The average Level 30 [Warrior] might triumph in a duel, but how many of the [Slavers] below were Level 30? Nor were the Skeleton Champions fighting fair. The one with a greatsword was trading cuts with a huge [Slaver], who was matching him with a lead club taking chips across the weapon. They were swinging on each other, going blow for blow, when the club-wielding [Slaver] gasped and half-turned.
One of the Skeleton Champions with daggers had buried its blades in his back. Then the greatsword fell.
No honor. No etiquette. Not for these foes. The Skeleton Champions went hunting for stronger foes. One raised a shield as a [Fireball] blew every zombie around it to pieces. It staggered as a [Mage] pointed at the skeleton still on its feet—
Pisces landed behind the [Mage] and beheaded the caster. His [Invisibility] spell failed as he lost concentration, and there was a cry.
“The—the—”
He was in the center of the [Slavers]’ defensive lines. The [Necromancer] went running at a wall of [Guards] who panicked. Half turned themselves up, and one went down as a Ghoul took them from behind and dragged them into the clutches of the hungry zombies. But the rest were aiming Skills at him—the [Necromancer] ran, and then something rose upwards.
A…slope? He ran up the ramp of bones, which carried him over the heads of the fighting [Slavers] and undead. The [Slaves] saw the [Necromancer] leap—that was how he’d bypassed their lines the first time.
He’d never performed this move on a chaotic battlefield. But Pisces had learned to animate structures in the Trials of Shields. He was a [Necromancer of Reclaimed Grandeur]—and he had needed to get that [Mage].
Necessity. Pisces turned in the air. He saw a cluster of [Archers] aiming at him and pointed at them.
“[Fireball].”
His aim was spot on. Two saw the roiling ball of fire shooting at them and dove away in time to survive the blast. They lay on the ground, stunned, as the undead pressed forwards without their support. And then the [Necromancer] was gone again.
“Yield! We surrender!”
A cry went up as the undead pressed the narrowing lines of [Slavers] back against the [Slaves]. The [Slaves] were clumped together—they were afraid of the undead, even if some of them were smiling. But the zombies did fall back. A pair of snarling Ghouls loped back a step—and the [Slavers] hesitated. A few tossed down their weapons and raised their hands, but then a figure shouldered aside the shorter zombies.
A Skeleton Champion, bones reinforced with Manticore ivory, stepped into place. Thirteen formed a circle around the [Slavers]. The two Ghouls joined their ranks, and the guards realized the zombies were falling back only because the [Necromancer] couldn’t control them if they got past them.
The Skeleton Champions waited. Then a [Deathbolt] flashed out of the fading light and hit one of the [Guards] in the chest. The [Necromancer] reappeared, and the Skeleton Champions advanced.
 
——
 
Easier the second time. All but eighteen zombies had been hacked down, but not a single Skeleton Champion had fallen. This caravan felt weaker than the other one—or maybe it was the lower-level undead.
The [Slaves] were still hard. Freeing them? He just cut the ropes free. But they asked him the same question.
“I…freed a caravan northwest of you. They were headed—”
Pisces hesitated. He didn’t know if he should say.
“I cannot escort you. I’m sorry.”
“But—we’re on foot. This is a trade road. We’ll be caught.”
This group wasn’t nearly as fit as the other. They hadn’t been in great condition, but neither had they been malnourished or visibly injured. Khormez hadn’t bought valuable [Slaves], though. Pisces saw open wounds or odd scars on the Stitch-folk.
It took him a moment to realize it was frayed skin that had been knotted off, leaving warped, puckered scar-tissue. A way to close damaged cloth-flesh if you had no fabric. Worse were the missing limbs, usually arms, or digits. He knew they could sew their limbs back on, but these people…
It did not make him angrier. He didn’t feel…angry. Rather, as he looked over a hundred dead men and women, some of whom he had killed, he felt—
Ah. He wiped at the dried blood on his cheeks, shook some off his robes and rapier, then got to work. He’d think of that later, later.
Just another connection between him and the man he’d used to think was a goal. Az’kerash.
So be it. If he was falling, then today he was diving. So this is what it was like, then…he pushed the thought away. He had dealt with the [Slavers].
But the [Slaves]—
“Sir, we will never make it. Is there no one else? No…route?”
“No.”
He stood there, and the hundreds of men and women moaned.
“You’ve doomed us. They’ll have us killed for betraying our masters.”
One shook his chains at Pisces, and the [Necromancer] looked at a Stitch-man. The figure shrank back behind the others. He looked noticeably better than the others, and he hadn’t been attached to the main slave-lines. Pisces remembered the [Slaves] who had taken Igheriz’s and Hrome’s sides…
His rapier was heavy as he addressed the group.
“You are free, now. I cannot escort you to safety. There are horses, and if you split up, disguise yourselves, you have a chance. Loot the dead for clothing. If you are Stitch-folk, you could change your face. I am sorry. But I can only halt the caravans. There may be help northeast of here or if you go to Tiqr, Pomle.”
Too far. They stood there until he pointed at random. A woman jumped.
“You. Gather what you need. If there’s anyone you trust, form a group. If—”
He almost didn’t say it, but he had let these people out.
“If you wish to remain [Slaves], the city is not far. Go there, but this is your chance. Your only chance, perhaps.”
Uncertainty. The woman Pisces had pointed at was glancing around—but then someone bent down and grabbed the [Slavemaster]’s whip. A young man who bore lash marks on his back. He began to check the man’s bag of holding, and that provoked a flurry of motion.
People began grabbing magical items like bags of holding, fighting over coins. Pisces stopped them from brawling and divided items up, but he was turning. Watching the road.
The undead were keeping travellers away, but after twenty minutes, he thought he could see a cloud of dust headed towards them from the city. He stood on the hilltop and told them to run.
Not all of them did. The [Slaves] scattered, most headed away from the city. Some stood there, waiting to be re-captured.
Well, they’d slow the garrison. Pisces saw more than one figure gazing up at him. Gold-rank adventurer with undead. He wasn’t helping them.
If it were me…
Most have no levels for combat or survival.
It’s a chance.
That was all he told himself. He could not…the [Necromancer] was busy. As the stripped [Slavers] lay there, he spoke one word that made all who heard it shiver.
“Arise.”
 
——
 
Ceria, Ice Squirrel: Heeeey, Pisces. Haven’t heard from you, assuming you’re just enjoying the endless dust. Don’t eat too much. Update on Yv. Etrikah is pretty good—she says Yvlon’s balances are off. Looks like a cure’s not known. Pretty interesting actually; to create it, they take some poor kid and load ‘em up with curatives but keep getting them sick. So whatever magical disease they’ve got is nasty. Bright side? Less Yvlon. Downside? Less Yvlon. She’s under maximum security rest.
Ceria, Ruler of Medain NOT MARRIED: Itkisa’s gotten off with a slap on the wrist. Keep mum about the fights and Tomb. Bit tricky over here. We want to do strategy and planning given circumstances. Thinking we should hit Tiqr…might be a possibility to tie up my stuff and do politics while we’re there. And Zenol. Lots to do.
Ceria, Archmage of Frost: Funny story, Pisces. Your carriage just pulled up. It’s empty. You okay? Obviously, if you’re kidnapped and someone’s reading this [Message] now we’re into hostage negotiations, and I’ve got a Relic-class circlet that makes me smart. Just let me know.
Ceria: Did you hit a caravan outside of that city we were in? I need you to get out of there right now if that is the case, and we can cover it. Answer, Pisces.
Colth: This isn’t a good idea, Pisces. Answer Ceria and meet us at Tyrant’s Rest, pronto.
 
He got all of that when he woke up. He assumed she’d been messaging him throughout the night. [Messages] didn’t have timestamps…at least not the ones he could cast.
He’d forgotten to answer them. Pisces sat up, and he’d been sleeping in another buried bivouac. This time, the sand hadn’t really gotten him, but he’d been safe.
…Mostly because of the undead around him. He was sore, his mana reserves were high, and he felt that mental strain from casting repeatedly—but despite it all, he got up almost trembling with energy.
Nerves, too.
He sent Ceria nothing at first. Pisces was thinking. He hadn’t been clever enough…but it was before dawn, and he was fresher after last night. He’d seen the [Slaves] off in the evening, used some of the zombies to slow down the garrison, and then taken the rest of the undead as far away from the roads as he could.
He’d gotten maybe eight hours of sleep since he’d actually gone to bed early—now he estimated it might be 3 AM. A good time. He got to work fast.
The Skeleton Champions stripped his meager camp as he chewed on some food he’d taken from the dead [Slaver] caravans. Pisces wrote fast on a scroll, then adjusted the spell and handed it to a Ghoul. He concentrated and took firm mental control of it. Then sent it sprinting westwards.
He took quick stock of the rest of the undead as he consulted a map. Pisces had trouble orienting himself in the darkness, but that was what the [Compass] cantrip was for; it pointed you at Wistram, at least, the version he’d learned. Wistram wasn’t north, but with the map that Lareceina had been given, he could orient. So he was going north…he wished he’d tossed down more mice on the roads in prep for today.
Or that he could animate flying creatures. How the hell did you make flying undead? If Pisces killed a bird, he doubted he’d get one flying properly, even if it was left in pristine condition. He had done Face-Eater Moths, but birds were totally different. Skeletons and muscle. He had no practice was the point.
“Another flaw in my studies.”
He was on the skeleton horse’s back and riding fast with the undead running after him within eight minutes of waking. Travel took a long damn time even with the skeleton horse. He had none to waste.
 
——
 
Pisces winged a myna bird after six misses and reanimated it, trying to figure out how to get it to fly. It actually managed a few flaps before it crashed and he had to get another.
He felt bad about that. Flying was very hard. But the nature of zombies meant that birds could fly just like zombies could run; you had the body’s natural muscle memory to draw on. It was then only a matter of giving the bird enough mana and direct control to keep it ‘active’.
Otherwise, it’d just crash. Pisces sent it flying up and lost track of it almost at once.
Keeping a mana-link in the skies was also a lot harder than on the ground. Pisces had once commanded a single bug at range, but that had been with his full focus, and it hadn’t gone nearly as quickly.
The fast-moving bird needed something…he didn’t know what until he read some of the books that Az’kerash had given him.
The answer turned out to be a simple rune you drew in the flesh that acted as a marker for your magic. A dagger would do, and he could trace it under the feathers, then send the bird up.
Scout acquired. Pisces killed two more birds, mainly by having the undead bird chase other flocks of birds up for him to shoot [Deathbolts] at. Other birds reacted to the undead ones like most animals: they either fought or ran, spooked. Mind you, they couldn’t tell another bird was a zombie until they got close…
That left three birds to work on. Two of which Pisces managed to animate to the level of Ghouls. This trick wasn’t even new.
“[Invigorate Corpse].”
That was a spell from when he’d been back in Ailendamus. Pisces hadn’t used it then since Feren had been making Ghouls. Back then, he’d had to cast it with six others to reliably get one. Today?
His first Ghoul-bird couldn’t withstand the death mana he pumped into it and exploded. After he’d wiped the bits off him, he did it more carefully.
A Ghoul myna bird was not a deadly creature, but it flew fast. Very fast. He used one to scout ahead of him. The other one he sent west, after the Ghoul.
This allowed Pisces to expedite the Ghoul-trick. He had it hand off the scroll to the Myna bird, then pulled the death mana from it, killing the regular Ghoul. It was a waste of undead, but it would have gone rogue or attracted attention otherwise.
Pisces had less undead to work with than he wanted. He’d lost almost all the original zombies, but replenished their ranks with about seventy-some zombies and a few Ghouls. No more skeletons; he hadn’t had time to process the bones.
He’d lost nearly a third of the corpses due to a phenomenon he was starting to realize was unique to Chandrar: Stitch-folk didn’t become corpses in the same way.
Oh, they turned into regular dead bodies when they died. They’d rise, dead flesh and stitching rotting—assuming you hadn’t hacked a limb off, in which case it would be cloth.
But there was the problem. If they lost a limb, it was cloth when you animated them. And when a zombie Stitch-person died, something odd happened.
They turned to cloth entirely. So unlike, say, a Human corpse, which you could animate, let ‘die’, then recycle by adding more death magic to it—unless it was completely destroyed—Stitch-folk would turn into shredded and tattered cloth.
…And bits of faintly glowing string.
Lifethread. Pisces had seen the other Stitch-folk [Slaves] blanching when he’d observed the phenomenon, and he didn’t have any idea what to do with the dust or Lifethread. But it meant that his undead force was far less renewable. Smaller, too.
Again, he had no solution here. Just observations. The undead bird was a win enough for the morning.
After three hours of riding, dawn was already breaking, but Pisces felt it was time. He had the distant Ghoul myna bird land, then, with great effort, pull the string he’d attached to the scroll. It finally got the damn thing open, and the [Message] scroll activated.

What Pisces didn’t know was that by the end of the first day, the other caravans were well aware…something was going on.
He had guessed, of course. The Slaver’s Guild of Chandrar was directly funded and organized through Lailight Scintillation. Roshal.
It was one of, if not the, most effective organizations in the world. Emir Yazdil’s talent could be said to be reflected here; he had ensured the caravans ran smoothly and reformed them from more lax standards in generations past. The other Slave Lords had made numerous changes to Roshal; in this, they had ceded to him.
For instance, the Slaver’s Guild had a number of departments devoted to various crises. Such as the Kidnapping and Ransoms department. Small, but nearly twenty members of the Guild were on-call to just…answer kidnappings of their membership.
Often, a lot of it was inter-Guild politics, but there were always thugs, bandits, and so on. They didn’t guarantee a member was freed unless they were in good standing. Business was business. But if someone actually answered the ransom note, did some negotiating, or even said, ‘we can’t pay that’, the odds of survival went up by at least 30%.
In the same vein, a substantially larger wing of the Guild was Caravan Crisis—a catchall term for obstacles or attacks on caravans. It monitored the Leashed Trails across all of Chandrar and issued alerts for weather, monster attacks, war, and so on.
It was so vast and important that it had regional headquarters, which in turn coordinated with nations, petitioning them to send out their law enforcement or hire adventurers—if needed, the Slaver’s Guild would do it themselves, but they preferred not to waste coin.
‘Never do what someone else can do for you’ was one of the quotes written in a faded gold plaque above the main headquarters’ doors. Naturally, the operators had [Slaves] for menial tasks, but this was a rare job that required freefolk workers exclusively.
Freeman Chilt was a [Remote Operator], Level 23, in charge of the day-crew for his sub-region in the South Eastern Leashed Trails division of the Caravan Crisis headquarters. One of over a thousand such employees.
It was not a prestigious job, though it paid decently. He had dreams of promotion to Lailight Scintillation, not having to live in the small headquarters in Nerrhavia’s Fallen. He enjoyed the two office [Slaves], but resented not having his own. He was a man with plenty of complaints about life, who would consider himself a normal man, like a Drake or Gnoll or anyone else around the world.
Until yesterday, he had never had a crisis too large for his job. Yes, the caravans had trouble all the time. [Slave Masters] were arrogant, touchy, and loved to send [Messages] to complain about things the Guild didn’t have to help them with.
Other [Slave Masters] stealing their earmarked [Slaves]—a matter for another department. Getting in trouble for collaring someone with the Watch? Another department.
The cheap speaking stones and [Message] spells from Wistram just made it worse. Now he was deluged with trivial complaints, and they had an entire person whose job it was to just respond nicely to the pampered idiots. However, Chilt’s job was to monitor the roads, and it had not been hugely stressful.
Sometimes, there were monsters. Sometimes, there were bandits. He’d had entire caravans wiped out from monster attacks. One time, Sand Worms had eaten a caravan of over two thousand.
Tragic, and he’d had to scramble alerts across the entire region. A Named-rank team had been called to hunt them down, but this did not distress Chilt. It was onerous at times, yes, but…he was still sitting in a padded chair as a [Slave] handed him drinks. At worst, he was reporting to a supervisor and sweating before he took out his frustrations on one of the [Slaves]. If the idiots on the Leashed Trails died, well, it looked bad if he hadn’t done his job, but that was their life. All risk, all reward, eh?
Today was different. Today, Chilt hadn’t slept. Grime from greasy food had left a patina across his unshaven face. His eyes were sleep-deprived and wanted to close, but the stamina potion mixed into his tea had given him the runs and nervous energy.
“Hello? Hello to Honored Slave Master Kitre? This is Operator Chilt of the Guild. Caravan Crisis—checking in.”
He was rasping into a speaking stone as an upset woman snapped back.
“Blessed sands, I have been on hold for twenty minutes! You incompetents, what is going on? And it is Slave Mistress, fool!”
He bit back a short reply; he’d done this for the last four hours.
“Standby, Slave Mistress. We pray your indulgence in this most-stressful of times. Please report your caravan’s condition and any notable incidents on the road—”
“Standby? You have had us standing by all night and into the dawn! If there is a monster, say so! But I have had to halt while—”
He didn’t have time for this. There were four other caravans in the area near the city marked in red on a map, and more would be headed along the road. That was caravans, mind you. There were other interests of Roshal that weren’t even part of this list, and Chilt snapped.
“Slave Mistress, we have declared an all-halt to caravans until we know the fate of two that have vanished, all presumed dead! The Blessed Chains and The Speedy Servant have both vanished close to the city of Halqued! We presume monster attacks or—or a creation of the Mad Ones or something else!”
One caravan was bad enough, but both had been decently large, and neither one had sent out a distress call. There had been no survivors. This was not in itself odd.
The scary part was that there had been no bodies. Halqued was not exactly filled with ultra-efficient members of Nerrhavia’s Fallen. When the Guild had finally cajoled the local garrison to check, they’d found the wagons only after hours of searching. The first caravan not reaching the city had been enough for Chilt to issue one of these warnings to others in the area.
He hadn’t thought much of it other than being annoyed at the delay of The Blessed Chains and expecting the Slave Mistress in charge to give him an explanation in an hour and having to do paperwork.
Then the second caravan, The Speedy Servant, had gone missing. Undead had been spotted near them, but not enough to…
The Guild’s internal systems had ways to deal with unexpected events like these. In this situation, Chilt had to call an all-halt to every caravan on the road headed into a dangerous region and find out what was going on.
The problem was…the local garrison had found nothing. No bodies, again. No wagons. They had been delayed hacking up some zombies, and when they’d gotten there, they’d discovered nothing.
Well, there had been [Slaves], but those didn’t count. The useless things had all given mixed accounts of what had happened, so Chilt had tossed those out as contradictory—unreliable. Given how many had run off, they were probably lying to protect any runaway [Slaves], but it meant that until one was interrogated properly, he wasn’t allowed to use their testimony.
And Nerrhavia’s Fallen’s stupid [Soldiers] had just claimed them as their property! The Guild was having an advocate deal with that, but it might be days of negotiating for them. What it meant was that there were two caravans, both wiped out in short periods of time with no reliable witnesses.
Nor had Nerrhavia’s Fallen’s garrison thought to bring [Trackers]; it had been lazy Hemp [Soldiers] searching for a fight and nothing else. The flaw in relying on local governance. So the Slaver’s Guild had Chilt arranging for adventurers to cover the shortfall…
Hence him being up; it was his head on the line if he didn’t figure out what was going on. Chilt snarled as the [Slave Mistress] gave him a lashing with her tongue. He thrust out a cup at a frightened [Slave], who took it and rushed off. The lazy idiots got rotated through his headquarters, and they were never high-level or attractive…
“Slave Mistress, Slave Mistress, I have other caravans to check on! Please report your status.”
He took some satisfaction in cutting her off. Chilt stared at the board as a weary co-worker tacked something onto it. It was scrawled notes in messy ink as the team put down conclusions.

The third caravan was waiting for him. So Pisces once again changed tactics. It seemed too alert, but it was the smallest yet, so he did the most expeditious thing he could: he cast [Invisibility] on the Skeleton Champions and sent them in.
[Invisibility] was a tough spell. It had always been known as a tough spell, even for Tier 4. Plenty of [Mages] never learned it because it had so much nuance to it.
For instance, you had to concentrate a bit to keep it up. Getting hit almost always knocked it out of you. Dust or clouds revealed you, and plenty of [Mages] could only keep invisible until they touched something.
Pisces could do four Skeleton Champions plus himself, and the four would lose it the moment they attacked. Not exactly ideal. If he’d had [Darkness Cloud] or the ability to raise a sandstorm he could have used that.
But what he did have was a unique trick. [Drain Death Mana] and a horde of undead. So, Pisces did this.
He and the Skeleton Champions moved past the [Slavers]’ defenses. They got close as they could to a group of the [Guards], then Pisces cast two spells.
[Muffle] and [Lesser Illusion]. He fixed an image of the camp in place and attacked with the Skeleton Champions. Then, once the fighting was done, recast the spell and advanced.
The trick was he was draining zombies of their mana to fuel this much spellcasting. It was hard. His head hurt, and he got a nosebleed the fourth time he did it. But it worked.
By the time they advanced past the walls, the [Guards] knew they were under attack. This is where it got—harder.
Unlike the other two caravans, this one knew something had been out there. They’d lacked for anti-invisibility spells, but they came out of their defenses and fought—hard.
The first Skeleton Champion went down as a [Power Strike] smashed a skull in. Another exploded, silently, as a Potion of Blast detonated. It overloaded the [Muffle] spell, but the only sound was a brief ‘clap’ as loud as someone smacking their hands together.
Then—silence. By the time other [Guards] were turning, two more Skeleton Champions were moving up, and the onslaught continued.
Pisces had to fight with the Skeleton Champions. He was higher-level, a Silver-bell [Duelist] with his Ring of Shatterbolt versus low-level [Guards] during a surprise attack. They still tagged him.
A blade slashing across his chest. An arrow striking him in the back—twice, the [Necromancer] staggered, then, to the horror of the [Slavers], turned and ran his attacker through. Stalker’s armor. That broke what nerve they had left. They had already been speaking his title like a curse, trying to run.
Three minutes of fighting did not go unnoticed, despite the muffling spells. The magic-users detected the foreign magic, but by that point…
It was too late; Skeleton Champions were marching between the wagons along with the rest of the undead who’d walked past the undefended walls. Then the caravan was trapped.
The [Slavers] had the horses hitched up, ready to go, but the Skeleton Champions had been smashing the wagon tongues, setting them free, and any time a [Slaver] appeared, they had died in seconds.
The [Slavers] had been trying to hide, thinking it was ‘just’ invisible monsters.
Hoping, perhaps, they’d be ignored or the undead would kill the [Slaves] and they could get away. Pisces had gone after the [Slave Master] when he’d heard the speaking stone, worried she’d report…

It corrupted everything. He ignored her gold and artifacts and picked up two things from her personal, neat wagon. A healing potion. She’d had two of the now-precious vials; he left the other for them.
The second was a map.

Stellar Ivory. He gazed up at it and then slept.
 
[Necromancer of Reclaimed Grandeur Level 45!]
[Skill – Advanced Undead Shaping Obtained!]
[Spell – Mend Undead Obtained!]
 
——
 
Pisces dreamed oddly in his sleep.
He dreamed of…
Ivery.
He was the Skeleton Champion. For a second, he was Bearbones, the two-headed warbear, ‘sleeping’ next to a bunch of oddly-sanguine animals, camels and horses, even a zorse. And Ivery, sitting cross-legged in a tent as people spoke around him.
Both. And a bunch of undead marching around a sleeping [Necromancer] glowing with undeath. Pisces was split between all these perspectives…
He was even in a bar with wiggling slime-breasts, serving drinks to—
…
His mind fuzzed, and the Skeleton Lord’s viewpoint snapped him into Ivery’s eyes. Then he was Ivery.
Bones scarred from combat. A bit stronger than before? Yes. It was his animating spell. He was quicker, more adept, but most importantly, his bones were stronger.
Different bones than the poor [Slavers]. Better bones. See here, this had been one of the [Slavetaker Champions]. And this was a bone from a dead [Slave Master] who’d nearly killed Bearig with a sword—
One bone per corpse. Lessons learned. Ivery knew this, of course. It was Pisces’ mind which absorbed it all.
Stronger, faster, better with a blade—but not as good as some. Frustration. The Skeleton Lord was frustrated. Too many Djinni. Too weak. It had eaten a [Lightning Bolt] the other day, and true, no one had died but…
“Good job, Ivery.”
The words echoed in its skull. The Skeleton Lord stopped picking at the sandy ground in the tent. Smiled. It glanced up, with Pisces, as someone spoke.
“—has to be him. No one else could do it, eh?”
“Why now? He’s too far inland to get there. We’ll never make it.”
“Someone must try. If it is him, he’s fighting alone. So are we cowards?”
The voices were familiar. To Pisces. Ivery knew them all, of course. There was Nathpe, the [Rebel] that the Horns of Hammerad had helped when she led a raid on a caravan along the Ekhot Straits. She was fiercely arguing with the other leaders, who’d ridden through the night to be here.
Risky, risky. But everyone was aflutter with the news. They’d heard it through their own sources and Roshal’s Guild. She was remonstrating with a huge Human man, a solid bloke named Amprel, over six and a half feet tall. He didn’t run fast, but he didn’t get into trouble like she did.
“Not cowards but, I think, practical. Merr’s closer. If we go this far into Nerrhavia’s Fallen, we may never come out.”
“If it’s him—”
“Let’s ask Bearig.”
That came from Qshom, of course. The [Tailor of Freed Thread] was working on an arm; he always was. So every head turned, and a man heaved himself up. Pisces, dreaming, felt a shock.
Of course, he hadn’t seen how much weight the [Cook] had lost. Or how he’d rebuilt his arms for more muscle. They were still thick, but he had a warrior’s trim in more than just body. It was a confidence, both in tone and how he held himself.
“We ride. Ivery’s gazed that way nonstop.”
“Even in battle, eh? Maybe we’ll get him upgraded, at least. Then we’re with you, Bearig.”
Nathpe leapt up, but Bearig held up a hand.
“Not every group. We have to be fast. Qshom, you stay with Nathpe. Amprel, if you run interference…”
She began arguing as the other man nodded, relieved.
“This I can do.”
“I’m going with you. We’re all going. If only Eloque were here…”
Qshom stood, and Bearig began to argue, then nodded. They were all talking, then, and Ivery’s head was turning. He got up to pace around the camp. Guard duty in case a Djinni attacked—not that he could do much. He’d ‘died’ sixty-eight times, but they kept putting him together.
Weaker than he should be for a Skeleton Lord. If a certain [Necromancer] were doing upgrades, Ivery could use something better than a crummy piece of glass, eh?
At this point, Pisces realized the Skeleton Lord was talking to him. In a way. He was stirring and trying to ask.
Eloque? Merr was elsewhere, but what had happened to Eloque? He saw Ivery pass by a temporary tent, and his reflection caught in the light from a glass lantern. A skeleton with glowing blue flames for eyes.
A camp of [Rebels].
Bearig, stepping out to call for Ivery.
“Ivery, we need to know where—”
A little figure was by his side. Ivery strode over, and Rophir pointed up. The half-Elf boy looked broadly the same, but his skin was sun-tanned now, and he seemed different. His eyes more focused. He had a turban on his head and he spoke.
“He’s in his eyes.”
Bearig jerked and stared at Pisces, and the [Necromancer]—
—woke—
—up.
 
——
 
He was feverish when he woke up. Head spinning, clouded. Pisces lay there until a Skeleton Champion unhooked a water flask and gave it to him. He drank thirstily.
“Bearig? Where’s Eloque. Ivery…”
He’d known the Skeleton Lord was still around, but—Pisces had no idea you could do that. He was learning a lot.
He hoped he wasn’t infected by the spear wound. He lay there until he was well enough to rise and pass water. Then he sat and thought.
 
——
 
It had been a Skill from the [Javelineer] which had gotten Pisces on the fifth caravan attack. The Stitch-woman had played dead.
Foolish of himself to go in like that, but the undead had needed backup. Pisces needed more bones. But the Stitch-folk attrition rate meant he was barely growing the horde.
…Well. It’d do. The Bone Horror and Skeleton Champions were the first beneficiaries of Pisces’ [Mend Undead] spell. He could fuse bones and fix them, but this was like a [Repair] spell. Far more convenient.
Pisces wished he’d gotten a new undead or attack spell, but life was not so convenient. If he’d been able to animate that Bone Behemoth…
No. Too big. Same with Crypt Lords if he could make them; too slow, and they thought.
He had a mix of zombies, over two hundred; Skeleton Champions, thirteen; a Bone Horror; and about twenty Ghouls. More than enough to wipe out an average caravan alone. And Pisces’ scouts told him the other caravans were going evasive. The one he’d tagged was deep offroad and trying to bury themselves under tarps in the sand.
Very clever, actually. They’d decided to hide rather than go for the city. There were, what, two more in the area he could hit? That he knew of. This one would have been all-but-invisible to Pisces.
Since he knew it was there, Pisces had a thought. He was immobilized while he healed. It was dark, and he was exhausted.
He glanced up, and a Skeleton Champion winked a yellow eyeflame at him.
We do overtime, boss.
Pisces was probably still a bit sick because he imagined the Skeleton Champion talking like Colth. Either way, it was a good idea. The Skeleton Champions took point and led the Ghouls and Zombies into the night, followed by the galloping Bone Horror. Pisces drifted off and dreamed of undead falling upon screaming [Slavers].
No, wait, that wasn’t a dream.
 
——
 
Attrition was decently high for the undead during the night battle, but they actually animated the rest of the corpses as zombies and came back. More importantly, Pisces had realized two things as he slept.
One: the Skeleton Champions were generating Stellar Ivory, that resource he still lacked much of. He had not yet made anything permanent out of it…
Two: a period of two full moons was approaching. The [Ritual of the Lord of Bones] could be cast, and at last, Pisces was close enough to bind something to Ivery again.
He’d slept on both things, especially Ivery. But the thought of the Skeleton Lord made Pisces resolve to do the ritual.
Anything’s better than a glass rock. He seems far more powerful, but I could potentially just remake him entirely. That…made Pisces feel guilty, but Ivery was like a hodgepodge of bones. If Pisces used the Manticore bones, he could make a Manticore Skeleton Lord.
Imagine one of those coming at you. With a bound [Fireball] in the mouth? Az’kerash had said that the ritual allowed for any spell Pisces knew—though the Skeleton Lord would need to use its personal mana reserves if Pisces didn’t help.
Bound [Fireball] at will?
No, no, bound [Invisibility] at will. Invisible Manticore Skeleton Lord.
He put that one in as ‘acceptable’. Pisces was more worried in the interim about the Stellar Ivory thing.
He was aware the Skeleton Champions were developing a bit of a personality. A bit of autonomy. Any undead of sufficient power could think; even Ghouls were a bit tactical. The Skeleton Champions might not be full leadership types, but he had to watch them. Make sure they didn’t think he would be better as a Skeleton Lich or go rogue.
The Stellar Ivory was a powerful piece of necromantic material. Would they want to hang onto it? He still didn’t fully know what it did aside from knowing it could partially-animate an undead even without a complete frame and was stronger and could generate mana…
As it turned out, the issue was a moot one. When the Skeleton Champions came tromping back, blades freshly blooded, they had a surprise for Pisces. He stared at the roughly femur-sized pile of bone scraps, each one pale and starlight bright.
The Stellar Ivory. They’d pulled it out of their bodies! Pisces saw a replacement finger on the Skeleton Champion with the bow, a missing piece from one’s head, a chunk carved out of another’s forearms—
“For me? Why?”
He croaked at them. For answer, the Skeleton Champions knelt while the one holding the bones presented it to Pisces like a [Knight] offering a great item to a [King]. It had that same feel.
Perhaps it was their growing autonomy. Or his lesson in seeing through Ivery’s eyes. But Pisces felt it, this time. A sense from the undead.
They weren’t able to think, let alone in concrete terms like Ivery. They were dimmer in intelligence. But there was a…feeling from them. Even the Ghouls and zombies. They gazed at the Stellar Ivory, at Pisces, and recognized him.
Necromancer.
The glowing ivory was valuable. Each undead wanted it, like a flower craved good soil or sunlight. But they recognized Pisces was the creator of it. That he could make greater undead.
They had…
Great expectations of him.
He shivered and realized they had always been waiting for him to level.
 
——
 
Pisces never found the 7th caravan. He suspected, like the 6th, it had gone to ground because he had multiple undead birds in the sky, and they saw nothing like it.
That was okay. He spent all of the third day resting. He was a bit feverish, but he thought he hadn’t been infected or he’d have been dead with that healing potion; he was good enough to rise on the 4th day and do what had to be done.
 
——
 
The city of Halqued wasn’t noticeably different after a few days since the Horns of Hammerad had fought Itkisa at the Mad Ones’ encampment. Life was back to normal.
Oh, it had been crazy for a moment there. There had been scrying spells, people had been going to see and then being told they might be inside a Gold-rank adventurer fight—it had been exciting!
Everyone had hoped for a bunch of cameras to come through so they could be on Nerrhavia’s Wonders—alas, only the Mad Ones got interviewed. And, reminded of that, people had visited their encampment and bragged to relatives and friends they’d been close to this news story, but it really hadn’t been A Thing.
There had been that incident with the Bane afterwards, but it hadn’t been much to hear tales of it. The Bane of Roshal hates slavery, shocking, more at eleven.
Even in the days after the Horns had left, things were fine.
Oh, sure, there had been that weird undead attack on the road, but they’d been killed. And maybe some [Soldiers] kept heading out on patrol; well, good, they might as well do something around here!
On the third day, perhaps you could see some agitation around the local Slaver’s Guild. It was oddly quiet without a regular shipment of [Slaves]. Everyone there seemed grumpy, but you could walk the city and never come across the Guild or its members.
So the city truly was placid, with its usual corruption or scandals unique to it. Was [Mayor] Heresha truly still sleeping with eleven different suitors? Yes. Had Master Dromet really bought some object from the Mad Ones which was allowing him to out-carpenter every other competitor, and had he been murdered by his son for said object? Investigations were still ongoing.
People entered and exited the city, local towns feeding the ore markets always hungry for more. In fact, a band of fifty were on the roads transporting a rather huge haul of ore from one of said local towns.
Copper, the good stuff. Every metal was useful, and fifty huge loads of copper in massive baskets as big as the carriers were headed towards the gates.
Ore was hard to transport because Bags and even Chests of Holding had hard limits to volume and weight. Even if it was only 40%, filling a Chest of Holding with copper ore was a good way to get an object impossible to move that would smash through any vehicle.
There were ways around the issue. Spells for lightening the weight, Djinni, or, and here was a Chandrarian method: [Slaves].
Fifty Hemp [Slaves] with [Laborer] classes was cheaper than other solutions. True, it wore down their bodies fast, but Hemp was cheap. It was just one of those things where Roshal had become part of the economy of Chandrar; they often sold [Slaves] cheap for first-time buyers because when you had one, you tended to get more.
They were in sight of the walls as a somewhat-harried Cotton Stitch-man with a whip chivvied the Hemps forwards. If he was impatient, well, it was damned hot, and the flies were biting. The Hemps ignored the whips on their backs as they plodded along, and pedestrians kept wide of the ore train.
One man even told the [Labormaster] off for flicking the whip a bit too close to his son; he might hurt someone! The [Labormaster] was hurling an expletive, telling the man to deal with Hemp for an hour and then he’d see, when someone walked out of the stream of people headed for the gates.
It was a figure to draw the eyes. Not because of his attire; he was wearing a wanderer’s clothing, dusky, sun-bleached fabric, mostly grey or brown, wrapped around his arms and legs. Cheap protection against sun, insect, and sand. If he smelled at all in this heat, it was of sweat and unwashed linen. His feet made no sound on the dry ground.
Nor did he speak as the babble of voices, the crack of that whip, filled the morning air. But what marked him and had faces turning, people stepping side and pointing covertly, was the mask.
It was a bone white mask that only had room for his eyes, which were between grey and green, perhaps with a hint of orange. They were wide, unblinking, and people took him at once to be an [Assassin].
Or an odd adventurer, a bounty hunter? Perhaps just someone hiding his face, a criminal, but not one you wished to be drawn into the proximity of. The [Guards] at the gates bestirred themselves as one marked the figure. More work. They hoped he was not some trouble…they began to argue who had to interrogate the fellow.
The [Labormaster] saw the stranger with the mask last. He was raising his whip for another blow when his head turned and he saw the figure. Instead of lifting the lash further, he lowered it, politely giving the person a wary nod.
“Watch the Hemp, stranger. They’ll hurt you if one should fall with all that weight.”
A conscientious man’s concern for a fellow traveller on the roads. The stranger with the mask said nothing, but he stopped on the road. Accordingly, the [Labormaster] did too. Then he saw the stranger had a sword. A long rapier, a thin blade with a strange coating to the sword’s edge halfway up. Or was it some odd…
He drew it. Every eye had already been focused on him, but now the people halted. The [Labormaster]’s mouth opened, and he half-glanced behind him, as if thinking…he raised the whip uncertainly, but it was no weapon to block a strike with.
“Sir, what is—”
The masked stranger’s blade went across the Stitch-man’s neck, and the head landed on the ground. It kept speaking, in that way only Stitch-folk could do, as his body crumpled.
“—going on? I’m just bringing…I’m…ah.”
He gazed up as blood spurted up from his corpse. It did not turn to cloth; too much of it had been connected to the Stitch-man’s body. It fell, and there was a scream. Someone covered her mouth. The father with his son backed away, fumbling for—
The masked stranger turned, and the Hemp-folk had frozen. They gazed at him, and he looked to them. To the walls. Then down at the head.
“You’re him.”
The [Labormaster] was dying. His eyes glazing over without blood or oxygen, but he gazed up, almost dreamily at the figure who shook blood off his blade. There was no response.
Then a call from the wall. A shout. The people didn’t panic or run—they were frozen for a man with a blade was among them. But he didn’t cut into the Hemp [Slave]. He just turned…and walked.
Down the road, away from the city of Halqued. A slow walk that stopped only once. At first, it was nonsensical to the travellers who flinched away from him, hoping to hear the Watch coming to their rescues. Then they saw the second figure he had stopped next to.
It was an older man. Human, the other common species wherever you went. He was far richer, dressed well, and less…well, one might never associate with his kind. Because he was taking a [Slave] for a walk.
Some beautiful Stitch-girl who had to crawl like an animal. Not far from the city since who could move like that? A [Master] taking a [Slave] for a walk, the kind of which…
Then it was like a little click ran through all’s minds, and they took in the mask. White as bone. And that rapier was the bigger clue. The old man trembled then.
“I—”
The second swing didn’t take his head off but halted against his spine. Even so, when the old man fell, he did not get up nor gasp for air. Dead.
The [Slave] on her hands and knees stared up at the figure as he halted. She whispered.
“My collar’s deathmarked if I run. If I—”
He didn’t pick up the fallen leash. The masked figure just bent down, and she flinched; blood was on his clothing and mask. Did he whisper something to her?
If so, no one heard it. Her eyes were round as he walked down the road. Then…the horns were sounding from the gates. There was shouting, and someone began running for Halqued. A scream—and people began to flood towards the gates, but they looked back.
That masked figure was on the roads. Walking away from the city mobilizing—slowly—too slowly—and there was suddenly that calm dread. Even excitement, however perverse.
He was walking down the road. Then the people asked the horrifying question—how many on this road might have one of them with them? Servant, company, labor?
[Slaves].
 
——
 
By morning, the babble of what had happened at the northern gates was the rage of the city. People were talking, speculating.
It had to be. But he had left! All had seen it! He had—
Someone should tell Wistram, surely. There had been horn calls all morning. A [Guard] had gone off-duty and was gossiping loudly with everyone else at the wells.
“We never found him. Not that it is a ‘he’ we know for certain, and the Watch Captain bid us all quiet—but we rode down the road, and there were but six dead for the span of three miles.”
“Six!”
“Less than you might think? Then the [Soldiers] took over, but you know the Hemp; slow to move, slow to march. Each deathblow was a single cut, but for one fellow who seemed to have tried to dodge; he was stabbed ere he lay.”
She was peering around, perhaps thinking to report this to a newspaper or the Mage’s Guild. The folk of Halqued were mostly excited, those who hadn’t seen the killings.
“Do you think I might get an autograph? It’s worth good gold, and I had not the chance earlier…”
An enterprising man spoke up, excited. Another licked his lips.
“You’d be a fool to ask. Hush a madman’s wishes or a Djinni will answer you with laughter. If it is so—”
“Bah, I’ve nothing to fear. I’m not rich enough to be a target!”
The autograph-wisher laughed, and there was agreement, an excitement in the air until there was, abruptly, a horncall again. Everyone turned, expecting it to be from the north, but it was not. It came…from the east.
Silence fell, and all turned to Guard Lortina, who fell silent, gulping water from a waterflask. She spilled her drink slightly, then smiled.
“Probably a monster or some other—”
Then the horn blew again. And again, urgently. And they did not know, of course. They stood in sudden silence until they heard shouting—and then the silence was broken by a City Runner.
Her name was Loqe the Lethargic for she often overslept. She was quick, though, and ran…
She was running now, pale-faced, and blood was on her tunic. She came to a halt in the square around the well and gasped.
“It—it—they’re all dead.”
“Who is?”
Someone peered north, but Loqe pointed back with a trembling finger.
“The—the road east. A masked figure’s appeared and is killing everyone on the road! There was a [Slave Trader] and eleven—he’s hacked them up. A [Swordsman]—”
She was stuttering, in shock. Then the smiles left everyone, and they turned.
A masked man? Surely one would not be so mad unless…
“It’s him after all.”
The fellow who coveted an autograph was smiling now. Hesitantly, forcing it a bit. Because he was safe. He was—
Loqe the Lethargic needed soothing, and they asked her what she had seen. She was mid-recounting the tale of violence where one man had taken out eleven so fast…someone was running to see what the Watch and garrison were doing for they had seen [Riders] streaming eastwards.
Then they heard more horncalls to the south. And west. Then there was a twisting in the stomach.
“One man cannot be in three places at once. It’s like the other times, I’ve heard, on the borders. Anyone can wear a face—”
The comment hung in the air, like the suspended bucket of water shedding droplets into the well. Right up until there was a scream.
“Undead on the road! Skeletons are slaughtering people! Help!”
Now a ringing. Summoning the Watch to arms. A [Rider] galloped into the square.
“It’s some kind of Skeleton Knight—six of them! They ignored me, but they’re butchering—”
Guard Lortina paled and backed up as every eye turned towards her. She protested she was off-duty, tired, sick—before the same thought hit her as everyone else.
Loqe the Lethargic swallowed and looked up.
“Undead, you said?”
“Yes! I’ve never seen one fight like that. Each had weapons and armor—are you mad?”
The terrified [Rider] was afraid until they saw how everyone eyed each other and marked this fact. Then it was like a fell wind blowing across the city.
“I hold no chains.”
The autograph-seeker said it slowly, as if to declare himself innocent of something. A few people in the crowd stared at him, and someone called out.
“We’re all citizens of Nerrhavia’s Fallen, man!”
“Yes. But in case anyone were listening, I wish to say that I hold no chains nor have held any. Nor would I be leaving the city if…”
The voice trailed off. Then Loqe muttered.
“How far up the road north did you say he went? Three miles?”
Silence. The city listened as horns blew and blew, and now [Soldiers] were marching left, right, shouting for citizens to clear the way, but they appeared—disconcerted. They started running, but never seemed to fight or find anything.
Then the bodies started coming into the city. Stained red. And the citizens of Halqued—yes, they woke up from that amusing dream they’d had. Adventurers doing adventurer things. Some had wished for more interest, more drama, more excitement worthy of the legend.
Djinnis laugh at you. Fool, for what you wish.
The first day of it had the city in uproar. The [Mayor] and three of her lovers standing behind her giving a speech assuring everyone the gates were solid, the garrison full of thousands of Nerrhavia Fallen’s finest. The Slaver’s Guild loudly calling for adventurers, for protection!
—After three days, someone said that a [Slave Trader] had been found dead on the road, fifty miles north of the city. Entrails spilt after being taken off his horse. Half his [Slaves] had fled into the city, the other half vanished.
By then, it was one of a hundred tales from the road. An unease that gripped much of the city. Anyone who had even so much as held a collar, or who had a friend, family who owned [Slaves] felt a great trepidation upon them. Of course, they knew they were safe behind the walls, but they demanded reassurances that were given. This would end, this would be the last time. And then another report came in, and another.
The Scourge had come to Halqued.
Now, they knew what it meant.
 
——
 
He knew time was passing. That he had to get back to his team, but he just thought of that girl, and he didn’t stop.
He was out of caravans, obviously. So he just…took to the roads. Walked up and down them and found them.
There were so many. At times, it was one in a thousand. Other times, there were so many he wondered what percentage of Nerrhavia’s Fallen, of Chandrar, held chains.
The disguise might not have done much. He still carried his rapier since he needed the weapon he knew. But it was deniability. Just a shred.
Pisces had had the vague thought, when he was feverish, to come up with an alibi for not reaching Tyrant’s Rest. He’d worked on a long ruse and been organizing a second bird with a [Message] scroll when he’d checked and realized he and Ceria shared the same single brain cell.
 
Pisces: Ahem, to my esteemed Captain Ceria (and team), I regret to inform you that my sojourn abroad has hit something of a snag. I was accosted on the road by a rather objectionable fellow who insisted I duel him. When I naturally refused, he claimed it was over an illicit relationship I had with his bride-to-be?
Whom I did not know. Whereupon I did clarify the issue, and it turned out I was the object of admiration—suffice it to say I have been at a wedding of some length.
They go on for days, allegedly, and I have been trying to excuse myself, but I may be delayed.
Ceria: You idiot, what? Are they eating cake?
Pisces: As a matter of fact, yes. And I have been propositioned, in rather scandalous terms, by several ladies—
Colth: You’d better take them up on their offer.
Pisces: I shall not respond to that. Rest assured I will be headed back as soon as I find out—
Pisces: I believe I am in the wrong city. Excuse me while I clarify.
Ceria: Hilarious. Yisame’s laughing her butt off. Get over here, dumbass.
 
To be clear, Pisces hadn’t written any of that. It was clearly a conversation she’d written up in his voice. If he logicked out what she was doing, she was probably arranging the same trick he had, albeit with perhaps one of Yisame’s people casting the other [Message].
It was all obfuscation, deniability. He felt guilty but…well.
He continued. He knew it was dangerous and that each day ran the risk higher, that Roshal had to know. But he could not enter the city; he’d seen how many [Soldiers] were there, and the gates were now watched by a small army.
But there was a madness in him, a kind of thought in his head.
If no one enters or exits the city from Roshal, they can’t sell her or anyone else.
All he had to do was…kill any of them he found. Birds flying the skies. Undead mice on the ground.
It was just madness. The darkness of his class. He’d always known, deep down, he was probably like this.
He was glad no one from home could see him.
For he didn’t stop.
 
——
 
He was not freeing [Slaves]. He was killing [Slavers].
There was a distinction. Most of the time, Pisces just walked past the [Slaves]. Many had magicked collars. They were on the road, with witnesses. They could not run.
They recognized him, of course, but most said not a word. Not one. They would stare at the ground, wide-eyed, or shrink away from him. Some even covered their masters with their bodies, weeping.
Was it real? He couldn’t tell, though at times he would see one glance up at him or smile, give the slightest nod. They were tiny signs, and the most common, from the [Slaves] who looked oldest, was this.
They would put forefingers or pinkies together, linking like two fishhooks in a simple gesture, then pull them apart. A quick motion while feigning fear or pretending to be mute or silent.
A gesture without equivocation. He wanted to free them the most, but he could not. Even when they begged, he just told them he couldn’t do anything. Walked on as guilt ate at him.
Some ran for it. Others offered to join him, and again, it was hard.
Once, a Stitch-boy who couldn’t have been more than sixteen had bent down to pick up a cane that had been lashing his back. He’d put it on one shoulder and asked Pisces who he was killing next. Pisces had almost let him tag along—but the Stitch-boy couldn’t cast spells. He was too young, too low-level.
Garuda were easiest because they could fly off, and he could believe that was that. One time, he ambushed a bunch of Slave-Adventurers, three Garuda and a Stitch-girl with a painted face who called herself a [Clown].
She wanted to join him; the Garuda all flew off, each in a different direction. They’d all been adventurers who’d been in debt and enslaved. The Stitch-girl had nowhere to go, and he’d hesitated—turned her down as she cried out they’d capture her on the road. She’d tried to follow him, but when she saw the horde of undead he used to screen his retreat as they fled backwards into the wilderness, she’d given up.
It ate at him, but he didn’t even know where safety was.
So he walked or ran, vanishing with [Invisibility] when the garrison rode out to get him. Pisces’ trick that had foiled the charioteers worked again and again.
They could defeat invisibility.
They could detect life. They could detect death, and sometimes, his undead got sighted.
They could not find someone who was invisible to death or life, a man who just lay down in the sand and waited for them to pass by. Perhaps there were [Trackers] or [Hunters] who could find him.
Pisces assumed they did not want to find him or he was getting lucky. He lost track of how many days it was; he would wake up at random, multiple times in the night, sleep in the day.
Not long, he assumed.
Not long. Just a while of waking up and walking down the roads, [Flash Stepping] along from town to village to the city’s gates. He kept finding people, and so he told himself after a day when he found no one, no one—he’d stop. Then he’d have done his best, right? Then…
Then he ran into the family.
 
——
 
There were five of them. Father, mother, young. Early thirties? Children, ten and nine? [Slave], mid-twenties, a Garuda.
They’d hidden her collar with a hood. Been hurrying towards Halqued, within three miles, when he’d reached them. By now, it was easy for Pisces to tell the signature of Roshal’s magic.
He appeared and drew his sword, and they screamed.
All of them—the father tried to make the horse pulling the little cart go faster. Pisces walked around it, cut the leads, and it galloped away. He saw the two Stitch-children frozen as their mother grabbed at them, and the man drew a belt-knife.
Pisces took slow aim and hesitated. The two children were staring at him, at the faded blood on the mask he hadn’t bothered to clean, and then the man lunged.
“[Quick St—]”
He missed. Pisces had seen Skills go off, and it was obvious. He leaned away, slashed the arm down to the bone, and the man screamed and fell onto the ground. Pisces raised the rapier to stab as they yelled at him, and someone threw herself on top of him.
The Garuda [Slave].
“Tirth! Master Tirth! Help! Help—”
She was shielding him. Then the mother leapt forwards, another shield, and Pisces stared down.
“Move.”
He was speaking to the Garuda, but she turned up huge eyes at him and shrieked back.
“Leave! Please! I don’t want to be free! He’s done nothing to you!”
Pisces had been—not calm. Not tranquil, but a steady thrum of intensity that had passed hours by without the strain of more than concentration. This shattered his focus. He blinked. Peered down at her.
“Bane, spare us! Chire, Doit, run!”
The two children were scrambling off the wagon, and Pisces just gazed down at the man, who was groaning, holding his arm.
“We’ve done nothing to you. You—you butcher. Spare my family! Take Yive. Yive, just go and—”
“Don’t hurt him!”
That was directed at Pisces. He was circling around. Then the mother rose.
“You’re trying to kill an innocent man!”
Pisces stared at the Garuda and the collar exposed from her hood. The young Garuda was named Yive? She rasped.
“They took me in when I was young. I’m family—if you want to stab him, you’ll have to stab me!”
“And me! Get back!”
The mother was swinging the fallen knife at Pisces. He was thinking as he held still.
His goal had been to kill the father. The children were innocent. Killing both parents…
No. He couldn’t do that.
He glanced down at Yive, and she paled.
“Shie, run! Run! He’s going to kill all of you—”
She threw herself up, arms spread, and the mother turned white. She tried for a slash—Pisces cut the dagger out of her hands, and red blood showered the ground.
“Mummy!”
Her daughter screamed in horror. The boy—Doit—ran at Pisces and tried to punch his leg. His previously-wounded one, which twinged. He punched Pisces in the stomach, hitting the Stalker underarmor, screaming.
“Stop it! Stop it, I’ll kill you! I’ll—”
Pisces almost kicked him, then the man, Tirth, tore his son back. He backed away, one armed, and the four Stitch-folk hid behind the Garuda. Pisces eyed Yive, and she was shaking.
“Bane or Scourge—it is you, isn’t it? We were just going home. We had been on holiday when you—if you have any reason, let us go. I don’t wish to be freed.”
They had done a lot of talking. Pisces felt like his own throat was filled with sand. He croaked.
“Why?”
The Garuda gave him a blank look, then earnestly turned her head towards the family. They were backing up towards the city, leaving her, but they were calling for her to run, to fly.
“They’re my family.”
“You’re in chains.”
“So? Not all of us are treated poorly! Where would I go without them? You—do you think everyone you killed is a monster? Let us go.”
Pisces stared past Yive, at the Stitch-folk. Tirth shouted at Pisces.
“You’re no Gold-rank hero worthy of Hraace! You cold-blooded killer—touch Yive and I’ll have every bounty hunter and assassin in Chandrar on you!”
He sounded so self-righteously passionate. He flinched, and Yive blocked Pisces. Perhaps thinking to stop a spell.
Like [Deathbolt]. She was panting, and Pisces spoke directly to her.
“If they loved you, they’d free you.”
Another blank gaze, then an incredulous laugh. She shook her head.
“And do what, employ me? I like my class. I’m a [Happy Slave]. You’ve only known poor slavemasters. They’re not all like that.”
His hand—twitched. She flinched and backed away, tensing to leap into the air. Pisces inhaled and exhaled slowly.
The Watch would be coming. He addressed Yive shortly.
“Not everyone is treated like you.”
“And? Are you going to free me against my wishes? Are you going to butcher everyone who has a [Slave] for the sins of a few?”
She flapped upwards and grew more confident, calling down at him as she circled. Pisces’ head turned, and he was cold.
“Yes.”
She faltered, and Pisces glanced at the family now running for the gates. He could hit the father with a [Deathbolt]…maybe. But it might go through him and hit a child. He lowered his finger as Yive swooped at him. She had talons outstretched.
“[Defend the Master]!”
He dodged her. She hit the ground hard and cried out. Then flapped around awkwardly. She stared down at him, and he imagined Cawe in her place.
He didn’t stab her. Pisces just felt at his hair.
“I didn’t think about killing parents in front of children.”
It was more of a statement to himself. He turned and began to stride away; he could sense figures racing out the gates. Yive called after him, a shrieking, angry note in her voice; she might have broken her own foot in trying to attack.
“Do you understand what you nearly did? What you’ve done, Bane? Are you regretting any of it?”
He turned back. Glanced at her. Then it came out of him.
Laughter.
Bitter laughter he hadn’t heard in a long, long time. The same kind of laughter he’d felt bubbling inside of him when Relc and Klbkch had nearly executed him. When he’d been taken captive by Montressa’s team. A dark, mirthless laughter bordering on hysteria. She flinched, and he walked off.
Laughing his head off until he cast [Invisibility]. He supposed, later, he should have reflected on that. Had a moment of conscience or doubt.
Instead, he just thought that it would have left a bad taste in his mouth, either way.
Cast [Sleep] first. He’d be more careful the second time.
He supposed he was going mad, then. Sinking deeper, but he didn’t hear the red class, if he had one. Just…
Silence.
That silence was an answer of its own. He murmured to himself as he continued his walk.
“Ah. So this is what it was like. When Perril Chandler became the Necromancer who destroyed Silvaria, the Kingdom of Paintings.”
He gazed down at his hands, flexing them.
“It doesn’t hurt at all. It’s too easy. I cannot feel myself falling. Just climbing a mountain I must carve out of their blood and flesh.”
Longing to breathe the air at the top, as if he could end the nightmare. He felt like a man in a dark sea, underwater, climbing the dark mountain of corpses he was building. Ever higher, that he might one day breach the surface and find a better world where he could be normal and happy, again.
Pisces turned back and stared at the city blaring alarms. His eyes shone in the darkness, and he feared they shone black and white. But all he said as he vanished was—
“I’m sorry, Erin. It appears you were wrong about me.”
 
——
 
Pisces didn’t sleep well that night. The sight of that Garuda chased him around, and he kept sitting up with things to tell her or say.
‘Did it ever occur to you that you should have been born in a world without being a slave?’
‘When they take off their mask, then you’ll see.’
‘You haven’t looked around at the others, you hypocritical—’
Stuff like that. Then he’d done some calculations. If you weren’t willing to kill the parents, you could put a hole through both knees. Though that might mean the children were without caregivers. How about one eye per person? And they were Stitch-folk, so any damage was healable…
How could she look him in the eye with that self-righteous fury? [Happy Slave]. Happy—was it a redline class? Delusion, like that [Guard] who’d thought all the [Slaves] were smiling at him?
Toss, turn. Toss—he was glad when he realized the 7th caravan had appeared.
They were making a break for it. Away from the city. They must have been hiding however long it had been. How much food did they have? Days? Not for weeks unless they’d overbought for whatever reason.
Time or desperation had forced their hands. Pisces sat bolt upright; he sensed eight open wagons racing northwards. He leapt up. Jumped in the saddle as the undead stirred.
Rode.
 
——
 
The undead were out of position, and the wagons were moving fast. He had to slow them down, so Pisces cast the one spell he could.
“[Stone Stalagmite]!”
The Tier 2 version of [Earthen Spire] wasn’t powerful. Nor was Pisces a good [Geomancer]; the piece of stone rose fast enough to hit you hard in the groin, and it was pointy-ish. But the resultant piece of stone was hard.
Hard enough to hit a wagon wheel and shatter the axle. Two of the eight wagons slammed into the ones already skidding out of line, and the frantic [Guards] leapt down to try to replace the wheel.
Sadly, even without the locking nut that made Izrilian wagons more secure—most other continents didn’t have screws—changing a wagon wheel was hard enough in the dark.
Harder still with a [Necromancer] firing [Deathbolts] at you and Ghouls leaping down from a ridge. Twenty Ghouls versus maybe twice that number? A bit more?
He might win with the Ghouls alone. But Pisces didn’t like the ambush; he felt like there was some powerful magic around him, but he couldn’t locate it. So he [Flash Stepped] away, went invisible and silent, and waited.
The [Caravan Master] soon proved his instincts to be accurate. The man emerged, waving a Wand of [Fireballs], and Pisces saw a [Lightning Bolt] from another [Guard].
Wand spells. He grunted as the Ghouls went down. Now the wagons were being frantically repaired, but here came…
“U-undead! More of them! Dead gods! Lailight Scintillation, protect us!”
The [Slave Guards] were waving at the air, screaming, perhaps under [Scrying] spells? Pisces hoped his personal protections shorted it out. He sat up, taking aim with his death-mana laser as the leader fired [Fireballs] frantically at the incoming horde. The Skeleton Champions dodged, but zombies were going down. Pisces murmured.
“[Death—]”
Then he felt the mana around him surge and looked up. He saw lightning and dove.
The Djinni came to earth riding a real lightning bolt. He had the head of a cat, the body Human, bronzed skin crackling with magic, and his lower half was that of a cloud that turned into a glowing nimbus of blue particles sparkling with magic.
He was bare-chested, naked, in his way, save for a pair of golden spectacles on his face with a link of metal looped around one ear. He had more magic in him than any being Pisces had met save for the most dangerous of monsters or people like Larracel.
More magic than Azam’du.
The impact knocked Pisces sprawling. Seemutor cursed as he arose, and he drew six scimitars with six arms.
“Scourge of Roshal, your hour comes for you are marked. I am Seemutor, who has battled the King of Destruction and Orjin of Pomle! As my previous master, the Greatly Foolish Merchant Almon bids, who was sold into servitude and now is in chains alongside me—all enemies of Roshal shall die.”
His address was long, carrying, and he stretched his body upwards, growing until he was eight feet tall. Then he stretched his back out like a cat, yawned—
“Djinni, kill the undead!”
The [Slave Master] was howling at him. Seemutor glanced down at the embattled caravan, which was outnumbered by the undead.
“My task is to kill the assailant, not protect you. As so—”
He pointed, and Pisces realized the Djinni could see him. The [Invisibility] spell did noth—
The lightning bolt was fast, and Pisces had no idea how to handle it. He had never learned barrier spells like Ceria and Montressa had. He could have used Ksmvr’s Forceshield…
Pisces ducked down behind the dune he’d been crouching behind, and the impact kicked him backwards and onto his feet, but aside from the ringing in his ears and feeling that the air had punched him all over, the lightning didn’t do much. He scuttled away as Seemutor laughed.
“A fine trick. And now, mine. This is real lightning, not your [Mage]’s kind!”
He began arcing lightning bolts, firing them from his scimitars over the hill. They would have blown Pisces to bits—if he were anywhere near there.
He’d already [Flash Stepped] away, and Seemutor tried to follow him, frowning. A bolt of lightning passed in front of Pisces, and the [Necromancer] halted.
Seemutor’s aim was as good as Pisces’. Which was to say, he had trouble aiming at range too. Thinking of that, Pisces pointed.
He shot a ray of death-magic at Seemutor, straight at the Djinni’s chest.
[Deathbolt]—!
Before he even cast it, he saw Seemutor twist around nimbly at the waist, dodging the—Pisces never fired the spell. The Djinni recovered, fired four lightning bolts at Pisces—the [Necromancer] was running again.
Into the center of the fighting with the [Slavers] and undead. He leapt towards the wagons, the only place where Seemutor couldn’t hit him.
Because of the [Slavers]. Seemutor laughed and rose upwards.
“Ah, adventurers. The cunning of rats, and the pride of Crelers! Bravi, bravi, avventurieri! It saves you naught.”
Then he swept down with scimitars raised, firing lightning at the undead before beheading the first Skeleton Champion with a sweep of four of his blades.
 
——
 
Monster.
Pisces had encountered many foes. Horrifying ones he wasn’t sure he could hurt like Tolveilouka, the horde of Crelers who might kill in moments, the overwhelming might of Gazi when he’d been low-level, Bograms who was invisible, lurking—
Djinni were the most adaptive foe he’d ever met. For one thing?
Seemutor flew. There was no getting around that single dreadful aspect. He was fast, hard to hit in the air, and able to attack in more dimensions than Pisces was familiar with. It reminded him of Valeterisa. Or worse, Amerys.
The Djinni lounged on the air, pretending to rest on a cloud he conjured as he hurled down lightning bolts that blew apart undead. He was only pretending to be so relaxed; when a Skeleton Champion rolled out of the undead to aim a bow up at him, he came down and slashed the champion to bits.
“Djinni, stop playing around and save us! The Guild commands it!”
The [Slave Master] with the Wand of [Fireballs] was screaming, firing at the undead and even hitting his own [Guards]. The Slaver’s Guild must have given him the artifact; he was blowing through charges.
And Pisces’ horde. The [Necromancer] was mixing with his undead, sweating as he tried to think. Ambush! Fool, fool—
His saving grace was that there weren’t many [Slavers], and but for the two artifacts, they would have been slaughtered by his undead. However, the two armed with magical wands had to die if Pisces wanted backup against the Djinni. He knew the Djinni was waiting for him, though; Seemutor flew back upwards and, again, stretched like a cat. He had cat’s paws, now, and a feline coat of black fur he licked with a long tongue. Slitted pupils roaming…
He kept watching the [Caravan Master] with the Wand of [Fireballs]. He knew Pisces had to go for the man. As luck had it, though—the problem solved itself. The screaming [Slave Master] was firing [Fireballs] at the zombies.
“Die, die, all of you! [Fireball], [Fireball], [Fireb—]”
His wand had been glowing red-hot, actually smoking as the ruby tip cast the powerful spell over and over. It had been made for that one purpose, charged up with magic, but Pisces saw the wand glow brighter, brighter—
Then the [Fireball] detonated inside the wand. Seemutor winced and clapped a hand to his forehead.
“Fools.”
That…took out a chunk of the defenders. But the one with the [Lightning Bolt] wand was still firing and targeting the Skeleton Champions. Pisces cursed, aimed—fired.
He took the woman out with a single spell; she turned grey, waxy, toppled over. She wasn’t dead, but one of the zombies grabbed her, and that was that. Seemutor saw, though.
“There you are.”
He came down, and the undead vanished around the Djinni as he threw a lightning bolt, landed in the impact, and swept around.
Six arms, whirling blades, each one slashing with grace and form—nothing.
The Djinni had diced the zombies, but when he swung around, his eyes narrowed.
Where is that [Necromancer]—?
The [Shatterbolt] hit one of Seemutor’s scimitars as he blocked it, and he cried out in mortal pain as it exploded. He turned, leapt, and slashed—
The Skeleton Champion grinned at Seemutor as the Djinni cut it to ribbons. The Djinni’s eyes widened, and he spun—but no attack came from his back.
Gone, again. He flew upwards, cursing. He did not remake the shattered blade but just pointed a finger crackling with lightning.
“I sense you, little mage. Where are you?”
He stared down, then grinned. Below, Pisces cursed. He’d been sneaking through the undead, but now—
 
——
 
Impact. He bounced off a wagon, gasped, and grabbed the lip of the roof. Heaved himself backwards and over on top of it with strength and dexterity he didn’t know he had.
[Manacharged Reflexes].
Seemutor blew apart the wagon’s walls. He aimed up—the [Barrier of Light] absorbed a lightning bolt and blew up. Pisces was already flying downwards.
He could not engage this Djinni in a spellcasting duel! Nor hide! How was he seeing Pisces, even amongst the undead?
Djinni were made of magic, Azam had said. If anyone could see Pisces’ magical signature…
The battle with the [Slavers] was going Pisces’ way. The [Slavers] were trying to drive the wagons northwards, and annoyed, Seemutor boomed.
“Stand and fight, worthless wretches!”
He scythed the zombies down from the waist, targeting Skeleton Champions. A few could block one lightning bolt or survive a single shot—but they were glowing ash in seconds. The Bone Horror charged Seemutor next. He grabbed it, four hands grappling with it as it clawed, bit, gouged at his body…
It didn’t do any damage. The Bone Horror was scraping at—at—a cloud. Seemutor’s flesh just vanished under it, and the dismayed undead realized the laughing Djinni was ripping it apart.
Pisces took the opening and emerged out of cover.
“[Fireball]!”
He fired one of the two spells he’d prepped at Seemutor. The Djinni spun and began to twirl away from the Bone Horror, letting the fireball flash past him—
It blew up in midair, and the Djinni staggered.
“Hm.”
That…had been Pisces’ hope, that if he burst it in midair the shockwave would at least hurt—the Djinni raised his fingers, pointed.
Five lightning bolts hit a [Bone Wall] and exploded. Seemutor hesitated. Took aim again.
The second volley blew up on impact too, and Pisces was running up a dome. Seemutor hummed.
Then he fired two lightning bolts from his left hands, three from the other. The last one was scratching at his side.
The first volley blew apart the [Bone Wall] that Pisces had conjured a third time. The other three hit the second [Bone Wall], which was thin, paper-thick—but caused the magic to detonate.
“Nice trick, [Mage]. But you’ve run out of undead.”
So saying, Seemutor swept around and began slashing the last undead to pieces. He dispatched the final Skeleton Champions with flourishes of his blades, but only used two of them—his other four hands were making finger guns.
Waiting.
