Seemutor was disappointed that the [Necromancer] didn’t rise to the bait. Still, he’d sacrificed all of his minions for that, and that was a [Necromancer]’s strength. The last of the powerful undead fell, and he dismissed the zombies as threatless; he floated past them, swinging his swords carelessly.
They couldn’t harm his body, not with their clawing hands. Now, Seemutor rose once more and saw the wagons of Roshal fleeing towards the city.
Their little distraction was done; the Slaver’s Guild had sprung its trap, and Seemutor, the agent of their rage, had his foe. He had marked the ways in which the one called ‘Scourge of Roshal’ could hurt him and was disappointed.
Orjin of Pomle had been more martially powerful, if limited. The King of Destruction and his vassals far more fearsome. This was just a middling adventurer, a nemesis to other small, low-level foes. Not to a Djinni of Seemutor’s caliber, and he was far from Drenirkessun.
Ah, Seemutor wearied of this battle already, for all it might be that of fame. What did he care for fame? If anything, he was slightly bitter to rid Roshal of another of its foes, even one undeserving of his reputation.
He peered around, his cat eyes focusing, hunting down the magic cast through the battle. The [Necromancer] used [Invisibility], as he had been told.
“That does not work on me.”
He’d dive and take the Human out in close-quarters combat. Seemutor’s ability to manipulate magic was actually fairly limited; there were others of his kin who could do far more than throwing parts of their body out like lightning. But in hand-to-hand combat, he was very experienced. The man could not outrun him. So…
…Where was he?
At first, Seemutor thought he’d just missed the [Necromancer] from his altitude, but then he realized he couldn’t spot…
But that was impossible. He could see [Invisibility] spells, which were just another form of magic, like a cloud. Yet the [Necromancer] was well and truly—
Dead? No, his corpse would be—
Seemutor began to fly closer to the ground. He swept left and right, staring around. But how? He searched for life magic, the energy of all beings. Then death magic, and saw plenty in the remaining zombies, the broken bones. But no vast signature like he’d identified in Pisces.
Then he remembered an old trick he’d heard [Necromancers] had used. One of the Djinni he’d served with in the Great Desert had once said—
He twisted around when he felt the death magic too late. Pisces nailed the Djinni in the chest with two [Deathbolts] and emerged out of the sand, rapier drawn. And Seemutor paused—
Then he laughed.
 
——
 
Pisces had hoped to hide, but he’d seen Seemutor start glancing his way. So he’d done it. He’d fired both [Deathbolts] dead on, without the deathmagic laser. He’d noticed Seemutor had been able to see even that.
Which meant that he’d probably used the same trick as everyone else. Seeing magic. Pisces’ ability to equalize magic had let him hide and land the first major spell of the battle. Two, straight through the Djinni’s chest.
The fur on Seemutor’s chest rippled and went dead white, as if scarred by the spells. His cloud-like lower half also paled, like someone had injected pale white in the whirling cloud. The Djinni did not stagger. He didn’t appear pained, just surprised.
Then he laughed.
“Ah, [Necromancer]. It would work on the living, empower the dead. I am more of a mystery than both. Now die.”
He swept at Pisces, swords drawn, and Pisces backstepped. The swords cleaved through the air, and Pisces saw them cross where he had been standing.
No way to parry that. Seemutor’s five arms were—Pisces saw the sixth hand pointing.
[Barrier of Light]. The explosion of lightning was blinding. He rocked backwards—
Three blades coming at him through the explosion! Pisces jumped.
[High Jump]. The blow carried him over the Djinni’s head. He slashed as he landed—his blade cut across Seemutor’s face and did…nothing.
Even the contact felt like cutting a hard sponge. The Djinni twisted, rueful.
“Sloppy, I’ve become. Now, [Mage]—”
He lunged, four blades spearing forwards, the last sweeping around. Pisces shouted.
“[Flash Parry]! [Joveln’s Parry]!”
He parried both the lunge and other blade, flicking his rapier up as his hand rang. The Djinni was grinning as he pointed that sixth finger at Pisces, charging up—and Pisces activated the [Bound Spell] in his rapier.
The Djinni’s eyes widened, and the [Light Spear] slashed outwards, into his chest. He howled, then. A cat’s howl which became roaring, echoing, and he sprang away, clutching at—
Steam? His chest was radiating crazy magic, and Pisces saw a hole had appeared there. Seemutor hissed.
“You—”
Pisces fired [Flame Swathe] from one hand, then [Ice Dart] from the tip of his rapier. Seemutor dodged both with ease. He closed on Pisces, four handed; two were holding his chest, swinging. Pisces ducked a slash, blocked another—the blow tossed him across the ground. Seemutor dropped a rapier, grabbed—
Pisces fired a [Deathbolt] three times into Seemutor’s chest and grabbed the glowing essence as Seemutor’s hand closed around his arm with crushing strength. A scimitar froze, glittering, above Pisces’ head as the [Necromancer] held his rapier up.
Both men froze. Seemutor was panting, steam still rising, and Pisces was gasping for air. He saw the white stain coating Seemutor’s fur, shifting particles, and Seemutor breathed.
“I have you, [Necromancer]. Submit and be bound by Roshal and I will not destroy you.”
“I have you, Djinni. Strike me and I’ll unleash all the mana I have left.”
A laugh. Seemutor’s eyes flicked around, but the zombies had collapsed; Pisces had pulled the death mana from them. He was filled with magic.
“You could hit me a thousand times with [Deathbolt] and nary trouble me.”
Pisces bared his teeth.
“Then I’ll cast [Light Nova].”
Then Seemutor’s smile vanished, and Pisces confirmed the theory he’d been working on in the fight. They stood there, gripping each other, and Pisces stared at the glittering scimitar. It was beautifully ornate, steel etched with decorative inlays. Impractical, perhaps, too gaudy. It looked to have golden hilts; a show-weapon.
…If it were even real. He nodded at it.
“My [Shatterbolt] destroyed that blade. But that’s just part of your body. Djinni fight with what they are in most cases. You couldn’t resist that.”
“You dropped your ring. Want it back?”
Seemutor had it in one of his hands. He dangled it casually, but Pisces didn’t glance away from the Djinni’s smiling face. The Djinni was all projected confidence, but he’d halted.
Why? Well, Pisces nodded at it.
“If it had more magic, perhaps I could hurt you that way. It’s a Tier 5 spell.”
“Tier 4. It’s simply…made well. By a better [Mage] from a better era. You have no magic even close to it.”
Pisces smiled.
“But I hurt you.”
“Not with [Deathbolt], and you lack for another spell as strong.”
“I did hurt you, Seemutor the Djinni. Not from [Deathbolt] alone, it’s true. But when I used [Light Spear], you took damage. Your fur’s gone white.”
Seemutor’s face was blank as he casually shifted, and he was imposingly huge. No smell of sweat, though, no sense of a body radiating heat. If anything, cool air seemed to come from him along with the faint feel of static electricity. A being of magic. Pisces glanced at the white stain in his body.
Was it shrinking? Ever so slightly, perhaps. He pushed more death magic into his hands, and Seemutor’s grip tightened on his shoulder, but Pisces glanced up. Now he was certain.
“Djinni are beings of magic. You live off of it. Generate it. Your bodies become what you desire—within limits. Each Djinni has an element, or so I read. Multiple ones, it’s true, but there must be limits to what you can absorb. You cannot absorb two conflicting types. If I hit you with light magic now, you’ll die.”
For answer, the Djinni exhaled with a huge sigh and relaxed his grip a bit.
“Wrong. I’ll be wounded, perhaps sorely, but I won’t die. And you will be dead.”
“Then why haven’t you killed me?”
“Perhaps I don’t wish to ruin my health for my master’s benefit.”
“Then we’re stalemated.”
Pisces concluded. They were locked together, and if he cast magic, Seemutor would take a lot of damage. Potentially die if he was bluffing how tough he was—but Pisces wouldn’t survive Seemutor’s counterattack.
The Djinni grinned, baring his teeth.
“Well then, shall we agree to a draw? I swear upon my honor and name, Seemutor the Bespectacled, the Wisdom of Sage’s Clouds, that I shall allow you safe passage if you do the same.”
Pisces blinked up at him, then frowned.
“What good is your word? You told me you have orders from Roshal. You’re a [Slave]; you’ve been ordered to kill me.”
The Djinni puffed up his chest, and Pisces dug his fingers warningly into his flesh. Seemutor relaxed, but he gave Pisces an arch look.
“Am I not a Djinni? My word is my bond.”
“That is, I believe, a common myth. You are not bound by any magic unless it comes from your container, and most were not given such safeguards. Anyone would be wise to trust your word only after enforcement magic is activated.”
This time, the cat-Djinni lost his proud expression and eyed Pisces sourly.
“Fancied yourself a Djinni, did you, [Necromancer]?”
Pisces shifted, glancing around for something, anything. But the ruined stretch of road was deserted. It was night.
He was in trouble, but he kept talking.
“No, I did my research for a friend who wanted to know about Djinni and her preconceptions of them. Then out of my own curiosity. I have met your kind before.”
“Everyone born on Chandrar has met my kind.”
Seemutor rolled his eyes, and Pisces saw two of his hands fold behind his head. One kept hold of Pisces, another holding the scimitar casually. Pisces spoke warningly.
“Hands where I can see them. I met one of your kind when I was a [Slave]. Azam’du. And Czautha’qshe, the Death of Chains.”
For the first time, Seemutor seemed to actually perk up and pay attention to Pisces. He lost the bored expression he’d been wearing and slowly, slowly lifted his hands. Each paw was holding an orb of a different color. Magic. It vanished as he opened his paws, then his four additional arms vanished.
“…Now that’s interesting. You aren’t lying, are you, little [Necromancer]? For I’d owe you a truly unpleasant death if you were. No…mine eyes see magic, and yours doesn’t waver. Did I hear…? Let’s speak then, in earnestness, for a moment.”
They stood in the cold desert as Pisces shivered. After a pause, he felt Seemutor’s fur under him warm, and the chill ended. He blinked as Seemutor’s fur turned orange from within his body, like there was a light inside him, and the Djinni grinned like a mischievous cat.
Pisces almost smiled, but never let go of the Djinni. They had nothing else to do. So they stood and talked a while.
 
——
 
“I do not follow the lives of adventurers. Nor do most of my kindred. Scourge, they called you, and I laughed for I thought it a joke. They were so serious. You are no Scourge, Adventurer Pisces.”
After some clarification, Seemutor was pleasant, if not actually friendly. But for the standoff, Pisces suspected they’d kill each other in a heartbeat. He kept putting death magic into Seemutor, preventing the Djinni from absorbing the already present mana. Seemutor didn’t mention that, but his eyes twinkled.
Dangerous indeed. He was everything Pisces had imagined when he’d read of Djinni. Clever, elegant liars by omission, and magically powerful. But the Djinni was also, well, convivial.
Especially when he heard Pisces had not only met another Djinni but been saved by Czautha.
“Truly? Truly, you saw her? Our sister who broke all chains? Prove it. How did she come?”
“By…rainbow?”
“Ach, anyone would know that. How else?”
“With Silvenia, the Death of Magic? She was a falling comet, and she claimed she only had a moment before she could leave. She freed as many Djinni as she could before attacking Lailight Scintillation.”
Seemutor rotated his neck around in amazing displays that would have broken even a cat’s neck. He screwed up his face.
“Ah, but anyone could claim that. You have it right, but if you had done any research…nor do I know Azam’du. He sounds young. Weaker than I.”
“He was, apparently. Still frighteningly powerful.”
“How many centuries?”
“I don’t know.  He was born in captivity. A few?”
Seemutor’s face fell, and his whiskers drooped.
“Hm. Being born in captivity means nothing; we have been captive for ages. But mere centuries old? So young. A rarity. This is not proof, nor did you meet them recently enough that I can sense their magic on you. Did they say any word that would make me know it was her? Likely not.”
Pisces wasn’t sure how to vouchsafe his bona fides to Seemutor, but he felt like this was his only chance, even if the Djinni had orders to kill. He thought, then spoke.
“My bag of holding, on my right side, had something Czautha thought to take back with her. But she didn’t, because she said I might need it. It’s a spellbook written by a Djinni. Can you see it?”
The Djinni blinked, then laughed.
“Hah! A good one. There are no such things written by my kin that—buried kingdoms, it is a spellbook!”
He stared at Pisces’ bag of holding and did a double-take. Then he seemed to believe, and his eyes rose slowly.
“Your chest. Is that the brand of your master?”
“Former master. He’s dead, and I’m no longer a [Slave].”
Pisces felt Igheriz’s brand on his skin, and the Djinni nodded. Then he smiled, once.
“Congratulations on your freedom, Adventurer. You have won what Czautha’qshe fights for and what all we Djinni dream of.”
The [Necromancer] began to smile back, and then Seemutor lost his smile, leaned in, and whispered.
“You should have never come back to Chandrar and stayed free. What possessed you?”
For answer, Pisces sighed.
“I left my friends here.”
He thought it needed explanation, the long story of the Horns and all the coincidences along the way, but Seemutor gazed at him, and his cat-ears dropped. He closed his eyes, and his touch became light as a feather.
“Oh. The trap of all Djinni. I am guilty of this, truly. The King of Destruction was easier than this. Orjin of Pomle was amusing. I wish I had not met you, [Necromancer] who knows my chains. You are a dead man, now.”
Infinite regrets were in his eyes when they opened, but he did not let go of Pisces. And now the [Necromancer] was staring across the horizon. Towards the city. He knew…
He was running out of time.
 
——
 
Seemutor did not desire this man’s death anymore. He never had, insofar as he had any choice. But he had orders.
The orders were not to risk his life, so he had taken this stalemate to spite his masters as he always did, but also out of pragmatism. The damage this man might cause to him in close-quarters was immense.
Plus, [Necromancers] always came back from the dead when slain, and grappling with a Skeleton Mage or worse was not appealing.
Now that he knew Czautha’qshe had freed this boy, it made it all the harder. But Seemutor was a slave, and so he just stood there.
All he had to do was hold Pisces Jealnet. Because the Guild did not bet its victory on just the Djinni. Seemutor was only the quick-response force assigned to odd jobs the Guild needed. There were other killers.
This was a dead man, but Seemutor still humored him. He owed one freed this little courtesy. All the while, though, he knew a force was coming to slay the [Necromancer], and when they arrived, Seemutor would join them.
Kinder to kill him than collar him, though. The Djinni would do that. Thus, he spoke, wishing the conversation were not so…amusing.
“So, you came by a Djinni’s spellbook, rarest of the rare, when raiding the tomb of one of the greatest [Necromancers] in existence to save a friend who came back from the dead.”
“Yes. Erin Solstice. Surely you’ve heard of her?”
Again, Seemutor threw his head back and laughed. He emoted grandly, but the [Necromancer] never lost his grip or stopped paying attention. Too clever. This was a dance, so Seemutor began to insult him, to see if the mortal had a temper to play on. He threw his head back and spoke honestly his contempt for this woman…whose name stuck in his mind.
“Pisces, adventurer. I have said it again and again: we do not pay attention! Some of my kin did not even know this King of Destruction except as a random king they had served until they heard of Drenirkessun being freed by him. Masters come and go, and we are old—wait, Erin Solstice? HER?”
His attempt at arrogant disregard fell to pieces in a moment when that name hit him in a heartbeat. It could not be. But of all the mortals Seemutor knew, and he knew so few—
Her? Seemutor remembered her, belatedly! He had met the woman who claimed to have met one of the great Djinni in death itself!
“You met her?”
It was Pisces’ turn to be shocked, and in that moment when he wavered, there might have been the scorpion’s chance to strike. But it was a risk, and Seemutor himself was so caught by this that he held still. Remembering his superior nature, he feigned indifference.
“I…yes. Some mortals do stick in the memory, and I had cause to meet her, in person. But it is a coincidence, my point remains. To ask a Djinni any mortal’s name, even one who was legend in their time, is pointless. Like as to ask what Nerrhavia’s true name was.”
That was another lie, actually. Some Djinni knew the true name of the Immortal Tyrant, but they feared to say it, even now. Seemutor omitted the part where he had told every Djinni he’d met about his encounter with the mysterious young woman who’d encountered a ghost of his people. It was a weakness, and he did not want to give the man he was about to kill any opening.
Pisces ducked his head slowly.
“I apologize. It must be a banal question. I am glad that you have met Erin, though. Of all mortals, hers is a name to remember, if I may offer that opinion.”
He was courtly enough, so Seemutor grew embarrassed, and his body developed a slight chill as his mana changed. He was the being of age, for all he was young and not like his greater cousins. So he shrugged.
“Eh. Que sera, sera. It is not your fault you have the same question as so many before you. The mountain should not rage at the chipmunk which digs the same holes again and again, just smile at the forests it plants.”
He quoted a Giant’s saying, and the [Necromancer]’s eyes brightened.
“That’s…a quote from Atvecius, the last of the Giant Kings. That other phrase. What does ‘que sera, sera’ mean? I think I’ve heard it.”
Two surprises. But Seemutor grinned with his cat’s sharp teeth. He liked cats, which is why he took this form.
“You have some knowledge, but you have never heard such language as that. It is more dead than the Mage’s Language. The kind of thing only Djinni carry. And Giants, I suppose.”
“You shouted something at me. ‘Bravi?’ It sounded like ‘adventurer’—”
“You noticed that? Yes, I learned it from a Djinni over twenty thousand years old, who had it from another—these are phrases. Quotes. So, you see, unless Czautha’qshe said that to you, you do not know ‘que sera, sera’. And even she would have been taught it, just as I was.”
He was quite tickled by the thought she used the same phrase he had learned, but Pisces tilted his head. Closed his eyes in an unguarded moment.
“No…I think I’ve heard her saying it. ‘What will be, will be.’ Is it a song?”
Seemutor nearly lost his grip on Pisces. The shock—
“How do you know that?”
For answer, Pisces just smirked up at Seemutor and then sneezed as he got some of the Djinni’s essence in his body.
“That’s from—achoo—a being of great mystery whom I was acquainted with. Erin Solstice.”
Twice, now, Seemutor was struck silent in conversation. A rarity. She knew one of the lost languages from before the First Goblin King’s rampage? He saw the [Necromancer]’s eyes brighten and feared this conversation was giving him strength.
Time to end this. Yet his biding of time was to a point, so the Djinni weighed his options. Which gave Pisces the chance to hit the Djinni with his final attack.
“I did not, in fact, hear Czautha say ‘que sera, sera’ either time I met her.”
“…You met her twice?”
“In a location I cannot disclose, a grand Skill where we encountered each other—very briefly. My team fled, but I saw her, the Death of Magic, and the Death of Wings.”
Pisces shivered, and Seemutor stared at him, wishing he could read the [Mage]’s aura perfectly because this had to be madness. But he was an adventurer, and the Death of Magic could go anywhere if she were truly healed…the words came out of him too fast, a rush.
“How did she look? Was she healthy? Happy? Have her wounds healed?”
He had to know. Pisces blinked and didn’t know—Seemutor pressed, asking about the color of Czautha’s magic, the elements in her body.
“I don’t…she was under a kind of illusion that let her appear like a different species. She appeared decent? Better than the Death of Magic.”
Seemutor let out a huge breath, and then he had something else to blab about to every Djinni, young or old.
“You do me a service, then, Necromancer. I shall remember it, even if I am bound to your death like an arrow. I regret it, now. But know that even this gives all her kin hope. She is our dream, young though she is. Barely older than I.”
“Young?”
That surprised Pisces, and Seemutor tossed his head, nodding prouder still.
“She was born after the Creler Wars. It is rare for a Djinni of her caliber to ever be created, let alone in these eras as Djinni die. That she freed herself, and has not stopped her war, makes her the greatest of our people, to me. I am younger than she by a thousand years, give or take.”
“So you are five thousand years old?”
Seemutor grew embarrassed at how astonished Pisces sounded.
“But five thousand and some, yes. I am young.”
Very young by some Djinni’s standards. It impressed Pisces to no end, though.
“I knew Djinni were old. But how can one live so long…?”
“Because we are bred, when they can. Because we are so valuable we are not wasted. And because we used to dot all of Chandrar, and the last of us are a dying breed.”
Seemutor rumbled with a sigh. Pisces licked his lips.
“Then you remember the end of the Creler Wars. All these ancient nations—”
Then Seemutor grew grumpy again. He shifted, mustering more power to his hands. He was a proud Djinni; he refused to be humiliated, either in combat or wordplay. He fancied himself a scholar, more intelligent than any short-lived being, but even a scholar grew tired of hearing the same question a million times. He’d once counted and it was over a million by now.
“Aye, perhaps. What of it? Would you want me to furnish you with stories? Even when I was young, I learned not to care who held my lamp. Kingdoms rose, and kingdoms fell. Have you a Djinni, you would do well to ask them another question than that.”
Pisces blinked at Seemutor, then nodded.
“Tell me how you met, Erin, then. I care more about that.”
This was…fair. So, Seemutor had to relate the encounter that had seen him fighting Orjin of Pomle. Erin Solstice had tried to save the [Martial Artist] and failed, but the conversation had made him speak of her to other Djinni.
But he hadn’t put that together with other modern events; Djinni didn’t watch the scrying orbs much. Maybe they should, because Pisces pointed out that there was only one woman who’d come back from the dead of late. Seemutor scoffed.
“Bah, that is a common thing amongst you mortals. You die, get to come back—I would have put good money on there being at least two at any given time. Had I money. Well, well. So you came to Chandrar for her. There are worse beings to put your life behind. But again: you have erred. Roshal is not a foe that the Death of Chains can stand against in open battle. What made you think you could do this?”
Pisces was staring across the desert.
“Madness. I know it was a fool’s errand, but I had to try.”
Ah, Seemutor wished those words could inspire his soul. If he were thousands years younger, he might have conceived of a great affection for this man of principle. Instead, he just felt a vague sadness, even a hint of contempt for the foolishness.
“Because you know two beings I hold in some esteem, a rarity in any age, I shall speak to you with a Djinni’s kindness. It is thought to be a joke, but now listen, Pisces Jealnet.”
The [Necromancer] glanced at him suspiciously, but in this, Seemutor was honest. He spoke quickly.
“If, by some unimaginable miracle, you should survive the next hour, flee this continent. For I am but one weapon, and Roshal shall hurl them until the continent cracks. That is how their authority is maintained. They cannot let a single challenge exist. And next time shall not be a falling Djinni, but a blade in the dark. I am mighty, but far from the most dangerous of my kind. Enough to hunt rebels—they shall send a true Face of the Assassin’s Guild after you.”
Pisces exhaled.
“So noted. But I have heard others claiming my name. I know my friends are alive. So it doesn’t follow that rebellion is instant death—”
“They are [Rebels] with Skills designed to be free. You are known. Roshal can tolerate the nibbling of flies, but not you, who stand openly against them. You will die.”
Now, the Djinni was angry. His voice was flat.
“You cannot best me. Nor, from your story, could you triumph against Azam’du. You have no right to call yourself Scourge of Roshal if you cannot even slay us.”
Pisces head bowed.
“I know that. I know it, and I never wanted that title. But I had…to try. This continent is strange to me, and we are fumbling around in Nerrhavia’s Fallen. I have a friend who knows this place, but I can’t fully trust him. I want to, but—”
His teeth ground together, and Seemutor spoke.
“Ah, if you are the guests of the [Queen], then you would be better served leaving twice quick. Nerrhavia’s Fallen is not so strong as it appears. Unwise wars. The Oresect plague. And the Hemp are gathering. As they do. They are usually torn to pieces, but perhaps this time, it will be different. Or are you blind to all that?”
Pisces eyed Seemutor.
“I—had noticed some hints. By organizing, do you mean rebelling?”
“What are [Slaves] by a different name to do? Not that they think of themselves wholly as such. Roshal has sold [Slaves] to them; in this way, no matter which cloth reigns, they win. But I am the Djinni sent to spy, deliver, and go about many tasks. I care nothing for great events, but I do observe empires falling with amusement.”
It was a hobby for him to guess which year they’d implode. Pisces nodded slowly and glanced over Seemutor’s shoulder.
The sun was rising. And the Djinni felt [Message] spells buzzing in his essence. The Guild was coming. The [Necromancer] seemed to know it too, for their truce was ending. Both were regarding the other, waiting for a chink in their poise.
If I simply get clear, I will not be caught by that magic again. If he sneezes—
Seemutor had a cunning idea. So he gave Pisces a sultry smile and shapechanged. The [Necromancer] had hold of Seemutor’s chest and blinked. He was suddenly holding an ample bosom as Seemutor took on the appearance of a female cat-lady. Pisces turned so red he might have been a Djinni—
He didn’t let go. But Seemutor was grinning. She leaned forwards.
“You are a funny one. Enough to make my kindred laugh. Some would weep and cheer you just for what you represent, doomed as you are. Not I. You are a dead man, blushing [Necromancer]. Your one hope was your undead. But those Skeleton Champions, that Bone Horror, could not slay me, only delay. You do not know how to fight Djinni.”
Her body was absorbing the death mana faster and faster now. She had finally configured her essence to absorb it easily. The stain of white on her chest-fur was fading, and the [Necromancer] saw it.
He tried to pour more death-mana into Seemutor’s body, but it was now a futile gesture. The Djinni tensed. She was ready to strike until she heard him rasp.
“That’s true. I don’t know how to fight Djinni. I have never wanted to, before.”
The Djinni’s scimitar lifted, and her magical arm tensed.
Then Seemutor gazed into Pisces’ eyes and saw fear. A mortal man’s fear of death. Uncertainty. All the flaws of his nature.
But not despair. 
The hands gripping the Djinni suddenly felt…
Cold.
A kind of cold that Seemutor didn’t know. Startled, she changed back to her regular form. A thicker coat of fur growing over his chest. As if he were…
Cold? But he was a being of magic. He didn’t feel cold except from the most chilling of spells, and even that was a kind of magic. Not this.
It felt like growing numb. A shivering of the being. Loneliness made sensation. A dreadful pull.
It felt like…
Death.
Then the Djinni glanced down and saw the death magic the [Necromancer] had been infusing his body with pooling. It was…leaving Seemutor?
Concentrating in his hands. At first, it was just the intensity of two [Deathbolts]. Then it gathered. And it felt like a Tier 4 spell.
Then a Tier 5 spell.
All the power of a [Mage] of his level. Drawing together. Seemutor’s eyes rolled around. The zombies. The undead he had destroyed. All their mana—
It was right here. And now…the magic was becoming visible to even the naked eye. Still, Pisces held Seemutor, and the Djinni hesitated.
Swallowed. He had faced [Mages] across his thousands of years, casting all manner of spells. Their boxed magic they were so proud of.
Few…had ever cast magic that did not have a name, a meaning outlined in their classes. But this—
Who is this? 
 
——
 
The Djinni did not attack. Pisces had thought Seemutor might. But the ruse worked.
Djinni were beings of magic and susceptible to its fluctuations. When the stalemate had seemed to end, and he’d realized Seemutor had become immune to his death mana, Pisces had done the only thing he could think of: copy Lareceina.
He was concentrating all the death mana he could into his hands. He didn’t have a spell to channel it; he didn’t have a spell that could contain this mana. But it probably appeared dangerous.
A bluff.
He was blinking sweat out of his eyes as he gazed up at Seemutor.
“I do not want to kill you, Seemutor. Can you not pretend you are in danger and flee to your masters?”
“A good joke, [Necromancer].”
Seemutor had gone alarmingly still. Pisces thought he saw lights crossing the road in the distance. The Guild? He smiled up at the Djinni. He was afraid, but…
“You’re not my foe. Please…”
The Djinni was shifting, and now, Pisces saw bobbing torches. There were [Riders]. The sun had risen, he realized, and it played off Seemutor’s fur. The Djinni’s head turned, and he murmured.
“You cannot stand against both them and I.”
“Move and die.”
The Djinni appeared to hesitate, but he held his ground. Pisces was counting.
At least a hundred, all mounted. Roshal’s own guards? There was nothing he could do; the moment he moved, the Djinni and he would fight, and he could not outrun Seemutor. So Pisces did the only thing he could think of.
“Once more. One last time. You have never been my salvation, as many times as I begged for it. But just once—I need your help. So, please…arise.”
He poured some of the magic in his hands outwards, and Seemutor’s fur rose. Pisces felt the ground around him stir as he poured magic into it.
[Death’s Ground]. He let it flow to each broken corpse, charred bone, dead [Guards]—and then he saw it.
Rising as bones swirled around it, armor cut to ribbons by Seemutor’s blades, but grinning, that being he loved and hated.
A Skeleton Champion saluted Pisces as it arose, then another. Zombies rising upwards, save for the String-folk corpses. And if only he could animate cloth.
Maybe…
But all Pisces did was stand there, and Seemutor’s head turned. The undead gathered around Pisces, and walls of bone arose. Shields from arrows. Protection. A maze…
“Who taught you this magic, [Necromancer]? This is no spell of labyrinths.”
“I like architecture. I walked this place. My best friend is an ice mage. These are her walls. Do I need a spell for everything?”
They were such simple answers, but the Djinni blinked down his bespectacled face at Pisces. They stood together, waiting, as the [Slavers] shouted, and the Skeleton Champions’ jaws clattered. Pisces stood there.
Waiting.
 
——
 
Undead fought the living.
Outnumbered, defending a maze of bones as the ground itself turned dead. When they were slain, the magic animated them in seconds—but the undead did fall, and their bodies were hacked down, bones ground to dust.
The [Slavers] were coming. Pushing for the two figures who stood together. Waiting for someone to break their stalemate. They cursed Seemutor. Ordering him to battle, but his eyes were on the [Necromancer].
Waiting…waiting for the young man to look away. Pisces Jealnet refused to, even as arrows cracked on the wall between him and the attackers. He saw the Skeleton Champions falling back, fighting frantically to defend him. Dying…
The moment was coming. He was smiling, feeling his strength running out. He was holding the last of his magic tighter and tighter, compressing it down like Lareceina had shown him. He knew, now, Seemutor was a bit kind, as Djinni could be.
He was playing up the danger to give Pisces a few last moments. He acted well; he even appeared a bit afraid. But then the [Slavers] were staring at Pisces, separated by that wall of bone.
“Scourge, we have you. Come out and be shackled or die.”
One called, and Pisces whispered.
“You do have me. Give me one moment. I’ll see you shortly. But you will never put chains on me again. Not even my corpse.”
They shuddered as his head turned, and those pupils were glowing. Glowing a color no one here had ever seen but the Djinni, who held still.
The eyes of a [Necromancer]. It was then that Seemutor’s hands grasped a blade in each palm, and they would have been sweaty if they had any to give. For this was the kind of story Djinni told Djinni. They did tell stories, if the mortal was worthy enough.
This man who came so much by chance, connected to other beings that Seemutor had met…
Perhaps something favored him after all. For his hands glowed with a magic that made Seemutor’s essence shrink against it. And a fell wind was blowing, as if conjured by his words.
It blew hard across the [Slavers], who shielded their faces against the blasting sand. Crouched against their horses as the ones who had taken the maze of bone walls backed up. Backed out of the ivory-white walls, despite their leader’s cursing and their numbers.
The Scourge was coming out, and they waited for the Djinni to do its job. But it stood silent, and the wind blew harder until it was a howl. The sand was odd and clinging. Softer than one thought…one of the [Veteran Slave Takers] spat and cursed.
“Djinni, do your job! The [Necromancer] is at his weakest—finish this by blade or chain!”
He coughed as more sand got into his mouth, but it didn’t taste like the usual grit. He hacked, coughed, and swiped at the damn powdery…white stuff?
The [Slave Taker] blinked at the odd material on one glove. Finer than even sand grains. He rubbed his fingers and a few other [Slavers] turned. That wasn’t sand. It looked like…
“Flour?”
Then he heard a ringing—his [Dangersense]. But it had rung the moment they’d approached the [Necromancer]. This was a second bell, though. Loud and urgent. The [Slave Taker] whirled.
“Flour? It’s a storm. Take c—”
He threw himself down as he saw the storm whirling around them—and it should have been a clear day—blowing harder. As if someone had called it. Powder in the air, so fine it was choking everyone. A storm of particles. And then—blooming in the storm, ignited, spreading as the dust itself caught—
Fire.
 
——
 
The explosion blew up the flour dust and didn’t kill as much as you thought. Dust explosions were a known phenomenon around grain silos, and flour was a good combustible.
Against [Warriors], in the open, it couldn’t kill them. Deafen? Absolutely. Knock flat, disorient, burn, and concuss?
Not kill—which was why the shrieking [Bandits] came down on the [Slavers] mere seconds later, riding through the smoke with practice. They stabbed down with long spears, leapt off their saddles to impale the [Slavers].
The band was only eighty-strong. But they rode and fought like their namesake, who led the charge in with an enchanted sword raised high.
Merr the Storm, one of the [Bandit Ladies] of Chandrar. She was howling.
“Don’t let a single one leave alive! Pisces! Pisces, m’boy, you’d better be alive or I’ll kill you twice!”
She was racing around, swearing, heart pounding. Was she too late? They’d ridden hell-for-leather the moment they’d heard about the attacks and realized it wasn’t…
The madness of it. She saw bones scattered everywhere. The glowing flames in a skeleton’s head going out. Then—she heard a boom. Laughter.
Bones exploded as a Djinni burst upwards, shattering a dome made out of ivory. Merr swore, and there were screams.
“Oh shit, Djinni, Djinni—we have to run!”
“Belay that, hold! We have to get—”
They were all damned dead if that thing was powerful. Merr had an enchanted blade, but Djinni were not something anyone fought—she was looking around. If he was dead, then…
Her storm was dying down, but her eyes could pierce past the dust and wind as if it were calm. So that was how she saw him.
Pisces Jealnet stood in the shattered dome of bones, staring upwards as Seemutor the Djinni rode a cloud higher. He was laughing, lightning booming around him, but he didn’t fire down at the [Necromancer]. He was fleeing—westwards. Fast as he could fly.
Away from the young man who stood there with a rapier in hand. As the storm subsided, light shone down around him. He was brushing flour from his hair. Blinking.
Were his eyes glowing? Merr rubbed her own eyes and got some of the flour dust in it and cursed. When she blinked, it was just him.
Pisces lifted a hand as he stumbled towards her. He had blood on his skin, and he was covered in dirt. His face was fuller from the privation she remembered, and he seemed…steadier. An air of magic hung about him that she didn’t remember.
But he was the same. She halted, then swung herself off her saddle.
“You crazy [Necromancer]. What are you doing, taking on all of Roshal by yourself? Where’s that damn team you kept whining about, eh?”
“Merr? I thought I was dead. How did you find me?”
“Your face, fool.”
She strode over. As her [Bandits] turned, she threw her arms around him in a hug and picked him up. He hadn’t gained much weight, and he blinked. Almost protested. Then, as she put him down, he smiled at her.
“Merr.”
“That’s my name.”
She’d forgotten what she was going to say to him. The [Bandit Lady] was just smiling, at the figure she’d escaped her chains with. An adventurer come a continent away, just like he’d promised.
Silly man. They’d troubled him with his false reputation. But when she glanced around, remembered the glow, and saw the Djinni, still laughing as he fled—she wondered if they had exaggerated it, truly.
All of it could wait. Pisces rasped as he became, for a moment, that awkwardly gallant figure she remembered. He stumbled, nearly tripped on his robes, and gazed at her.
“I’m glad you found me, Merr. I missed you all.”
A smile broke across his weary, bloodstained face, and his eyes shone a second under the rising sun.

10.75 H (Pt. 1) (2026-08-30)

<I am taking a month-long break due to a death in the family and to rest. Read my announcement here—I’ll post a new chapter on October 3rd. Also the 2nd half of this chapter on Tuesday.>
 
 
Merr the Storm looked different than Pisces remembered. His nightmares were honest. His waking memories less.
He remembered an attractive Stitch-woman, body sewn up with Silk—even if it was looted and thus a tiny bit inconsistent—dark of hair streaked faintly red with brown skin, like the dunes of the Great Desert when the rising sun caught the sand just right.
In his nightmares, she was gaunt. Not starved; they hadn’t been starved, but humbled, a tired, dirty [Slave] trudging along with the rest of them. Again, his memories of her were different, and they matched the woman who had come to find him.
This was Merr the Storm, a [Bandit Lady] of Chandrar. Her cloth-skin looked even better than before. Not as smooth or like that of a [Lady], but almost…cleaner? The vitality of an adventurer rather than someone who kept their complexion up by illusions or makeup, if that made sense.
She was also heavier than he remembered, in sheer physique, another shock. Stitch-folk truly could change anything they wanted. She still looked and moved fast as she paced around, giving orders to her [Bandits], but she might have outweighed Pisces. Closer to Briganda, another high-level warrior.
The reason for that, too, became plain as Merr strode about the ruins of the bone maze and battlefield where Pisces had thought to meet his end. Some of the [Slavers] had been playing dead after the explosive dustcloud attack. But the [Bandits] were doing, well, cleanup, stabbing each body through the head.
You could survive a stab to the chest, maybe even two or three, hope to drink a healing potion or use a survival Skill. A chop to the neck was fatal, let alone one that destroyed the brain or Lifethread therein. As Merr strode around, a [Slaver] leapt up.
“[Claim Blade]! Don’t move or your leader dies!”
He had Merr’s sword, a scimitar, from its sheath in a second and tried to do the standard thing he’d probably read about in adventure books or had done with friends. Namely, grabbing Merr and putting a blade at her throat so he could back up and grab a horse.
He got the blade. He executed the grab. Whereupon Merr seized his chest, lifted him up, and slammed him flat on the ground.
He broke five ribs before she stomped in his face, and then eight arrows hit the corpse. Merr kicked the body, spat, and shouted.
“Make sure they’re fucking dead. Not bad, though, not bad. I think this is the best muscle fiber bundle I’ve gotten yet. Qshom’s levelling.”
She flexed one arm and half-turned. The [Bandits] cheered their fearless leader, and Merr called out.
“You won’t believe what Bearig looks like. Well, when he’s not wearing your face. Y’do know about that, right? We can’t send [Messages], and I stuck the last scrying orb we found up a bastard’s ass. Hey, you awake, Pisces my boy? Mana-burnt? You look too much the same, you know. Everyone’s gotten a makeover but you. That’s Humans for you. You don’t even have more muscles. Scrawny as can be. Don’t they feed you in Izril?”
Merr talked like she fought and operated. A storm of words, and she went over to prod him. He was swaying a bit—he was exhausted, incredulous.
Relieved. She frowned at him.
“Hey, someone get a good mana potion over here! And anyone with a healing Skill! We got any?”
“I think that was Zamanta, and she ate a crossbow bolt last week, Boss.”
“Damn, well, who’s got a healing potion?”
“Here! Here, Boss Merr!”
Someone came racing over, eagerly waving a potion. Pisces saw a unique-looking [Bandit] wearing silver bells for earrings and with a face painted white—with red lips and even a blue nose—dash over.
He stared.
Sometimes you knew you weren’t dreaming by how stupid the world was. Merr grabbed the potion and eyed it critically.
“What grade is this?”
“Um, high, boss? I took it off a [Mage].”
“Idiot, who are you again? No, wait, I know you. One of the new girls. Chimes? If it’s good, you put it in the loot chest.”
“S-sorry.”
“Don’t be sorry. If someone thinks you’re hoarding the loot, you get shanked in the night or someone steals it, and then I have to either kill you or break toes. Think!”
A cuff to the head, and Merr grabbed the potion and inspected it. She jerked a thumb at the cringing [Bandit].
“Look at what I’m working with these days. I can’t get any honest [Bandits]. Most are weirdos like this kid. See the face? Former [Performer]. It don’t even come off. But hey, you recruit some, you lose some…”
The [Bandits] around Merr were all female, Pisces realized, wore a hodgepodge of armor, usually light, and were looting the dead. One called at Merr, grinning as she tugged down her facemask to reveal a huge scar across her lips.
“Honest [Bandits] don’t wanna work for Merr the Anti-Slaver, boss! They’re nervous you’ll split them from head-to-groin for dealin’ in them, just like the Scourge.”
“Don’t call me that! It’s Merr the Storm, not—and I’m not one of the [Rebels]. I’m independent!”
Loud jeering from all around turned to yelps when Merr threw the potion meant for Pisces so hard she took one of the [Bandits] off their feet. She called back.
“Shut up, stop whining, and toss it back. Pisces, drink.”
“I’m fine, Merr. I don’t need to waste one. I’m just…it’s good to see you.”
She eyed him, then spun on her heel.
“Yeah, yeah. If you’re going to burst into tears, do it after we’re riding, would you? This lot will eat you alive if you get all sentimental. Hey, lookouts, any sign of reinforcements? Tell me that Djinni’s still leaving.”
She would have strolled off as Chimes glumly scurried the potion over to a lockbox of quality loot, but Pisces caught up with Merr. Now he was coming alive again, the feeling of strange calm leaving him. That had been when he’d been amplifying the death mana in him. A kind of reaching for something he had never…
He’d think on that later. She turned, put a hand out.
“If you hug me, I’ll kneecap you.”
She sounded half-serious, and amused, but Pisces just shook his head.
“Thank you for finding me, Merr. I would be dead without you. I’ve wanted to see you since I left Chandrar. I’m sorry how it happened, and now…I’m back. So, thank you, truly.”
She blinked at him with sable eyes, the rising light of dawn reflected in them, and then they were back there, together. Seeing the Death of Chains depart. Marching along the Glass Straits, fighting to find a path to freedom as Roshal pursued them.
Merr riding off into the distance only to return with reinforcements—
He had not known her long, but she was one of the few people in this world Pisces thought he could call a true friend. A number that had grown exponentially since coming to The Wandering Inn. But of all of the people who bore that dubious distinction—she, Eloque, Bearig, Qshom, Cawe, and Rophir were the only ones he’d befriended without being around Erin Solstice.
His friend.
She reddened faintly as they stood there. Then the wind blew around them, and dust covered her and Pisces. He shielded his face, and she spoke.
“Yeah, well…what am I supposed to say to that, idiot? C’mon, mount up, and let’s ride! Of course I had to come on by. Don’t make a big deal about it.”
She kicked him and stomped off. Pisces just smiled, and then he felt lighter. Truly.
 
——
 
Merr’s Bandits, or the Dustbandits as they were known, were highly amused by their leader’s reaction to meeting the Scourge of Roshal. Well, they’d wanted to meet the genuine article for a long time. You heard all the stories, of course.
It was part of Merr’s legend, and a [Bandit Lord] or lady was all reputation. It was sort of, well, like fan clubs in bandit society.
Okay, maybe that was a weird comparison, but Chandrar had lots of [Bandits] due to the wide desert and the literal bandit-kingdom of Savere. In other continents, you had a higher proportion of [Rogues] or so on in your criminal classes. But Chandrar had bandit culture.
Which meant as an aspiring [Bandit], sure, you might strike out on your own with a pointy stick and a dream to hold up an [Emir]—but that tended to mean you ended up as paste on the ground. Smart [Bandits] joined groups.
Many were exclusive, like the Bleakbeaks, who had been a Garuda group who hated…Garuda. Look, the gangs didn’t have to make sense. You found a crew, stuck with it, and if it didn’t work, tried to trade up. ‘Course, you had to offer your new crew something to get them to let you in most times, prove your loyalty.
Everyone who was in this for life knew that you had to be careful with tattoos if you weren’t a Stitch-person. Sure, the first bandit group you could tattoo your arms or a leg. But a cheek? What happened when your gang-for-life split up or the leader got axed? Then you had a giant-ass tattoo of your previous affiliation that you needed to cover up to get into your new one. Some poor loser shows up with sixteen gang-tattoos on their body and they didn’t exactly paint a winning record there.
…The point was that bandits had celebrity culture. Famous gang-leaders attracted people by their deeds, personalities, and of course other factors like how much gold they shared out, what kind of work they did.
But [Bandit] life was often short, hard, and it might be worth a few less silver in your pocket per haul to have a leader that got you or one you could admire. You savvy?
It was why Rasea Zecrew of [Pirate] fame had such a diehard crew. And it was also why Merr had her appeal.
Oh, regular [Bandits] didn’t stick with her much these days. Not enough profits, too much fighting Roshal—and they held a grudge—but she still got recruits, and she drew from the [Slaves] she freed.
She had a good rep in Savere. Sure, don’t cross her on the [Slave] thing, she’d gotten a bit ‘moral’ these days. But that’s still Merr the Fucking Storm. You ever see her blow through a gate after exploding flour dust across every [Guard]’s face? Her having freed herself and riding with Pisces the Scourge had only added to her reputation, really. Plenty of tough types got collared and never came out the same.
So, yes, Merr was popular. Her Dustbandits, the ones who rode in her principal gang with her, sometimes had it rough. They hadn’t liked a daring raid this deep into Nerrhavia’s Fallen. But dead gods, it was worth it to see her blush.
“I ain’t never seen the boss flush. You think she and he were a thing?”
Some of the veterans, who included Dustbandits from before the time Merr had been captured, were riding side-saddle, sometimes two-to-a-mount, and close together to gossip. One group even had dice rattling around on a tray held between two horses. They were good riders; Merr’s entire thing was hit-and-run, speedy assaults.
One of them was Chokin’ Casep, a Human [Dustrider Veteran]—a former Trick Rider of Jecrass, believe it or not. She hated her nickname, but her entire thing was the lengths of rope she carried on her belt and saddle. [Rancher]-style ropes used for corralling loose animals. Only, Casep’s trick was, uh, tossing a loop of rope around your neck and galloping off while she dragged you behind her. It was an effective strategy, but she resented the name.
Another old [Bandit], Scarlips, was grinning. They were all watching as Pisces and Merr rode together, he on his weird skeleton horse, she on a Nightmare, a magical horse that could turn invisible and liked eating meat. A vicious mare she’d nicknamed Toothie.
“Don’t let her hear you say that or she’ll swing on you. You talk to those [Rebels] often, Casep?”
“Bah, they’re too uptight. Can’t get ‘em to trade nothing good, and they got all offended one time—why?”
“Just asking if anyone’s heard rumors back when they were all [Slaves]. She’s never said anything went down, but the boss keeps that kind of thing close to the chest. Never loosens her stitching on personal affairs. Which I respect!”
Everyone nodded; that was just good business. You hated to see a boss sleeping around and getting all entangled. Scarlips went on, pursing said lips.
“Just…can’t think of an hour the last damn week she wasn’t telling us to ride faster to catch him.”
“True, true.”
Such interest. The Dustbandits were thinking. They were thinking this rescue of the Scourge put a target on their backs, even if Nerrhavia’s Fallen wasn’t after the [Necromancer]—yet. Roshal was, and he was crazy; he’d slaughtered hundreds of [Slavers] this week alone.
“So much for the boss sayin’ he wasn’t all that. You saw him facing down that Djinni? And from how many were dead before we got to him—”
“Well, that’s a Goldie for you. Stands to reason.”
“Sure, sure, but did you hear about the sea battle? Or the Crossroads of Izril?”
“They didn’t get to them, that’s a rumor; don’t be spreading lies, Hacksey.”
“Not lies! I have it from a pen pal I write all the time in Izril that they were in the sky itself! Everyone saw it!”
“Your friend’s a [Con Artist], Hacksey.”
“So? They’ve never lied to me a day in my life. Don’t judge people by classes; we’ve been pen pals eleven years—and the Horns were at the Village of the Dead.”
“Stands to reason he can fight. But if we’re placing bets on the boss and him—I heard he slept with the Arbiter Queen.”
“So? You know adventurers. Worse’n [Whores]. Male, female, you mark me, you ever shack up with one, you make sure they’re not carrying something nasty first.”
“All I’m saying is this had better not be drama with the boss. What if he’s sleeping with the Silver Killer?”
“…If he is, he’s probably lost his genitals. Problem solved. What makes you think they’re together? Is it that book you keep reading? You know that’s fiction. The [Writer]’s trash.”
“It’s by Heartslayi, and she’s amazing. I’m just saying I want to settle some questions for the record. Just so when we get to Savere I can tell everyone—”
The Dustbandits knew danger might come to them. But on the other hand—it was hugely entertaining. So things were looking up. Bandit life, bandit mentality.
 
——
 
If they were thinking Pisces and Merr were having some heart-to-heart talk or deep romantic exploration of past flames, the Dustbandits were dead wrong.
In fact, they hadn’t said a word for the last five minutes. Pisces was beet red, and Merr was rolling her eyes. She was listening to the voices of her Dustbandits, which were somehow blowing into Pisces and Merr. They eventually cut off, and she grunted.
“[Voices on the Wind]. Idiots never think I can use it on them. Morale’s good. You have to check on it constantly. If you ever lead people—well, you got a taste for it when we were freed, but a full-time group needs you to have a finger on the pulse nonstop. ‘Specially [Bandits]; they just leave when they think something’s bad.”
He didn’t know what to say. She’d shushed him, and then the rumors—Pisces had been all gratitude, feeling solemn even, this massive weight lifting as part of his vow of months past had finally been fulfilled moments before his death by seeing Merr.
But instead of that, he blurted, red-faced.
“I did not sleep with Jecaina, and I do not conduct myself like—like—we did get to the Crossroads, but I didn’t know we were in the sky! Was it that magical road? Vofea told us it was magic! Should I clarify to them for your good reputation?”
He would have ridden back this instant to clear this up, but Merr threw her head back and laughed. Then she reached over and slapped him on the back.
“There’s the fellow I came to rescue. Less of being an adventurer out of stories, more this. Let ‘em yak. It does my reputation good. Mystique. Don’t play it up, mind. Just don’t talk to the underlings about stuff you don’t have to. Dead gods, we’ve too much to say to each other. So you did meet the Arbiter Queen herself? How many [Bandits] is she hanging per day?”
“Er, uh, what? None that I saw. She does have new courts she told me she was building, and she was laying out cities to be rebuilt or restructured with the money King Fetohep gave her—and she has Lawriders—”
Merr was pulling on a lip.
“Yeah, I heard. Bandit world’s all abuzz about Jecrass. So no mass-hangings?”
“No.”
“Hmm, might be worth a shot, then. Y’see, the thing is, you hear Arbiter Queen and you imagine a lot of things. Gallows, headman, guillotine, being tied to a pole and set on fire—Nerrhavia’s Fallen loves that, and it is a bad way to go—so most gangs are avoiding Jecrass. Lawrider…do they have a class?”
Pisces thought they did, and Merr shuddered.
“Anti-crime classes. Gah! Hate them! Shivers those timbers I keep hearing about. Well, I’m not keen on going through Jecrass anyways. There’s good money stealing horses, but they’re always mounted, and I hate fast pursuit. So she really hosted you?”
“Her and King Raelt, yes. They were very hospitable.”
Merr listened as Pisces gave her a garbled account of the events that had led him across Chandrar to find his team. He realized she didn’t know about the rest, but in fact, she even knew about him and Colth coming off the undead ship. She tapped one ear now, knowingly.
“You think I don’t have an ear to the wind, Necrolad? Gossip about you is all but free, and the [Rebels] have no end. So you were there, dueling her with rapiers—yeah, I see how someone says that and you get the wrong impression. She wasn’t interested in you?”
A huge hesitation which made her head snap around.
“Well, I mean—Colth told me after the fact—but I didn’t see the alleged signals he said were out there. And besides, she was a [Queen]—”
Merr started laughing even harder. She clutched at her sides, nearly falling off the Nightmare, whom Pisces realized was laughing at him as well.
“Oh, dead gods! Argh, pop my stitching, this is what I’ve missed! The man loses a chance with a real [Queen]—hey, girls, guess what? This fool missed his shot with the Arbiter Queen and didn’t even know she was flying the freaky flag! Turns out both of ‘em flirt as well as camels!”
Instantly, the Dustbandits started howling with laughter. Pisces spluttered and remembered, too late—
Merr could be hurtful. He went to shove her lightly, and she jostled him.
“How’d you end up so late to Chandrar, eh? The Ice Squirrel washed up faster than you, and the Silver Killer walked, but nooo, you were a week late! Bearig was chewing a hole through leather by the time you showed up!”
He hissed at her, red-faced.
“That wasn’t my—I didn’t know we were supposed to be enchanted! The Death of Magic cast a spell on the driftwood we were on, but I thought a ship would—”
Merr had been laughing. Then she gave him a puzzled grin.
“Oh, pull the other leg, I’ve got spares. The Death of Magic? Please, I know the Arbiter Queen was real, but what, were you romancing her?”
“What? No, she actually cast a spell on the driftwood that Colth and I were on. She—”
Pisces did not mention the fact that Colth was actually in league with the Demons and an agent of one of the Deathless, but Merr only stared at him. She realized he was not joking.
“Wait, you’re not fooling with me? Because if you are, say so now or I’ll hit you, no jokes.”
“No jokes, Merr. On Cawe, that was her—”
Merr drew in a breath. Then she recoiled, glanced around, and waved back the Dustbandits coming over to laugh at Pisces up close. She drew over, hissed at him.
“What?”
 
——
 
The Death of Magic was a level far beyond even meeting and failing to romance the Arbiter Queen. Oh, one might sound like the other, but Merr was actually an individual worldly enough to understand that the Death of Magic was at the top of…everything. It was the most rattled Pisces had seen her.
“Zeikhal swallow me ‘n spit me out. You actually…they blocked the scrying spells when she appeared, you know.”
“I know. I’ve seen some of the battle. Hard to follow.”
Most of it had been other ships being boarded or chaos. No one had even mentioned the flying Dragon, though some of Teriarch’s magic and fire had been seen in the chaos. Merr rubbed at her nose.
“Was she…was she as terrifying as they say?”
“I don’t honestly know. It was so much like—like armageddon at the end that she just sort of fit it. I can’t imagine how many spells she was blocking or dodging, but they were firing them at Erin.”
“Your [Innkeeper], yeah. Saw her too. It was the first time I’d laid eyes on her, y’know, after she came back? You did it, I remember thinking. But I never got a good look at her. Me and scrying orbs, we’re like distant lovers. Can’t mix or I get hunted down since we know Wistram sells locations on bandits. But I saw the recording, and I thought…yeah. Yeah, she fits the woman who had you do all that. Flaming hat, knifing Bloodtear Captains like they were rookie [Deckhands]. She okay?”
Pisces’ head bowed, feeling oddly gratified to hear Merr speaking of Erin like that. He wondered how they’d interact if they met. He wished it had happened.
“I…yes?”
“I heard she was in Baleros. With the Titan. Safe enough. Woman took a city in battle.”
“Yes. I—I heard. If that’s her, it’s good she’s safe.”
Merr was glancing ahead; she was following some kind of internal map, taking them in odd directions now and then, perhaps to throw off pursuit, and some of her Dustbandits would fall back then gallop to rejoin or go ahead. Erasing tracks? Scouting? Pisces couldn’t pay attention. Now, she twisted around.
“If that’s her?”
“It doesn’t seem like her. I think it isn’t.”
He had no proof of this. Lyonette, Mrsha, the inn had contacted his team and said all was well, but he’d thought maybe there was a hint of a lie? Ceria wasn’t sure, but she’d said it was all too possible. Pisces only had the Erin he’d seen on the scrying orb for confirmation, but…he felt like it wasn’t her.
Plus, she hadn’t contacted him. She’d sent [Messages] to Ceria and asked about him, but he felt like the real Erin would have done something. Maybe. Maybe it was him, not…he only told Merr this because he felt like he had to.
Like he could tell her anything. Then Pisces worried he was blabbing, but Merr just nodded.
“Interesting. You know her best. And your teammate, Ksmvr. He ain’t here. We don’t know where he is. Did he…”
“He’s alive. Baleros. Lost in the jungles. We’ll find him and Vofea. We just have to finish our business first, but we’re headed there right away.”
Merr exhaled and squared her shoulders.
“Right, well, that makes sense why you came here. Had to grab that Relic-class sword, right? You’d best steer clear of Savere. The Siren still hates the Ice Squirrel for the stunt she pulled. Reckon you want to meet Bearig; his force is slower than mine, but he’ll be moving. Qshom’s with him, and so’s Rophir. Kid talks now, you know? Once in a blue moon. So, once a night. Eloque’s not with either, but you came for ‘em. Just like you said. I miss anything?”
“Um, Yvlon’s friends, but she did rescue them—”
“Seems easy enough to do, the sword aside. At least you’ll find the Empress of Beasts easy; she’s got a real army, even if I think she’s still more fucked than a lone heifer in a bull pen. Getting that sword from her? Good luck. I could get you a [Thief], but—eh, that’ll do. Got anyone else who wants a ticket to Izril? Bearig, Qshom, Rophir, Eloque are the real crew. Few others who turned out good, but those were the ones you wanted, right?”
“And you, Merr.”
She blinked at him, then grinned.
“Me? I’m Merr the Storm, Pisces. A [Bandit Lady]. Look at my gang. We’ve been raiding, I’ve rebuilt the Dustbandits better’n before—I came here to help you, but I’m fine.”
He met her gaze, and Pisces said the things he’d waited so long to say.
“Even so, Merr. I’ll charter a ship to take you and all your Dustbandits to Izril. You, all these [Rebels], and Eloque too. I don’t want any of you where Roshal has power. I want to find Ksmvr and Vofea and get to Erin, but you’re on that list.”
She stared at him, nonplussed, wide-eyed, and then turned her head abruptly.
“Now I know you’re a Gold-ranked adventurer. Too big for your damn britches. You rescuing [Bandit Ladies] because I’m weak? Who’s got a higher level? C’mon, whip yours out and we’ll measure ‘em! You think I wasn’t levelling?”
“Merr, I didn’t mean—don’t kick me! Merr!”
He protested, but she was very nimble in the saddle, and he had to ride away from her as the Nightmare did the same. The Dustbandits watched as Merr cursed at him, and one whispered.
“Hey, anyone got a Skill that lets them talk to Savere? Tell ‘em to open up a betting pool on the Boss and the Scourge.”
“Done and done. On whether they’re a thing or will be?”
“Why not both?”
 
——
 
Pisces levelled up in his sleep that night. He did sort of nod off by the end of his ride; it was longer than he thought. Merr wanted to get out of any pursuer’s range, and that included more Djinni.
He was exhausted, but when he woke, he found the Dustbandits already making breakfast. Pisces was not a ‘morning person’, but he’d grown used to it during his raids on Roshal. To his surprise, he didn’t turn into his usual lethargic self in the morning. He felt…
Well, he met with Merr straight off. She was relaxing around a smokeless ‘fire’ that showed him she really had rebuilt her fortunes, because it was bandit-tech.
Namely, magical stones that acted like embers. No smoke, but you could grill anything. Perfect for not being detected. They had a pot that erased scent, anti-scrying charms, lucky talismans, even a loot chest.
“It’s Beithday! Anything in the chest goes to the Siren! She’ll teleport it out via her Skill, so empty your pockets!”
A [Bandit] tasked with making sure the Siren got her cut and the most valuable items were converted to gold was stomping up and down the tents, waking people up. Another was strolling about.
“Anyone got an infected cut or some shit? Shout it out or you’re dead the next time we use a potion, and if we waste one on you, we’ll kill you!”
She daubed anyone with an infection with a bit of orange on their right shoulder. Efficient. Pisces sat down.
“I forgot you’re so good at this.”
He didn’t know many leader-types. Merr kicked him as she chewed on sausage mixed into some grits.
“Shut up.”
“What did I—”
“How the hell do you have six levels on me? I’ve been fighting damn wars with Bearig, and I hit Level 40 last month!”
She was very upset. Merr had been in her mid-thirties before being taken as a slave, and her rise since then had put her on the map of top [Bandits]—but Pisces had been through a few adventures. Merr grumbled as he smiled.
“At least my class is better than yours. [Ladies] always are harder to level.”
“Er, Merr, you’re a [Bandit Lady].”
Another kick.
“A [Lady]’s a damn [Lady] no matter what! You’re just some [Necromancer of Reclaimed Grandeur]. Sounds stupid.”
“I can animate structures!”
“Oh, structures. I’m so afraid. What, are you gonna animate a wall and have it fall on me?”
He glowered until he was handed breakfast, and the hot, fresh food cheered him up instantly. Merr relented.
“Argh, fine. Don’t get sniffy with me. Do you still do that? All the girls want to see; none of ‘em believed that was a thing. I like your undead. Ivery’s a hoot, and I came around to Bearbones. Saw a few more corpses of late, and I see your point. Rotten flesh? Yuck.”
Another thing about Merr was her complete unfazedness when it came to undead. She actually really liked them, and Pisces almost sniffed, saw everyone turn to stare at him, and let out a breath instead. They sighed.
Oh, this was strange. He felt so light, but he did gaze at her.
“I should have animated the [Slavers] I killed, but I was too tired.”
She waved it off.
“Eh, we’d have outrun them.”
“I could have had them run through the night. The undead don’t stop moving, and they can follow me even when I’m asleep.”
She raised one eyebrow at that.
“Oh? Even the zombies can run? Interesting…I’d have probably vetoed the suggestion anyways. A running zombie can be marked or followed, and some of my Skills for speed or stealth only affect the Dustbandits. But hey, we run into any bastards between here and Bearig’s group and we can do that. Though I’d trade ten zombies for one Ghoul. Can you do that? Can you…upgrade undead or mash the low-tier ones into a single good one?”
The thought hadn’t ever really occurred to Pisces, and he hesitated.
“I know some [Necromancers] would keep body piles together to form better undead. One can upgrade them—I’m decent at that with my Skeleton Champions, and I did reclaim most of their bones. But you mean change their actual…species? I’ve never tried.”
You could make Wailing Pits and Crypt Lords out of piles of the dead, but that was just natural undeath. Merr winked.
“Lookit me, lecturing [Necromancers]. I knew you weren’t thinking like a rat bastard without me. Okay, I’ll make sure to keep the corpses more intact. But best case is we never run into anything on our way east. We link up—I’m hoping Bearig’s not gone too far into Nerrhavia’s Fallen searching for us. We can find each other. Then we splinter. If you’re not wanted by Nerrhavia’s Fallen, you catch one of those damn Wistram Carriages back to your team, then we all move to wherever we agree on. We can talk ships and who’s on them when everyone’s there. Damn, forgot Eloque…eh, she won’t be part of the initial meeting, but we’ll send word. Deal?”
Pisces blinked at this plan. Merr drew it out over her own rough map, and she seemed to know approximately where everyone was. It was a good plan, but he shifted.
“I…do want to meet Bearig. And Eloque and the others, Merr. But I’m actually—I need to stay here. Around the city of Halqued.”
She stopped chewing on her food. The Dustbandits glanced up, and Merr leaned forwards.
“So you didn’t just start attacking Roshal at random. I thought you held it together well. [Rebels] wanted you to do more butcherin’, but I thought you knew the score. This was crazy, Pisces. So crazy I wondered if they’d tried to collar you or…what’s in the city? A teammate? A friend?”
Pisces was aware of every eye on him. He replied slowly.
“Just a caravan of [Slaves]. I couldn’t…I can’t fight in the city. I’d be killing Nerrhavia Fallen’s soldiers and guards. But I thought that if I hit caravans around the city, I could—”
Merr sat back, and suddenly she wore a pained expression. The Dustbandits began moving around loudly, but she just gazed at him. Not with incredulity as he’d feared his team might look at him like—excepting Colth—just pain.
“Ah, Necrolad. I forget you left Chandrar. To you, this has got to hurt twice as bad, a wound reopened. You still got that bastard’s scar on your chest?”
Pisces felt at it, and she gazed at him.
“Humans. Rophir’s got his, but even Eloque’s…you can’t save ‘em all.”
“I know that, Merr. I just—”
“You can’t save whomever that is.”
He met her eyes. For a moment, Pisces nearly said something harsh. He bit his tongue, turned his head. Stared at the ground and saw a headless corpse collapsing. Just a few more—
“I know. I know it was madness, and that was before the Djinni found me, Merr. But I’ve already done the worst. I’ve killed every single [Slaver] I could find. Not just caravans. The ones on the road, anyone—I should have done more the moment I landed, but I was afraid. I don’t want to go back to Tyrant’s Rest and get my team in trouble. When I do, I’ll pay the price, but right now, I—we’re here. You’re a [Bandit Lady], right?”
She nodded, warily, eying him. Pisces glanced around and saw, even here, a few marks. Someone with scars on their wrists. A [Bandit] joking with the others who had a mark around her neck or a brand somewhere visible. They glanced at him, and unlike the regular [Bandits], there was something in their gaze that spoke to him.
Like Merr. Like Colth. Something unifying that they could never forget. A hatred, a desire. Pisces whispered.
“But you’re one that frees [Slaves]. You understand.”
She opened her mouth, and he just glanced at her.
“I know you’re not a full [Rebel]. I know Merr the Storm has to do her own thing. That’s what you told me. But you understand, don’t you? Merr, I have to do this. I…”
He was gazing at the map, then around, and he didn’t realize it but it seemed suddenly, to Merr, as if the [Necromancer] were still hungry. Not for breakfast, but he was peering around like someone hunting for something. She sat back as her skin prickled, and she felt her heart pumping.
Agh, damn. She knew she shouldn’t have come here, even though she had to. Just like him—she was going back in time. Then he peered at her, both a memory and a stranger, one changed. But better. More sure of himself, perhaps. Higher-level.
“Merr. I need your help.”
“Doin’ what, exactly?”
Pisces glanced down at the map and saw where they were—far further from Halqued than he could have ever gotten alone, even with the skeleton horse. Merr was a [Bandit Lady] known for speed; her Skills had carried them far, far in the night. He drew a circle with one finger.
“They’ve kept all the caravans away from Halqued. Stopped, but they probably knew where I was, roughly. How many…are around us now, Merr? Or going north to avoid the city?”
They’d have to choose more roads along the Leashed Trails. Predictable ones. Merr gazed at Pisces, then sighed.
“I do this for profit, Pisces. I don’t go beyond certain limits, and you’ve pushed past them. Bearig and his lot are hunted, but even they didn’t dare do what you have. They’re not high-level enough. If we hit more caravans? They sent a Djinni after you.”
“Yes. But there are ways to lose pursuit, aren’t there? Your class is an expert in that. And they’ve hunted you all this time.”
They had to have. Roshal would never forget, and Pisces had thought Emir Yazdil especially would not relent. He’d only been surprised Yazdil hadn’t done anything until now. Merr drummed her fingers on her legs.
“We have them riled up. Every day we stay here—”
“Not long, Merr. Just a day. Two, at most. How many could we hit?”
“My girls don’t fight for nothing, Pisces. You could get me—”
He glanced at them. Over half Merr’s girls were former [Slaves]. Pisces eyed Merr.
“I can pay them.”
“Hah! You have any idea what a crew like mine runs? We need gold, more than even you’ve got without a Merchant’s Guild.”
“Then you can have the [Slavers]’ gold. I don’t want any. C’mon, Merr. You must loot them and know how much each one has.”
She was hesitating. Merr inspected her fingernails, glanced up at him, cursed, and stood up.
“Those freed [Slaves]—what did you do with ‘em?”
Pisces hung his head.
“I pointed them towards safe places and let them scatter or organize. I couldn’t…I didn’t know where to send them. I should have done more.”
Merr walked in a circle, muttering.
“Yeah, most might not have—no, you get inventive, and more make it than you think. But the smart move is to send ‘em to a hideout. Not your fault; you didn’t know. But we’d have to put them on horses, and we don’t have enough! Then you ride them at a [Rebel] group, but too many? Too easy to spot. I’d have to break up the Dustbandits, call in one of the peripheral bands, make contact with [Rebels] around here, or hire help and do small parties. D’you know how hard that is? And they will be pursued by the Slaver’s Guild.”
Pisces sat there, and he was trembling. Trembling with that same energy of the last few days. It hadn’t left him at all. It had just grown worse, if anything. And he saw it in her too, for all she sat and tried to dismiss it all.
“But you’re a [Bandit Lady]. If anyone can do it, it’s you, Merr. Besides…there won’t be as many pursuers, just scrying spells.”
She stopped gnashing on her cooling breakfast and gave him a look like he was genuinely stupid, full of actual irritation for once.
“How do you reckon that? Did you or did you not walk into an ambush that—”
“There won’t be any pursuers if we get them too.”
She stopped. Pisces sat there, and she shivered.
“We cannot fight that many. We don’t have the numbers, Pisces.”
“Not unless I start animating legions.”
Her eyes were flickering, and Pisces threw in one last thing.
“Doesn’t Roshal arm their retribution forces with enchanted items? I saw your Dustbandits looting the ones after me. Imagine it, Merr.”
He stared around at the group of eighty-some Dustbandits.
“You could have every single Dustbandit armed with an enchanted blade and armor. Every single one of Merr’s Bandits.”
The [Bandit Lady] rubbed at her nose, stared down at the map, then folded her arms. She gazed up at the sky, then cursed as she leapt to her feet.
“You think my crew’s just eighty bandits? This is only the core. I could have four hundred with me in a day’s time—we have plenty of enchanted swords!”
“We could arm all four hundred. If we kill enough [Slavers].”
She studied him, and he held her gaze, lips trembling almost like he was laughing. Madness…but then she put him in a headlock and tousled his hair.
“Argh. That’s damn good logic. I can only give you two days, tops! Dustbandits, get ready.”
There was a whoop, and Pisces’ heart leapt. He hadn’t actually thought she’d go for it, but he looked up at her, and there they were again. As if they hadn’t stopped. Chained together by something other than metal.
So, once more, as if he had never left Chandrar…
The Scourge rode with the Storm.
 
——
 
Some people had all the luck. In that however bad their day was, and it could really suck—a terrible boss, annoying co-workers, stepping in poop so bad it slushed into your boots and socks…
You weren’t being kidnapped into slavery or in the middle of a war. That didn’t make it better, of course. Everyone was the [Hero] of their own story, and being told someone else was being stabbed repeatedly didn’t cheer you up unless you really hated their guts.
That was why stories mattered for the people with all the luck. It was an escape. A window out of their world into another one that sucked more—and that was the point. Someone who was hurt worse than you or rising higher. A flying swallow screaming skywards or a falling comet burning its way into the bowels of the earth—
That was what drew the likes of Lord Molen to the television. Oh, he enjoyed the japes and jabs, the silly stuff. Videos of cats doing cat-things, and there were nearly a hundred catalogued cat subspecies, enough for a lifetime of cats. But that alone would sicken him, like a man who only ate ice cream all his life. He craved, at times, something to make him weep or rage. To feel alive, and for the moment, the television of this world was too honest. It delivered just that and needed no manufacturing.
…But why, then, did other men, like Nuvityn, watch television? The King of Myths needed no more grief. He was a man bereaved. A father on a quest of vengeance. A [King]. He, who stood at the height of power any being, mortal or immortal, might ever aspire to…why did he watch the same television as ordinary folk?
Perhaps to understand what they thought. To understand normality, Miihey believed.
Miihey was a half-Elf [Barbarian] of Forem, a tribe in the Kingdom of Myths. He was exceptional in every way. Not only was he over Level 40, but he was a half-Elf with such an uncouth class. He was a member of one of Erribathe’s diverse peoples; Forem were hillfolk, who wrestled bears—and befriended them. A half-Elf so divergent from others that he had set Gaiil-Drome on its head with his very presence.
Miihey was a half-Elf, you see, who lived with Humans as equals. Not ‘among Humans’ as half-Elves were known to condescend to do—with the other members of his tribes. He was just Miihey to them. Yes, he aged slower, but he brawled and talked with them as equals. No respect was given for his age. Forem had learned to treat the children of Elves as the same as all else, the lesson of millennia, and the reward was just creating half-Elves like Miihey. Ones who cared nothing for their age or blood.
It would not make him live long; in fact, Forem half-Elves tended to die pretty young given their penchant for punching a grizzly bear who’d started raiding their food supplies. But it did mean he was grounded. A trusted advisor to even the King of Myths. For who better to speak plainly than the [Barbarian]?
It was more than just lifestyle. Miihey embodied a certain savagery, a wildness and deliberate incivility. He rather resented the fine arts and crafts of ‘better’ folk and the pretentiousness that came along with it. Not that he hated people who were a certain way genuinely. He hated the thought it made you better.
For instance, he had not quibbled much with Calanfer, who played politics as a way to survive and whose folk could be genuine, for all they treated the Eternal Throne like the beacon of all that was good and holy.
