10.75 H (Pt. 2) (2026-09-02)

<I am taking a month-long break due to a death in the family and to rest. Read my announcement here—I’ll post a new chapter on October 3rd.>
 
 
“A Face of Chandrar has come for you, Pisces Jealnet. Throw down your blade or die. I am the [Jester].”
She was still dancing on that stage as a bright haze of pink and blue surrounded her, like a performer coming out of backstage. There was a spotlight fixed on the [Assassin]’s body, highlighting her torso.
The bells that swung from her silly hat and chest that never rang. Her face, painted white, with black mascara highlighting her eyes and lips. An artful jewel of ice drawn on one cheek, a jagged bolt of lightning crossing her other eye.
No colorful red nose.
[Jester], not [Clown]. Nor [Fool]. The nuance…Pisces’ rapier was raised, and he had set himself sidelong. He was trapped behind the table, next to the others in the booth. Heart pounding.
She killed Casep and the others. She’s been following me since the palace. Idiot—if I’d drunk that whiskey, I’d be dead. 
Or in chains.
A deeper certainty spoke to Pisces as he tried to analyze her. Those bells. He knew them. Idiot only looking at her breasts—
Those were the bells of [Duelists]. Which meant she might have earned one silver one and one gold one, but the rest…she’d taken them from the people she’d killed. Unless it was a bluff. Anyone could commission a bell—
It wasn’t a bluff. She was the genuine article. He hadn’t noticed it when she was hiding her abilities, but now she swayed to the right and left, drawing a pair of long blades. They seemed like oversized daggers. Handleless, with that long, stabbing point.
Dirks? She was wielding both in her hands, not reversing one like he’d seen Seborn use. Pisces didn’t know how they would move. But she was here.
A song from the [Popstar] of Terandria was blasting from the back of the club as the Jester sauntered forwards. She ignored the gasps, the incredulity from the people around her. Even laughter.
Her eyes were just focused on Pisces, and they gleamed, yellow coins spinning like a [Gambler] tossing one last bet onto the table. He watched her balance shifting.
Perfect form. Just like the Maestro or Raelt. He felt like she was stabbing him from there. His lungs were pressed against his ribs. Even more than Itkisa—he remembered this feeling from meeting the King of Destruction.
She was over Level 50. And he was almost out of magic.
Her clothing wasn’t visibly enchanted, but if he’d failed to notice her, then it might b—
Pisces slammed into Lareceina and knocked her flat. She went headfirst into the table so hard her nose started bleeding. A blade stabbed through the cushioned seat where he had been, then he ducked.
The second slash cleaved through a guard’s chest, spilling red gore onto the table. The Jester tsked as Pisces stabbed, and his rapier rang as she backflipped up. She threw something—his [Barrier of Air] exploded.
The second dirk tumbled through the cloud of debris and landed in a booth next to his; Pisces saw the third one coming at him and deflected it with his rapier. It exploded as he flicked it across the room, and there were screams.
All of this before Lareceina finished saying ‘wh—?’. His foot was on the cushioned seats again, the other one on top of the table. He was panting. Feeling at his side.
She’d torn through his robes. Missed his skin. The Jester winked.
“Exalted royals of Nerrhavia’s Fallen. You may wish to run.”
She called out, voice playful and carrying. Only, her attack had created another moment of paralysis. No one was laughing at the strange woman now.
Most hadn’t even seen her move. Lareceina staggered upright, clutching at her nose, eyes wide. Pisces kept his attention on the Jester, desperate. The moment he’d lost the tiniest focus to check her clothing, she’d attacked.
She’s faster than Colth. She’d jumped from the stage into the booth in a single move. He heard a voice croak.
“A Face of Roshal? Ridiculous. I am Prince Weith of—of—”
Weith was dragging himself upright, face pale. He went for his sword, and the Jester didn’t even glance at him. She just spoke off-handedly.
“Anyone in this building in a minute’s time is dead, along with him. This is just between us, Adventurer. It’s a duel. I challenge you for the honor of Roshal.”
She pointed her rightmost dagger at Pisces, and he tensed. Weith hesitated. He looked to the unconscious Yosoc; Princess Lithic was on her feet, pushing to get out of the booth with her bodyguards. There were whites in the corners of Weith’s eyes.
He was afraid. But he still reached for his sword.
“This man is under the protection of House Dabrei and Nerrhavia’s Fallen, woman. Leave or—”
Someone lunged. Weith half-turned. But the hand that slammed into his, stopping him from drawing the blade, wasn’t one of the Jester’s accomplices. It was one of the [Bodyguards].
The woman with the younger brother tackled the [Prince], and her buddy with the grandparents grabbed his legs. They heaved him over the edge of the booth, and Yosoc’s people were doing the same.
“Out! Out—”
Princess Lithic was running for the doors, the only way out. Stitch-folk were standing at the edge, and they were a story up. It was a long dr—
Lithic pushed a Stitch-man out, then leapt herself. The cursing Prince Weith was shouting obscenities.
“Put me down! My h—”
The [Bodyguards] tossed him out the door, then leapt themselves. Prince Yosoc’s people were right behind them. They just bailed out onto the street. Breaking the [Prince]’s legs in a fall?
Far better than having him minced by a Face of the Assassin’s Guild. This was their job. You had to admire it. Exemplars of the class, really.
They knew exactly what would happen if they’d stayed. Pisces saw it all out of the corner of his eyes as he stood there. They’d cleared the booth; Lareceina was edging out as well, and he needed the space. He would have leapt from the booth to the floor, but he was afraid to move.
The Jester had let the others go. She kept flipping a dagger up in her right hand, twirling it, catching it. Baiting him. She flipped it, caught the blade between two fingers, and winked at him.
“One gets in trouble for killing royalty. But I can kill anything I need to accomplish my goals. You should have taken me as a helper, Scourge. I’d have given you a night to remember, then you’d have woken up in a box to the harbor.”
“You killed Casep, Chimes. Were you after Merr, or was that just to get at me?”
He needed an opening to drink a mana potion. He needed a strategy. Or to just—
Flip. The rightmost dagger twirled in the air, and Pisces’ eyes were caught by it. A hypnotizing twirl.
[A Hypnotizing Trick].
She was a blur, leaping across the room, off the walls of another booth, striking from the side, and he couldn’t look away for the crucial moment. She attacked into his blind spot, and he—
—parried—
The dagger. Tried to pivot and reset as the Skill let him go, but they were nose-to-nose, and she was grinning.
Inside the guard of his rapier. His hand came up.
“[Deathb—]”
Her empty right hand punched him in the ribs, hit his jaw, and struck his chest a second time. Pisces flew backwards, into an adjoining booth, as Lareceina whirled. The Jester dove, dodging a stream of black magic. Her right hand was filled with a fan of enchanted daggers, and she threw them, conjured another set, threw them, then threw a third volley.
Explosions. Only then did she pause, cocking her head, and shook out her right hand ostentatiously.
“Nice armor.”
Pieces of wood were raining down as Lareceina shielded herself with a wall of air. The smoke cleared and revealed splintered wood and fabric; the booths where Pisces had been standing were shredded.
Pisces? He was crouched behind a [Wall of Bone] spell, clutching at his chest. But his hand still held his rapier. Lareceina saw his wide eyes and shredded robes. The Jester was eying him, gaze bright, smiling, but tensed.
 
——
 
She’d broken his ribs and jaw. That free hand had punched so hard—
She backed off when I cast [Deathbolt]. Even Roshal doesn’t know necromancy well.
Flickers of thoughts as he poured death mana into his bones. Pisces spoke despite his broken jaw. He had to.
“Armor made from Stalker, the guardian of Liscor’s dungeon. I trust you hurt your hands?”
“Want to kiss them to make them better?”
She grinned; she had a playful, casual tone, but the Jester was circling now, letting the fog effect in the club engulf her. Pisces rose, trying to keep her in sight. She just kept…
“Doesn’t cover your arms or legs. Let me see if I can stab through it.”
“No thank you. Tell me—how does a [Jester] become one of the Assassin’s Guild’s deadliest killers? Or is that just a cover? I’m rather dismayed. I had hoped my end would be a bit more…dignified.”

The door standing in the center of the performance area of The Djinni’s Hour. Untouched by the utter destruction around it. Or the Jester’s blade. It had a strange handle. It was familiar, even though he’d never seen it before. The [Necromancer] knew it. He gazed at the door. The Jester saw him smile.
Then they were fighting, her stabbing around one edge of the door, trying to break through it—
He fired a [Deathbolt] around the door and ducked as she flipped over it, stabbing down with the boot-daggers. She flipped back over as he slashed upwards.
Landed. Pisces dodged a slash as she riposted. Both their blades glanced off the wooden frame as they snarled at each other.
Blood in one of her eyes. Red footprints tracing around the door.
Separation. Lareceina pulled one of the daggers out of her shoulder, but her arm hung limp. She wanted to cry. To apologize to Pisces.
All her magic, all her spells and she’d only hit the Jester directly once. Just once. It wasn’t going to save him. She saw Pisces leaning against the door. But he didn’t reach for the handle. She was waiting for him to bleed more. The slightest sheen of sweat on her skin. He beckoned her weakly.
“Would you just finish this? I have an appointment after this.”
She watched blood drip down onto the floor as the Jester swung her blades up.
“You might miss it.”
Pisces chuckled.
“Don’t worry. She’ll see me one way or another.”
He drew himself up slowly, and Lareceina tried not to let the world blur over. She blinked the tears out of her eyes to watch the end of his duel.
 
——
 
He was out of tricks. Even Lareceina’s technique hadn’t swung the odds. Not against her. Pisces was relieved, though. He just had to do his best. Then he’d…
Let his [Innkeeper] down. Make her cry. He tried to push himself up a bit more. Think of something. But what?
There was death magic around him. He’d spent his mana on this building that reeked of undeath, but the Jester wasn’t letting him animate anything. He could parry her—so what? That just put them on equal footing.
Still too fast. Still can’t hurt her enough. It reminded him of a grinning Djinni with a cat’s face.
…Yes. She was cautious. He began to pull mana into his hands. It had almost worked last time. Almost…almost…
The Jester hesitated. She tried to intercept him, sprang forwards as he concentrated. Two slashes. A blow that knocked him backwards, skidding. But he didn’t lose focus.
All the mana he had left in his hands. For a spell.
He didn’t know the spell. It was directionless. Useless. So cold. The antithesis of life. So concentrated, now, that even he couldn’t carry it.
“Pisces. Your hands.”
Lareceina warned him, and he gazed down. That was why the Jester was waiting, again. He saw some of his skin just…peel away. Flesh cracking, turning white, then developing black lines.
It was killing him. He sighed, and the Jester waited. She didn’t want him to touch her. He glanced at the door.
“One second, Erin.”
He took a step—and his heart stopped. A cold hand was grasping it, and the death magic was trying to overwhelm, reanimate—
The [Necromancer] gasped. He had to hold it. Had to, but he was dying. No receptacle. Nothing but his bare hands and…
He looked at his right hand, and the gleaming blade of Stellar Ivory glinted. Pisces gazed at it, then smiled—and forced the magic up the hilt.
“There.”
That’s what he had been trying to do.
His unenchanted rapier was almost all bone, now. Magical bone, but that was all. Perfect for little except storing the one thing that belonged there.
Death magic. He concentrated it until it was running along the blade he knew so well. Infused into every part of it. All the mana he had left. All of the magic in this building he could draw on until it was like a Death’s Door, but better.
A wound into the living world. A little sliver to something that lay beyond. Pisces lifted the rapier, and he heard an oath.
The Jester gazed at the [Necromancer], and he held an enchantment she had never seen before. She had memorized every single one in the Assassin’s Guild’s annals. But they had fewer records on rare classes. Like [Necromancers].
She had to stop him. The Jester cartwheeled forwards, rotating, building speed with each rotation. [Performance: The Comedian’s Death].
Flip and twist in the air. He saw her coming, but he was so focused on the blade, and she was falling, blades twirling, a grin she didn’t feel on her lips. So focused she didn’t see the marble stuck to her pant legs turn white-hot until it exploded—
The detonation would have blown a leg off if the Jester hadn’t sensed the motion and performed an [Aerial Flip] to mitigate the blast. Her skin was still burnt, her costume blown to pieces. She stumbled, half-turned.
The [Mage]. She should have killed her, not marked her for the Naga. Rage was in the Jester’s being, and she raised her daggers to throw, then twisted around and set herself. She exhaled.
Too late.
The blade had changed colors. It still glowed, but instead of the pale ivory, it was…black. The color was black, but it was still bright. The magical color was coating the rapier, like an aura, an enchantment that hurt the eyes.
He let it rest along the floor, as if holding it were heavy, and she saw the floorboards change colors. Where the tip of his blade met the wood, it turned grey. Dusty. Rotten. As if he were killing…
The wood itself. She gritted her teeth.
This is why she had tried to take him by surprise. Why adventurers were hardest.
Counter-levelling. She drew herself up and saw him gazing at that door again. He was drawing strength from it.
“One last dance, [Necromancer]? Now we have a proper duel. To the death, then.”
She licked her lips, watching that blade. She couldn’t let him touch her with it. The bones scattered around them were rattling. Pieces of Stellar Ivory swirling around, as if the sword was reanimating everything.
He was all but dead. Just kill him—he grinned at her, and his eyes were gleaming.
“Death is not the end, Jester. Let me show you.”
His rapier rose, and a little bell of a color she didn’t know hung from the hilt. It made her feel like she wasn’t a master, but an apprentice still on a great journey. Now, it rang.
The Jester listened to it as it rang across the waiting city. Such a beautiful sound. She sighed, then bowed, the fool, the joker with pranks played upon her head by fate. Then she advanced.
 
——
 
Two blades versus one. They stabbed, trying to take him from either side, but a burst of mana forced her back a step. The deathly blade swung over her head, and she ducked it. Unwilling to merely lean out of the way.
He came forwards, a stumbling pirouette, spinning and cutting. She went to punish the opening, her leg kicking up with that hidden dagger in her boots.
A tiny marble exploded, and she jerked back. It hadn’t even gotten near her. Lareceina had flicked it with paralyzed fingers, but it let Pisces press the Jester back. She did a handspring, slashed as she backflipped.
His [Flash Step] carried him into a lunge as she landed. She nearly beheaded him with a sweep of her daggers. He pulled his head back, and she was walking along the counter of the bar. Blocking his rapier with her vibrating blades and kicking glasses at his face. One of her boot-daggers—
She leapt off the counter, and they were fighting along the walls. He kicked a chair at her. She jumped on top of it, kicked him in the face, and was gone. Landed, and he rushed her. Locked blades and felt the rapier sucking at her energy as it drew too close to her skin. Shoved him back, snarling.
He was bleeding from multiple deep wounds, but he was fighting without regard for his reserves. She just had to hold out, wait for the last stand to finish. He couldn’t keep that enchantment up forever.
His face was a mask of concentration and blood. Smiling at her. Not even cursing her for refusing to risk a final clash. Too much respect.
She performed another [Fool’s Dodge], cartwheeling out of a lunge. Hopped back, grasping a dagger with the toes on her right foot. Back against the wall, waiting for him to—
An arm locked around the Jester’s throat and she stabbed backwards, wildly. The [Mage]? Her team? That damn [Prince]? How—
Her blades stabbed into the wall of the nightclub. The Jester felt nothing, but the [Necromancer]—
Ran her through the chest. Then she felt the cold blade sucking her life away. She screamed—ripped herself off the blade, and was stumbling away. He had been staring at the person who’d grabbed her. But who…
She swung back as her Skill tried to knit her flesh, yet she was suddenly slower. Weaker. No potion could heal…again, she put her back to the w—
The arm grabbed for her again, and she spun. Daggers raised. She stared down at the figure who’d caught her by the waist.
A face made of bone. But not a skeleton’s skull. Someone had carved features out of bone. Stellar Ivory that was so finely detailed you could see her short-cropped hair moving. It would have been brown in real life, but this undead was colorless. Mischievous, hazel green flames stared out of carved eyes above smiling lips.
A Human’s face. An [Innkeeper]’s wrought in ivory. Like Venitra, a woman of bone. No…Pisces had never laid eyes on Az’kerash’s Chosen.
This was like Cognita. A woman, but half-formed. Only her upper torso and face were even visible, and they were incomplete. There was not enough Stellar Ivory to animate her, so the pieces ended abruptly, like a jigsaw puzzle. What was there was still…
The undead woman was holding the Jester. She had risen out of the floorboards and grabbed the Jester around the waist. Even now, the floorboards were adhering to her body. Melding upwards, as if she and the floor were one thing.
An undead? The Jester had never seen—the Assassin’s Guild didn’t study—
Her daggers stabbed the fake-Erin’s face, but the bones merely cracked. The undead sank back into the floorboards as the Jester slashed wildly, dodging the [Necromancer] from the side. Then the Jester was leaping, head whirling—
The floor again. Hands reached out, and she stomped, but despite breaking the bones, they just came again as she leapt. This time, the Jester leapt onto a table. That had to be s—
A hand tried to grab her, and she saw the undead rising from the table as the Jester dove again. Instead of following, the undead grabbed a chair and hurled it. Then she was sinking again.
Like a Sandworm or a shark. This entire damn building was her hunting ground. She was melding with the walls. The Jester knew this trick. But that face—
The undead had that face the Jester recognized from the Naga’s files.
“This is your undead?”
She whirled, trying to sneer at him, and the [Necromancer] was looking around. Tracing something only he could see. He’d re-animated the building. She’d thought it was a great opening. A pointless use of mana…fool!
She’d halted for too long. A hand rose, and she was too slow. Again, the undead innkeeper rose, her body already mended. She was holding the Jester’s legs, still smiling. But that glittering flame was colder than any other undead’s the Jester had met.
Other undead just want to kill you. I know why you should die. It’s personal.
The Jester slashed that face, tore free with all the Galas muscle she had. It was just a moment’s opening.
All he needed, of course.
The Scourge stabbed her through the shoulder. Her arm went dead as she slashed at his chest and swept one blade down to free herself. She hopped away on her remaining foot. Fumbling for a spare arm and foot.
A scarecrow of a woman, strings trailing, stuffing coming out of her. The [Necromancer] lunged at her, seeking to end the fight.
She tossed her arm at him and grinned as his eyes widened, and he tried to st—
The explosion knocked them both flat. She did a pratfall and came up, hoping…no. His damn skeleton had pulled him out of the way. Damn armor; he might have broken a rib or two, but her trapped arm hadn’t killed him. And she was…
The Jester eyed the undead skeleton sinking into the floorboards as the Scourge got to his feet. She nodded tightly, then gritted her teeth. She crunched the upper right molar in her mouth and rasped.
“Jester requesting emergency teleport. Right now.”
She heard a muted affirmative as she whirled, teeth bared. She was slow, one-armed. She wasn’t going to make it…
He was leaning on someone supporting him. The smiling undead wearing the [Innkeeper]’s face. Pisces’ blade of undeath was aimed at her, but he had paused.
“Where is it?”
“Take them from me. One bell’s yours.”
She gestured at the golden bells hanging from her, but he was just searching her.
“No. Where’s…your collar?”
He searched her bare neck, her wrists and leggings, and she blinked at him. Then started giggling. She wheezed, leaning on the table, laughing.
“Boy, they don’t leave it where you can break it. It’s right here.”
She tapped her heart. His eyes found hers, and she shook her head. He raised the rapier, and she felt distant magic take hold of her. A second’s teleportation for a Face.
Too slow. She waited in that moment as the rapier shone and saw his center of gravity lower. Lower…until the strange undead laid him down on the floor. Then the rapier stopped glowing, and he lay face-first on the ground.
The Jester ran at him, laughing, blade stabbing, and vanished in a spiral of glowing motes of light.

<Title – A Face of the Assassin’s Guild, Unmasked: Defier of Hidden Blades Assigned!>

The gold bell dinged off Pisces’ head. Which told him he’d only passed out for a second. Just long enough to gain his levels—and for Lareceina to pour a healing potion on top of him.
She was lying on the floor when he raised his head.
“Paralysis. Sucks. You alive? Please be, I’m too emotionally invested in you for you to die right now.”
“How’re you moving?”
He thought she should have been completely helpless given the Jester paralyzing her. Which he’d assumed was for her to take Lareceina as a [Slave] or something. So the Jester was a [Slave]. He’d thought she must be.
Her heart. He should have killed her. He knew that. But he’d realized she was a [Slave], and he couldn’t do it. Just like Wildcard. It was his weakness, Pisces guessed.
Lareceina spoke to the ceiling of the ruined nightclub, which began to crumble inwards. A piece slammed down a dozen feet away. Neither adventurer moved.
“Mana. Forced it through my body and moved it like a puppet. Can’t move well, and it hurts.”
Wham. Another piece fell, and Pisces tried to sit up.
“Dying when masonry hits us would be a terrible way to go.”
“Haha. Yeah.”
Neither one moved. Pisces was healing sluggishly, but the potions he’d looted from Roshal had saved him. He’d taken a few truly deadly wounds in the battle; the armpit stab had been the worst, but he might have saved himself by using death magic on himself. It had slowed the rate he was bleeding out.
He gazed at his hands; there were still faint scar lines from the death mana he’d held. Might be permanent. It beat Yvlon’s hands, or Ceria’s, so he put it out of his mind.
A piece of wood came spiraling down from the ceiling and hit the little wall of floorboards that Bone-Erin conjured to shield Pisces and Lareceina. Both Gold-rank adventurers felt splinters of wood land on them. Lareceina sat up.
“Er—maybe we should cast a barrier.”
“Right. We could leave, but if the Jester had accomplices…”
Pisces was glancing around. He had something to do. Lareceina kept staring at the undead-Erin.
“Is this your newest undead?”
“Sort of. I didn’t know—that is to say, she’s incomplete.”
The Stellar Ivory that made up the undead’s face was incomplete. But she could sink into the floorboards and manipulate buildings he’d animated with death magic. That was…
Very scary if she were a rogue undead. Pisces shuddered to imagine an undead capable of shifting into the walls and ambushing you. He coughed.
“She, um, she looks like—”
“The [Innkeeper]. Whom you’re in love with? I don’t know if she’d appreciate this…”
Lareceina waved a hand, and Pisces hesitated.
“It’s not romantic. Platonic—it was an unconscious thing! I didn’t expect it. And I…I was doing everything I could in that fight. All the bits and pieces. Lareceina, thank you. Without you, I’d have been—and the [Mana Burst Parry] and [Death’s Blade] spell were because I was thinking about your techniques!”
She blinked at him.
“Is that what the spells are called?”
“Yes, they are. I imagine you could do the parry technique yourself.”
She nodded slowly, eyes lighting up.
“It looks easy enough, but the timing could get you killed. I can’t believe we survived.”
“She was a cautious Face. I think she wanted to bait out every attack I had and was wary about me having something else. I also wonder if she wanted me alive, for all her talk.”
Pisces rubbed at his armpit as he conjured a little dome of bones for them to hide under. Lareceina shuddered.
“That would explain it. Although she might have just been psyched out.”
“By what? Me being a [Necromancer]?”
“No, your face.”
“…What about it?”
The [Compression Magus] opened her mouth, peered at Pisces, then turned her head.
“If you don’t understand, I don’t feel like explaining it right now. I sense you won’t get it. One question: what was that door that appeared mid-fight?”
The door. Pisces pushed himself up slowly, and it was still there. He walked towards it.
“That’s…I think it’s her. I need to answer it. I’ll be back. Just pretend I’m hiding if I—”
It was her. He knew it. He turned back.
“Lareceina? Thank you, I owe you my life. I will repay you, but I just have to—”
She was brushing at her face, shaking her head.
“I think you’d have been…well, maybe I did save your life, but I didn’t feel very useful in that fight. I need to brush up on my close-combat techniques. Kusal and Leo would have made that a lot easier. Go do what you have to. If that is Erin Solstice, you have to see the person you’re in love with. Just don’t leave me to clean up all this mess or the royalty might actually execute me. You’re lucky I like you; I’d have left your Captain behind in a heartbeat.”
She sat back with a groan in the inside of the little shelter, and Pisces hesitated. The bones of Nekhret and his possessions were scattered across the entire damn place—what hadn’t been vaporized in the fight. Yet somehow…he knew that the door wouldn’t take long.
Just a second, really. How he knew it, he wasn’t sure, but he trusted the door. He began to nod, scratched at the back of his neck, and hesitated.
Hm? It was an odd feeling. Almost like he was on the practice courts, but entirely mental. Pisces frowned, then tried it anyways.
“Well, I, ah, don’t know if I want to fight a second Face ever again, Lareceina. But I would, for you. I shudder to imagine what I’ll have to do for a favor since I owe you far more.”
She blinked at him, and he blinked at her. Then he closed his mouth.
Was that a [Seduction Counter]—?
Pisces strode over to the door, opened it, paused a second, then vanished. Lareceina stayed where she was, then laid back down on the floor. Then she began kicking around in a circle.
How he had picked up on that? She hadn’t even been obvious about her feelings! Did he mean—? Well, obviously she liked him. Who wouldn’t admire someone with his principles?
She was not prepared for Pisces to come out the door a second later. But that moment…
To him, it was still occurring in a place only two people existed.
 
——
 
It did feel like a dream. As if he had died and this were just…a pleasant way of letting him down. One moment, he was levelling, the next, he was walking through the void on a path of cobblestones towards a building suspended in the middle of nowhere.
With the woman he most wanted to talk to waiting for him.
It wasn’t love, at least, the kind that he thought many people assumed it was. Pisces was no expert on love. He felt like he’d mostly peaked in Wistram on that front, to be honest. He’d been his most popular then, and after that, it had been far less easy to get to know people.
Your average [Necromancer] tended to be male, at least, the kind you found in cabals, and regardless, they weren’t all that fun to be around sometimes. Pisces could also admit he hadn’t been at his best back then. Hygiene, always an issue…
Why was he thinking about that? He’d just fought a Face—
But he was somehow more nervous than then. Because…he kept slowing to peer at her. It was her, wasn’t it? Was she the same woman who was in Baleros? She looked…
Different.
She felt it. This new place, well, that suited her. If Erin Solstice had sailed across Nerrhavia’s Fallen on a ship christened ‘The Wandering Ship’, Pisces Jealnet would have blinked for about five seconds, then gotten on board and asked her if she now served adequate seafood.
He would believe anything of her. Just as Ceria had once said—they were her team. His life had changed when he’d met her in that inn, long ago. He was just worried he’d disappoint her.
She was gazing at him like he was a stranger too. He halted halfway up the gazebo’s steps and took in her discolored hair. The scars.
One look at Erin Solstice, the real Erin, and he saw how flawed and fake the skeleton he’d made of her was. That was just the [Innkeeper] in his heart. The one he remembered, longed to see, with a frying pan in hand when things were at their darkest.
The first one he’d met, who’d fed a hungry, lost [Necromancer] with no good reason other than he was hungry.
The last time he’d seen her…her face had been bruised and swollen. Magical paint and seawater clinging to her skin. A flaming pink hat on her head, eyes locked on the thing only she could see.
This Erin, the one who made him halt in his tracks, was the woman who’d survived that moment. No part of her wasn’t scarred.
Her hair wasn’t the same color. It was regrowing, but it had fallen out and was uneven on one side, reshorn so it was deliberate instead of…it was seared into different colors, white or multicolored in places. Magical contamination he’d only seen in textbooks in Wistram.
The same with her skin. Erin was noticeably thinner. It looked like someone had carved skin off her arms with a bloodless blade. Odd, puckered skin from more spell damage. But it was her wrists, her neck, that revealed the truest scars. Discolored skin burned dark. Collar and manacles.
He hadn’t seen it the last time. Now, Pisces reached for his rapier and almost turned around and left this place. Excused himself so he could walk over to Roshal and come back after…
Her expression stopped him. She was wearing strange clothing: a shirt that looked like it had been woven from a single blade of grass, but detailed, soft tufts of dandelion’s fuzz padding her elbows and shoulders. Leggings made of some dark chitin, like a bug’s.
A stranger he might have taken for some twisted, alternate version of Erin Solstice if they’d passed on the streets of Liscor. Missing the top of her right ear. But that hesitant expression became a smile when she saw him and they locked eyes.
It was wearier than he had ever remembered seeing on her face. A tired woman full of the fears she never cared to share. Uncertainty, oh, yes.
But it was still the same smile as the first one he’d earned from her. It felt like it gave Pisces more than he could return. A smile just for him, welcoming him into her home, wherever it was and however strange it got. That was how he knew it was her each and every time.
Pisces still wanted to go and set all her foes to flight. But he was tired, and there was a chair waiting for him across the chess table.
Too weak. Too weak, too far…he sat down across the chess board from her, adjusting his robes. Realizing they were almost torn off his body, revealing the scarred armor underneath.
“I, ah—hello, Erin. I’m sorry I’m a bit of a mess. And that I took a moment to reply. I was occupied.”
“The Pavilion said…what happened to you? You look like you’ve been in a war.”
Even her voice sounded different. Maybe a bit raspier, deeper. Or perhaps it wasn’t her bubbly cadence that held the real Erin. He drank in how she looked once more and then glanced back. Shrugged, because he’d almost forgotten the Jester.
“Just a continuation of the war you were in.”
He favored her with a slight smile, a self-depreciating quirk of the lips. She sat there, and then her face filled with guilt.
“Roshal?”
She knew it in a moment. And the guilty joy that had been on her face was extinguished so fast he tried to lie.
“N—”
No lies here. The rules had popped into his head as he’d entered. Pisces hesitated and chose his words carefully.
“It was purely my own affair. Nothing to do w…it was entirely selfish on…there were a lot of extenuating circumstances.”
He couldn’t tell those lies. Not to her. But she looked so guilty…Erin was shaking her head.
“Chandrar. Chandrar. I knew you were all there, but I’ve been too scared to use this Skill. This is the [Pavilion of Secrets], Pisces. You know the rules, but I could have—I’ve been guilty, and they tried to kill you, didn’t they? Are you okay?”
“I’ll be fine, Erin. I beat the Face they sent at me.”
“A Face?”
“…Only one.”
Lying was hard, and he was not mentally ready for this. Erin sat up, then sat back in her chair. She seemed…she rubbed at her chest.
“Sorry. I’ve been a bit sick. And distracted. Stupid stuff. I—you were the first person I thought of, after the inn. I took too long to contact you, and there was this thing with Garry.”
“Garry? Is he well?”
“…Yes? Now he is. He was dressing up as Santa and delivering bread to Drakes. Then they blew him up, but he survived, and—yeah.”
Pisces let that information roll off him. Solstice event. Then he tried to parse it and started grinning. Erin grew flustered.
“I’m very sorry, Pisces. I didn’t…I wasn’t thinking of you. I was asking the [Pavilion of Secrets] who was in the most mortal danger at that moment and it must have not been you at that time. He was, but then I developed tunnel vision, and I was fighting with Ulvama, and—your robes.”
She looked at him again, and he glanced down.
Ah, that was a lot of blood on them. The charm that meant they couldn’t get dirty had been shredded with the fabric. Pisces touched the robes and felt…a bit of a pang. Ryoka had bought them for him a long time ago. There were plenty of better robes he could have bought. But these had been his.
“It’s just clothing, Erin. I am fine. I didn’t even lose any digits, see?”
He hesitated, then tucked his hands under the table. Erin’s eyes were drawn downwards.
“I’m glad you didn’t lose your hands. What do they look like?”
“…Hands? They’re perfectly serviceable as far as I know, Erin.”
“Pisces, show me your hands.”
His damned mouth. When he showed her the cracked skin and damage from the death magic, she just exhaled. Pisces began to speak quickly.
“That was my own doing! You see, I was using death magic to create a powerful spell—it was pure improvisation, really. A powerful new attack. My most dangerous magic by far! It’ll revolutionize how I fight. Also where I need to fight from; I’ll need to be up front, but not even Colthei can insult me anymore. And my other spells and Skills—it’s a resounding victory. I chased a Face off and…and…”
“Roshal’s still after you. They won’t stop until they’ve got you, Pisces. I’m so, so sorry for not talking sooner.”
Her quiet voice, and the way she gazed at her own hands made Pisces reach out. He grabbed her arm, scattering chess pieces off the table.
“I—sorry. Erin, don’t blame yourself for this. This was my doing. I was just…killing [Slavers]. Raiding caravans. I did it with Merr and by myself. I raised hordes, and I slaughtered them. The only person who put my team and myself in such danger was me.”
She looked at him, bleak.
“But why did that happen, Pisces? Did they try something or…?”
He gazed past her and sat back in the chair. He was so tired, but he wouldn’t have closed his eyes for anything.
“I just…met a little girl they’d taken as a [Slave], Erin. I couldn’t stop myself. I tried to kill all of them because I couldn’t do anything less. Because of you and what they did to me and everyone else, yes. But they deserve it.”
His head bowed, and he sat there. Then he was filled with fear. But he had to say it. Honesty…Pisces looked up and gave Erin a wretched smile.
“Erin, I’m rather afraid I’ve become a monster. I—I’m sorry, because you put such faith in me. But of late, I don’t think I’m better than anyone else. I think I’ve stepped upon that dark path that all [Necromancers] seem fated to walk. Because I enjoyed killing the [Slavers]. It felt right.”
That was the thing he hadn’t said out loud. He’d realized it after a while. He had stepped off the cliff and was falling, and he couldn’t stop. He waited for her to pull away, tell him how disappointed she was, or just…
Erin blinked at Pisces, and the guilt burning behind her eyes turned to surprise. Then she studied him and, abruptly, threw her arms around him.
“You silly, smelly [Necromancer]. You could change a hundred thousand times and it’d always be you. C’mere.”
She tried to ruffle his hair, and he protested.
“Erin! Erin, I’m serious! Stop that.”
She was laughing all of a sudden! Laughing, and he feared she didn’t understand…then Erin stopped. She coughed, and he grew worried at the rattling in her lungs. But it was gone in a moment, and she wiped her mouth.
“Sorry. I still got a bit of that soul fracture stuff. Pisces…you’re the bravest, best guy I know. You just pretend really well you’re not, sometimes. And you killing evil people doesn’t change that.”
“But I’ve killed…”
“They keep [Slaves], Pisces. You and I have both seen what that is. They put me on a ship. They took you to Roshal. I’d kill them all, one-by-one, if I had to.”
Erin’s eyes were burning again. Not her hat. She leaned over the table, and she shook her head.
“You silly goober. ‘Look at me, I’m so evil for killing [Slavers]. Bleh, I’m a terrible person’!”
She made little devil horns on her head, and it was so silly that Pisces started laughing. Chuckling, then laughing as he hadn’t done since—since—
Since they’d sat in an inn and done this last time. Erin started laughing too.
“Hey, don’t make fun of me! I’m making fun of—listen, pal—ah, you dummy! Why hasn’t Ceria, Colth, or Yvlon told you how stupid you’re being?”
He stopped laughing abruptly.
“I got separated from them. And it’s…it’s not been perfect.”
Erin blinked at him, then leaned forwards. She gestured at the table, and he went to pick up the pieces that had fallen, but they were all arrayed nice and evenly in a moment. He went to move a pawn, but Erin just eyed the chess set, then brushed an arm across the table.
It all vanished. Then she stood, and the world changed.
For a moment, they sat in The Wandering Inn, and the common room smelled of Calescent’s food. It was cold—but the door to the beach garden was open. Pisces’ eyes widened, and his heart hurt. He half-rose…but then saw Erin’s face.
Regret, sadness, longing.
She banished it.
Then they were in the [Garden of Sanctuary], hers, staring up at the night sky full of stars. But that too vanished after a moment. Erin Solstice stood in the gazebo, the world flickering as she tried to find something…
And found nothing. The world vanished, even the gazebo, and then they stood in the void, a sea of infinity, and she sat down. Just sat on the ground. Pisces walked over and sat next to her. He pulled his knees up to his chest, and she murmured.
“Tell me, Pisces. Tell me how it’s been, please?”
So he closed his eyes, and because they had ages…
He told her.
 
——
 
The two sat there a long time. In the real world, another Pisces was doing things like collecting his possessions, continuing to heal, extricating himself and Lareceina from the crumbling nightclub, and rendering some explanations as her team raced over.
He pitied that Pisces. Because here was where he wanted to be.
“The Horns of Hammerad, fighting? Not in sync?”
Erin finished listening to his account of how things felt so…so bad. It was a relief for Pisces to tell her about his gripes with Ceria’s leadership, the way Colth was acting. And his own guilt for not always being with them. He waited for her to pass judgement, even if she found him in the wrong, but Erin just laughed softly.
“Some things never change.”
“What? Erin, it has not been pleasant. Without Ksmvr—and Vofea—we’ve been at each other’s throats. We nearly killed other adventurers. I went on my own because I couldn’t trust my team and—and Yvlon’s sick and—”
The [Innkeeper] just chuckled more and waved a hand. Little images flashed across the void, tiny as motes of light. Memories.
“Pisces. Do you remember when you guys formed a team after the crypt? You didn’t even have Ksmvr, I just suggested him last-minute. And you and Yvlon hated each other. Remember?”
“I…well, yes. But we worked things out.”
“Sure you did. And there were times you guys got along great. Right up until Yvlon nearly beat you all down because she was so mad. And Ceria’s circlet was going nuts, and—you guys always fight.”
“Not always.”
But he saw her point. There had been moments when he’d thought he’d quit this stupid adventuring team at the start. Wondered what he was doing and…Erin shook her head.
“Colth’s the new kid. He’s been on, what, one big adventure with you? Technically, there was the Stalker raid, but that was pretty short. It was just the Crossroads and the sea battle, really. This is your second long adventure. Of course he’s not fitting in. Low self-esteem issues, that guy.”
“Colth. Colthei. Are we talking about the same fellow? He’s always telling us what real Named-rankers do…”
“Well, yeah, Pisces. Don’t you think all of his senior friends from Larracel’s inn tell him that all the time?”
Pisces opened his mouth, and it was like Erin had levered his head open and inserted a shovelful of understanding. He closed it.
“—He does talk about the inn a lot. And I had observed how he told us stories of them treating him—”
Erin shook her head as she conjured an image of Larracel and her Haven.
“I wish I’d hung out with Larra more, but I feel like we’d have fought. Now? I think we could get along a bit better. I think if she realized how Colth was treated, she’d say he wasn’t being treated fair, Pisces. The guy was a [Slave], and he’s a [Supporter]; he was a kid when they were all Named-rank. They never really let him grow up around them. With you, he’s trying to be the adult, but all the ‘veterans’ sucked.”
“I hadn’t thought about it like that. There was this moment where he didn’t want me to talk with a [Trader] because he was worried she’d prey on me…”
“See? He’s trying to look out for you, and maybe it’s a good lesson, but he’s doing it wrong. Colth’s problem is that he’s good at lots of stuff.”
“…How is that a problem? I don’t follow.”
Again, Erin chuckled.
“It’s a problem because when he’s not good at something, I think he doesn’t realize it. He thinks he’s got to know it all. But you know what? If you guys said, ‘Colth, this is how it’s gotta be, back us up’, I think he might be happy. He’s a [Supporter], not a [Leader]. Sort of, y’know. In the class?”
She waggled her eyebrows at him, and Pisces opened his mouth to refute this Erin-logic…and then just laughed.
“I wish you’d called us all ages ago, Erin.”
He regretted saying that because it was true and it hurt her. She turned her head away.
“I’ve been selfish, Pisces. I was using this place to hurt myself at first. A lot of Skills, actually. Then I stayed away because I was afraid of how everyone would blame me.”
“For what?”
He had no idea what anyone could possibly blame Erin for. Being the target of an evil being’s attack? Getting kidnapped? Erin gazed at him, wide-eyed, then shook her head.
“You really are…hey, Pisces?”
“Yes, Erin?”
“Sorry.”
She leaned against his shoulder, staring into the distance. He couldn’t quite see her face, so he just held still.
“What do you need to apologize for?”
“I’m sorry because I’ve been having a great time in Baleros. I’ve been selfish and not talking to the people I should.”
He gazed down at her wrists. Scarred so badly. And her hair. And her arms which looked…Pisces whispered.
“A great time?”
“As much as I deserve. But you guys didn’t deserve that. You followed me and saved me when I was fighting at sea. You all nearly died, and I didn’t even ask about you for…I don’t know. Ksmvr and Vofea are still missing. Some [Innkeeper], huh?”
He tried to think of words to say.
“I…don’t blame you for that, Erin. You needed help. Vofea told us, so we went. It’s as simple as that. Even if you had known what was coming, if you’d asked, we’d have agreed. I know that. If you threw us into hell itself, you wouldn’t do it without a reason.”
She didn’t answer him. She was only silent, and he didn’t break the silence until she sniffed. Not like he did, haughtily. Just an intake of shuddering breath.
“I’m sorry. I was afraid you’d hate me. Or that you were hurt, and I’d never be able to forgive myself…”
“You were kidnapped by Roshal too, Erin. You survived. I only wish I’d come sooner. And look at you, you’re…”
Fine. He couldn’t say it. Erin glanced up at Pisces, then down at her wrists. She felt at her neck.
“I had a fight with Ulvama, Pisces. She’s with us…I’ve been a really terrible person a lot of the time. Selfish. I’m—I’m not okay, Pisces. I think I broke something on that ship. Or afterwards. Just like every time my friends die.”
He stared at his clenched fists. They were trembling. Pisces shook his head.
“They can’t break us. Not you, Erin. I’m—I’m the one who’s not better. I nearly got myself killed. My team is still in danger. I did it all for something I know won’t change…and I want to do it again. You say I’m not monstrous for killing them? I’d bathe in their blood, Erin. I could kill a thousand of them each day and sleep without problems. That may not be wrong, but it’s not ‘alright’. I’m afraid of what they might make me into.”
Someone who killed without a thought. He hadn’t ever wanted to take lives, but he had done it so easily—Erin glanced up at him, and she understood that, he thought. She brushed at her eyes.
“If you’re worried you’re evil, Pisces, then show me how evil you are. Show me the Necromancer in your heart, or someone as bad as Yazdil.”
He exhaled.
“I…well, I can’t. If it’s there—”
“You can show me any memory you want. Say something horrible, go on.”
“I can’t when you’re watching me.”
He protested, and she chuckled. Put out an arm and hugged him, surprisingly strong.
“Pisces. I have a thousand things to tell you. A thousand things to say. But after hearing what you’ve been doing, none of that is to say, ‘stop, you’re wrong’.”
“But I can’t be better than they are, Erin.”
He whispered it, and she frowned at him. Then pushed herself up. It seemed to take great effort, but then she was standing. He remembered when she’d been bound to a wheelchair. She even felt taller, but perhaps that was her level. Older…she stuck out a hand.
“I never said you couldn’t be angry, Pisces. You have more right to be angry than anyone. You’re allowed to hate them. If you think you’re turning evil or going too far…I can’t read your soul.”
You can’t? He just gazed up at her as she smiled down at him.
“…But I can do what I’ve always done. Which is watch you, Pisces. If you go too far, if I think you’re slipping, I’ll tell you. Until then? Arise, my necromancer.”
He gazed at her fingers, then took her hand, and she pulled him up. Erin patted Pisces on the shoulders.
“I wasn’t there for you. I’m still not. I’m lost on another continent, and it’s taking a long time for me to find my way back. I think…I’m figuring it out. But I promise I’m gonna come back home, Pisces. Maybe different. But when I do—I’ll be there for you again. Okay, Pisces?”
“You’ve been there every moment I needed you. I was just relieved we made it when we did. If only we’d been a bit faster.”
He gazed down at her, and she shook her head, exasperated, eyes shining—then she flicked the hair on his forehead back.
“I’m so dumb. I shouldn’t have worried. It’s easy to talk to you. Ceria, now, she might be weird if she’s actually cursed. But I’ll find the others. Each one. Ksmvr, Vofea…everyone. Just—”
She stared across the empty void.
“There’s so much going on, Pisces. And I can’t be there.”
He touched her arm.
“I don’t expect you to. This is enough.”
She started and shook her head reflexively.
“Don’t be stupid, Pisces. It’s not. I’m leaving you all behind while you’re fighting and dying. I can’t even save a silly [Baker]. I just hurt people around me—”
Her fingers dug into her flesh, and he stopped her as he shook his head. Then he turned and gestured to the door.
“Your door saved my life, Erin. When I saw it, I knew it was you. That got me through my duel.”
“It did? I thought it felt weird when I was waiting, but…”
Her head rose urgently, but Pisces just sniffed, then exhaled. He couldn’t even pretend with her anymore. He just rested a hand on her shoulder.
“That’s all we need, Erin. That’s all we’ve ever needed from you. A moment of encouragement, a drink, or some food when we’re tired. A place to rest. We don’t want you to solve every problem in our lives. We just keep coming back for those moments of wonder we can’t capture anywhere else.”
She shook her head, averting her gaze.
“I’m out of wonder, Pisces. Out of flames, and…I try not to charge you all for it, but the tab always ends up being everything. That’s what it costs to be one of my guests, my friends. I can’t repay it. You’re supposed to be my guests.”
The [Innkeeper] wanted to turn away, but he wouldn’t let her. The [Necromancer] clung to her, for support now, because he was so tired.
“How many of these things did you start? Did you start any war? Every monster, each time you call on us, it’s to save someone else. You never told us to do anything. I have always done what I wanted, Erin. You just…make it easier to be that better person. You may say you cannot help us, far as we are. But Erin, I’m tired. It’s been…a long few days.”
She looked up at him, and whatever he read in her, saw in her changed appearance, she seemed to take in an ocean of changes. She just nodded.
“I’m sorry, Pisces. I’m sorry I haven’t asked until now.”
“That’s quite alright, Erin. But if I may…may I lean on your shoulder a second? I just need to rest.”
She gazed at him, then straightened a bit.
“Yeah, sure.”
He did, lightly, and smiled. He felt then like he could keep standing for a long time.
“I have my team with me, some of them. And another team—a good one—I need to get back to. I am hardly alone. But Erin, if we have a moment, could you tell me about what you’ve been through? And I do have more to share, if you’ll listen.”
“Of course.”
After a bit, Pisces took a step into the empty infinity, and Erin walked with him. She supported his weight as Erin began to talk, and Pisces listened as she sketched out a world as seen through a Fraerling’s eyes, and he noticed how she lied, by omission or just her perspective. But he wouldn’t have interrupted her for anything.
In time, he was strong enough to walk on his own. That was all he needed. Just a moment.
Then it was his turn to tell her more. More and more until he wondered if the other Pisces was…
How long has passed, neither could have said. Erin eventually broke off.
“Darn. I’m the only person who has to spend time here. We could do this for ages. But Ulvama will be worried. And I’m, uh, hungry.”
Her stomach was rumbling. Pisces smiled.
“Why don’t you just call me later?”
“Why don’t I?”
She said it as if the thought hadn’t occurred to her, then a spark appeared in her hazel eyes, and she grinned.
“I will. You’ve gotta go back to doing your Pisces thing, right? The Scourge of Roshal rides again.”
He shook his head.
“That’s not me. It’s just an idea. It’s Bearig and Merr and everyone.”
“Sure it is, buddy.”
“I’m serious, Erin.”
“Okay, pal.”
He caught her arm as she walked him back to the door, and his heart hurt. His hand was trembling suddenly.
“Erin. I can’t even save one girl. I don’t deserve to be called anything. Even if…”
Even if there was an opportunity in the Jester’s attack on him. Erin’s eyes flicked to Pisces, and she saw it in him. She was, after all, far smarter than most people gave her credit for. Then her wondrous gaze twinkled, and for a moment, she laughed.
“Pisces, you made a promise. Not to her or me, but to yourself. If I were Roshal, I’d tremble. Well, actually, if I were Roshal, I’d kill myself. But you know what I mean.”
“I might be too late. I might fail.”
His entire body was shaking, now, with nerves. Back to fear. She turned, and like always, the [Innkeeper] watched one of her first guests wavering. So she gave him a little push. Just in a different way each time.
“You’ve got to try. So let’s make it official, Pisces.”
She closed her eyes. Then her lips moved—and she lifted something up in her hands. A glowing little scroll. She posted it into the side of the doorframe with a hammer and a glowing nail, and he heard it.
Toc.
Then she pushed at his back, laughing. Cackling, really. She flung the door open, and he heard her as she kicked him out of her inn. But he was running before his foot passed through the doorway, and he opened his eyes.
 
<Personal Heroic Quest — Save Her!>
Find Lleta, Pisces. Bring her to safety, no matter what it takes.
Optional Condition (Impossible): Save them all.
 
——
 
The television was abuzz with the latest. Pisces the Scourge attacked in a nightspot by a Face of Chandrar and…victorious?
No one had footage of the battle. The most you could see were explosions, parts of the nightclub blowing outwards, the animation spell before that—
Some eyewitnesses, but everyone had fled when the fighting had started. One Stitch-girl described being held captive and Pisces the Bane coming back in to save her—
Roshal’s Slaver Guild, unavailable for comment.
Ceria Springwalker, unavailable for comment.
Plenty of people available for comment. All of whom didn’t count, weren’t important, and who didn’t know anything.
Prince Weith was fighting with Princess Lithic to be on television as an exasperated Drassi tried to get anything useful out of them.
“—attacked under our royal protection! They shall regret that, Assassin’s Guild or not!”
“Right, right, but if you could move aside so I can see the club? I get it, you bravely ran away. Also, your kingdom tried to assassinate me, so shut up.”
With that, she leaned out of the scrying orb again. She dangled from her waist as everyone recoiled.
“Darn, I can only get this far out. Also, it only works on one person at a time. Excuse me! Pisces? Sneeze twice if you’re dead! Can anyone actually brave carry me up there for a look?”
The sight of a Drake half-leaning over her desk, tail suspended in the air, was a good sideshow. But everyone was waiting.
Alive meant a lot of things. How many limbs did he have? How much poison? And had he levelled?
About two hours had passed, and the only people who’d gone in were Wildcard; the [Soldiers] were keeping everyone else back, even the royals.
Well, the royalty were highly attached to their own heads, and if the Face were around…a second attempt when everyone had let their guards down was very likely, as Weith and Lithic well knew. But they’d been insulted, so they were preparing to castigate Drassi before heading up.
Sadly, they lost the momentum to Prince Yosoc, who arose, tossing his cloak out behind him.
“As I was sadly poisoned, I missed the fighting. But let it not be said that I, Prince Yosoc, hide behind [Reporters]. Miss Drassi, I should be delighted to give you a view of the fighting, even should the entire Assassin’s Guild fall upon my head!”
That bastard. He had the scrying orb and was ascending a [Light Bridge] spell before Weith and Lithic could move, and his bodyguards were fighting theirs as they tried to grab the orb from him. However, the floorshow gave way to a figure appearing in the ruined opening of The Djinni’s Hour. Everyone recoiled, and Yosoc held his cloak up like a shield…then paused.
Oh.
It was only Lareceina. She had blood on her robes, was filthy, and looked like someone had, well, collapsed half a building on top of her. She limped down the stairs with Kusal and Leo flanking her.
“Is that…the team the Horns fought? No, they were on guard duty. At least one of them earned their keep.”
Kusal and Leo were very unhappy by Drassi’s commentary, but she was taking no prisoners today. Nor slaves.
Lareceina halted midway down the [Light Bridge] and cast a simple [Loudness] spell. Without preamble, she called out.
“I am Lareceina of the Gold-rank team Wildcard. We have executed our task in defending Pisces Jealnet, known as the Scourge of Roshal—or possibly Bane—from a Face of the Assassin’s Guild. The Jester has fled after prolonged battle, and I hereby declare my contract fulfilled in good faith given what is about to happen next.”
Everyone stared at her. She was making sense, but not being the most helpful about actual details they wanted. Lareceina went on.
“Furthermore, I would like to take this moment to clarify that my team, Wildcard, are upstanding Gold-rank adventurers that neither endorse nor support Pisces the Bane’s attacks on Roshal. We took this contract purely out of monetary desire as well as a favor to the crown of Nerrhavia’s Fallen. I personally disagree with any breaking of laws—”
At this point, Kusal and Leo rolled their eyes, and Drassi leaned forwards.
“Prince Yosoc? You wouldn’t happen to have a brick you could huck at her head, would you?”
He was obligingly hunting around for one when Lareceina broke off. She had insisted on maintaining her team’s good reputation, or at least, neutrality with everyone. Given how nasty a Face of the Assassin’s Guild was…even her teammates couldn’t really blame her.
Really, Pisces had to admire her too. Because Lareceina was an untruther on the level of Bird the Liar. No one was actively casting [Detect Truth] on her, so she was getting away with it. Drassi’s smile was fixed as she watched Lareceina, eyes flicking past her to the open club.
Good statements from Wildcard. If Pisces could have avoided a second attack from the Assassin’s Guild on him…well, he wouldn’t. But Wildcard weren’t ready to make an enemy of Roshal. They had to live here for the moment.
He had promised to go home with someone. But first…he had made another promise.
When he emerged in the opening above the street, everyone pointed. Lareceina kept talking for a bit, then Kusal nearly kicked her down the light bridge. She turned, and he stood there.
He could have changed clothing and freshened up in the two hours he’d had. But he’d felt, accurately, that this left more of a dramatic impression. And he’d been waiting to know what Erin said.
Now…the <Quest> was in his mind. He didn’t think she could see him. That was okay. He’d tell her in a bit. Or they’d record it.
“Pisces!”
Drassi broke the silence first. She had [Greater Resistance: Surprise]. Pisces nodded to her, but he began walking down the [Light Bridge] spell.
He still hurt all over. But Wildcard had helped patch him up a bit more and gathered all the damn bones. He hoped he hadn’t missed any. They’d done a bit of talking, waited to see if the Jester was coming back—he suspected she might have teleported all the way back to Lailight Scintillation, or a base at least.
She would return. But as Erin had alluded to, there was something Pisces had to do.
“Pisces, I’m glad you’re alive! You’re on television. Are you, uh…dying? Because we can get a [Healer]. Ancestors, he’s covered in blood.”
Drassi called out as Pisces did his best not to trip and fall face-first down the ramp. Which was a real possibility. New levels or not, he was exhausted.
“Yonder stands a true adventurer, one who has fought a Face of Chandrar! Better to fight a sandstorm of blades than to cross blades with one—and still he stands. I ask, is this a Gold-rank adventurer to fight a Face, whom all and sundry know is above Level 50? Or is this a Named-rank adventurer?”
He punched a fist into the air, still holding the brick, and he was pulling at the people on the street. They began to cheer. Yosoc was manufacturing a moment for Pisces.
It wasn’t even a bad one, and he did have social Skills. But Pisces interrupted the [Prince]’s flow by reaching Yosoc…and walking straight past him. Drassi half-turned, holding a microphone out.
“Er, Pisces? Pisces, Drassi here. Selys’ friend? C’mon, I served you drinks at—wait, is he doing that thing where he walks out and collapses? Does he have arrows in his back? No? Good, phew.”
He didn’t say anything. He didn’t turn. He just walked down the [Light Bridge], onto the street, and past Prince Weith and Lithic. They wanted to clap him on the shoulders, pose for the cameras…he strode past them. The people on the street began to jostle forwards—then pulled back.
Possibly because he’d just drawn his rapier. The blade was still made of Stellar Ivory, and it would remain that way. Unenchanted. After all, Pisces had just learned the only enchantment he needed.
An active enchantment. He walked towards the [Soldiers], who took one look at him and slammed to the side of the street. One of them shouted.
“If any [Assassin] is among us—kindly reveal yourselves, as we are but humble soldiers of Nerrhavia’s Fallen and not part of a second bloodbath!”
‘Second bloodbath’ also worked to clear people away. Chandrarians were a very funny people, Pisces decided. Self-aware about stories.
He kept moving. He saw people parting in front of him, pointing, staring at his bloody armor…
“Pisces? Pisces. What’s going on? Is the Face around?”
Drassi appeared next to him as Prince Yosoc jogged to keep up. Pisces’ head was turning right and left. He hoped she was playing dumb. He hoped no one got it. But he didn’t know…
It was, in the end, a very technical thing he was counting on. Wording. He bet Ceria would get it and only hoped she could tell Yisame. The [Queen] was a savvy woman. But he supposed he had to say it to give her an excuse. So he turned and glanced at Drassi.
Her eyes were wide and full of worry. But there was also that strange expression there. Pride. She was looking at him like…it was embarrassing, so Pisces glanced past her. Down the street.
“Drassi. I was instructed by Queen Yisame to return to the capital. By the order of Nerrhavia’s Fallen, she gave me clear instructions. She forbade me from attacking any member of Roshal or anyone aligned with the Guild of Slavers. Any unprovoked attack would incur her personal wrath.”
“…Okay? And how do you feel about that, Pisces?”
The Drake stared at Pisces. He couldn’t tell if she was playing dumb; she was on camera. But maybe there was a twinkle in her eyes, suddenly.
Pisces just turned and kept moving. During the two hours he’d been gathering his strength, he had been making a crude plan of sorts. Very basic.
One of the things Wildcard had brought was a map. And he’d been staring at it for a while as Lareceina cast some [Message] spells for him. Just polite inquiries. Harmless. In theory.
He was striding now, blade still bared, and Yosoc turned the scrying orb as he went. The [Prince] was mouthing too.
“Of course the Queen would do nothing less to an ally such as Roshal’s. But they have offended her—with some cause. It shall be a matter for the Court of Silks, much less an assassination in royal presence, but there are precedents. Why, though, would…”
He figured it out around the same time as some of the viewers in the audience. Princess Lithic got it and drew in a sharp breath.
Prince Weith took a bit longer. He glanced around suspiciously. Pisces was jogging, now. Moving down the street faster.
You could just see the little gears turning in people’s heads. One of the Mad Ones, who had come out to see what was going on, was spelling it out for a few in the audience.
“He’s talking about what he was told he couldn’t do. If he attacked anyone first, she’d have to have him arrested. The key word is ‘unprovoked’. Now, there was just a Face of the Assassin’s Guild, which belongs to Roshal, attacking him. We call this ‘provocation’. Also, Adventurer Lareceina did say ‘what comes next’. That’s called foreshadowing. Now—”
Ah.
It was the kind of wording a [Necromancer] paid attention to. Or an [Innkeeper]. Some people still didn’t get it until they saw Pisces’ jogging transition into a full run. Then they stared at the sword. His eyes, which were intent as he ran down the street.
His name. Which everyone knew—but—but this was a city. He hadn’t attacked in here because of the law. Because…
No one had tried to attack him inside the city’s gates. But if there was any cause that might excuse a man’s actions, perhaps ‘nearly being assassinated by a Face of Roshal’ might…
At that point, an alarm bell began to ring. Not [Dangersense]; that had been going off in every single person’s head who had the Skill, oh, half an hour ago. They’d put it down to something else or the Face and the Scourge fighting.
The alarm bell in this case was an actual alarm bell, an enchanted one in the Slaver’s Guild. It was the one you rang when everyone had to just run. It was loud, and yes, it had been triggered by the Slaver’s Guild’s headquarters in Lailight Scintillation.
They weren’t idiots. The moment they’d seen Pisces draw that sword, some of the people there had figured out what might happen. Sadly—
The television was on a five minute delay.
 
——
 
The [Slavers] were pouring out of their Guild and into the streets, trying to saddle horses or just ride or run.
That helped Pisces quite a bit; they should have hidden inside and locked the doors. He was leaping down the street. [Flash Step]—not the other spells. [Flash Leap] actually had a lot of momentum, and you jumped with it. He had no practice with that.
They were armed. And surely, they could see how wounded he was. The Scourge looked like a dead man running. Some took aim, glancing from left to right to assure themselves of victory. They wavered when they saw the undead at Pisces’ back, Skeleton Champions running.
Even so…they saw him pointing a finger over their heads and took cover. The [Slavers] were snarling, rats prepared to fight to the death in front of their warren. Until he cast the only spell he had mana left for.
A flash of dazzling light. The guards threw themselves down, crying out. They thought it was aimed at them until they looked up. He’d missed?
No. The illusion spell was just that. It passed overhead, shooting over the city of Halqued, glowing particles landing on the roofs, pieces of a rainbow falling as the citizens peered up. Bits of color; a comet shooting across Chandrar’s skies.
It sapped the strength in the limbs of the [Slave Guards] who saw it. Conjured that name to their lips. Then they saw him running towards them. Blade drawn.
In that moment, the two became a single idea. Death of Chains. Scourge of Roshal. The first archer tossed down her weapons, just dropped them and fled, shedding everything she could carry. Then the next—and the next—
A [Slave Master] tried to rally the guards, but they took one look at the [Death’s Blade] that Pisces held, under the glowing comet’s light, and they fled.
Or maybe it was the two bells hanging from the rapier. One was the Bell of Challenges, which lay silent. The other?
Gold. And it did ring, because he was no expert beyond reproach. He had just earned it the old-fashioned way. Besting a Gold-bell Duelist.
No one could argue with that. Not even…
“Padurn Jealnet?”
The [Fencer] was a block of wood. A pillar of ice. A statue with [Eternal Stasis] cast on it. He only reacted the sixth time Drassi called his name.
She was smiling as the scrying spell zoomed out. Prince Yosoc was sprinting after Pisces, but she’d gone back to her studio.
“Mister Jealnet? I was wondering if you had thoughts on your son’s newest bell. We appear to be watching the Scourge of Roshal taking vengeance for his near-assassination. Which seems at least partially justified. I’m no expert on Chandrarian law, but Guild of Assassins, Roshal.”
She made two boxes on the desk with her claws. Overlapped them.
“Tragic. Viewers may wish to look away. Anyways, Fencer Padurn! How does it feel to have your son surpass you at less than half your age?”
She folded her claws together and rested her chin on them. Padurn did respond, then. The entire Court of Ailendamus was watching his broadcast. People across the Kingdom of Glass and Glory, across Terandria, the world, saw Padurn fix his eyes on his lifelong obsession. His son, still covered in blood. Then Padurn drew a breath and said—
“A Gold-bell won through a duel with a Gold-bell [Duelist] is unequivocally earned.”
Drassi exhaled and smiled. She opened her mouth, and Padurn continued.
“—If it were earned in a solo duel. Which it was not. A Gold-bell [Duelist] has the right to bestow such a bell only if two or more such duelists are in agreement.”
Drassi Tewing sat utterly still for a moment, just staring at Padurn. Then she exhaled.
“…Huh. You know, I didn’t expect anything better of you, but wow. Okay, let me just, uh, call up the Maestro and King of Duels. How about that?”
Padurn’s eyes never left the scrying orb.
“The individual known as the ‘Jester’ is not a recognized Gold-bell Duelist. A roving [Assassin] who slaughters actual Gold-bell—”
Drassi would have jumped through the screen, but one of her [Journalists] grabbed her.
“Drassi, don’t—”
“Let go of me, I just want to hit him. Let go of—”
“He’s a [Fencer]! He’ll cut you, and we don’t know if you actually bleed with the Skill!”
“I’m just going to—”
Her image turned black, which left Padurn Jealnet as the only host of Channel 2 news. The worst [News Anchor] in Channel 2 history stood there in dead silence for half a minute.
The Scourge was fighting down the street. Cutting down fleeing [Slavers]. But he was running. He didn’t want them? Padurn whispered, perhaps forgetting he was on television.
“I have never attempted to understand what goes on inside that head of yours. What are you doing? Is there no limit to how many rules you must break?”
The Scourge was advancing. And he was not alone; Prince Weith was running after him, sword raised, and his [Bodyguards]. Even some civilians. Nerrhavia’s Fallen had been attacked after all, insulted. And perhaps the Scourge’s words to the [Prince] still burned.
Skeleton Champions were sprinting after Pisces. Padurn’s face twisted in a grimace as Pisces ran on. He only slowed once and turned his head, questing left and right, as if hearing something foul. Then he shook his head and ran on.
Five minute delays. It took about that long for Padurn to figure out what was going on. He saw, of course, [Slaves] being led out onto the street. A Gnoll, who was being unshackled—other [Slaves] who’d been in holding, awaiting masters.
That was Wildcard’s doing. They were pounding ahead of Pisces, shouting.
“Set them free! Set them free or he’ll kill you!”
Captain Leonardo was riding on a horse, shouting, and he had run into the Slaver’s Guild to tell them to unshackle whomever they had—then run. One of the Guild’s [Receptionists] was clinging to his arm.
“You have to stop him! Please—”
Leo looked back at Pisces, who was running towards them. The [Tennis Champion] eyed the glowing blade, Pisces, and raised his hands.
“Uh…we’re not being paid enough for that.”
He turned his head so no one caught his expression as Pisces ran by.
No sum in the world.
But that was only…half of what Pisces was aiming for. He advanced past the Guild, leaving the Skeleton Champions and the others to keep fighting. He was headed for somewhere else, the viewers and Padurn realized. He was running faster now, desperate.
 
——
 
It was, in fact, the same district where Pisces had stayed twice. A rich area with mansions for the wealthy in the city of Halqued. A Silk district. It was where a prominent [Slave Trainer] lived.
Pisces was out of mana again. He tried gulping down a mana potion, but he was well and truly in mana burn. Body agonized and beaten, newly healed.
Yet he kept going.
There. He saw the mansion was in chaos, doors open, staff and guards in the streets. Because of course, the moment the owner of the mansion had seen him charge the Slaver’s Guild, she must have had a thought.
Once they’re dead, what about me? And she had bought [Slaves] from the Slaver’s Guild, the same ones he’d been involved with.
At least one.
The people of the city were in the streets, staring at him. Rich Silk-folk who shrank back from his bloody passing, trying not to catch his eyes. Those with nothing to fear holding scrying orbs showing a [Fencer] on screen, watching a running figure’s progress from above.
Pisces saw it all, and yet it all blurred before him. He was searching the street, the [Slaves] being loaded onto carriages as they took off, for a single figure. A flash of scales. Where—where—
He thought he saw a tail being whisked into a carriage as the [Driver] lashed the horses and drove it forwards. Another was being loaded up with children dressed like miniature [Butlers] and [Maids]. Pisces hesitated, but there was more than one—
“Back, back! We are law-abiding citizens of—”
A panicking Stitch-man tried to swing a long paddle at Pisces. Something you’d hit someone with to discipline them. It bounced off of Pisces’ armor as he climbed up into the carriage seat. His glowing blade rammed through the Stitch-man’s chest, and the figure convulsed. Fell over, then rose, a zombie. The other [Slavers] screamed as the zombie came at them.
Another wagon—Pisces flicked his wrist. [Shatterbolt]—it blew one of the wheels to pieces, and the terrified [Slavers] got out and started fleeing.
At least two carriages going towards the gates. He should have had Skeleton Champions secure them. The children inside the carriage stared at him.
“Don’t let them take you again. I’ll be back.”
He shouted and started running down the street. The inhabitants of the mansion who were [Slavers] were either hiding or already long fled. All save for one.
A Stitch-woman was running down the street ahead of Pisces. It looked like a horse had kicked her out of the saddle. She must have lashed it too hard, because the [Slave Trainer] who owned the mansion and all the [Slaves] was fleeing just ahead of Pisces. He sprinted at her, sword raised. Eyes roaming for the carriages—
“Unbelievable. First, you break the law. Then you turn your sword on the unarmed, the helpless? They cannot fight back. How low must you sink?”
A voice made Pisces stumble. He slowed—and he would have known that voice anywhere. But how—?
It was in dozens of scrying orbs around him, held by the crowd. A single face sneering at him, or the image of him. It still looked like Padurn Jealnet was staring right at Pisces.
His father. Pisces froze, gazing into the scrying orbs. The man was white-faced with anger and shock. He truly…
Didn’t understand anything. But he saw what he saw: Pisces, his son, a Silver-bell duelist about to cut down an unarmed woman from behind. His eyes were filled with such abhorrence.
Just like when he looked at undead. Or anything that Pisces had ever loved besides the sword. The young man was frozen, standing there.
He knew they were all running. The screaming [Slave Trainer]. The carriage with Lleta. But Padurn’s words were like a brand on his back. Pisces just halted there until Padurn whispered.
“Can you hear me, boy?”
Five minutes of delay. Pisces jerked and saw the [Slave Trainer] almost at the end of the street. The carriages—he raised a hand, and a skeleton horse began to rise from the bones flowing from his bag of holding, but that damn voice.
“She has no weapon. She is unarmed. Innocent. You do not know her. She did not attack you.”
Padurn Jealnet spoke like the training master he had been, barking every sentence down like it was set in stone. His eyes were a cold grey blaze in his face, and Pisces raised his rapier. Studying the weapon of bone. The bells that hung there were silent.
Then Pisces took a breath and pulled himself up onto the skeleton horse’s back. He turned and his face was caught by every scrying orb.
 
——
 
The Arbiter Queen was watching from her throne with her father, who was listening, studying his own golden bell. Admiring the other Pisces carried, which he had nothing like.
 
——
 
Selys Shivertail was sitting on the counter of her Guild as the [Assassins] watched a man who had bested a true legend from their home. Rhata was running around in circles as Haldagaz waited, a scholar listening for an answer to an argument he could have made.
 
——
 
Ceria Springwalker was sitting in the magical carriage that had come to a halt on its mad rush, next to Colthei and a slumbering Yvlon. The [Armsmistress] was smiling in her sleep. Colth was covering his mouth as Elena and Delitandra hugged each other, waiting.
 
——
 
So many more. Little Gnoll girls, [Princesses] off and on ships, and Archmages. And…
The Death of Chains was sitting in the air. Gazing down at a spark that people said she had fanned into being. She had done nothing, barely paid attention to him. She had merely set him free.
It was…everything, she knew. Now, she waited. Hearing her own voice in her ears to answer this little man. Waiting for his.
She saw the Scourge of Roshal turn, and Pisces Jealnet spoke once as he kicked the undead horse forwards.
“Innocent? You ignorant fool. It was not empty when she grabbed their collars. It was not empty when they raised their hands and you could not see what they did. No hand which holds chains is empty.”
Then he was riding down the street, sword raising. Czautha saw it flash down once as he passed the [Slave Trainer]. He didn’t look back, didn’t gaze at the blood on his blade. He was riding onwards, now, through the gates. Chasing the fleeing carriages.
The Death of Chains exhaled as the father stood there.
Trying to come up with a reply to best his son. But Pisces couldn’t hear him anymore.
He was trying to keep his promise.
 
——
 
…But he was failing. At last, his strength had given way. It was just…
His skeleton horse was galloping as fast as it could move. The carriages were heavier, but there was a team of horses being whipped to run, and the wheels were enchanted. The [Drivers] must have had Skills.
That was all.
Had he the mana, he might have caught them with [Flash Step]. But the trail of dust kept getting smaller. He was gasping.
“No. Please…”
She was right in front of him. Almost. Almost…he was reaching out, as if he could pull them back from the horizon. And perhaps there was magic for that too. But he couldn’t focus. Pisces’ head dipped down. He saw the two dustclouds separate…and there were more figures moving.
He was losing them among the traffic on the road ahead of him. Pisces didn’t have tracking spells, and if they got away or just bought time until Roshal sent reinforcements or Yisame ordered him to halt again?
Pisces’ eyes followed the leftwards trail of dust, a tiny cloud rising. It ran into a cluster of dots. More dust on the horizon. Then he lost track of the carriage. He was riding closer and trying to pick it out.
