But all he saw were figures, mounted…Pisces galloped forwards. Then he saw blades catching the light.
Guards. There were dozens—no, maybe over a hundred of them. He glanced down at the unenchanted rapier he carried. He was out of Skills, out of mana.
He kept riding. The little riders were circling around. Defending the carriage and its escort, which had come to a halt. One, then. He’d lose the other, and it was one versus…
Wait. Pisces saw one of the [Riders] hacking at something as he galloped forwards. They were cutting at…the carriage? And it had stopped. Surely they’d escort it onwards and block him.
But the [Slavers] on horseback were racing right and left. And the new [Riders] were…chasing them? Pisces saw one figure on horseback racing away from the road. Turning—then jerking.
Falling. Then he saw a figure leap down and plant a sword in their back. Drive the blade down three times, then raise it.
The other [Slavers] were dropping. And the wagon—someone was opening the doors, lifting figures out, pointing a bow into it at someone who came out, hands raised. They fell to their knees before an arrow nailed them to the side of the coach. The dead [Slaver] hung there, blood running into the sand.
Another [Rider] swept past the carriage, bow raised. They loosed, drew an arrow, loosed again. Pisces saw the number of living bodies in the carriage decrease by two.
A man was on the ground, running towards another [Slaver] who had jumped out and was trying to mount one of the horses missing a rider. He ignored the panicked blade that slashed across his face and chest and swung down.
More red. He hacked the body three times on the ground, then turned. The [Slavers] were all dying.
It was so quick. This group fought like they had no care for their wounds, shouting, a note of wild fury in the air. And triumph.
Pisces hadn’t looked in a mirror since he’d left Halquad all that time ago. So the sight of this attack astonished him. He halted for a moment.
“Is it…?”
He didn’t believe it at first. There was no dustcloud. And she had been leaving. But then Pisces had another thought.
What if…it wasn’t Merr? He focused ahead, and there was something familiar about another group of [Riders] streaming rightwards. After the second carriage. A very familiar feeling indeed.
Death magic. He could almost see through the eyes of a figure who sat cross-legged on the back of a running bear made out of bones. It was racing after the others, and they were being led by someone who held a short weapon in both hands.
Cleavers. They were following the second carriage. Now he knew who it was. Pisces whispered as his heart leapt.
“Bearig.”
The [Rebels] were shouting and finishing the [Slavers] as Pisces galloped past them. He saw a Stitch-woman tug down her veil.
“Scourge, the other one is there! Go, go! [Let Evil Not Escape]!”
Half the [Riders] with her saw the pursuit and whirled. They rode behind Pisces, shouting, and then he was amidst them. He turned his head and saw the man who’d been on foot grabbing an arm and being hauled onto a horse’s back.
Scars all over his body. Hemp—he was barely cut from the blade, and his eyes were locked on the second carriage. He was holding a dagger between his teeth, and he’d been carrying a huge scimitar in one hand, throwing daggers in the other.
The woman he was riding with had a recurve bow and was putting another arrow to the string. But Pisces had never seen arrows as jagged at these. Each one had tiny little nails fused to the arrowhead, angled so they’d enter but catch if you pulled them out. Hand-made barbed tips.
The armor of both [Rebels] was also mixed and matched. The archer wore three different pieces of chainmail, each one enchanted, cobbled together.
The woman that Pisces recognized was mounted on a new horse. A charger with barding, eyes covered. She had a lance in hand and was riding like a [Knight]. They were all following the other carriage.
“It is getting away! [Weighed Down by My Pain].”
The Hemp Stitch-man saw the second carriage was faster and flung out a hand. Pisces’ head whipped around, and he saw the carriage—slow. Was something hanging off it?
The [Rebels] and Pisces were streaming down the road, but Pisces’ eyes were on the man leading the second wave, trying to catch the carriage.
The enchanted carriage was throwing everything it had at them. The [Rebel] broke off slashing at one wheel and threw up a hand—a [Lightning Bolt] shot at him. He—bounced the spell off his cleavers, but the carriage accelerated.
Cursing, Bearig kicked his horse after it, but another [Lightning Bolt] was being fired from the window. A figure rode into it, and it illuminated Ivery’s bones. But then the Skeleton Lord was spreading his arms. Grinning like Toren once had.
He ate two more [Lightning Bolts] as the Warbear, Bearbones, reached the carriage’s side. Ivery grabbed the roof and swung himself onto it. He hurled a rock down at the roof, began stomping, and then drew his sword—
Spears from the inside jabbed through the roof and hit him in the chest. The Skeleton Lord wobbled, then slashed at the driver. He managed two blows before a swerve threw him; he grabbed onto one door and began dragging along the ground. The carriage door opened, and spears struck at him as he hung on. His glowing flame-eyes were fixed on something behind him.
Hurry up, hurry up this sort of hurts—
The distracted occupants of the carriage didn’t realize that Bearig had caught them until the man threw the cleaver.
It went through the driver’s chest, and the horses began to slow. The second cleaver hit a wheel, and the carriage was turning in a circle, now. Slower…
Bearig re-armed himself and leapt from the saddle as the rest of the [Rebels] encircled the carriage. Then—Pisces heard his voice.
“Exit the carriage without the [Slaves]. There’s no hostage to take nor anywhere to run. Hurt them and we’ll make this slow.”
Pisces was suddenly amongst them. Riding forwards. Bearig turned, and the two halted in astonishment.
The [Necromancer] was tall for a Human, and he remembered a shorter, fatter man with a timid smile and gentle bearing. Now, the [Rebel] was of a height with him and barrel-chested. Muscle was taut as he lifted a bloody cleaver, the edge battle-worn, just like his expression. His voice was a bellow, a solid note in the air, and he smelled of fury and sweat.
Yet when he put out an arm to stop Pisces, his eyes widened, and then he smiled. And that was Bearig. When his eyes turned to the coach, he focused on the children, and he only saw them.
Not the [Slavers].
The last of the [Slavers] were crouched in the open carriage. Each one had a blade to the throat of at least one child. A shaking Garuda, Stitch-child, and a Drake girl…
She wasn’t trembling. She was staring at him as Pisces dismounted. One of the [Slavers] screamed.
“Give us horses and you get them alive—if not, corpses! No arguments! We’ll kill them all, our honor on it!”
Bearig spat on the ground.
“We don’t negotiate. You’ll die ten thousand deaths. Come out and meet your fate. You of cloth—you have just as many lives to live if we restitch you. I swear that upon your worthless honor.”
His voice was thunderous. He was still the huge [Cook] in some ways, but he was imposing. The same determination that had emerged at the battle of the oasis turned into a fierce confidence. Again, he stopped Pisces from drawing a bead on one of the [Slavers]. He could hit one with [Deathbolt] if they didn’t react, but the other two…
“You’ll damn children. Be reasonable!”
One of the [Slavers] cried. There were at least a dozen children in the carriage with him, and he had an enchanted dagger. Pisces was frozen with indecision, but then Bearig’s voice became cool.
“Reasonable says the man who takes children as [Slaves].”
“They’re worth more than you or I. Listen, we’ll ruin a fortune and countless lives. You wouldn’t want that.”
They were trying to negotiate in something like earnestness, but even how they spoke…Pisces shifted, then went still. Bearig raised his brows, putting his cleavers into holsters at his side. The [Slavers] relaxed fractionally, but they were watching Pisces, tensed.
“Aye, a fortune, is it? Then what’s the half-Elf worth? Ten fortunes? None will save you. So put them down, and maybe there’ll be mercy as you deserve.”
The half-Elf? One of the [Slavers] turned and grabbed the half-Elf boy, abandoning the Drake girl.
“Listen, we’ve gold. You can have both it and the children if—”
He was thinking to have them just bring horses out. Then he’d grab a child and ride; they’d be afraid of hitting him. Damn the others. The [Slaver] was so desperate it only occurred to him after half a second to question something.
Half-Elf? Slave Mistress Hisqua loved buying prospective [Slaves], but half-Elves were in high demand since they lived so long. They were somewhat rare and expensive. She didn’t have any—
Rophir slashed off the second [Slaver]’s arm and stuck a shiv up the third’s jaw, into his brain. He grabbed the arm before it could spasm and cut his hostage. The boy hopped out of the carriage as the children screamed, and the two [Slavers] spilled onto the ground.
The Stitch-man who’d been holding a dagger at Rophir’s throat admired the simplicity of the attacks.
A true [Assassin]’s action. Splendid, glorious work. The trainer of this boy had been a genius. Vaguely, he wondered why he hadn’t reacted or done anything when the boy had revealed his true colors.
Then it occurred to the [Slaver].
Ah, of course. He was already dead.
 
——
 
[Delayed Kill]. The third [Slaver] fell over as two diagonal wounds nearly cleaved his head from his body. Rophir paused, turned, and lifted two fingers on each hand. He posed with his daggers.
“Endless silks, Rophir! You had us sweating! Enough with the showing off!”
Rebel Nathpe swung herself out of the saddle, laughing. Pisces just stood there as the half-Elf boy gave her a frown.
He opened his mouth, glanced at Pisces, then closed it and sidled around the carriage. He began poking at the Skeleton Lord, who was still clinging to one carriage door, two spears buried in his ribcage.
Ow, ow, ow. Stop that. Was I cool?
Ivery sat up as Bearbones loped over. Only then did the second group of [Rebels] and the reinforcements appear. Qshom came galloping down the hill.
“We don’t have long. Is he here? I—Pisces!”
The [Necromancer] was swaying on his feet. Bearig had turned to him after checking the children were unharmed. He strode over, arms spread, but then stopped.
“Bearig?”
Pisces looked like he had just been freed from slavery. Possibly…worse. His robes were torn, and he was pale and sweating. Mana burnt. Exhausted, hair blown crazily, desperate. Bearig studied him, then extended a hand.
“We came as fast as we could, but Merr got word to us, and then we heard you had been found by Nerrhavia’s Fallen. When we heard of the Face…I thought they’d come from this gate if they took you prisoner. It was all we could do.”
They’d been preparing to ambush a Face? Pisces blinked at him, and Bearig turned to indicate the [Rebels].
“We couldn’t bring that many. We’re wanted both by Nerrhavia’s Fallen and Roshal. I’ve stolen your face for this, Pisces. No one would fear a [Cook], and my family is still out there. I’m sorry. I hoped you’d underst—”
He broke off. Pisces had stumbled forward and put his arms around Bearig’s shoulders. The [Necromancer] half-collapsed as Bearig caught him.
“My friend. You made it. Thank you. Thank you for catching them. I’m…I’m a bit tired, Bearig. I’m sorry, but will you help me? Just for a second?”
He just needed a shoulder. Bearig gazed down at Pisces, and the same adventurer who had fought and helped keep the [Cook], the [Tailor], the other [Slaves] alive when they’d been freed…
Bearig put an arm around Pisces’ shoulder, then picked the [Necromancer] up. Pisces protested faintly, but Bearig just turned.
“You’ve lent us blade and magic and face for so long—of course. Anything we can pay back. Someone get to fuzzing scrying spells on us. They’ll be coming out of the city. Get the children mounted and ready to go. Do we hit the gates?”
“They freed the ones in the city.”
“Then we don’t risk it. I want us riding in one minute!”
Bearig did put Pisces down so the [Necromancer] could ride his horse; he seemed to object to being carried in Bearig’s arms, even if the former [Cook] assured him he could and had done it before.
Pisces had something to do first. He took a few wobbling steps over the sand, ignoring the blood and the bodies. His eyes were fixed on a little figure who stood there, staring up at him.
Lleta was wearing a black-and-white [Maid]’s outfit speckled with blood. [Slave] training. Her dusky green scales were dusty, and her eyes were big as she glanced around at the dead bodies. But she just waited until Pisces sank to one knee.
That took the last of his energy. The [Necromancer] searched for words.
I’m sorry I took so long. 
I wish I’d done this from the start. 
I’m so sorry.
He didn’t know what she’d been through already. On this long and terrible journey or when she’d been sold. He was afraid to know.
Lleta was the first one to break the silence. She fumbled for something in her outfit’s pockets, then produced a tiny, white handkerchief. She wiped at his face.
“Adventurer, you’re hurt.”
He blinked at her, lost for words. The little handkerchief didn’t really do much to the dried blood on his face. But the Drake girl kept dabbing.
“I knew you’d come back. I knew it. Verg didn’t believe me. No one did. But I kept waiting because I knew you’d do something. Then everyone heard about the caravans and I knew. I just had to wait, because…because that’s what adventurers do.”
Her voice was trembling. She put down the handkerchief after a moment. Swallowed.
“Even when it was really scary and hard, I just kept waiting. Did you save Verg too?”
Pisces had seen the Gnoll when he’d run past the Slaver’s Guild. He didn’t know where he was, but he looked into those huge, brown eyes and rasped.
“I’ll get him. You’re safe now, Lleta.”
“Yes. I know.”
Solemnly, she folded the handkerchief and put it in her pockets. Then she stepped forwards and hugged him. Hesitantly at first, then she buried her head in the remains of his robes.
“Did they hurt you, Adventurer Pisces? You look really, really bad. You must’ve had to kill a lot of bad guys. I’m sorry.”
He heard a muffled sound, and she started crying. The [Necromancer] patted her on the back.
“No. No…it’s fine, Lleta. It was easier than the Adult Creler. I would do it again. A thousand times. You’re safe now.”
“I know.”
She kept crying. He didn’t know what to do, so Pisces just kept patting her on the back until someone turned. Bearig was back.
The former-[Cook] was gentle, but he picked the girl up. They’d cleared the carriage out. She didn’t want to get back inside, though, so he let her ride with him. Pisces saw his skeleton horse was waiting for him, too. He got on it as Lleta watched him.
Then they were racing away from the city, and Bearig was asking about the [Slaves] that Roshal would surely re-collar. He sent volunteers to see if they were there and saw the [Slaves] riding out the gates, half on horseback, others bundled into carriages.
Wildcard’s doing. Or perhaps someone in the city who understood. Then they were streaming eastwards, dodging tracking spells, and Pisces felt himself falling asleep. So Rophir did a flying leap off his horse and grabbed the reins. Pisces blinked and—
 
——
 
—Found himself riding into the night as Bearig split the groups a third time, sending decoys with his face racing north—
Ivery and Bearbones were riding next to Pisces, and the Skeleton Lord was menacing a trio of Skeleton Champions sitting in a commandeered carriage. The lesser undead were staring at the weirdest undead they’d ever seen. Ivery was silently telling them to be nice to the [Rebels] or he’d smash their skulls in.
Nice? To the living? He was crazy. They only stopped staring at Ivery when Pisces whispered.
“He’s everything you need to become. Don’t you see?”
The Skeleton Champions’ jaws fell off their heads, and Ivery nearly laughed himself out of his saddle. Then Pisces blinked as Rophir started sniggering—
 
——
 
“—your bloody time! Bah, you made it, and he’s…eugh. He looks like underwear after it’s been shat in and someone spent a day riding about with it attached to a camel’s backside.”
Pisces didn’t even open his eyes.
“That’s Merr.”
When he did pull his head up, Merr was riding next to them, her Dustbandits whooping and cheering. She turned to him and spoke as Bearig made a gagging sound.
“Do you have to speak so, Merr? Rophir’s just a boy. Pisces doesn’t look that bad. He’s like…a ham gone slightly green. Might be bad all the way down, and you should probably toss it, but I’ve known fellows who’ll carve the other bits off and serve it up as good.”
It was Merr’s turn to give Bearig a gaze of horror.
“I’d stab a man who did that. Pisces, you alive?”
“Please stop analogizing me.”
Laughter. Bearig slapped his stomach and chuckled, deep in his belly, and Merr threw her head back. Qshom rolled his eyes as he carried his head in the crook of his arms, a smile the Dullahan’s only concession to the moment.
Merr rode over.
“We’ll stop soon as we have a break. You’re mostly dead, but you did it. Did you get her?”
“No. I’m sorry. She was a [Slave] too. I didn’t think about Casep. I hesitated and…she got away.”
Her voice was gentle.
“Argh, you soft Necrolad. You’ve humiliated a Face of Chandrar. Casep would laugh at that alone. Get some rest. But turn down half the levels, eh? I can’t have you hit Level 50 first. What about my reputation?”
Pisces rather feared…he fell asleep then and there, and someone did carry him [Princess]-style. But if so, he was smiling.
 
——
 
The [Rebels] did not spend long in the wilderness outside of Halqued. The [Queen] had sent her chariots back and hired Gold-rank teams, and scrying spells were combing the area for a sight of the Scourge.
Even with their Skills, and Merr’s, they couldn’t linger. But Bearig had a plan.
“Always have two plans. Running a rebel group that frees [Slaves] is rather like running a restaurant. I shall now explain.”
Rophir rolled his eyes as he lounged in a hammock where he napped. He rolled himself up like a caterpillar and hung upside-down. It was, apparently, the only way he would sleep.
Lleta was sitting in the tent, staring at Rophir. She looked…Pisces hoped she hadn’t been hurt. The Gnoll, Verg, was also here. As far as Pisces could tell, they’d freed all the [Slaves] in that caravan and many more from the city.
But he hadn’t heard the <Quest> update. Bearig was curious about that, as were the other [Rebels]. They’d been besieging Pisces with questions. Even asked him for autographs or for him to demonstrate his best [Slaver]-killing move—until Merr had chased them away.
Even now, they were sitting outside the tent, but a [Silence] spell gave them privacy.
Qshom, Bearig, Verg, and Lleta—because the girl insisted on being near Pisces—Merr, Rophir, and Ivery, who was standing in a corner, pretending to be a lamp, eyes aglow.
All but Eloque. Pisces watched Bearig go over to the maps.
“Like a restaurant, you always have a backup plan if things go wrong. If the ingredients are off or your best [Waiter] gets sick. Sometimes, you serve the local [Magistrate] a fishhook anyways, but two plans. Three or four, preferably. If we can’t meet up easily, you’ll know how to get in contact with a group that knows us.”
“Savere knows me. So long as the Siren and your half-Elf don’t start shitting in the same pot, she’ll help get word to me. I could even head that way, but I think we have to keep wide of each other.”
Bearig and Qshom’s faces screwed up with the most appalled expressions ever, and Lleta clapped her claws over her mouth and started giggling. That was enough to make Pisces smile. Rophir didn’t care for the Merr-isms, though, and hucked one of his shoes at the back of her head.
Hard. She swore and went to toss it back at him, but gently.
“This is why I don’t hang around you lot. Too sensitive. Eloque, now, she’s a girl that understands me. This? A boy’s club.”
She pointed at the Stitch-man, Dullahan, and half-Elf, who all stared at her. Qshom murmured.
“Eloque asked you to stop with your colorful expressions when we ate.”
Merr turned up her nose, sniffing.
“I don’t recall this.”
“Old.”
Rophir resumed caterpillaring when Merr glowered at him. Lleta edged over.
“Is that fun? Can I try?”
The half-Elf stared at her, unblinking, then spoke.
“Only cool people can.”
“Oh. Sorry.”
The Drake girl scuffed at the ground; she was still wearing a [Maid]’s outfit. But they’d removed the collar. Pisces saw Rophir hesitate, then unwind and pat the hammock.
“Careful.”
They all watched the girl try to tangle herself up like he had, until her neck spines were poking out the holes in the fabric and Rophir was trying to untangle them.
Pisces was just sitting there as Qshom got up.
“There are contacts in cities. A network of informants and people, but Pisces cannot endanger them. It is risky. So risky. But we can meet, especially if you leave the borders or go to places where Roshal has less power.”
“He’ll be followed by their Guild of Assassins and eyes. But yeah, I’ll pick up some countermeasures. No one’s getting the drop on my gang twice.”
All Pisces wanted to do was sit with them. His heart felt overfull and was tired. But relieved. They were so busy talking that Bearig only noticed Pisces faint smile after a moment.
“Pisces? Do you need more rest? Food? I still make food—better than ever, I’d say. Strange how hacking up [Slavers] gives you ideas for new recipes to try. And looting caravans bound for Roshal means you never run out of odd ingredients.”
Pisces shook his head slightly.
“I just want to stay here for a while. I know you’ve all gone to such lengths and we cannot, but…”
That’s all he’d wanted. All this time. To just go back and be here. To know they were as well as they could be.
And to bring them to his home.
Merr sniffed, and Pisces thought she was mocking him, but she just rubbed her eye.
“Damn dust. Idiot gets to leave Chandrar, and he comes back all high and mighty. Adventurers.”
“She’s missed you. She starts sniffing and talking like how she thinks Izrilians are when she gets lonely.”
Qshom whispered, and Merr scowled at the [Tailor]. Pisces started laughing softly. He knew he had to go back to his team; Ceria was spamming him with [Messages], telling him that he had better come back, and no more incidents this time, because they had enough trouble.
He knew he had to go back. But just for a moment…he lingered with them, and then they were sitting around a fire again.
Changed, different—but in a way, the same.
Not a bunch of former-[Slaves], because they weren’t defined by that. Just some friends thrown together by fate. And a Skeleton Lord, who saw the [Necromancer] glancing at him now and then. Ivery flopped down in the center of the tent, spread-eagled, staring up at Pisces.
 
What? I’m not mad…Father. Creator? Dad sounds weird. You got taken on a flying carpet, it’s fine, it happens. I wanted to stay. Plenty more interesting bones and fights over here. These chumps you’ve got following you around don’t know nothin’. Me? I’m experienced. Tough. Everyone likes me.
Sure, I lost to an actual Skeleton Lord we ran into one time, and Bearig had to bail me out. He was trying too hard. I’m not mad about the stone thing. It’s funny. Ha-ha, everyone gets a good laugh.
We don’t need to get all touchy-feely about things. Hurt people hurt people, that’s why Rophir is so good at what he does.
I know you didn’t bring me any gifts. It’s fine. Look at Bearbones, he’s got no expectations. Zen. Practically a [Sage]. I heard how the other guy went nuts, but not me. I have friends.
You could have given me a voice, but hey, when life gives you lemons, you’re glad that a half-Elf didn’t poop on them. Just like Merr says.
 
Pisces kept staring at Ivery until Merr broke the silence.
“You trying to win a staring contest with him? Because I’ve done that and only won once.”
He rubbed at one ear as he broke away from Ivery.
“…You won? Er, uh—no, I was trying to understand what he was thinking about. And either he’s, ah, changed a bit or I’m projecting onto him in quite a number of ways. Merr, do you have a saying about half-Elves pooping—”
“On a lemon? Favorite saying. You gotta ask yourself, Pisces m’boy. Whenever you get some fruits from the Claiven Earth—and they are the best—how do them half-Elves make fertilizer? Because I’ve heard they’re nature-freaks up there. Just think about it.”
He stared at her. Ivery shrugged. Pisces wasn’t sure if he was hoping this was some elaborate prank or not. He gazed at Ivery, then nodded.
“I suppose I am a bad…creator.”
Phew, he didn’t go the dad route. Ivery wiped at his forehead. Crisis averted. Pisces paused.
“I loved undead, but I guess I never thought of them quite as—as people. Ama and Gewilena, they saw it differently. They might have been more right after all. But my first true creation I treated poorly. I didn’t warn Erin.”
He reflected on Toren, perhaps for the first time in those terms. He’d always questioned if the bones of Nekhret had been at fault, his spell, the part he’d left blank—but he glanced at a covered scrying orb that Bearig sometimes used to monitor news.
“I’ve been a bad parental figure. I suppose I’ve never known what I was supposed to do right.”
Ooh. Merr, Ivery, and every eavesdropping [Rebel] winced. Merr began to signal for backup from Bearig, an actual father. But Pisces just got up, dusting his kilt off. That was all that was left of his robes. He might need new clothing. He walked over and held out a hand.
“Then again, you found people to love you and learned the only lesson I had to teach. I wouldn’t make you go anywhere but here. Here is where you’re needed.”
Ivery stared at Pisces, then took the hand and pushed himself up. He made a show of dusting down his patchwork armor.
Well, yeah. Obviously. You don’t have to be dramatic about it. Of course I’m guarding Bearig. Man wouldn’t survive midday soup without me. Ask him about the soup incident, go on.
“…What’s the soup incident?”
Bearig began spluttering explanations and defending his cooking, which had only nearly murdered someone twice. Whereupon Pisces did learn that most [Rebels] thought that Bearig was an inspiring leader, a brave and canny fighter, but who made utterly cursed food. And he smiled, but he watched Ivery out of the corner of his eyes.
 
——
 
Much else was said and done before Pisces the Scourge made it back to civilization, but he did return to the city of Halqued where Wildcard was waiting to escort him back to the palace.
The city’s gates were locked, and barrier spells were glowing behind every entrance as the [Guards] on the walls took cover and loudly talked about their poor families and pets that were waiting for them to come back home.
But the Scourge just passed beyond the walls and rode to a small outpost a mile outside the city.
The Mad Ones didn’t fear him, though they did invite him with a bit more interest than last time.
“Beat your first Face? That gets you a drink, actually free for once. Want some overpriced food?”
Master Otevious admired Pisces’ Stellar Ivory rapier with a sigh as he had Pisces recount the duel with the Jester. It wasn’t like they were immune to enjoying a good fight, and Pisces’ detailing of the way she’d fought caught their interest.
“Vibrations? I wonder if we could rig up a blade to do that. Anyone interested in collaborating on a spell? I think a mechanism would be too hard…”
“Why create the spell? Let’s go to a brothel that does sex toys and start from there.”
Pisces opened and closed his mouth and really hoped that this wouldn’t go down as his contribution to the advancement of weaponry. Otevious cackled, but he rested on his haunches. After a moment, he tapped the rapier.
“The tyranny of levels. Very well done, though. Your magical innovation? It may be only applicable to you, but there is genius there.”
Pisces regarded his rapier, then took something out of his pocket.
“Yes, well, the funny thing is, Master Otevious—this only came about because I didn’t have an enchanted rapier, you see. My channeling death mana only would work on a piece of unenchanted ivory; it’d clash with a regular enchantment.”
The man’s eyes gleamed.
“Ah. Another truth: there is no avenue not worth exploring. Though I imagine the mana-costs of an active enchantment are substantial. Still, [Death’s Blade] sounds nasty enough that I can’t imagine even Mars wants you to hit her with it.”
Pisces hadn’t figured out what tier it was, but his guess was that it was a Tier 5 spell. If not as instantly destructive as [Deathblast]…if you were good with a sword, you’d be doing a lot of applications of the magic.
He coughed and glanced at his escort. Wildcard was haggling for some of the Mad Ones’ gear, though they didn’t have that much gold. A very happy Yisame had paid them, but Lareceina refused to eat any of the overpriced snacks, and Kusal was talking with the resident Earther and haggling for upgrades for his tech.
They might become very fearsome…Pisces thought Lareceina had levelled, but he wasn’t sure how much. That was reassuring; an allied Gold-rank team in Chandrar was important to have.
Allies. Both here and riding into the distance. Pisces shifted.
“Well, Master Otevious, it occurred to me that the Guild of Assassins will come again.”
The man nodded.
“It will, and that’s the least of what you should have with you. Nice bell; it’ll help, but don’t rely on it.”
He indicated both the gold bell and the silent Skeleton Champions standing behind Pisces. The [Necromancer] nodded. Then he placed a piece of Stellar Ivory in front of the Mad One.
“Yes, Master Otevious. But if my current blade, and the one I’m likely to use for the foreseeable future, is just plain bone…Stellar Ivory is hard to shape unless one knows death magic. Very, very hard to collect. I don’t have enough to upgrade any one Skeleton Champion with it. Not nearly enough.”
Yeah, yeah, it’s rare stuff. Anyone can get more if they just work hard. Not like we need handouts.
Three of the Skeleton Champions turned their heads slightly to look at the fourth, who was more…scruffy looking than the others. He had a bit of Stellar Ivory on him, unlike the others, and he seemed more…animated than the rest. Bouncing on his heels, glancing around—then snapping to attention.
Odd. However, Otevious was distracted by the pieces of it in front of him. And Pisces’ rapier.
The Mad One picked up the ivory, and his eyes stole to the prototype shortsword on his walls.
“Why, if it was the blade you were going to use all the time…it might be handy to conceal it. Though how handy is that?”
“If I could ask for a quote, sir?”
Pisces conferred with the Mad One for some time in private. But despite a good hour’s long negotiations, in the end, he didn’t come away with a deal. The Stellar Ivory was too hard to work in Otevious’ mind, and a concealable blade was not going to win Pisces a fight.
“It’s a fine idea, young man. But if the price makes you flinch…”
The [Necromancer] didn’t seem that disappointed as he shook Otevious’ hand and walked out of the camp. But several observers who reported to their masters did so with a bit of relief.
The last thing the Scourge needed was a Mad Ones-style upgrade. 
 
——
 
That was that. Pisces Jealnet left Halqued empty-handed, and Wildcard joined him in a carriage ride to Tyrant’s Rest. It was a long journey, but they seemed companionable enough, and Halqued finally breathed a sigh of relief when the Scourge was gone. Even then…they kept watching the roads.
You never knew if he might come back. And his deeds would echo there. Even in his absence, the building he’d reanimated still stood over the city. The Slaver’s Guild lay empty, and they had seen what the Scourge of Roshal truly meant.
The magical carriage with Wildcard in it stopped only once since it was late. It was a moonlit night when Pisces Jealnet got out to stretch his legs. He stared up at the twin moons and scuffed around on the ground for a while. His Skeleton Champions stood there, and one of them joined him.
They got to bickering over the exact details of one part of the glowing lines on the ground. Even shoved each other until Lareceina came over and both sides agreed that hurtful things had been said and thought, and you know what? You could compromise.
Then, and only then, did Pisces step back and activate the [Ritual of the Lord of Bones]. Ivery was posing like Rophir in the center of it. That already made Pisces self-conscious, but he knew the spell, and he’d been thinking for a long while on it.
You could do a lot of bindings—if you had the knowhow and materials. There was such a thing as going overboard, so Pisces kept it light.
Ivery had wanted [Fireballs]. Instead, Pisces bound [Flash Step] to his feet. He placed an [Invisibility] spell on the Skeleton’s chest, and [Barrier of Air] in the skull. He didn’t have room for any more spells, and he frankly might have failed to do all of that properly, let alone more.
However, a certain master of magic had given him a few tips when calling to congratulate him about a parrying technique.
That alone would have been good enough, but for a fellow who might have to fight other Skeleton Lords or a Face…Pisces had been thinking about Ivery’s gear. Or lack thereof.
Ivery saluted the little glass pebble as it re-materialized in front of him. The weapon that had slain half a dozen [Slavers] lay there as Pisces put a replacement item there instead. It confused his observers, some of whom had been waiting here for hours.
“The fuck’s that?”
Merr was grumpy because she’d had to help set up the damn spell circle and then wait around for him. But she’d wanted to see, and she had to ride Ivery back to Bearig and the others. The other Dustbandits shushed her; she’d been the one insisting on helping the actual [Mages] among them.
The item in question was very strange to Merr. It made her nervous on principle, because she knew where Pisces had gotten it. It was like a [Rogue]’s weapon…and if the spies who had been watching Pisces had been any good at all, they would have noticed its absence from Master Otevious’ tent.
Sadly, they’d fallen for the most obvious trick in the book. The inventor had handed it over to Pisces, and they’d taken the hour to fashion a good-looking replacement, which was hanging on his walls. But the genuine article was now glowing in the light.
It was…a battleaxe. Or rather, it looked like one that someone had married to a bunch of compressed wire coils. Only a single trigger stood between you and enough force to blow through a chestplate of enchanted armor.
A weapon that Otevious was very proud of, but which he’d acknowledged had many flaws. Such as the recoil which could break your arm. Or the trigger, which, again, was delicate and if it went off, would kill you dead.
Or the springs, which would break and become risky without [Repair] spells after each activation—and the fact that each one needed to be hand-tightened with a custom mechanism he’d invented.
An utterly, utterly impractical weapon to use at scale, and a one-shot for even a [Rogue]. A lovely prototype, but not worth the gold.
…Unless you were a Skeleton Lord who would conjure the weapon bound to him as it had been, each and every time. Pisces was sweating as he poured mana into the spell, but when the air flashed and kicked him onto his back—
Ivery the Skeleton Lord held the spring-loaded battleaxe over his head. He checked it. Swung it up, tossed it through the air after arming it—
The explosion of sand and a stray coil made everyone duck. Merr slapped the back of the Skeleton Lord’s head. Then she saw him raise his hand, and a spring-loaded axe re-appeared in his grip.
“Worms of Zeikhal shit out of the desert’s ass—Necroboy, are you trying to get us killed?! Put it down! Down, Ivery—”
He was smiling.
Best birthday gift ever. It made up for all the other ones Pisces had missed.
“I didn’t miss any—why is he so weird?”
Pisces shouted at Ivery, and Merr stumped over. She sighed.
“He hung out with Rophir too much. Two strange little lads…well, he looks happy, and that should put paid to everything but a Djinni coming after Bearig’s lot. Ivery was already damn tough, he just couldn’t kill much. He was getting more adept, but now?”
She shuddered. Pisces nodded at the happy Skeleton Lord menacing the Skeleton Champions running away from him.
“I did all I could. I’ll see you all again, Merr. And when I do, I’ll make sure I’m prepared for the other upgrade. For Bearbones too, if I can manage it.”
His fingers already hurt at the thought of all that intricate needlework, but…yes. He was afraid of that power, but if anyone deserved it—
Ivery slowed. His head turned, and all the Skeleton Champions came to a dead halt. One exploded as the spring-loaded axe malfunctioned, but they just—
Merr blinked. She was yawning, eying Wildcard, who were pretending not to see all the Dustbandits as they let Pisces ‘stretch his legs’.
“Second upgrade?”
Pisces just smiled at her.
“I’ll tell you when we’re away from prying ears. Not that I don’t trust everyone, it’s just that some secrets are so big I can only trust Merr the Storm with them. Not even Wildcard, yet.”
They jumped, and Pisces suspected it was Kusal or Lareceina who’d been listening to them. He grinned as Merr chuckled.
“Ah, that’s worth the ride. Alright, you lot! Get mounted! So you’re bound for the capital? Less trouble, I take it?”
He nodded as they prepared to say farewell, just for now.
“I am. I need to check on Yvlon, and Ceria and Colth have been up to their own adventures.”
“Well, you just let me know if you want company or someone to knock some sense into them. Hopefully I’ll meet them. Tell the Silver Killer that Rexel and Leprel can join the gang if they haven’t gotten soft, yeah? Then get some damn sleep.”
She punched Pisces in the shoulder, and he almost fell onto his face. He was still weak and recovering, and he really, really hoped the Jester wasn’t going to be coming around for a rematch any time soon. Hopefully the [Death’s Blade] kept her weak.
Hopefully they hadn’t killed her for failing. He rubbed at his nose and sniffed, which earned him a chortle from Merr.
“I’ll try to get some rest, Merr. A bit of relaxation after all this. Keep an eye out for Lleta, Ivery. And the others. I’m just planning on two meetings, and then I’ll sleep until next month.”
Merr rolled her eyes.
“Queen Yisame wants you to tell her all about your heroics? Careful with that one. Rumor is she has a sex dungeon larger than the entire nightclub you blew up. Don’t go re-animating that.”
Pisces paused, opening and closing his mouth. He tried not to ask more questions, but everything Merr did invited comment. He spluttered.
“Wh—I’m sure I’ll talk to Yisame, and it will be quite chaste. She’s had no designs on me—not that I expect any royal I meet to be interested in me!”
The [Bandit Lady] rolled her eyes as she checked on her Nightmare, then put a foot in the stirrups.
“Sure, sure. Let’s count. The Arbiter Queen, the Queen of Nerrhavia’s Fallen isn’t into you, yeah, sure, nor’s the King of Destruction, nor the King of Duels—careful or they’ll all have you in bed. Actually, stay away from Revine while you’re at it.”
The things she thought of. Pisces shook his head, grinning, as he walked away.
“It’s just a talk with a friend, Merr. And a date with Lareceina, that’s all.”
“What’s that?”
Pisces waved as Merr went over the saddle and landed on the other side with a thump. She sat up as he smiled.
“I’ll see you later.”
“Wait a—what did he just say?”
The [Necromancer] wandered off as the Dustbandits turned from riding away. He waved at Lareceina, who hesitantly waved back as Merr pulled herself upright. He’d asked her if she was open to a date after he’d exited the [Pavilion of Secrets], and he was glad to put all the jokes behind him.
Plus, there was that weird Skill—he utterly missed the commotion behind him.
 
——
 
Pisces Jealnet, Scourge of Roshal. A man of infinite amusement at times. And perhaps…potential.
He would have made an unsurpassed [Slave]. The fact that he had never come to Roshal to be turned into something as glorious as the Jester? Tragic.
But his war on the nation was…disastrous. One man’s actions had tarnished Roshal’s name.
“It was not his actions, but yours, Pazeral.”
Shaullile hissed across the table where the [Slave Lords] of Roshal had gathered. She was tired and wet; a Courier’s ship from Zeres was not fun to ride, but she’d had to move fast to get here.
Now they were talking. Arguing, rather, over what should happen next.
It was actually one of the first true arguments they’d had. They’d disagreed over many issues before, but talked out their differences. Acceded where one was strong. Who would argue with Andra over matters of coin? How it should be spent, yes. How to optimize it?
No.
This was different, though. This was an argument over what should be done next, and they were not aligned, to each’s displeasure. Pazeral was still clutching at the angry violet streaks in his side. The poison had yet to leave him, so he sat, unable to rise. He hissed back.
“If there is error in my actions, I take it. But we have been made fool twice, then. For we bared ourselves to the world, and they recoiled—but we also failed to revenge ourselves and humiliated our Guild of Assassins! Finest in the world, hah!”
He spat that at the Naga, Emir Yazdil. The only mortal [Slave Lord] of Roshal was coiled in on himself, and his voice was…overly patient.
“A man who could best a Face is better acquired than lost.”
“And he is better dead than an enemy. Let alone one you’ve levelled.”
Shaullile snapped back. She raked a claw through her neck-spines.
“This Face is incompetent, regardless. She should have gone for the kill, and she failed.”
“Her r-record is good. Anomalies do exist.”
Andra demurred. She was reviewing the files on the Jester, and the last [Slave Lord] to speak, Thatalocian, murmured.
“Her name. I wish to weigh her true name. 10-5-19-20-5-18. Even the name is hard to read. A mockery of digits. A run of three, two numbers divisible by the smallest…”
His fingers were tapping a tool he’d brought out, a series of dials. Each face of each dial had a different letter and number on it, and he was sorting it.
“11-9-11-9-1-17. Another sign of trickery. Not an even number among them. Bah. Had the last one been ‘e’, it would be a portent indeed.”
They ignored his insanity lest they catch it. Shaullile was annoyed.
“A Face failed. In my day, they were killed or punished.”
“She is well-made.”
Yazdil snapped. Andra nodded.
“I do not dictate Assassin’s Guild policy. Whatever the current law is…”
Thatalocian folded his arms, refusing to weigh in, so Yazdil and Shaullile were deadlocked. It was Pazeral who hissed.
“Send her to me. I shall evaluate her. If I’m pleased, she lives.”
The [Slave Lords] glanced at each other, and Shaullile threw up her claws.
“I don’t care. Now, you will listen to me. Leave the diplomacy to me. And some of what we will do is be silent and take our lumps. If any of you, any of you, rock this ship, I will kill you.”
The [Slave Lords] did not like threats, but they nodded slowly, and Shaullile turned to Andra.
“Good. Andra?”
“Every surviving [Slave Master] in the region attacked by the ‘Scourge’ is d-demanding reparations from the Slaver’s Guild. Compensation for losses incurred while sheltering. Assurances, security, that they will not fear such attacks again. We shall, of course, increase security and ref-fuse the compensation.”
This was the heart of their disagreement, actually. Instantly, every single [Slave Lord] disagreed. Yazdil’s tongue flicked out.
“It is customary to make whole any caravan who is failed by the Guild.”
“By paying their every little complaint?”
Shaullile was incredulous. She stabbed a claw down onto the table.
“This isn’t our problem. This is each nation’s fault. The Queen of Nerrhavia’s Fallen is making a mistake. We should remind her of it, politely.”
Yazdil was calmer than she was and lifted his tail and shoulders in a shrug.
“She has a penchant for the team. Of course our [Diplomats] are already pressing the issue. But are we not all Roshal?”
The words needled Pazeral, who spat.
“Do we protect them or find these [Rebels]? Levy each master for forces and we shall go hunting!”
Andra tsked loudly as the other two [Slave Lords] argued.
“This is overblown. If we increase the existing protocols—we do not need to make exceptions for—”
They were bristling, auras pressing against each other, so Shaullile deflected with her usual tricks. To the wrong person this time.
“Thatalocian. Give us some numbers-based wisdom. How about the old 1-2-buckle-my-shoe logic? What would you do?”
The [Slave Lord] was usually disinterested in most answers, except to consult the numbers and give a ‘yes’, ‘no’, or abstain. However, they were all suddenly reminded of his presence as he folded his arms. He loomed there, and his voice was quiet.
“We will give them nothing.”
Shaullile and Pazeral began to smile, but Yazdil’s eyes narrowed.
“Nothing, Thatalocian? We do promise that the Leashed Trails are secure. The Slaver’s Guild is devoted to the sale of [Slaves]. These [Slave Masters] have some right to complain.”
The other four nodded at that. But Thatalocian’s face was stony.
“We give them nothing.”
“Right, so the fact that the Scourge and [Rebels] killed over a dozen caravans is just…peachy?”
This time, Shaullile’s voice grew sarcastic, and Pazeral made a twirling motion with one finger as he glanced at Andra. Thatalocian’s eyes narrowed.
“If they object, which I am sure they will, the [Slave Masters] may come here. Then, address their complaints to us. They whine and beg for gold. If they are upset—let them bring it with voice and deed. If not? They level or die.”
“Your favorite method for everything. One has to wonder if you ever found a better method.”
Yazdil murmured to himself, and Thatalocian spoke to him.
“Your methods would create pretty toys to break like glass in the Long Night, Yazdil. Just like you.”
The Naga’s eyes turned venomous, and Andra raised a quavering hand.
“Some recompense would be merited. If we agree to a number, we may discuss th—”
Thatalocian’s fist hit the black marble table and cracked it. All four [Slave Lords] recoiled, though only Pazeral was fast enough to have a hand on a blade. Thatalocian roared.
“Do we cover this up? We are Roshal, and our blood lies upon the sand! Will you pay gold and let these [Slave Masters] wipe their sweat away and pretend they were not in fear for their lives? I will not allow us to pretend we are not bleeding or hurt, however small. Let them fear the Scourge. Let him slaughter a thousand caravans. The ones who live will become worthy of this place.”
Four pairs of eyes glittered at him as he shrank slightly, and each one of the [Slave Lords] of Roshal held their ground. Shaullile’s forked tongue flickered in the shadows she stood in.
“That may be the Roshal you know and love, Thatalocian, but mine remembered every insult. He’s crossed a line. Let’s say…I agree that we’ve got a weak crop of [Slave Masters]. Everyone agreed on that?”
Yazdil hesitated. But Andra, Pazeral, and Thatalocian nodded. Shaullile pulled up a chair and put her feet on the broken table.
“Good. Then we’ve got a point of agreement. Let’s negotiate the rest. Thatalocian’s right. If they can’t even deal with one adventurer, even one approaching Named-rank, we’ve got a lot of maggots crawling around our towers. Let’s hatch them or find new ones.”
The Naga said nothing as he saw the other three leaders of Roshal picking at his careful garden. Where few blooms save the ones he allowed to grow rose to any prominence that could threaten him. He wished to object…but he was one voice among five. And—he glanced at the image of Pisces Jealnet and sighed.
He was not certain they were wrong.
Even so, the Naga marked it. This was not the first time he had been forced to compromise. That was no failure he held against himself; it was politics at any level, give or take.
But this time, he had been well and truly overruled. Yazdil also paid attention to his reaction. He had not been willing or confident enough to force the issue. He had observed his fellow [Slave Lords], analyzed their faults and competencies, and found them wanting in so many ways…but he could not remove any one of them. He no longer even wished to; they were vital.
Yet the Naga was not happy. He did not stand among equals, not among even ghosts. Not in his home. To once again make Roshal his own, he would have to take risks. Play the only pieces he had left that none of them had access to. They might be superior [Slave Masters] of ancient days, who had seen and done what he could not imagine.
But they were still just those beings of old. What was a [Slave Master] without capable [Slaves]? His were very fine, and he had laid a great foundation not even the other [Slave Lords] were aware of. Like eggs, carefully incubating in the warm sands. Time, then, to hatch them and change the world. He sighed, simply regretful.
He had not longed for the changing of an age. But he would rather slither atop the ruins of a new one than share space with any other.

Of course, everyone had an opinion on the Scourge’s duel and war against Roshal. Again, most were inconsequential and did not change the world.
Just…perhaps their world. And perhaps only as much as any one moment could. A pebble’s width towards a different point of view. It wasn’t enough, but it was something.
The world was not fair, just, or good. It did not reward the deserving and often only gave those with power and wealth a favor.
Trader Hexata knew that. So when she celebrated the Scourge’s victory against a Face with her brothers, they were so drunk as to have alcoholic piss. They had bought out a pub in the city where they’d stopped—not Halqued—and were buying everyone drinks.
The pub, which was on the Scourge’s side, passing guests, even the camels. The largesse of a [Trader] who’d been paid well and just made some inroads with the black market.
Humble, you might say, for a woman who could claim she was part of the Scourge’s tale. Dangerous, if anyone ever thought to take revenge for that link.
Trader Hexata did not rage against fate or blame the Scourge in any way for missing out on treasures or fame. She was a humble woman who had run into a legend.
And who had also scurried over to the Mage’s Guild the moment she’d seen the first caravan attacks on the news. There was a group of [Mages] in Wistram who took bets on news stories, run by the Illusion Faction—she’d put half of all the money she had on Pisces Jealnet surviving.
Just…surviving. The odds had been very, very low when the Face had appeared. Plenty of counter-bets from Lailight Scintillation. The Illusion Faction had paid out her bet and even sent her a note of congratulations.
That was all. In this world, if there was no reward to be had, then it was one you had to make for yourself. So Hexata had a bit of coin to burn and a story to trade on—carefully. She could accurately tell [Slavers] that she had held the Scourge back from a bloodbath the first time, after all.
She toasted Pisces as she and her brothers danced on tables into the night.

There was no dancing in Ailendamus’ courts, for all they had plenty of ballrooms. Plenty. Baron Regalius had once gone on a ‘Dancing Tour’ of the palace with refreshments, fine music that went from ballroom to ballroom, and he’d had to quit after the fifteenth.
No, there was no dancing. That would imply to an observer that Ailendamus supported the [Necromancer]’s actions. And there were enough diplomats in the palace who could observe the talk of the court to infer a simple correlation.
Politics was sometimes very simple. Yes, it could be the dynamic, complicated web of interests, the push and pull of economy, military, society, and culture upon the will of a throne. Or, sometimes, it was just a [King] wanting something really badly or popular sentiment.
Why did a [King] divorce his wife and marry someone a third his age? Because he really wanted to, and no one told him ‘no’. That was the…the blunt edge of the beautiful world that Regalius liked.
His older brother, the late Baron Digeneral, had never liked it. He’d gotten it, but he’d hated a world ruled by emotion and not logic and rationality as he’d seen it. Regalius himself had once made a decision out of pure emotion that had changed the course of nations. A decision not to marry a [Princess]…
He wondered if he should pay for that sin, sometimes. If his brother’s obsession that had led to his death, the passing of his fiancée in a tragic accident, the misery of the Cursed Princess, Seraphel, was all due to his actions. Fate was indeed unkind because it had not punished Regalius himself for any of it.
This was life. This was why a man drank, at times. Or had cats to cuddle. It was reality that if a [King] backhanded you, you might level because he was a [King]. It was not right.
Regalius was only glad that he hadn’t seen such in his kingdom. He had to also applaud the King of Bows. King Itreimedes was not a subtle, calculating man. But his honesty continued to win him points among his people and abroad. He had no head for politics. The instincts of the [Archer King] meant he shot at the right targets, however. So that was a head for politics, in a sense.
You know who had no instincts diplomatically? Padurn Jealnet. The same footwork that was so flowing on the dueling grounds wasn’t flatfooted in the Court of Ailendamus; it just didn’t exist. He didn’t seem to realize he could apply his class or any of the skills he’d won to this setting.
Disappointing. The man’s latest performance on television had been so disastrous that over ten thousand letters had been sent to the palace from outraged citizens.
Baron Regalius brought the man a drink. No one else was talking to Padurn, and he seemed rather surprised anyone was smiling at him at the moment.
“Thank you, Lord…”
“Baron Regalius, Fencer Padurn. May I say that it has been a pleasure to have you at court? You have turned us all upon our heads, we polished, privileged folk. To hear you speak so honestly and openly is a delight.”
Padurn Jealnet stared at Regalius and took the Baron at his word, smiling back. Which was fair because Regalius meant everything he had said. Just perhaps not as Padurn had heard it.
“I am glad someone feels so, sir. I had the impression I was unwelcome, despite conducting myself to every standard I know.”
His eyes stole to a certain [Battle Princess], Princess Ozena, the eldest daughter of King Itorin II, who was shooting him evil eyes as she remonstrated with her parents. She was not the only one who disliked him.
House Shoel seemed rather split on Padurn. Half of them didn’t seem to care about him one whit, but Lord Uziel and his cohort regarded the man with an odd dismay. As if they would have loved to embrace his plain-spoken, honest ways, only they weren’t quite sure how he’d gotten to where he was with all his earnest integrity.
Nobility were a bit less kind. Padurn was a hard man to enjoy speaking to, and his conduct on television had not won him any points. In fact, you could argue that Padurn was a sinking anchor tied around any pro-Roshal sentiment, and he had made the best case for killing [Slavers], necromancy, and filial impiety in the history of Ailendamus’ courts.
Hence why Regalius pumped his hand up and down.
“Nonsense, Fencer. Nonsense. True, some people may object to your presence, but we would hardly be such a diverse nation full of wonderful ideas if we all got along. You should have met my brother. I wonder if you two would have been friends.”
An odd thought. They were so alike and yet different. Two upright men who stared only at the line they saw, not anything else. Regalius paused, and Padurn bowed gracefully.
“I was not aware your brother had passed. Allow me to express my condolences, sir.”
“Thank you, thank you. Now, Fencer Padurn, I believe that given the Scourge is departing the city, there may be less call for you on television.”
Those Drakes don’t want you back, and our networks aren’t going to endure you either. Padurn’s head bowed.
“It has been a delight to visit the royal courts. I only wish I could have spoken to Their Majesties.”
Odd that they hadn’t spoken to the man, but royalty was busy. And they could hear. Regalius kept beaming, but he lowered his voice and activated [For Your Ears Only].
“Well, Fencer, I know you and your delightful family do have your own life to get back to. But speaking as the Baron of Ceremonies, I am empowered to promote my own diversions and necessary entertainments. I have a discretionary budget.”
It went to parades for the Knights of the Hydra, mostly. Padurn stared at Regalius, wondering why the man was saying this, but Regalius was looking ahead.
“It occurs to me that fencing is a noble art which our palace enjoys—but might see more of a resurgence. One can dream. Would you be open to a tutoring position at court? I should love to see more of you.”
Padurn blinked. He looked around, then smiled and straightened his already-immaculate posture. Regalius began to talk numbers—it would be a modest stipend, of course, and the man had a job.
But it would be wonderful to see him in court now and then, eh? Naturally, someone might complain, but Regalius could claim it was a bureaucratic mixup. The fellow’s contract would be magically locked in, and he’d have access to the palace. And if someone asked him for his opinion and he gave it…
What a boon to the man’s enemies, eh? Of course, you might not see it that way.
Yietha, Regalius’ wife, sighed as he waved her over to signal success. Even though she’d suggested the entire plan, he thought it was fair.
Regalius had a plan, and that plan was mostly confined to what he was good at: making a spectacle, making Ailendamus beloved. He was also, like Trader Hexata, a betting man. He wagered he could pay Padurn out purely from the winnings on betting on Pisces’ survival…though he felt like Padurn wouldn’t get the irony or appreciate it.
It sounded funny and silly. But Regalius felt like this was a strong move in a game that was quite difficult. Ailendamus was a nation made of various cultures. Traditionally Terandrian in many senses, for all it was thought to be progressive.
Roshal? Roshal existed, and most Terandrians fancied themselves to be like Noass. Above such things, but they gave it no thought. They did not think of history beyond Az’kerash, either. No love for [Necromancers]. They could object to something abhorrent, then forget about it.
You needed to repeat the conversation, to force them to engage with it. What better tool than a son of Ailendamus? Or his father, who was like a dog with a bone with any topic?
Look. Regalius excused himself from Padurn after a moment and turned. His [Survey the Courts] Skill picked out any moments of interest, a glow in his sights.
He saw, quite clearly, Princess Ozena speaking at the high table. And he could hear thanks to Yietha’s [Share Senses: Hearing] skill. Always good to be a loving married couple.

“—bit of merriment, Father.”
“And why would I call for a party, Ozena?”
King Itorin II was amused. Not in a ha-ha kind of way, but at his daughter. He was of mixed emotions, as a man of his age and understanding was allowed to be.
He swirled the pear juice around in his cup. Good, fresh stuff from half-Elves. He didn’t want something stronger or he might dwell on, well, the [Slaves]. It had been an entertaining last few days.
Funny to imagine that Gold-rank adventurer was a son of Ailendamus. Another one who’d gotten away. Necromancy…now there was a topic that Itorin hadn’t heard brought up outside of Rhisveri or the Noelictan conflict last year. Itorin II had thought the bloody war with that Pisces fellow to be a bit overblown.
But he’d seen some of the point at the end. Children in chains or dressed up like servants. It made you wonder…dark things. And, unfortunately, Itorin II was in possession of a lot of information specialists. He did not have to wonder, merely ask, and he got answers in detail of what might have occurred or what did occur in Chandrar.
Hence, his mercurial mood. His wife, Queen Oiena, was less sympathetic towards Pisces the Scourge. But that wasn’t personal; he thought she’d also been inclined to cheer the fellow liberating children. It was just that her kingdom, the Taimaguros Dominion, did have links to Lailight Scintillation. Nothing so open, but she was weighing things as a Daughter of Gura.
Ozena saw things more simply, and sometimes that was lovely. But King Itorin II wished his daughter had a bit more savvy. He was amused by her attempts to get him to throw a party.
“I don’t believe there is a moment that merits spending that much coin, Ozena. We are at war, and we should not indulge while the populace toils.”
He reminded her, and she tossed her head of green hair.
“Who said I would ever ask for a party for us alone? We could choose three cities and…”
“Ozena, it would appear as though we’re celebrating events overseas as you have presented no good reason for us to celebrate here.”
Queen Oiena flicked a hand-fan out and peered at her daughter, a warning tone in her voice. They weren’t under privacy spells. This was fine. King Itorin II chuckled as Ozena bit her tongue. She knew better than to say she wanted to celebrate the Scourge out loud.
“…The King of Bows is throwing a party in Avel.”
“Are we linked to Avel or the King of Bows in any way, Daughter?”
“In a fine appreciation for men?”
Ozena’s comment made one of the people listening spit out their drinks. Itorin, trained from birth, didn’t cough out his drink, but he did laugh. Queen Oiena did not.
“Ozena, your comments are an insult to Avel and ourselves. Control yourself!”
Her daughter bowed her head. Itorin tried to salve Oiena’s wrath; it was just a joke, and no one who knew the King of Bows would take umbrage to that statement. Dangerous, though. What were they teaching in the magical academies for Ozena to come out with that? In Kaaz, such a statement might get her a death-duel if it were said to the wrong person.
Maybe she was too sheltered there after all. Maybe the culture of the young [Mages] and students was rubbing off on her. But they didn’t want their daughter to be like the Princess of Keys and go off to risk her life on adventure. Itorin sighed.
All this because of a [Necromancer]. One with a golden bell. A first for the history books in two centuries, he suspected.
Itorin II wasn’t blind. He’d heard the talk in the courts, and one of his people had just pulled a contract that Baron Regalius had filed with a certain [Fencer]. Itorin II didn’t block it; he wasn’t sure he disagreed with Baron Regalius at this moment.
Sometimes, as a monarch, you steered the horse of a kingdom through the briar patch or deep waters. And sometimes you just rode and let it take you where it willed, listening to it. Often, he had to listen to the whims of the Wyrm who rode both [King] and kingdom, so Itorin was in a unique position.
His freedom was that he was still a [King], and a kingdom was not something even an immortal being could rule perfectly, at least, not Rhisveri and his cabal.
The King of Ailendamus surveyed his court as his eldest daughter withdrew. He saw Padurn Jealnet smiling—until a [Lady] strode over to ask him what kind of a father wouldn’t acknowledge his son’s deeds. To argue about the right of a man to hold chains.
“It is their law.”
Itorin could read Padurn’s lips. No excuses, no second thoughts. Just a man pointing to a sign. Because someone had written on the sign, it was correct.
Is that morality? Itorin doubted it. He rather wished his friend, Ryoka Griffin, were here to set the Court of Masks to delightful chaos. He closed his eyes and gazed at the last image they’d seen.
Just a kneeling [Necromancer] with a little Drake girl hugging him. That was when Itorin II had been sold on the Scourge.
Not at any moment before. A [Necromancer]. If he became like so many others…it was just one man. You could claim he changed. But the decision to embrace any figure was still a choice. Let alone for the Crown to sanction anything. He had been deliberately obtuse this entire time. But Itorin just let the image replay.
What terrifying things Wistram had invented. The television was changing this world. He heard a voice.
“Father…?”
He opened his eyes, and there, overlaid with the image of the little Drake girl, was his youngest daughter.
Princess Oesca Zessoprical was a year older than the girl that Pisces had rescued. She blinked, as if wondering why her father focused on her with such intensity. But she curtsied in the skirts she didn’t want to wear.
Children changing. He smiled at her.
“Yes, Oesca? Has something happened?”
She gave him a solemn nod.
“Father, a very important thing has happened today. I would like to report…that I’ve lost my last baby tooth.”
He blinked at her. Oiena stopped whispering with her other daughter, and they peered at Oesca.
Human children lost their teeth rather early on, most of the time. Like their Earth counterparts, but even quicker given how years were longer in this world. Or so Itorin was being briefed…he put Earthers from his mind.
Oesca’s final baby tooth had left her mouth, and she presented him with a gap-toothed smile as the court murmured. Some of the non-Humans appeared appalled; they didn’t do ‘baby teeth’. But there were voices of congratulation, and Oesca shuffled her feet.
“My word. Then I imagine the coins might transmute if the Alchemist of Teeth needs one for his concoctions tonight.”
Amazing how that fellow got around. Turned teeth into coins or candy. Oesca showed him the tooth—covertly—and Itorin eyed it.
It was stuck in a hard piece of candy. Quite deep. Oesca hadn’t liked losing her baby teeth, which did hurt when they came out. She normally stayed away from anything that would lose it. But perhaps she’d been hungry and forgotten.
Or really wanted to lose a tooth? She was giving him the most innocent of stares, and she was good. He smiled.
“Well then, perhaps we should throw a party.”
“Dear.”
Oiena was hesitating, but Oesca turned up the charm, and she spoke to her mother.
“I know it’s just teeth, Mother, but now I’m almost ready to turn ten! And there’s nothing like a set of adult, Gura-chomping teeth, is there?”
A nod to Oiena’s beloved half of Taimaguros and the [Queen] was smiling. Itorin II just chuckled and made his choice.
“Very well, a little party. Let’s have some entertainment and choose some cities to celebrate—a tooth festival, perhaps!”
The idea took root fast among the court, who all agreed it was a fine thing! A moment of whimsy! Even nobles who might protest the waste of coin on frivolous things—odd how they were suddenly in favor of celebrating teeth.
A few courtiers protested, and Itorin II took note of them. But he saw the mood of the courts was with Oesca, and he spoke out of the corner of his mouth as he activated a silencing spell, just for a moment.
“Oesca, you might wish to avoid giving your sister a glance of triumph. A tad too obvious.”
The young [Princess] jumped and blushed. But that was just a father looking out for his daughter. Itorin II rose to dance with his daughter in one of the many ballrooms of palaces Ailendamus had conquered and taken to their capital.
In honor of baby teeth as a [Necromancer] slept.
Small things. Like children, growing up so quickly.
